What factors affect competitiveness? Some factors in recent years seem to indicate that developments in the exchange rate are primarily of importance for the cost competitiveness of the business sector. Competitiveness is also influenced by several factors other than just the exchange rate. In a longitudinal view, the stability of the economy in general, and the upsurence of a competitive business sector in particular, must be seen in the context of how the use of petroleum revenues affects the economy. They can be illustrated by a look back at our close economic history. E is 1970 we have two periods of clear impairment of competitiveness. The first took place in the 1970s, when competitiveness - as measured by real wage costs in a common currency - deteriorated by almost 20 per cent. The deterioration in competitiveness during this period was due to a combination of counter-cyclical policing, persistent pressures in the labour market and, moreover, that over a period of time we was tied to the German mark - and thus strengthened the krone exchange rate in relation to many of our other trading partners. The reason for this development was, among other things, the fact that Norway was an oil nation, which also made it possible to finance deficits in government finances with loans abroad in favour of interest rate terms. The second period of deterioration in competitiveness is most of the 1980s. Even then, the Norwegian economy was characterised by oil wealth, strong growth in demand and a shortage of jobs. From 1980 to 1988, the krone exchange rate for our trading partners was depreciated by a total of 12 per cent, which in isolation should have contributed to improving competitiveness abroad. However, the depreciation of the krone could not prevent competitiveness this time due to persistently high wage growth - deteriorating by almost 10 per cent from 1980 to 1988. In other words, developments in competitiveness in the 1980s contradicted what the nominal krone exchange rate should indicate. In addition, the Norwegian price range was also considerably higher than among our trading partners. In the two periods of strong improvement in competitiveness - in the late 1970s and between 1988 and 1994, wage growth in Norway on the other hand, was clearly lower than among trading partners. Nor during these periods was there an unambiguous correlation between developments in the krone exchange rate and developments in competitiveness. The improvement in competitiveness towards cunning in the 1970s, including a price and wage halt, can to some extent be explained by a somewhat depreciation of the krone. But the significant improvement that took place in the 1990s occurred as we know against the background of a largely stable krone exchange rate. Part of the reason for this is to be found in the way the labour market and wage formation have functioned. Job scarcity and craggy growth in demand - and also a significant price gap - are factors that consistently exacerbate competitiveness. Similarly, experience shows that competitiveness tends to improve when the labour market is less tight, growth in demand is subdued and price inflation is low. These factors have traditionally been heavily influenced by how financial policing is encrovisored. Increased use of petroleum revenues will lead to increased demand for goods and services from sheltered industries, thereby reducing the resources in the economy that are available for competitive activities. If pressures arise in the economy in this way, price and cost inflation will each increase and competitiveness will deteriorate. Noen vil ogs kunne ta opp nye ln med pant i boligen for  nansiere andre investeringer, for eksempel kjp av bil eller andre varige forbruksgoder. Generelt medfrer en rentenedgang at husholdningene fr kt sine muligheter l  betjene en strre gjeld, i hvert fall p kort sikt. Men heri ligger ogs en risiko for at husholdningenes nansielle situasjon kan bli svekket nr renten igjen m e s ge. Prisene p bruktboliger - mlt i nominelle termer - kte med 11 prosent p rsbasis fram l og med erde kvartal i or. Husholdningenes boligformue kan forsik g ansls l rundt 700 milliarder kroner. Boligprisveksten det siste ret har dermed gi husholdningene en nominell formuesgevinst p om lag 70 milliarder kroner. Over d m vi alts regne med at noe av denne formuesgevinsten frer l en kning i det private forbruket. Lignende mekanismer gjr seg gjeldende i andre deler av konomien, blant annet kny et l egenkapitalsituasjonen i nringslivet og kommunenes nansieringskostnader. Bde bedri enes og kommunenes investeringsniv blir ogs pvirket av renteendringer. Strrelsen p disse virkningene er imidler d svrt usikker. En indikator p utviklingen i publikums og nringslivets nansformue, og ogs p muligheten l  f inn ny egenkapital, kan vre utviklingen i aksjeverdiene. Aksjeverdiene p Oslo Brs steg i lpet av 1996 med over 30 prosent. Med unntak av Helsinki og Reykjavik var de e den sterkeste verdis gningen p noen europeisk brs. Nr formuesprisene vokser s sterkt, kan det tyde p en kende risiko for "nansielle bobler", der den nominelle verdiveksten ikke ndvendigvis representerer en lsvarende permanent kning i underliggende realverdier. De e kan vre en ustabil situasjon. Risikoen s ger for at bedri er og husholdninger overvurderer sine reelle formuer, og eksponerer seg for mye p gjeldssiden. Vi har drlig veiledning i vre modeller og annet erfaringsmateriale l  tallfeste virkningene av renteendringer. Det skyldes dels at det generelt er vanskelig  nne stabile sammenhenger som kan forklare utviklingen i den nansielle sparingen og i investeringene. Dels er det ogs slik at vi gjennom de store endringene i nansmarkedene det siste ret ikke ndvendigvis kan trekke sterke konklusjoner p grunnlag av dligere erfaringer, spesielt ikke erfaringene fra fr kredi reguleringen ble opphevet midt p 1980-tallet. Samspillet mellom nans- og pengepoli kken Derimot gir vre erfaringer et - rik gnok noe usikkert - grunnlag for  analysere sammenhengene mellom nans- og pengepoli kken og hvordan disse to delene av den konomiske poli kken har pvirket konjunkturutviklingen det siste ret. Norge sto i en rela vt guns g statsnansiell situasjon ved utgangen av 1980-rene, blant annet takket vre de hye oljeinntektene. De e gjorde det mulig  legge om nanspoli kken i ekspansiv retning i 1989. Mlt ved det ak vitetskorrigerte underskuddet, gav nanspoli kken en s mulans l den samlede e ersprselen p over 7 prosent av BNP for Fastlands-Norge i rene 1989-1992. Sysselse ngen i staten og i kommunene kte betydelig. Sam dig s mulerte denne poli kken den private delen av konomien. Til tross for den ekspansive nanspoli kken, fortsa e imidler d lavkonjunkturen i Norge fram l og med 1991, og ledigheten ndde si hyeste niv - p om lag 6 prosent - frst i 1993. Sysselse ngen i nringslivet begynte ikke  vokse for alvor fr i 1994. En vik g rsak l at nedgangen ble s langvarig, var den kra ige gjeldskonsolideringen som fant sted i privat sektor. De ekspansive impulsene fra nanspoli kken, som normalt ville gi kt sysselse ng ogs i nringslivet, ble mer enn oppveiet av denne gjeldskonsolideringen. Nr konsolideringen av gjelden tok s lang d, hang det ogs sammen med innretningen av penge- og valutapoli kken i denne perioden. Norge fulgte, i likhet med de andre nordiske landene, en fastkurspoli kk som bandt pengepoli kken l renteutviklingen i Tyskland og resten av Europa. P grunn av hykonjunkturen i forbindelse med den tyske samlingen, var rentenivet i Tyskland hyt ved inngangen l 1990-rene. De e frte l at land som var kny et l D-marken ogs kk hye realrenter. Nr en sammenholder innretningen av pengepoli kken med utviklingen i sysselse ngen, synes det noks klart at pengepoli kken gjennomgende har virket ekspansivt i hykonjunkturer og kontrak vt i lavkonjunkturer. Det er med andre ord et gjennomgende trekk at innretningen av pengepoli kken i Europa har frt l at pengepoli kken i Norge ikke har vrt lpasset den norske konjunktursituasjonen. I midten av 1980-rene var den norske hykonjunkturen langt mer markert enn ellers i Europa og prisveksten sterkere. De e frte l at realrenten ble lav i Norge, og pengepoli kken virket ekspansivt. Mot slu en av 1980-rene og frst p 1990-tallet var det lavkonjunktur i Norge, mens hykonjunkturen i Tyskland gav et hyt norsk realrenteniv og en kontrak v pengepoli kk. N er situasjonen igjen den at Norge er i en hykonjunktur, sam dig som lav vekst p kon nentet bidrar l rela vt lave realrenter og en ekspansiv pengepoli kk i Norge. Vi kan alts konstatere at pengepoli kken i Norge de siste rene gjennomgende har medvirket l  forsterke konjunkturutviklingen, og derved stort se motvirket de stabiliserende eektene av nanspoli kken. Jeg kan vel trygt si at de e fortsa er lfellet, e er at vi n har redusert renten betydelig. Et sprsml man kan s lle seg er om pengepoli kken ikke bare har forsterket konjunkturene, men ogs i betydelig grad vrt noe av drivkra en bak. De e sprsmlet er ikke enkelt  besvare. Ogs andre faktorer - som blant annet oljeinvesteringer og konjunkturene i utlandet - er med og pvirker konjunkturutviklingen i Norge. Det som synes klart, er at de kra ige endringene i realrenten m ha spilt en vesentlig rolle for styrken bde i oppgangs- og nedgangskonjunkturene. Et moment som kan bidra l  belyse de e sprsmlet, er hvordan utviklingen i den renteflsomme delen av nringslivet har bidra l svingningene i sysselse ngen. Jeg tror spesielt utviklingen i bygg- og anleggsnringen, som er blant vre mest renteflsomme sektorer, kan illustrere de e. Sysselse ngen i bygg og anlegg steg med nr 25000 personer fra gjennomsni snivet frst p 1980-tallet l 1987, med et pflgende fall p over 50000 personer l 1993, da sysselse ngen ndde et bunnpunkt. Gjennom varekrysslpet mellom ulike produksjonssektorer kan en endring i e ersprselen som direkte sysselse er tusen personer i bygg- og anleggsnringen, ansls  bidra med rundt 750 arbeidsplasser i resten av nringslivet - hovedsakelig innen industri, varehandel og transport. Ringvirkningene av svingninger i bygg- og anleggssektoren er sledes betydelige. Nr vi tar hensyn l disse ringvirkningene, har bygg- og anleggsektoren st for mellom 30 og 50 prosent av svingningene i den samlede sysselse ngen i nringslivet de siste femten rene. Fr noen trekker forhastede slutninger p grunnlag av disse betraktningene, vil jeg minne om at forholdet mellom pengeog nanspoli kken samlet se m vurderes i lys av erfaringene dlig i 1980-rene. Sa inn i denne sammenhengen, m vi kunne si at penge- og valutapoli kken de siste rene p mange mter har vrt vellykket. Vi har maktet  bringe priss gningen ned p et lavt niv, rentedieransen mot utlandet er eliminert og nringslivets konkurranseevne er bedret. Vi har med andre ord lykkes i  gjenvinne troverdigheten i pengepoli kken, og en stabil valutakurs har fungert som et nominelt anker for inntektsoppgjrene. Jeg mener imidler d ogs det er grunnlag for  si at denne innretningen av pengepoli kken har ha en kostnad. Som vi har se , tyder mye p at pengepoli kken i betydelig grad har vrt med p  forsterke de store konjunkturutslagene vi har ha i Norge de siste rene. At slike eekter vil kunne forekomme nr en velger et kursml i pengepoli kken, er verken ny eller overraskende. Det er et moment som inngr i avveiningen av sterke og svake sider ved ulike regimer i pengepoli kken. Et system med stabil valutakurs innebrer at ansvaret for stabiliseringspoli kken llegges nanspoli kken. Finanspoli kken har da ogs gjennomgende motvirket konjunkturene det siste ret, og sledes virket stabiliserende. En vik g erkjennelse ser imidler d ut l  vre at selv ikke betydelige omlegginger av nanspoli kken i denne perioden har kunnet forhindre rela vt store konjunkturutslag. En u ordring Det synes klart at pengepoli kken i den nrmeste den vil bidra l y erligere vekst i e ersprselen innenlands. Dersom denne innretningen av pengepoli kken fr sl gjennom i den innenlandske konomien, m vi regne med at hykonjunkturen i sektorer re et mot innenlandske markeder kan bli mer markert. Vi m ogs regne med at denne hykonjunkturen kan bli avlst av en lavkonjunktur og nedgang i sysselse ngen. Bde i Norge og i andre land har vi erfaring for at slike svingninger i konomien har varige virkninger, blant annet i form av en permanent kning i arbeidsledigheten. P bakgrunn av de erfaringene vi har med samspillet mellom nans- og pengepoli kken, mener jeg det er grunn l  understreke den u ordringen som innretningen av pengepoli kken n s ller nanspoli kken overfor. U ordringen blir ikke mindre av at nanspoli kken ogs har andre oppgaver. Gjennom budsje prosessen fastlegges de konomiske rammevilkrene for fordelingspoli kken og for produksjonen av en rekke oentlige tjenester. Hensynet l konomisk eek vitet og forutsigbarhet i rammevilkrene legger dessuten begrensninger p hvor langt vi kan g i retning av sterke endringer i ska e- og stnadssatser. Jeg m si at vanskelighetene med  lpasse nanspoli kken l konjunktursituasjonen, som ne opp oppstr fordi nanspoli kken skal ivareta ere hensyn, gir grunn l en viss uro. Vi har vel alle i klar erindring at reduksjonen av rentefradraget i 1980-rene - som var helt ndvendig av hensyn l den langsik ge balansen i vr konomi - ikke akkurat tra helt godt rent dsmessig i forhold l konjunkturutviklingen. Eventuelle reformer i boligbeskatningen kan bli et parallelt eksempel, om enn ikke av samme dimensjon som de dligere reformene av ska esystemet. I lys av hvordan pengepoli kken er innre et, ville eventuelle le elser i boligbeskatningen n ikke akkurat bidra l  dempe presset i boligmarkedet. Den ne opp avslu ede hstsesjonen i Stor nget avdekket hvilke vanskelige avveininger vr nasjonalforsamling m g gjennom hver hst i et forsk p  imtekomme alle de ambisjoner og ulike hensyn som legges l grunn i u ormingen av nanspoli kken. I mi foredrag her for et r siden la jeg vekt p  f fram hvilke langsik ge u ordringer den norske velferdsstaten str overfor, og hva som kan bli krevet av prioriteringer for at det oentlige skal kunne u re sine oppgaver i frem den. Jeg forskte  peke p en del vanskelige avveininger vi str overfor p lang sikt, kny et l prioriteringer av ulike oentlige ytelser som for eksempel helsetjenester og pensjoner. Disse langsik ge u ordringene legger fringer p hvordan det oentliges midler kan fordeles i frem den, og dermed ogs p mulighetene en har l  endre vesentlig p ulike budsje poster. Jeg skte i min redegjrelse i or ogs  pvise at hensynet l konomisk eek vitet legger begrensninger p muligheten for en y erligere kning i det alminnelige ska e- og avgi snivet. Ska e- og avgi skostnadenes rent konkurransemessige betydning synes dessuten stadig mer fremtredende i en verden preget av frie vare- og tjenestestrmmer og store kapitalbevegelser over landegrensene. Generelt kan vi kanskje si at langsik ge hensyn lsier et behov for noenlunde forutsigbare og stabile rammevilkr. De e se er srlige krav l u ormingen av en nanspoli kk som sam dig er llagt ansvaret for stabiliseringspoli kken - et hensyn som lsier at innre ngen av nanspoli kken m kunne variere mye. Det sier seg selv at det ikke all d vil vre like enkelt  kombinere disse to hensynene. En alterna v fremgangsmte kunne vre at en i u ormingen av pengepoli kken i strre grad avveide hensynet l kursutviklingen mot hensynet l stabiliteten i konomien for vrig. Formlet ville vre  unng at pengepoli kken i for stor grad forsterket konjunktursvingningene, slik at realkonomien og sysselse ngen i mindre grad ble utsa for "sjokk" via renten, og slik at belastningen med  gjennomfre stabiliseringspoli kken i noen grad kunne fordeles mellom nans- og pengepoli kken. Ulempen med en slik mer ak v u orming av pengepoli kken er frst og fremst at valutakursen i strre grad vil flge de konjunkturelle svingningene i konomien. I store land, der utenrikshandelen utgjr en rela vt liten andel av samlet BNP, vil valutakursendringer ha liten eekt p den generelle konomiske utviklingen. Stabilitet i valutakursen kan dermed llegges begrenset vekt i de store konomiene, mens den interne stabiliteten m llegges stor vekt. I sm land med en rela vt stor utenrikskonomi vil derimot valutakursendringer ha strre betydning for den innenlandske utviklingen, spesielt dersom eksportsektorene ogs str for en betydelig andel av sysselse ngen. Det er dermed heller ikke mulig ukri sk  overfre erfaringene fra store land med en - rela vt se - liten utenrikskonomi l sm land, som Norge, med en pen konomi. Jeg innledet mine betraktninger her i kveld med  fremholde at sentralbanken har fulgt det rd som Chris an Michelsen e er sigende skal ha gi l Bjrnstjerne Bjrnson: "Nu gjelder det at holde kj !". De e er selvsagt en meget kortsik g strategi. De u ordringene vi n str overfor gjr det kanskje like naturlig  flge Bjrnsons rd: "Nu gjelder det at holde sammen!". Eller re ere sagt: N gjelder det  f systemet l  holde sammen! Da m vi frst erkjenne at alle de tre hovedpilarene i den konomiske poli kken er under press fra ulike hold. Jeg har forskt  f fram at selv om presset akkurat n kanskje er mest aku p kronekursen, er problemene i vel s stor grad kny et l den generelle stabiliseringen av den konomiske utviklingen. I et system med stabil valutakurs er de e frst og fremst nanspoli kkens oppgave. Med stabil valutakurs fungerer dessuten kursnivet som en nominell forankring for inntektsoppgjrene ved at lnnsutviklingen slr direkte gjennom p den kostnadsmessige konkurranseevnen. Det er vesentlig at en n makter  viderefre lnnsmoderasjonen, slik at ikke den sterke e ersprselsveksten slr ut i kende lnns- og priss gning. Sam dig m vi erkjenne at ogs partene i arbeidslivet har begrensede virkemidler l rdighet, og at de ikke med bindende virkning kan fastlegge lnnsutviklingen. Partene utver sin innytelse i frste rekke i de sentrale inntektsoppgjrene, mens vi m anta at markedsforhold har en betydelig innvirkning nr de lokale oppgjrene gjennomfres. Selv om forstelsen for lnnsmoderasjon e er hvert synes grunnfestet i store deler av befolkningen, vil en kende knapphet p arbeidskra i forskjellige regioner og blant ulike yrkesgrupper derfor kunne pvirke lnns- og kostnadsutviklingen for nringslivet betydelig. Jeg vil understreke at retningslinjen om stabil valutakurs ligger fast. Norges Bank har innre et - og vil fortsa innre e virkemidlene i pengepoli kken i trd med retningslinjene i valutaforskri en. Vi m sam dig innse at det  holde en stabil valutakurs ikke er noen enkel oppgave i en verden der markedets vurderinger av kursen kan sl gjennom med stor tyngde. Selv om sentralbanken eller andre kan mene og vite at markedet tar feil, vil ikke det i seg selv ndvendigvis fre l en korreksjon i markedet. For at systemet skal holde sammen, gjelder det derfor  utve pengepoli kken med atskillig tlmodighet. Som jeg har forskt  belyse her i kveld, er en stabil nominell valutakurs dessuten ikke noen garan verken mot svingninger i konkurranseevnen eller i den konomiske utviklingen mer generelt. Erfaringene lsier tvert imot at en slik u orming av pengepoli kken kan forsterke de realkonomiske svingningene, og dermed ke pkjenningene p nanspoli kken og inntektspoli kken. Dersom en i u ormingen av de vrige elementene i den konomiske poli kken ikke makter  ta hyde for de ekspansive impulsene fra pengepoli kken, vil svingningene i e ersprselen fr eller senere ogs sl ut i pris- og kostnadsveksten innenlands, med den flge at konkurranseevnen og grunnlaget for sysselse ngen svekkes. For at et system med stabil valutakurs skal fungere e er hensikten, er det derfor en grunnleggende forutsetning at myndighetene gjennom andre virkemidler i den konomiske poli kken lykkes i  stabilisere den konomiske utviklingen. Title: Bank of Norway's role as manager of Norway's foreign exchange reserves and the government petroleum fund
text: Bank of Norway's role as manager of Norway's foreign exchange reserves and the government petroleum fund Leif Eide, Execu ve Director. EMEAP (Execu ve Mee ng of East Asia and Pacific Central Banks) reserves management seminar, Singapore, 26/27 February 1997. Background informa on 1. It may be appropriate to begin by providing a brief overview of Norway and the importance of petroleum to the economy. The Kingdom of Norway is a mountainous, coastal na on with a popula on of about 4 1/2 million and a land area of about 324 000 square kilometres. It is a li le smaller than Finland, thirty per cent larger than Great Britain and 20 per cent larger than New Zealand. Mountains and plateaus cover 73 per cent of the surface while produc ve forests make up 23 per cent. Due to low temperatures and a short growing season, Norway has always been dependent on food imports. (Agricultural area accounts for only 3.5 per cent of the total surface). Historically, fish and forestry products were the main exports, but shipping became a major export industry one hundred years ago. Norway was then one of the poorest countries in Europe. Abundant supplies of energy, however, have been developed in this century. Numerous waterfalls were harnessed to produce hydroelectric power in the period 1910-1960. Large oil and gas fields in the North Sea have been developed since the 1970s. Towards the end of this century Norway thus emerges as one of the richest countries in Europe, with a welldeveloped welfare system. Norway is now the world's second largest exporter of oil. As a result of substan al oil tax revenues and the state's direct financial interest in the petroleum industry, government budgets show a surplus equivalent to 5-8 per cent of GDP, the country's current-account surplus corresponds to 8-12 per cent of GDP, and infla on is 1.5-2.5 per cent. Norway is now a creditor na on, with net foreign assets equivalent to 10 per cent of GDP. These assets are projected to rise in the period to the year 2000 to about 40 per cent of GDP. Norway is now in its fi h year of strong growth, and unemployment has declined to about 4 per cent. The petroleum sector accounts for approximately 18 per cent of GDP, but only 3.5 per cent of total employment. Oil and natural gas represent 35-40 per cent of total exports of goods and services. The sector also has a substan al impact on government revenues, with taxes and royal es from the petroleum sector accoun ng for about 8 per cent of central government revenues. Including other oil-related revenues, the share is 16 per cent, or a good 6 per cent of GDP. The chart shows es mated government revenues from the petroleum sector along with government pension expenditure. The es mates are based on prudent assump ons concerning oil prices, known oil fields and exis ng technology. Each me the curve for projected revenues is redrawn, it shi s to the right and in an upward direc on in the chart. This reflects increasingly cost-effec ve produc on, new oil finds and improved technology. The chart also shows rising government expenditure on pensions as the popula on ages. Norway shares this trend with many other countries. Unlike these countries, however, Norway can cope with this situa on without having to raise taxes or implement deep welfare cuts. This can occur if we do not refer to the pumping of oil from the North Sea as revenues which are included in other budgets - but as the conversion of oil wealth to foreign assets. This financial wealth should provide a current return which will alleviate government finances later in the next century. When the Government Petroleum Fund was established in 1990, it was therefore important to determine how much oil revenues were immediately consumed in the domes c economy. It was also deemed inappropriate to keep capital in the Petroleum Fund if the government had to borrow to finance its expenditure. It was thus decided that the annual alloca on to the Petroleum Fund should be equivalent to the difference between total government oil and gas revenues and the government budget deficit, excluding oil and gas revenues. No alloca ons were made between 1990, when the Fund was established, and 1994, because the budget deficit exceeded oil and gas revenues in this period. The Petroleum Fund then only showed that total government revenues from the oil sector were added to the Fund and automa cally withdrawn and transferred to the government budget. Even though long-term challenges were the star ng point for the establishment of the Petroleum Fund, the principles for transferring capital entail that the Fund is also a "buffer" fund. If oil prices or the cyclical situa on in the years ahead result in a budget deficit, including oil revenues, the government can draw on the Fund. This means that the investment strategy must place considerable emphasis on liquidity. This was par cularly true in earlier years when the es mates for the size of the Fund were considerably smaller than the level now being projected. 2. When oil revenues proved to be so high that there was a balance in the Petroleum Fund at the end of the year, the Ministry of Finance issued a regula on for its management. The regula on s pulates that Norges Bank is responsible for the opera onal management of the Fund on behalf of the Ministry of Finance. The Fund is placed in a separate krone account in Norges Bank, and the Bank shall invest this capital in its own name in assets denominated in foreign currency. In Norges Bank's balance sheet this appears as follows: FINANCIAL ASSETS Foreign assets Interna onal reserves Government Petroleum Fund investments Other foreign assets 256 587 196 622 46 265 13 700 Claims on Norwegian financial ins tu ons Loans to private banks Other assets in the form of deposits, securi es, loans and overdra s Provision for losses on loans to banks LIABILITIES AND CAPITAL Foreign liabili es IMF holdings of NOK Other foreign liabili es 4 815 4 849 21 -55 14 753 4 589 10 164 Notes and coin in circula on 40 642 Domes c deposits Treasury Government Petroleum Fund Other public administra on (excl. municipali es) 194 525 134 261 46 265 3 355 Private banks Other financial ins tu ons Other Norwegian sectors - 7 802 2 717 125 It is important to emphasise that the Petroleum Fund in itself will not provide any extra resources for the future. The Petroleum Fund is basically no more than an accoun ng technique. The purpose of the Fund is to provide an instrument for be er, long-term budget discipline in a situa on with government financial surpluses. If resources were not allocated to the Petroleum Fund, a sound economic policy would have resulted in roughly the same macroeconomic developments and accumula on of Norges Bank's interna onal reserves equivalent to what is now being transferred to the Petroleum Fund. Central government claims on the central bank would also have been the same, but the en re amount would have been placed in an ordinary sight deposit account. It was assumed that Norges Bank would not build up the foreign currency component of the Petroleum Fund by reducing its own foreign exchange reserves. This means that the central bank's net foreign currency purchases over a period will, as a minimum, correspond to the alloca on to the Fund. The annual alloca ons, however, depend on many factors, and are consequently very uncertain. Alloca ons depend on oil prices, the USD/NOK exchange rate, oil produc on and the non-oil budget balance - in other words general trends in the Norwegian economy. The es mates for the Petroleum Fund therefore fluctuate considerably during the year. At the start of 1996, we es mated that the Fund would amount to about NOK 50 billion (USD 7-8 billion) in the year 2000. This was a modest figure compared with Norges Bank's ordinary foreign exchange reserves. The central bank would probably not be facing any major challenges in managing a fund of this size. However, in the autumn of 1996 this figure was revised upwards to NOK 270 billion (USD 40-45 billion), and this entails challenges of a completely different nature. The es mates for the alloca on for 1996 were also revised upwards by a considerable margin during the year. The decision to establish the Petroleum Fund also entailed that the Ministry of Finance would channel government capital abroad. As the public sector will be inves ng a share of the foreign currency surplus in foreign assets via the Petroleum Fund, Norwegian interest rates will have to be somewhat higher than if the private sector were to account for the en re capital ou low. The substan al foreign currency inflow in 1996 accentuated a monetary policy problem which is a result of the high oil revenues and sizeable current-account surpluses. In Norway, it is the Government which formulates the monetary policy mandate of the central bank. There has been widespread concern that the very profitable oil industry might result in such a strong krone exchange rate that other industries would no longer be compe ve interna onally. This would create problems when oil produc on declines. This was one of the reasons Norges Bank was given the mandate of orien ng monetary policy towards exchange rate stability. Due to the domes c cyclical upturn and the pressures which began to emerge in the economy, the central bank was reluctant to reduce official interest rates sharply, and instead intervened heavily in foreign exchange markets. Foreign currency purchases, however, reached such high levels that the Bank had to abandon this approach on 10 January this year. Interven ons were halted and interest rates were reduced to German levels. The central bank also stated that the responsibility for avoiding pressures in the economy and higher infla on now rested with the Government's fiscal policy if the central bank's monetary policy mandate remained unchanged. The krone has appreciated in effec ve terms by 5-7 per cent since then. 3. Norges Bank manages foreign assets equivalent to a total of USD 35 billion. The foreign exchange reserves correspond to USD 27 billion or 6/7 months of imports of goods and services. In addi on to requirements regarding liquidity, the regula ons specify rules concerning exchange-rate risk, interest-rate risk and credit risk in par cular. Actual management ac vity may be characterised as rela vely passive, and is kept close to the benchmark. The main ac vity comprises selec ng profitable close subs tutes for securi es included in the given benchmark. The prac cal work involved in such investments is carried out by the Market Opera ons Department, which is also responsible for the bulk of analy cal work in connec on with investments. The department was established in 1986, when the opera onal sec ons of the former Foreign Exchange Department and Credit Policy Department merged. As far as I know, we were the first central bank to organise ac vi es in this way. In connec on with the substan al growth in the foreign exchange reserves in recent years and the tasks assigned to the Bank in connec on with the Government Petroleum Fund, the department has recently started the process of increasing its staff and enhancing its exper se. We now employ 52 persons, of which two work in the somewhat broader field of research in the Research Department. Total es mated resource used in Norges Bank in connec on with asset management amounts to 24 person-years. This is probably insufficient, in terms of both resources and exper se, in view of the challenges facing the central bank. A working group is therefore now assessing the ambi ons and resources used in connec on with asset management, including a possible out-sourcing of some of the work to a subsidiary. The Bank has an advisory commi ee, the Investment Commi ee, which reviews the department's reports on investment ac vity, and which also evaluates proposals for changes in guidelines, new instruments, etc., before they are submi ed to the Governor or Execu ve Board. The commi ee is chaired by the Deputy Governor and comprises representa ves from each of the policy departments and the Research Department. The commi ee normally meets four mes a year. Since 1 January this year, the Bank's organisa on is composed of 3 wings which cover the central bank's core ac vi es, plus one administra ve wing. The Market Opera ons Department is in Wing I - Monetary Policy. 4. In spring 1996, the Execu ve Board carried out an assessment of strategies for the central bank's further development. One conclusion was that the Bank should concentrate on its core ac vi es. Another was that the Bank should strive to make its ac vi es more transparent. Accordingly, it was decided that the Bank should replace the internally constructed benchmark with an externally constructed one, when measuring the result of investment ac vity. We also intend to publish these results. J.P. Morgan was selected to construct the benchmark. The Ministry of Finance has selected Bacon and Woodrow (CAPS) to undertake the work on a benchmark for the Government Petroleum Fund. In addi on it was decided to transfer the management of some funds to external por olio managers. This decision was announced and more than 100 ins tu ons subsequently expressed their interest. Drawing up a short-list and making the final selec on was therefore an extensive process. We made it quite clear to the candidates that the purpose of having external managers was to establish a coopera on that would entail the transfer of exper se to Norges Bank, and at the same me provide a be er basis for comparison for Norges Bank's own management ac vi es. ABN AMRO Asset Management, London, was given responsibility for managing a por olio equivalent to DEM 150 million for European currencies, and Goldman Sachs Asset Management, New York, was assigned the management of a por olio equivalent to USD 100 million for investment in USD and CAD. Norges Bank signed a contract with the Bankers Trust Company for deposit services and returns analysis in connec on with the external management. B. Strategic management choices 1. Equity Norges Bank's foreign currency holdings are now larger than those normally required for interven on purposes. Furthermore, the country no longer has a fixed exchange rate, but operates an official floa ng exchange rate regime, which entails that the reserves should to a greater extent be perceived as na onal wealth. The establishment of the Government Petroleum Fund has increased the need to look at alterna ves to the current strategy which comprises secure, liquid investments in interest-bearing instruments. There are three important reasons why Norges Bank would consider using equity in the management of the Government Petroleum Fund, and possibly also in the management of the ordinary reserves: 1. Historically, stocks have proved to be a be er hedge against infla on than bonds. The most important objec ve of the management of the Petroleum Fund and foreign exchange reserves is to maintain the reserves' interna onal purchasing power - and it is the real purchasing power that is important in this context. 2. Stocks have historically had a weaker correla on to oil prices than bonds. This is important as Norway's total na onal wealth declines in value when calcula ons are based on lower oil prices. Historically, equity yields higher returns than bonds, and there is reason to assume that this will also be the case in the future. Stocks are also more vola le than bonds, entailing a greater risk of losses in the short term. In the longer term, however, the expected return is higher. If the investments have a sufficiently long me horizon, a number of years with weak (unrealised) results may be acceptable. As there is no perfect correla on between the return on equity and bonds, some diversifica on gains may be achieved by combining equity and bond investments. If we look at the past twelve years, nominal returns in both interna onal equity and bond markets have been high and the risk premium on stocks has been higher than the average recorded in the period from 1950. If this was used as the basis for determining the acceptable share of equity, the conclusion would be that the likelihood of losses in any given year would be limited, even with a high propor on of equity. This can be illustrated by a simple example: if we take return figures from interna onal equity and bond indices in America, Europe and Asia and weight them, it is possible to calculate average returns and standard devia ons for varying equity propor ons in the por olio. This would also provide informa on about the probability of losses in the por olio in any given year. Even though such probability calcula ons rely on dubious assump ons, the rela onship between the equity propor on and risk is clearly illustrated. As regards the point about avoiding nega ve returns, the main risk factors are: that returns on both bonds and equity will fall, that the risk premium on stocks will be reduced in rela on to bonds, that the correla on between the equity and bond markets increases. For example, if it is assumed that bond yields fall by 4 per cent (to 5.5 per cent) and the risk premium is reduced from 4.5 to 2.5 per cent (ie the return on equity is 6.5 percentage points lower), the probability of nega ve returns in some years is naturally greater. However, it is not only important to be prepared for the probability of short-term nega ve returns, it is equally important to have some idea of magnitude of the nega ve returns. And it is not necessarily the por olio with the higher equity propor on - which increases the likelihood of nega ve returns in a given year - that will incur the poten ally largest losses. As there is no perfect correla on between bonds and equity, substan al losses in bonds and stocks do not necessarily coincide. Based on historical figures, an equity propor on of between 30 to 40 per cent would incur the smallest losses in the unadjusted returns series. Based on adjusted figures, equity propor ons between 0 and 40 per cent would result in roughly the same level of losses in the worst year. If we were only interested in minimising the downside risk, and were of the opinion that the adjusted figures were the most representa ve of future market developments, we would not recommend any investment in equity. But such an extreme aversion to risk is hardly relevant in our case. What should then the equity propor on of the Government Petroleum Fund be? This is decided by the Ministry of Finance, not Norges Bank, and depends on the government's risk preference. If we were sufficiently certain that historical rela onships would be repeated in the future, and only emphasised long-term returns, the answer is obvious: everything should be invested in equity. In terms of the Petroleum Fund, which is not likely to be realised in the short term, it could be argued that li le emphasis should be placed on short-term vola lity. However, we do know that a en on would be focused on very poor annual results even though the objec ve of the investment is long term. It is possible that very poor short-term results would erode poli cal support for the Government Petroleum Fund and contribute to an increase in domes c consump on via the central government budget. Public opinion may also press for a reduc on in equity exposure and thereby force the realisa on of losses. If such a scenario is a cause for concern, a ceiling should be set for propor on of equity in the por olio. 2. Currency and market distribu on As men oned in the introduc on, the currency distribu on of the Petroleum Fund is based on import weights. Even though the aim is to maintain, and preferably to boost, the Fund's interna onal purchasing power, it is not given that import weights minimise risk. First: It should actually have been based on future import weights, as the Fund will probably be realised some me in the future. The problem is, of course, that we know what today's import weights are, but can hardly guess what these weights will be in 20 years. Another point is that the import weights are not adjusted for trade flows with third countries. Germany and Sweden account for the largest share of Norwegian imports. But Swedish and German industry also rely on imports from other countries. Without having studied this further, there may be reason to assume that adjus ng for trade with third countries would bring the import weights closer to global export weights, which show individual regions'/countries' share of total world trade. One may also raise the ques on of whether developments in the Norwegian economy should be taken into account when establishing the market distribu on. Norwegian import weights are fairly similar to our export weights. This may entail that the return on the Petroleum Fund, given the current set of weights, is posi vely correlated with developments in our na onal economy, which in an interna onal context must be perceived as being very open. The supply of domes c and foreign goods may therefore move in pace, which may have an unnecessarily large impact on the total supply of goods. Another important factor is that the goods we import are priced in an interna onal market, where near subs tutes are produced in various countries. Therefore, there may not be any immediate effect of the movement in a given currency in rela on to the Norwegian krone on the price of goods produced in that country. It may be that in the long run a country's export capacity or produc on capacity has a greater impact on future exports to Norway than the current import weights would imply. Global export weights, or global GDP weights, have their appeal from this perspec ve. It would also be an advantage to invest in other markets than the current import weights would suggest - namely transac on costs associated with maintaining an import-weighted distribu on. In principle, one can build on the assump on that there is a correla on between the size of a market and the transac on costs associated with making large investments in that market. Market capitalisa on weights will then minimise these transac on costs. Both GDP weights and global export weights are closer to the market capitalisa on weights than the Norwegian import weights. Finally, one may consider the purpose of an in-depth analyses of the distribu on of investments by country. If the assump ons of purchasing power parity and interest parity apply, there should not be significant differences in return according to investment country in the long run. However, in the short and medium term there will be differences, which probably form the basis for performance measurement. We are thus le with a number of op ons which are to some extent quite dis nct from each other. The differences are illustrated in the chart: What is the conclusion? So far we have applied today's import weights, although there are strong arguments in favour of a more diversified por olio that reduces the propor on invested in Europe in favour of North America and Japan/Southeast Asia/Oceania. 3. Risk management The points raised with regard to equity and currency/market distribu on are essen al to determining the composi on of the benchmark por olio. But the composi on of this por olio is not the only determining factor as regards return. Another decisive factor relates to management constraints, that is the restric ons on taking posi ons that deviate from the benchmark por olio. In this connec on, two ques ons must be answered: How should the manager's degree of freedom in rela on to the benchmark be formulated? How should the por olio's risk be measured? The current guidelines for the management of foreign exchange reserves set out separate limits on currency distribu on and dura on. The percentage point difference allowed between the currency share in the benchmark por olio and the actual por olio is defined, as well as the maximum devia on in dura on allowed in each currency. The problem with such par al limits is that they easily prove to be inconsistent, and that they do not take into account underlying vola li es and correla ons in the market place. The guidelines may be inconsistent in the sense that, for example, one has the possibility of increasing the risk of the por olio to a much further extent through the choice of currency distribu on than the choice of dura on. Separate limits for each currency may entail that a small change in dura on in all currencies is allowed - which is poten ally high-risk - while large matching posi ons in two highly correlated markets are prohibited. The la er strategy may easily be less risky than changing dura on by a small margin in all markets at the same me. In Norges Bank we have discussed the drawbacks of tradi onal risk measurement tools, and have recently decided to complement in part, or replace in part, today's par al limits with one overall limit for the en re por olio's rela ve vola lity, or "Tracking error" against the benchmark por olio. As is the case for measuring the por olio's absolute vola lity - Value at risk - one needs informa on about underlying vola li es and correla ons in and between markets in order to es mate the tracking error. For prac cal reasons, we have chosen to use data from J.P. Morgan's Risk Metrics, which is daily and is available on Internet and can be used freely. We are now tes ng this with the inten on of using it on a full scale in the near future. The use of "Tracking error" as an opera onal limit for the total por olio represents a substan al methodological step forward compared with par al limits. But the methods "Value at risk/Tracking error" have certain drawbacks. They are not conducive to es ma ng the risk associated with instruments that contain op on elements, and the underlying assump ons that returns in capital markets have a normal distribu on and no serial correla on are dubious. Direct measurements of "Tracking error" with the aid of "Risk Metrics", or other data sources, must therefore be combined with stress-tes ng of the por olio. At the same me, it may a good idea to keep some of the enhanced par al risk limita ons in order to avoid "extreme" composed por olios, but use "Tracking error" as the opera onal risk limit. The management of the Petroleum Fund entails new challenges as regards the defini on of risk limits. Limits must not only be defined for fixed-income por olios, but also for por olios with a high probability for equity investments. In view of the public focus on the Fund, it is especially important to define thoroughly considered risk limits. One advantage of using "Tracking error" as an opera onal management tool for risk control is that the methodology can also be applied to equity por olios and balanced por olios (stocks and bonds). Ideally, the government's preference for absolute risk should therefore be defined in the guidelines for the Petroleum Fund through a clear defini on of the benchmark por olio - and the rela ve risk preference in the form of a limit for "Tracking error". There is probably some gap between what is ideally desirable and what can realis cally be formulated in the guidelines, which leads me to believe that the guidelines which are drawn up will be rela vely general in character. It will therefore be our task, as managers, to develop our own internal risk management tools so that at any given me we will be in a posi on to control the por olio's overall risk in an effec ve manner. 4. Opera onal aspects A fairly substan al share of the Petroleum Fund, which at the end of 1997 will come to at least USD 15 billion, might be invested in interna onal stock markets in 1998. (This will come in addi on to any investments of the ordinary foreign exchange reserves in equity). The es mated size of the Petroleum Fund in the year 2000 implies that the Fund may become a substan al investor in the capital markets of some countries. As the central bank lacks special competence in equity investment, whether it be in the front or back office, a number of opera onal ques ons must be considered. There are three ques on in par cular that we have considered so far, notably ques ons rela ng to liquidity, ownership and internal/external management. a. Liquidity Na onal equity markets, par cularly in smaller countries, will be affected if we should decide to transform foreign exchange reserves/bonds into an equity por olio. It will probably be necessary to spread the purchases over a longer period. This will create problems when comparing against the benchmark por olio. As regards our neighbouring Scandinavian markets, the Fund will become so large that this in itself is a strong argument in favour of reducing the market share in these countries. b. Ownership It goes without saying that Norges Bank, as the central bank, avoids investments that entail expecta ons of ac ve ownership on the part of the Bank. With a broad diversifica on strategy in each market, we will contain our ownership interests to a only a small frac on - even with a large Petroleum Fund. Another problem is that we may have ownership interests in companies that are poli cally controversial (for example, companies that are in legal conflict with the Norwegian state, or known for pollu ng the environment, or that have an industrial base in countries with human rights problems, etc.) This could put the central bank in an unfavourable light in the public opinion. It would be an impossible task for the central bank to define which investments are "acceptable" and which are not. If we are to take such aspects into considera on, we must receive instruc ons s pula ng the companies in which we are not allowed to invest. This ques on also makes synthe c equity investments poten ally interes ng. c. Internal/external management The management of equity por olios requires broad competence in an organisa on. In the front office the competence required will obviously depend on the management style adopted. Ac ve management, where one takes posi ons in individual companies and industries, requires more resources than a more risk-averse strategy such as indexing. I would assume that Norges Bank will require several years of prepara on before we will be in a posi on to take responsibility for ac ve management of an equity por olio. However, indexing does not require the same insight into individual companies, but is more a ques on of having the necessary technological support and flexibility for combining direct investments and deriva ves. Moreover, it should be possible to implement indexing strategies or so-called enhanced indexing with a limited increase in resource use and with a substan ally shorter prepara on me than in the case of ac ve management. But equity investments also require considerable resources for purposes of se lement, accoun ng, and control. In an equity por olio which replicates an index, there will be constant movements every day merely due to corporate ac ons. When these amounts are to be invested, it will generate a number of smaller transac ons in a large number of individual stocks. This requires an adequate risk-monitoring system and a sufficient number of people to carry out the necessary se lement procedures. Such a system is not implemented overnight. The fact that we have a limited period to make the system opera onal favours out-sourcing as much as possible in the start phase, both in terms of management, se lement and accoun ng. The se lement and accoun ng func ons will probably be about the same whether we are talking about ac ve or risk-averse management strategies. But we are hesitant to define mandates for external managers which we are not able to control ourselves. This means that the share of tradi onal ac ve management will be limited in the beginning phase. It will thus be appropriate to use external managers in order to develop the broad competence which our own organisa on requires, and to help us assess the resources required for internal management. It will then be possible at a later stage to assess whether we should take over the opera onal management of the "passively" managed por olio. If at a later stage the central bank performs this func on at a lower cost than private managers, there are solid grounds in favour of internal management. 27. februar 1997 14:00

text: Stabilisation policy in discourse for the central bank Speech by Governor Kjell Storvik at NFF's spring conference on Wednesday 21 May. If one were to take the misery that I have received in the e-mails literally, I could have one in short in the following way: The stabilisation policy irreordination for the central bank is - according to the fixed division of responsibility between the various elements of the economic policy - to stabilise the krone exchange rate. I assume that the organizer has not made such a short post, but I have intended to elaborate on the indistingsure Norges Bank considers to be too unschedelled by the economic policing more generally. This includes a need to take a somewhat more than what lies in Norges Bank's opera to be responsible for the course management. I would like to invite you to comment on developments in money and foreign exchange markets over the past few months, and to try to see this development in the context of the other parts of the economic policy. I will be based on the exchange rate scheme adopted on 6 May 1994, which forms the basis for Norges Bank's exercise of monetary and foreign exchange policing - together with the unsubstaged guidelines in the Revised National Budget for 1994 and later the bidding documents. Both the Government and Norges Bank have emphasised throughout the period e is that the share price crisis was adopted in the spring of 1994, emphasising that a successful policing for a stable exchange rate requires close interaction between different policy areas: First, when monetary policy is tied to the objective of a stable exchange rate, the fiscal policy must bear the main responsibility for ensuring stable economic developments. This means that when there is high growth in the economy, the bidding must be made so that it reduces pressures on the economy and ensures a prudent balance in government finances. Second, stability in the value of the krone measured against European currencies provides the basis for ensuring that income policing can ensure sound cost competitiveness, and provides a so-called "nominal anchor" for the economy. By maintaining a stable exchange rate against countries with low inflation, inflation will also be able to achieve a correspondingly low inflation rate above d. The Revised National Budget for 1994 states that the operatic guideline for "Norges Bank's ongoing exercise of monetary policy is that it shall be oriented towards stability in the value of the krone measured against European currencies, based on the exchange rate range since the krone began to float on 10 December 1992." The exchange rate prediction also states that "In the event of significant changes in the exchange rate, instruments shall be incorporated with a view to ensuring that the exchange rate e is each brought back in the initial range". They entail that the objective of monetary and foreign exchange policy is to stabilise the krone exchange rate, also in a situation where, due to the situation in the market, funds are driven outside the usual exchange rate range. The Government also stated that there are "no specific fluctuation margins for the krone and that it will not be appropriate to use such strong instruments in terms of the purchase and sale of NOK and short-term interest rate changes in order to keep the krone exchange rate as within a fixed exchange rate regime". Sam dig, who has clearly stated that a stable krone exchange rate is the main objective of monetary policy, it is also clear that Norges Bank is not obliged to raise the exchange rate by "all means" - such as This trap, for example, is within a narrow fixed exchange rate regime with defined and public fluctuation margins. The e is a result of the experience in connection with the international currency crisis in the autumn of 1992 and the winter of 1993, which I want to come lbake l later. What lies in these is that Norges Bank can assess whether it is appropriate to defend the current exchange rate, or whether it may be more appropriate to give e are funds dig, and then bring the exchange rate back later. But in other words, "instruments shall be incorporated with a view to ensuring that the exchange rate is each brought back in the initial range". In the bidding that followed e is Revised National Budget 1994, only minor adjustments were made to the monetary policy. In light of the marked upturn in the Norwegian economy, the Government wrote in the National Budget in 1996: "Within the limits of exchange rate prediction, the monetary policy should contribute to ensuring fast-term low price inflation and stable economic developments." Furthermore, it was opened up for Norges Bank to use interventions to stabilise the krone exchange rate to some extent by purchasing foreign exchange somewhat beyond the build-up of the Petroleum Fund. These guidelines were set out in Revised Budget 1996 and in the National Budget for 1997. Until late summer 1996, the system worked reasonably well. Norges Bank lowered interest rates to - and at times below - European interest rates, which helped bring Norway out of recession. Through 1995 on In the autumn of 1996, it was possible to maintain an interest rate policy that contributed both to stable domestic economic developments and was consistent with the objective of a stable exchange rate. The Norwegian economy had healthy and balanced growth - weaving pulses came both from abroad via exports and domestically, among other things. a from private consumption. Private consumption was based on income growth and not loans. In the years from 1993 to 1996, almost 130 000 more people came into work, there was low price growth and solid real income growth for wage earners. It was not until autumn 1996 that more pronounced pressures arose in the foreign exchange market. Norges Bank responded by selling NOK and looking down the interest rate. In total, we sold more than NOK 90 billion in 1996. They were twice as much as was necessary based on the allocation in the Petroleum Fund. Norwegian money market rates fell from 4.5 per cent in November to 3.9 per cent at the end of the year. There were several reasons l that tensions arose in the economic policing: In a world of free capital movements and an increasingly integrated international economy, one must expect that there may occasionally be pressure on the krone. As I said before, it is taking into account such situations in the course investigation. Such pressures do not necessarily have to reflect real economic conditions in Norway, but can be driven by expectations of a return ratio in other countries or by the real return ratio between different investments - what is known in the professional language as "portfolio ips." The figures for the Norwegian economy that have been could indicate that the Norwegian economy is strong both in relation to other European economies and in relation to what we envisaged. The estimate for forward-looking petroleum revenues has been revised upwards. In 1996, the surplus on the drizzle was about 7 percent of GDP, and the surplus on the state budget was almost 5 percent of GDP Norway. What was an incipitated cyclical upturn in the spring of 1994 has developed into a crash, with signs of pressure in parts of the labour market, high growth in domestic demand and an economy close to full capacity growth. Even though prices are very low, there are signs that domestic contributions in the price range are increasing. They have probably give the impression that the Norwegian economy "needed" a cooling down and combined with the figures for the foreign economy, there was speculation about an appreciation of the krone. I'd like to invite the rest of the e-mails l to discuss these matters any closer. Exchange rate management and capital movements The krone exchange rate has been adjusted a total of twelve times in the last 20 years. Nine of these exchange rate adjustments took place in the period 1976-1984, and were in reality devaluations with a view to increasing competitiveness that was weakened as a result of stronger price and wage growth than among trading partners. Common to these nine exchange rate adjustments was that they were in the past by the authorities to correct for an unfortunate restructuring of cost developments, and not the result of pressure from the market. The exchange rate adjustments in May 1986, December 1992 and January 1997 were not planned or desired by the authorities, but were more or less forced through market pressures. They illustrate that the authorities have limited opportunities to maintain a stable exchange rate if market participants believe that the exchange rate is not "rich g". Changes in market expectations can quickly result in large movements in and out of individual currencies. For Norway, these developments can be exacerbated by the uncertainty surrounding the establishment of EMU. This uncertainty may increase investors' interest in spreading risk by investing in NOK and other "rand currencies". They can in turn lead to large movements in and out of nok as a result of international portfolio skis. It appears that the Norwegian krone was "discovered" in earnest by financial market participants during 1996.
