Store intervensjoner kan i en aku situasjon i valutamarkedet vre et lite egnet virkemiddel se fra sentralbankens side. Det skyldes at nr markedsaktrene e erspr store kronebelp, vil lsvarende store intervensjoner fra Norges Bank kunne oppfa es av markedet som et signal om ubalanse i markedet - det oppstr en skalt "one-way bet" situasjon, der e ersprselen e er kroner ker i takt med intervensjonene. Hvis sentralbanken derimot unnlater  intervenere, m markedsaktrene inng veddeml mot hverandre - i stedet for mot sentralbanken. Ne opp fordi erfaringene med skalte "one-way-bets" lsier at intervensjoner har begrenset virkning i en aku situasjon, kan det vre mer fornu ig  bye noe av, for s senere  komme lbake l kursleiet nr forholdene i markedet har roet seg ned. Det er denne strategien som ligger l grunn for det Norges Bank har foreta seg de siste mnedene. Gjennom rentenedse elsene i januar str aktrene i markedet sam dig overfor en lavere avkastning p norske kroner sammenliknet med de este andre europeiske valutaer. I trd med retningslinjene har vi alts innre et virkemidlene med sikte p at kursen e erhvert skal bringes lbake l utgangsleiet. Siden begynnelsen av februar har valutakursen svekket seg med mer enn 5 prosent. Kursen har ligget i omrdet 101,5-102 mot ECU den siste uken, og den er alts lbake p nivet i november i or. Det er vanskelig  vite nyak g hvilke kre er som har bidra l - skal vi kalle det - en normalisering av kursnivet. Jeg nevnte vr virkemiddelbruk. Det er grunn l  tro at investorer, nr det ble mer usikkert om en vesentlig appresiering ville nne sted, har redusert sine posisjoner i norske kroner. Tilbakevendingen av kursen har videre sammenfalt med et fall i oljeprisen. Det kan ogs ha spilt en rolle at det i denne perioden ser ut l at ltroen l MU har kt. Jeg vil sam dig understreke - slik jeg ogs har gjort ved dligere anledninger - at kursutviklingen selvsagt er usikker. Forholdene i valutamarkedet pvirkes bde av internasjonale forhold - som for eksempel forventningene kny et l MU og utsiktene for oljeprisen - svel som andre utviklingstrekk innenlands. Blant annet vil lnns- og prisutviklingen innenlands kunne pvirke kursutviklingen. Alt annet likt vil en hyere pris- og kostnadsvekst innenlands kunne dempe forventningene om en appresiering av kronen. Jeg ser ikke bort fra at prisutviklingen de siste mnedene sammen med den rela vt ekspansive innretningen av pengepoli kken, kan ha bidra l  ke forventningene om frem dig priss gning i Norge, og sledes bidra l  dempe forventningene om en nominell appresiering av kronekursen. Endrede utsikter Et sprsml som naturlig melder seg i denne sammenhengen, er hvor sterke appresieringsforventningene er, og hva de bygger p. I Revidert nasjonalbudsje 1994 presenterte Regjeringen langsik ge beregninger som viste et underskudd p statsbudsje et, inklusive oljeinntekter, i strrelsesorden 15 l 20 milliarder kroner i rene 1994-1998. I 1996 ble overskuddet p statsbudsje et 47 milliarder kroner, mens det i r - i flge Revidert Nasjonalbudsje 1997 - er ventet et overskudd p 57 milliarder kroner. Grunnen l at overskuddene er bli oppjustert, er for det frste at oljeproduksjonen har vrt hyere enn hva som dligere ble lagt l grunn. For det andre er veksten i fastlandskonomien bli sterkere sam dig som nanspoli kken er bli strammet inn, slik at ska einngangen har kt og enkelte oentlige utgi er redusert. Det siste poenget kan illustreres ved at det i 1997 er ansl et underskudd p statsbudsje et utenom oljeinntekter p om lag 23 milliarder kroner, omtrent lsvarende anslaget for underskuddet inklusive oljeinntekter i Revidert nasjonalbudsje 1994. Oppjusteringen av petroleumsproduksjonen har videre frt l at utsiktene for utenrikskonomien er bli vesentlig forbedret. Mens anslagene i 1994 viste et overskudd p dri sbalansen i strrelsesorden 5 prosent av BNP i 1997-98, er n dri soverskuddet - i flge Revidert nasjonalbudsje 1997 - ansl l om lag 8-10 prosent av BNP i r og de nrmeste rene framover. Iflge Lang dsprogrammet vil Norges ne ofordringer overfor utlandet komme opp i over 100 prosent av BNP i lpet av de neste rene. Anslagene for oljeprisen er penbart avgjrende for Norges og statens frem dige oljeinntekter og fordringer. Anslagene i Lang dsprogrammet er basert p en gjennomsni lig oljepris p 115 1997-kroner pr. fat. Oljeprisen har siden slu en av 1980-rene gjennomgende ligget i omrdet 110-140 kroner pr. fat. Oljeprisen m med andre ord vesentlig under 90renes "normalniv" for  motvirke den oppjustering av oljeinntektene som har skjedd gjennom blant annet kte anslag p petroleumsreserver og -produksjon de senere rene. Oljeprisen har imidler d vist store svingninger og den frem dige prisutviklingen er meget usikker. Prognoser for oljeprisen p noe sikt varierer over et intervall fra rundt 60 kroner pr fat l 210 kroner pr fat. Konsekvensene for oljeformuen av endringer i oljeprisen er betydelige. I Revidert nasjonalbudsje 1997 ppekes det at dersom oljeprisen faller med 20 kroner reduseres oljeformuen lsvarende vel 50 prosent av BNP. Den stadige oppjustering av oljeformuen gjennom de siste rene innebrer at det kan hevdes at Norge fak sk er bli rikere. Med de e som utgangspunkt er det grunnlag for kt konsum bde i innevrende og frem dige perioder. En del av det kte konsumet vil vre re et mot skjermede produkter der e ersprselen bare kan mtes gjennom kt produksjon i Norge. En varig kning i forventede frem dige inntekter innebrer dermed at mer ressurser over d skal brukes i skjermet sektor. Gi at norsk konomi allerede opererer nr full kapasitetsutny else, innebrer de e resonnementet at det i den fremover bare vil vre rom for en vekst i e ersprselen lik veksten i produksjonskapasiteten om det skal legges grunnlag for  oppre holde nvrende omfang p konkurranseutsa sektor. Ved sterkere e ersprselsvekst vil ltakende press i arbeidsmarkedet e er hvert frt l en nedbygging av konkurranseutsa sektor og overfring av arbeidskra sressurser l den skjermede sektor. Behovet for  oppre holde et visst omfang av konkurranseutsa virksomhet for  le e overgangen l en situasjon med fall i oljeinntektene og den store usikkerheten forbundet med de frem dige oljeinntektene - kny et blant annet l priser og teknologisk utvikling - trekker imidler d i retning av at Norge ikke br bli for oljeavhengig. Sammen med det forhold at de store oljeinntektene som n blir synliggjort kan betraktes som en overfring av formue fra Nordsjen l fordringer p utlandet - og sledes isolert se ikke innebrer at vi er bli rikere - lsier at myndighetene br ske  motvirke en nedbygging av den konkurranseutsa e sektoren. Ved  fre en lstrekkelig stram nanspoli kk kan myndighetene holde en stabil nominell valutakurs sam dig som inasjonen holdes nede. Gjennom valutakjp l petroleumsfondet vil en stram nanspoli kk sam dig bidra l  nytralisere virkningen i valutamarkedet av store overskudd i utenrikskonomien. De e reiser imidler d et grunnleggende sprsml om forholdet mellom pengepoli kken og nanspoli kken. Dagens styringssystem bygger p at pengepoli kken skal bidra l lav inasjon og moderate 1nnsoppgjr gjennom stabil valutakurs. Finanspoli kken skal innre es med sikte p stabilisere den konomiske utviklingen. Dersom det av hensyn l stabil valutakurs blir ndvendig  fre en pengepoli kk som bidrar l  forsterke konjunktursvingningene, flger det at nanspoli kken m ta en lsvarende strre belastning. Prosyklisk pengepoli kk? Som nevnt oppsto det et markert appresieringspress mot norske kroner i lpet av hsten 1996, noe som isolert se lsa en rentenedgang med sikte p  stabilisere kronekursen. P den annen side var det klart at det ut fra innenlandske konjunkturhensyn ikke var nskelig med en betydelig rentenedgang. De e illustrerer at et pengepoli sk styringssystem som er re et inn mot stabil valutakurs ogs kan ha kostnader. Siden begynnelsen av 80-tallet synes det noks klart at pengepoli kken har virket prosyklisk: Pengepoli kken har gjennomgende virket ekspansivt i hykonjunkturer og kontrak vt i lavkonjunkturer. En mte  illustrere de e p kan vre  ta utgangspunkt i den skalte "Taylor-regelen" for pengepoli kken. Denne regelen ble opprinnelig utviklet for  prve  simulere hvordan pengepoli kken i USA blir utvet. I USA frer sentralbanken en produksjons- og prisstabiliserende pengepoli kk. Taylor-regelen kan sies  reektere det en kan kalle en "op mal" pengepoli kk, nr en utelukkende tar hensyn l virkningene av pengepoli kken p konjunkturutviklingen innenlands. Denne regelen indikerer sledes hvordan renten m lpasses for at konomien skal ha hy kapasitetsutny ng og hy sysselse ng sam dig som presset i konomien ikke blir s sterkt at priss gningen ltar. Avviket mellom den renten Taylorregelen antyder og den fak ske renten kan derfor indikere i hvilken grad pengepoli kken er lpasset konjunkturutviklingen. La meg presisere at ingen sentralbank beny er en mekanisk regel for innre ngen av pengepoli kken, heller ikke den amerikanske sentralbanken. En kan heller ikke vurdere pengepoli kken isolert fra de vrige poli kkelementene, for eksempel nanspoli kken, slik denne regelen gjr. Sm land som Norge vil videre uanse m e ta hensyn l valutakursen, slik at det aldri vil vre aktuelt for Norge  innre e pengepoli kken e er en slik regel. Likevel kan en slik regel antyde om renten har bidra l  forsterke eller dempe konjunkturutslagene. Taylor-regelen antyder at renten burde vrt hyere i strste delen av 1980-tallet, men at renten var for hy i begynnelsen av 1990-tallet. Fra 1995 er det strre samsvar mellom Taylor-regelen og fak sk rente og mot slu en av 1996 peker beregningene i retning av at renten burde vrt noe hyere. Jeg vil understreke at disse beregningene er begrenset l innenlandske rentevirkninger og ikke vurderer rentens eekt p valutakursen og konsekvensen av de e for konomien. Jeg vil spesielt peke p at kostnaden ved en feil lpasset rente m sees i sammenheng med gevinsten for konkurranseutsa sektor ved at valutakursen holdes stabil. Det er videre et vik g poeng at det har vrt ulike bakenforliggende forhold som har bidra l at renten ikke har vrt lpasset konjunktursituasjonen. Avviket mellom Taylor-renten og den fak ske renten kan sledes ikke mekanisk tolkes som en kostnad ved dagens kursstyringssystem. Eksempelvis i den sterke oppgangen i 1984-86 var veksten i Norge i takt med konjunkturene internasjonalt. Vi ble alts ikke pfrt et for lavt renteniv utenfra. Den alt for sterke oppgangskonjunkturen vi kk hadde sammenheng med det lave poli ske bestemte rentenivet og den store verdien rentefradraget hadde. Det var sledes ikke hensynet l valutakursen som medfrte at at renten var lav. I likhet med mange andre land fant det i Norge sted en kra ig reduksjon i inasjonen fra slu en av 1980-tallet l begynnelsen av 1990-tallet. En slik nedgang i priss gningen ville ha krevet en stram pengepoli kk uanse hvilket pengepoli sk regime vi hadde. Det er lite som tyder p at kostnaden ved  bringe priss gningen ned i Norge var spesielt mye hyere enn i andre land. Tvert i mot var oppgangen i ledigheten i Norge mindre enn i de este andre land. De e hadde sammenheng med at vi (e erhvert) gjennomfrte en nanspoli sk ekspansjon som andre land ikke hadde muligheten l (eller nsket). Det eksible arbeids lbudet i Norge var nok ogs medvirkende l at oppgangen i ledigheten ble mindre enn i andre land. Fra slu en av 1989 og fram l i dag har pengepoli kken i Norge mer entydig bidra l  forsterke konjunkturene som en direkte flge av mlse ngen om  holde en stabil kronekurs. Mot slu en av 80-tallet og begynnelsen av 90-tallet var det lavkonjunktur i Norge, sam dig som hykonjunkturen i Tyskland bidro l et hyt norsk realrenteniv og en kontrak v pengepoli kk. N er Norge igjen inne i en hykonjunktur, sam dig som lav vekst p kon nentet bidrar l lave realrenter og ekspansiv pengepoli kk. De lavere rentene vi e erhvert kk i Norge fra 1993 var trolig en vik g drivkra i den oppgangen vi har ha i norsk konomi. Det synes ogs klart at pengepoli kken i den nrmeste den vil bidra l y erligere vekst i e ersprselen innenlands. Realrenten e er ska for ln e er de guns gste vilkrene er n rundt  prosent. Nr pengepoli kken er re et inn mot  holde fast valutakurs, er det nanspoli kken som m srge for  stabilisere den konomiske utviklingen. Et vik g premiss for at nanspoli kken fak sk skal kunne ivareta sin rolle, er at den kan justeres lstrekkelig dersom pengepoli kken blir mer ekspansiv. De e er blant annet et sprsml om hvor renteflsom konomien er i forhold l den kontrak ve virkningen av en nanspoli sk innstramming. Mye tyder p at norsk konomi er rela vt renteflsom. I strre grad enn i utlandet lner husholdninger og bedri er l ytende rente. Renteendringer med sikte p  pvirke valutakursen vil derfor sl rela vt sterkt ut i realkonomien. Det er ogs grunn l  tro at formueseekter gjennom virkninger fra lavere renter p boligprisene kan vre sterkere i andre land enn i Norge. I forhold l utlandet er det en rela vt stor andel av nordmenn som eier sine egne boliger. Videre er det grunn l  tro at en lavere rente ikke i srlig grad reduserer husholdningenes disponible inntekt i Norge, mens den vil virke kontrak vt mange land hvor husholdningene gjennomgende har en strre rentebrende nansiell formue enn i Norge. I Norges Banks siste inasjonsrapport ble det redegjort for hvordan renteendringer kan pvirke realkonomien. Disse beregningene var basert p hvordan de historiske erfaringene var nedfelt i Norges Banks makrokonomiske modell RIMINI. En nedgang i pengemarkedsrenten p 1 prosentpoeng som raskt slr fullt gjennom i bankrentene, vil i flge disse beregningene e er to r fre l en vekst i innenlandsk e ersprsel opp mot 1 prosent og nesten  prosent hyere sysselse ng. Andre konomiske modeller for norsk konomi viser noe svakere rentevirkninger enn de e. Generelt er tallfes ngen av renteendringer usikre. Bde i Norge og i utlandet har det vist seg vanskelig  nne stabile sammenhenger som kan forklare utviklingen i sparing og investeringer. De store endringene i nansmarkedene det siste ret innebrer at det er vanskelig  trekke sterke konklusjoner p grunnlag av dligere erfaringer. Spesielt gjelder de e trolig erfaringene fra fr kredi rasjoneringen ble opphevet midt p 1980-tallet. U ordringene vi str overfor i stabiliseringspoli kken vil ogs avhenge av om Norge vil vre i konjunkturfase med de landene vi har kny et valutaen l. Dersom vi er i en hykonjunktur sam dig med landene vi stabiliserer valutaen overfor, innebrer det at rentenivet ogs vil vre lpasset den konomiske situasjonen. Gjennomgende ser det imidler d ut l at Norge har vrt mer i konjunkturfase med de engelsksprklige landene enn med landene i Kon nental-Europa. Det vil vel ikke vre helt uventet om de e kan fortse e i de nrmeste rene nr landene i Europa gjennomfrer de signaliserte innstramminger i nanspoli kken for  oppfylle kravene l deltakelse i MU. Det er imidler d hverken ny eller overraskende at en mlse ng om stabil valutakurs kan fre l at pengepoli kken i perioder kan bidra l  forsterke konjunkturutslagene. De e forhold var med i de vurderinger som ble gjort da rollefordelingen mellom de ulike poli kkelementene ble etablert. I vrt brev l Finansdepartementet i 1994, hvor Norges Bank lrdde en viderefring av en stabil valutakurs mot de europeiske valutaer, understreket banken betydningen av at det var bygget opp en bred forstelse av stabil valutakurs som en fast ramme for den konomiske poli kken og for lnnsoppgjrene. S langt m vi konstatere at denne ansvarsfordelingen har virket e er forutsetningene. I perioden e er 1986 er inasjonen og inasjonsforventningene i Norge redusert, blant annet ved at en stabil valutakurs la grunnlag for gjennomfring av moderate 1nnsoppgjr og en ansvarlig nanspoli kk. De e har vrt med p  legge grunnlaget for den guns ge utviklingen i 1990-rene, blant annet gjennom lavere realrenter. Finanspoli kken er strammet inn og gjennom inntektpoli kken har en oppndd lavere nominell lnnsvekst enn det vi kunne ha fryktet i en s sterk oppgangskonjunktur. Jeg vil avslutningsvis understreke at den rentenedgang Norges Bank m e foreta i r for  stabilisere valutakursen og den sterkere vekst som n ansls for innevrende r i Revidert nasjonalbudsje , understreker behovet for en stram nanspoli kk. P denne bakgrunn er det bekymringsfullt at innstrammingen i nanspoli kken for innvrende r er redusert i forhold l det regjeringen la opp l i Salderingsproposisjonen. PUBLISERT 21. mai 1997 14:00

Title: Management of the Government Petroleum Fund
text: Management of the Government Petroleum Fund Speech by Governor Kjell Storvik at the Bergen Conference on Oil and Economics 5-6 June 1997 When the Act on the Government Petroleum Fund was adopted in 1990, the main purpose was to highlight the use of government petroleum revenues. In the early years, the fund was also an account through which petroleum revenues flowed before they were used in priority public tasks. It was not until 1995, when we made a surplus in the central government accounts for the first time in a long time, that there has been money in the fund. For a broader understanding of the importance of the Petroleum Fund in a broader economic-policy context, it is necessary to look at the particular policing on which we rely in Norway and where fiscal policy plays a decisive role: The fiscal policy, i.e. the state budget, is a key element of stabilisation policing. The fiscal policy will be used to smooth fluctuations over cyclical cycles, and fiscal policy will be incorporated with a view to stability in economic developments. In Norway, monetary policy does not have quite the same function as it has in many other countries, but is primarily aimed at ensuring a stable krone exchange rate measured against European currencies. In this way, monetary policy does not form part of the stabilisation policy instruments. The distinctive third element of economic policing in Norway is income policing, which is intended to contribute to low price and cost inflation through moderate income settlements based on solidarity salts. While the last two elements, namely monetary policy and income policing, aim to create a stable nominal path, it is primarily fiscal policy that will contribute to stabilising real economic developments. The Petroleum Fund must be assessed in this context. The fund is formally viewed as a krone account in Norges Bank. The provisions in 1995 and 1996 have been equal to the surplus on the government accounts. Through the determination of fiscal policy, the Great Will take into account how much of the petroleum revenues can be used each year based on the consideration of prudent application regulation. In recent years, large parts of government petroleum revenues have also been used every year. Thus, the amounts desisted in the Petroleum Fund cannot be raised domestically without weakening the role of the government bidder as a management tool. The funds must therefore be channelled abroad. In the face of a fall, the fund's domestic investments will result in a question beyond what the Great No. The funds in the Petroleum Fund will be channelled abroad by Norges Bank acquiring foreign exchange in the market. They will contribute l curbing appreciation pressures on Norwegian kroner. In the event of a lockout one of the year, an amount of the surplus on the state budget will then be transferred from the government's sight deposit account in the Petroleum Fund. Some of Norges Bank's foreign exchange holdings will be lordnet fund. The interest rate on the fund's krone account will then be determined by the return norges bank achieves on the lorded foreign exchange holdings. When assessing the importance of the Petroleum Fund, it is important to be aware that what we call revenues from the petroleum activities are not revenues in the usual sense. The counterpart is an unealthing of the oil. Thus, when money is deposited into the Petroleum Fund's account, there is a transfer of wealth from oil in financial assets. This wealth should represent a "buffer" that provides greater freedom of action in economic policing when - or if - oil prices or the acroon of the mainland economy falter. Such situations may be met with a weakened bidding balance, albeit within the limits of the question regulation. With a somewhat longer ds horizon, we know that pension payments are each going to burden public spending. They are a situation that is common to many Western countries. In contrast to them, we will then be able to draw on the fund and thus avoid the release of any of the increases that other countries will have to implement. E are the current guidelines, the Ministry of Finance is responsible for the management of the fund. The Government has also given Norges Bank the operatic responsibility for the management of the Fund. Given the size of each fund, it is very important that management takes place in a satisfactory manner. Even a modest excess return can have major consequences for the fund's size, and any excess return in e-year must not come as a result of the manager taking an unintended risk. Then let me move on to the real theme of the e-mails, namely the management side of the fund. The funds in the Petroleum Fund have been managed e are corresponding principles as applies to the ordinary foreign exchange reserves. The e are primarily related to the limited scope of the Petroleum Fund. The provision for 1995 amounted to NOK 2 billion, and in connection with the presentation of the Revised National Budget for 1996, the provision for 1996 was estimated at NOK 25 billion. The fund's limited size meant that it could not rule out the need to draw on the fund in the coming years. The guidelines for the Petroleum Fund were thus established as a compromise between the longitudinal purpose and the short-term purpose. The guidelines cover factors that are intended to safeguard currency risk, credibility risk, risk, interest rate risk and liquidity requirements. Foreign exchange risk is safeguarded by preserving the fund's international purchasing ratio from this year by having a currency distribution that is close to the individual countries' share of Norwegian imports. Kredi risk is safeguarded by limiting the likelihood that borrowers cannot meet their obligations by limiting investments in high collateral investments. Interest rate risk is safeguarded by the fact that an upper limit has been defined for how much the market value can change as a result of a change in interest rates. Liquidity requirements are safeguarded by placing the fund's funds mainly in instruments with high liquidity. In the Lang d programme for 1998-2001, forecasts have been prepared for developments in the Petroleum Fund indicating that it will be significantly larger than projected. According to these projections, the fund will amount to more than NOK 400 billion at the end of 2001. Furthermore, it now appears that it will take longer d before it becomes necessary to draw on the fund. The Petroleum Fund is also expected to increase and reach a peak around 2020-2030, and will then account for 130% of GDP. The outlook for a large fund and a long investment horizon raises questions about whether the guidelines for the Petroleum Fund should be adjusted. Conditions should be laid down in order to increase the longitudinal return. The Petroleum Fund may become a key instrument for securing public finances and is that petroleum reserves have been drained. The difference between good and medium returns can mean a great deal for the ability to solve public priority tasks 20-30 years ahead. In a letter of 10 April d.y. l the Ministry of Finance - on the view of these considerations - has recommended that the guidelines for the management of the Petroleum Fund be amended on two factors. First, it is recommended that it be permitted to invest in equity instruments by the fund having a substantial equity share. Furthermore, Norges Bank pointed out in its letter that there are factors that suggest that a larger share of the Petroleum Fund will be invested outside Europe than is currently the case. They are both factors that are of great importance in the further management of the Petroleum Fund, and I would also like to go into more detail about why Norges Bank has recommended that these changes in the management of the fund be applied. When it comes to different classes of shares, experience from virtually all quarters as well as the theorek ske plan suggests that the return in the long term will increase if some of the fund's funds are also invested in the form of equity instruments. Norges Bank points out that Norwegian and international funds with a long-term investment horizon usually distribute the bulk of their financial investments between equities, bonds and real estate. Large pension funds, life companies or state investment firms comparable to the Petroleum Fund all have a substantial share of their total assets invested in equity capital. When there is widespread practice among asset managers with long-term investments to invest significant portions of their portfolios in equities, this is due to the fact that equities experience a higher return than bonds. Surveys from a number of international capital markets show that equities have returned higher than bonds over longer periods. In a survey conducted by the G10 countries in 1995, the excess return on equities in a historical context was estimated at 4 per cent. There is no guarantee of an excess return on equities of 4 per cent in the year ahead, but there are reasons to suggest that there will soon be an excess return on equities compared to bonds. Although the return may vary to a greater extent from one year in the other if the fund's funds are invested to a greater extent in equity instruments, the likelihood of a higher return on investments in equities increases if the ds horizon expands. In the US market, equities have returned higher than bonds for 60 per cent of the years from 1871 to 1992. If a basic five-year period for this assessment is based on the same period, equities have an excess return for more than 70 per cent of the five-year periods. In excess of these general experiences and recognitions with regard to the profitability of investing in equities in the long term, conditions of a somewhat distinctive nature apply to Norway: Stocks have historically been nega vt correlated with oil prices, while bonds have been posi vt correlated. If they are in force, investments in equities may contribute to stabilising the total value of oil wealth and financial wealth in relation to investments limited in pure bond investments. It seems that the return on equities and bonds is not strongly correlated, and diversification gains will be achieved by combining equity and bond investments. Men ogs det at det bygges opp et fond med en signikant strrelse i internasjonal sammenheng, vil gi posi ve ringvirkninger l det norske nansmiljet. Norges Bank har hi l ha stor glede av samtaler og seminarer med det norske forvaltningsmiljet. Det er vik g for oss at det er et kompetent milj for risikostyring og forvaltning i vr nrhet. Vi tror at vi ogs gjennom den kompetanse og erfaringsbakgrunn vi n bygger opp, og gjennom vr rolle som en krevende innkjper, vil kunne gi vik ge impulser lbake l det norske miljet. Forslaget om investeringer i egenkapitalinstrumenter er som kjent l behandling i Stor ngets nanskomit. P bakgrunn av komitens merknader, vil Norges Bank i lpet av noen mneder gi en mer presis lrding om hvordan de nye retningslinjene for forvaltningen av fondet skal u ormes. Denne lrdingen vil vre en del av bakgrunnsmaterialet for departementet nr de fastse er retningslinjene, muligens i forbindelse med fremleggelsen i Nasjonalbudsje et for 1998. Hvis vi ikke stter p u orutse e problemer i gjennomfringen, vil nye retningslinjer kunne vre opera ve fra januar 1998. PUBLISERT 5. juni 1997 14:00

Title: The outlook for the Norwegian economy
text: The outlook for the Norwegian economy Deputy Governor Jarle Bergo. Seminar organized by Unibank Markets/Radisson-SAS Plaza on September 24, 1997. The organizer has asked me to give "an assessment of the Norwegian economy with particular emphasis on the risk of overheating, bottlenecks and the possibility of lower inflation". As usual, it is not my job here today to spread laughter and op-ed in the congregation. When we look at the situation in the Norwegian economy today, it does not appear to be a basis for black vision. We have been through five years of high growth, but price inflation and cost inflation have so far shown signs of taking off. Sam dig has Norway large surpluses in the foreign economy and in government finances. Minister Gudmund Hernes wrote in his previous career about the more bizarre legalities in our existence: "Why everything goes wrong(1) . The starting point for the book is the well-known "Murphy's Law: Everything That Can Go Wrong Goes Wrong, and at its Worst Imaginable dpoint". Some would say Murphy was an op-ed; also what cannot go wrong goes wrong, and at the worst possible point. In line with the task the organizer has assigned to me, I will try to see how these laws can possibly be applied to the Norwegian economy. About everything that can go wrong... The economy is growing at a rapid rate. Mainland GDP growth Norway is rapidly high, and employment growth is strong, particularly in the public service sector. It seems that 1997 will again be a year in which we underestimated the growth in employment in advance, and to some extent also the demand. In the case of interest rate-driven demand, growth in petroleum investments and municipalities is particularly high. Despite the e, we have not yet seen signs l that price and wage growth are taking off. In our June Inflation Report, we estimated prices at 21/2 per cent this year and 2 per cent next year. Much of the decline in prices is due to developments in electricity prices this year. After all, the "underlying" price slide is on the rise. Based on these figures, it does not appear l l that for now there is some reason l to sound the alarm. The projections in the Inflation Report are based on some significant assumptions that will not necessarily hold up. This applies, among other things, to the impending of economic policing, not least the fiscal policy. Moreover, in the more recent episodes of overheard that we have , it has often been the case that inflation is the last thing that takes off, and only when everything else has gone badly wrong. On the other hand, inflation is difficult to bring down again, and it has in some cases required large sacrifices once it has reached a high level. There are plenty of ng that could go wrong in the next year. Or put another way: we are seeing more risk factors now than we saw a year ago, and the longer it goes with high growth rates, the more likely it will be that one or more of these will impact the economy. The most obvious risk lies in developments in the labour market. We know from other countries that a period of high unemployment tends to lead to a hard time getting unemployment down again in what it was. Over the past year, we have seen a relatively dramatic increase in the number of unemployed workers reported in the employment offices. As with several other indicators, they indicate that more and more people are now unable to get their hands on the jobs they need in the market - despite the fact that unemployment is rapidly high on a historical scale. They may indicate that labour market tightness is now increasing, and that it may be tempting for workers to bid up wages. The Solidarity Salterna knows has been successful, and probably contributes to the fact that unemployment has been able to fall as much as it has, without a much increase in wage growth. However, it is probably limited how long such policing can take full effect when the growth in demand drives the economy towards or even above the capacity limit. If the imbalances become large, we must expect that market creeds will sooner or later take over. Employment is already on an "all-me high" and it is difficult to speed up with today's wicket for very long. With the current situation in the labour market, it will be quite important to seek to hold back domestic demand growth, so that we are able to produce what is requested without the price glut. On the e-demand side of the economy, I see two major risk factors at the moment. It is the fiscal policy and developments in household credibility. Monetary policy is an objection to a stable krone exchange rate. This means that the interest rate must be adjusted for conditions in the foreign exchange market. The fiscal policy programme shall both ensure stable economic developments, prudent developments in government finances (e.g. tie in the National Insurance Scheme's economy) and an appropriate and effusive use of resources in public administration, in relation to the tasks the public sector is so close to solving. In the system we have, it is therefore essentially the task of financial policing to regulate the level of accompaniment domestically. I would like to stress that the e follows from policing decisions tie a division of responsibility in the economic policing. Over the past year, there has been a certain debate in the academic community and in the media about what is the most appropriate division of responsibility between the elements of the economic policing, give the situation Norway are now in. I'm not going to address this discussion here, but I'm going to start with the regime we have and discuss the opportunities and indis words they're facing us. Let me just say that a changed monetary policy regime, e.g. in the direction of an inflation target is not a sesame sesame that inconveniently solves our trade-off and priorities. There will be no need for a tight fiscal policy as the cornerstone of the economic programme. In recent years, the treasury has also contributed to a significant tightening of domestic demand - a figure of just over 5 per cent of mainland Norway GDP over the past four years. I'd like to mean a few comments in the e. First, it may be worth noting that fiscal austerity has slowed in recent years, as the situation in the economy in isolation would rather indicate that the need for austerity was diminishing. Those who will have the word in deba one later undoubtedly have better preconditions than me l explain why it has been so. Nevertheless, let me say that it appears that various costs of such austerity - including what they entail for the development of the public service - make policing's task more difficult as it goes. It may also be that the large surpluses that are now depositing in the Petroleum Fund do not exactly contribute to making this task laughable. To make the task more demanding, I would also like to remind you that it is not indifferent how fiscal austerity is achieved. We know that there are some large real economic costs at a high level, and the level of Norway is already high compared to other countries. Fiscal policy tightening should therefore be made as far as possible through lower growth in public releases. As there have been significant tightenings in fiscal policy, monetary policy is considerable, particularly at the beginning of the upturn in 1993, but also later, partly during the last year. In his to the Supervisory Council in February this year, the Governor addressed how monetary policy in recent years appears to be pro-cyclical. This means that monetary policy in the Norway, under the guidelines on a stable exchange rate, will generally contribute to amplifying cyclical developments. They are a cost of the system that must be weighed against the advantages entailed by the system, including the tie-in of wage formation and a clear division of responsibility in the economic policing sector - in order to distribute a stable exchange rate in itself for, among other things, competitive business. The fundamentals of the economy seem to give market participants a strong edge in the krone exchange rate - we have, among other things, high growth combined with large surpluses in the foreign economy and, quickly, low inflation. They entail that the interest rate must be low in order to avoid an appreciation of the krone. Low interest rates are higher than high interest rates, but how strongly changes in interest rates affect economic developments is uncertain. The fact that the changes in interest rates during the 1990s have affected the cyclical situation in the Norwegian economy is indisputable. They can be illustrated by the relationship between developments in house prices and the real interest rate. Norges Bank has, using our macroeconomic model RIMINI, make calculations that can illustrate the effect of a decline in interest rates. With all the caveats that all d will have to be taken by such model calculations, the model indicates that well over half of house price growth, and 20 l 50 per cent of growth in domestic demand and output since 1992, is due to the decline in interest rates. Today we have a very low real interest rate level, and there is reason to believe that the effects of a change in interest rates on asset prices and real economic variables are even stronger now than in a situation with a higher interest rate level. By extension, there may be reason to emphasise the risks associated with the interaction between financial and monetary policy. In the current situation, as mentioned, it is necessary to tighten economic policing in order to avoid an overheating of the economy. A fiscal tightening will also lead to higher government surpluses and the foreign economy. One should not disregard the fact that they can influence expectations in financial markets in the direction of increased confidence in an appreciation, so that Norges Bank must lower interest rates more easily on the part of stability in the krone exchange rate. The effects of fiscal austerity will then be partially offset by the easing of monetary policy. Other factors, such as changes in the global economy or oil prices, may also give rise to such "monetary shocks". It is not difficult to imagine that the cunning effect of the e can be that the economic policing, including monetary policy, as a whole will be less tight than would be desirable from a stabilisation policy point of view. The consequence may be that e demand is rapidly growing also e is that the production side cannot lby more goods and services, with the consequence that wages and prices are starting to struggle to balance it all. It is not fair to think that we will be able to cover the growth in demand by exclusively purchasing goods and services from abroad, thereby avoiding the price and cost effects of e-demand growth. A certain proportion of growth must be covered by domestic production, and experience has shown that the rise in prices for imported goods and services also picks up when the temperature in the economy becomes high enough. For now, it appears that developments in monetary aggregates are under control - that is: there is not yet an uncontrolled growth in e-demand generated by low interest rates and high credibility - in progress. Household growth has now been opposed to claims in the form of insurance claims, bank deposits and purchases of securities, and households are now in a far healthier financial sector than in the 1980s and 1990s. But it is also a paradox that the solid financial woes in households may mean that we have some kind of monetary overhang, which can suddenly be triggered, with strong consumption growth and lax price and cost inflation as a result. Even now, growth in the money supply and gdp is higher than nominal GDP growth. The monetary wealth that we see signs l in monetary indicators may initially find its way in capital markets, and have an impact on higher house prices and equity prices. In turn, and especially if credibility - and the rise in money supply - is accelerating, such a monetary integrity will almost inevitably lead to a rise in prices sooner or later. All in all, they indicate that we must now not get more monetary shocks into the economy if we are to avoid an increase in price and wage growth. Sam dig I must say that it does not seem entirely unlikely that we can have such monetary shocks in the future as well. ... going wrong, ... In our most recent Inflation Report, we tried to illustrate how any overheating of the economy might have an impact next year. We looked at the effects of two conditions. First, a situation where the labour market became so tight that it was no longer possible to hold back on wage growth, with the result that wages returned to the level of historical experience of the 1980s. Second, a situation where household saving was influenced by the low interest rate level in line with what we saw in the 1980s (we basically assumed a somewhat more different attitude among households). The effects of such fluctuations would only be felt for a few years, partly because they could generate strong fluctuations in the economy that force a tightening of economic policing. We have not assessed the longitudinal effects, nor the effects of more people going wrong together, but only look at the effects e years ahead in d isolated (separately). Even such a limited exercise shows that there is considerable upside potential, both for developments in wage growth (and thus, of course, also the price range and competitiveness) and for growth in private consumption. There is reason l assume that a development in line with what we see in the alterna vein in the chart, rela vt could quickly lead to serious imbalances in the economy, give the situation we have in the first place. ... at the worst possible point l've been talking to Li about what can go wrong, and li about what can happen if things go wrong. To complete the analysis of Murphy's legalities, e-mails remain - namely, how they might happen at the worst possible point. It is generally very difficult to predict when turning points or marked changes in the growth trajectories occur. This is partly due to the fact that such turning points have to do with changes in household expectations and bedri is - and such expectations are notoriously difficult to predict. In part, such turning points and events will occur due to e or other shock that, by definition, cannot be predicted. If we were to take Murphy's law seriously, the worst-case scenario for an e-commerce shock would be the moment when the economy is resilient so that production capacity is already expanding and a more erratic increase in demand cannot be satisfied by increased production. Unfortunately, for those of us who have laughed about being concerned, the situation I have described is very reminiscent of the situation the Norwegian economy is currently in. In other words, we're not very far away from the worst possible moment for a shock that hurts the growth in demand or prices. As I've been aware, it's also not hard to spot any candidates in such a shock. This may be part of the reason why Norges Bank could probably envisag a larger "margin of safety" in the economic programme that will soon be presented to the new Stor nget. I would also suggest that one in the e-mails should take into account the impact of a pro-cyclical monetary policy and the possibility of more monetary shocks generated by the situation in the foreign exchange market. about what can't go wrong.... l have l now concentrated on what can go wrong. But what if what can't go wrong still goes wrong? We cannot rule out the possibility that there will be a sudden disapproval in foreign exchange markets, that Norwegian bedri is suddenly increasing its price margins, that strikes are erupting, or that the labour market is significantly reduced as a result of labour market reforms. Such shocks may also induce imbalances and turning points with substantial real economic costs if safety margins are poor in principle. The worst possible point for this type of nega ve shock is likely to be when the debt ratio and asset prices have reached a very high level. Again, we may be heading for such a point, even if we are not in the 86 situation yet. In the e-mails I have tried to give an assessment of the Norwegian economy, with particular emphasis on risk factors. Maybe there's reason to stress that there are risks I've talked about, and that of course it doesn't have to go so badly. We can be lucky and avoid unpleasant shocks. However, the balance of risks should nevertheless trigger certain actions. Most houses don't burn, at least not every year. Nevertheless, few people do not see the value in paying li to guard themselves financially for the fact that something should happen. Transferred on the Norwegian economy, we can say that we have been through a long drought period where the forest around Det norske hus is bone dry and shelter can catch fire. When it is not certain that some cooling of the economy has any cost at all in the form of lower growth than the one we could potentially have , our choice should be reasonably simple: Let's take out the insurance and not play with the guys. 24 September 1997 13:00

Sentralbanksjefen kom blant annet i sin rstale l representantskapet i februar i r inn p hvordan pengepoli kken i de senere rene ser ut l  virke pro-syklisk. Det vil si: Det ser ut l at pengepoli kken i Norge, under retningslinjene om stabil valutakurs, gjennomgende vil medvirke l  forsterke konjunkturene. De e er en kostnad ved systemet som m veies opp mot de fordeler systemet innebrer, blant annet kny et l lnnsdannelsen og en klar ansvarsdeling i den konomiske poli kken - i llegg l de fordeler en stabil valutakurs i seg selv innebrer for blant annet konkurranseutsa nringsliv. Med alle de forbehold som all d vil m e tas ved slike modellberegninger indikerer modellen at godt over halvparten av boligprisveksten, og 20 l 50 prosent av veksten i innenlandsk e ersprsel og produksjon siden 1992, skyldes nedgangen i rentenivet. I forlengelsen av de e bildet kan det vre grunn l  understreke de risiki som ligger i samspillet mellom nans- og pengepoli kken. En viss andel av veksten m uanse dekkes ved innenlandsk produksjon, og erfaringene har vist oss at ogs prisveksten p importerte varer og tjenester tar seg opp nr temperaturen i konomien blir hy nok. text: Financial perspek ver Governor Kjell Storvik's speech at Norges Bank's Annual Meeting of the Supervisory Council on Thursday 19 February 1998 Background Over the past six months, we've witnessed a severe economic downturn in Asia. There have been considerable problems with refinancing both foreign and domestic debt, and gradually it is becoming clear that countries in Asia are facing a financial crisis. Growth in international capital flows over the past year has resulted in a new dimension in developments towards a global economy, with increased cross-border competition, but also wider fluctuations and vulnerability to imbalances in economies. The crisis in Asia demonstrates, like crises elsewhere, that even the most growth-craggy economies will sooner or later face strong market reactions if macroeconomic imbalances occur, or if a country's financial system is not functioning properly. Globalisation also creates a need for internationalisation of economic policy instruments. International institutions such as the IMF and the WTO - the new World Organization for Trade - now have a more prominent place in monitoring and regulating international economic relations than the other. In our own part of the world, the EU countries are in the process of forming an economic-policing superstructure over national markets through the economic and monetary union - EMU - and through the rise of the EU's internal market, of which we ourselves are a part. There is every reason to assume that developments towards increasingly integrated capital and commodity markets will be hasty, perhaps even with a stronger element of what international perspek knows in the unprecedented nature of economic policing. In other words, there is also reason to assume that the ineptness that the integration of our own economy with the rest of the world has already s lt us facing will be reinforced in the years to come. We have long been aware of some of these misconditions. These include new restrictions on the exercise of monetary policy, the increased need for oversight and control of financial markets, and restrictions on the imposed framework conditions for the business sector - including the system. Other inconsistenceables have so far been less in the spotlight. I believe that this applies not least to the impact on the structure of our business sector, and thus also to the structural policing of the authorities. I also think we can quickly improve our understanding of the relationships between the different policing areas - between on the one hand a prudent macroeconomic policing and on the other hand how structural policing can best be incorporated to meet the objectives of the economic policing. I will use this opportunity l to try to shed light on some of these contexts, and what consequences we can draw for the inemence of economic policing. I don't want to say that there are answers, but I see a clear danger that in the light of our oil wealth we are failing to take the misconditions seriously. It is my view that there is a need for a profound and fundamental debate about the choices we face. I hope in all modesty that with the e I can contribute l such a deba . From protectionism l integration... As the Second World War was to rebuild the economy of Europe, it was seen as essential to avoid the "everyone's struggle against all" that characterised protectionism and nationalism in the 1930s. The regulation of commodity markets that must e l in the early e-war years gradually became one of a system of increasing cross-border trade. A number of organisations - including GATT, the OECD and the IMF - were also built to address the need for international regulation and monitoring. Not least small countries that Norway benefited from the growing international commodity city. They enabled us to specialise in our economy and build up the business sector in sectors where Norway either had special advantages or particularly high competence. Thus, resources were also freed up from less profitable industries in the production of new goods and services where demand increased. E is that most of the trade barriers were erred, the reduction of restrictions on international capital movements began. They were associated with - and were a consequence of - the increased integration of economies into e-war it. The development of the international city of goods predicted e-payments and settlements in international currency. E is each, it became difficult to limit such foreign exchange settlements to pure capital transactions, and large international markets also developed for capital movements. The release of cross-border capital flows was a consequence of this development, and the deregulation of the markets can thus be seen as the "last stone" in the construction of international agreements and integrated economies that were formed e is the war. At the beginning of the 1980s, most Western countries were in a situation with very large deficits in the foreign economy and in public bidding, high and falling unemployment, and a far higher price level than worse. The major imbalances created a need for a more flexible financial system, which could channel savings across national borders and manufacturing sectors. In order for them to be able to recover, large sums of money were required in exchange rates as well as interest rates, and it became increasingly clear that direct regulation of financial and capital markets was not appropriate. In many countries, these regulations , together with high inflation and unsuitable systems, had each been recognised l that the return requirements for investments were partly very low, and partly that the required rates of return varied considerably between different types of investments. The consequence of those e - not least in Norway - was that high investment rates e are each left little in the form of increased economic prosperity, and the amount of directly unprofitable investments was increasing. Sam dig also led technological developments in that market regulations gradually lost effect. It became clear that it was neither possible nor desirable to maintain the regulation of capital flows. ... and global required rates of return As the regulations have each fallen away, investments in e-countries must be compared with competing projects in other countries - in principle, around the world. Some of the best profit opportunities turned out to be in countries that had not come as far as the rich countries in their development, and where the potential for profitable investments was consequently greatest. Not least, the countries of Asia - at least in recent years - have benefited from this development. As capital flows accelerated, the high profit opportunities in Asia probably led to at least some higher required rates of return in western countries as well. The result was that investment in our part of the world fell significantly, as investment increased in developing countries. A larger share of savings in western countries is now invested elsewhere than on their own territory, and there has been a very strong growth in capital outflows from OECD countries. Also in Norway, the low return on capital in the 1970s and first half of the 1980s was an indication that financial markets were not functioning well and that the capital market in Norway was partly isolated from the rest of the world. The interest rate was largely policing, and the system provided for a very low and partly nega v real interest rate e er ska . Both meant that the capital market did not provide "correct" information - in the form of interest rate signals - neither in savers nor borrowers. The result was partly that the overall level of investment was too high, partly because the investments were wrongly collated by the rationed credibility not finding its way into the most profitable investments. E is each it became clear that the regulation of capital markets could not be raised in Norway. Housing and property markets, the credice market and the foreign exchange market were deregulated during the 1980s. With the rising international capital movements and more effusion in markets - which quickly created an arbitrage opportunity - the bias in the system had wider consequences, which included the strong credicle expansion of the 1980s. Ska ereform in 1992 teased many of the differences that existed between different forms of savings and types of investments. In this sense, the reform was a natural consequence of the changes that had taken place in capital markets. E is the deregulation of capital markets and the 1992 tax reform is the required rate of return in Norway more in accordance with the required rate of return internationally, and the kredi market distributes kredi more efficient vt and l more profitable investment projects for society. I think there is now a broad consensus that both are necessary prerequisites for investing in competitive ge projects and promoting profitability in the business sector. Have the reforms yielded us a manufacturing win? Profitability in the business sector would be a meager consolation if these changes did not also have an impact on increased value creation. At first glance, it appears that the most important consequence has been that investments fell. If we compare investments and production developments in the current cyclical upturn with the upturn in the 1980s, it turns out that we now have somewhat higher output growth, despite lower investment rates. In other words, it appears that investments are considerably more manufacturing than in the 1980s. Now some will immediately object that high GDP growth during the upturn is primarily related to the strong employment growth. Instead, in order to distinguish the effects of cyclical developments in the labour market, we can compare developments in capital expenditure and productivity over a longer period. Increasing capital investment is a common explanation for growth. The fall in investment rates we have seen in the 1990s should therefore be traditional explanations leading to a fall in manufacturing growth as well. The growth in production per meverk was almost exactly the same in the 1978 period in 1986 and the eleven years from 1986 to 1997. But in the period from 1978 to 1986, manufacturing increased primarily as a result of very high investments and a strong growth in the amount of capital behind each meme. Fak sk increased capital expenditure somewhat more strongly than the product during this period. In the last 11 years, this trend has reversed. We can say that we now have an "unexplained" production growth - a growth in manufacturing that cannot be explained by increased capital investment. Moreover, we should note that the decline in capital growth is considerable - from 21/2 per cent per an an year in the early 1980s to 11/4 per cent per year in the last year. Nevertheless, the growth in manufacturing has been well held up. There can be many reasons in this development. Part of the explanation may be that we quickly live on overcapacity from the previous cyclical upturn. We have also been going through a period of introduction of new technology, and it is possible that this new technology has significantly increased the production knowledge. It may also be that today's work crashes are in themselves more manufacturing, for example through an increased level of education. It is striking that such a large "unexplained" improvement in manufacturing has taken place at a time when we have undergone significant reforms in capital markets - both the deregulation of capital markets and the reform of 1992. One of the objectives of the reform was to improve the functioning of capital markets and increase the socio-economic return on our investments. While there may be many reasons for the improvement in capital's socio-economic return - measured in the way we see in Figure 4 - it is difficult to get around the fact that these reforms can have a significant impact. In other words, it is appropriate to interpret the developments in capital markets - together with the 1992 reform - all in all, to increase the return on the capital we as a nation are investing, which may also lead to higher growth than the dligere. New surroundings increase the requirements for stability and restructuring ability Participation in international capital markets also entails disadvantages and inconveniences. Some will see it as a disadvantage that we as a nation are more exposed to international events, and that the crevasses in the international economy are forcing us through reschedings we may not immediately see a new one of. Others may see them as an advantage, perhaps even as a kind of "garan" against the policing of governments being or upholding economic secrecy and regulations. A are others may think that the increased return on capital has unfortunate distributional effects that are necessary to correct. It is also part of the picture that market participants do not seem to be acting rationally - at least not in the way the authorities would like them to behave. For me, it is important that in the long run Norway neither can nor should "opt out" of the worldwide integration process and the international agreements regulating the flows of goods and capital in the world economy, or evade influence from international capital markets. In our domestic deba there are o e disadvantages of these markets on which it is being focused, and we tend to forget the obvious benefits Norway have of being able to participate in international markets and achieve an acceptable return on the nation's savings. Not least, they apply to the part of savings that is channelled through the Government Petroleum Fund, which is invested abroad in its entirety. So we must take as a give - and there is no revolutionary insight - the frameworks for our economic policing that are provided through the way the international community organizes itself. The fact that capital flows freely across borders is a fact that we may or may not like, but that is a fact - and there is little we can do about it. Norway's a small country. The most fertile and realis we can do is focus on how best to make sure that we are in the framework conditions that apply. Then, of course, we can work in international forums to change the aspects of the system we don't think well of. We can hardly expect all this to have an impact on our views, but working outside the system is also not a viable path, at least not for small nations. The consequences of the new environment for economic policing and the dismantling of the framework conditions of the business sector can be summed up in two terms: stability and resilience. The Norwegian authorities must provide the business sector with framework conditions that make it possible to adapt to globalisation and meet international competition for capital. There are requirements for stability and credibility in the implications of these framework conditions, and there are limits to the costs we can charge to the business sector - including in terms of burden and administrative costs. Through economic policing, the authorities can also contribute to stable economic developments, so that we avoid major macroeconomic imbalances and new crises in the financial sector. The requirement for respites is applicable in many areas of economic policing. First, the shift in markets and the world economy means that we must be prepared for sudden and unexpected changes in our environment - changes that may make it necessary to change larger or smaller parts of the economic policy. A policing that seems excellent for a period of time doesn't have to be rich g medicine in the next round. Second, the part of economic policing that particularly affects the framework conditions of the business sector - structural policing - must be addressed in return for the fact that the business sector can quickly change its mind and face new inconveniences. Stabiliseringspoli kken under press The changes in the world economy are of great importance for the exercise of monetary and foreign exchange policy. From a system of policing exchange rates, small capital movements and policy-controlled interest rates, we have gradually moved into a situation of large capital movements, more unstable conditions in the foreign exchange market and an interest rate level that is largely influenced by interest rates and market conditions internationally. In Norway, norges bank seeks to maintain a stable exchange rate, with the consequence that the interest rate level must be adjusted so that the foreign exchange market balances. For Norway, the e - in broad terms - means that the interest rate level in Norway is largely fixed in Frankfurt, based on the considerations that the German monetary policy authorities choose to emphasise. It dares to be well known in this assembly that our policing authorities and Norges Bank have a somewhat different view on the question of how monetary policy should be incorporated into the current situation. Norges Bank has not changed its assessment since or autumn, when the Bank gave an unearthable justification for its views in the Government. I would like to emphasise that Norges Bank takes the authorities' view in this direction, and the Bank loyally follows up the guidelines for monetary policy as established by the policing authorities. I'm therefore not going to do them on any topic here tonight. Nevertheless, I find it necessary briefly to remind you of the consequences of the choice in monetary policy. When the authorities choose to use the interest rate l to stabilise the exchange rate, fiscal policy remains as the only real instrument in stabilisation policy. In a system with a stable exchange rate, it is therefore crucial that the authorities are able to implement fiscal policy in such a way that there are no major and undesirable cyclical movements in the economy. It can be challenging to reconcile stabilisation policy with all the other considerations that need to be taken into account in fiscal policy. The problem has been clearer in the last year than in this upturn. In the specific irrecondition of fiscal policy, the bidding for 1997 and 1998 has consistently resulted in a near-neutral fiscal policy, despite the fact that the upturn is about to peak. In other words, monetary policy seems to be expanding due to the prevailing conditions in the money and foreign exchange market. In other words, we can't get around the fact that neither monetary policy nor fiscal policy at the moment seems to be contributing to stabilising economic developments in Norway. In this situation, the policing authorities seem to place much of the responsibility for the stability of the economy on the parties to the income settlements. They are my view - and with all due respect to the parties - a responsibility that goes beyond the possibilities and instruments that the parties are concerned about. There are therefore clear limitations to what we must reasonably expect income policing to handle. All in all, it seems to have the presumption that we will be able to manage the economy so that we avoid a turnaround in a few years. We must at least be prepared for the fact that the upturn is first accelerating, because you are slowing down due to constraints on the supply side of the economy - primarily in the labour market. Norges Bank's projections may indicate that the cyclical turnaround may be marked. As I was in the introduction, we cannot rule out that capital markets will react to such a situation, and if so, also amplify the turnaround - as we have seen these markets react more closely, both to the situation in the Norway and in other European countries in the 1990s, and most recently to developments in asian economies. If economic policing cannot deliver the stability we really all want, the following question becomes central: Is the Norwegian economy - our business sector and our households - today better equipped l to withstand a cyclical turnaround than in the slush one of the 1980s? Again, they are my view a matter of stability and resilience. The basic preconditions for us to get upright through such a turnaround will be that underlying structures are inconspicuously stable. In turn, this requires that the economy does not falter under the weight of the cyclical turnaround - and that the business sector is stretchable to quickly meet the amended framework conditions. To put it bluntly, they're pretty much over-the-top themes. There is hardly an unambiguous answer to what should l for the economy to have the desired characteristics. To make the task easier - and without claiming that with it I have given an indecent discussion - I will concentrate on two factors that I believe can be decisive: First, I would argue that the stability of the economy will largely depend on a substantial financial solvency - in the business sector in general and in the financial sector in particular. Without such a solidity, domino effects of the kind we have recently seen in Asia - and as we experienced ourselves in the 1990s - could arise where bankruptcies in some sectors are and sectors quickly forge over into other parts of the economy. In light of developments in Asia, I also believe that financial strength in the financial sector in particular will be decisive for how tight international markets react, and thus also for how crass the turnaround needs to be. Second, I would argue that the resilience of the business sector will largely depend on the fact that we can quickly ensure a reasonable allocation of capital. We will depend on the fact that the investments we make are solidly founded and have such high profitability that they can also be defended in bad ones there. After all, it is the new investments, the new capital, that will in turn provide growth. In light of the changes I have sought to shed light on - with strong competition for capital and increased cross-border required rates of return - I would also argue that the actual organisation of the capital market can be decisive. Not least, it is my opinion necessary to focus on the importance of conditions on the ownership side in the business sector and in the financial sector, including the state's ownership role. Financial equity/assets ratio The financial crisis in Asia and our own banking crisis illustrate the close relationship between stability in the financial sector, events in foreign exchange markets and economic policing and domestic developments. Overall, our and others' experiences over the past few years show that a financial sector with tensile strength and solidity is necessary if we are to get through the next round of cyclical turnarounds and currency turbulence without too much difficulty. A fundamental problem for the authorities in regulating the financial system is what mechanisms we really have to ensure that the financial sector's dispositions do not lead us, as a society, to take too much risk. There are several reasons l that isolated interest rate decisions in the individual incentive may contribute to weakening the stability of the financial system as a whole. One possible reason may be that a single bank is only concerned with the risk the bank itself is incurred, and not the risk it indirectly imposes on others. This systemic risk is related to, among other things, the interaction with international financial markets and the interdependent dependence of Norwegian banks on each other in the Norwegian credice market. For example, a Norwegian bank's credibility abroad will depend not only on the Bank's own system, but also on how the financial strength of the entire Norwegian banking system is assessed. We have found that in the event of turbulence in parts of the financial market, foreign funding also disappears for those incentives that did not initially have liquidity or solvency problems. As a result, there may be a risk to the financial system as such, tying a l how individual banks are run. They have probably also been an important element in several crises internationally, most recently in Asia. As in the vast majority of other Western countries, in Norway we have a broad range of regulations to address these and other types of risks that might otherwise arise in the financial industry. An example of such a regulation is the requirements of capital adequacy, which are intended to ensure some financial strength in the sector and thereby counteract systemic risk. I would like to stress that even with the regulations and views we currently have for the industry - and although both the industry and its customers today undoubtedly both have better financial strength and are far more concerned with risk management and control than we did years ago, we cannot rule out that the financial system may again come under pressure if the situation in the economy deteriorates. Conditions in the money and foreign exchange market suggest that monetary policy in the Norway must be exchanged expansionary in order to keep the krone exchange rate stable. In most other European countries, monetary policy is also expansionary, but the economic situation is clearly different from that of Norway. The consequence of these is that the level of the real interest rate in Norway - measured as market rates adjusted for inflation - is now just below the level in the mid-1980s. When we disregard risk premiums, investments for it may be considered profitable with a return down to 2-3 per cent. In light of the fluctuations we have seen in interest rates - which may repeat themselves - there is reason to ask how such a return on marginal investments would affect the solvency of the business sector, at least if such investments were to occur to a large extent. With the e-low interest rates, we have also seen a high growth in credit demand. We must assume that any wider fluctuations in the interest rate level may result in an increase in banks' losses and that some sectors may again have problems with their debt burden. With lending growth that is barely strong, it cannot be ruled out that more of banks' lending portfolios are becoming more risk atown. Sam dig has led some weakening of banks' capital adequacy over the past two years. They are li paradoxical, e as we would normally expect it to be in good there that the incentives can strengthen the solidity. Low interest rates and increased loss risk must also be viewed in the context of developments in the property market. As a result of rising demand and affordability, house prices have risen by more than 40 per cent in real terms since the bottom point in 1993, and the real price of housing is now approaching the highs of the 1980s. The rise in prices for commercial properties has also been very strong. In light of the considerable fluctuations we have seen, there is reason to assume that a possible turnaround in the economy will again lead to a fall in property values. Some of the price risk they entail must be assumed to fall on banks through loans secured on real estate. One development that is due to the fact that a substantial share of growth in banks' lending is now financed abroad. Total foreign funding amounted to almost NOK 190 billion at the end of November. This means that this type of financing has increased by about 120 billion over the past two years. The sharp growth in foreign funding is to some extent related to banks having their credibility upgraded by foreign agencies, thereby achieving cheaper financing in international bond markets. However, as seen in Chart 9, financing through such bonds is a smaller part of the growth in total foreign debt. In other words, a significant portion of foreign funding - around three pea parts - is card-like. I would assume that banks normally hedge this type of borrowing against foreign exchange risk through transactions in futures markets, among other things, so that banks' foreign exchange exposure does not increase. Furthermore, the Norwegian financial sector meets the international and national requirements of financial strength, and there are substantial surpluses in the Norwegian banking industry. Nevertheless, I would argue that several of the developments we are seeing are pointing in the wrong direction. If the direction doesn't change, it may not be too long-term to worry. The danger of a large shortfall in financing abroad is that the financial sector as a whole - as a system and above d - can present a significant liquidity risk. If the credice from abroad were to suddenly stop or be reversed - for example in the context of an economic downturn or a failure of our currency - such financing could cause significant payment problems, as we have seen in Asia, for example.
