Title: Experience and challenges in Norwegian monetary policy
text: Experiences and indiscibles in Norwegian monetary policy Governor Kjell Storvik's speech at the conference "U ordringer i norsk okonomi", Norwegian Association of Economists, Wednesday 25 February 1998 Let me initially say that the topic of today's conference - "indistingsions for the Norwegian economy" - is a topical problem for us at the central bank, which, the more than most people have a reputation for casting worrying glances at it. And there are several reasons l that the topic is more relevant now than in several years. First, Norges Bank has long questioned whether it was possible to get a prudent landing of the Norwegian economy e is the strong growth period that started in 1993. As is certainly known to this assembly, our assessment in the autumn was that there was a significant risk that the economy could enter unstable developments. We therefore recommended a policy change so that monetary policy could contribute to some stabilisation or at least not lead to more destabilisation of the economy. Let me also remind you of another vik g u ordring the Norwegian economy faces in the next few years - and which other speakers will also get into - namely the establishment of EMU and the introduction of the euro in Europe. Mi's contribution will be to discuss some of the inept words and choices facing the establishment of EMU's Norwegian monetary policy. Economic development A broad background for the recommendations we made in our letter this autumn on monetary policy was the current economic situation and the risk we intended to see for an unstable development ahead. Let me therefore start by outlining how we assess economic developments. The Norwegian economy is now entering the fifth year in a row with a strong upturn. The upturn has lasted about as long and has been about as strong as the upturn in the 1980s. So far, there is little evidence of dampening in e-demand, and growth in both the private and public sectors is high. The strong employment growth has led to an ever-tighter labour market, and there is a shortage of qualified jobs in many sectors. Capacity growth has thus increased markedly in recent years, and there are indications that the mainland economy is close to or even above the capacity limit. In the Inflation Report presented by Norges Bank in December, it was pointed out that the Norwegian economy may be ahead of a period of a marked cyclical path. Strong growth is likely to continue in the current year and next, but restrictions on The lbuds side, among other things, in the form of a labour crash scarcity, will l slush lead to a cyclical turnaround. In the Inflation Report, it was suggested that such a backlash could come around the turn of the century. Employment growth will come to a halt and we may again see an increase in unemployment. The cyclical turnaround is related to the deterioration in competitiveness - wage growth may, according to projections, reach 6 per cent. Together with an expected decline in petroleum investment, The Sam dig will weaken profitability and lower capacity growth, leading to a decline in business investment. There is obvious uncertainty associated with the assumptions behind the projections for future developments. Among other things, it is conceivable that we may have underestimated the longitudinal growth potential of the economy. I can tell you that more and more people are now sharing our view of the economic situation. The OECD's country report on Norway clearly underlined the danger of over-overheating the Norwegian economy. Both the possibility of a strong overhaul of the economy and the risk of new shocks amplifying cyclical developments mean that one thinks through whether the Norwegian economy is icyly equipped l to withstand a severe economic turnaround. We must also try  as far as possible  to correct a development that entails a significant risk of incurring significant costs in the forward. The "safety margins" in the economy are now very small and even minor deviations from the assumed developments may have serious longitudinal consequences. Financial and revenue policing In the case of fixed exchange rates, the authorities give up an instrument - the interest rate - in stabilisation policy. Or resentfully: they choose to use the e-instrument l stabilise the exchange rate rather than use the interest rate directly in the question regulation. They entail that fiscal policy is left as the only real instrument in stabilisation policing. In a system with a stable exchange rate, it is therefore crucial that the authorities are able to implement fiscal policy in such a way that there are no major and undesirable cyclical movements in the economy. During a boom, as we are now in, fiscal policy should contribute to curbing demand for domestic production resources. Such austerity can be achieved by increasing the number of people who are giving up or by reducing public spending. It is not without significance how austerity is imposed. Increased ska er and emit is will reduce the affection in the economy through the twisting effects we know are ignited. The main purpose of the reforms in the 1990s was to improve the effigies, and we must be careful to undermine what we have achieved here. Our opportunities to enter us with a significantly different level than our competitor countries have also been weakened as a result of increased market integration. Such considerations may therefore indicate that stabilisation policing should first and foremost be initiated on the bidding side. However, it is also not the case that we can reduce the issue without consequences for e or several of the other targets in the financial policy area. Daily media coverage of shortcomings in the health and social care sector, in our school and university system, raises serious questions about whether more austerity in fiscal policing is traditionally a viable path. Moreover, unfortunately, we must assume that we only see the beginning of the e-priority issue. E is questionable, and the requirements l, several of the central tasks that the public sector today is ears, will rather increase than decrease with rising revenues in the years ahead. We must assume that technological and general societal developments will rather indicate an increase than a reduction in these tasks' share of value creation. In llegg, we know that the share of value creation will increase - this follows from the guidelines that have already been laid down for, among other things, the age pensions. Now I don't mean by the e to say that there are no opportunities l to reduce publishing in the public sector. I would like to point out that there is a difficult conflict of objectives between on the one hand the objectives of stabilisation policing and on the other hand all the other considerations that need to be taken into account in fiscal policy. Over the past couple of years, the financial policy has not tightened, despite the fact that the upturn is about to peak. The proposed 1998 government budget entails a tightening of 1/4 per cent of mainland GDP, as measured by the change in the oil, interest rate and interest rate-adjusted surplus on the state budget. Our assessment this autumn was that a fiscal tightening of about 11/2 per cent of mainland GDP was necessary Norway if fiscal policy alone were to curb economic growth now so that we could avoid a fall around the turn of the century. The solidarity salt has so far been successful, and probably contribute to the fact that unemployment has been able to fall as much as it has, without a much increase in wage growth. But there are limits to how long such policing can take full effect when demand growth drives the economy towards, or even above, the capacity limit. If the imbalances become large, we must expect that market creeds will sooner or later take over. Employment and occupational participation are already higher than ever. In other words, it is not an insignificant task for the social partners when they start the spring wage negotiations. To get a continuation of the successful line they have led hi l will undoubtedly be more leniency if the financial policing had steadied one up below the moderation line. Money and currency policy In our letter this autumn, Norges Bank's assessment was that we could no longer assume that fiscal policy would ensure stable economic developments, and that we seemed to have found a situation where the achieving of the operatic objective of exchange rate stability was not consistent with the fundamental objective of full employment and sustainable economic growth. As is known, today's monetary policy management system is set out in the foreign exchange crisis on 6 May 1994 with the guidelines in the various bidding publications. In accordance with the e, monetary and foreign exchange policy is against keeping the exchange rate stable and they are also in line with the recommendations made by Norges Bank in a letter in April 1994 l Ministry of Finance: "Monetary policy under floating exchange rates". In its e-mails, Norges Bank attached great importance to the long tradition Norway had for fixed exchange rate policy and also underlined the role of monetary policy and the exchange rate as a nominal anchor for wage settlements and the framework for financial policy. In our 1994 letter, we pointed out that the overriding objectives of economic policing are to provide conditions for low unemployment and sustained economic growth, and that the most important contribution of monetary policy in stable economic developments was to maintain low price and cost inflation. Although at the time we recommended exchange rate stability as an opera vt intermediate target, we therefore also pointed out that the e opera ve intermediate target in certain situations should be adjusted: "If the economy is affected by severe economic disturbances or prolonged and strong cyclical fluctuations, the derived exchange rate target should be adapted to the target for monetary policy." Norway has experienced a strong and prolonged cyclical upswing in recent years that is now affecting increased pressures in many areas of the economy and we are in a situation where we have a crash in the cyclical movement and where the management system for monetary policy is the Bank's view has contributed and contributes to strengthening these problems. In this context, let me remind you that much of the burden on fiscal policy can be attributed to a procyclical monetary policy: for example, the tightening of fiscal policy over the past two years has largely been neutralised by the easing of monetary policy. During the last (just over) year, interest rates have been lowered by about 1 percentage point. Calculations made in Norges Bank's rimini economic model indicate that a 1 percentage point decline in the interest rate must be matched by a tightening of fiscal policy of up to 3/4 per cent of GDP in order for the overall orientation of the policy instruments to have a neutral effect on the economy. Such calculations are uncertain and other models for the Norwegian economy may probably produce somewhat different results. Nevertheless, it is obvious that low interest rates have worked and have an expansionary effect on the Norwegian economy. One reason why monetary policy has seemed procyclical is that Norway since the mid-1980s the systema sk has had a different cyclical development than the countries in Kon nental-Europe. The interest rate level in the countries against which the krone is tied has thus generally not been consistently consistent with the cyclical situation in Norway. While in the early 1980s it was obviously necessary to pursue a tight monetary policy in order to resurrect the krone and bring inflation down so that there was not necessarily any conflict between the exchange rate target and the final objectives of the economic policy cycle, it is worrying that monetary policy in recent years has contributed to amplifying the upturn. Of course, it's possible that the year we have behind us is special. The overheating of the Norwegian economy in the mid-1980s had major consequences for economic developments in the following years. Furthermore, the reunification of Germany in the early 1990s had a major impact on cyclical developments and monetary policy in Europe. We can hope that we are not exposed to such shocks again. Nevertheless, there are some fundamental features of the Norwegian economy that may indicate that we will soon have a systemic cyclical development than the countries in Kon nental-Europe. First, the industrial structure of the Norway is different from most countries in Kon nental-Europe. In llegg l the obvious importance of the oil sector, there is also reason to believe that large parts of the mainland industry are out of step with the countries at the convention. Our export drive, for example, is highly commodity-oriented, while exports in Kon nental Europe are to a much greater extent finished goods producers. There is also reason to believe that the sensitivity to fluctuations in interest rates in Norway is greater than in many countries in Kon nentalEuropa, and this will reinforce the effect of us being in a different cyclical phase than these countries. They may be particularly related to the fact that interest rate changes have a major effect on Norwegian household wealth because housing ownership is very prevalent in Norway. Experience has shown that there is a close relationship between changes in the real interest rate and changes in house prices in Norway, which is the most important component of Norwegian household wealth. In most other European countries, housing is a much smaller share of household wealth and changes in house prices thus have a smaller impact on household wealth, even if they are to some extent offset by households in other European countries having larger equity wealth that is also affected by changes in interest rates. Furthermore, a large part of lending rates in Norway are tied to the short-term interest rates. In Kon nental-Europe, the public's borrowing rates are fixed throughout the loan run d and households and are thus to a lesser extent affected by fluctuations in interest rates. Some have argued that household interest rate sensitivity may have been reduced compared to the 1980s because households now have higher financial assets and that higher interest rates may therefore have an impact on household income. I don't think they're obvious. It is rich that household ne o financial assets are now higher than in the 1980s, but the chart also shows that the ratio of interest-bearing debt to receivables is approximately the same as in the latter part of the 1980s. The income effect for the household sector during an interest rate increase is thus quickly nega v. The increase in household assets is partly due to an increase in household holdings of equities. An interest rate increase will have an impact on the value of equities and thereby give households a nega v wealth effect. It is therefore conceivable that interest rate sensitivity has increased compared to the 1980s. Low borrowing costs are about to have a knock-on impact on growth in credit lending, particularly from banks, and there is reason to believe that strong lending growth has made a number of financial institutions more risk ailing. Although the solidity of the since the mid-1980s, the financial industry has clearly strengthened, and strong lending growth may soon conflict with the requirements of banks' holdings of core capital. As I pointed out above, there is a significant correlation between interest rates and property prices. Low interest rates have contributed to a 40 per cent increase in house prices since 1993. If interest rates were to rise substantially again, we must expect property prices to fall. A fall in property prices will initially affect households and households and reduce their demand. We have more likely to see that they can have a forging effect on banks if they are and households have difficulty servicing their loans as the value of banks' collateral has been reduced. Possible changes in monetary and foreign exchange policing Norges Bank's letter in the Ministry of Finance this autumn discussed whether monetary policy could make a greater contribution to stabilising economic developments than norges bank believes is possible with the guidelines we currently have for monetary policy. Norges Bank recommended a restructuring of the current exchange rate path in the direction of providing greater flexibility in the short term, but where the objective of exchange rate stability is maintained. Specifically, we advised that the price against which monetary policy is directed - the "initial range" - is defined further than today. They will be able to do so by avoiding the problems of a strong pro-cyclical monetary policy in situations with renewed pressure on the krone exchange rate. Under such an alternation, one will mainly be able to continue the basis for the existing division of responsibility in the economic policing, especially in relation to income policing, in that the exchange rate will quickly serve as a nominal anchor. In responding to our advice on more flexibility in the exercise of monetary policy, the Government showed "that there is already some flexibility in the exercise of monetary policy in that no central exchange rate has been established for the krone with fluctuation margins." Furthermore, it pointed to the need for clear objectives and responsibilities between government agencies in the government's view is safeguarded in the current guidelines. Norges Bank has  as the executive authority for monetary policy  taken the Government's response in the direction of the monetary policy and will of course implement the monetary policy in line with the exchange rate policy and the guidelines that have been drawn up for monetary policy. The Government's response must also mean that we can foresee the other elements of the economic policing being laid out so that there are no conflicts of objectives in monetary policy. They will be necessary for us to pursue a monetary policy that is consistent with the overriding objectives of the economic policy within the guidelines on stability in the krone exchange rate. Based on the picture I drew for the Norwegian economy above, I must nevertheless note that there is a considerable probability that we will not be able to avoid a cyclical turnaround in a few years. It may well be that we will have to rely on low growth and perhaps a reduction in asset prices and employment. In such a situation, capital markets must also be expected to react and probably amplify the turnaround, as we have experience for in Norway and in other European countries, and recently in the Asian economies. In other words, it is not difficult to spot moves that are worrying and that may cause a flashback to be stronger than what we dare to base in our estimates. The purpose of highlighting these factors is not to claim that they will happen, but rather to underline the dangers of market participants being exposed to factors that cannot persist over d. In the cyclical upturn that led up to the over-accumulation of the Norwegian economy in the 1980s, few people were expected to suggest that real interest rates could be as high as they were a few years later. I hope that Norges Bank's failures in our Inflation Report and elsewhere have contributed to dampening unrealistical expectations of both interest rate levels and income growth - even if we do not all d arrive with our advice - or perhaps raise it. EMU and Norwegian monetary policy Let me say a few words about EMU and the indiscibles they are facing. The strong policing will behind the plans and the fact that many countries now appear to meet most of the so-called Maastricht criteria suggests that EMU will be established as planned. The euro will thus most likely be introduced on 1 January 1999 and it appears that 11 countries will participate in EMU from the start. The redress of EMU and a common currency in Europe will further enhance global financial integration. Member states' national financial markets are merging into deep and liquid markets, and they are likely to initiate major structural changes. We will probably see a trend towards several large and capital-strong players that could amplify the trend in large capital flows internationally. Dersom det skulle bli store kursuktuasjoner i de internasjonale valutamarkeder, vil en te euro- lknytning gi betydelige svingninger i kronens eek ve kurs. Den eek ve kronekursen er, i hvert fall p kort sikt, vik g for lnnsomheten i konkurranseutsa sektor og gir - i llegg l utviklingen i det rela ve kostnadsniv - vik g informasjon om utviklingen i industriens konkurranseevne. Jeg har ovenfor pekt p at dagens kursstabiliseringsregime har bidra l prosyklisk pengepoli kk - hovedsakelig som flge av ulik konjunkturutvikling i Norge og Kon nental-Europa. Konjunkturforlpet i anglosaksiske land synes derimot  vre mer i samsvar med det norske. Stabiliseres kroneverdien mot en kursindeks som ogs omfa er bri ske pund og amerikanske dollar, kan sannsynligheten for at pengepoli kken skal virke prosyklisk, bli noe mindre. Et alterna v l en euro- lknytning kan vre  stabilisere kronen mot konkurransekursindeksen, som gir u rykk for valutakursens bidrag l endringer i industriens konkurranseevne. Det ville innebre en lbakevending l det kurvsystemet som vi hadde i perioden 1978-90, men med en forskri som pner for strre eksibilitet i kronekursen. Lykkes det  holde kronens verdi mlt mot konkurransekursindeksen stabil, vil uktuasjoner i de internasjonale valutakursmarkedene ikke pvirke industriens gjennomsni lige konkurranseevne, og vi blir mindre srbare overfor devalueringer og revalueringer i andre land. Det er ikke penbart at et eventuelt valg mellom euro og en handelsveiet kurv vil innebre store forskjeller for pengepoli kken. Denne guren viser handelsveiet og euroveiet rente og valutakurs. I perioder har det vrt forskjeller, men hovedinntrykket er at rammebe ngelsene ikke vil bli vesentlig forskjellig. Det kanskje noe overraskende forhold at euroveiet rente er svakt hyere enn den handelsveide renten fra 1990 har blant annet sammenheng med det svrt lave rentenivet i Japan. De e har motvirket at rentene i Storbritannia, USA og Sverige er hyere enn for euro-landene. Enkelte har hevdet at euro e erhvert vil kunne bli anvendt i innenlandske betalinger i land utenfor unionen. En slik anvendelse av utenlandsk valuta kalles gjerne valutasubs tusjon. Et stort omfang av bruk av euro i Norge innebrer i sin y erste konsekvens at vi ikke lenger har noen pengepoli kk fordi vi ikke lenger vil ha noen nasjonal valuta. Dersom de e skulle skje vil valget av kurs lknytning selvsagt vre uten interesse. Det er imidler d f eller ingen eksempler p land med ordnede konomiske forhold som rammes av et stort omfang av valutasubs tusjon. Hvilke forhold er det s som kunne lsi at euro skulle bli ta i bruk og fortrenge norske kroner som betalingsmiddel i Norge? Norske bedri er som handler med bedri er bde i Norge og MU vil kunne nske  beny e euro ogs i Norge, for p den mte  sikre at inntekter og utgi er blir i samme valuta. Det er allerede stor oppmerksomhet i nringslivet om virkningene av euro, og de store bankene forbereder seg p  kunne lby et bredt spekter av nansielle tjenester i euro l sine kunder. Hvor rask og omfa ende en slik utvikling vil kunne bli er selvsagt meget usikkert. Betydningen av euro i det norske markedet vil blant annet kunne avhenge av hvor stor handel vi har med euro-omrdet. I 1996 ble EU-landenes valutaer beny et som oppgjrsvaluta for 22 prosent av vr eksport og 37 prosent av vr import. Tilvarende tall for dollar var henholdsvis 57 og 23 prosent og for norske kroner henholdsvis 18 og 34 prosent. Den hye dollarandelen i oppgjret av eksportbetalinger har blant annet sammenheng med at olje og gass stort se handles i dollar. I llegg er ere av de strste industribedri ene og skipsfarten i hovedsak dollarbaserte. U ormingen og prak seringen av det penge- og valutakurspoli ske styringssystemet kan i seg selv f betydning for bruk av euro i Norge fordi de e vil pvirke stabiliteten i kronekursen overfor euro. Med en rela vt streng valutakurs lknytning l euro, vil kroner og euro kunne bli svrt nre subs tu er, i hvert fall s lenge en slik lknytningen er troverdig. De e kunne bidra l kt bruk av euro. Ved en mer eksibel kronekurs, vil svingningene i valutakursen bli strre, og valutakursusikkerhet kan skape en barriere mot valutasubs tusjon. En av grunnene l at valutasubs tusjon i liten grad har skjedd i de industrialiserte land er trolig at det bare er den nasjonale valutaen som er tvunget betalingsmiddel. De e innebrer blant annet at det bare er den nasjonale valutaen som kan brukes l betaling av ska er og avgi er. Det er vel neppe noe som tyder p at euro vil bli et tvunget betalingsmiddel i Norge i den nrmeste frem d. La meg avslutningsvis ogs peke p at Canada, som jo har den amerikanske dollar som svrt nr nabo og som har den strste delen av sin utenrikshandel med USA, fortsa har sin egen valuta og sin egen selvstendige pengepoli kk. Forvrig vil jeg minne forsamlingen om at det i henhold l valutabestemmelsene ikke er lla for  for nordmenn  gjre opp sine mellomvrender i utenlandske kontanter. Vi vil nok derfor fortsa se den norske kronen anvendt i betydelig i grad i Norge ogs e er at euroen blir introdusert. PUBLISERT 25. februar 1998 13:50

Title: Petroleum Fund: Strategy, Guidelines and Management
text: Petroleum Fund: Strategy, Guidelines and Management Address by Central Bank Governor Kjell Storvik. Conference on the Norwegian Petroleum Fund, New York, March 12 1998, held by The Norwegian-American Chamber of Commerce INC. The new guidelines for the Petroleum Fund specify a benchmark por olio with investments in both equity and fixed income instruments. The investment management aims at high long term returns within acceptable limits of risk exposure. To induce general confidence, adequate risk controls and transparent repor ng of performance will be essen al. Future petroleum revenues are expected to be very large in rela on to the Norwegian economy, but there is a substan al risk a ached to them. The revenues are based on the extrac on of a non-renewable natural resource. Intergenera onal jus ce and economic policy considera ons suggest that these revenues should not all be spent as they are earned. The risk of seeing very low petroleum revenues in the future makes it essen al to retain the compe veness of a broad range of other industries, to reduce our dependence on petroleum. This implies that only a limited sum of the expected petroleum revenues should be spent domes cally at any me. The Norwegian economy will s ll be fairly dependent on these revenues, and would face a difficult transi on period if they should suddenly evaporate. The Petroleum Fund thus has a double purpose. It serves as a buffer in case we are hit by an external shock, such as a fall in petroleum prices. It is also an instrument for saving part of Norway's petroleum revenues for the next genera on. That genera on will for instance have to cope with a drama c change in the age structure of the popula on, with pension payment obliga ons that are expected to reach 15 per cent of GDP in 2030. The size of the Petroleum Fund is increasing rapidly. It may reach 70 billions dollars within four years, and is likely to con nue increasing for the next 20 years. The central bank proposed last year that at least 30 per cent of the Fund should be invested in equi es. The Minstry of Finance agreed to the 30 per cent floor and set a maximum of 50 per cent, with the rest of the Fund invested in fixed income instruments. The chosen split between equity and fixed income implies some risk diversifica on, but should mainly be regarded as a compromise between high expected returns and low annual variability. That kind of compromise is probably familiar to most of you. The ra onale for having equi es in the Fund por olio will also be familiar to most of my audience. With a long investment horizon, there is ample interna onal evidence that the return on equity investments has nearly always been higher than the return on fixed income. There is also evidence that a diversifica on gain can be obtained by combining equity and fixed income por olios. Norges Bank is managing the Petroleum Fund on behalf of the Ministry of Finance. Because of the poli cal importance of the Fund, this is rather more than an ordinary por olio management contract. We feel it is important that we obtain widespread na onal confidence in the way Norges Bank manages the Fund. If that confidence is lacking, it may become very difficult for our poli cians to ensure that a sufficient share of our petroleum revenues are being saved for the future. In a sense, then, the whole Norwegian popula on should be regarded as our customers, rather than just the Ministry of Finance. I believe the Ministry had several reasons for choosing Norges Bank as the manager of the Fund. As a central bank with large foreign reserves, we have a long experience of managing interna onal por olios, with par cular insight into fixed income instruments. No other Norwegian manager has similar interna onal experience. Secondly, as a central bank we are subject to the supervision of a council elected by the Norwegian parliament, which can thus keep a close watch on the quality of our opera ons. We also have a close rela onship with the Ministry of Finance. These rela onships probably contribute to the na onal confidence needed for the management of the Fund. The Ministry of Finance set new guidelines for investment of the Petroleum Fund from 1 January this year. The guidelines are based on counsel from Norges Bank formally submi ed to the Ministry in April and August 1997, and on an ongoing dialogue between the two ins tu ons. This advisory role regarding the strategic guidelines for investment is a part of the Bank's general obliga on to provide professional advice to the poli cal authori es. In addi on to prescribing large equity investments, the new guidelines also introduced revised country weigh ngs in the por olio. The weigh ngs used to be based on Norwegian import shares, which meant that about 75 per cent of the Fund was invested in Europe. With a short investment horizon, this may have been a reasonable strategy rela ve to the basic goal of maintaining the interna onal purchasing power of the Fund. With a larger Fund and a longer investment horizon, such concentra on of investments on one of the five con nents would leave us with too much exposure to certain non-quan fiable risks, such as wars and natural disasters which may involve a number of countries simultaneously. We also realised that subs tu on could change the import weights significantly over me. Given a distant horizon, it seemed a be er idea to take a more balanced look at all produc on ac vi es outside Norway. We therefore recommended that European investments should be limited to 40-60 per cent of the por olio, whereas investments in North America should be in the 20-40 per cent interval, and investments in the Pacific Area in the 10-30 per cent interval. We also recommended that a small share be invested in emerging markets, but on that point the Ministry disagreed. The reason was partly the greater variability of return in these markets, but mainly a wish to avoid capital markets without well developed infrastructures or without a high degree of liquidity. The Ministry selected companies quoted on the major exchanges in 21 countries as eligible for investment from the Fund. Within each of the three regions, we recommended different country weigh ngs for the equity and fixed income por olios. For the equity por olio we opted for standard market capitaliza on weights, which means that the investments will be concentrated in the largest and most liquid markets. Market capitaliza on weights also reduce the need to rebalance the por olio when markets perform differently. For the fixed income por olio we recommended GDP weights, which give a well diversified por olio. Since these weights are closely correlated to market capitaliza ons, the liquidity of the investments will also be ensured. Within each country the Ministry has chosen to define the benchmark por olio by means of the Footsie equity index (FT/S&P Actuaries World Index) and the Salomon Smith Barney government bond index. The Footsie index was chosen partly because it is the worldwide equity index most frequently used by other investors. The choice of a government bond index should be regarded as a preliminary choice, since the Fund is actually also allowed to invest in non-government bonds. The guidelines set by the Ministry state that the Petroleum Fund may not own more than 1 per cent of the share capital in any one company. The reason for this is not merely to compel diversifica on. It also reflects the view held by our poli cal authori es that the Fund should be a purely financial investor, and should not in any way interfere with the opera ons of the companies in which it owns shares. This implies that the Fund will not be used for strategic investments. Certain na onal business interests would no doubt have welcomed the Fund's assistance in their market posi oning efforts abroad. But the Ministry has made it clear that any such assistance, if found desirable, will be given through other vehicles than the Petroleum Fund. The maximum ownership rule is closely related to an issue that is at present the subject of lively discussion in Norway, namely the ques on of having ethical guidelines for the Fund investments. The purpose would be to avoid investments in companies that operate in a way considered unethical. The present guidelines reflect such concerns to some extent through the investment universe chosen. The government may soon be looking further into this issue, to decide whether extended guidelines would be desirable. We are awai ng their conclusions on that point. The slide illustrates the two roles of Norges Bank, as a professional advisor rela ve to the investment guidelines, and as the Ministry's chosen investment manager. The la er role is somewhat unusual for a central bank. We are aware of the poten al conflicts between our role as a central bank and our investment ac vi es. To preclude any actual conflict, the execu ve director of investment management has been detached from all central bank ac vi es. He does not take part in the general management of the Bank or in any economic policy discussions, and he is not given access to any confiden al informa on that we receive in our capacity as a central bank. We have in fact tried to establish a nearly independent investment unit within the Bank, and intend to keep a watchful eye on how the zone of poten al conflict develops over me. Norges Bank wishes to behave as a professional investment manager, comparing its costs and performance to other large funds around the world. In order to achieve that, it is important that the new investment unit is slim and of high quality, with very competent people in key posi ons. Consequently, the Bank has had to offer more flexible wage schemes than have tradi onally been available. I believe we are going to succeed in establishing a highly efficient investment unit. The guidelines state that we should maximise returns on the Fund por olio within certain risk limits. The Ministry has set some limits in terms of the country alloca ons, the propor on of equi es allowed, and in terms of modified dura on of the bond por olio. However, the effec ve limit on devia ons from the benchmark por olio is set in terms of tracking error. The expected tracking error of the total por olio, as defined in a BARRA total plan risk model, may not at any me exceed 150 basis points. This method of defining limits to market risk-taking is not yet standard in the investment management industry, but our experience so far has been encouraging. Every morning we compute the tracking error of the por olio as it was at the end of the previous working day. This is possible because we keep track of our fixed income por olio in our internal accoun ng system, and because our global equity custodian daily transfers files describing our en re equity por olio. We have spent a considerable amount of effort ge ng these informa on rou nes in place, since they will be essen al to our control of the por olio. This way we shall be able to follow every external manager and also the total por olio very closely. We started this year with a fixed income por olio of about 15 billion dollars. During the year we shall increase the share of equity investments from zero to approximately 40 per cent. At the same me, the por olio will grow as more government savings are allocated to the Fund. We are therefore engaged in an extensive transi onal process, of establishing a new equity por olio. The transi on will con nue throughout the year, with the assistance of the four index managers. The iden ty of these managers will not be disclosed while the transi on process is s ll under way. The slide illustrates our use of external services. From the outset we established close rela onships to one legal advisor and one investment advisor; both companies of high interna onal standing. These advisors have assisted us in the design of management contracts and in the planning of management mandates. We have appointed Chase Manha an Bank as our global equity custodian, and will partly depend on their services for our compliance controls and repor ng. The four appointed external index managers will each take over their parts of the equity por olio once it has been established. Their defined index is equal to the benchmark equity por olio supplied by the Ministry. The index mandates were announced publicly in July last year, and a ques onnaire was sent to a large number of poten al managers and also made available on the internet. On the basis of the informa on obtained from the ques onnaire, and the advice of our external investment consultant, we established a short-list of candidates for the final nego a ons. We had specified all our legal requirements in a standard contract drawn up in coopera on with our external legal advisor, and had our condi ons accepted in essence by all the managers. We also paid visits to their offices in order to obtain an impression of the quality of their organiza ons. We made sure that our people would have the opportunity to visit the managers for training purposes. The process lasted through the autumn, and the four contracts were only signed in December. There are several reasons for ini ally choosing an index equity por olio. Indexing carries substan ally lower fees and normally also lower transac on costs than ac ve management. Empirically the return to ac ve management net of fees and transac on costs has not been superior on average to the return obtained by indexing. This conclusion has been documented to us by our external investment consultant, and is also in line with most of the academic literature in this field. Furthermore, indexing is a low risk strategy in that the tracking error rela ve to the benchmark is very limited. This does not mean that we intend to con nue indexing the en re equity por olio. On 2 February we announced ac ve equity management mandates, with 27 February as the deadline for applica ons. As before, the invita on was made available on the internet. The mandates are regional, covering five different regions within our investment universe, and with a mixture of tradi onal ac ve and enhanced indexing styles. There are two reasons mainly for not giving global mandates: We do not want more than a couple of ac ve mandates in each market, in order to limit the frequency of counterac ng bets from different managers. We also believe there is a wider choice of good quality managers for regional mandates. The announcement did not specify the investment styles in detail, and it also contained a reserva on to the effect that the number of mandates actually awarded will be decided upon later this spring. There are three reasons for this: First, we would like to see what offers we get. Second, we are not sure how much of our internal control organisa on will be in place by midsummer. We will absolutely not take on more mandates than we are able to follow up very closely. Third, the Ministry of Finance will make new transfers to the Fund at the end of each quarter, but the size of the transfers will depend on the realised costs and revenues in the government's budget. Since the growth rate of the Fund is very high in its ini al phase, uncertainty about the actual size of new transfers may be of significance. We have received some 260 applica ons from about 140 ac ve managers. The selec on process is going to be as thorough as it was for the index mandates, and will proceed for several months. A er a first sor ng of applica ons, a further ques onnaire will be sent to a selec on of managers. We primarily want the managers to convince us that their proposed strategies are sound and that they have implemented sa sfactory risk controls. A er a second sor ng a number of managers will receive visits or be invited to Oslo. Before summer we expect to have a short list of poten al ac ve managers, and the final contract nego a ons will start. The actual management under the mandates may nevertheless be delayed un l late in the autumn. As already men oned, we are aware of evidence that the average ac ve manager is not able to produce excess return, a er correc ons having been made for higher fees and transac on costs. When we have s ll opted for some ac ve mandates, the reason is that we hope to be able to select a group of managers that are more competent than average. Our external investment consultant has produced some evidence of his selec on skills in this respect. We shall therefore give ac ve management a try for at least a few years. Even with a firm belief in ac ve management, however, we would probably retain indexing as the investment style for most of the equity por olio. The reason is that a large number of ac ve mandates may easily produce counterac ng posi ons, which net out in the overall por olio. That would imply paying ac ve management fees for what turn out to be passive posi ons. In order to reduce the probability of such occurrences, we intend to limit the number of ac ve mandates in the same markets. Norges Bank has no previous experience of equity management. But we have brought in people with an equity background, and we intend to do some of the equity management in-house. This ac vity will be small scale at the outset, but may be expanded later on, depending on the experience gained. At any rate, we do not see 100 per cent external equity management as desirable. Some internal investment ac vi es will be important for keeping track of what the external managers are doing, and for ensuring an efficient transi on into equity por olios when new transfers are made to the Fund. The en re fixed income por olio is now managed in-house. Norges Bank has long experience in this field, from inves ng the central bank's foreign reserves. That investment has mostly been passive, with some rela ve value trading. The passive indexing style will s ll be the dominant one, for the reasons given above regarding the equity por olio. But we are also preparing for some ac ve management, partly in-house and partly by external fixed income managers. A few fixed income mandates may be announced already this spring. With all these new investment ac vi es, Norges Bank this year will primarily be concerned with ge ng the simple things right. The single most important thing will be to get the risk and compliance controls running smoothly. We shall be able to measure both market risk and credit risk on a daily basis, and we shall endeavour to reduce opera onal risk as much as possible. Handling opera onal risk is generally important in investment management, and even more so for this par cular Fund with its key role in macroeconomic policies. I end the talk as I started it by stressing the importance of our public rela ons, and of our informa on ac vi es directed towards the Norwegian people. Losing their confidence might be very detrimental to the Fund, whatever the reason for such an eventuality. 12. mars 1998 14:00

Title: Current stabilisation policy challenges for the central bank
text: Current stabilisation policy for the central bank Governor Kjell Storvik's speech at the Economic Forum 1998, organized by the Norwegian Financial Analysts Association and the Social Economists' Association on 19 May 1998. I have been asked by the organizer as usual in the e-mails to address "current stabilisation policy issues for the central bank". I assume that the organizer with the e also believes that current stabilisation policy is viewed on the part of the central bank, and not just the indiscibles for which Norges Bank itself has a direct responsibility. (In the last trap, I could, in parentheses noted, make a very short post.) Some may address the situation so that we economists tend to become bleaker in the minds of the Norwegian economy. I would therefore already now acknowledge that if someone were to invent my mood here as characterized by such undue gloom, then it does not have its background in a special or Puritan layer of anger, where joy in the situation itself arouses concern. Rather, the reason for our concern is due to the lack of capability - or lack of capability - that we have shown over the past fifteen years when it comes to stabilising economic development in this country. Norway is becoming an economy that fluctuates more than any other Western European country. I will therefore spend a great number of years here today discussing the consequences of such fluctuations, and why seeking stability in itself may be necessary to ensure a favour with economic development in the longer term. Four days ago, the Government presented the Revised National Budget for 1998, which this time in the customary bidding material also contains a review of Norway's conditions in EMU and the krone's forward course. It is natural for me to comment on both of these topics in the . Economic developments - wage settlement No one can claim that the current developments in our economy could not be predicted. I guess it's a question of whether you wanted to see it. In this context, I would like to highlight the summary found in Norges Bank's Inflation Report in December 1996, i.e. 11/2 years ago. This report cited a projection of economic developments with rapidly high growth and an increase in capacity growth in the latter half of the 1990s. About the outlook for the labour market and for wage and price developments, it was called: "... the projection shows ... a gradual fall in unemployment of almost 3 per cent in 2000. Sam dig shows a gradual increase in price and wage growth, up to 3 and 51/2 per cent per year, respectively, during the cunning one of the calculation periods. If these projections are met, they mean that the business sector's me wage costs will increase about 6 per cent more than among our trading partners during the latter half of the 1990s." In Norges Bank's letter to the Ministry of Finance on the economic programme for 1998 last autumn, we summarized the economic situation that follows (and I quote): "On the basis of the overall balance of risks for economic developments ahead, Norges Bank is concerned that it will be relatively small l before a development with imbalances in several parts of the economy, for example in the labour market and in the market for assets. Such imbalances will sooner or later have an impact on higher price and cost inflation and real economic fluctuations as a result of changes in the private sector. The e can e is Norges Bank's view avoided by bringing growth in demand down to underlying growth in production capacity..." Developments in the labour market and the economy in general are the main picture in the documents I cited from. If anything, the development may have been even faster than what was in the basis of these documents. In April, a record 22,000 unemployed people were registered - a doubling in the last 16 months alone - while growth in employment for it stands at well over 60,000 people on an annual basis. While in 1993 there were 20 unemployed persons per unemployed person, the number today has been reduced l closer to 2. I would particularly like to highlight developments in imports for the time being. In the first quarter of this year, the value of Norwegian imports of goods was 25 per cent higher than in the same period last year. This is probably due to the fact that Easter fell in the second quarter of this year, while in or fell in the first. Nevertheless, the increase in imports has been sharp. The e is primarily a regret that the growth in e-demand is too strong. But they are also a clear sign of the underlying problem in the Norwegian economy, namely that the lbuds side is unable to meet the increased demand. Our projections now show that labour market pressures will continue to increase over the next year. They are of course a decisive factor in assessing how long the upturn can take. Provide the restrictions that must be Instead in the labour market, the question of the turnaround is not coming, but when. It is possible that some people will see them as "black paint". I can agree that the contrast in the everyday life of the upturn can be great. I would argue that the above reasoning is merely a description of very simple economic relationships. Anyone who these days seeks e-demanded services or workers can be concerned e. When Norges Bank now points out that the potential for rapid growth must soon be unsuitable, we therefore note neither more nor less than an obvious fact. Our analyses have pointed out that the prolonged and strong cyclical upswing sooner or later must be expected to have an impact on rising price and cost inflation. The events in recent years are - rather than decrees - the analyses that have been carried out by Norges Bank. The fact that some people choose to call these "prophets of doom" testifies instead to the long tradition that applies to messengers with bad news. Led by the settlement in the workshop industry in mid-April, settlements in the private sector were perhaps easier than many had feared, in the sense that strikes were avoided . Although not all wage settlements are yet fully completed, and local settlements have not begun, there are few factors to indicate that our estimate of wage growth from the Previous Inflation Report of 51/4 per cent should be too high. Many have expressed disdy at the fact that this year's egg was unexpectedly large. It has been a long time since we have seen general salary inlays of NOK 10,000 or more. E's my view is not surprising. From our experience with wage formation in Norway developments are rather consistent with expectations. The result of the wage settlement hardly has its primary explanation in any culture of greed, not in workers or managers, but in fundamental economic conditions. In order to support e de e, I would like to show a chart showing Norges Bank's projections for wage growth over the past five years together with projections from Sta's central agency and the Ministry of Finance. For all the estimates, the projections are in December of the year before the forecast year. Our projections are based on experience of how fundamental economic conditions, such as developments in unemployment, manufacturing and profitability in the business sector, affect wage growth. As we can see, Norges Bank's projections appear to have struck reasonably well, and we are closer to the factual developments than any of the other incentives. But all the incentives have in common that lax wage growth has been expected. I think this chart illustrates an important point: the explanation for the fact that wage growth is now primarily in the economic policing that has been waged in recent years and is now creating pressure in the labour market. And so there's no reason to be surprised. The division of responsibility in the economic policing As the interrogators are probably familiar with, a division of responsibility has been established in Norwegian economic policing, where the social partners shall lay a necessary basis for employment through moderate wage increases, which both provide a reasonable income development and contribute to the competitiveness of the business sector. The Monetary and Foreign Exchange Policy Shall ensure a stable exchange rate against European currencies, while the financial policy has the main responsibility for ensuring stable developments in overall demand. In order for the division of responsibility in the economic policing to work e is the purpose, it is important that all parts of the policing function are the prerequisites. The consideration of a balanced economic development requires a successful interaction between all the different elements of the economic policing. For Norges Bank's part, I would like to excite myself in the assertion that we have delivered the e-conditions in this context. Despite some turbulent periods in the foreign exchange market, the exchange rate has been reasonably stable when viewed over the past six to seven years under e . Nevertheless, they have made the task difficult for the other elements of the economic policing. When the interest rate must be used l to keep the exchange rate stable in relation to European currencies, we will normally end up with approximately the same interest rate level as the anchor countries. The interest rate in Norway will therefore not be determined on the terms of domestic economic conditions, but will be appropriate to conditions in the economies of anchor countries. In con nental Europe, the interest rate for the interior is based on considerable unemployment and low capacity renewal, especially in Germany and France. Of course, they're over to us. The Norwegian interest rate has largely fallen since the beginning of the 1990s, which we are now seeing results from in credic growth and in sharply rising house prices. Now, an expansive monetary policy would not necessarily have been a problem in the current situation if fiscal policy had been aimed at neutralising these effects. But the fiscal policy has so far failed to deliver on the assumptions. The 1998 state budget means that the fiscal policy has shied away from being contracted to seem almost neutral this year. Nor in 1997 did the fiscal policy seem particularly austerity. Et annet forhold er introduksjonen av en felles valuta i store deler av Europa. MU og konsekvenser for norsk penge- og valutapoli kk Ogs pengepoli kken m ses i lys av de begivenheter som skjer rundt oss i disse dager. Som vi ser av guren har det historisk imidler d vrt rela vt sm forskjeller mellom kursindeksen for MU-landene og den handelsveide valutakursen. Ogs nr det gjelder renteutviklingen har det historisk se vrt mindre forskjeller enn man kanskje skulle tro. Det lsa at det br foreligge forholdsvis tungtveiende grunner fr en eventuelt foretar slike endringer. Ut fra hensynet l kon nuitet og llit l pengepoli kken lrdde Norges Bank p denne bakgrunn at Regjeringen holder fast ved de eksisterende retningslinjene for pengepoli kken. Valutakursforskri en gir ingen konkret veiledning om hvilke europeiske valutaer som kronens verdi skal holdes stabil mot. I praksis blir det vel o e anta at de e innebrer at kronens verdi skal stabiliseres i forhold l ECU. ECU - som er en kurv av tolv av EU-landenes valutaer - er imidler d en synte sk valuta som neppe vil ha noen prak sk interesse nr euroen blir innfrt. Som utgangspunkt for Norges Banks gjennomfring av pengepoli kken, vil euro inng som den vik gste europeiske valutaen, p samme mte som ECU i dag er en sentral styringsparameter. Kursforholdet mellom ECU og euro vil bli sa lik 1:1 p overgangs dspunktet. Hovedfokus i mi foredrag her i dag har da heller ikke vrt rundt de e, men p den ustabile utviklingen vi n er i ferd med  f i norsk konomi. Det ser ut som om myndighetene har lagt vel mye av ansvaret for  stabilisere konomien p partene i arbeidslivet. Som jeg dligere har hevdet, er de e e er mi syn et ansvar som gr ut over de muligheter og virkemidler som partene fak sk rr over.  f l en viderefring av den vellykkede linjen partene i arbeidslivet har frt hi l, ville utvilsomt vrt le ere om den konomiske poli kken i strre grad hadde st et opp under moderasjonslinjen gjennom  stabilisere den konomiske utviklingen. Nr pengepoli kken er re et inn mot  stabilisere valutakursen, er de e nanspoli kkens oppgave. Videre har Norges Bank pekt p at den sterke veksten fr eller senere vil m e avlses av mer normale vekstrater, eller i verste fall stagnasjon. Vre modeller indikerer at et slikt omslag kan komme rundt rhundreski et. Jo sterkere e ersprselsveksten er, desto kra igere blir omslaget nr lbudssiden i konomien frst se er begrensninger. Gjenta e advarsler om den konomiske utviklingen synes imidler d  ha falt p stengrunn. De har i hvert fall ikke ledet l noen innstramminger i den konomiske poli kken. Det er kanskje ikke oppsiktsvekkende. Det synes ikke  vre vilje l, eller poli sk oppslutning om, ltak som p en eek v mte kunne redusert presset i konomien. Ingen vil ha forandringer, ubehageligheter og innstramminger i en situasjon av den karakter vi n gjennomlever. Vi er p en mte inne i den store fordelingspoli ske fase hvor det poli ske system synes  vre tjent med  gjre alle l lags. En glemmer o e at konomisk poli kk, i den konjunkturfase vi gjennomlever, er  gjre noe folk ikke liker i nuet, men p en mte som fr folk l  forst at det likevel er l deres eget beste i et lengre dsperspek v. Som jeg nevnte innledningsvis, er historien full av eksempler p budbringere med drlige nyheter som, i beste fall, ble viet liten oppmerksomhet. En slik budbringer blir ikke mer populr av  dukke opp mens festen enn pgr. Det behver ikke bety at det ikke er p de  avslu e selskapet, mens det enn er hp om  begrense ubehagelighetene dagen derp.
