Title: About Norges Bank's regional departments and the production and distribution of banknotes and coins
text: About Norges Bank's regional departments and the production and distribution of banknotes and coins Speech by Governor Svein Gjedrem Norges Bank at the Supervisory Council seminar on 13 January 2000. Part1. Norges Bank's tasks in the payment system, with emphasis on cash handling The purpose of the talks is to provide a briefing on Norges Bank's tasks in the payment system, with an emphasis on the production and distribution of banknotes and coins. We are accounted for in terms of the wording of the cash handling, and the alterna ve vein. Norges Bank's various tasks in the Norwegian payment system. Through the Central Bank Act, Norges Bank is required to issue notes and coins, and to promote a good payment system. Norges Bank is also the "bank of banks", and lbyr banks kon . According to the law, banknotes and coins are legal tender 1 . In llegg l norgespengene (cash and banks' account receivables at Norges Bank), banks issue money. This money, which is receivables to the banks, is called deposit money. Payments are then made largely by transferring this money from the account in the account. If the payer and mo aker do not have an account in the same bank, the transfer takes place via the regulation of the banks' consensus in Norges Bank or in a private settlement bank. Norges Bank thus has a settlement function. Norges Bank's settlement system (NBO) has been introduced and further developed in the period 1997-99, and is aimed at reducing the risk in the settlement of payments. Clearing systems calculate the various banks' positions against each other, so that there are a large number of positions settled in Norges Bank. Settlement of large interbank transactions takes place individually and continuously. Banks request cash from Norges Bank and distribute them to the public via ATMs, etc. Cash holdings (from the cash registers etc.) are handed in to banks, both for security reasons and to obtain interest. For the same reason, banks submit surplus cash holdings in Norges Bank. In the new Act relating to payment systems, Norges Bank has been given responsibility as a licensing authority for interbank systems, i.e. systems for clearing, settlement or transfer of money between credibility. Systems for payment services must be approved by Kredi lsynet. Norges Bank also maintains an account for the government. All liquidity is collected in the government's corporate account in Norges Bank. The government does not accept that there is a float in government payments. Developments in the payment system Figure 2 shows the development in the use of giro, payment card, check and ATM in the period 1988-98. The number of payments using cards has increased sharply throughout the period, as check usage has been reduced. The use of electronic giro services has also increased, at the expense of the blank based services. ATM shares have also increased, but they must also be seen in the context of a reduction in the number of cash cash cash over the counter. We do not have figures for the number of payment transactions with cash, but we have estimated that the number of transactions with cash was more than 1 billion in 1994 2. Measured in amounts, the picture is slightly altered, as shown in Figure 3. They reflect that giro, especially electronic, and check are used in large amounts compared to payment cards and cash. Developments are in the same way; the use of online services and cards is increasing, while paper-based services are losing ground. The amount of cash in circulation has grown approximately in line with private consumption in the 1990s. About 70% of the cash turnover measured in value consists of 1000-krone notes. International studies show that up to 70% of the largest denominations are used l to store wealth. We cannot therefore draw definitive conclusions about the use of cash in payment transactions, but developments in the use of cards make it reasonable to assume that cash use has declined. Prices and costs Chart 4 shows price developments, unepressed by the price of a selection of banks on selected services. The glossy based services have increased the most in price in the 1990s, while prices for electronic services have only increased marginally. It is also evident that the banking industry has increasingly paid for cash handling, through higher prices for ATM cash. In assessing price developments, it is interesting to look at the extent to which price differences represent cost differences for banks. We do not have up-to-date data on cost developments divided into simple jenester, but a survey of the costs was carried out in 1994 3 . Figure 5 shows the unit costs for a number of services. The chart shows that online services are significantly less costly than the glossy based services. As mentioned, prices for blank-based services have increased in the 1990s. Sam dig has reduced the use of these services and the use of online services has increased. They provide a clear indication that services are priced more "costly" than and that pricing has an effect on the usage pattern. As a follow-up to the cost survey from 1994, calculations were made of the economy in the payment system 4. As revenues, transaction prices and float were included, and one found that banks' results varied for the various services. Some services gave posi vt results, but the conclusion was that banks had accumulated a deficit in the payment system. The deficit was estimated at barely NOK 1.5 billion. An answering survey was carried out in 1989, but the methods used were so different that the figures cannot be compared directly. In other terms, there was a clear tendency to increase coverage via direct prices at the expense of floa ntekter compared to the 1989 figures. In 1999, an projection of the costs from the 1994 survey was made, based on assumptions based on general developments 5. Combined with prices for 1998, these figures indicate that payment services are no longer a deficit for banks. This cost projection is based on personal customer services only. In the 1994 survey, banks' total costs in the payment system, incl. cash, were estimated at about NOK 6 billion. These were distributed as follows: - Personnel costs: 30% - Premises/branches: 10% - External suppliers: 25% (data centers etc.) - Key features: 25% (staffs, overhead, etc.) - Other: 10% Drivkre er The projections indicate that costs have been significantly reduced over the past year. The cost reductions have primarily taken place in paper-based Giro services. In essence, we assume that there are three factors that have been the driving force behind this development: - Technological developments. New and more efficect instruments are being developed. - More rich ge prices. As shown, there has been a trend towards the fact that the prices that users face to a greater extent than they do reflect the cost differences in the various services. The e must be assumed to be related to a lesser degree of cross-subsidy, partly as a result of greater competition and more squeezed margins in the deposit and lending market. - The indirect subsidy of postgiro is take away. The subsidy that took place through large government deposits that were not required to be interested on entailed a competitive shift that, among other things, made it difficult for banks to withdraw prices that covered the costs. Cash As mentioned above, banks are requesting cash from Norges Bank. The public takes out banknotes from the banks via ATMs, etc., and the bucks collect change. E is to have been used in payment transactions, the cash ends up large looking up in the bows, which at today's sluice deliver the cash reserves in the banks. In order to achieve interest rates, banks have an interest in handing in surplus holdings in Norges Bank as quickly as possible. Transports of varying scale and frequency are organised into Norges Bank's district departments. Transport costs are covered by banks. Norges Bank counts and credits banks' consensus. As a general rule, banks' wives are credited on the same day as the cash is filed, predicting that submission will take place before 16:00 (or 13:30 if there is no co-ordinated transport system). It is agreed to carry out a trial period where all submissions are credited to the banks' consensus on the same day as submission, combined with access to submission 24 hours a day. Norges Bank checks that the notes submitted are genuine and sorts them in different qualities. Banknotes that are sheathed are destroyed. When banks requisition cash, controlled (or new) banknotes are handed out. Norges Bank charges for ATM quality notes, but other notes are handed out gra s. Costs The cost survey from 1994 estimated the banks' and Posten's costs in distribution, deposits/o ac, processing and storage of cash l about NOK 2.5 billion. Based on the e, investigations have been carried out of other actors' costs in cash handling. In cooperation with Hakongruppen AS, Norges Bank has made calculations of the retail and service sector's costs in transport, security, settlement against the customer and tender settlement 6. Norges Bank's costs in developing, producing, distributing, controlling and destroying banknotes and coins in 1994 have also been estimated. The total costs were estimated as follows: Norges Bank NOK 0.5 billion Banks and Posten NOK 2.5 billion The retail and service sectors receive NOK 1.0 billion. Total NOK 4.0 billion Developments in the use of cash As mentioned above, the amount of cash in circulation has increased in line with private consumption in the 1990s. In 1998, there were approximately NOK 43.6 billion in circulation, about 70% of the e are 1000-krone notes, which are partly used in value retention. Cash makes up a large part of all payment transactions. On the basis of a survey conducted by Norwegian Opinion, cash in 1993 was estimated to be used in about two-and-a-half parts of all payment transactions. The number of cash robberies was then estimated at 1 billion. The survey from 1993 showed that cash was used in over 95% of all transactions under NOK 100. The forward-looking use of cash will, among other things, be affected by: - Users' costs in cash compared to alterna vein. The costs of holding cash can be divided into unexcupsideled costs, which are fees and other costs that depend on the Availability, including banks' distributions, new distribution patterns such as cash-back in payment terminals, and alterna v costs, which are lost interest income and the risk of losing or being stolen cash. Users themselves may to some extent influence the costs of choosing an unexxed size, and the price per payment transaction depends on the number of payments per a. - Development within alterna ve means of payment. Distribution and use of arc terminals is increasing. It is expected that money cards will arrive each, but that it is unlikely to significantly reduce cash use right away. It is also reasonable to assume that the lliten l new payment instruments will increase e is each as the audience gains more experience with them. - Developments in "payment needs". They are influenced by developments in private consumption, changes in consumption patterns, etc. It must be assumed that cash will play a important role within the payment system, and that notes and coins will be cost-effective in small transactions. The development of new payment services and banks' caps, including the use of prices, to shift usage to less costly services means that cash's share of payment transactions is expected to be reduced. Nevertheless, price inflation and growth in private consumption may mean that the amount of banknotes and coins in circulation is not reduced. Norges Bank's role in the cash area Norges Bank currently undertrobies a number of tasks, some of which follow from the statutory issuer liability 7 and some are services of a more business nature:  Production of banknotes and coins - production - distribution of new banknotes and coins in the district departments  Further distribution and processing of banknotes and coins (u cents at district departments) - grossis unction between manufacturer (NBS and DKM) and retailer (banks) - inventory function - warehouse as wholesaler - stock over now one for banks - redistribution central bank - between banks/branches with profits and deficits - provides the basis for contributing l coordination of transport - sorting and packing of banknotes and coins for banks and the mail - agreed services for banks and the mail - counting and aggravated sorting from na safe and coin machines - packing and mo ak directly l/from banks - packing in ATM box is - authenticity control - destruction and replacement of damaged/slip notes and coins The tasks related to production, distribution in the district departments, destruction and replacement of damaged and slip notes and coins, as well as authenticity control can be said to be central bank tasks (government tasks). The others are services that are unsecured for banks. Central bank tasks are monopoly tasks, while the other services are not in competition with others. As mentioned above, we must assume that banks submit surplus holdings in Norges Bank in order to achieve an interest rate return, and that this comes into play when choosing a service provider. Banks have also organised coordinated transports that largely run daily, which also contributes to a large entrance into Norges Bank. Norges Bank processes (controls and sorts) everything that is handed in. It is difficult to say for sure how much market share Norges Bank has of its business tasks. For example, we do not know how much banks and others do in terms of manual or machine quality sorting. For sorting and packing for banks and the mail, Norges Bank's market share is estimated at about 70% (55% for banknotes and 95% for coin), and for the agreed services, the market share is estimated between 20 and 25%. Agreed services are unpaid for a fee. Sorting and packing for banks and the mail is partly for payment, by charging for ATM quality and coin-in-roll notes. The costs of the other activities are borne by Norges Bank. Today's activities and price policy provide Norges Bank's regional departments (incl. the Oslo department) with revenues from the sale of processed banknotes and coins of about NOK 39 million, and revenues from agreed services of about NOK 47 million. The costs are approximately NOK 246 million, so the business provides an annual ne o cost for Norges Bank of about NOK 160 million. Labour is about 450 man-years. Directions in Norges Bank's cash treatment. Today's price policy makes it difficult to assess how appropriate large parts of Norges Bank's activities in this area are. A number of services for banks are unsecured without payment or in a payment that is probably low relative to the costs. They give Norges Bank a large market share and a basis for maintaining an rebuilt organisation and machine park, which in turn can give the Bank the opportunity to expand into paid services by making marginal costs relatively low. Banks may see themselves served by entrusting Norges Bank with unearthed services that they would otherwise have provided themselves or purchased by others. There may also be a shift in the demand for services for which no services are paid. In some areas, there has been a tendency for banks to increasingly request standard quality controlled notes (for which they are not paid) and use them at ATMs. It may be questioned whether we have a prudent management of the use of resources in Norges Bank when the Bank produces grassroots services together with international services, and the Bank covers 2/3 of the costs. If Norges Bank is to compete with banks and value companies, a substantially larger share of the revenue must come from sales in customers. Competition with value insurers and banks takes place across a wide range of services. Compared to others who can use these services, Norges Bank has a competitive advantage in that customers receive interest on the money while they are being processed or redistributed. In addition, Norges Bank has an exemption. Among other things, they mean that we may be in a dubious frontier in relation to competition legislation. The valuation rules and the rules that follow from Norges Bank's special role in society should not be a competitive advantage for Norges Bank's services of a business nature. It is therefore necessary to price the services in order to avoid undesirable distortion of competition. It is also necessary to price Norges Bank's services to a greater extent to ensure a better balance between customer needs and Norges Bank's use of resources. The bank cannot continue the current arrangement. Distinguish between issuer tasks and management services In general, it should be a requirement in all cash management at Norges Bank that it is not as effective as possible, and in line with best international practice. As long as Norges Bank has both an issuer role (government task) and a role as a service provider for banks and other customers, it is important to distinguish between these as clearly as possible. It must be ensured that the statutory issuer tasks are safeguarded in a prudent manner. Among other things, this means that Norges Bank does not charge to produce the money and keep stock to make it available to the banks in the district departments. If Norges Bank is to provide treatment services for banks and other customers, we must be sure that there will be no cross-subsidy. Possible road choices It is against the background of the above two alterna ve roads: - Develop the treatment services as a business activity - Cultivate the issuer role (the authority function) Develop the treatment services as a business activity. The alterna knows on the basis that the infrastructure and expertise in cash management that Norges Bank has built up over a number of years should be able to be developed with a view to the best possible effusive knowledge in the overall cash system. It lbys a wide range of products to further the bank's knowledge and market position. The considerations mentioned above are addressed by renewing the room for manoeuvre we have for using prices. Pricing may change a significantly larger share of the business without conflicting with the statutory issuer obligations, and cost surveys indicate that current prices must be increased in order to achieve cost coverage. Increased use of prices will help to ensure effek v resource use in the bank, and l to balance the needs of our customers against our costs so that the services are not available to an extent beyond what someone is willing l to pay for. Cost-based pricing will also help us not cross-subsidize the competitive services by drawing on the seignioragen, which is revenue from the issuer monopoly. The pricing will have to be redeemed in order to avoid distortion of competition as a result of valuation and scrapping rules. The cost-based pricing is achieved by providing a profitability requirement in this part of the business. Alterna knows that the treatment business is established as a performance unit, which is required to achieve a posi vt financial result. The unit will sell treatment services to banks, and will not accept the relevant central bank statements in return for remuneration from Norges Bank. Prices will need to be increased both in width and level. It must be assumed that norges bank's current deficit (in the order of NOK 150 million) is a small amount in relation to the total costs society has in the cash area, cf. the overview on page 7. Nevertheless, it is hardly realis sk that banks or others will be willing to pay the prices necessary to cover the current cost level in Norges Bank. Title: Monetary policy experience and challenges for the central bank
text: Monetary policy experiences and misconditions for the central bank Deputy Governor Jarle Bergo, Gausdal 27 January 2000 The main task of monetary policy is to deliver nominal stability. In Norway, we have chosen to tie the objective formulation l stability in the krone exchange rate. For a small, open economy, the exchange rate is important for price developments. Moderate price and cost inflation will jointly be a prerequisite for stable exchange rate developments over d. With the e as a starting point, I would like to discuss both the experience, but primarily about the inconvenience the central bank will be able to face in the future. Experiences Central banks have traditionally used short-term interest rates and interventions in the foreign exchange market as instruments to pursue the objective of nominal stability. At times, central banks have also tried to talk the market into question. They are no longer a prominent element, if ever there has been. On the other hand, greater emphasis has been placed on improving the effect of the other instruments through transparency on objectives, analyses and the exercise of judgement. There are also lfelle in Norway. Over recent years, we have gained experience with restructuring and sustained purchases and sales in the foreign exchange market in order to influence the exchange rate. These experiences are generally poor, both during the later phase of the fixed exchange rate period and under our current regime. If the central bank is heavily involved in steady purchases, a game situation has arisen where market participants are perceived by the central bank's interventions as an interesting profi opportunity. Market participants know that a situation where the krone exchange rate is held up only because Norges Bank is buying up NOK cannot persist. It is then tempting to take positions in the foreign exchange market against the central bank. They entail that re-end and sustained interventions over d can exacerbate the pressure on the krone, so that the volume of necessary steady purchases is steadily increasing. The foremost example of such a game situation was that Sweden had floated its crown on 19 November 1992. Over the course of six trading more than two days, more than NOK 50 billion in foreign exchange came from Norges Bank's reserves. Similar experience in the spring of 1997 and autumn 1998 may indicate that foreign exchange interventions can only curb pressure on the krone exchange rate for a short period. Even our large foreign exchange reserves are disappearing small in relation to the turnover in the global foreign exchange market. Large foreign exchange purchases are also not up to date. This pushes down large amounts of krone liquidity and pushes down money market interest rates. Liquidity can in principle be revoked by posting government securities with a short run d, but this gives the government increased interest costs. There may also be questions about how effek v such a liquidity bond will be. From the individual bank's point of view, an increased holding of short-term government securities may be considered highly liquid, and may thus form the basis for a more offensive lending strategy. If market participants also assume that Norges Bank will use the interest rate l to defend certain levels of the krone exchange rate, this may open the door to a game situation. A sharp rise in interest rates to defend the exchange rate will lead to deflationary deflation. The market may therefore try to test how high Norges Bank is willing to see the interest rate. In autumn 1998, speculation against the krone was combined with speculation that Norwegian interest rates would rise when the krone depreciated. If Norges Bank had not spared a "game" by stopping interventions and interest rate increases, the economy could have entered a nega v spiral. Norges Bank does not wish to act in a way that could provoke such game situations. Nor can we expect other central banks to come to our rescue. The Bank may nevertheless use interventions to a limited extent if the exchange rate is substantially outside what we consider to be reasonable on the basis of fundamentals or in the event of large short fluctuations in thin markets. In such situations, the risk of falling into a losing game against foreign exchange market participants may be less. In light of our experience with the use of interventions, it is the interest rate that is the central bank's most important instrument in monetary policy. When interventions can be difficult to use, it is obvious that the central bank cannot fine-tune the krone exchange rate. The interest rate is not an instrument that can be used to control the exchange rate from day today, week in week or month in month. Our monetary policy regime is unique and gives the central bank considerable scope for exercise of discretion. I can understand that it is not immediately easy to understand either for the general public or market participants. In order to function well, we have felt that it is necessary for Norges Bank to be transparent with regard to how we interpret the mandate and exercise its discretion. That's what we've been trying to do. It is my impression that the message is consistently enlightened and understood , but I would still like to renew the opportunity l to recapitulate the main features. A more thorough review of the e was given in the so-called "Budsje letter" last autumn. In the currency research crisis even 2 it says: "Norges Bank's ongoing exercise of monetary policy shall be adjusted towards stability in the krone's value against European currencies, on the basis of the exchange rate rent e is that the krone began to float on 10 December 1992. In the event of significant changes in the exchange rate, instruments shall be incorporated with a view to each return to the exchange rate. This does not apply to fluctuation margins with a duty for Norges Bank l to intervene in the foreign exchange market." (Norges Bank's highlights) Let me briefly review our understanding of this section. This is based on the fact that we have a floating exchange rate. However, instruments shall be adjusted towards stability in the value of the krone against European currencies. "European currencies" Norges Bank has chosen to define as euros from 1 January 1999. The last sentence of the forecrimination specifies that our system is not a traditional fixed exchange rate system. A central rate has not been established within specific fluctuation margins. To the extent that the scheme provides associations in the direction of a fixed exchange rate regime, the concept of the initial range should be understood as a broadly drawn central exchange rate that the krone can fluctuate around without fixed y er limits. The second sentence refers to significant changes in the exchange rate in relation to the initial range. Essentials must be given a financial content. A reasonable interpretation is that a "significant change" is a change that influences expectations concerning price and cost developments so that the change in the exchange rate becomes self-reinforcing. The unsuitables with a view to, e are each, rees towards and on the basis of showing that Norges Bank is giving great scope for exercising discretion. The requirement in the forewing of the krone exchange rate in the initial range may - if it is said at the forefront - have too strong an element of paripoli kk in it. In an imaginary situation, for example e is a large and permanent fall in oil prices, the krone exchange rate may remain outside the exchange rate range for a longer period. If Norges Bank then tries with a high interest rate to squeeze the krone back into the exchange rate range, monetary policy may result in a downturn there of a nature that will weaken the krone. Similarly, appreciation may arise situations where the interest rate must be viewed so low to bring the krone to the initial range that inflation is generated. This weakens the basis for exchange rate stability. Norges Bank cannot, with open eyes, intervene in policy instruments in such a way that they create inflation or a downturn d with deflation. If a situation arises where Norges Bank cannot get the exchange rate back without such consequences, the Bank will submit to the government authorities that there is a need for Intact by anyone other than the bank. There may then be talk of fiscal policy that makes it possible to bring the krone exchange rate back towards its initial range and stabilise it. If there have been fundamental changes in the framework conditions for the Norwegian economy, it may, on the other hand, be rich to consider changes in the guidelines for monetary policy. In its exercise of monetary policy, Norges Bank focuses on the fundamental preconditions for stability in the krone exchange rate. In order to achieve exchange rate stability against the euro, instruments must be re-incorporated so that the price and cost benefits come down to the point aimed at by the European Central Bank (ECB). Sam dig, we must avoid that the monetary policy itself contributes l deflation, because it may weaken the krone. If we look at the past year, the stability of the krone exchange rate has been considerable, not least in light of the large movements we have seen in the exchange rate relationship between the major currencies and oil prices. At the beginning of 1999, the krone exchange rate was rapidly weak relative to the initial range. When the euro was introduced we had to pay 8.88 kroner for it. Through 1999, the euro depreciated significantly compared to the other major currencies. The krone has also depreciated against the US dollar and the Japanese yen over the past year, but appreciated against the euro. In relation to a review of our trading partners, the krone exchange rate has been very stable. U ordringer Confidence in monetary policy is fragile and vulnerable. It takes you to build up the llit and it takes little l to destroy it. If lliten fails, it will take a lot to win it back. We all remember the price we have to e pay to get out of devaluation syndrome in the latter half of the 1980s. The biggest unearth in the future therefore lies in many ways in rebuilding and reinforcing the llit we have already accumulated. Prerequisites for success First, let me get into some necessary requests that must be fulfilled if we are to succeed in achieving nominal stability. First, it is important that the various policing elements pull together to achieve the overall objectives. In Norway, the fiscal policy has played a important role in stabilisation policing. This is due to the fact that solid government finances provide freedom of action. In other countries, burdensome government debt has meant that fiscal policy can no longer be used particularly for stabilisation purposes, at least not in decline there. Through the income settlements, the social partners have the opportunity to influence the overall level of employment above d. Compared to other countries, Norway generally have a low unemployment level and a high proportion of the population in work for the past twenty-five years. Many countries that have been through long and deep recessions have experienced a significant and prolonged increase in unemployment. A important feature of wage formation in Norway has been that the competitive conditions in the business sector have been given considerable weight in wage negotiations. They also apply to wages in sectors that are not particularly exposed to competition from abroad. The willingness to take longitudinal considerations has contributed to stabilising framework conditions in the internationally exposed sector and keeping employment at a high level. The most important contribution that income policing can make is to speed up the conditions for structural unemployment in Norway to remain low and employment at no high level. In the short term, fiscal policy may influence developments in output and employment. In a longer perspek v, the inequacy of fiscal policy, including the system, public investment and publishing, for example, is a major impact on the growth potential of the economy. In addition, the growth in public publishing is, as the authorities put it, affecting the distribution of labour crashes and capital between different sectors of the economy. Unless there are vacant reserves of labour coerc or capital, increased use of resources in the public sector will impose production factors that could be raised in the private sector. Above d, developments in the price level can be influenced by monetary policy. Employment can be affected by wage formation. The distribution of resources between the sheltered sector and the competitiveness of the business sector can be influenced by fiscal policy. The size of the internationally exposed sector is determined by d in a battle over real resources between the public sector and the business sector. It is important to note these assessments of what the various policing elements can influence in the long term, even when formulating the operatic objectives for policing in the more short term. There seems to be quite a lot of agreement on the longitudinal division and interdependence in economic policing. When the Minister of Finance presented to the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs on 4 November 2015, he said: "In conclusion, I would like to emphasise that there is no contradiction between Norges Bank and the Government when it comes to the interpretation of the monetary policy guidelines or in terms of the division of labour in economic policing. In a discussion of the division of labour, it is essential to take into account the interdependence and the close interaction between the different policing elements. It is not, and cannot be watered e shoes between the different parts of the economic policing. A successful implementation of monetary policy is therefore dependent on the failure to get out of exchange." I agree with them. I said that our monetary policy regime is unique, but what really sets us apart from other countries we would otherwise like to compare ourselves with is the oil. There is reason to give the policing system credit for the mechanisms built up through the petroleum fund scheme in order to ensure proper management of petroleum revenues, and, even more so, that these mechanisms are allowed to work. Not that we do not use domestic petroleum revenues, but at least we have managed to limit what the economy can reasonably tolerate. It will be important, also for the monetary policy, that the Petroleum Fund function is the purpose. The Fund plays a significant role in stabilising economic developments. When foreign exchange revenues from the petroleum sector are invested abroad, the balance sheet in the market for NOK is maintained. This dampens impulses from fluctuations in oil prices at the krone exchange rate. The Petroleum Fund also acts as a shock absorber against short-range fluctuations in petroleum revenues. Since much of the money flow from petroleum activities is direct to the government, fluctuations in oil prices will initially cause allocations in the fund to vary in size. A change in oil prices will thus not have a full impact on public releases. This makes the Norwegian economy more resilient to fluctuations in oil prices and thus less dependent on oil, also in the short term. An example can illustrate the e. Let's assume that oil prices increase by NOK 10 per barrel, or less than USD 1.50 per barrel. There is a slight change in oil prices, well within the normal variations from e year l the next. Government revenues - and thus the surplus - will then increase by around NOK 10 billion in the first year and NOK 12-13 billion over the next year. This is close to 1 per cent of Norway's annual GDP. Increased releases require an increase in the public sector's use of real resources - primarily work scraps . Then 1 per cent of GDP is very much. If the increase in petroleum revenues is used domestically in this way, it will, for example, generate almost half of the annual growth in the mainland economy in a normal year. If the private sector of the economy is also growing, and the economy is already close to the capacity limit, such a policy will quickly lead to strong pressures on resources in the economy. It gives rise to wages and prices. The idea behind the Petroleum Fund is that revenues from such a small increase in oil prices should flow the fund and be invested abroad, and that the increase in oil prices does not affect the share price. In this case, the increased revenues will not affect the domestic economy, but will be invested abroad through the Petroleum Fund. Similarly, one would not have to go into public release if oil prices were to be low for a period. There is an indistering to keep this mechanism intact. Policy instruments and transparency The most important instrument in monetary policy is the interest rate. Norges Bank has control over only the very short-term interest rates. In practice, they are primarily the sight deposit and D-loan rate - which is the interest rates commercial and savings banks have when they have deposits and pay when they have loans in Norges Bank. Signalling rates are renewed  as far as we know  not in other transactions that are important for economic developments. The direct effect of a change in these interest rates is therefore limited. Monetary policy has macroeconomic effects only to the extent that it can influence prices in financial markets that have an impact on households' and assets, such as banks' interest rates to the public and long-term bond yields, but also exchange rates, equity prices and other asset prices. These variables will in turn affect the economic impact of two years ahead in d. Through the effects on the real economy, the interest rate e will each also influence prices and wages. Monetary policy can also influence such nominal variables directly through the formation of expectations. In normal situations, changes in signalling rates have a fairly direct impact on short-term money market rates. The effect on market rates with longer maturities there and on asset prices depends on how the change in interest rates affects the economic outlook and what expectations are generated about monetary policy going forward. A reduction in signalling rates may in a situation trigger fears of overheating and rising inflation and lead to a sharp rise in interest rates to make the yield curve good. In such a situation, it is likely that an increase in the short interest rate would have had a smaller impact on long-term interest rates, or even brought them down, because the central bank's ceiling seemed ill-advised in relation to ensuring nominal stability. Can we find an impe piece of money for a country's monetary policy, i.e. the ability l in a certain sense to deliver nominal stability? Based on the yield curve, we can calculate implicit forward rates. Forward rates can be interpreted as expected interest rates between two forward-looking points. Forward rates can be used l to say something about inflation expectations if we foresee that the nominal interest rate is approximately equal to the sum of the expected real interest rate and expected inflation. In the short term, interest rate expectations will be influenced by expected cyclical developments. It may then be difficult to know exactly how much can be written in the expected real interest rate and how much can be iscribed from expected inflation. In the long term, i.e. up to the year ahead in d, it seems unlikely that market participants have specific expectations concerning the cyclical situation. The forward rate can then be interpreted as the sum of the expected real interest rate and expected inflation when the economy is in equilibrium. Inlays come any risk or run dspremier. If the equilibrium real interest rate is the same between countries, the difference between Norwegian and foreign forward rates can be interpreted as differences in expected inflation plus any risk premium. The long-term interest rate differential between Norway and Germany will then tell us something about the will of the participants lit l that the economic policy over d will result in inflation developments in line with that of the euro area countries. The chart shows that the forward rate differential between Norway and Germany, i.e. the difference between the short-term interest rates on forward-looking points, is fairly low when we go a few years into d, and not much greater than for the other Nordic countries. It can be interpreted as the economic policing contributes to providing a good nominal anchor. Credibility and llit can contribute to making the effects of monetary policy more predictable. With the current monetary policy, the real economic costs of a monetary policy can be reduced by rapidly normalising inflation expectations when the central bank signals a need for a tightening. As a result, low inflation would also come down without the central bank having to keep interest rates high for longer periods of time, with nega veer effects on output and employment. Now the world is probably not so straightforward and the connections are not so simple. It costs to erote inflation - even in countries where it has succeeded in creating a large amount of monetary policy. This is due to the fact that the assumption of full credibility for the central bank and perfect foresight in the markets never fully applies. We must therefore assume that it costs to bring down inflation that has been allowed to develop. The lowest costs will be if we ensure that price and wage growth never get out of hand. This is where the central bank's cove is located. The central bank may, in other terms, contribute to reducing the costs of erasing inflation through transparency and good communication abroad about monetary policy. They are aware that Norges Bank has attached great importance to transparency on objectives, analyses and the exercise of discretion. As I pointed out above, money policing works through complicated mechanisms and with significant dse erslep. A key basis for Norges Bank's interest rate ng is our analyses of the economic outlook and price developments a couple of years ahead. Norges Bank attaches great importance to communicating the assessments of the economic outlook ahead, primarily through the Bank's inflation reports, which are four times a year. We are open about our analyses, the use of models and the assumptions that underlie them. In the presentation of the Inflation Report, all d press conferences are held where the Bank's management informs about the analyses and answers questions. Analyses of the latest errors are designed to be able to make better and more accurate estimates through improvements to our analytical apparatus and our use of the e. Therefore, the estimates are systema sk, and in the quarterly crisis Money and Kredi . By pre-announcing dates for meetings of the Executive Board where the interest rate question is normally dealt with, all participants are familiar with when any interest rate changes can be expected to occur. The Bank's management has attached considerable importance to informing which assessments have been decisive when the interest rate has changed, both by inviting in press conferences and through other channels. We also hold meetings with the press even though the interest rate has not changed. The interaction between the policing areas is important for us to succeed in achieving nominal stability. The indispatients in the monetary policy are asked whether the bidders and the social partners are doing their part. In other terms, there will be a risk that an unfortunate policing composition may occur. There may be situations where Norges Bank, on the basis of its assessment of the economic outlook, maintains a high interest rate, while the government authorities increase their share of the government bid to increase their employment. They are a real dilemma. Transparency about our analyses and reaction patterns is probably the best way to address this indiscible. The government authorities can then take into account the effect on interest rates when deciding on a state budget. The target for monetary policy is to tie an exchange rate, but without such specific requirements in developments in this in the short term. A precondition for exchange rate stability above d is low inflation. It is therefore natural that developments in inflation and the krone exchange rate form the basis for assessing whether the monetary policy that has been pursued has been successful. But developments in these variables may also shed light on whether other parts of the economic policy have been well aware of the situation. It is reason to emphasise that developments should be assessed over a longer period. One cannot judge the results simply by looking at exchange rate and price developments. It must also be assessed discretionarily whether the exchange rate and inflation could have been stabilised with lower real economic costs. The prospect of success in the near future d With regard to the prospect of success in achieving nominal stability in the years ahead, it is natural for us to start with the last Inflation Report presented before Christmas. As I pointed out, the analyses in the Inflation Report, together with the ongoing assessment of the outlook for price and cost inflation and conditions in money and foreign exchange markets, form the basis for decisions concerning the orientation of monetary policy instruments. The economy is entering a period of lower growth than we experienced in 1994-98. Norges Bank expects mainland GDP Norway to increase by 3/4 per cent this year. Next year, growth is expected to pick up to 11/2 per cent. You're looking for growth to pick up in the long-downward trend growth in the economy. The risk of a marked downturn in the mainland economy now appears to be less than envisaged by us. Consumer price inflation is expected to slow over the next two years and come down to the rate aimed at by the euro area countries. These projections are based on wage growth slowing from 33/4 per cent this year. Our projections impound the developments we consider most likely, result in key variables such as interest rates, exchange rates and public demand developing as predicted , and there will be no structural changes in the economy. The world is difficult to predict, and many conditions can change along the way. The turnaround appears to be particularly concentrated in manufacturing, partly as a result of deteriorating profitability and lost competitiveness, but also because petroleum investment will fall. The impact of the turnaround on the overall share of the Norwegian economy will depend, among other things, on the resilience of the parts of the industry that are affected. We expect an increase in demand from the public sector and service industries. It is uncertain how wage formation will function with major changes between sectors of the economy. Traditionally, the industry has been a wage leader. This means that wage growth slows when profitability in this sector deteriorates. Tensions in the labour market and rapidly high demand in parts of the labour market may contribute to a pick-up in wage growth, even with some increase in overall unemployment. Inflation will then also be higher than projected in the March Inflation Report. The systemic assessment of dligere projections shows that a substantial part of the forecast errors for the real economy and e-demand growth in mainland Norway have been tied to an underestimation of growth in the public sector. In recent years, and perhaps especially in the or, there has been a tendency for growth in public releases to be higher than adopted during the bidding process. They may indicate that there is a relatively strong underlying pressure on the public sector. We cannot rule out that they are a more enduring trend. If growth in public sector output is higher, demand and the level of growth in the mainland economy will also show stronger growth than projected. The pressures in the labour market will thus increase and may contribute to the fact that wage and price inflation does not come down, but rather can lta. Conclusion We do not want to repeat the bad experiences of the 1970s and 1980s with high inflation and large cyclical fluctuations. Nominal stability will be central to avoiding such developments. In accordance with our mandate, Norges Bank will place great emphasis on realising the e. We exited the 1990s with the prospect of a reasonable balance in the Norwegian economy e are the problems that threatened to build up. In order to prevent nominal instability, the monetary policy was tightened in 1998. As fiscal policy and wage developments became more adapted to the economic situation, the interest rate could be reduced, even if the krone exchange rate was rapidly weak. Thus, we prevented the overall arrangement of the policing system from becoming too tight. Some people think that the short-range interest rate is also a measure of how successful economic policing has been. It may therefore be reason l to repeat myself; the interest rate is an instrument, not a target. Above d, there is a need for symmetry in the interest rate period, in the sense that the instrument must be used with the same collar both to slow down as to slow down the economy. Such a symmetry is necessary to uphold the lliten l nominal stability. It cannot be the case that we only increase the interest rate when it is absolu necessary, but lower it as fast as we can. 27 January 2000 00:00

I den utstrekning opplegget gir assosiasjoner i retning av et fastkursregime, br begrepet utgangsleiet forsts som en bredt tegnet sentralkurs som kronen kan svinge rundt uten fastlagte y ergrenser. Den andre setningen omtaler vesentlige endringer i kursen i forhold l utgangsleiet. Vesentlige m gis et konomisk innhold. En rimelig tolkning er at en "vesentlig endring" er en endring som pvirker forventningene om pris- og kostnadsutviklingen slik at kursendringen blir selvforsterkende. Ogs u rykkene med sikte p, e er hvert, re es inn mot og med utgangspunkt i viser at Norges Bank er gi stort rom for  utve skjnn. Kravet i forskri en om lbakevending av kronekursen l utgangsleiet kan - om det blir sa p spissen - ha et for sterkt element av paripoli kk i seg. I en tenkt situasjon, for eksempel e er et stort og varig fall i oljeprisen, kan kronekursen i lengre d bli liggende utenfor kursleiet. Dersom Norges Bank da forsker med hy rente  presse kronen lbake l kursleiet, vil pengepoli kken kunne skape nedgangs der av en art som vil svekke lliten l kronen. Tilsvarende kan det e er appresiering oppst situasjoner der renten m se es s lavt for bringe kronekuren lbake l utgangsleiet at det skapes inasjon. Da svekkes imidler d grunnlaget for kursstabilitet. Norges Bank kan derfor ikke med pne yne innre e virkemidlene slik at de skaper inasjon eller nedgangs d med deasjon. Dersom det oppstr en situasjon hvor Norges Bank ikke kan f kursen lbake uten slike konsekvenser, vil banken underre e statsmyndighetene om at det er behov for ltak av andre enn banken. Det kan da vre tale om nanspoli ske ltak som gjr det mulig  bringe kronekursen lbake mot utgangsleiet og stabilisere den. Dersom det har skjedd fundamentale endringer i rammevilkrene for norsk konomi, kan det derimot vre rik g  vurdere endringer i retningslinjene for pengepoli kken. I utvelsen av pengepoli kken fokuserer Norges Bank p de grunnleggende forutsetningene for stabilitet i kronekursen. For  oppn kursstabilitet mot euro, m virkemidlene re es inn slik at pris- og kostnadss gningen kommer ned mot den s gningen Den europeiske sentralbanken (ESB) sikter mot. Sam dig m vi unng at pengepoli kken i seg selv bidrar l nedgangs d med deasjon, fordi det kan svekke lliten l kronen. Ser vi p det ret som er g , har stabiliteten i kronekursen vrt stor, ikke minst i lys av de store bevegelser vi har se i kursforholdet mellom hovedvalutaene og i oljeprisen. Ved inngangen l 1999 var kronekursen fortsa rela vt svak i forhold l utgangsleiet. Da euroen ble introdusert m e vi betale 8,88 kroner for den. Gjennom 1999 svekket imidler d euroen seg rela vt betydelig i forhold l de andre hovedvalutaene. Ogs kronen har svekket seg i forhold l amerikanske dollar og japanske yen i lpet av det siste ret, men styrket seg mot euro. Se i forhold l et gjennomsni av vre handelspartnerne, har kronekursen vrt svrt stabil. U ordringer Tilliten l pengepoli kken er skjr og srbar. Det tar d  bygge opp llit og det skal lite l for  delegge den. Svikter lliten, vil det kreve mye  vinne den lbake. Vi husker alle prisen vi m e betale for  komme ut av devalueringssyndromet i siste halvdel av 1980-tallet. Det strste u ordringen fremover ligger derfor p mange mter i  bygge opp om og forsterke den llit vi allerede har opparbeidet oss. Forutsetninger for  lykkes La meg frst komme inn p noen ndvendige be ngelser som m vre oppfylt dersom vi skal lykkes i  oppn nominell stabilitet. For det frste er vik g at de ulike poli kkelementene drar sammen for  oppn de overordnede mlene. I Norge har nanspoli kken ha en vik g rolle i stabiliseringspoli kken. Det har sammenheng med at solide statsnanser gir handlefrihet. I andre land har tyngende statsgjeld frt l at nanspoli kken ikke lengre kan brukes srlig ak vt for stabiliseringsforml, i alle fall ikke i nedgangs der. Gjennom inntektsoppgjrene har partene i arbeidslivet mulighet l  pvirke det samlede nivet p sysselse ngen over d. Sammenliknet med andre land, har Norge gjennomgende ha et lavt ledighetsniv og en hy andel av befolkningen i arbeid de siste tjuefem rene. Mange land som har vrt gjennom lange og dype lavkonjunkturer, har opplevd en betydelig og langvarig kning i arbeidsledigheten. Et vik g trekk ved lnnsdannelsen i Norge har vrt at konkurransevilkrene i nringslivet er bli llagt betydelig vekt i lnnsforhandlingene. De e gjelder ogs for lnningene i sektorer som ikke er srlig utsa for konkurranse fra utlandet. Viljen l  ta langsik ge hensyn har bidra l  stabilisere rammebe ngelsene i konkurranseutsa sektor og l  holde sysselse ngen p et hyt niv. Det vik gste bidraget det inntektspoli ske samarbeidet kan gi, er  fortse e  legge forholdene l re e for at den strukturelle ledigheten i Norge forblir lav og sysselse ngen hy. P kort sikt kan nanspoli kken pvirke utviklingen i produksjonen og sysselse ngen. I et lengre perspek v har u ormingen av nanspoli kken, herunder ska esystemet, oentlige investeringer og utgi er l for eksempel forskning og utdanning, stor betydning for vekstpotensialet i konomien. I llegg vil den vekst i oentlig utgi er som myndighetene legger opp l, pvirke fordelingen av arbeidskra og kapital mellom ulike sektorer i konomien. Med mindre det er ledige reserver av arbeidskra eller kapital, vil kt ressursbruk i oentlig sektor legge beslag p produksjonsfaktorer som alterna vt kunne beny es i privat sektor. Over d kan utviklingen i prisnivet pvirkes gjennom pengepoli kken. Sysselse ngen kan pvirkes gjennom lnnsdannelsen. Fordelingen av ressursene mellom skjermet sektor og det konkurranseutsa e nringslivet kan pvirkes gjennom nanspoli kken. Strrelsen p konkurranseutsa sektor bestemmes over d i en kamp om realressursene mellom det oentlige og nringslivet. Det er vik g at en har med seg disse vurderingene av hva de ulike poli kkelementer p lang sikt kan pvirke, ogs nr en formulerer de opera ve ml for poli kken p mer kort sikt. Det synes  vre noks stor enighet om den langsik ge rolledelingen og den gjensidige avhengigheten i den konomiske poli kken. Da nansministeren redegjorde for Finanskomiteen 4. november i or, sa han blant annet: "Jeg vil avslutningsvis understreke at det e er min oppfatning ikke er noen motsetning mellom Norges Bank og Regjeringen nr det gjelder tolkningen av de pengepoli ske retningslinjene eller nr det gjelder arbeidsdelingen i den konomiske poli kken. I en dr ing av arbeidsdelingen er det helt sentralt  ta med i betraktningen den gjensidige avhengigheten og det nre samspillet mellom de ulike poli kkelementene. Det er ikke, og kan ikke vre vannte e sko mellom de ulike delen av den konomiske poli kken. En vellykket gjennomfring av pengepoli kken er derfor avhengig av at nans- og inntektspoli kken ikke kommer ut av kurs." De e er jeg enig i. Jeg sa at vrt pengepoli ske regime er unikt, men det som virkelig skiller oss fra andre land vi ellers gjerne sammenligner oss med, er oljen. Det er grunn l  gi det poli ske system honnr for de mekanismer som er bygget opp gjennom petroleumsfondsordningen for  f en forsvarlig hndtering av oljeinntektene, og, enda mer, for at disse mekanismene har f lov l  virke e er forutsetningene. Ikke at vi ikke bruker oljeinntekten innenlands, men vi har iallfall for den greid  begrense de e l hva konomien med rimelighet kan tle. Det vil vre vik g, ogs for pengepoli kken, at Petroleumsfondet fungere e er hensikten. Fondet spiller en vesentlig rolle for  stabilisere den konomiske utviklingen. Ved at valutainntektene fra petroleumssektoren plasseres i utlandet, oppre holdes balansen i markedet for norske kroner. Dermed dempes impulser fra svingninger i oljeprisen p kronekursen. Petroleumsfondet virker ogs som sttdemper mot kortsik ge svingninger i oljeinntektene. Siden store deler av pengestrmmen fra oljevirksomheten lfaller staten direkte, vil svingninger i oljeprisen i frste omgang fre l at avsetningene l fondet varierer i strrelse. En endring i oljeprisen vil dermed ikke sl inn med full tyngde i oentlige utgi er. De e gjr norsk konomi mer robust overfor svingninger i oljeprisen og dermed mindre oljeavhengig, ogs p kort sikt. Et eksempel kan illustrere de e. La oss anta at oljeprisen midler dig ker med 10 kroner per fat, eller li under halvannen dollar fatet. Det er en liten endring i oljeprisen, godt innenfor de normale variasjonene fra e r l det neste. Statens inntekter - og dermed budsje overskuddet - vil da ke med rundt 10 milliarder kroner det frste ret og 12-13 milliarder kroner det neste ret. Det lsvarer nrmere 1 prosent av Norges rlige BNP. Hvis de kte inntektene blir ta inn i konomien gjennom kte utgi er eller reduserte ska er i statsbudsje et, blir den samlede e ersprselen innenlands pvirket. kte utgi er krever en kning i det oentliges bruk av realressurser - frst og fremst arbeidskra . Da er 1 prosent av BNP svrt mye. Dersom kningen i oljeinntektene p denne mten brukes innenlands, lsvarer det for eksempel nesten halvparten av den rlige veksten i fastlandskonomien i et normalr. Hvis ogs den private delen av konomien vokser, og konomien allerede er nr kapasitetsgrensen, vil en slik poli kk raskt fre l et sterkt press p ressursene i konomien. Det gir opphav l lnns- og priss gning. Tanken bak Petroleumsfondet er at inntektene fra en slik mindre kning i oljeprisen skal lyte fondet og plasseres i utlandet, og at kningen i oljeprisen ikke pvirker budsje et for vrig. I s fall vil de kte inntektene ikke pvirke den innenlandske konomien, men investeres i utlandet gjennom Petroleumsfondet. Tilsvarende vil en ikke behve  g l drama ske ku i oentlige utgi er om oljeprisen skulle vre lav en periode. Det er en u ordring for frem den  beholde denne mekanismen intakt. Virkemidler og penhet Det vik gste virkemiddel i pengepoli kken er renten. Norges Bank har bare kontroll over de helt kortsik ge rentene. I praksis er de e frst og fremst folio- og D-lnsrenten - som er de renter forretnings- og sparebanker mo ar nr de har innskudd og betaler nr de har ln i Norges Bank. Signalrentene beny es - s vidt vi vet - ikke i andre transaksjoner som er vik ge for den konomiske utviklingen. Den direkte virkningen av en endring i disse rentene er derfor begrenset. Pengepoli kken har makrokonomiske virkninger bare i den grad den kan pvirke de priser i nansmarkedene som har betydning for husholdningenes og bedri enes lpasning, som bankenes renter overfor publikum og de langsik ge obligasjonsrentene, men ogs valutakurser, aksjekurser og andre formuespriser. Disse strrelsene vil igjen pvirke den konomiske ak viteten e l to r fram i d. Via virkningene p realkonomien vil renten e er hvert ogs pvirke priser og lnninger. Pengepoli kken kan ogs pvirke slike nominelle strrelser direkte gjennom forventningsdannelsen. Endringer i signalrentene har i normale situasjoner noks direkte gjennomslag i de helt kortsik ge rentene i pengemarkedet. Eekten p markedsrenter med lengre lpe der og p formuesprisene er avhengig av hvordan renteendringen pvirker de konomiske utsiktene og hvilke forventninger som skapes om pengepoli kken framover. En reduksjon i signalrentene kan i en gi situasjon utlse frykt for overopphe ng og kende inasjon og fre l at de langsik ge rentene s ger slik at avkastningskurven blir bra ere. I en slik situasjon er det trolig at en kning i den korte renten ville pvirket lange renter mindre, eller endog brakt dem ned, fordi sentralbankens ltak virket llitskapende i forhold l  sikre nominell stabilitet. Kan vi nne et u rykk for lliten l et lands pengepoli kk, alts evnen l i en viss forstand  levere nominell stabilitet? Med utgangspunkt i avkastningskurven kan vi beregne implisi e terminrenter. Terminrentene kan tolkes som forventet rente mellom to fram dige dspunkter. Terminrentene kan brukes l  si noe om inasjonsforventningene hvis vi forutse er at nominell rente er lnrmet lik summen av forventet realrente og forventet inasjon. P kort sikt vil renteforventningene vre pvirket av den forventede konjunkturutviklingen. Da kan det vre vanskelig  vite eksakt hvor mye som kan lskrives forventet realrente og hvor mye som kan lskrives forventet inasjon. P lang sikt, dvs. opp mot r fram i d, virker det derimot lite trolig at aktrene har bestemte forventninger om konjunktursituasjonen. Da kan terminrenten tolkes som summen av forventet realrente og forventet inasjon nr konomien er i likevekt. I llegg kommer eventuelle risiko- eller lpe dspremier. Dersom likevektsrealrenten er lik mellom land, kan forskjellen mellom norske og utenlandske langsik ge terminrenter tolkes som forskjeller i forventet inasjon pluss en eventuell risikopremie. Den langsik ge terminrentedieransen mellom Norge og Tyskland vil da fortelle noe om aktrenes llit l at den konomiske poli kken over d vil gi en inasjonsutvikling p linje med eurolandenes. Figuren viser at den terminrentedieransen mellom Norge og Tyskland, alts dieransen mellom de kortsik ge renten p frem dige dspunkter er noks lav nr vi gr noen r ut i d, og ikke srlig strre enn for de andre nordiske landene. Det kan tolkes som at den konomiske poli kken bidrar l  gi et godt nominelt ankerfeste. Troverdighet og llit kan bidra l at virkningene av pengepoli kken blir mer forutsigbare. Med lstrekkelig llit l pengepoli kken kan de realkonomiske kostnadene kny et l en pengepoli sk lstramning reduseres ved at inasjonsforventningene raskt normaliseres nr sentralbanken signaliserer behov for en lstramning. Dermed ville ogs den fak ske inasjonen komme ned uten at sentralbanken behvde  holde renten hy over lengre d med lhrende nega ve virkninger p produksjon og sysselse ng. N er antakelig ikke verden s grei og sammenhengene ikke s enkle. Det koster  erne inasjonen - ogs i land hvor det har lykkes  skape stor llit l pengepoli kken. Det har sammenheng med at de s liserte forutsetningen om full troverdighet for sentralbanken og perfekt forutseenhet i markedene aldri gjelder fullt ut. Vi m derfor ta som utgangspunkt at det koster  bringe ned inasjon som har f utvikle seg. Lavest blir kostnadene om vi srger for at pris- og lnnsveksten aldri kommer ut av kontroll. Her ligger sentralbankens vik gste u ordring . Sentralbanken kan imidler d bidra l  redusere kostnadene med  erne inasjonen gjennom penhet og god kommunikasjon utad om pengepoli kken. De e er mo vet for at Norges Bank har lagt stor vekt p penhet om ml, analyser og skjnnsutvelse. Som jeg poengterte ovenfor, virker pengepoli kken gjennom kompliserte mekanismer og med betydelige dse erslep. Et vik g grunnlag for Norges Banks rentese ng er vre analyser av de konomiske utsiktene og prisutviklingen p et par rs sikt. Norges Bank legger stor vekt p  formidle vurderingene av de konomiske utsiktene fremover, frst og fremst gjennom bankens inasjonsrapporter som utgis re ganger i ret. Vi er pne om vre analyser, den modellbruk og de forutsetninger som ligger l grunn for dem. I lknytning l fremleggelsen av inasjonsrapporten arrangeres det all d pressekonferanser der bankens ledelse orienterer om analysene og besvarer sprsml. Analyser av dligere feil er vik g for  kunne lage bedre og mer tresikre anslag gjennom forbedringer av vrt analyseapparat og vr bruk av de e. Derfor e erprves anslagene systema sk, og publiseres i kvartalskri et Penger og kredi . Gjennom  forhndsannonsere datoer for mter i hovedstyret der rentesprsmlet normalt behandles, er alle aktrer kjent med nr eventuelle renteendringer kan forventes  komme. Bankens ledelse har lagt betydelig vekt p  orientere om hvilke vurderinger som har vrt avgjrende nr renten er endret, bde ved  invitere l pressekonferanser e er rentemtene og gjennom andre kanaler. Vi holder ogs mter med pressen selv om renten ikke har vrt endret. Samspillet mellom poli kkomrdene er vik g for at vi skal lykkes i  oppn nominell stabilitet. U ordringene i pengepoli kken le es om budsje poli kken og partene i arbeidslivet gjr sin del av jobben. Det vil imidler d all d vre en risiko for at det kan oppst en uheldig poli kksammensetning. Det kan tenkes situasjoner der Norges Bank ut fra sin vurdering av de konomiske utsiktene holder hy rente, mens statsmyndighetene p sin side ker utgi ene over statsbudsje et for  s mulerer sysselse ngen. De e er et reelt dilemma. penhet om vre analyser og reaksjonsmnstre er trolig den beste mten  mte denne u ordringen p. Da kan statsmyndighetene ta hensyn l virkningen p rentese ngen nr vedtak om statsbudsje et fa es. Mlet for pengepoli kken er kny et l valutakursen, men uten at det er sa bestemte krav l utviklingen i denne p kort sikt. En forutsetning for stabilitet i valutakursen over d er lav inasjon. Det er derfor naturlig at utviklingen i inasjonen og kronekursen danner grunnlag for i e er d  vurdere om den pengepoli kken som har vrt frt, har vrt vellykket. Men utviklingen i disse strrelsene kan ogs kaste lys over om andre deler av den konomiske poli kken har vrt vel lpasset situasjonen. Det er grunn l  understreke at en br vurdere utviklingen over en lengre periode. En kan ikke bedmme resultatene bare ved  se p valutakurs- og prisutviklingen. En m ogs skjnnsmessig vurdere om valutakursen og inasjonen kunne vrt stabilisert med lavere realkonomiske kostnader. Utsiktene l  lykkes i den nrmeste frem d N det gjelder utsiktene l  lykkes i  oppn nominell stabilitet i rene fremover, er det naturlig for oss  ta utgangspunkt i den siste inasjonsrapporten som ble lagt frem fr jul i or. Som jeg var inne p, er det analysene i inasjonsrapporten, som sammen med den lpende vurderingen av pris- og kostnadsutsiktene og forholdene i penge- og valutamarkedene, danner grunnlag for beslutninger om innretningen av virkemidlene i pengepoli kken. konomien gr inn i periode med lavere vekst enn vi erfarte i 1994-98. Norges Bank venter at BNP for Fastlands-Norge vil ke med  prosent i r. Neste r venter vi at veksten vil ta seg opp l 1 prosent. Dere er ser det ut l at veksten tar seg opp l den langsik ge trendveksten i konomien. Risikoen for en markert nedgang i fastlandskonomien synes n  vre mindre enn vi dligere s for oss. Vi venter at konsumprisveksten i lpet av de nrmeste to rene vil avta og komme ned mot den s gningstakten eurolandene sikter mot. Disse anslagene er baserer seg p at lnnsveksten avtar fra i or og kommer ned i 3 prosent i r. Vre anslag u rykker den utvikling vi anser for mest sannsynlig, gi at sentrale strrelser som rente, valutakurs og oentlig e ersprsel utvikler seg som forutsa , og det ikke skjer strukturelle endringer i konomien. Verden er imidler d vanskelig  forutsi, og mange forhold kan endre seg underveis. Omslaget synes  vre srlig konsentrert om industrien, dels som flge av svekket lnnsomhet og tapt konkurranseevne, men ogs fordi oljeinvesteringene vil falle. Hvor store konsekvenser omslaget fr for den samlede ak viteten i norsk konomi, vil blant annet avhenge av oms llingsevnen i de delene av industrien som blir berrt. Vi venter fortsa kt e ersprsel e er arbeidskra fra oentlig sektor og fra tjenesteytende nringer. Det er usikkert hvordan lnnsdannelsen vil fungere med store oms llinger mellom sektorer i konomien. Tradisjonelt har industrien vrt lnnsledende. Det lsier at lnnsveksten avtar nr lnnsomheten i denne sektoren svekkes. Spenninger i arbeidsmarkedet og fortsa hy e ersprsel i deler av arbeidsmarkedet , kan bidra l at lnnsveksten tar seg opp igjen, selv med en viss kning i samlet ledighet. Da vil ogs prisveksten bli hyere enn vi anslr i siste inasjonsrapport. Den systema ske e erprvingen av dligere anslag viser at en vesentlig del av prognosefeilene for realkonomien og e ersprselsveksten i Fastlands-Norge har vrt kny et l en undervurdering av veksten i de oentlige utgi ene. De siste rene, og kanskje srlig i or, har det vrt en tendens l at veksten i oentlige utgi er har bli hyere enn vedta under budsje behandlingene. De e kan tyde p at det er et forholdsvis sterkt underliggende press p de oentlige utgi ene. Vi kan ikke utelukke at de e er en mer varig trend. Dersom veksten i oentlige utgi er blir hyere, vil e ersprselen og ak vitetsnivet i fastlandskonomien ogs vise sterkere vekst enn ansl . Presset i arbeidsmarkedet vil dermed oppre holdes og kunne bidra l at lnns- og prisveksten ikke kommer ned, men snarere kan lta. Avslutning Vi nsker ikke  gjenta de drlige erfaringene fra 1970 og -80-tallet med hy inasjon og store konjunktursvingninger. Nominell stabilitet vil vre sentralt for  unng en slik utvikling. Norges Bank vil, i samsvar med vrt mandat, legge stor vekt p  realisere de e. Vi gikk ut av 1990-rene med utsikter l en rimelig balanse i norsk konomi e er problemene som truet med  bygge seg opp. For  hindre nominell ustabilitet ble pengepoli kken strammet kra ig l i 1998. E er hvert som nanspoli kk og lnnsutvikling ble mer lpasset den konomiske situasjonen, kunne renten se es ned i or, selv om kronekursen var fortsa svak. Dermed forhindret vi at den samlede innretning av poli kken ble for stram. Noen synes e er de e  mene at den kortsik ge renten ogs er et ml p hvor vellykket den konomiske poli kken har vrt. Det kan derfor vre grunn l  gjenta meg selv; renten er et virkemiddel, ikke et ml. Over d er det vik g med symmetri i rentese ngen, i den forstand at virkemiddelet m brukes med samme kra bde for  bremse opp som  s mulere konomien. En slik symmetri er ndvendig for  oppre holde lliten l nominell stabilitet. Det kan ikke bli slik at vi bare ker renten nr det er absolu ndvendig, men senker den s fort vi kan. Title: Developments in the Norwegian economy and challenges ahead
text: Developments in the Norwegian economy and in the period ahead By Deputy Governor Jarle Bergo. The Norwegian Municipalities' Economics Conference, Trondheim 20 March 2000 We have been through a long period of high economic growth in the 1990s. This upturn was longer and stronger than the growth period we remember from the more turbulent 1980s. Despite the e, there are many unresolved issues. The health and care system is constantly being criticized from various quarters. The elderly and the chaos between countries will see the welfare state face major incursions. There is also, in a more brief way, uncertainty about where the Norwegian economy is going is the slowdown of the past year. Today I will try to discuss the developments as we see them today as well as some of the more longitudinal changes. Developments in the Norwegian economy The Norwegian economy was in a very strong growth period from the 1990s until the mid-1998 period. At that time, wage growth was very high, fiscal policy was not tight, and oil prices were low. The outlook for the Norwegian economy was rather uncertain. A certain cooling was necessary to avoid overheating. The interest rate was terminated in order to contribute to nominal stability, and economic growth slowed. We envisioned a growth pause, or even nega v growth, for a period ahead. The risk of a severe downturn in the Norwegian economy appeared to be less against cunning one of the years. In the latter half of 1999, growth appeared to be on the rise again, and that the growth pause was already over.
