Samspillet i den konomiske poli kken Her i Trondheim er det fremstende personer som o e bruker ordet samhandling som et vik g suksesskriterium innen sport, kanskje srlig fotball. Samhandling er ogs et meget vik g suksesskriterium for den konomiske poli kken, men den m ta utgangspunkt i individuelle ferdigheter. Dersom stabilitet og vekst skal oppre holdes, er det vik g at de ulike poli kkelementene bidrar l  lse oppgavene innenfor sine mulighetsomrder. Finanspoli kken Finanspoli kken har i Norge ha en vik g rolle i stabiliseringspoli kken. De e har vrt mulig p grunn av statens sterke nansielle s lling. Andre land det er naturlig  sammenlikne seg med har langt svakere statsnanser, og er dermed ikke i stand l  drive stabiliseringspoli kk p samme mte som i Norge. Finanspoli kken har imidler d ogs andre oppgaver enn  stabilisere konjunkturene. Den skal bidra l  dekke e ersprselen e er oentlig nansierte goder og bidra l  pvirke fordelingen mellom grupper og generasjoner. P lang sikt vil strukturen i nanspoli kken, herunder ska esystemet og oentlige investeringer, kunne pvirke vekstpotensialet i konomien. I llegg vil den vekst i oentlig sektor som myndighetene legger opp l, pvirke fordelingen av arbeidskra og kapital mellom ulike sektorer. Med mindre det er store ledige reserver av arbeidskra eller kapital, er imidler d stabiliseringspoli ske ltak ikke egnet l  pvirke det samlede nivet p produksjon og sysselse ng over d. En ekspansjon av oentlig sektor i en konomi med hy kapasitetsutny ng vil sledes over d fre l en lsvarende reduksjon av ak viteten i privat sektor. Et ml p statsbudsje ets samlede virkning p e ersprselen er den skalte olje-, rente- og ak vitetskorrigerte budsje ndikatoren, som er vist i denne guren. Budsje ndikatoren viser at nanspoli kken stort se har virket dempende p veksten i oppgangs der og ekspansivt i nedgangs der. De e er imidler d en grov indikator for budsje ets samlede virkning. Det er derfor ogs ndvendig  vurdere budsje ets sammensetning, herunder veksten i utgi ene, for  danne seg en oppfatning av den samlede virkningen av nanspoli kken. kte oentlige utgi er kan i prinsippet nytraliseres gjennom en kning av ska ene, slik at kt oentlig ak vitet motsvares av en lsvarende nedgang i husholdningenes e ersprsel. Imidler d er det i praksis vanskelig  f l en kning i ska er eller avgi er som ikke ogs rammer nringslivet. Lnnstakere og andre vil kunne reagere med krav om inntektskninger for  hindre at kte ska er og avgi er demper veksten i realinntektene, og de vil gjennomgende lykkes bedre dess strammere arbeidsmarkedet er. Det synes lite trolig at det over d vil vre mulig  gjennomfre en poli kk med stadige innstramminger overfor husholdningene gjennom ska e- og avgi skninger. En vesentlig ekspansjon i oentlig sektor ut over det den underliggende veksten i konomien lsier, vil derfor normalt innebre en overfring av realressurser fra konkurranseutsa l skjermet virksomhet. Det er ikke gi hva som er den rik ge strrelsen p oentlig sektor, og e ersprselen e er tjenester fra det oentlige kan endre seg over d. En sterk og eek v oentlig sektor er et vik g element i samspillet i konomien som kan bidra l kt vekst og velferd. Imidler d er ogs den oentlige sektoren avhengig av at det skapes verdier i nringslivet som kan holde inntektene oppe nr oljevirksomheten ikke lenger dominerer konomien. Den konkurranseutsa e sektoren er srbar. Det er store svingninger i inntektene og globaliseringen ltar. Med den oljeavhengigheten norsk konomi allerede har, tar vi en risiko dersom vi svekker grunnlaget for fastlandets nringsliv y erligere. Det lsier at veksten i utgi ene i statsbudsje et normalt ikke br vre strre enn den trendmessige veksten i fastlandskonomien. Betydningen av petroleumsfondet for stabilitet De e kan vre en srlig u ordring for en rik oljenasjon som Norge. Vi har en oljerikdom som de siste rene har gi staten store overskudd som er plassert i Petroleumsfondet. Det er grunn l  gi det poli ske system honnr for de mekanismer som er bygget opp gjennom petroleumsfondsordningen for  f en forsvarlig hndtering av oljeinntektene, og, enda mer, for at disse mekanismene har f lov l  virke e er forutsetningene. Ikke at vi ikke bruker oljeinntekter innenlands, men vi har iallfall for den greid  begrense de e l hva konomien med rimelighet kan tle. Det vil vre vik g, ogs for pengepoli kken, at Petroleumsfondet fungerer e er hensikten. Fondet spiller en vesentlig rolle for  stabilisere den konomiske utviklingen. Ved at valutainntektene fra petroleumssektoren plasseres i utlandet, oppre holdes ogs balansen i markedet for norske kroner. Dermed dempes impulser fra svingninger i oljeprisen p kronekursen. Petroleumsfondet virker ogs som sttdemper mot kortsik ge svingninger i oljeinntektene. Siden store deler av pengestrmmen fra oljevirksomheten lfaller staten direkte, vil svingninger i oljeprisen i frste omgang fre l at avsetningene l fondet varierer i strrelse. En endring i oljeprisen vil dermed ikke sl inn med full tyngde i oentlige utgi er. De e gjr norsk konomi mer robust overfor svingninger i oljeprisen og dermed mindre oljeavhengig, ogs p kort sikt. Et eksempel kan illustrere de e. Siden regjeringen la fram Nasjonalbudsje et for 2000 har oljeprisen steget kra ig. I Nasjonalbudsje et er det kalkulert med en oljepris p 125 kroner per fat i gjennomsni for 2000. I januar og februar var oljeprisen 210 kroner i gjennomsni , alts 85 kroner hyere. Bare ekstrainntektene i rets to frste mneder i forhold l Nasjonalbudsje et er p om lag 13 milliarder kroner. Det lsvarer mer enn 1 prosent av Norges rlige BNP. Hvis de kte inntektene blir ta inn i konomien gjennom kte utgi er eller reduserte ska er i statsbudsje et, blir den samlede e ersprselen innenlands pvirket. kte utgi er krever en kning i det oentliges bruk av realressurser - frst og fremst arbeidskra . Da er 1 prosent av BNP svrt mye. Dersom kningen i oljeinntektene p denne mten brukes innenlands, lsvarer det for eksempel halvparten av den rlige veksten i fastlandskonomien i et normalr. Hvis ogs den private delen av konomien vokser, og konomien allerede er nr kapasitetsgrensen, vil en slik poli kk raskt fre l et sterkt press p ressursene i konomien. Det gir opphav l lnns- og priss gning. Tanken bak Petroleumsfondet er at inntektene fra en slik kning i oljeprisen skal lyte fondet og plasseres i utlandet, og at kningen i oljeprisen ikke pvirker budsje et for vrig. I s fall vil de kte inntektene ikke pvirke den innenlandske konomien, men investeres i utlandet gjennom Petroleumsfondet. Tilsvarende vil en ikke behve  g l drama ske ku i oentlige utgi er om oljeprisen skulle vre lav en periode. Det er en u ordring for frem den  beholde denne mekanismen intakt. Avsetningene i petroleumsfondet utgjorde ved utgangen av orret i overkant av 222 milliarder kroner. Selv om de e er mer penger enn de este av oss kan fores lle seg, s lsvarer det ikke mer enn om lag 50 tusen kroner per innbygger i Norge. Fondet er med andre ord forelpig ikke veldig stort. 222 milliarder kroner er heller ikke nok l  kjpe kleskjeden Hennes og Mauritz, for  gi et eksempel. Norges samlede nansformue er ogs forholdsvis liten dersom en sammenlikner med andre formueskomponenter. Nasjonalformuen kan grovt deles inn i petroleumsformue, som er neddiskontert verdi av frem dig ne o kontantstrm fra petroleumsvirksomheten, verdien av realkapitalformue, nansformue og dagens verdi av frem dig arbeid, eller menneskelig kapital. Figuren her, som er hentet fra regjeringens lang dsprogram, viser at verdien av petroleumsformuen og nansformuen i frem den er liten i forhold l realkapitalformuen. Det mest slende ved disse anslagene fra lang dsprogrammet, som det selvsagt er stor usikkerhet ved, er i hvilken grad dagens verdi av menneskelig kapital dominerer den samlede nasjonalformuen. Vr strste rikdom er alts oss selv og vr skaperevne. Men petroleumsfondet kan komme godt med, det ogs. Petroleumsfondet ker e er hvert som oljen hentes opp og petroleumsformuen blir mindre. Statens inntekter fra petroleumsvirksomheten plasseres i utenlandske verdipapirer og nansformuen ker. Oppbyggingen av petroleumsfondet er med andre ord bare en omplassering av formue. Hyere oljefond i seg selv gjr ikke Norge rikere, men oljefondet vil forhpentligvis gi god avkastning. Oljefondet bidrar l at nasjonalformuen spres p ulike ak va og reduserer dermed risikoen for store verdifall. P den mten reduseres srbarheten for et eventuelt frem dig prisfall p olje. Det er grunn l  presisere at petroleumsfondet er en ren nansiell investor. Hensikten er ikke  vre en strategisk eier, men heller  investere i en andel av verdens verdiskapning fremover. Gjennomfringen av pengepoli kken Petroleumsfondsmekanismen er som nevnt meget vik g ogs for pengepoli kken, ved at den legger l re e for strre stabilitet i realkonomien og valutakursen. Mlet for norsk pengepoli kk er stabilitet i kronekursen mot europeiske valutaer, siden 1. januar 1999 denert som euro. I utvelsen av pengepoli kken legger Norges Bank vekt p  oppfylle de grunnleggende forutsetningene for stabilitet i kronekursen mot euro: Virkemidlene i pengepoli kken m re es inn slik at pris- og kostnadsveksten kommer ned mot den s gningen Den europeiske sentralbanken (ESB) sikter mot. Sam dig m Norges Bank unng at pengepoli kken i seg selv bidrar l nedgangs d med deasjon, fordi det kan svekke lliten l kronen. Erfaringene fra 1970- og 80-rene viser at pengepoli kken i lengden ikke egner seg l  styre konkurranseevnen eller strrelsen p den konkurranseutsa e sektoren. Slike grunnleggende realkonomiske forhold kan derimot pvirkes gjennom nanspoli kken og samarbeidet mellom partene i arbeidslivet. Det pengepoli kken p lengre sikt kan bidra med, er  gi konomien et nominelt anker, det vil si srge for stabile priser og stabil verdi for den norske kronen. Det skapes ikke vekst og fremgang av  trykke mer penger. Norges Bank kan ikke med pne yne bidra l  skape inasjon eller nedgangs d med deasjon. Det ville fre l en ustabil krone. Det er derfor ikke konikt mellom  re e virkemidlene i pengepoli kken mot lav og stabil inasjon og mlet om stabilitet i kronekursen. Selv om pengepoli kken ikke egner seg l  styre konkurranseevnen, kan endringer i kronekursen i visse situasjoner gi et dlig varsel om at det konkurranseutsa e nringslivet er i ferd med  bli svekket - eller styrket - i kampen om realressursene. Nr nanspoli kken lykkes i  jevne ut svingningene i innenlandsk e ersprsel og produksjon, og nr inntektsdannelsen fungerer like godt som fra slu en av 1980-tallet, blir det lagt et godt grunnlag for en stabil krone. Den vik gste faktoren som pvirker kronekursen er lliten l den nominelle stabiliteten. Hvis det frst er en slik llit, kan kronekursen variere p kort sikt uten at det fr konsekvenser for kursnivet over d. Tilliten avhenger blant annet av myndighetenes vilje l  prioritere nominell stabilitet. Under fastkurspoli kken fram l 1992 bandt vi oss l masten ved  erklre klart hvor kronekursen skulle ligge. I et system med ytende krone og strre rom for skjnnsutvelse, kan penhet om analyser og reaksjonsmnstre bidra l  styrke lliten l det nominelle ankerfestet. Det forutse er sam dig at det reaksjonsmnsteret som varsles, ogs blir fulgt. Norges Bank har lagt stor vekt p penhet rundt pengepoli kken. Langsik ge u ordringer for velferdsstaten La meg n g nrmere inn p enkelte strukturelle u ordringer som norsk konomi, og ikke minst kommunekonomien str foran. Kommunesektoren under oppgangsperioden p 90-tallet De siste par rene er det bli en mer markert todeling av konomien. Lnnsomheten i industrien har falt, og investeringene bde i oljevirksomheten og fastlandsindustrien faller trolig i r for andre r p rad. Sam dig har husholdningenes forbruk vokst sterkt gjennom mesteparten av 90-rene og fram l n. Spesielt e ersprselen e er tjenester har vokst betydelig i det siste. De e har bidra l sterk vekst i produksjon og sysselse ng i tjenesteytende virksomheter. Denne utviklingen vil trolig fortse e i rene fremover. Det er en kjensgjerning at jo hyere inntekten i et land blir, desto hyere vil e ersprselen e er tjenester bli, deriblant helse- og omsorgstjenester som kommunesektoren str for. For denne siste type tjenester er det spesielt slik at nansieringen i det vesentligste skjer over oentlige budsje er, slik at prismekanismene ikke i srlig grad virker begrensende p e ersprselen. Sam dig vil det vre klare begrensninger p hvor mye inntektsrammene l kommunene kan ke. Det kan dermed oppst en ubalanse mellom kommunenes inntekter og utgi er i frem den. Kommunene vil derfor e er alt  dmme bli utsa for et kt press i retning av eek visering og prioritering mellom ulike forml. Sysselse ngskningen i kommunesektoren fra 1993 l 1999 var 57 tusen personer, de e lsvarte 24 prosent av den samlede kningen i denne perioden. Sysselse ngen i kommunesektoren utgjr n om lag 1/4 av den totale sysselse ngen. Andelen kte frst og fremst p begynnelsen av 1990-tallet, mens den de siste fem rene har vrt rela vt stabil. De e m ses i sammenheng med den sterke samlede sysselse ngsveksten de siste rene. Figuren viser at det i forrige oppgangskonjunktur var noe sterkere vekst i sysselse ngen i privat sektor enn i oentlig. Det har vrt en markert vridning innen oentlig sysselse ng i denne perioden: sysselse ngen i staten har falt (mye av de e skyldes frre sysselsa e i Forsvaret og at statlige forvaltningsbedri er er g over l  bli aksjeselskaper) mens oppgangen i sysselse ngen i kommunesektoren, frst og fremst i primrkommunene, har vrt formidabel. kningen i kommunesektoren gjenspeiler kt ak vitet med satsing p helse, omsorg og undervisning. Spesielt innen helse- og omsorgstjenester har sysselse ngen kt betydelig de seneste r. Sam dig har kommunenes konomi utviklet seg i nega v retning. Overskudd fr lnetransaksjoner er en indikator ved vurderingen av utviklingen i kommunekonomien. Ser vi p 1990-tallet har kommuneforvaltningen ha et underskudd fr lnetransaksjoner i alle rene unnta i 1994, men underskuddene var beskjedne fram l 1998. Vi m lbake l 1987 og 1988 for  nne underskudd i den strrelse vi opplevde i 1998 og 1999. Sta s sk sentralbyrs anslag for underskuddet i 1999 er vel 6 milliarder kroner, eller 3,2 prosent av de totale inntektene. Det er imidler d stor usikkerhet rundt de e tallet. Kommunenes Sentralforbund anslr underskuddet l omtrent det dobbelte, iflge avisoppslag. Underskuddene de to siste rene m rik gnok ses i sammenheng med hye investeringer i lknytning l eldresatsingen, hvor staten i siste omgang plukker opp mye av regningen, men selv om en korrigerer for de e er underskuddet trolig stort. Andre vik ge faktorer bak det store underskuddet i or er en sterk vekst i lnnskostnadene, som flge av kt lnn per meverk, kt antall sysselsa e, og kte ne o renteutgi er. Gjennom mesteparten av 1990-tallet var det hy vekst i kommunale utgi er. kningen var gjennomgende hyere enn ansl i nasjonalbudsje ene samme r i perioden 1996 - 1999, som denne guren viser. Avvikene var spesielt store i 1997 og 1998. Denne glidningen er et problem og en u ordring for s vel kommunene som for den makrokonomiske styringen. P tyve r er det bli 240 000 ere sysselsa innenfor helse, omsorg og utdanning. Det er rundt 60 prosent av kningen i den samlede sysselse ngen i Norge i denne perioden. I helse- og omsorgssektoren ble antallet sysselsa e mer enn doblet p tyve r. Det arbeider n ere i denne sektoren enn i industrien samlet. Likevel fr vi daglig meldinger om personellmangel p sykehusene, i eldreomsorgen eller p skolene. Myndighetene varsler stadig kning i bevilgningene for  f bukt med problemene. Norge importerer personell fra andre land for  dekke ressursmangelen. Hvordan kan de e henge sammen? En rsak er at kravene l helsetjenester og dermed samfunnets utgi er p de e omrdet s ger markert nr inntektene s ger. I forhold l inntektsnivet har Norge likevel ikke spesielt hye helseutgi er internasjonalt se . En annen mulig rsak kunne vrt sammensetningen av befolkningen. Vi vet at vi om noen r m regne med sterk vekst i helseutgi ene p grunn av eldreblgen. Men i dag lsier slike demograske forhold ikke et srskilt press. U ordringene vil ke betydelig i rene som kommer. Fortsa inntektsvekst og eldreblgen vil ke presset for y erligere utbygging av helse- og omsorgstjenester. Det vil dessuten bli mulig  lby tjenester og behandlingsformer som ikke er lgjengelige i dag, men som trolig vil vre kostnadskrevende. Alt de e skal innpasses innenfor stramme personalrammer og budsje er som vanskelig kan vokse mer enn den samlede verdiskapingen, jf dr ingen av grenser for kningen i ska enivet dligere. Utgi er l pensjoner i Folketrygden vil legge beslag p en stadig strre andel av statens samlede utgi er. Selv med en vellykket oppbygging det nrmeste ret av en statlig nansformue gjennom blant annet Petroleumsfondet, m vi regne med at denne sparingen ikke vil vre mer enn det som trengs for  dekke kningen i pensjonsutgi ene, som illustrert i denne guren. Siden ska enivet i en stadig mer globalisert verden neppe kan heves srlig mye, vil andre oentlige utgi er dermed ikke kunne vokse mer enn den samlede verdiskapingen. Jeg vil illustrere de e. Figuren viser Norges Banks anslag for oentlige kjp av helse- og omsorgstjenester. Anslaget bygger p at det oentlige skal nansiere en like stor del av det samlede tjeneste lbudet som i dag. Anslaget for oentlig konsum er hentet fra det siste Lang dsprogrammet. Det grunnleggende problemet er at presset mot disse ytelsene vokser raskere enn inntektene fra ska er og avgi er. r for r, budsje for budsje , vil det bli vanskeligere  mte kravet om kt lgang p helse- og omsorgstjenester. Det vil vre grenser for hvor langt staten kan g i  redusere bevilgningene l andre vik ge samfunnsoppgaver, som utdanning, forskning og re svesen. Her m noe gi e er. Selv e er alle omlegginger de senere rene kan helse- og omsorgs lbudet trolig organiseres mer eek vt. En slik eek visering er likevel neppe lstrekkelig l  lse u ordringene. I llegg kan brukerne derfor i vesentlig strre grad selv m e st for nansieringen, enten ytelsene produseres i oentlig eller privat regi. Men det er grenser for hvor langt det oentlige kan g i retning av brukerbetaling uten at det blir uakseptable fordelingsvirkninger. Et privat forsikringssystem gir ikke et fullgodt svar p de e. Det er derfor vanskelig  forst annet enn at det oentlige m denere sine kjerneoppgaver klarere, bde innen helse og omsorg og p de andre omrdene. Det er behov for  avgrense hva det oentlige skal nansiere over ska eseddelen. Avslutning La meg oppsummere. Vekstpausen i norsk konomi var trolig over allerede i or. Til forskjell fra situasjonen da norsk konomi kom ut av nedgangs dene p begynnelsen av 1990-tallet, er utgangspunktet n en situasjon med meget hy kapasitetsutny else. Det er en desto strre u ordring  holde pris- og kostnadsveksten nede de nrmeste rene. De e er vik g blant annet for  unng at rammebe ngelsene l utekonkurrerende virksomheter, eller konkurranseutsa sektor, forverres y erligere og svekker grunnlaget for sysselse ngen og veksten i denne delen av konomien. De e vil trolig ogs kreve varsomhet nr det gjelder ekspansjon i oentlig sektor, for ikke  beslaglegge for mye av landets arbeidskra fremover. Oentlig mtehold kan vre ndvendig for at vi skal ha et oppegende nringsliv nr oljeinntektene begynner  falle. De e blir en krevende u ordring for myndighetene lokalt s vel som sentralt, gi det press for kt oentlig tjeneste lbud vi m tro kommer. kning av ska enivet for  nansiere kte oentlige utgi er er neppe noen holdbar lsning. Ska enivet i Norge er allerede hyt internasjonalt se og det pgr en ska ekonkurranse mellom landene som vi m tro vil skjerpes. Begrensningene i arbeidsmarkedet vil heller ikke lses ved kte ska er. Det er ogs vik g at de ulike poli kkelementene spiller sammen ved at de se es l  lse de oppgavene de er best egnet l. For at den konomiske poli kken skal fungere godt og n mlene om balansert langsik g vekst og varig hy sysselse ng, er det vik g at mekanismene rundt petroleumsfondet holdes intakt. Hvis vi klarer det, vil midlene i oljefondet ogs vre med  nansiere velferdsstaten nr Norge mter eldreblgen. Pengepoli kkens vik gste oppgave er  sikre et nominelt ankerfeste for konomien. Finanspoli kken er langt p vei avgjrende for fordelingen av realressursene i konomien. En nanspoli kk som bidrar l  dempe svingningene i realkonomien, og en lnnsdannelse som ivaretar hensynet l sysselse ngsgrunnlaget i konkurranseutsa e nringer, vil gjre Norges Banks ml om nominell stabilitet le ere  oppn. Title: The economic situation in Norway
text: The economic situa on in Norway "Diploma oredraget" - address by Governor Svein Gjedrem to invited foreign embassy representa ves, Norges Bank, Thursday, 30 March 2000 Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen In my address to you last year, I highlighted a turnaround in the Norwegian economy. A er six years of strong growth with increasing imbalances in the economy, the fall in oil prices, the interna onal financial crisis and slower growth in the world economy led to a period of sluggish growth. In Norges Bank's view, there was a risk of a defla onary recession. In fact, this par cular risk would now seem less prominent. At this me last year, oil prices stood at USD 10 a barrel. At present, oil prices are USD 24 a barrel, a er having hovered around USD 30 a barrel for a while. The period of sluggish growth now appears to be transient. European economies are expanding while the US economy is s ll booming. Even a er a year of slower growth, economic ac vity in Norway is s ll high. In my speech here today, my focus will be on explaining special aspects of the Norwegian economy, which is largely based on a limited number of commodi es. I shall discuss the importance of the petroleum sector and the challenges associated with vola le oil prices. Then I will give you a historical overview of monetary policy in Norway over the last 30 years. Against this background, I will try to explain how we conduct monetary policy today and give you our latest assessment of the prospects for the Norwegian economy. The importance of the petroleum sector Extrac on of North Sea oil started in the 1970s, and the produc on volume has increased over the years. The petroleum sector employs only a small part of the total labour force, but brings in substan al revenues. A main challenge to Norwegian economic policy is therefore to stabilise the Norwegian economy in the face of high, fluctua ng petroleum revenues. Some figures will illustrate the importance of the petroleum sector in the Norwegian economy. Given the current es mates for exis ng resources, produc on is expected to be at its maximum between 2000 and 2010. It is then expected to decrease gradually as the remaining resources are reduced. The future level of oil produc on is highly uncertain. Employment in the petroleum sector and related industries is only around 4 per cent of total employment. Investment in the petroleum sector has been substan al compared to investment in the rest of the economy, and as a share of GDP. Investment accounts for an import share of about 1/3. This means that investment rela ng to the petroleum sector has had a substan al effect on industries in mainland Norway. The petroleum sector is an important source of revenues for the government, both through taxes and through direct government ownership. Projec ons indicate that revenues will remain at about the same level un l around 2008, when they are expected to decrease gradually as petroleum produc on declines. The Norwegian government is running a budget surplus including petroleum revenues. The columns show the budget surplus (or deficit), excluding petroleum revenues. The line represents total net government surplus, which is transferred to the Government Petroleum Fund. The surplus also includes returns on Fund investments. We note that the amount of petroleum income used to finance public expenditure varies from year to year, while a large por on of the income is saved. Oil prices and hence petroleum revenues fluctuate over me. A er a period of high prices in the 1970s, when OPEC first demonstrated its power, and the early 1980s, oil prices have been fairly stable. Focusing on the last 15 years, somewhat larger fluctua ons have been observed since 1997. In 1998 the price of oil dropped temporarily below USD 10 a barrel. Last year the price increased substan ally above the USD 15 to USD 17 a barrel price range that we consider a more "normal" level. Today, the price is around USD 24 a barrel. Fluctua ng oil prices and economic stability: Dutch disease and the Government Petroleum Fund Oil revenues increase consump on poten al. However, it is a challenge to manage these resources in a way that increases welfare for current and future genera ons. A rapid expansion of the sheltered sector based on uncertain and perhaps temporary increases in petroleum revenues may lead to the situa on called Dutch disease. The impact of oil price fluctua ons on the exchange rate and on economic stability in general will depend on the speed at which petroleum revenues are used. In general, income can either be used now, or saved by accumula ng assets abroad, so as to redistribute the income and thus consump on between genera ons. If petroleum revenues are to be used for increased sheltered goods consump on, such as services like health care and educa on, a real exchange rate apprecia on, that is, a loss of compe veness, will be needed to ini ate the realloca on of resources to the sheltered sector. The extent of the realloca on will depend on how fast the revenues are used and how much is saved for future consump on. Suppose, as one extreme, that all government budget revenues were used in that same period. This means that an increase in the oil price would increase government revenues and domes c demand, encouraging a realloca on of resources from the exposed to the sheltered sector. If the oil price fell again later, Norway would be le with an exposed sector that is too small, resul ng in a current account deficit and expecta ons of an exchange rate deprecia on that would be needed to restore the exposed sector. Such fluctua ons in the use of oil revenues would lead to considerable instability in the Norwegian economy and large fluctua ons in the exchange rate over me. Norwegian economic policy is organised to counteract such instability. The key issue is to prevent increased petroleum revenues from leading directly to increased government consump on, in other words to reduce the dependence of government spending on oil revenues. The share of government spending financed by oil revenues varies over the business cycle. For the past few years this share has averaged around 3 per cent, and it is expected to be kept at about that level over the coming years. To this end, Norway has created the Government Petroleum Fund. The Fund receives revenues from the petroleum sector, transfers the amount necessary to produce a balanced government budget and invests the surplus abroad. As long as the increase in petroleum income is kept outside the domes c economy, there will be less need for structural change and thus less need for exchange rates to change. The Petroleum Fund serves many purposes. It is a means of storing wealth and redistribu ng income from oil extrac on between genera ons, of buffering against changes in oil prices, and of facilita ng demand management. Thus, the Fund facilitates the fiscal policy tasks of maintaining the desired size of the exposed sector and stabilising the economy. Historical perspec ve Let me now give you a longer term perspec ve to how the petroleum sector has impacted on the Norwegian economy and at the same me give you a background for monetary policy in Norway today. The post-war fixed exchange rate system - the Bre on Woods System - collapsed in 1971. A few years later, the Yom Kippur War broke out and OPEC countries suspended oil deliveries, triggering the first oil crisis. The sharp rise in oil prices led to a recession in the western economies. Moreover, infla on took root in most countries. In Europe, only Germany and Switzerland were able to keep infla on more or less at bay. In Norway, the welfare state and support schemes for businesses were rapidly expanded partly based on expecta ons of large future oil revenues. Furthermore, economic policy was oriented towards building a bridge over what was expected to be a temporary downturn in the world economy. This led to a tug of war for real resources between the business sector and the public sector - between the exposed and the sheltered sector. The cost level in manufacturing industry was driven upwards and compe veness detoriated. Two forces were behind economic developments from the beginning of the 1970s. First, the deteriora on in compe veness was caused by the expansion of the Norwegian welfare state and a transfer of real resources from the exposed sector to the sheltered sector. Second, infla on expecta ons took root as a result of low administered interest rates and compe ve devalua ons. Nominal interest rates were kept low although price infla on and the value of taxdeduc ble interest expenses rose. Frequent devalua ons in the period from 1976 were ul mately ineffec ve with regard to preven ng a rela ve decline in manufacturing industry. On the contrary, the devalua ons proved to be self-reinforcing. This chart proves the point. It shows consumer prices in Norway compared with consumer prices in Germany and the value of NOK against DEM since 1970. Over a period of 15 years from 1973 to 1988 consumer prices in Norway rose twice as much as in Germany. In the same period, the value of the krone was virtually halved against the Mark. While we paid around 2 kroner for one Mark in 1973, 15 years later we had to pay close to 4 kroner. Since then the krone has remained rela vely stable against the Deutsche Mark. Today the exchange rate is around 4 kroner and 15 ore. The last devalua on came in 1986 a er the fall in oil prices. Therea er, the krone exchange rate was fixed. The Norwegian economy had to go through a severe economic turnaround. Confidence in the krone had to be restored in order to avoid persistent infla on. This required very high interest rates. The Norwegian economy entered the worst recession experienced since the interwar period. Unemployment rose from about 2 per cent in 1987 to almost 6 per cent in the winter of 1992/1993. Many companies went broke and households were faced with debt problems. The financial sector was hit by crisis. The fixed exchange rate regime led to a gradual decline in price infla on, but not to defla on as was the case in Norway as well as in many other countries in the 1920s. An improved wage-se ng process, in conjunc on with an ac ve fiscal policy, contributed to curbing the real economic costs. Hence, the experience of 1986 and the beginning of the 1990s probably provides a realis c picture of the minimal costs associated with stamping out high infla on. In Norway, high infla on has been a war phenomenon and a phenomenon of the 1970s and 1980s. In the a ermath of high infla on, we experienced substan al real economic losses and financial instability. The cost of infla on has been high. History shows that lower unemployment cannot be achieved in exchange for higher infla on in the long run. A monetary policy that fuels infla on does not generate economic growth. On the contrary, the result is booms and specula ve bubbles, which are the precursors of recession and unemployment. In the absence of nominal stability, employment and produc on will not show stability either. The economy must be endowed with a nominal anchor. This is the task of monetary policy. The Norwegian economy was lacking a nominal anchor during the period of low interest rates and devalua ons in the 1970s and 1980s. This led to rising infla on and instability. From 1986 the fixed exchange rate regime restored confidence in monetary policy and subsequently laid a founda on for more stable economic developments. Through the 1990s, infla on has been on a par with or below infla on in Europe. While the average annual rise in prices was a good 8 per cent in Norway in the 1970s and 1980s, the annual rise in consumer prices has been confined to 2 per cent in the 1990s. The subdued rate of increase in consumer prices has coincided with a strong expansion. In 1999, the number of employed was 10 per cent higher than in 1990. We had to abandon our fixed exchange rate policy in December 1992, primarily as a result of the system's inherent weaknesses in a world of free flows of capital and deep interna onal financial markets. When the fixed exchange rate policy was formally abandoned, there was a risk that the Norwegian economy would again lose its nominal anchor. However, the krone exchange rate showed li le change and quickly found a new trading range. In the first years a er the fixed exchange rate regime was abandoned in 1992, the krone exchange rate was very stable, also on a daily basis. When we now look back at developments in the Norwegian foreign exchange market in the 1990s, we see no significant change in 1992. On the contrary, we witnessed a pronounced shi in January 1997. It was from this point in me that daily quota ons and month-to-month varia ons in the exchange rate show that the krone is floa ng. In 1996 and in the autumn of 1998, Norges Bank a empted to reduce movements in the krone exchange rate through exchange market interven ons. On both occasions, interven ons prompted a game situa on between the central bank and market par cipants, as was also the case during the currency crisis in the autumn of 1992. When a central bank trades its own currency, market operators make a play for profits on the premise that the exchange rate does not reflect market fundamentals. In a world where capital flows freely, this game situa on can quickly trigger large capital movements. The experience of the 1990s shows that Norges Bank does not have the instruments to fine-tune the krone exchange rate. Today's monetary policy The objec ve of monetary policy is exchange rate stability against European currencies, defined as the euro from 1 January 1999. Norges Bank's mandate - which is the Exchange Rate Regula on - takes into account that the krone may remain outside its normal range. The Exchange Rate Regula on states that "in the event of significant changes in the exchange rate, monetary policy instruments will be oriented with a view to returning the exchange rate over me to its ini al range". The concept "significant changes" is not quan fied and must be given an economic content. Norges Bank interprets a "significant" change in the exchange rate as a change that fuels expecta ons of price and cost infla on to the extent that the change in the exchange rate becomes self-reinforcing. Monetary policy can counter such a self-reinforcing movement in the exchange rate by contribu ng to low and stable infla on without recession. In its conduct of monetary policy, Norges Bank therefore places emphasis on fulfilling the fundamental precondi ons for exchange rate stability against the euro: Monetary policy instruments must be oriented towards bringing infla on down to the level aimed at by the Eurosystem. At the same me, Norges Bank must prevent monetary policy from contribu ng to a defla onary recession as this may weaken confidence in the krone. Fiscal policy and the Government Petroleum Fund have proved to be effec ve in terms of sheltering the mainland economy from more normal varia ons in oil revenues. A permanent change in the krone exchange rate will occur if there is an increase in the use of oil revenues through a shi in expenditure growth. In this context, instruments other than those available to Norges Bank must be used to return the krone to its ini al range. Over the last 15 years, the business cycle in Norway has differed from the cycles in most European countries. The output gap provides a rough indica on of the phase of the business cycle. The chart shows a specifically Norwegian upturn in the mid-1980s and a subsequent downturn. While the downturn bo omed out in Norway in 1990, other European economies were booming. Subsequently, the business cycles have remained different. The economic fluctua ons in Norway can to some extent be traced back to the disturbances in the Norwegian economy in the 1980s and the economic shock in Europe in the wake of the fall of the Berlin Wall. The divergence in business cycles is the main reason behind the infla on differen al between Norway and euro area countries. The very low rate of infla on in Europe primarily reflects the downturn in the 1990s. A fundamental precondi on for exchange rate stability against the euro is that the infla on rate in Norway is brought down to the level aimed at by the Eurosystem. In recent years, the rate of increase in prices has been higher in Norway than among euro area countries, which is reflected in the interest rate differen al between Norway and the euro area. The economic situa on Signs of an overhea ng of the Norwegian economy, with a sharp increase in wage growth, low oil prices and interna onal financial turbulence, contributed to a marked deprecia on of the krone exchange rate in mid-1998. In an environment of strong pressures in the economy, there was a risk of a self-reinforcing deprecia on of the krone. In response to these developments, Norges Bank raised its key rates by a considerable margin in the period to end-August 1998. When the euro was introduced as a common currency in the 11 euro area countries on 1 January 1999, the krone stood at 8.86 against the euro. At the same me, the three-month money market rate in Norway was 8 per cent, or 4.5 percentage points higher than the level in the euro area. The high level of interest rates in the la er half of 1998 and a ght central government budget for 1999 dampened the pressures in the economy. At the same me, the growth prospects for the interna onal economy were weak. At the beginning of 1999, the outlook for the Norwegian economy implied a reduc on in price and cost infla on over the following years to the level aimed at by the euro area. Furthermore, Norges Bank's analyses pointed to a risk of a downturn that could weaken confidence in the krone. The objec ve of exchange rate stability over me thus implied that it was appropriate to reduce interest rates. In the course of 1999, Norges Bank lowered its key rates from 8 percent to 5 per in five steps. There was a marked apprecia on of the krone exchange rate in the same period. Norges Bank has le its key rates unchanged since September 1999. One week ago Norges Bank its most recent analysis of the outlook for the Norwegian economy in our Infla on Report for the first quarter. Our analyses indicate that the current consolida on in the Norwegian economy, a er a decade of strong growth, may be less painful than expected earlier. Developments in 1999 indicate that the slowdown in the Norwegian economy came to an end last summer. With the excep on of fixed investment in the petroleum sector, all demand components exhibited an upward movement in the second half of last year. A number of indicators point to higher growth in private consump on in recent months. Retail sales and credit growth are rising. House prices con nue to dri up. Normally, higher house prices lead to lower saving and higher private consump on. Households are increasingly op mis c about their financial posi on and the economic prospects for Norway. Norsk Gallup's consumer confidence indicator con nued to rise in February, reaching its highest level since the summer of 1998 when interest rates were increased. This consumer confidence indicator usually provides a good indica on of movements in private consump on. The growth outlook for trading partners has improved. Growth in the world economy recovered rela vely quickly a er the crisis in the autumn of 1998. The chart shows forecasts for global GDP growth in 2000 at various points in me. Economic developments in the crisis-hit countries in Asia were reversed more quickly than an cipated. At the same me, the long period of expansion in the US has con nued, and growth rates in Europe have con nued to rise. Tradi onal merchandise exports have increased in recent months, reflec ng higher growth in the global economy. Es mates for export growth have been revised upwards. Oil prices have more than doubled compared with the same period last year. A year ago, our es mate of the current account surplus for this year was around 2 per cent of GDP. Now, our es mate is 11 per cent of GDP, or NOK 150 billion. Business investment is expected to con nue to make a nega ve contribu on to growth this year. But the fall in investment is now es mated to be more moderate than earlier projected. This, combined with improved global economic prospects and expecta ons of higher consumer demand, has led us to raise the forecast for mainland GDP growth to 1 % in 2000 and 2% in 2001. While fairly moderate, these forecasts are considerably higher than envisaged one year ago. Pressures in the labour market remain strong. So far, the contrac on in manufacturing has been more than offset by con nued high employment growth in the public and private service sectors. Against the background of an upward revision of output growth this year and next, the turnaround in the labour market is now expected to be less pronounced than earlier projected. Our es mates point to a very moderate rise in unemployment from 3 per cent this year to around 3 per cent in 2001 and 2002. The risk of a downturn in the economy now appears to be limited. The risk of rising price and cost infla on has increased. In the light of recent economic trends and the balance of risks, the probability that the next change in interest rates will be an increase is greater than the probability of a reduc on. Conclusions Let me conclude by summing up as follows. The Norwegian economy is highly dependent upon a few basic commodi es, of which oil and gas naturally are the most important. Oil prices and revenues from the petroleum sector vary. We must learn to live with that. To this end, Norway has created the Government Petroleum Fund, which serves among other things as a buffer against changes in oil prices. Since inves ng the surplus abroad, the domes c economy is more or less sheltered from fluctua ng oil prices. The Fund therefore also supports monetary policy in Norway, by helping to keep the exchange rate stable. The period of sluggish growth envisaged last year seems to be over. Our latest projec ons indicate that economic growth will pick up to more normal levels in one or two years. The pressure in the economy is s ll high. Norges Bank must therefore use the means necessary to secure stable economic developments, thereby stabilising the krone exchange rate. Thank you for your a en on. I will now be happy to answer any ques ons you may have. 30. mars 2000 14:00

Title: Economic developments in 2000, expectations for 2001. Impact on business and society
text: Economic developments in 2000, expectations for 2001. Impact on business and society Speech by Governor Svein Gjedrem. Trondheim Business Association, 31 August 2000 One of the biggest inconsistenceable effects on the Norwegian economy today is the high e-demand e is a workhorse compared to the current one. Sam dig will be the number of workers in health and education services increasing in the years ahead. As a result, there will be less unemployment in manufacturing and business. The tight labour market, strong lending growth and a fairly weak krone have contributed to higher interest rates in Norway than in many other countries with which we compare ourselves. There has been sluggish growth in mainland labour production Norway in recent years. Economic developments The Norwegian economy has a long upturn behind it. Since 1993, we have had solid economic growth, only to be interrupted by a slight pause in growth from the summer of 1998 in the summer of 1999. Although the 1990s started with high unemployment in Norway and crisis in the financial industry, we can say that the 1990s were a golden year. From 1993 there was strong growth in output and employment, and unemployment fell from about 6 per cent l slightly above 3 per cent in 1999. High economic growth has coincided with low and stable inflation. Norges Bank's projections from June showed that if economic policy was not tightened l, consumer price inflation this year would be 3 per cent and around 21/2 per cent over the next two years. This is in excess of what we can expect to be consistent with exchange rate stability measured against the euro. The European Central Bank has said it aims to keep the price slide in the euro area low and it is likely to succeed. The economy is now at a period of somewhat lower growth than we experienced from 1994 in the first half of 1998, but higher than in the second half of 1998 and 1999. Norges Bank expects the bridge international product for mainland Norway to increase by 13/4 per cent this year. Growth is expected to be 11/2 per cent over the next two years. The risk of a marked downturn over the next two years is small, but has been reduced as a result of higher-than-expected growth in business costs. The risk of higher price and cost inflation has also increased. The situation in the Norwegian economy is currently characterised by strong growth in the 1990s. The number of unemployed has quadrupled since the beginning of the 1990s. Today, there are more than 20,000 vacancies in Norway. There have never been more. Labour force participation is at a record high and the labour market is becoming very tight. Three-thirds of the population between the ages of 16 and 74 are in the labour force. Only Iceland has higher occupational participation than Norway. The high professional frequency means that it is probably limited how many more people we can draw into the labour force. Perhaps more young people will choose work over education if labour market pressures continue. In recent years, e-demand e is partly covered by work crashes from abroad. Better prospects for economic growth in our neighbouring countries, such as Sweden and Finland, may contribute to this spring drying up, even though wages are high in Norway for many groups. Measures such as cash-strapped parents and contractual pension schemes have contributed to increased welfare. But the ltaks mean that more people are choosing to pull out of the workforce. In a year from Sta sk central agency, it is estimated that cash-steady an isolated se has reduced the workforce by 3 500 l 4 500 man-years. The survey was carried out only a few months e is that the reform was fully developed. It is conceivable that the effect will be greater as the reform has worked. The number of persons with a contractual pension scheme has increased markedly since the scheme was introduced in 1989. During 1999, 10 000 people chose to retire, and at the end of the year there were about 25 000 people on this Scheme. This year, the number of AFP schemes in the private sector has increased by 16 per cent from the same period last year. They are a trend that is likely to intensify in the years ahead, partly as a result of more people in the relevant age group (62-66 years). A sharp increase in the number of disability pensioners in recent years has also contributed to reducing the workforce. About 10 per cent of the population between the ages of 18 and 67 were in or out of retirement. During the year there were 12 000 new disability benefits. The AFP scheme has therefore not visibly reduced the disability pension scheme, as was expected. Sickness absence has also shown a strong increase since 1995, e is that from 1989 in 1994 there was a decrease every year. The number of sick pay days increased by 5 per cent per employment from 1998 to 1999. In the end, it is decided to extend the holiday for most occupational groups by a total of four days over the next two years. Four extra vacation days in isolation reduce the amount of work it does by just under 2 per cent per year. Some of the e will be matched by more over ds jobbing and more working days for part dsansa e, so that the ne o effect will be less. Norges Bank has estimated that the growth potential for the mainland economy will be reduced by about 1/4 percentage point both over the next two years as a result of these e. If these tendencies are not matched by increased employment among young people, for example, growth in the labour force will be lower in the years ahead. This will contribute to a tighter labour market. It's going to be an even bigger u-wording to hold. price and cost inflation down. There are signs of geographical and business imbalances in the labour market. There is strong growth in employment in large parts of the private and public services sector, while employment in manufacturing is declining, particularly in the workshop industry, which is largely located along the coast. Nevertheless, I do not want to draw too dark a picture for industry and business. There are bright spots and op-eds in many industries. Large parts of the business sector are benefiting from a severe international upturn. The development this year has been posi v for large parts of traditional exporting a business. Many industries report high capacity renewal and high exports. The fish farm industry and the aluminium industry are examples of industries that are doing well. This chart shows county-distributed figures for registered unemployed. It is particularly in agder counties and western Norway that unemployment has increased over the past year. Unemployment has been more stable in the inland and in the large urban areas where private and public services are of greater importance. The sell-off in employment in manufacturing is largely due to lower investment in the North Sea. Moreover, the competitiveness of the industry and the profitability of exports have deteriorated. Labour costs in Norway are growing considerably stronger than among our trading partners. For the period 1997 - 2001, we can expect wages to increase by 10 percentage points more in Norway than in a survey of other countries. Through the latter part of the 1990s, competitiveness in isolation was improved by the depreciation of the krone exchange rate. The business sector has also been helped in recent months by a rela vt weak krone, particularly against the US dollar and the british pound. The competitive situation is somewhat in the short term. However, the depreciation of the krone has been hand in hand with higher price and cost inflation than abroad. Sooner or later, higher costs measured in NOK that do not have a counterpart in increased production will probably have an impact on deteriorating cost competitiveness. The cost-cutting in Norway and low earnings in large parts of the business sector can result in a faster sell-off of jobs and jobs. This may have an impact on the outlook for cost and price developments, for the exchange rate and for the interest rate ahead. The economic outlook for the world economy and for our trading partners has been revised upwards in the last three or four economic reports presented by Norges Bank - the ones we call the Inflation Report. Growth in the US has remained high for a long time, and growth is expected to continue for some time l. The situation among the euro area countries and Japan has also improved. Sweden is in a period of rapid growth driven by exports, private consumption and investment. The stronger growth in other countries means higher demand for Norwegian goods and services. Strong growth abroad will be a driving force for the Norwegian economy this year and next. Pengepoli kken The monetary policy objective is stability in the krone exchange rate against European currencies, since 1 January 1999 defined as the euro. The mandate allows for discretion in the exercise of monetary policy. In its exercise of discretion, Norges Bank places emphasis on the fundamental preconditions for stability in the krone exchange rate: In order to achieve exchange rate stability against the euro, monetary policy instruments must be tightened so that price and cost inflation comes down to the point aimed at by the European Central Bank (ECB). In isolation, Norges Bank must avoid that monetary policy itself does not contribute to deflationary deflation, because this may weaken the krone. There is therefore no conflict between adjusting monetary policy instruments against low and stable inflation and the objective of stability in the krone exchange rate. Norges Bank has raised key rates three times by a total of 1.25 percentage points since April this year. The key policy rate - banks' deposit rate in Norges Bank - is 6.75 per cent. With these e, we have made significant changes in the interest rate that is rich based on the analyses we presented in our Inflation Report in June this year. Nevertheless, there is a probability that the next change in the interest rate will be an increase. It is the combination of higher interest rates abroad, a weaker krone against some currencies and the prospects of a particularly Norwegian price and cost glg over a long period that has led Norges Bank to increase its interest rates. The global upturn has also led to prospects of higher inflationary pressures abroad. Since last summer, the US Federal Reserve has raised its key policy rate by 1.75 per cent to 6.5 per cent. Many other central banks have also raised their key rates over the past year. Interest rate increases reflect a pick-up in economic growth in countries. Developments also have an impact on the interest rate in Norway. Among other things, higher interest rates and returns in other countries may make it more of a priority for the business sector and financial players to invest funds abroad. This may weaken the krone. In addition, interest rate increases from Norges Bank this spring must be viewed on the basis of exchange rate developments. The Norwegian krone has been weak for a long period. Over the past year, it had depreciated by 3 1/2 per cent against a scent of other currencies. The weakening comes in what we pay for the U.S. dollar. A year ago, a dollar cost 7.80. Now we pay li over 9 kroner for it. The impact on the euro has been smaller. This is due to a very weak euro for it. We must take into account that the euro in the coming years may be strengthening. The depreciation of the krone contributes to higher prices for goods and services that we buy from abroad and contributes to higher prices in Norway than in other countries. U-wording in the economic policing Norway is now benefiting from high oil prices, which result in high petroleum revenues and large surpluses in the current balance sheet. A substantial share of these revenues is invested abroad through the Government Petroleum Fund. As a result, the Norwegian mainland economy is significantly shielded from the impact of large petroleum revenues. They are a victorian purpose of the oil fund. The relatively weak krone therefore now reflects developments in the Norwegian mainland economy. Government finances in Norway are boosted by high petroleum revenues. The surplus on the state budget for this year - before transfers in the Petroleum Fund - is estimated at more than NOK 120 billion in the revised national budget. The amount will be much larger if oil prices remain around the level seen in recent months. Petroleum revenues provide substantial fiscal relief. We have the opportunity to curb growth in the upturn there, and see more of a slowdown there. In other countries, burdensome government debt has meant that fiscal policy can no longer be used particularly for stabilisation purposes, at least not in decline there. The build-up of the fund takes into account the distribution of petroleum revenues between generations and contributes to stability in the government's finances in the long term. The larger the fund, the less dependent it will be on petroleum revenues. What is most eye-catching about government finances, however, is, as the chart shows, the ell of obligations in the form of pensions that the government pushes ahead of it. The government's pension is estimated to increase from 8 per cent of GDP in 1998 to about 17 per cent of GDP in 2050. Public consumption has increased steadily. In the short term, fiscal policy may affect developments in output and employment no. In a longer perspek v, the unequality of fiscal policing, including the system, the public investments and publishing are, for example, research and education, of great importance for the growth potential of the economy. In llegg the growth in public publishing is, as the authorities put up l, affect of work crashes and capital between different sectors of the economy. Unless there are vacant reserves of labour coerc or capital, increased use of resources in the public sector will impose production factors that would be renewed in the business sector. Norway are among the countries with the highest share of public sector employment. The demand for employment in the health and social care sector will increase significantly in the period ahead. They are due to the age of the population. In addition, a continuation of the current lbud and the implementation of a number of reforms in the municipal service will contribute to a sharp increase in the need for work crashes in the municipal sector going forward. One possible solution to these could be to curb growth in the part of the business sector that does not compete on the world market. That would require higher ska er. As Norges Bank expressed in our letter from October in Or do households today have a strong sledging in the labour market and the sheltered ones are a strong sing in the product market. One may therefore fear that any increase will largely be overturned in the form of higher labour costs and higher price margins and thus higher domestic price and cost inflation. Ska competition between countries is also a factor. Another solution would be a sharp increase in manufacturing in the future. Should manufacturing in the business sector grow more than expected, inflation may be lower than projected . If economic developments are to be balanced, with low inflation and high employment, any increase in demand and output must be largely countered by increased productivity. New economy or old connections? Recently, there has been considerable interest in the strong developments in the US economy. From 1995 to 1999, there was an annual growth in production of more than 4 per cent. In July, the US entered its 105th consecutive month of growth in industrial production. That's a record. The product's growth has increased and inflation has been low. The economic upturn in the US through the 1990s has led to claims that the relationships in the economy have changed. That is, it is a "new economy". Although the new economy is not an unambiguous term, there are three features in particular that characterize the new economy. First, it appears that there has been an increase in underlying product growth. Growth in the labour output increased by about 1 percentage point from the first half of the 1990s in the second half. Some prominent AMERICAN researchers believe that the majority (2/3) of this acceleration is due to high investments in information technology, and more affect the production of computer equipment. Second, the high investments in information technology and a strong belief in high earnings in IT companies have led to a sharp rise in the share price in this industry. Many of these shares have fallen in value in recent d, as it has proved too high and unrealisical expectations in terms of earnings in these companies. Third, many believe that flexibility in the labour market increased. This means that unemployment may be lower without inflation rising. The special feature of the upturn in the US in the 1990s is that inflation has remained low and that product growth has increased. The upturn in manufacturing growth has come at a stage of the cyclical cycle, where experience could indicate that it was slowing. There is a close connection between these two phenomena. Trondheim kan se p seg selv som en stor eksportr av kunnskapskapital. Avslutning La meg avslu e med  g lbake l pengepoli kken. Som nevnt prver vi  holde valutakursen stabil overfor euro. Det krever at priss gningen konvergerer mot europeisk standard. Det er ere forhold som har bidra l at Norges Bank kte renten for  styrke grunnlaget for stabil kurs.
