When the idea of a government petroleum fund was discussed in the Long -Term Programme 1986-89, the government at that me stressed the importance of establishing a fund structure that limited the opportuni es for rent seeking behaviour: "The use of government petroleum revenues shall exclusively take place via the central government budget, partly for financing purchases of goods and services and transfers, and partly as a source for financing loans to state credit ins tu ons gran ng loans to other sectors. Except for financing of the State's direct financial interest in the petroleum sector (SDFI), the transfers [to the fund] shall not be earmarked for par cular purposes. This implies that the transfers are part of the budget's financial basis in general." This point of view was repeated in the Government proposi on to establish the Government Petroleum Fund in 19908: "The investment alterna ves for the Petroleum Fund must be strictly limited. The Petroleum Fund shall not be an alterna ve source of financing for programmes that are given lower priority in the compe on for budget expenditure. Fixed investment in Norway should be financed as previously, and not specifically through the Petroleum Fund. Even if this ini ally could be defined as a use of fund income in accordance with long- term guidelines, fixed investment financed in this way will increase domes c demand. Further, fiscal discipline would deteriorate, by reducing the constraints on the various spending programmes in the central government budget." The risk of rent seeking is par cularly high when assets including elements of economic rent are transferred from the state, and when the price is agreed in bilateral nego a ons. Where a market exists, the state should generally prefer to check any price against other interested par es in the marketplace. The transfer of economic rent directly to the state has been the key argument for maintaining significant parts of the State Direct Financial Interest (SDFI) [in the petroleum sector] in public ownership. Because of the large element of economic rent, SDFI ownership cannot be confused with the discussion about state ownership in enterprises. Varying SDFI ownership according to the size of economic rent is far simpler than varying the marginal tax between fields. Secondly, it is doub ul that the state would receive a fair price if a large part of SDFI assets were sold. The buyer should be expected to have be er informa on than the state itself about the underlying value of these assets. The buyer will also face uncertainty about the future tax system, nega vely affec ng their willingness to pay. 4. To ensure a high rate of return on petroleum wealth and financial assets in public ownership The Government Petroleum Fund is s ll limited in size compared with the net present value of SDFI and future royal es, taxes and tariffs in the petroleum sector. During the next years, we will see a substan al transforma on of wealth from petroleum to financial assets. This represents, as I commented ini ally, a diversifica on of risk and transfer of wealth into high yielding assets. The current investment strategy of the Petroleum Fund is based on diversifying the market risk over interna onal equi es and fixed income products in twenty-seven countries in more than 1750 individual companies and more than 450 bonds. This does not protect the fund from nega ve por olio effects resul ng from a global downturn. However, the strategy protects the por olio from significant problems in a single enterprise, sector or country. The basic por olio decision is the choice between expected long- term return and short- term risk. The Ministry of Finance is responsible for this decision, primarily through the limits it has set for equi es in the por olio. There has been opposi on to the strategy of broad diversifica on. An alterna ve strategy of large and focused business investments in selected foreign companies has been suggested. In order to recommend such a strategy, one needs to be convinced that a significantly higher expected return from concentrated business investments compensates for the extra por olio risk. However, the evidence is not compelling. The alterna ve to large, concentrated investments in a limited number of enterprises will at any me in the future be an investment in a broadly diversified equity por olio. The la er por olio entails lower risk. If a concentrated por olio s ll should be preferred, this por olio must produce an expected return above the expected return of the equity market in general. There might be a link between the size of the capital in the Fund, and the pressure to spend part of the capital on projects where elements other than the financial return and risk level are important. While the fund is not earmarked for future pension payments, these future outlays are an obvious reason for saving significant parts of petroleum revenues today. The construc on of the Government Petroleum Fund may be cri cised for not making the inten on to save sufficiently clear. When the Petroleum Deple on Commi ee first suggested a petroleum fund in 1983, the inten on was to provide a buffer against short -term fluctua ons in oil revenues. Later, petroleum ac vi es were substan ally expanded, based on an explicit assump on that it is possible to separate explora on from the use of revenues. The public need for saving has gradually become a more important issue for the Petroleum Fund, not least because of significant upward revisions of es mates for future welfare expenditure. It has been suggested that earmarking the Petroleum Fund assets for future re rement payments will make future use of these assets more transparent, and increase public support for saving a large part of the revenues today. Such earmarking may be accomplished either by changing the Petroleum Fund to a state pension fund, or by pre-funding a mandatory pension saving scheme outside the public sector. In the la er case, pension commitments will also be transferred from the state to pension fund suppliers. If the responsibility for saving for future supplementary pensions is moved from the state to the individual, a likely solu on will be to compensate saving requirements through a reduc on of compulsory pension insurance payments to the state. In their recent economic survey of Norway, the OECD has also discussed such reforms. A transfer of an equal amount of assets and pension commitments from the public sector to the private sector does not reduce the challenge to financing the future welfare system. On the other hand, further improvements in the part of the pension system that has been transferred will no longer be a public responsibility. Earmarking the Petroleum Fund for future pensions will reduce the government's financial flexibility. The effect on public and private saving is uncertain. Saving takes place in a global context. Individual saving is increasingly channelled through interna onal funds. Capital seeks poten al return, and the na onal markets are evermore integrated into the global market scene. Norwegian enterprises will receive capital only to the extent investors are offered a compe ve expected return. Any analysis of the impact of an individual based pension saving scheme should take this fact into considera on. Concluding remarks Norway has an opportunity to turn petroleum wealth into a long - term advantage. A posi ve outcome depends on our ability to learn from the mistakes of other resource abundant na ons. A cau ous phasing in of oil revenues into the Norwegian economy counteracts instability related to oil prices. By applying a cau ous and long-term oriented approach to spending oil revenues, an excessive crowding out of the interna onally exposed sector, resul ng in a loss of growth capacity, will be avoided. Thank you for your a en on. Footnotes: 1 Na onal Budget 2001 2 See, for example, Sachs/Warner: Natural Resource Abundance and Economic Growth, NBER Working Paper no. W5398, (Harvard, 1995) 3 IMF Public Informa on No ce, IMF concludes Ar cle IV 2000 Consulta ons with Kazakhstan, December 2000 4 IMF Staff Country report, Islamic republic of Iran, September 2000 5 Hanneson (2001): "Inves ng for Sustainability, The Management of Mineral Wealth". 6 Ugo Fasano: Review of the Experience with Oil Stabiliza on and Savings Funds in Selected Countries, IMF Working Paper WP/00/112, June 2000 7 See A.J. Auerbach and L.J. Kotlikoff (1987): Dynamic Fiscal Policy, Cambridge University Press, Cambridge and E. Steigum Jr. (1993): "Accoun ng for Long-Run Effects of Fiscal Policy by Means of Computable Overlapping Genera ons Models", in: S. Honkapohja and M. Ingberg (eds.), Macroeconomic Modelling and Policy Implica ons, Elsevier Science Publishers, Amsterdam. 8 Ot.prp no. 29(1989-90) 7. mars 2001 14:00

Title: The economic situation in Norway
text: The economic situa on in Norway "Diploma oredraget" - Address by Central Bank Governor Svein Gjedrem to invited foreign embassy representa ves, Norges Bank, 15 March 2001 Norway's economy is today characterised by substan al petroleum revenues, sharp growth in government expenditure, a ght labour market and high cost infla on. High oil prices and sizeable petroleum produc on are contribu ng to surpluses on the current account and the central government budget. This has also resulted in a vigorous rise in Norway's disposable income. The current account surplus in 2000, which was about 14 per cent of GDP, is among the highest surpluses recorded by an OECD country in the post-war period. The total general government budget surplus also rose sharply, reaching 141/2 per cent of GDP. With the excep on of a brief pause in growth from the summer of 1998, the Norwegian economy has been expanding since 1993. Employment has risen and unemployment has fallen to just over 3 per cent. A shortage of labour in many sectors has resulted in a rela vely sharp growth in labour costs. Whereas the upturn was balanced for a long period, the public sector has laid claim to a large share of the increase in the labour supply in recent years. Manufacturing employment has fallen markedly since 1998. Working me reforms, increased use of sick pay and disability benefits and a reduced supply of labour from other Nordic countries are restraining growth in many sectors. Moreover, there is no evidence sugges ng that produc vity growth in Norway has picked up to the levels in some of our neighbouring countries. The economic situa on The mainland economy features some aspects that are associated with a boom period, although growth is low. A er several years of mainland GDP growth in the order of 3-4 per cent, ac vity is now increasing by less than 2 per cent a year. Economic growth slowed towards the end of last year, but there is s ll a shortage of labour. The economy is opera ng near capacity limits, and wage and price infla on is higher than among our trading partners. Consumer prices increased by an average of 3.1 per cent last year. Excluding changes in electricity and fuel prices and indirect taxes, the underlying rise in prices was 2.4 per cent. Last year Norges Bank increased its key interest rates four mes by a total of 1.5 percentage points. At the end of the year the sight deposit rate stood at 7 per cent. The interest rate differen al vis-a-vis the euro-area widened somewhat to 23/4 percentage points through the year. Last week Norges Banks its most recent analysis of the outlook for the Norwegian economy in our Infla on Report. Norges Bank projects consumer price infla on at 3 per cent in 2001. If interest rates remain unchanged at the current level, price infla on may approach 2 per cent from the end of 2002. Consumer price infla on is influenced by the increase in oil prices. The sharp rise in 1999 and 2000 is expected to con nue to have an impact on prices for goods and services, par cularly this year. Our analysis indicates that the slowdown in ac vity that started in the last half of the previous year will con nue this year. From next year, however, we expect ac vity to pick up somewhat. Increased op mism in some manufacturing sectors and higher petroleum investment would indicate more posi ve developments in manufacturing. On the other hand, interna onal developments have been somewhat weaker than expected. The uncertainty surrounding interna onal developments is primarily associated with the severity of the downturn in the US and how long it takes before growth picks up again. A pronounced downturn that has an impact on the world economy will reduce consumer price infla on interna onally. The effects of such a turnaround on the Norwegian economy will, however, be mixed. Substan al parts of the Norwegian export industry are already producing near capacity, and the slowdown is expected to have li le impact on this sector. The effects on developments in commodity prices and exchange rates are uncertain. If the interna onal slowdown develops into a situa on where commodity prices are severely nega vely affected, the Norwegian economy may suffer. I will elaborate on the risks and uncertain es in the interna onal situa on later. Mainland GDP is projected to grow by 11/4 per cent in 2001. With unchanged interest rates in the period ahead, annual mainland GDP growth may be 11/2 per cent the next two years. The rela vely high interest rates - the three-month money market rate is currently at around 71/4 per cent - will contribute to modest growth in private consump on and fixed investment. Public expenditure is expected to grow in line with poten al output at around 2 per cent. Pressures in the labour market remain strong. We expect the unemployment rate to remain at just over 3 per cent in the years ahead. Underlying this projec on is an employment growth of roughly 1/2 per cent, equal to the growth in the labour force. The increase in labour costs has been higher in Norway than among our trading partners in most of the last decade. This situa on will con nue, even if wage growth is expected to fall somewhat in the years ahead. High growth in labour costs is the main reason consumer price infla on increased through last year. The interna onal environment In the last few years, interna onal developments have led to major changes in the outlook for the Norwegian economy. In 1998, the crisis in Russia triggered a strong deprecia on of the krone, rising interest rates and weakening domes c demand. At the same me weak developments in Asia contributed to falling oil prices and a slower rise in prices for imported goods. The interna onal recovery was fast, and through 1999 and 2000 world trade expanded. The price of crude oil increased from USD 10 per barrel at the beginning of 1999 to USD 29 per barrel on average last year. Rising oil prices contributed to higher consumer price infla on. Interna onal equity prices declined sharply last autumn. The downward trend con nued in the first months of this year. In the US, output and employment are stagna ng. As shown in the chart, the risk premium in capital markets on long-term credit to enterprises has increased. In addi on, many interna onal enterprises now have a poorer credit ra ng than earlier. At present it is not clear how severe the downturn in the US economy will be. The con nuing upturn during the 1990s was driven by high growth in produc vity, increased fixed investment and a steady decrease in household saving. If the downturn entails a complete reversal of this development, the economic slowdown will be more severe than we have an cipated. The effect on the Norwegian economy will to a large extent depend on the reac ons in commodity, financial and capital markets. Lower interna onal economic growth and infla on could induce a further lowering of short-term interest rates abroad in the next months. The interest rate differen al between Norwegian rates and interna onal rates may then widen. The price of crude oil plays a major part in interna onal economic cycles. If the oil price falls significantly, infla on will decrease due to reduced imported infla on and lower energy prices. On the other hand a falling oil price may trigger a weakening of the krone, offse ng the effects of reduced import and energy prices. The pricing of op ons in the oil market indicates that market par cipants are uncertain with regard to future developments. This uncertainty must be viewed against the backdrop of low oil stocks, high capacity u lisa on in a number of OPEC countries and unrest in the Middle East, which may have contributed to fears of high prices. OPEC has previously stated that the oil price should lie within a target range of USD 22-28 measured as an average of various grades of oil. For North Sea oil (Brent Blend), this corresponds to an interval of USD 23-29. The ver cal lines in the chart indicate that at the end of February market par cipants priced in a 10 per cent probability that the oil price in December 2001 would be less than USD 18 per barrel, and a 10 per cent probability that it would be higher than USD 35.5 per barrel. Should a significant fall in the oil price occur, this would dampen ac vity in the Norwegian economy, in contrast to an expected boost in oil impor ng countries. Reduced income in the petroleum sector will reduce fixed investment, and consumer confidence may be nega vely affected. Monetary policy The long-term objec ve of monetary policy is to provide the Norwegian economy with a nominal anchor - domes c price stability - and thereby the basis for a stable krone. Nominal stability is the best contribu on monetary policy can make to economic growth and prosperity. A nominal anchor is also a necessary precondi on for stable financial markets and property markets. By linking movements in the krone to the euro, we have chosen to follow the same standard for nominal stability in the economy as set by the euro area countries. Our experience is that changes in the Norwegian interest rate level only have a predictable effect on the krone exchange rate when the change in interest rates also contributes to stabilising infla on. However, the rela onship between interest rates and price and cost developments is uncertain. The se ng of interest rates thus requires the use of professional judgement and discre on. The basis for exercising discre on is subject to limita ons, however. Should any doubt arise as to whether the interest rate is oriented towards nominal stability, this would trigger substan al capital movements. Since 1997, infla on has been higher in Norway than in the euro area. The difference partly reflects a period of strong growth in Norway, while the level of ac vity in Europe has been low. The higher level of infla on in Norway cannot be sustained, however, as this would undermine the basis for stability in the krone exchange rate and confidence in monetary policy. As I men oned earlier, in our projec on price infla on approaches 2 per cent from the end of 2002 if interest rates remain unchanged at the current level. Short-term capital inflows and ou lows are probably the most important factor determining movements in the krone exchange rate from day to day, from week to week and from one quarter to the next. They are governed by expecta ons concerning future returns. Changes in expecta ons concerning the future value of the krone can trigger extensive capital movements. As a rule, Norges Bank does not intervene in foreign exchange markets with a view to influencing the krone exchange rate. The krone is floa ng, and the value of the krone fluctuates in periods by the same magnitude as exchange rates in other open economies. Nevertheless, the prevailing stability of the krone is largely a reflec on of confidence that infla on in Norway will be kept at a low level. Interac on with income forma on A precondi on for a stable krone exchange rate against European currencies is that price and cost infla on in Norway must over me not exceed the corresponding aim for infla on of the European Central Bank (ECB). The ECB orients monetary policy instruments towards price stability, and has defined price stability as an infla on rate below 2 per cent. The rise in prices for imported goods is expected to con nue to be rela vely low, leaving room for a somewhat higher rise in prices for domes cally produced goods and services. Over me, produc vity growth determines the level of wage growth that is consistent with stability in prices and the exchange rate. With produc vity growth around the average for the 1980s and 1990s, i.e. in the order of 11/2 per cent per year, nominal wage growth should be brought down to between 3 and 4 per cent. There will be room for higher wage growth if produc vity growth increases. In recent years, cost infla on in the euro area countries and among trading partners has been rela vely low. Growth in labour costs in Norway has been roughly 11 percentage points higher than in the euro area in the past three years. A number of other small open economies have recorded a decline in unemployment and lower growth in labour costs than Norway. In Sweden, unemployment has shown a substan al decrease over the past five years and wage growth is below 4 per cent. Three-year wage agreements are now being concluded, underpinning the basis for low cost infla on. In the Netherlands, unemployment has fallen to a very low level. Wage growth has picked up, but is lower than in Norway. In Denmark, unemployment has come down without an increase in wage growth. In Finland, unemployment has fallen sharply from the high level that took hold in the 1990s, and wage growth has slowed. In the euro area, unemployment has dropped without an increase in wage growth. In Norway, the high growth in labour costs may be a source of rising unemployment. Norwegian key rates are currently 11/2 percentage points higher than in the US, 21/4 percentage points higher than in the euro area, and 3 percentage points higher than in Sweden. In some countries, short-term interest rates are now moving down and in other countries expecta ons of interest rate increases have receded. Norges Bank has a neutral bias with regard to interest rates developments, partly reflec ng price and cost developments in Norway, as illustrated in the chart. Interac on with fiscal policy It is important that the annual budgets are based on a long-term strategy that takes into account possible fluctua ons in oil revenues from one year to the next. With large and, to some extent, varying budget revenues, the basis for determining central government expenditure and taxes from one year to the next may easily be impaired. If budget spending is allowed to vary in step with oil prices, the Norwegian economy may experience abrupt shi s and instability. Changes in oil prices may then quickly influence wage and price expecta ons, the exchange rate and long-term rates. In addi on, short-term rates would have to be changed frequently and sharply. In recent years, central government real underlying spending growth has accelerated somewhat. Both in 2000 and 2001, spending growth has been higher than 2 per cent, which is above poten al growth in the mainland economy. At the same me, taxes have increased. Fiscal policy has thus had a virtually neutral effect on domes c demand for two years while wage growth has been substan ally higher than in other countries. A possible interpreta on of this development is that it is more demanding to use the government budget to dampen cyclical fluctua ons during an upturn than during a downturn. The willingness and ability to pursue a counter-cyclical policy may in itself be cyclical. Another interpreta on is that a neutral fiscal policy in a year featuring a sharp increase in government financial assets reflects a balance between using the government budget to stabilise the economy and phasing in higher financial revenues in the economy. Irrespec ve, a gradual shi in economic policy is taking place. While fiscal policy is having a neutral impact on domes c demand, monetary policy is having a contrac onary effect. This is partly reflected in higher short-term rates compared with long-term rates. The focus of the income se lements may also be said to have changed somewhat since the mid-1990s, with less emphasis on balanced labour market developments. Natural resources and growth capacity Petroleum revenues fluctuate widely, with substan al uncertainty as to future developments. This raises the ques on of how quickly petroleum revenues shall be used. The term "Dutch disease" was first used to describe the situa on in the Dutch economy in the 1970s and 1980s a er revenues from the large gas finds in the Groningen field were used to finance strong growth in public expenditure. When the gas revenues declined and growth in the economy came to a halt, a ghtening of policy was necessary and unemployment rose. An abundance of natural resources should be considered a gi of nature and an advantage for any country. At the same me, the experience of other countries indicates that in the long run the supply of natural resources can prove to be just as much of a disadvantage as an advantage for a na on's economy. Many countries with an abundance of natural resources are poor today. They have not used the resources to provide for sustainable higher income. It would appear that easy money could reduce the growth capacity in an economy. I will address four main challenges in turning petroleum wealth into a sustainable benefit for the current and future genera ons of Norwegians: First, in countries with substan al revenues from natural resources, growth condi ons for the interna onally exposed sector may become less favourable. The exposure of large parts of the economy to intense foreign compe on provides a breeding ground for learning, innova on and development. Compe ve pressures in sheltered sectors, such as internal trade and public enterprises, are normally more limited. In my view, it is essen al to maintain a broad exposed sector in the mainland economy, primarily because of the effect this has on the growth capacity of the economy. Second, substan al petroleum wealth can weaken financial discipline in enterprises that are financed or assume that they can be financed by the public sector. The moral hazard problems associated with our "from cradle to grave" welfare systems may also be compounded. If enterprises assume that the central government will provide support, resources may be squandered and the risk of substan al losses may be given li le emphasis. The organisa on of public enterprises is thus important. The central government's financial responsibility for individual enterprises and for other levels of public administra on must be delimited in a credible manner. Third, petroleum produc on generates a profit in excess of a normal return, i.e. economic rent. As economic rent accrues to the state, the central government is accumula ng substan al capital in the Government Petroleum Fund. A strong interest in gaining access to this capital can easily arise. There is a risk that entrepreneurship, talent and energy in the business sector and poli cal life are used to acquire a piece of the economic rent rather than for innova on, restructuring and growth. Decision-making forms in economic and poli cal life must provide an effec ve shield to prevent special interests from gaining a dominant influence and control over petroleum wealth. The EEA Agreement restricts the scope for favouring individual enterprises or groups of enterprises. It is important for growth capacity in the Norwegian economy that both na onal and interna onal compe on authori es engage in effec ve supervision in order to avoid the development of a business sector that is dependent on protec on. Last, but not least, we must aim to ensure a high rate of return on petroleum wealth and financial assets in public ownership, within acceptable risk limits. This pertains to both the Government Petroleum Fund, the state's direct financial interest in petroleum ac vi es and other public assets such as the state's direct ownership interests in enterprises and assets in the Na onal Insurance Fund. Conclusions Let me conclude by summing up as follows. Con nued high oil prices have reduced income growth in many countries and are contribu ng to the turnaround in the US. The effect of high prices for oil and other commodi es is different for the Norwegian economy, with large profits in some export industries and substan al surpluses on government budgets and the current account. The high level of oil prices is boos ng petroleum investment and holding up household income expecta ons. The Norwegian mainland economy is opera ng near capacity limits, although growth is low. Wage growth and infla on are higher than among our trading partners and in the euro area. As a result, we have a higher level of short-term interest rates than in most other European countries. Title: Developments for the Norwegian economy
text: Developments for the Norwegian economy Speech by Governor Svein Gjedrem, SpareBank1- SR Bank, Stavanger 23 March 2001 Monetary policy targets and frameworks The task of monetary policy is to ensure that the economy has a nominal anchor - a stable domestic price level and thus a basis for a stable krone. Economic agents shall be very confident in developments in the value of money. Agreements on purchases and sales, loans and interest rates become cunning in nominal nok. Decisions in both the public sector and the business sector take place on the basis of the current krone value. The system is in nominal rates. When the price level fluctuates sharply, it becomes more difficult to predict the real content of such agreements and bidding. High inflation and a fluctuating exchange rate therefore impair the function of prices as information carriers. Unexpected fluctuations in the price level may laugh at undesirable fluctuations in the real economy and a lack of stability in financial and property markets. This may lead to animals d and declines following each other and in arbitrary redistribution of income and wealth. Nominal stability is therefore the best contribution monetary policy can make to economic growth and prosperity. The mandate for monetary policy is enshrined in the forescription of the krone exchange rate scheme adopted by royal decree on 6 May 1994. Section 2 of the forecrimony states: "Norges Bank's ongoing exercise of monetary policy shall be adjusted towards stability in the value of the krone against European currencies on the basis of the exchange rate range e is that the krone began to float on 10 December 1992. In the event of significant changes in the exchange rate, instruments shall be incorporated with a view to each return to the exchange rate. This does not apply to fluctuation margins with a duty for Norges Bank l to intervene in the foreign exchange market." Norges Bank does not have instruments to fine-tune the krone exchange rate. The exchange rate will vary in the short term. Norges Bank has chosen to include instruments in monetary policy with a view to meeting the fundamental preconditions for stability in the krone exchange rate. Since January 1999, the term "European currencies" is defined as euro. In order to achieve exchange rate stability against the euro, monetary policy instruments must be tightened so that price and cost inflation comes down to the level aimed at by the European Central Bank (ECB). In isolation, Norges Bank must avoid that monetary policy itself contributes to deflationary deflation, because this may weaken the krone. The interest rate is our instrument The interest rate on banks' deposits in Norges Bank, the sight deposit rate, is the most important instrument in monetary policy. Changes in the sight deposit rate affect market rates with different maturities d. The sight deposit rate has a fairly strong impact on short-term money market rates, i.e. daily and weekly rates. Interest rates on money market investments with somewhat longer runs there are not affected as directly. Here, market expectations in the central bank's trading pattern and economic developments also play a part in the level of short-term interest rates. Price and cost inflation is influenced by the money policy through several channels. When the interest rate increases, it becomes more profitable to save and to see out consumption l later. This will reduce growth in household consumption. A higher interest rate could increase the required rate of return and thereby reduce investments in the private sectors. In the case of the direct effect on e-demand, an interest rate increase may reduce the question through reduced access to liquidity, loss of value on assets such as securities and real estate, and a stronger exchange rate. A stronger exchange rate will also reduce the rise in prices for imported goods, which account for 40 per cent of the goods and services in the consumer price index. An interest rate increase may also have an impact on inflation expectations. Expectations of lower inflation will increase the real interest rate and may thus have an effect on the real economy. Inflation expectations may also have an impact on price and wage formation and the exchange rate. In general, we must assume that the relationships between interest rates, expectations, inflation and inflation are not stable. Analyses of how interest rate changes affect the economy in different countries have been published. In December, Norges Bank presented an analysis that suggests that an interest rate increase of 1 percentage point reduces GDP growth and inflation by barely 1/2 percentage point. A substantial part of the effect on inflation was due to effects via the exchange rate(1). The central banks in England and Sweden have calculations showing effects of approximately the same magnitude. It normally takes a couple of years for an interest rate change to have a material effect on price and cost inflation. Monetary policy is affecting prices and cost inflation with a dse erslep of perhaps three years. Monetary policy must be forward-looking in order for Norges Bank to implement the target set. In the interest rate period, the assessments of the economic outlook therefore play a important role. Economic developments; a little flashback and the outlook ahead Today, the Norwegian economy is characterised by high petroleum revenues, strong growth in public releases, a tight labour market and high cost inflation. Good oil prices and large petroleum production contribute to a surplus in the foreign economy and in the government's finances. This has also resulted in a sharp increase in Norway's disposable income. The surplus of about 14 percent of GDP is among the highest surpluses in an OECD country in the world. The overall surplus on public couriers has also increased, reaching 141/2 per cent of GDP. The Norwegian economy had a long upturn behind it when it was interrupted by a pause in growth in the summer of 1998. The growth pause was triggered by turbulence in international foreign exchange markets, partly as a result of the crisis in many Asian countries. The Asian crisis resulted in low international demand, low oil prices and weak price developments for other Norwegian export goods as well. In addition to the effects of particularly Norwegian cost inflation e, the wage settlement in 1998, we faced major changes in the victorian sector of manufacturing. At the beginning of 1999, Norges Bank assessed the risk of a strong downturn in the economy that was large. Sam dig saw price and cost inflation come down to the slack aimed at by the euro area countries. Norges Bank therefore reduced the interest rate. Over the course of nine months, the interest rate was reduced 5 times by a total of 21/2 percentage points. This contributed to stabilising the Norwegian economy and therefore the krone. The international economy reversed unexpectedly rapidly. Asian countries managed to recover from the crisis faster than most had expected. Oil prices rose. Together with, among other things, the decline in interest rates contributed to renewed op-eds among Norwegian bedri er and households. The economic downturn showed e is every clear increase in consumption and output. Since the summer of 1999, the Norwegian economy has again been growing. Through the latter half of 1999, economic indicators indicated that economic growth had underestimated. The projections for price and cost inflation and growth in the mainland economy in the coming years were revised upwards. The wage settlement in the spring of 2000 resulted in significantly higher growth in labour costs than projected . The result of this year's tariff settlement means that cost growth over the past three years has been between 10 and 11 percentage points higher in Norway than the countries we compete with. The sharp increase in labour costs gave new impetus to the domestic price range. These developments led Norges Bank to consider raising the key policy rate by a total of 1.5 percentage points on four occasions. The krone depreciated markedly through the first half of the year, but appreciated again during the summer and autumn. Measured against the import-weighted krone exchange rate, which best provides a push for importing price impulses directly from exchange rate developments, the krone depreciated by 2 per cent. Weaker effek v krone means that it will be more expensive for us to buy goods and services from abroad. The decisions to increase key rates were made at a time when the krone had depreciated against a close of trading partners, but was stable against the euro. The latter reflected the weak developments of the euro. In the situation in which the Norwegian economy was in, we considered that an unchanged interest rate would not contribute to bringing price and cost inflation down to the level aimed at by the ECB. An unchanged interest rate would thus undermine the objective of a stable exchange rate above d In the previous quarters, private consumption showed a more subdued trend in the second half of the year. There were signs of some stabilisation in house prices. House prices have now reached a very high level. In real terms , i.e. adjusted for the general price range, house prices are almost 10 per cent higher than when they peaked in the 1980s. Household growth slowed somewhat towards sluggish one of the years, but is still very high. Global growth has long been expected to slow, but the turnaround in the US economy now appears to be stronger than previously assumed . To mitigate the impact, the Federal Reserve has been slowing the Federal Funds rate target by a total of 11/2 percentage points since the end of the year. Many expect the turnaround to be short-lived. But both the duration and strength of the decline are uncertain. Doubts about further developments in Japan have also increased. E is that the bubble burst in the early 1990s, growth has never started again. The banking sector is struggling with considerable problems. Growth in Europe is expected to remain relatively solid. If developments are approximately as assumed, the effects of the global turnaround on the Norwegian economy may probably be limited. This is partly due to the fact that our equivalence is largely characterised by the capacity of the individual bedri that determines the extent of exports and the importance of oil and gas exports. In the event of a marked decline in oil prices and other commodity prices and a strong impact on financial markets, we will also feel the impact. The high oil price we now have results in lower growth in revenues in many countries and contributes to the turnaround in the US. But in the short term, the impact is significantly different on the Norwegian economy. We will have large surpluses in parts of the ecb, on the current balance sheet and in government finances. Therefore, there is no prospect of a significant reduction in pressures in the Norwegian economy. The decline in petroleum investment appears to have stalled. The optimism among industry leaders is greater than just a few months ago. Growth in household income is expected to remain high and form the basis for an increase in private consumption without compromising saving. There is little available resources in the Norwegian economy. The participation rate of the profession is high. We can't expect the workforce to increase significantly. More labour reforms and increased use of disability and sickness benefits are reducing the gap in work crashes . In large parts of the Norwegian economy, there is a shortage of work crashes. There have never been any more vacant slings registered. Especially in the health care system, the school system and the construction industry, there are many uninhabited issues. There are not enough nurses, teachers, plumbers or carpenters. In Eastern Norway, unemployment has fallen over the past year. They are a region where private and public services weigh heavily. There is therefore much to suggest that the labour market in service industries is very tight. Even though there is a shortage of jobs in the Norwegian economy, the situation is different in parts of the country. In southern and western Norway, unemployment increased in or. This largely reflects developments in manufacturing, where there have been fewer employment in the past year. Several factors now indicate a somewhat brighter outlook. There are signs of increased order intake in the industry in Southern and Western Norway. A shortage of jobs is mentioned, among other things, as a growing problem both in sta s sk central agency's Business Tendencyometer and in the business cycle report from the Norwegian Confederation of Technology. We expect manufacturing employment to remain approximately at current levels over the next two years. Sam dig is expected to be working hard to increase in public and private services. Unemployment therefore appears to remain approximately at current levels over the next two years. The tight labour market contributes to a high level of wage growth. We expect that growth in labour costs will slow somewhat and fall to 41/2 per cent in 2002. This is higher than wage growth is expected among our trading partners and in the euro area. Several other small and open economies have seen a decline in unemployment, but combined with lower growth in labour costs than Norway. In Sweden, unemployment has fallen sharply over the past five years, and wage growth is below 4 per cent. Three-year pay agreements will now be entered into that will consolidate the low cost gap. In the Netherlands, unemployment has been reduced at a very low level. Wage growth has lta , but it is lower than in Norway. In Denmark, unemployment has fallen without wage growth having lta . In Finland, unemployment has been reduced from the high level that first festered in the 1990s, and wage growth has fallen. In the euro area as a whole, unemployment has fallen without an increase in wage growth. Since 1997, inflation has been higher in Norway than in the euro area. Inflation has slowed over the past six months, even as we ignore the rise in oil prices and the increase in VAT at year-end. Total consumer price inflation was 3.6 per cent from February last year. Excluding the contributions from emitting, electricity and petrol prices, inflation was 2.9 per cent from February last year. This is 0.7 percentage point higher than a year ago. Inflation is expected to be 3 per cent this year. You are expecting a gradual decline in inflation in 21/4 per cent in 2003. When Norges Bank forecasts economic developments, we must make assumptions about a number of key variables. These include international developments, fiscal policy, oil prices, the exchange rate and the interest rate. If these do not become as predicted, they may result in a different path for both the real economy and nominal developments. The path I have now described is based on the interest rate developing in line with market expectations as reflected in forward rates at the beginning of March. Market participants expected the interest rate to fall by a total of 1-11/4 percentage points over the next two years. On the other hand, if the interest rate is kept constant at the current level(2), our calculations indicate that price and cost inflation will come down faster. The chart shows the possible path for inflation in the period 2001-2002 with the falling (red) and unchanged interest rates (the blue one), respectively. When the interest rate is kept unchanged, inflation may fall to 2 per cent from the end of 2002. It is then assumed that such an alterna v interest rate path will entail a stronger import-weighted krone exchange rate in the same period (3). The effects of inflation will be rapid when the exchange rate strengthens. E is the result of a decline in the effect via the exchange rate, the effect via the real economy will dominate. Higher interest rates will curb demand growth in the Norwegian economy, particularly growth in private consumption. They will in turn curb output growth. The projections indicate that mainland GDP growth Norway at such an alternation of interest rates to be around 11/2 per cent over the next two years. Pressures in the labour market may ease somewhat and curb wage growth. That's all the uncertainty. The estimates are due to the fact that a number of key variables develop as predicted . Moreover, it is not a good thing that the model apparatus and our use of the e capture the changes that are taking place in the economy. There are factors that can push up inflation. Growth in the labour force may be lower than the population trend is. Wage formation, where manufacturing has been the key to settlements in the sheltered sector, may be under pressure. In recent years, we have seen tendencies in that the sheltered sector, where the lack of a work crash is high, has had a bearing on overall wage developments. Growth in public demand may be higher than assumed. Oil prices may remain high. The krone exchange rate may be weaker than assumed. On the other hand, there are credibility that can contribute to pushing down inflation. The turnaround in the global economy may be stronger than we have assumed. Growth in the Norwegian economy may be weaker than projected , e.g. if the household chooses to save a larger share of income. Product growth may increase, as we have seen in other countries. Oil prices may fall faster. The krone may be stronger than expected. Overall, we consider the uncertainty surrounding the price projections to be symmetrical. Inflation is just as likely to be higher than our estimate as it will be lower. U word rings ahead The Norwegian economy is vulnerable to abrupt skiing in the world economy. The big oil sector is amplifying that. For every dollar of oil prices The Norwegian economy is vulnerable to abrupt skiing in the world economy. The big oil sector is amplifying that. With every dollar of oil prices rising, the value of the country's total output is up nearly 1 percent. And vice versa. Oil prices have been very high over the past year. We know from the point of view that oil prices may fall again abruptly. We cannot fully shield ourselves from "shock" from the outside world, but we can mitigate the effects. The economic policing can create the basis for stable economic growth through a successful interaction between the various elements of policing; that is, between fiscal policy, monetary policy, the system of income settlements and other ltaks to improve the functioning of the economy. The financial policy, i.e. developments in the state's output and in the ska er and is, have Norway have a important role in stabilising demand and production. If the authorities allow the government to publish a government bid in line with oil prices, there will be abrupt skies and instability in the Norwegian economy. There is a risk that changes in oil prices will quickly forge ahead with expectations of a big wage and price hike, on the exchange rate and on long-term interest rates. In those years, it will be very demanding to secure the value of the money. The short-term interest rates will have to be changed frequently and sharpened, and interest rates will increase because there is greater risk associated with investments in NOK. If economic developments are to be stable, it is therefore important that the annual bidding is anchored in a long-running strategy that takes good account of the fact that petroleum revenues may fluctuate from this year. The Government Petroleum Fund shall serve as a buffer against short-range fluctuations in petroleum revenues. Since much of the revenues from petroleum activities accrue to the government, fluctuations in oil prices and petroleum revenues will primarily result in changes in allocations to the Petroleum Fund. Since the Fund is invested in its entirety abroad, such changes will not in principle affect the economy. The foreign exchange market remains in balance since the petroleum fund mechanism acts as a "revolving door" for foreign exchange flows. This makes the Norwegian economy more resilient to fluctuations in oil prices and thus less dependent on oil, also in the short term. We can say that petroleum revenues enter the Norwegian economy through an external and internal cycle. The distinction between the external and internal cycles is important for the stability of the exchange rate. This means, among other things, that short-range changes in oil prices should not affect the orientation of economic policing. If the distinction between the two cycles were to break down, and petroleum revenue spending fluctuated more in line with oil prices, we would have a more volatile economy. The state has generated revenues from petroleum activities since 1971. Since then, total revenues from petroleum production have been an estimated NOK 1,100 billion. If, over the same period, government budget deficits add up (excluding petroleum revenues), they can be estimated at just over NOK 800 billion. It is petroleum revenues that are included in the economy. The build-up of financial wealth abroad through the Petroleum Fund takes into account that future generations will also benefit from petroleum wealth. Sam dig contributes to stability in the government's finances in the long term. The larger it gets, the less dependent it will be on developments in oil and gas prices. The e can come in handy. The Norwegian economy is facing major inecursions ahead as a result of an increasing proportion of elderly people in the population and strong growth in In pensions and in nursing and care services. The number of age and disability pensioners is projected to increase by 50 per cent by 2030, and the government's disability pension is projected to increase from about 7 per cent of GDP this year to 15 per cent in 30 years. Demographic developments mean that growth in the labour force will be fairly small in the period ahead. Norway is a pretty rich country. We're rich partly because of the oil. But wealth doesn't give us any more work. As shown, we have used a very large share of the petroleum revenues. This is reflected in the labour market. Compared to the others Nordic countries have increased their employment markedly in the public sector. Oil wealth can do little - at least in the short term - with the shortage of nurses, doctors, teachers, carpenters or plumbers. If we want to have more people in the health service and the school system, more l to build roads and improve school buildings we need more work crashes . But it's not the kind of work we're missing. To get more of it, there needs to be less work in other businesses. Such a struggle will be a weakening of the basis for the competitive sector. This makes us even more vulnerable if petroleum revenues fail. Experience from other countries that access to natural resources in the long run may as well be a disadvantage as an advantage for a nation's economic development. Asia and European countries without much access to such resources are among the world's richest. It appears that laughing money can impair the growth potential of an economy. A comparison of economic developments in recent years between Norway and our Nordic neighbours may also provide a basis for turbulence. Their business sector now appears to have a stronger growth rate than ours. In countries with high revenues from natural resources, the international sector may experience poor growth conditions. When a large part of the economy is exposed to intense competition from abroad, it becomes fertile ground for learning, innovation and development. Competitive pressures in sheltered sectors, such as trade and public sector enterprises, are probably more limited. It is important to maintain a broad competitive sector in the mainland economy, primarily for the sake of growth capacity in the economy. Conclusion Norwegian key rates are currently two percentage points higher than in the US, 21/2 percentage points higher than in the euro area and three percentage points higher than in Sweden. In several countries, the short-range interest rate level is now degrading. Norges Bank has a neutral view of interest rate developments. This is partly due to the price and cost outlook in Norway and the fact that oil prices have now remained high and shielded us from the possible nega effects of subdued growth abroad. Footnotes: 1 It was assumed that the krone exchange rate developed in accordance with uncovered interest rate parity. 2 For the first quarter of 2003. 3 Computational engineering, we have assumed that the exchange rate will change in line with the theory of uncovered interest rate parity. A higher interest rate on the Norwegian krone is then matched by an immediate appreciation and you are a steady depreciation in the initial level so that the expected return on investments in NOK is unchanged. 23 March 2001 14:00

En rentekning vil ogs kunne virke gjennom inasjonsforventningene. Forventninger om lavere fram dig inasjon vil ke realrenten og kan dermed i seg selv ha en eekt p realkonomien. Inasjonsforventningene kan ogs ha betydning i prisog lnnsdannelsen og for valutakursen. Vi m imidler d regne med at sammenhengene mellom rente, forventninger, e ersprsel og inasjon ikke er stabile. Det er publisert analyser av hvordan renteendringer pvirker konomien i ulike land. Norges Bank la i desember i or frem en analyse som antyder at en rentekning p 1 prosentpoeng reduserer BNP-veksten og prisveksten med knapt 1/2 prosentpoeng. En vesentlig del av virkningen p prisveksten skyldtes virkninger via valutakursen(1). Sentralbankene i England og Sverige har publisert beregninger som viser eekter om lag i samme strrelsesorden. Det tar normalt et par r fr en renteendring gir vesentlig eekt p pris- og kostnadsveksten. Pengepoli kken pvirker prisog kostnadsveksten med et dse erslep p kanskje e l tre r. Pengepoli kken m vre fremoverskuende for at Norges Bank skal kunne gjennomfre det mlet som er fastsa . I rentese ngen spiller derfor vurderingene av de konomiske utsiktene en vik g rolle. Den konomiske utviklingen; et lite lbakeblikk og utsiktene fremover Norsk konomi preges i dag av hye petroleumsinntekter, sterk vekst i oentlige utgi er, et stramt arbeidsmarked og hy kostnadsvekst. God oljepris og stor petroleumsproduksjon bidrar l overskudd i utenrikskonomien og i statens nanser. Det har ogs gi en sterk kning i Norges disponible inntekt. Overskuddet p dri sbalansen i or p om lag 14 prosent av BNP er blant de hyeste overskuddene i et OECD-land i e erkrigs den. Ogs det samlede overskuddet p oentlige budsje er har kt kra ig og ndde 141/2 prosent av BNP. Norsk konomi hadde en lang oppgangsperiode bak seg da den ble avbru av en pause i veksten sommeren 1998. Vekstpausen ble utlst av uro i internasjonale valutamarkeder, blant annet som flge av krisen i mange asia ske land. Asiakrisen ga lav internasjonal e ersprsel, lav oljepris og svak prisutvikling ogs for andre norske eksportvarer. I llegg l virkningene av srnorsk kostnadsvekst e er lnnsoppgjret i 1998, stod vi foran store oms llinger innenfor vik ge deler av industrien. Ved inngangen l 1999 vurderte Norges Bank risikoen for et sterkt lbakeslag i konomien som rela vt stor. Sam dig s pris- og kostnadsveksten ut l  komme ned mot den s gningen eurolandene sikter mot. Norges Bank reduserte derfor renten. I lpet av ni mneder ble renten sa ned 5 ganger med i alt 21/2 prosentpoeng. Det bidro l  stabilisere norsk konomi og derfor ogs kronen. De internasjonale konjunkturene snudde imidler d uventet raskt. De asia ske landene klarte  hente seg opp av krisen raskere enn det de este hadde ventet. Oljeprisen kte kra ig. Sammen med blant annet rentenedgangen bidro de e l fornyet op misme blant norske bedri er og husholdninger. Den konomiske sta s kken viste e er hvert klar oppgang i forbruk og produksjon. Siden sommeren 1999 har det igjen vrt vekst i norsk konomi. Gjennom siste halvdel av 1999 tydet konomiske indikatorer p at vi hadde undervurdert den konomiske veksten. Anslagene for pris- og kostnadsveksten og veksten i fastlandskonomien de nrmeste rene ble oppjustert. Lnnsoppgjret vren 2000 frte l vesentlig hyere vekst i lnnskostnadene enn dligere ansl . Resultatet fra orrets tarioppgjr innebrer at kostnadsveksten de siste tre rene har vrt mellom 10 og 11 prosentpoeng hyere i Norge enn landene vi konkurrerer med. Den sterke kningen i lnnskostnadene gav nye impulser l priss gningen innenlands. Disse utviklingstrekkene frte l at Norges Bank vurderte det som rik g  ke styringsrenten med i alt 1,5 prosentpoeng ved re anledninger i or. Kronekursen svekket seg rela vt markert gjennom frste halvr i or, men styrket seg igjen i lpet av sommeren og hsten. Mlt mot den importveide kronekursen, som best gir u rykk for importere prisimpulser direkte fra valutakursutviklingen, svekket kronen seg med 2 prosent i or. Svakere eek v krone innebrer at det blir dyrere for oss  kjpe varer og tjenester fra utlandet. Beslutningene om  ke styringsrentene ble fa et i en periode da kronen hadde svekket seg mot et gjennomsni av handelspartnerne, men var stabilt sterk mot euro. Det siste reekterte euroens svake utvikling. I den situasjonen norsk konomi befant seg i, vurderte vi at en uendret rente ikke ville bidra l  bringe pris- og kostnadsveksten ned mot den s gningen ESB sikter mot. En uendret rente ville dermed undergrave mlet om en stabil valutakurs over d E er kra ig vekst de foregende kvartalene viste det private konsumet en mer dempet utvikling i andre halvr i or. Det var tegn l en viss stabilisering i boligprisene. Boligprisene har n kommet opp p et svrt hyt niv. Reelt se , det vil si korrigert for den alminnelige priss gningen, er boligprisene nrmere 10 prosent hyere enn da de p si hyeste p 1980tallet. Kredi veksten l husholdningene avtok noe mot slu en av orret, men er likevel fortsa svrt hy. Det har lenge vrt ventet at veksten internasjonalt ville dempes, men omslaget i amerikansk konomi ser n ut l  bli sterkere enn dligere anta . For  dempe utslagene, har den amerikanske sentralbanken, Federal Reserve, m de e med  senke mlet for federal-funds renten med i alt 11/2 prosentpoeng siden rsski et. Mange forventer at omslaget blir kortvarig. Men bde varigheten og styrken av nedgangen er usikker. Tvilen om den videre utviklingen i Japan har ogs kt. E er at boblen brast p begynnelsen av 1990-tallet, har veksten aldri kommet i gang igjen. Banksektoren sliter med betydelig problemer. Vi venter at veksten i Europa vil holde seg forholdsvis godt oppe. Dersom utviklingen blir omtrent som anta , kan virkningene av omslaget internasjonalt p norsk konomi trolig bli begrenset. Det har blant annet sammenheng med at vr ekspor ndustri i stor grad er preget av det er kapasiteten i den enkelte bedri som bestemmer omfanget av eksporten og betydningen av olje- og gasseksporten. Dersom vi skulle f en markert nedgang i oljeprisen og andre rvarepriser og sterke utslag i nansielle markeder, vil imidler d ogs vi merke avma ngen. Den hye oljeprisen vi n har gir lavere vekst i inntektene i mange land og bidrar l omslaget i USA. Men p kort sikt er virkningen vesentlig annerledes p norsk konomi. Vi fr store overskudd i deler av ekspor ndustrien, p dri sbalansen og i statsnansene. Det er derfor ikke utsikter l nevneverdig reduksjon i presset i norsk konomi. Nedgangen i oljeinvesteringene ser ut l  ha stoppet opp. Op mismen blant lederne i industrien er strre enn bare for noen mneder siden. Veksten i husholdningene inntekter vil ventelig holde seg oppe og danne grunnlag for at det private forbruket kan ke uten at de e gr ut over sparingen. Det er lite ledige ressurser i norsk konomi. Yrkesdeltagelsen er hy. Vi kan ikke vente at arbeids lbudet vil ke nevneverdig. Flere arbeids dsreformer og kt bruk av ufre- og syketrygd reduserer lgangen p arbeidskra . I store deler av norsk konomi er det mangel p arbeidskra . Det har aldri vrt registrert ere ledige s llinger. Srlig innenfor helsevesenet, skoleverket og byggebransjen er det mange ubesa e s llinger. Det er ikke nok sykepleiere, lrere, rrleggere eller snekkere. P stlandet har ledigheten falt det siste ret. De e er en region hvor privat og oentlig tjenestey ng veier tungt. Det er derfor mye som tyder p at arbeidsmarkedet i tjenesteytende nringer er svrt stramt. Selv om det er mangel p arbeidskra i norsk konomi se under e , er situasjonen annerledes i deler av landet. P Sr- og Vestlandet kte ledigheten i or. Det gjenspeiler i stor grad utviklingen i industrien, hvor det har bli frre sysselsa e det siste ret. Flere faktorer tyder n p noe lysere utsikter. Det er tegn l kt ordreinngang l ver sindustrien p Sr- og Vestlandet. Mangel p arbeidskra er blant annet nevnt som et kende problem bde i Sta s sk sentralbyrs Konjunkturbarometer og i konjunkturrapporten fra Teknologibedri enes Landsforening. Vi venter at industrisysselse ngen holder seg om lag p dagens niv de nrmeste to rene. Sam dig forventes e ersprselen e er arbeidskra  ke i oentlig og privat tjeneste y ng. Arbeidsledigheten ser derfor ut l  holde seg omlag p dagens niv de nrmeste to rene. Det stramme arbeidsmarkedet bidrar l at lnnsveksten holder seg hy. Vi regner med at veksten i lnnskostnadene vil avta noe og komme ned mot 41/2 prosent i 2002. Det er hyere enn den lnnsveksten som er ventet hos vre handelspartnere og i euroomrdet. Flere andre sm og pne konomier har ha nedgang i arbeidsledigheten men sam dig ha lavere vekst i lnnskostnadene enn Norge. I Sverige har ledigheten g sterkt ned de siste fem rene, og lnnsveksten er under 4 prosent. N blir det inng trerige lnnsavtaler som vil befeste den lave kostnadss gningen. I Nederland er ledigheten redusert l et meget lavt niv. Lnnsveksten har lta , men den er lavere enn i Norge. I Danmark har arbeidsledigheten g ned uten at lnnsveksten har lta . I Finland er ledigheten redusert fra det hye nivet som festnet seg frst p 1990-tallet, og lnnsveksten har falt. I euroomrdet samlet har ledigheten falt uten at lnnsveksten har kt. Siden 1997 har prisveksten vrt hyere i Norge enn i euroomrdet. Prisveksten har lta det siste halve ret, ogs nr vi ser bort fra oppgangen i oljeprisen og momskningen ved rsski et. Den samlede konsumprisveksten var 3,6 prosent fra februar i or l samme mned i r. Tar vi bort bidragene fra avgi er, strm- og bensinpriser, var prisveksten 2,9 prosent fra februar i or. Det er 0,7 prosentpoeng hyere enn for e r siden. Vi venter at prisveksten innevrende r blir 3 prosent. Dere er venter vi en gradvis nedgang i prisveksten l 21/4 prosent i 2003. Nr Norges Bank lager prognoser for den konomiske utviklingen, m vi gjre forutsetninger om en rekke sentral strrelser. Blant disse er blant annet utviklingen internasjonalt, nanspoli kken, oljeprisen, valutakursen og renten. Dersom disse ikke blir som forutsa , vil de e kunne resultere i et annet forlp bde for det realkonomiske og nominelle utviklingen. Forlpet jeg n har beskrevet er basert p at renten utvikler seg i trd med markedets forventninger slik de var reektert ved terminrentene i begynnelsen av mars. Markedsaktrene forventet at renten ville g ned med l sammen 1-11/4 prosentpoeng i lpet av de neste to rene. Holdes derimot renten konstant p dagens niv(2) tyder vre beregninger p at pris- og kostnadsveksten vil komme raskere ned. Figuren viser mulige forlp for prisveksten i perioden 2001-2002 med den henholdsvis fallende (den rde) og uendret rente (den bl). Nr renten holdes uendret, vil prisveksten kunne komme ned mot 2 prosent fra og med utgangen av 2002. Da er det lagt l grunn at en slik alterna v rentebane vil innebre en sterkere importveid kronekurs i den samme perioden(3). Utslagene i prisveksten kommer rela vt raskt nr valutakursen sam dig styrker seg. E er hvert som utslagene via valutakursen avtar, vil eekten via realkonomien dominere. Hyere rente vil dempe e ersprselsveksten i norsk konomi, srlig veksten i det private konsumet. De e vil igjen dempe produksjonsveksten. Anslagene indikerer at veksten i BNP for Fastlands-Norge med en slik alterna v rentebane blir rundt 11/2 prosent de to neste rene. Presset i arbeidsmarkedet kan komme l  avta noe og dempe lnnsveksten. Det er all d usikkerhet kny et l anslagene. Anslagene er be nget av at en rekke sentrale strrelser utvikler seg som forutsa . Dessuten er det ikke gi at modellapparatet og vr bruk av de e fanger opp de endringene som skjer i konomien. Det er forhold som kan trekke prisveksten opp. Veksten i arbeidsstyrken kan bli lavere enn befolkningsutviklingen lsier. Lnnsdannelsen, der industrien har vrt toneangivende for oppgjrene i skjermet sektor, kan bli sa under press. De siste rene har vi se tendenser l at skjermet sektor, der mangelen p arbeidskra er stor, har sa si preg p den samlede lnnsutviklingen. Veksten i oentlig e ersprsel kan bli hyere enn lagt l grunn. Oljeprisen kan forbli hy. Kronekursen kan bli svakere enn vi har lagt l grunn. P den andre siden er det kre er som kan bidra l  trekke prisveksten ned. Omslaget i internasjonal konomi kan bli sterkere enn vi har lagt l grunn. Veksten i norsk konomi kan bli svakere enn ansl , f.eks. hvis husholdningen velger  spare en strre andel av inntekten. Produk vitetsveksten kan ke, slik vi har se tendenser l i andre land. Oljeprisen kan falle raskere. Kronen kan bli sterkere enn anta . Samlet vurderer vi usikkerheten om prisanslagene som symmetriske. Det er like sannsynlig at prisveksten blir hyere enn vrt anslag som at den blir lavere. U ordringene fremover Norsk konomi er srbar for br ski i verdenskonomien. Den store oljesektoren forsterker det. For hver dollar oljeprisen Norsk konomi er srbar for br ski i verdenskonomien. Den store oljesektoren forsterker det. For hver dollar oljeprisen ker, s ger verdien av landets samlede produksjon med nesten 1 prosent. Og vise versa. Oljeprisen har vrt svrt hy det siste ret. Vi vet fra dligere at oljeprisen br kan falle igjen. Vi kan ikke skjerme oss fullt ut mot "sjokk" fra omverdenen, men vi kan dempe virkningene. Den konomiske poli kken kan skape grunnlag for stabil konomisk vekst gjennom et vellykket samspill mellom de ulike elementene i poli kken; det vil si mellom nanspoli kken, pengepoli kken, systemet for inntektsoppgjrene og andre ltak for  bedre konomiens virkemte. Finanspoli kken, det vil si utviklingen i statens utgi er og i ska er og avgi er, har i Norge ha en vik g rolle i  stabilisere e ersprsel og produksjon. Dersom myndighetene lar statsbudsje ets utgi er svinge i takt med oljeprisen, vil vi f br ski og ustabilitet i norsk konomi. Da er det fare for at endringer i oljeprisen raskt smi er over p forventningene om fram dig lnns- og priss gning, p valutakurs og p langsik ge renter. I de e lfellet vil det vre svrt krevende  sikre pengenes verdi. De kortsik ge rentene vil m e endres hyppig og kra ig, og de langsik ge rentene vil ke fordi det er strre risiko forbundet med plasseringer i norske kroner. Skal vi f en stabil konomisk utvikling, er det derfor vik g at de rlige budsje ene er forankret i en langsik g strategi som tar god hyde for at oljeinntektene kan svinge fra r l r. Statens petroleumsfond skal virke som en buer mot kortsik ge svingninger i oljeinntektene. Siden store deler av inntektene fra oljevirksomheten lfaller staten, vil svingninger i oljeprisen og oljeinntektene i frste rekke resultere i endringer i avsetningene l oljefondet. Siden oljefondet i sin helhet plasseres i utlandet, vil slike endringer i utgangspunktet ikke pvirke ak viteten i konomien. Valutamarkedet forblir i balanse siden petroleumsfondsmekanismen virker som en "svingdr" for valutastrmmene. De e gjr norsk konomi mer robust overfor svingninger i oljeprisen og dermed mindre oljeavhengig, ogs p kort sikt. Vi kan si at oljeinntektene kommer inn i norsk konomi gjennom et ytre og et indre kretslp. Skillet mellom det ytre og det indre kretslpet er vik g for stabiliteten i valutakursen. Det innebrer blant annet at kortsik ge endringer i oljeprisen ikke skal pvirke innretningen av den konomiske poli kken. Hvis skillet mellom de to kretslpene skulle bryte sammen, og bruken av oljeinntektene svinge mer i takt med oljeprisen, ville vi f en mer ustabil konomi. Staten har mo a inntekter fra petroleumsvirksomheten siden 1971. Den samlede inntektene fra petroleumsutvinningen har siden da og fram l i or vrt anslagsvis 1100 milliarder 2000-kroner. Dersom en over samme periode summerer underskuddene p statsbudsje et (utenom oljeinntekter) kan de ansls l i overkant av 800 milliarder 2000 kroner. Det er oljepenger som er ta inn i konomien. Oppbyggingen av en nansformue i utlandet gjennom Petroleumsfondet ivaretar hensynet l at ogs kommende generasjoner skal nyte godt av oljeformuen. Sam dig bidrar Fondet l stabilitet i statens nanser p lang sikt. Jo strre det blir, desto mindre avhengige av utviklingen i olje- og gassprisene vil vi bli i frem den. De e kan komme godt med. Norsk konomi str overfor store u ordringer fremover som flge av en kende andel eldre i befolkningen og sterk vekst i utgi er l pensjoner og l pleie- og omsorgstjenester. Antall alders- og ufrepensjonister ansls  ke med 50 prosent fram l 2030, og statens utgi er l alders og ufrepensjon er ansl  ke fra om lag 7 prosent av BNP i r l 15 prosent om 30 r. Den demograske utviklingen innebrer sam dig at veksten i arbeidsstyrken vil vre noks liten fremover. Norge er et ganske rikt land. Vi er rike dels p grunn av oljen. Men rikdommen gir oss ikke mer arbeidskra . Som vist dligere har vi bruket et meget stor andel av oljepengene. Det reekteres i arbeidsmarkedet. Sammenliknet med de andre nordiske landene har sysselse ngen kt markert i oentlig sektor. Oljerikdommen kan gjre lite - i hvert fall p kort sikt - med mangelen p sykepleiere, leger, lrere, snekkere eller rrleggere. Dersom vi nsker  ha ere i helsevesenet og skoleverket, ere l  bygge veier og utbedre skolebygg trenger vi mer arbeidskra . Men det er ne opp denne type arbeidskra vi mangler. For  f mer av den, m det bli mindre arbeidskra i andre virksomheter. En slik kamp vil e er noen d svekke grunnlaget for den konkurranseutsa e sektoren. Da blir vi enda mer srbare dersom oljeinntektene skulle svikte. Erfaringer fra andre land p at lgang l naturressurser i det lange lp like gjerne kan bli en ulempe som en fordel for en nasjons konomiske utvikling. Asia ske og europeiske land uten stor lgang p slike ressurser er blant verdens rikeste. Det kan se ut som om le jente penger kan svekke vekstevnen i en konomi. En sammenlikning av den konomiske utviklingen de seneste rene mellom Norge og vre nordiske naboland kan ogs gi grunnlag for uro. Deres nringsliv ser n ut l  ha sterkere vekstkra enn vr. I land med store inntekter fra naturressurser kan den konkurranseutsa e sektoren f drlige vekstvilkr. Nr en stor del av konomien er utsa for intens konkurranse fra utlandet, blir det grobunn for lring, innovasjon og utvikling. Konkurransetrykket i skjermede sektorer, som handel og virksomheter i oentlig regi, er nok o e mer begrenset. Det er e er mi skjnn vesentlig  oppre holde en bred konkurranseutsa sektor i fastlandskonomien, frst og fremst av hensyn l vekstevnen i konomien. Avslutning Norske styringsrenter er i dag to prosentpoeng hyere enn i USA, 21/2 prosentpoeng hyere enn i euroomrdet og tre prosentpoeng hyere enn i Sverige. I ere land gr n det kortsik ge rentenivet ned. I Norges Bank har vi et nytralt syn p renteutviklingen. Det har blant annet sammenheng med pris- og kostnadsutsiktene i Norge og at oljeprisen l n har holdt seg hy og skjermet oss fra mulige nega ve virkninger av dempet vekst ute. Fotnoter: 1 Det ble lagt l grunn at kronekursen utviklet seg i samsvar med udekket renteparitet. 2 Fram l frste kvartal 2003. 3 Beregningsteknisk har vi lagt l grunn at valutakursen endrer seg i trd med teorien for udekket renteparitet. Hyere rente p norske kroner motsvares da av en umiddelbar appresiering og dere er en jevn depresiering lbake l utgangsnivet slik at forventet avkastning p plasseringer i norske kroner er uendret. Title: Economic self-management in a global economy
text: Economically self-advisers in a global economy Submission by Deputy Governor Jarle Bergo, Partner Forum Spring Conference, 9 May 2001 Introduction Internationalization is a major issue that has many phases - something that today's program has undoubtedly shown. I will look at some aspects of developments towards a "global economy" and the possible consequences of this for the "economic self-management one". As the conference's el invites l, I would mainly like to see this self-advising one within the framework of the nation-state. Nevertheless, the theme is both large and wide. I want to start with an attempt to discuss what might be in self-advice and internationalization and whether we have a global economy. You are, we will look at the consequences of the Norway and how they affect our self-advisers and whether they are problematic. The answer to the latter may be that it depends on the eyes that see, or re-ere, what one thinks about the desirability of various economic inequalities. Om selvradere Discussions about self-counselling don't infrequently degenerate. It may therefore be appropriate to have a "clinical" approach, and at least try to establish a definition of the term that does not invite particularly strong feelings. With full economic autonomy for the nation-state, we understand that representatives of the national state ("the authorities") determine the framework for economic assistance in the country without any restrictions other than those a resulting from conditions internal to the country and naturgi e conditions. The frameworks will consist of laws and regulations of importance for economic activities, e.g. in relation to the imposition of the system, the disposal of public releases are and perhaps l and with to enslu e what (part of) the result of the economic objective should be (cf. the more centrally directed planning economies). Let's imagine that we can illustrate all possible decisions, and combinations of decisions, of importance to the economy that the authorities can make by a two-dimensional figure, the "decision room". Here, then, self-counsellors are a whole and uncut. The countries that come closest to them are probably North Korea and Cuba. But of course there are also limitations to these, the law of gravity applies fully and one cannot stray from climate and geographical location. However, the WTO agreement will not impose formal restrictions on the decision-making room. But the decision-making space is nevertheless limited by the behaviour of other nations and economic actors. Cuba may be happy to sell bananas in the U.S. for 1 cent per kilogram, but still won't be able to sell anything. Similarly, in Norway we cannot decide both that the price of Norwegian oil should be USD 40 per barrel and that abroad should buy in that price. So already initially there are many limitations in the decision room, but we will not invent the e as intervention in self-advising one. There is a conjecture in the or of the conference and the that we are now influenced by some developments that we call "internationalization" and "globalization" that place ever greater restrictions on our opportunities in order to preserve the framework for economic activity in the country, i.e. that the decision-making space is shrinking. Internationalization and globalization The developments we are thinking about are particularly that there are more financial transactions and more dissemination of ideas, culture and attitudes across borders than worse. From the public debate one gets the impression that international integration and globalization are something new , or at least have accelerated markedly in recent years. There may be something in it, but it may still be in its place to look at developments in a longer perspek v. Already in the slush one of the 19th century there was a high degree of openness between the economies of Europe, both in terms of goods, capital and work crashes . Many economies outside Europe were also open. Figure 3 shows that before World War I, goods exports accounted for about 9 per cent of the world's total production. World wars and the Depression of the 1930s led to new restrictions and falls in world trade. It wasn't until 1970 that the trade lbake at the level from the beginning of the century. We also note a significant increase since 1970. Developing countries have contributed to the sharp increase. It may also be worth noting that the transfer of resources between countries has probably not increased since the cunning of the 19th century. Chart 4 shows an index of ne o capital flows based on the current account in a number of advanced economies and emerging economies. On the other hand, bru o capital flows have increased significantly, especially within the last 20 years. International currency exchange has almost exploded, and in April 1998, the daily currency exchange was estimated at nearly 1,500. billion USD. Chart 6 shows figures for foreigners' share of AK VA (financial and real capital). For de land som har valgt  pne sine konomier og utny e de muligheter de e gir, gjelder det n betydelig strengere krav l det  fre en ansvarlig makro-konomisk poli kk med vekt p  hindre at det oppstr store ubalanser, internt som eksternt, enn det gjr i lukkede konomier som Nord-Korea. De e er neppe s galt. At tydelige markedsreaksjoner roper varsko fr selvrdere en er brukt fullt ut l  bringe konomien i alvorlig ubalanse, er en fordel. Et problem er at markedet ikke sjelden reagerer sent, men for sterkt nr det frst skjer (Mexico, Sr-st Asia). Likevel vil jeg hevde at internasjonaliseringens disiplinerende eekt samlet se er en fordel. Vi m videre anta at ny innsikt og bedret teknologi vil pne nye muligheter for spesialisering og utny else av kompara ve fortrinn. Kanskje srlig p tjenesteomrdet synes slik muligheter  pne seg. For sm land kan det imidler d vre forbundet med betydelig risiko  forske  utny e de e hvis det ikke er forankret i internasjonale avtaler som binder opp andre aktrer. En videreutvikling av det internasjonale avtaleverket kan vre en forutsetning for at vi skal kunne ha glede av utvidede muligheter. Internasjonale konomiske transaksjoner (vare- og tjenestestrmmer, bevegelser av kapital og arbeidskra , know-how og intellektuell eiendom over landegrensene) vil nok i kende grad bli underlagt et felles internasjonalt regelverk.
