Bde nans- og pengepoli kken har i hele e erkrigs den, med unntak av siste halvdel av 1970-tallet og frste halvdel av 1980-tallet, vrt basert p slike regler. Pengepoli kken har vrt klart forankret siden 1986. Handlingsregler er heller ikke sregent for vrt land. Inasjonsmlet forankrer forventningene om frem dig inasjon og renter. Inasjonsmlet er sa l 2 prosent. Pengepoli kken virker med et dse erslep. Inasjonen i dag gir ikke lstrekkelig holdepunkt for hva renten br se es l n. Vre analyser tyder p et en vesentlig del av virkningene av en renteendring vil komme innen to r. To r er derfor et rimelig dsperspek v for  n inasjonsmlet. Ser det ut l at inasjonen med uendret rente blir hyere enn 2 prosent, vil renten bli sa opp. Ser det ut l at inasjonen med uendret rente blir lavere enn 2 prosent, vil renten bli sa ned. Her er det symmetri. Det er like vik g  unng for lav som for hy inasjon. Norges Bank la fram sin siste inasjonsrapport 27.februar. Vi venter at priss gningen blir rundt 2 prosent om to r, hvis veksten i verdenskonomien tar seg opp igjen som forutsa . Samlet vurderer vi risikoen rundt anslaget for inasjonen  vre balansert. Det stramme arbeidsmarkedet vil trolig fortsa gi temmelig hy vekst i lnnskostnadene og noks sterk vekst i prisene p hjemmeproduserte varer og tjenester. Siden 1997 har lnnskostnadene kt med mellom 5 og 7 prosent per r. Vi anslr en rlig lnnsvekst p 5 prosent fremover. Lav prisvekst p importerte konsumvarer har bidra l  trekke den samlede prisveksten ned. Denne trenden vil trolig fortse e en d fremover. E er hvert som verdenskonomien tar seg opp, vil prisveksten p importerte varer lta. En vekst i lnnskostnadene p mer enn 5 prosent vil bare vre forenlig med inasjonsmlet hvis kronen fortse er  styrke seg. Til grunn for anslagene i inasjonsrapporten er det teknisk forutsa at kronekursen holder seg stabil. Kursene mellom de store valutaene svinger kra ig. Eek v kurs p amerikanske dollar har steget med mer enn 30 prosent siden 1995. Tyske mark (senere euro) er svekket med om lag det samme. Eek v kurs p yen har beveget seg i kra ige blger. Mindre land har ogs opplevd store endringer i valutakursen. Svenske kroner har endret seg mye de siste 10 rene og er n 10 prosent svakere enn sommeren 2000. Australske dollar har svekket seg med over 30 prosent siden vren 1997. Det er en tendens l at land som eksporterer mye rvarer fr store svingninger i sin valutakurs. Australia er et eksempel. Tradisjonelt har stabil kronekurs vrt det nominelle ankerfestet for norsk konomi. Lnnskostnadene hos handelspartnerne var en vik g referanse. N er det inasjonsmlet som er det nominelle ankerfestet. Svingninger i rvareprisene frer l endringer i forholdet mellom eksport- og importprisene, eller by eforholdet. Svingningene i by eforholdet slr ut i valutakursen, og det bidrar l  dempe virkningene p lnnsomheten. Valutakursen virker som en buer. P 1990-tallet var svingningene i Norges by eforhold srlig store. Endringer i oljeprisen var en vik g rsak. Kronekursen har ikke variert mye sammenliknet med andre land. Petroleumsfondet virker som en buer mot svingninger i oljeprisen fordi fondets kapital plasseres ute. Det bidrar l  stabilisere kronekursen. Lav og stabil inasjon om lag p vre handelspartneres niv vil over d ogs bidra l  stabilisere kronekursen. Vi m likevel vre forberedt p svingninger i kronen, p linje med de svingningene vi har se i andre land. Endringer i verdenskonomien kan pvirke kronekursen. Valutakursen kan ogs reagere p og bidra l  dempe virkningene av innenlandske forstyrrelser. Den ytende valutakursen er i det store og hele et egnet instrument l  fange opp uforutse e forstyrrelser som konomien blir utsa for. En sterkere krone kan for eksempel motvirke at innenlandsk e ersprselspress slr ut i hyere priss gning. Som historien og andre lands erfaringer har lrt oss, er det vesentlig strre realkonomiske tap kny et l  erne hy inasjon og dempe inasjonsforventningene enn l variabel nominell valutakurs. Hvis oljeprisen skulle falle l et s lavt niv at investeringene p norsk sokkel stopper opp, ville en svakere krone bidra l  le e oms llingene i nringslivet og norsk konomi for vrig. Handlingsregelen for nanspoli kken forventes hvert r i mange r framover  bidra l  s mulere e ersprselen i norsk konomi og l  holde e ersprselen e er arbeidskra oppe. kt bruk av oljeinntekter vil fre l at de tjenesteytende nringene trenger mer ressurser. Kampen om arbeidskra en blir skjerpet. For  holde inasjonen i sjakk m pengepoli kken trolig vre ganske stram i rene framover. Over d vil strrelsen p den konkurranseutsa e delen av nringslivet pvirkes av hvor mye oljeinntekter som tas inn i norsk konomi. Et vedvarende press i konomien kan, nr vi sam dig har lav og stabil inasjon, dvis komme l utrykk i en sterk krone og svekkelse av konkurranseevnen. Pengepoli kken kan p lang sikt verken pvirke den samlede sysselse ngen eller fordelingen mellom ulike nringer. Lavere rente ville ha frt l kt pris- og kostnadsvekst, som ogs ville ha svekket konkurranseevnen. Resultatet ville vrt det samme for sysselse ng og produksjon, men vi ville i llegg f hy inasjon. Hvor sterk kronekursen er, kan likevel pvirke hvor raskt endringene i nringslivet skjer. Historisk har sysselse ngen i konkurranseutsa sektor falt i blger. Srlig i perioden fra 1977 l 1984 og fra 1987 l 1992 var det kra ig avskalling i industrien. Forut for begge nedgangsperiodene svekket industriens kostnadsmessige konkurranseevne seg betydelig. Det er en risiko for at vi n str overfor en ny periode med nedgang i industrien. For hy lnnsvekst - bde i industrien og andre nringer - vil ramme det konkurranseutsa e nringslivet p to mter. For det frste vil hy lnnsvekst i seg selv svekke inntjeningen og sysselse ngen. For det andre vil renten se es opp og forsterke denne eekten. Industrien vil derfor merke utslagene av for hy lnnsvekst enda sterkere enn fr. S lenge lnningene vokser s mye som de har gjort de siste rene, vil nringslivets konkurranseevne svekkes. Denne svekkelsen vil bidra l  bygge ned sysselse ngen i vareproduksjonen. Det er store forskjeller i produk vitetsveksten innenfor ulike deler av industrien. Det kan se ut l at produk viteten i nringsmiddel- og grask industri har falt de siste rene og det trekker i s fall industriens samlede produk vitet ned. Siden 1995 har lnnskostnadenes andel av verdiskapingen steget med 17 prosentpoeng for denne nringen. Utenom nringsmiddel og grask industri har lnnskostnadenes andel av verdiskapingen steget med om lag 6 prosentpoeng siden 1995. Over de siste 10 rene har lnnsandelen holdt seg konstant i gjennomsni . Utviklingen for norske foretak behver ikke  bli nega v. Enkelte bedri er vil kunne vre i forkant i den teknologiske utviklingen og ke eek viteten i raskere takt enn den srnorske kostnadss gningen. Mange foretak lokaliserer strre deler av sin produksjon l utlandet. Norske industriforetak vil fremdeles kunne vre lnnsomme selv om industriens betydning i norsk konomi blir redusert. Likevel tar vi en risiko nr industrien bygges ned. Det gjr konomien mer srbar. Vekstevnen i konomien - grobunnen for lring, innovasjon og utvikling - kan bli svekket nr mindre av nringslivet blir utsa for intens internasjonal konkurranse. PUBLISERT 5. april 2002 10:00

Title: Oil on book and oil at root
text: Oil on book and oil at root Let me compliment the organizers with a punchy elk at the inaugural . Punchy tels create a drop for speakers, but at least it was nice to get the chance. I want to address three topics: First, I want to look at the composition of our national wealth and discuss its management. It is natural there to place particular emphasis on the fact that Norway has a financial wealth that was once petroleum and a rapidly substantial asset component consisting of petroleum under the seabed. My approach will be wealth management in general, and many of the special, technical and environmental aspects of oil as a wealth object will be simplified away. Secondly, I look at the experiences of other countries with significant non-renewable natural resources. How have they managed their wealth, and what can we possibly learn from them? The last topic is how we ourselves have so far adapted with regard to the management of wealth and the use of the income that this wealth provides. Management of wealth - trade-off of return and risk. In the nation's accounts, there are two assets related to petroleum: recoverable reserves that have not yet been recovered ("oil at root"), and the part of the produced reserves that have been sold and said in book in the Petroleum Fund. Both make up large amounts and are part of our national wealth, which is the basis for the country's consumption opportunities in a long-running perspek v. It is therefore crucial that national wealth is managed in a sense and satisfactory manner, so that the return is good and the risk acceptable. In the bigger picture, these two components become relatively small. It is the discounted value of our own work that is the dominant asset. We are probably an oil-producing nation, but oil doesn't mean much to our prosperity. By looking at asset figures, we take away the fact that the national accounts consider wealth to be income. What we make a living from, and will live on in it, is our ability through work to produce goods and services that are demanded, and to make them better year by year through creativity and creativity. But that must not prevent us from being enamonched when it comes to getting the greatest possible new e of the other components. What are we occupying, what is included in the new assessments? Returns of course - and risk. By risk, I mean how much return rates vary over d. In a national asset survey, the ideal contribution from the various asset and debt components in expected return and risk should be assessed collectively. In any case, the state should seek to manage its share of the wealth so that a favourable relationship between return and risk is achieved. Figure 1 suggests that the largest relocation of national wealth over the next three years will be from oil at root l oil on book. Are there any wrongdoings in return and risk considerations? Hotelling's1 rule states that the real price of a non-renewable resource above d should tend to be higher at a rate equal to the real interest rate. In that case, it would yield a return on "oil at root" that could be compared with the return on a financial wealth ("oil on book"). In terms of return, there should be no strong arguments for transforming oil into financial assets faster than is necessary based on how much one wants to use of the return/wealth. Experience shows that over a long period, real oil price inflation has been lower than the real interest rate on US bonds (which may be an indication of the more theore ske real interest rate). The chart shows developments from 1986 l now. The return on oil is clearly below bonds. Even if we had invested in oil 50 years ago and sold it today, we would have a worse return than by investing in bonds, but it would have been a few years in the 70s and early 80s where we could sell at a profit. If we look at the period from 1986 and compare nominal oil price developments with the return on a fund that followed the Petroleum Fund's investment strategy  a global portfolio with a distribution of 60-40 on bonds and equities  we see that the fund would generate a markedly higher annual return. So what about the risk, how is it affected by a relocation between oil and financial wealth? History gives us a clear, albeit perhaps somewhat surprising, message. A relocation from oil in financial wealth increases returns and reduces cohabitation risk. The e has to do with the fact that the wealth under the seabed (somewhat simplified) consists only of e ak vum, petroleum, while a broadly invested financial wealth is strongly diversified in many objects whose returns do not vary completely in pace. In a financial portfolio, much can also be done to steer towards a "good" city's relationship between return and risk. If financial investments are made less diversified by investing only in equities, we see that the risk reaches a minimum for a portfolio that contains a small proportion of petroleum. The return is also increasing with an increasing equity share. Today, the composition is about 20-80 between financial wealth (the Petroleum Fund) and petroleum. If we dare to steady ourselves in historical contexts, it is quite obvious that we have too much oil in our portfolio and that the asset relocation in the direction of financial wealth that is taking place is guns g. We don't have any guarantee that history will repeat itself, but to put it against us requires great courage. Rather, it can be argued that one should try to speed up the relocation. In principle, it can be thought of done in several ways: The state has sold "oil in a mess" through the disposal of SDFI shares. Y is more divestment is possible in principle, but it is a question of whether it is able to fully realise the values of the state's petroleum wealth. Buyers may have better knowledge of the share than the seller. Uncertainty about the forward-looking system may also contribute to pulling the price down. By increasing the recovery rate, oil reserves could move into the Petroleum Fund's diversified portfolio more quickly. I do not have an overview of what technical possibilities there are for them. Moreover, another major producer that Norway must assess the price effects of a sharp increase in the rate of recovery. In theory, oil price risk could also be uncovered in the market by selling a portion of the oil for forward delivery in a price that is currently being agreed upon. For large producers, the market for such commodity instruments is hardly well enough developed l to handle the large volumes and long runs where needed, should it be. Looking from a wealth management standpoint, the review seems so far to say that it is nice to have wealth, and the greater the better, but more of it should have been in financial wealth and less in petroleum. All else being equal, it would be better to have more oil on book and less at root. But e is each we will get there. But is it really an advantage to have large natural resources? A quick glance at the countries where oil or other non-renewable natural resources make up a large part of the industry base may be given a say in the question of whether oil, etc., is really a blessing. Developing countries with oil as the most important export commodity have generally had significantly lower growth than other developing countries. Norway has growth on a par with other advanced economies. Several studies2 of the relationship between longitudinal economic growth and the impact on natural resources also show that countries with a large impact on natural reserves tend to have lower economic growth. Why? Large natural reserves are basically an advantage for a country's economy. The production of petroleum and other natural resources provides a profi that overlooks the normal return on invested capital, a base rate or superprofi ("economic rent"). If this profi current was permanent and stable, it might be easy to handle it. Non-renewable resources such as oil can represent significant inconveniences because the profi current is uncertain and volatile, and because it does not last forever. The biggest danger is that an innre is as if this flow of money was stable and lasted forever. Then something can happen to our ability l make ourselves new e of the most important resource we have, our ability to work and crea vitet. The term "Dutch disease" alludes to the nega ve effects that the use of basic interest rates from natural resources received for the Netherlands. The large revenues that the Netherlands received from gas deposits from the slush in the 1960s financed a strong growth in public releases. The release led to a loss of competitiveness and job closures in the competitive sector. Developments went too far and large deficits in the foreign economy and government finances made it necessary to tighten so that unemployment rose sharply in the first half of the 1980s. The Netherlands is not the first example of a nation that suddenly gains access to valuable natural resources and does not deal with it. A very clear example can be found in Spain as early as the 17th century. The colonization of South and Central America gave the country lgang l great natural resources and l gold. Spain chose to spend a large part of its profits on luxury and war. The attitudes l work that they e led l did not laugh ere to get the land back on its feet when the gold took cunning. The historian David Landes describes them in his book "The Wealth and Poverty of Na ons". Why have many countries failed to exa lent the laughing girl wealth? The reasons can be several. An economic-policing explanation is that the wealth of resources leads l extreme focus from different groups on making as much of the profits from the natural resource as possible. The battle for the profits is often referred to as "rent-seeking behavior". Resource-rich countries may be more concerned with extreme rent-seeking than resource-based economies. The competition between the various factions can lead to an ineffective depletion of the natural resource and the inexorable use of the revenues. Entrepreneurship, talent and energy in the business sector and policing are used to share in these revenues instead of in more production in both the public and private sectors. For the individual bedri or grouping, this ak viteten may seem rational - a 10 percent chance l winning the big lottery ticket may be better than betting on an ordinary return of capital in ordinary business. For the country, it can be devastating. A sociological explanation is that le jent wealth weakens the insen vein in innovation and work. We feel like we're getting rich and want to have a good time. One possible economic explanation is that a large and broad sector, which is devout for competition from abroad, creates learning and development. In countries with a high level of impact on natural resources, the sector can be reduced, while sheltered sectors are built up. The competitive intensity of the economy may be diminished and the ability and willingness of innovation to weaken. We should be very careful about drawing safe conclusions from historical comparisons. I guess we'd rather assume that we manage our assets better. Nevertheless, there may be particular reason to highlight two critical factors in order for us to succeed. Figure 10. What conclusions can we draw from historical comparisons? First, the forms of decision-making and processes in policing and economic life must provide effek vt protection against special interests having a disproportionately strong control over and share of petroleum wealth or accusations of high petroleum revenues. Second, it is important for the growth capacity of the economy that we preserve a broad sector of the mainland economy that works under intense competition so that we preserve and develop incentives to acquire knowledge and innovation. Let me give a small example that illustrates the e: If a perception that with oil we are getting so rich that we can relax li should lead to a reduction in annual product growth of less than a quarter of a percentage point, i.e. a reduction in underlying growth in the economy (GDP) from the current level of about 2 percent l 1 3/4, it would reduce our income base more than any return on "book" or "mess" would give us. A good handling of the inconsecurities of non-renewable natural resources probably requires the recognition of two factors: that it is a asset and that it should be managed as it is that the return on this wealth can fluctuate considerably, and that this should be taken into account when taking into account how the return is disposed of. Several countries with large natural resources have sought to separate the extraction of resources from the consumption of sales revenues by raising special funds. Such funds have partly been stabilisation funds for managing income fluctuations, partly savings funds for future generations and partly both. The IMF has conducted a study3 of whether such funds have worked for the purpose. Big see, they don't. The intentions may have been there, but the implementation is too difficult. The funds have also proved to be functioning poorly because they are not integrated with the state budget, or because the rules for provisions and non-profit are circumvented or changed. It probably does little to raise a fund if there is no clear willingness and ability to conduct responsible financial policing, even in areas not directly affected by the fund. According to the IMF study, a longitudinal fiscal policy must be set up with a focus on preserving a carrier-wrecking balance sheet excluding oil, holding back on the growth as oil prices rise and having transparency about all aspects of financial policy and any fund structures. Give them e, a fund can be a new g mechanism. The IMF study claims that the Norwegian Petroleum Fund is successful because Norway have a tradition of, even before the raising of the Petroleum Fund, accountability in fiscal policy and macroeconomic policing in general, with a high degree of transparency. How do we get one? Government cash flow from petroleum activities is transferred to the Petroleum Fund. The Fund invests in a broadly combined portfolio of bonds and equities abroad. E is the new fiscal rule for fiscal policy, the estimated real return on the Fund's investments, sguled at four per cent, will be transferred in the bidding and used in the domestic economy. They provide an expansive impulse of around 0.4 per cent of the bru o national product into the Norwegian economy every year for many years to come. This raises questions about the fact that the Petroleum Fund is invested in its entirety abroad. In this discussion, it is important to distinguish between the use of petroleum revenues and the management of the Petroleum Fund. As for the first problem, it is reason to point out that since oil production began in the early 1970s, more than half of the government's proceeds from petroleum activities have been used domestically. So we've already spent a lot of our wealth. In the years ahead, the aim is to ramp up the use of petroleum revenues in line with the fiscal rule for fiscal policy. An excessively sharp increase in the use of domestic petroleum revenues, or an erration of them, would create balance problems in the economy, both in the short and longer term. Some have advocated that if parts of the fund are invested in Norway, it will help l develop the Norwegian capital market. The Governor discusses this problem in the in or, and I reproduce some of the factors. First, there may be reason to remind that today there is a high degree of capital mobility between Norway and abroad. The Norwegian capital market is part of a Nordic market that is once again being woven together with a global market. The e-market allows the state's choice as an investor and the choice of the people who are interested in capital to be separated. The state can choose the composition, requirements of returns and risk profile on its financial investments without reflecting the financing needs of Norwegian enterprises. Norske bedri, on the other hand, can choose its loan and equity structure independently of the government's financial investments. We should not treat the distribution of the state's financial investments and make one's choice of financing as if we have a city economy. After all, it's one of the great acts of markets that we must not demand "the double morphation of desires". The international capital market is also at the disposal of Norwegian bedri is, directly or indirectly via Norwegian financial institutions. It can hardly be argued that there is a lack of capital in Norway. Private saving in the mainland economy has been high in recent years. Real investment in the business sector has also been the case. In other words, any failure of the capital market will not be due to the fact that we invest and save little. Developments in the 1990s mean that equities and funds account for an increasing share of total household assets. The enterprises' equity ratio has increased in the 1990s, particularly for the new equity raised in the market. Capital markets are effek ve tools for channelling funds from the saver in the person investing. Nevertheless, the Norwegian loan and capital market is likely to have weaknesses, with thin securities markets and little breadth in the investor and ownership environments compared with some countries. Partly it's because we're a small country. We can do little about that. But it probably also has a background in the shambles of the various assets, in a large state ownership of bedri is and perhaps in the way we fund our pensions. We can do something about that. The new fiscal rule for fiscal policy and petroleum fund construction takes into account both the consideration that the generations e are us should also benefit from the oil wealth, and the consideration of preventing large fluctuations in oil prices from having an impact on the ups and downs of the Norwegian economy. The rule that only the return on the Petroleum Fund is to be used means that it is not eaten by the wealth. The Petroleum Fund will increase as long as the government has a posi v cash flow from petroleum activities, and when the conversion from oil in financial wealth has been carried out, no more shall be taken out than that the real value of the wealth is maintained, in principle. l evig d. The model addresses stabilisation considerations by only using the return on the part of petroleum wealth that has been transformed in financial capital, so that its use is shielded from the wide fluctuations in oil prices. In llegg, a l basis for its use lays a squirt, but realis slashes the real return of four per cent and screens this against the annual variations in the factual return. If we stick to the e, and remember that it is the return of the human capital on which we live largely, it may become the conclusions of leading historians that we managed our talents well, both the pecuniary and the intellectuals. Figur 1 antyder at den strste omplasseringen av nasjonalformuen de neste tre rene vil vre fra olje p rot l olje p bok. Er det fornu ig u ra avkastnings- og risikobetraktninger? Hotelling's1 regel sier at realprisen p en ikke-fornybar ressurs over d burde tendere l  s ge med en rate lik realrenten. Det skulle i s fall gi en avkastning p "olje p rot" som skulle kunne sammenlignes med avkastningen p en nansformue ("olje p bok"). Avkastningsmessig skulle det da ikke vre sterke argumenter for  transformere oljen over i nansielle fordringer raskere enn det som er ndvendig ut fra hvor mye en nsker  anvende av avkastningen/formuen. Erfaringene viser imidler d at over lang d har realprisveksten p olje vrt mindre enn realrenten p amerikanske obligasjoner (som kan vre en indikasjon p den mer teore ske realrenten). Figuren viser utviklingen fra 1986 l n. Avkastningen p olje ligger klart under obligasjoner. Ogs om vi hadde investert i olje for 50 r siden og solgt den i dag, ville vi f drligere avkastning enn ved  investere i obligasjoner, men det ville vrt noen r p 70- og begynnelsen av 80-tallet der vi kunne solgt med fortjeneste. Ser vi p perioden fra 1986 og sammenligner nominell oljeprisutvikling med den avkastning et fond som fulgte Petroleumsfondets investeringsstrategi - en global porteflje med fordeling 60-40 p obligasjoner og aksjer - ser vi at fondet ville gi en klart hyere rlig avkastning. Hva s med risikoen, hvordan pvirkes den av en omplassering mellom olje og nansformue? Historien gir oss et klart, om enn kanskje noe overraskende, budskap. En omplassering fra olje l nansformue ker avkastningen og reduserer sam dig risikoen. De e har med det  gjre at formuen under havbunnen (noe forenklet) kun bestr av e ak vum, petroleum, mens en bredt plassert nansformue er sterkt diversisert i mange objekter hvis avkastning ikke varierer helt i takt. I en nansporteflje kan en ogs gjre mye for ak vt  styre mot et "godt" by eforhold mellom avkastning og risiko. Hvis en gjr nansplasseringene mindre diversisert ved bare  plassere i aksjer, s ser vi at risikoen nr et minimum for en porteflje som inneholder en liten andel petroleum. Avkastningen fortse er imidler d  ke med kende aksjeandel. I dag er sammensetningen omtrent 20-80 mellom nansformue (Petroleumsfondet) og petroleum. Hvis vi vger  st e oss p historiske sammenhenger, er det ganske penbart at vi rela vt se har for mye olje i vr porteflje og at den formuesomplassering i retning av nansformue som foregr, er guns g. Vi har rik gnok ikke noen garan for at historien gjentar seg, men  legge det motsa e l grunn krever stort mot. Det kan heller argumenteres for at en burde forske  forsere tempoet i omplasseringen. Det kan i prinsippet tenkes gjort p ere mter: Staten har solgt "olje p rot" gjennom avhending av SDE-andeler. Y erligere nedsalg er i prinsippet mulig, men det er et sprsml om en i s fall er i stand l fullt ut  realisere verdiene av statens petroleumsformue. Kjperne kan ha bedre kunnskap om andelen enn selger. Usikkerhet om det frem dige ska esystem kan ogs bidra l  trekke prisen ned. Ved  ke utvinningstakten kunne oljereservene raskere komme over i Petroleumsfondets diversiserte porteflje. Hvilke tekniske muligheter det er for de e har jeg ikke oversikt over. Dessuten m e nok en stor produsent som Norge vurdere prisvirkningene av en sterk kning i utvinningstakten. I teorien kunne ogs oljeprisrisiko avdekkes i markedet ved  selge en del av oljen for frem dig levering l en pris som avtales n. For store produsenter er markedet for slike rvareinstrumenter neppe godt nok utviklet l  hndtere de store volumer og lange lpe der det ville vre behov for, skulle det monne. Se fra et formuesforvaltningsststed synes gjennomgangen s langt  fortelle at det er nt  ha formue, og jo strre dess bedre, men mer av den burde vrt i nansformue og mindre i petroleum. Alt annet likt ville det vrt bedre  ha mer olje p bok og mindre p rot. Men e er hvert vil vi komme dit. Men er det virkelig en fordel  ha store naturressurser? Et raskt blikk p de land der olje eller andre ikke-fornybare naturressurser utgjr en stor del av nringsgrunnlaget kan f en l  s lle sprsmlet om olje m.v. egentlig er en velsignelse. Utviklingsland med olje som vik gste eksportvare har gjennomgende ha en betydelig lavere vekst enn andre utviklingsland. Norge har en vekst p linje med andre industriland. Flere studier2 av sammenhengen mellom langsik g konomisk vekst og lgang p naturressurser viser da ogs at land med stor lgang p naturreservene har en tendens l lavere konomisk vekst. Hvorfor? Store naturreserver er i utgangspunktet en fordel for et lands konomi. Produksjon av petroleum og andre naturressurser gir en pro som overs ger normal avkastning p investert kapital, en grunnrente eller superpro ("economic rent"). Hvis denne pro strmmen var permanent og stabil ville det kanskje vre rela vt enkelt  hndtere den. Ikke-fornybare ressurser som olje kan imidler d representere betydelige u ordringer fordi pro strmmen er usikker og vola l, og fordi den ikke varer evig. Den strste faren er at en innre er seg som om denne pengestrmmen var stabilt stor og varte evig. Da kan det skje noe med vr evne l  gjre oss ny e av den vik gste ressurs vi har, vr arbeidsevne og krea vitet. Begrepet "hollandsk syke" henspiller p de nega ve virkningene som bruken av grunnrente fra naturressurser kk for Nederland. De store inntektene som Nederland kk fra gassforekomster fra slu en av 1960-tallet, nansierte en sterk vekst i oentlige utgi er. Utgi sveksten frte l tap av konkurranseevne og nedleggelse av arbeidsplasser i konkurranseutsa sektor. Utviklingen gikk for langt og store underskudd i utenrikskonomien og statsnansene gjorde det ndvendig  stramme inn slik at arbeidsledigheten steg sterkt i frste halvdel av 1980-tallet. Nederland er ikke det frste eksempelet p en nasjon som plutselig fr lgang p verdifulle naturressurser og som ikke hndterer det. Et svrt tydelig eksempel nner vi i Spania allerede p 1600-tallet. Koloniseringen av Sr- og MellomAmerika ga landet lgang l store naturressurser og l gull. Spania valgte  bruke en stor del av gevinsten p luksus og krig. De holdninger l arbeid som de e ledet l gjorde det ikke le ere  f landet p fote igjen da gullet tok slu . Historikeren David Landes beskriver de e i sin bok "The Wealth and Poverty of Na ons". Hvorfor har mange land ikke klart  utny e den le jente rikdommen? rsakene kan vre ere. En konomisk-poli sk forklaring er at ressursrikdommen frer l ekstrem fokusering fra ulike grupper p  legne seg mest mulig av overskuddet fra naturressursen. Kampen om de e overskuddet betegnes gjerne som "rent-seeking behavior". Ressursrike land kan vre mer utsa e for ekstrem "rent-seeking" a erd enn ressursfa ge konomier. Konkurransen mellom de ulike fraksjonene kan fre l en ineek v u mming av naturressursen og ufornu ig bruk av inntektene. Entreprenrskap, talent og energi i nringslivet og det poli ske livet brukes for  f del i disse inntektene i stedet for l mer produk v virksomhet i bde oentlig og privat sektor. For den enkelte bedri eller gruppering kan denne ak viteten fortone seg rasjonell - en 10 prosent sjanse l  vinne det store lodd kan vre bedre enn  satse p en ordinr avkastning av kapital i vanlig virksomhet. For landet kan det vre deleggende. En sosiologisk forklaring er at le jent rikdom svekker insen vene l innovasjon og arbeid. Vi fler vi er bli rike og vil ha det godt. En mulig konomisk forklaring er at en stor og bred sektor, som er utsa for konkurranse fra utlandet, skaper lring og utvikling. I land med stor lgang p naturressurser kan sektoren bli bygget ned, mens de skjermede sektorene bygges opp. Konkurranseintensiteten i konomien kan bli mindre og evnen og viljen l innovasjon svekket. Vi skal vel vre svrt varsomme med  trekke sikre konklusjoner av historiske sammenligninger. Vi vil vel helst legge l grunn at vi forvalter verdiene bedre. Det kan likevel vre srlig grunn l  trekke frem to kri ske faktorer for at vi skal lykkes. Figur 10. Hvilke konklusjoner kan vi trekke av historiske sammenligninger? For det frste: Beslutningsformene og prosessene i det poli ske og konomiske livet m gi eek vt vern mot at srinteresser lriver seg en uforholdsmessig sterk kontroll med og andel av petroleumsformuen eller besky else i ly av de hye petroleumsinntektene. For det andre: Det er vik g for vekstevnen i konomien at vi bevarer en bred sektor i fastlandskonomien som arbeider under intens konkurranse slik at vi bevarer og utvikler insen vene l  erverve kunnskap og l nyskapning. La meg gi et lite eksempel som illustrerer de e: Hvis en oppfatning om at vi med olje er bli s rike at vi kan slappe av li skulle lede l en reduksjon i den rlige produk vitetsvekst p mindre enn et kvart prosentpoeng, alts en reduksjon i den underliggende vekst i konomien (BNP) fra dagens niv p omlag 2 prosent l 1 3/4, s ville det redusere inntektsgrunnlaget vrt mer enn all avkastning petroleumsformuen p "bok" eller "rot" vil gi oss. En god hndtering av de u ordringer stor lgang l ikke-fornybare naturressurser byr p, krever trolig erkjennelse av to forhold: at det dreier seg om en formuespost og at den br forvaltes som det at avkastningen p denne formuen kan svinge mye, og at det br hensyntas nr en tar s lling l hvordan avkastningen disponeres. Flere land med store naturressurser har skt  skille utvinning av ressursene fra forbruk av salgsinntektene gjennom  oppre e spesielle fond. Slike fond har dels vrt stabiliseringsfond for  hndtere inntektssvingninger, dels sparefond for frem dige generasjoner og dels begge deler. IMF har gjennomfrt en studie3 av om slike fond har virket e er hensikten. Stort se har de ikke det. Intensjonene har kanskje vrt der, men gjennomfringen er bli for vanskelig. Fondene har o e vist seg  fungere drlig fordi de ikke er lstrekkelig integrert med statsbudsje et, eller fordi reglene for avsetninger og u ak er omg eller endret. Det hjelper trolig lite  oppre e et fond hvis det ikke foreligger en klar vilje og evne l  fre en ansvarlig konomisk poli kk, ogs p omrder som ikke direkte berres av fondet. Det m, iflge IMFstudien, legges opp en langsik g nanspoli kk med fokus p  bevare en brekra ig budsje balanse utenom olje, holde igjen p utgi sveksten nr oljeprisene ker og ha penhet om alle forhold rundt nanspoli kken og eventuelle fondskonstruksjoner. Gi de e, kan et fond vre en ny g mekanisme. IMF-studien fremholder det norske Petroleumsfondet som suksessfullt - ne opp fordi Norge har en tradisjon for, ogs fra fr oppre elsen av Petroleumsfondet, ansvarlighet i nanspoli kken og den makrokonomiske poli kken generelt, med stor grad av penhet. Hvordan har vi innre et oss? Statens kontantstrm fra oljevirksomheten overfres l petroleumsfondet. Fondet investerer i en bredt sammensa porteflje av obligasjoner og aksjer i utlandet. E er den nye handlingsregelen for nanspoli kken vil den beregnede realavkastning p fondets plasseringer, s pulert l re prosent, overfres l budsje et og brukes i den innenlandske konomien. De e gir en ekspansiv impuls p rundt 0,4 prosent av bru o nasjonalproduktet inn i norsk konomi hvert r i mange r fremover. Til der reises det sprsml ved at Petroleumsfondet i sin helhet er plassert i utlandet. I denne diskusjonen er det vik g  skille mellom bruken av oljepengene og forvaltningen av Petroleumsfondet. Nr det gjelder den frste problems llingen, er det grunn l  peke p at siden produksjonen av olje startet opp p begynnelsen av 1970-tallet, er over halvparten av statens proveny fra petroleumsvirksomheten brukt innenlands. Vi har alts allerede brukt mye av formuen. I rene fremover tas det sikte p  trappe opp bruken av oljeinntekter i trd med handlingsregelen for nanspoli kken. En for sterk kning i bruken av oljeinntekter innenlands, eller en erra sk bruk av dem, ville skape balanseproblemer i konomien, bde p kort og lengre sikt. Enkelte har ta l orde for at dersom deler av fondet investeres i Norge, vil det hjelpe l  utvikle det norske kapitalmarkedet. Sentralbanksjefen dr et denne problems llingen i rstalen i or, og jeg gjengir noen av momentene. Det kan for det frste vre grunn l  minne om at det i dag er hy grad av kapitalmobilitet mellom Norge og utlandet. Det norske kapitalmarkedet er del av et nordisk som igjen i s gende grad blir vevd sammen med et globalt marked. De e markedet gjr at statens valg som investor og bedri enes valg som e ersprrer av kapital kan adskilles. Staten kan velge sammensetning, krav l avkastning og risikoprol p sine nansielle investeringer uten  skjele l nansieringsbehovet l norske foretak. Norske bedri er p sin side kan velge lne- og egenkapitalstruktur uavhengig av statens nansielle investeringer. Vi br ikke behandle fordelingen av statens nansinvesteringer og bedri enes valg av nansiering som om vi har en by ekonomi. Det er jo ne opp en av de store a raksjoner ved markeder at vi ikke m kreve "the double coincidence of wants". Det internasjonale kapitalmarkedet str l disposisjon ogs for norske bedri er, direkte eller indirekte via norske nansins tusjoner. Det kan vanskelig hevdes at det er mangel p kapital i Norge. Den private sparingen i fastlandskonomien har vrt hy de senere rene. Det har ogs realinvesteringene i nringslivet vrt. En eventuell svikt i kapitalmarkedet kommer alts ikke l u rykk i at vi investerer og sparer lite. Utviklingen p slu en av 1990-tallet, frer l at aksjer og fonds utgjr en stadig strre andel av husholdningenes samlede fordringer. Foretakenes egenkapitalandel har kt p 1990-tallet srlig gjelder de e ny egenkapital som er hentet i markedet. Kapitalmarkedene er eek ve verkty for  kanalisere midler fra den som sparer l den som investerer. Det norske lne- og kapitalmarkedet har trolig likevel svakheter, med tynne verdipapirmarkeder og liten bredde i investor- og eiermiljene sammenliknet med enkelte land. Dels skyldes de e at vi er et lite land. Det kan vi gjre lite med. Men det har nok ogs bakgrunn i ska leggingen av de ulike formuesobjekter, i et stort statlig eie av bedri er og kanskje i mten vi nansierer pensjonene p. Det kan vi gjre noe med. Den nye handlingsregelen for nanspoli kken og petroleumsfondskonstruksjonen ivaretar bde hensynet l at ogs generasjonene e er oss skal ha glede av oljerikdommen, og hensynet l  hindre store svingninger i oljeprisen i  sl ut i kra ige opp- og nedturer i norsk konomi. Regelen om at bare avkastningen av Petroleumsfondet skal brukes innebrer at det ikke spises av formuen. Petroleumsfondet vil ke s lenge staten har en posi v kontantstrm fra oljevirksomheten, og nr omvekslingen fra olje l nansformue er gjennomfrt, skal det fortsa ikke tas ut mer enn at den reelle verdi av formuen oppre holdes, i prinsippet l evig d. Modellen ivaretar stabiliseringshensynet ved at en bare bruker avkastningen av den del av petroleumsformuen som er transformert l nanskapital, slik at bruken skjermes mot de store svingningene i oljeprisen. I llegg legger en l grunn for bruken en s pulert, men realis sk langsik g realavkastning p re prosent og skjermer slik mot de rlige variasjonene i den fak ske avkastning. Holder vi fast ved de e, og husker at det er avkastning av den menneskelige kapital vi i all hovedsak lever av, s kan det bli konklusjonene fra frem dige historikere at vi forvaltet vre talenter vel, bde de pekunire og de intellektuelle. The inflation target is 21/2 per cent. As it goes, we will gain experience with inflation targeting. E years are short. The price hike over the past year is also a result of monetary policy before the inflation target was introduced. It may also be interesting to look at experience from other countries with an inflation target. The last time I gave a here at CME was "Monetary Policy, Forecasting and Marketing Communication" . One issue then was transparency and predictability in the implementation of monetary policy. Transparency can be defined as the external presentation of decisions consistent with the internal decision-making process. In a report presented in the Center for Economic Policy Research (CEPR) under the elen "How Do Central Banks Talk?" 1 emphasises that transparency should contribute l that the public understands and perhaps foresees the central bank's decisions and sees each one of them as a logical conclusion in the series of more accurate and forward-looking decisions with the intention of achieving a clearly defined objective. If a change in interest rates is largely expected, it will be priced into the money market in advance and will have a small impact on market rates when it arrives. If we look at 2001 under e , the market was essentially expecting a more expansive monetary policy than the one that was carried out. Market interest rates therefore generally rose at the edge of monetary policy meetings. The exception is the December meeting where the sight deposit rate was reduced by 0.5 percentage points. The market had not expected such a large interest rate cut at the e-meeting, and the one-month rate fell by almost 0.2 percentage points. Nor had analysts expected an interest rate reduction of this magnitude. At the monetary policy meetings in January and February this year, both market participants and analysts expected a reduction that did not come then. Such patterns remain in many countries. In the UK, the impact was large throughout the year. In part, market rates will reflect the fact that various monetary policy meetings are possible. In addition, the central bank may assess economic developments differently from market participants. We must therefore assume that market rates will have an impact when the sight deposit rate changes or when the central bank publishes a changed view of the inflation outlook. Another example is the interest rate cut in Sweden of 0.5 percentage points in September, which came at a meeting that was not pre-announced. But the impact was generally small throughout 2001. Nor in the period from 1999 do the effects appear to be particularly large. This indicates that interest rate changes were largely priced in before monetary policy meetings. The impact on the Norwegian one-month rate is somewhat above a broad international level from 1999. One explanation may be that our inflation target is new , and that it may take something d before market participants and Norges Bank gain experience with trading patterns and communication. Another possible reason is that we have changed the interest rate by 1/2 percentage point, while central banks in countries with a lower interest rate level have more frequently adjusted the interest rate by 1/4 percentage point. We can also form a picture of how predictable monetary policy is by looking at developments in market expectations in forward-looking interest rates, known as FRA rates. In general, there is a tendency for the impact on market expectations to be greater than changes in Norges Bank's sight deposit rate. At the beginning of 2001, it was expected that the interest rate would fall in the spring. Six months later, interest rate expectations were higher than what was to be unealthed. From autumn 2001, the picture has again been reversed, and interest rate expectations were well below what was unearthed. It was probably rich to see developments. More generally, it appears that the market sometimes prices in forward-looking changes in the interest rate that do not come. There is no basis for saying that market participants' expectations were wrong at the point at which these FRA contracts were entered into. On the contrary, both in the autumn and on other occasions, there was reason to fear the effects of the international recession. They were reflected in interest rate expectations. When new information later showed that risk had been reduced, both market expectations and the central bank's view of developments changed. Frequent changes in interest rate expectations do not necessarily mean that the market is unstable. Det er ogs en tendens l at ere sm valutaer utenfor de store valutaomrdene har styrket seg. Ogs under Russland-krisen i 1998-1999 var utviklingen i disse premiene en vik g faktor6. Nr risikoen globalt vurderes som liten og internasjonale renter er lave, kan det vre mer a rak vt  investere i valutaer med hy rente. Siden sommeren 1999 har dieransen mellom norske og internasjonale renter trolig ogs vrt vik g for utviklingen i kronekursen. En gradvis hyere rentedieranse har g sammen med sterkere krone. kningen i rentedieransen avspeiler forskjeller i konjunkturene mellom Norge og andre land. Dieransen i tolvmnedersrentene har steget kra ig siden ny r, og ser ut l  fye kronekursutviklingen bedre enn dieransen i tremnedersrentene. Lengre renter pvirkes i strre grad enn kortsik ge renter av forventninger om den konomiske utviklingen fremover. E er ny r har det vrt tegn l at aktrene reagerer p kt press i konomien ved  justere opp sine renteforventninger p noe lengre sikt. De e slr ut i renter med lengre lpe d. Det er mulig at kronekursen styrkes nr det er kende knapphet p realressursene i Norge og ledige ressurser blant vre handelspartnere. Forskjeller i konjunkturene har ogs dligere pvirket rentedieransene mellom ulike land. Historisk er en renteforskjell p 3 prosentpoeng ikke uvanlig, verken for Norge eller for andre land. Fra begynnelsen av 1990-tallet og fram l 2001 har forskjellen i renten l Tyskland for Norge, Sverige og Storbritannia variert mellom -1 og 4 prosentpoeng som rsgjennomsni 7 Den norske kronen var mer stabil p 1990-tallet enn valutakursen for andre sm pne konomier som Canada, Sverige og Storbritannia. Det siste halve ret har bevegelsen i kronekursen lignet mer p bevegelser de andre landene har ha i sine valutaer. Kronen yter, og kronens verdi svinger periodevis som valutaene l andre sm pne konomier. Det er mulig at forventningene om den konomiske utviklingen i Norge n spiller en strre rolle for kurs- og rentedannelsen. Hvis markedsaktrene venter en innstramming i pengepoli kken, kan det i seg selv fre l at kronekursen styrker seg. Det kan bety at reaksjonsmnsteret for kronen er endret. Mens vi dligere s en tendens l svakere krone e er kostbare lnnsoppgjr, har kronen n styrket seg. Styrkingen av kronen virker som en automa sk stabilisator p priss gningen. Nr kronekursen styrker seg, blir ogs de monetre forholdene samlet se strammet l. En vik g grunn l  vre pen om reaksjonsmnsteret i pengepoli kken er, som nevnte, at pengepoli kken da blir mer eek v. Det har vi f illustrert denne vren. De monetre forholdene er bli strammere selv om Norges Bank bare har varslet et endret syn p utsiktene. Inntektsoppgjret viser at det var p de med en innstramming. Pengepoli kken skal sikte mot stabilitet i den norske krones nasjonale og internasjonale verdi, herunder ogs bidra l stabile forventninger om valutakursutviklingen. Det beste bidraget pengepoli kken kan gi l stabile forventninger om kursutviklingen, er  sikte mot  oppfylle det opera ve mlet om lav og stabil inasjon. Vi m imidler d ogs framover vre forberedt p svingninger i verdien av vr valuta som er mer p linje med de svingningene vi har se i andre land. Valutakursen vil variere p kort sikt. Et annet forhold er at terminkursene sier at kronen vil depresiere. Det reekterer at det er den posi ve rentedieransen som holder kroneverdien oppe. Terminkursen treer erfaringsmessig ikke srlig godt som prognose p utviklingen i spotkursen. Den viser likevel at dagens kurs er forenelig med en langsik g likevektskurs om lag p det nivet vi har ha dligere. Utviklingen i den nominelle kursen kan ogs vurderes i lys av utviklingen i den reelle valutakursen. Andre land, som Sverige, Australia og Canada har opplevd en trendmessig svekkelse av realkursen. Dels reekterer det trolig at disse landene produserer varer som er bli mindre verd p verdensmarkedet, dels kan det reektere at de har ha lavere vekst i sin produk vitet enn noen andre land. I andre land, blant annet Storbritannia, kan det se ut l at realkursen varig har lagt seg p et hyere leie. Vi har historisk ikke se tegn l en slik utvikling i norsk konomi. Det ser vi klarest nr vi sammenlikner med tysk konomi. I lpet av femten r, fra 1973 l 1988, steg konsumprisene dobbelt s mye som i Tyskland. I den samme perioden ble verdien av kronen nesten halvert mot tyske mark. Over d har forholdet mellom tyske og norske priser holdt seg noks stabilt mlt i felles valuta. Det kan tyde p at kjpekra sparitet mot andre europeiske land slr gjennom over d. Nyere forskning gir ogs st e l denne hypotesen.8 Norges eek ve realvalutakurs har svingt rundt et rela vt stabilt niv de siste tre rene. Gjennomgende reekterer disse svingningene forskjeller i konjunkturene. Nr det er press p realressursene i konomien, svekkes konkurranseevnen og realkursen ker. Nr det er ledige ressurser, styrkes konkurranseevnen og realkursen faller. De siste rene har presset i norsk konomi vrt markert sterkere enn i andre land. Vi ser at realkursen er sterkere n enn det historiske gjennomsni et. Den er ogs nr niver vi ikke har se dligere. Den konomiske poli kken i Norge bygger p handlingsregler for nanspoli kken og pengepoli kken. Handlingsregelen for nanspoli kken sier at bruken av oljeinntektene over statsbudsje et skal svare l den forventede realavkastningen av Petroleumsfondet. Pengepoli kken re es inn mot lav og stabil inasjon. Mesteparten av innfasingen av oljeinntektene kommer i de neste rene. Med en avkastning av oljefondet p 4 prosent vil bruken av oljeinntektene ke l nrmere 5 prosent av BNP for Fastlands-Norge i 2010. Handlingsregelen innebrer at nanspoli kken vil bidra l vekst i e ersprselen innenlands hvert r i ere r fremover. Pengepoli kken er llagt et strre ansvar for  stabilisere den konomiske utviklingen. I r er den underliggende nominelle veksten i statsbudsje ets utgi er beregnet l 7 prosent. Da er handlingsregelen fulgt nye. Mye av de e gr l  dekke kte priser og lnnsutgi er. Samlet prisvekst p oentlige utgi er er beregnet l 4 prosent. Den reelle underliggende utgi sveksten er 2 prosent. Men det er srlig overfringene som ker. Den reelle veksten i konsumet av oentlige tjenester er ansl l 1 prosent. Det er et ny trekk i bildet at utgi ene i statsbudsje et kes spass vesentlig nr det er sterkt press i arbeidsmarkedet. I Norge fr vi n et sammenfall i d - uten at det er en rsakssammenheng - mellom hyere lnns llegg og hyere oentlige utgi er. Hy lnnsvekst ville i et fastkurssystem tendere l  svekke lliten l kronekursen. N styrker kronen seg, og det kan skyldes at aktrene i valutamarkedet venter innstramming i pengepoli kken. Title: Monetary policy in an oil economy
text: Monetary policy in an oil economy Speech by Governor Svein Gjedrem. Norwegian Confederation of Trade Unions, 21 August 2002 The world economy is characterised by turbulence in financial markets, low growth and rising unemployment. Even though the turbulence abroad has had an impact on parts of norway's business sector, the overall growth in the Norwegian economy and solid growth in e-demand are goods and services. The demand is driven by a sharp rise in household incomes. There is also a strong case in the oil sector and high oil prices. Petroleum investment remains high. The labour market is tight. There's going to be a very high number of norwegian wages. For several years, the rise in labour costs in Norway has been considerably higher than among our trading partners. This hits the industry hard, along with bad ones out there and a strong krone. We take a risk when the industry is built down. This makes the economy more vulnerable. The growth capacity of the economy  the breeding ground for learning, innovation and development  may be weakened when less of the business sector is exposed to intense international competition. High wage growth affects the international sector in two ways. First, it in itself weakens earnings and employment. Secondly, the monetary policy must be tightened l. As a result, the krone is strengthening, so that earnings and employment are depreciating y more. Wage growth as a whole for all groups influences the inflation outlook. But large sums for individual groups can lay the groundwork for wage spirals. Wages for employees in the business sector have risen sharply for several years in a row. This year, it also appears that particularly in the public sector and in parts of the private service sector, high wages are taking out high wages. A year and a half ago, the Government and the Storting adopted new guidelines for economic policing. The real return on the Petroleum Fund is planned to be used each year. As a result, most of the petroleum revenues will be phased into the economy in the coming years. With a return on the Petroleum Fund of 4 per cent, annual use of petroleum revenues may increase by almost NOK 60 billion measured in today's prices in 2010. Sam dig fastsa e Government a new opera vt mandate for monetary policy. Norges Bank shall view the interest rate with a view to low and stable inflation. The mandate has the following wording: "Monetary policy shall be aimed at stability in the Norwegian krone's national and international value, including contributing to stable expectations concerning exchange rate developments. The monetary policy will co-connect the financial policy by helping to stabilise developments in production and employment." Norges Bank is conducting the operatic implementation of monetary policy." "Norges Bank's conduct of monetary policy shall, in accordance with the first subsection, be exchanged against low and stable inflation. The operatic target for monetary policy is to be annual consumer price inflation of close to 2.5 per cent." The first of these appears to be a purpose. The latter of these says more specifically what Norges Bank should do. The first sentence of the mandate refers to the value of the krone. Stability in the krone's national value means that inflation shall be low and stable. It's the best contribution monetary policy can make to economic growth and prosperity. It is also a necessary precondition for stability in financial and property markets. It also states that monetary policy should be aimed at stability in the international value of the krone. The krone exchange rate fluctuates from day today, from week in week and from month in month. We have open trade with foreign countries and free capital movements. We don't have instruments l fine-tune the krone exchange rate. In Norges Bank's letter to the Ministry of Finance on 27 March 2015 on the new guidelines for economic policy, we expressed the view that when monetary policy is aimed at low and stable inflation, they are the best contribution monetary policy can make to stability in the krone exchange rate above d. The interest rate influences price inflation, for example through the krone exchange rate. A stronger krone dampens inflation. If we counteract the apparel of the krone when there is pressure in the economy, we reduce the possibility of keeping inflation in check, and we increase the risk of wide fluctuations in the economy. In other words, the consideration of stability in the krone's national value must go first. In addition, stability in the international value of the krone depends on low and stable inflation when other countries follow such a line. In the second subsection of the research, the implementation of monetary policy has been delegated to Norges Bank. This means that it is the Bank's understanding of the research - as it appeared in the letter in the Ministry of Finance in March last year - that is the basis when we look at the interest rate. In our interpretation, we place emphasis on the Government's basis for the forewing, on the purpose as it is unclear in the first term, and on our knowledge of the relationships between interest rates, the krone exchange rate, output, employment and inflation. The operative target for monetary policy is low and stable inflation. The inflation target is 21/2 per cent. A monetary policy that results in high and variable inflation would have led to wider fluctuations in output and employment. There would also be an uptnding of turbulence in foreign exchange markets. There is therefore close agreement between the first subsection - the inflation target - and the first paragraph on stabilising economic developments and exchange rate expectations. Growth in the Norwegian economy is currently particularly driven by a sharp increase in private consumption and strong growth in household disposable income. Real growth in household income is expected to be close to 5 per cent this year. It's historically high. Growth in domestic credibility remains high. Household borrowing is high. House prices have risen sharply, albeit unevenly, for several years. The sharp growth in e-demand is a tight monetary policy. However, the strong krone exchange rate pushes down import prices and thus contributes to keeping interest rates low. It is not the case that the consideration of smoothing out production and employment ng lsier a le ere pengepoli kk. Had we placed greater emphasis on this consideration, monetary policy could have been tighter and interest rates higher to guard against a borrowing and consumption boom. The interest rate influences inflation in two ways: Through e-demand, goods and services are domestic and through the krone exchange rate. When interest rates rise, it becomes more profitable to save and more expensive to borrow. This curbs consumption and investment. In turn, lower demand l helps to curb the rise in prices and wages. Higher interest rates also make it more of a priority to invest in NOK and borrow in other currencies. Normally, a higher interest rate will therefore lead to a stronger krone. It makes imported goods cheaper. Llegg dampens a strong krone, profitability and wage capacity in the competitive sector, and hence cost pressures in the Norwegian economy. The mandate for monetary policy states that the interest rate must be adjusted to the outlook for the Norwegian economy. If it appears that inflation with an unchanged interest rate will be higher than 21/2 per cent, the interest rate will be terminated. If it appears that inflation with an unchanged interest rate will be lower than 21/2 per cent, the interest rate will be reduced so much. Such a monetary policy will normally also contribute to stabilising production and employment. Money polity works with a dse erslep. Inflation today therefore does not provide a sensitive basis for what the interest rate should see now. Our analyses indicate that a substantial share of the effects of an interest rate change will occur within two years. Two years is therefore a reasonable dsperspek v for achieving the inflation target. Nevertheless, it is conceivable that if inflation should be very high, and economic developments are weak, we may choose to spend somewhat longer than two years to achieve the target of inflation of 21/2 per cent. By influencing inflation over d, we avoid that monetary policy in itself inflicts unnecessary disturbances on the economy. Norges Bank has an e-instrument. It's the interest rate. The effects are wide-ranging. Money policy cannot therefore be resentful of stabilising developments only for the internationally exposed sector. This would create substantial imbalances in the Norwegian economy. The low interest rate and devaluations of the 1970s and 1980s are an example of how wrong such policing can be. The monetary policy was re-aimed at preventing the competitiveness of the industry from deteriorating. The krone was devalued several times. But wages accelerated to compensate for higher inflation. The result was a wage and price gap that hit the entire economy. E is another expensive wage settlement and a sharp fall in oil prices, came the last devaluation in the spring of 1986. From then on, the monetary policy was changed. The fixed exchange rate policy contributed to a Norway inflation that is each in line with inflation in other countries. But the Norwegian economy has to go through a crash from the latter part of the 1980s. Confidence in monetary policy and the Norwegian krone must be raised to prevent high inflation from persisting. It took a long d and required very high interest rates before the nominal anchor was rebuilt. The economy first came into a more stable development when wage and income formation was clearly anchored in the monetary policy objective, which was then stability in the krone exchange rate. They illustrate that it must be commonplace in the Norwegian and international foreign exchange and financial markets to ensure that inflation in the Norway remains low and stable. If this rate is not present, a decline in short-term interest rates will lead to higher long-term interest rates and a sharp fall in the krone. They would in turn lead to wider fluctuations in the economy. Today, the competitiveness of the business sector has deteriorated. The krone is strong because wage growth is high and demand is growing. If wage growth slows and we may have expected it to remain low in the coming years, the interest rate differential against other countries may be reduced. This will normally lead to a fall in the krone exchange rate. Overall, it appears that wages in Norway will be about 15 per cent higher than in the years from 1998 to 2003. The krone is now around 7 per cent stronger than in the 1990s. Developments in the krone are probably reversible, but the loss of competitiveness and jobs caused by the particularly Norwegian wage growth is difficult to recover. In the solidarity salts of the 1990s, the stable exchange rate and wage growth among our trading partners should be anchored for the social partners. Until 1997, they held the anchor. But the rise in labour costs made a jump in 1998. It has since been around 2 percentage points higher than among our trading partners - between 5 and 6 per cent each year. This year's wage settlement appears to be joining this row and also points to high wage growth next year. Wage growth is high compared to earnings in many years. It is demanding to effect quickly enough l to keep up with the growth in labour costs. Wage growth in Norway has not been anchored in recent years by wage growth among our trading partners. In the public sector, wages are growing substantially more than the government budget was built on. It affects service production. Public funding is growing by 7 per cent from this year. This is considerably more than the growth in value creation in the mainland business sector, which can be estimated at around 4 per cent in current NOK. The fiscal rule has then been followed closely. Real growth in public consumption is estimated at 11/2 per cent. For 2003, growth in service production is estimated at only 3/4 per cent. In other words, there will only be moderate real growth in public service production, even though public releases are increasing considerably. The explanation is that the costs of producing public services are high. This reflects high wage growth. Moreover, transfers in households in our social schemes are growing a lot. Most of the high growth in government appropriations therefore ends up as strong growth in household income and consumption. We may also have to expect this when wage and cost pressures are so strong in the first place. Should the government compensate businesses for giving wages a particular lie , the result will be a new round on the wage spiral. Our projections in the March Inflation Report in July showed that with an unchanged sight deposit rate - which at that time was 6.5 per cent - and a krone exchange rate equal to the krone in the second quarter, inflation two years ahead could be more than 21/2 per cent. Sam dig showed that inflation could be lower than 21/2 per cent in the short term. Should we have tried to achieve the inflation target in the very short term, by looking down the interest rate and thereby contributing to a weaker krone and higher inflation, we know that in the e-year d we will probably have to have raised the interest rate considerably more than we have now done. This would have led to more uneven developments in production and employment. During the 1990s, unemployment declined as long as wage growth in the Norway was lower than wage growth among our trading partners. They took cunning in 1998. At that time, the social partners said no in the line of moderation. The decline in unemployment came to a halt. The sharp rise in labour costs in recent years is a factor in higher unemployment. The interest rate is a major instrument for addressing lower inflation and rising unemployment when stronger demand does not translate into higher wage growth or unstable financial markets. But there is little monetary policy that can be done to prevent an increase in unemployment that is driven by high cost inflation. When real wage growth is greater than growth in manufacturing, profitability deteriorates. The business sector will then consider fewer and terminate more people. In the public sector, there will be a greater conflict between the bidding framework and the requirements for service production. High wage growth increases the demands of the private sector and in public sector enterprises. This reinforces the benefits of the labour market in various social security and pension schemes. Over the past three years, the industry has been built up in waves. Especially in the years from 1977 l 1984 and from 1987 l 1992 there was kra ig peeling. Profitability in manufacturing had deteriorated in the past. It may take d before such a weakening strikes lower production and employment ng. But once the cover arrives, it often happens quickly and quickly. We are probably now in a new period of shelling. The Norwegian krone has appreciated markedly this year. Developments in wage settlements have probably been a vik g drivkra . Foreign exchange market participants have behaved as we would expect. High wage growth provides the basis for high interest rates. This makes it a good idea to invest in NOK and to borrow in other currencies. The krone is strengthened. We are and must be prepared for the exchange rate to fluctuate, as we have seen in other countries. We have free goods and services and free capital movements. The krone is floating. This means that economic agents cannot assume that the krone will be stable against the euro, against the dollar or against a weighed-through of foreign currencies. Compared with other small currencies, fluctuations in the krone exchange rate do not stand out. A large share of petroleum revenues is invested in foreign equities and bonds through the Petroleum Fund. Changes in oil prices affect the fund's size, but to a limited extent the use of domestic petroleum revenues. The Petroleum Fund thus acts as a buffer against fluctuations in oil prices and shields the krone exchange rate. Nevertheless, we must be prepared for the exchange rate to fluctuate in line with other small countries' currencies. But the krone is flexible in both directions. It will not continue to strengthen. What has driven the krone exchange rate over the past two years is the high and widen interest rate differential between Norway and abroad. This interest rate differential reflects the particularly Norwegian wage development. So it is laughe understandable kre is that has driven the crown. They are also probably reversible. Persistently lower wage growth, more in line with global growth, will go hand in hand with a smaller difference in the interest rate. Above d, growth in real wages must correspond to the growth in workers' output. With an inflation target of 21/2 per cent and trend growth in manufacturing at around 2 per cent, according to updated figures from the National Accounts, annual nominal wage growth is around 41/2 per cent. The figures are well in line with developments in the 1990s. Wage growth was at 41/2 per cent. This resulted in inflation of 21/2 per cent. The krone exchange rate was stable. The high interest rate and the strong krone reflect real economic drivers, high petroleum revenues, a tight labour market and strong growth in household income, consumption and borrowing. New features of wage formation may have contributed to a particularly high overall wage growth. If these credis are curbed, there is also hope that the pressure on monetary policy may diminish. The competitiveness of the business sector will have a special lie if wage growth should slow. Lower wage growth will in itself strengthen earnings and employment. The interest rate may look down. Normally, this will cause the krone to depreciag, so that earnings and employment are strengthened more. Manufacturing may therefore feel the posi ve effects of low nominal wage growth even more strongly than before. With wage growth anchored in the inflation target, and when we preserve financial market spending, monetary policy could also be a blow to the overall demand for goods and services.
