Vi har pen handel med utlandet og frie kapitalbevegelser. Vi har ikke virkemidler l  nstyre kronekursen. I Norges Banks brev l Finansdepartementet 27. mars i or om de nye retningslinjene for den konomiske poli kken ga vi u rykk for at nr pengepoli kken sikter mot lav og stabil inasjon, s er de e det beste bidraget pengepoli kken kan gi l stabilitet i kronekursen over d. Renten pvirker priss gningen blant annet via kronekursen. Sterkere krone demper inasjonen. Hvis vi motvirker at kronen styrker seg nr det er press i konomien, reduserer vi muligheten for  holde inasjonen i sjakk, og vi ker risikoen for store svingninger i konomien. Her m alts hensynet l stabilitet i kronens nasjonale verdi g frst. Dessuten er stabilitet i kronens internasjonale verdi avhengig av at vi har lav og stabil inasjon, nr andre land flger en slik linje. I forskri ens andre ledd er gjennomfringen av pengepoli kken delegert l Norges Bank. Det betyr at det er bankens forstelse av forskri en - slik den kom l u rykk i brevet l Finansdepartementet i mars i or - som er grunnlaget nr vi se er renten. I tolkningen legger vi vekt p Regjeringens grunngivning for forskri en, p formlet slik det er u rykt i det frste avsni et, og p vr kunnskap om sammenhengene mellom rente, kronekurs, produksjon, sysselse ng og inasjon. Det opera ve mlet for pengepoli kken er lav og stabil inasjon. Inasjonsmlet er sa l 2 prosent. En pengepoli kk som gir hy og varierende inasjon ville frt l strre svingninger i produksjon og sysselse ng. Det ville ogs vrt en oppskri for uro i valutamarkedene. Det er derfor nrt samsvar mellom forskri ens tredje ledd - inasjonsmlet - og det frste leddet om  stabilisere den konomiske utviklingen og valutakursforventningene. Veksten i norsk konomi er i dag srlig drevet av en kra ig kning i det private forbruket og sterk vekst i husholdningenes disponible inntekter. Vi regner med en realvekst i husholdningenes inntekter p nr 5 prosent i r. Det er historisk hyt. Veksten i innenlandsk kredi holder seg oppe. Husholdningene lner mye. Boligprisene har steget kra ig, om enn ujevnt, i ere r. Den kra ige veksten i e ersprselen lsier en stram pengepoli kk. Men den sterke kronekursen trekker importprisene ned og bidrar p den mten l  holde renten nede. Det er ikke slik at hensynet l  jevne ut produksjon og sysselse ng lsier en le ere pengepoli kk. Hadde vi lagt strre vekt p det hensynet, kunne pengepoli kken vrt strammere og renten hyere for  gardere mot en lne- og forbruksfest. Renten pvirker prisveksten p to mter: Gjennom e ersprselen e er varer og tjenester innenlands og gjennom kronekursen. Nr renten ker, blir det mer lnnsomt  spare og mer kostbart  lne. Det demper forbruket og investeringene. I neste omgang bidrar lavere e ersprsel l  dempe veksten i priser og lnninger. Hyere rente gjr det ogs mer a rak vt  plassere i norske kroner og lne i andre valutaer. Normalt vil derfor en hyere rente fre l en sterkere krone. Det gjr importerte varer billigere. I llegg demper en sterk krone ak viteten, lnnsomheten og lnnsevnen i det konkurranseutsa e nringslivet, og dermed kostnadspresset i norsk konomi. Mandatet for pengepoli kken lsier at renten m lpasses utsiktene for norsk konomi. Ser det ut l at inasjonen med uendret rente blir hyere enn 2 prosent, vil renten bli sa opp. Ser det ut l at inasjonen med uendret rente blir lavere enn 2 prosent, vil renten bli sa ned. En slik pengepoli kk vil normalt ogs bidra l  stabilisere produksjonen og sysselse ngen. Pengepoli kken virker med et dse erslep. Inasjonen i dag gir derfor ikke lstrekkelig holdepunkt for hva renten br se es l n. Vre analyser tyder p et en vesentlig del av virkningene av en renteendring vil komme innen to r. To r er derfor et rimelig dsperspek v for  n inasjonsmlet. Det kan likevel tenkes at dersom prisveksten skulle vre svrt hy, og den konomiske utviklingen sam dig svak, vil vi kunne velge  bruke noe lenger d enn to r p  n mlet om en prisvekst p 2 prosent. Ved  pvirke prisveksten over d, unngr vi at pengepoli kken i seg selv pfrer konomien undige forstyrrelser. Norges Bank har e virkemiddel. Det er renten. Virkningene favner vidt. Pengepoli kken kan derfor ikke re es inn mot  stabilisere utviklingen bare for konkurranseutsa sektor. Det ville skapt store ubalanser i norsk konomi. Lavrentepoli kken og devalueringene p 1970- og 1980-tallet er et eksempel p hvor galt en slik poli kk kan bre av sted. Pengepoli kken ble re et inn mot  unng at industriens konkurranseevne ble svekket. Kronen ble devaluert ere ganger. Men lnningene skjt fart for  kompensere for kt inasjon. Resultatet var en lnns- og prisgalopp som rammet hele konomien. E er nok et dyrt lnnsoppgjr og et kra ig fall i oljeprisen, kom den siste devalueringen vren 1986. Fra da av ble pengepoli kken lagt om. Fastkurspoli kken bidro l at inasjonen i Norge e er hvert kom p linje med inasjonen i andre land. Men norsk konomi m e gjennom en kra ig snuoperasjon fra siste del av 1980-tallet. Tilliten l pengepoli kken og den norske kronen m e re es opp for  unng at den hye inasjonen skulle vare ved. Det tok lang d og krevde svrt hye renter fr lliten l det nominelle ankerfestet var gjenreist. konomien kom frst i en mer stabil utvikling da lnns- og inntektsdannelsen ble klart forankret i mlet for pengepoli kken, som da var stabilitet i kronekursen. De e illustrerer at det m vre alminnelig llit i de norske og internasjonale valuta- og nansmarkedene l at inasjonen i Norge holder seg lav og stabil. Dersom denne lliten ikke er l stede, vil en nedgang i de kortsik ge rentene fre l kte langsik ge renter og sterkt fall i kronen. De e ville igjen fre l strre svingninger i konomien. I dag er konkurranseevnen for nringslivet svekket. Kronen er sterk fordi lnnsveksten er hy og e ersprselen vokser. Hvis lnnsveksten avtar og vi kan ha llit l at den vil forbli lav de nrmeste rene, kan rentedieransen mot utlandet reduseres. Det vil normalt fre l at kronekursen faller lbake. Samlet ser det ut l at lnningene i Norge vil s ge vel 15 prosent mer enn ute i rene fra og med 1998 l 2003. Kronen er n rundt 7 prosent sterkere enn gjennomsni et for 90tallet. Utviklingen i kronen er trolig reversibel, men det tapet av konkurranseevne og arbeidsplasser som skyldes den srnorske lnnsveksten, er vanskelig  hente inn. I solidaritetsalterna vet p 1990-tallet skulle den stabile valutakursen og lnnsveksten hos vre handelspartnere vre ankerfestet for partene i arbeidslivet. Fram l 1997 holdt de e ankerfestet. Men veksten i lnnskostnadene gjorde et hopp i 1998. Den har siden vrt rundt 2 prosentpoeng hyere enn blant vre handelspartnere - mellom 5 og 6 prosent hvert r. rets lnnsoppgjr ser ut l  fye seg inn i denne rekken og peker ogs mot hy lnnsvekst neste r. Lnnsveksten er hy i forhold l inntjeningen i mange bedri er. Det er krevende  eek visere raskt nok l  holde tri med veksten i lnnskostnadene. Lnnsveksten her hjemme har de siste rene ikke vrt forankret i lnnsveksten blant vre handelspartnere. I oentlig sektor vokser lnningene vesentlig mer enn det statsbudsje et bygde p. Det rammer tjenesteproduksjonen. Oentlige bevilgninger vokser med 7 prosent fra i or l i r1. Det er vesentlig mer enn veksten i verdiskapingen i nringslivet p fastlandet, som kan ansls l rundt 4 prosent i lpende kroner. Da er handlingsregelen fulgt nye. Den reelle veksten i oentlig forbruk er ansl l 1 prosent. For 2003 er veksten i tjenesteproduksjonen ansl l bare  prosent. Det blir alts bare en moderat reell vekst i den oentlige tjenesteproduksjonen, selv om oentlige utgi er ker mye. Forklaringen er at kostnadene ved  produsere oentlige tjenester s ger sterkt. Det gjenspeiler den hye lnnsveksten. Dessuten vokser overfringene l husholdningene i vre sosiale ordninger mye. Mesteparten av den hye veksten i statlige bevilgninger ender derfor opp som sterk vekst i husholdningenes inntekter og forbruk. Det m vi nok ogs kanskje regne med nr lnns- og kostnadspresset er s sterkt i utgangspunktet. Skulle staten kompensere virksomhetene for at de har gi lnningene et srlig l , blir resultatet le en ny runde p lnnsspiralen. Vre anslag i forrige inasjonsrapport i juli viste at med uendret foliorente - som den gang var 6,5 prosent - og en kronekurs lik gjennomsni et i andre kvartal, ville prisveksten p to rs sikt kunne bli over 2 prosent. Sam dig viste anslagene at prisveksten p kort sikt kunne komme l  bli lavere enn 2 prosent. Skulle vi ha prvd  n inasjonsmlet p helt kort sikt, ved  se e ned renten og dermed bidra l en svekket krone og kt prisvekst, vet vi at vi om e rs d trolig m e ha sa opp renten vesentlig mer enn det vi n har gjort. Det ville ha frt l en mer ujevn utvikling i produksjon og sysselse ng. Utover p 1990-tallet kk vi nedgang i arbeidsledigheten s lenge lnnsveksten i Norge var lavere enn lnnsveksten blant vre handelspartnere. De e tok slu i 1998. Da sa partene i arbeidslivet nei l moderasjonslinjen. Nedgangen i arbeidsledigheten stoppet opp. Den sterke veksten i lnnskostnadene de senere rene er en kime l kt arbeidsledighet. Renten er et slagkra ig instrument for  mte lavere e ersprsel og kende arbeidsledighet nr sterkere e ersprsel ikke slr ut i kt lnnsvekst eller ustabile nansmarkeder. Men det er lite pengepoli kken kan gjre for  hindre en kning i ledigheten som er drevet av hy kostnadsvekst. Nr den reelle veksten i lnningene er strre enn veksten i produk viteten, svekkes lnnsomheten i bedri ene. Nringslivet vil da anse e frre og si opp ere. I oentlig sektor fr vi en strre konikt mellom budsje rammer og kravene l tjenesteproduksjonen. Hy lnnsvekst ker kravene l eek vitet i bedri ene og i oentlige virksomheter. Det forsterker utst ngen fra arbeidsmarkedet l ulike trygde- og pensjonsordninger. De siste tre rene er industrien bli bygget ned i blger. Srlig i rene fra 1977 l 1984 og fra 1987 l 1992 var det kra ig avskalling. I forkant var lnnsomheten i industrien bli svekket. Det kan ta d fr en slik svekkelse slr ut i lavere produksjon og sysselse ng. Men nr omslaget frst kommer, skjer det gjerne raskt og kra ig. Vi er trolig n inne i en ny periode med avskalling. Den norske kronen har styrket seg markert i innevrende r. Utviklingen i lnnsoppgjret har trolig vrt en vik g drivkra . Aktrene i valutamarkedet har opptrdt slik vi m forvente. Hy lnnsvekst legger grunnlaget for hy rente. Det gjr det a rak vt  plassere i norske kroner og  lne i andre valutaer. Kronen styrkes. Vi er og m vre forberedt p at valutakursen vil variere, slik vi har se i andre land. Vi har fri vare- og tjenesteby e og frie kapitalbevegelser. Kronen yter. Det betyr at aktrene i det konomiske livet ikke kan legge l grunn at kronen vil vre stabil mot euro, mot dollar eller mot et veid gjennomsni av utenlandske valutaer. Sammenliknet med andre sm valutaer, skiller ikke svingningene i kronekursen seg ut. En stor del av petroleumsinntektene investeres i utenlandske aksjer og obligasjoner gjennom Petroleumsfondet. Endringer i oljeprisen pvirker fondets strrelse, men i liten grad bruken av oljeinntektene innenlands. Petroleumsfondet virker dermed som en buer mot svingninger i oljeprisen og skjermer kronekursen. Vi m likevel vre forberedt p at valutakursen vil svinge p linje med andre sm lands valutaer. Men kronen er eksibel i begge retninger. Den vil ikke vedvarende styrke seg. Det som har drevet kronekursen de siste to rene er den hye og kte renteforskjellen mellom Norge og utlandet. Denne renteforskjellen gjenspeiler den srnorske lnnsutviklingen. Det er alts le forstelige kre er som har drevet kronen. De er ogs trolig reversible. Varig lavere lnnsvekst, mer p linje med veksten ute, vil g hnd i hnd med mindre forskjell i renten. Over d m veksten i reallnningene svare l veksten i arbeidstakernes produk vitet. Med et inasjonsml p 2 prosent og en trendmessig vekst i produk viteten p rundt 2 prosent, iflge oppdaterte tall fra Nasjonalregnskapet, lsvarer det en rlig nominell lnnsvekst p rundt 4 prosent. Tallene stemmer godt overens med utviklingen p 1990-tallet. Lnnsveksten var i gjennomsni 4 prosent. Det ga en inasjon p 2 prosent. Kronekursen var stabil. Den hye renten og den sterke kronen speiler realkonomiske drivkre er kny et l de hye oljeinntektene, et stramt arbeidsmarked og sterk vekst i husholdningenes inntekter, forbruk og lneopptak. I llegg kan nye trekk ved lnnsdannelsen ha bidra l en srlig hy samlet lnnsvekst. Hvis disse kre ene dempes, er det ogs hp om at presset mot pengepoli kken kan avta. Det konkurranseutsa e nringslivet vil f et srskilt l dersom lnnsveksten skulle avta. Lavere lnnsvekst vil i seg selv styrke inntjeningen og sysselse ngen. Sam dig vil renten kunne se es ned. Normalt vil det fre l at kronen svekker seg, slik at inntjeningen og sysselse ngen styrkes y erligere. Industrien vil derfor kunne merke de posi ve eektene av lav nominell lnnsvekst enda sterkere enn fr. Med en lnnsvekst som er forankret i inasjonsmlet, og nr vi bevarer lliten i nansmarkedene, vil ogs pengepoli kken kunne vre et slagkra ig virkemiddel dersom den samlede e ersprselen e er varer og tjenester skulle svikte. Title: Using Financial Soundness Indicators to Assess Financial Stability
text: Using Financial Soundness Indicators to Assess Financial Stability Presenta on by Deputy Central Bank Governor Jarle Bergo at an IMF Conference, Tuesday, September 17, 2002 The paper by Craig and Sundararajan provides an excellent road map on how to work on assessing financial stability by using FSIs, alone or in combina on with other indicators or methods of economic and financial analysis. It is a very important contribu on of value both to central banks that have just embarked upon macro-pruden al analyses as well as to those that have been working in this area for some years. The authors give us a clear understanding of the limita ons of relying on FSIs alone and provide a thorough and highly relevant discussion on how to combine different sources of informa on to enhance financial sector surveillance. I appreciate the way the authors carefully point out possible pi alls of the different approaches and their sugges ons of tests and extensions of the analysis to overcome shortcomings. This greatly adds to the paper's usefulness as a manual for central banks and others charged with promo ng financial stability. I found li le to object to in the paper. That being the case, and since the paper concentrates on giving a general overview, probably the best I can do is to share with you some of the prac cal experiences we at the Bank of Norway have gathered over the years in our efforts to assess financial stability. The par culari es of the Norwegian experience are perhaps of limited interest but I think there are elements in our general approach and methodology that can be of value for other prac oners. You will see that we have followed the stages outlined in the paper, star ng with simple FSIs for the financial sector, later complemen ng them with non-financial FSIs and then on to linking the FSIs to macroeconomic models to make forecasts and perform stress tests. I will give my comments on specific points in the paper as I go through our experience. The Bank of Norway is a non-supervisory central bank, but has responsibility for the payments system and is explicitly charged with promo ng a sound and efficient financial system. Norway experienced a serious banking crises in the early 1990s. As a consequence of that we started work on early warning FSIs for the banking sector. The analysis compared developments in the banks that needed financial support during these years with those that never became problem banks. To ensure coverage of the most important aspects, it followed the CAMEL (Capital Adequacy, Asset Quality, Management, Earnings, Liquidity) system of banking supervision, the same framework that the IMF has applied in its proposal for a Core Set . The result of this study showed that it was not necessary to have a very extensive set of banking sector indicators. Actually the study suggested just four banking sector indicators for early warning purposes. Apparently a model with a small set of indicators would provide the same informa on as a larger set of indicators. One can only wonder if the crises might have been be er contained had these indicators been used and correctly interpreted in the years leading up to the crises! However, we gradually came to the conclusion that a set of FSIs for the banking sector only was too narrow. Even if problems showed up clearly in the simple FSIs we wanted to know when poten al problems were moun ng before they showed up in the banks' accounts. As pointed out in the paper, FSIs for the non-financial sector can help detec ng weaknesses in the financial sector at an early stage. So in 1995 we issued our first semi-annual Financial Stability Report where a number of Encouraged set indicators for the non-financial sector was included. Our experience indicates that it is especially important to evaluate the effect of macroeconomic condi ons on the debtservicing capacity of households and enterprises, and thereby on the credit risk of banks. We have put major emphasis on assessing the poten al for losses on loans to households and enterprises. Of par cular concern in this regard is the enterprise sector, where about 85 percent of bank losses in the banking crisis of the early 1990s occurred. But it would be a mistake to neglect household behaviour and their debt burden in evalua ng the credit risk confron ng banks. The assessment of the household sector's robustness and possible spill-over effects to the enterprise sector in the event of a major macroeconomic shock is very important. I will come back to this a li le later. Another point underlined in the paper and where our experience supports the conclusion is the emphasis on collec ng and analysing disaggregated data, both for the household and enterprise sector. In our view, this is of considerable importance in order to comprehend more fully how these sectors are affected by macroeconomic shocks. Just to give you an example: Norwegian households' aggregate debt burden compared with the period just before the banking crisis is s ll rela vely low. When we look at disaggregated data, we see that the high debt burden at that me was largely due to high debt to income ra o of the 10 percent of households with the highest income. This can to a large extent be a ributed to the tax system at that me with high deduc ons for interest rate payments for the high-income households. The tax system has later been changed. The majority of households, however, actually have a historically high debt burden today, and this could cause problems for the financial sector in the event of a macroeconomic shock. As part of our Financial Stability report exercise we survey on a regular basis some 30-40 FSIs. However, we have more and more adopted a model-based approach to assessing financial stability. By building the FSIs into our macro-economic models, we can make forecasts and do stress tests. Let me give you a few examples of how we work in this area. To help assess the risks associated with loans to the enterprise sector, the Bank u lizes data from the annual accounts of all Norwegian limited companies. (Admi edly, we are fortunate in Norway to benefit from the availability of extensive and high quality data.) This has enabled us to develop a credit risk model es mated using data for these companies for the period 1990-1996. The model predicts individual bankruptcy probabili es as a func on of age, size and industry characteris cs, in addi on to account variables like corporate earnings, liquidity and financial strength. The reduced form of the motel is set out in the chart and the signs of the parameters indicated. I will not go into details on the model specifica on but refer to the references in the handout. Since the model generates individual probability es mates, it can be used in a number of areas related to credit risk analysis. Mul plying the debt of individual enterprises by their bankruptcy probability and adding them up provides an es mate of "risk-weighted debt". This variable may be considered an indicator of expected loan losses, given no collateral security. As the chart indicates, the developments in long-term debt and risk-weighted long-term debt have been different the last decade. Even though the debt level is now considerably higher than before the banking crisis, the associated risk predicted by the model is lower. As pointed out in the paper, a further enhancement of the financial stability analysis is to introduce stress tes ng. In order to assess risks both to the household and enterprise sectors, the Bank also uses its own macroeconometric model RIMINI and the macroeconomic forecasts produced for the Bank's Infla on Report to give forecasts of FSI, and to carry out stress tests. Stress tests can indicate how exposed financial ins tu ons are to macroeconomic changes, and are becoming an important tool for central banks in their surveillance of financial stability. In our latest Financial Stability Report, we es mated econometric models for financial ins tu ons' losses on loans both to the household and enterprise sector and incorporated these into our main econometric forecasts model. The model explains actual losses fairly well and also has good out-of-sample proper es. By doing this we were able to produce es mates of the effects on financial ins tu ons' loan losses as a result of different shocks to the real economy. In the first alterna ve scenario, house prices gradually fall by about 25 percent in rela on to the baseline scenario up to 2004. In the second alterna ve scenario, wage growth is 2 percentage points higher than in the baseline scenario in 2002. To counteract the effect this would have on infla on, the interest rate is assumed to be raised by 2 percentage points compared to the baseline scenario as from 2002. As you will see from the charts, the losses on loans to households are quite small even when the household sector is subject to a severe shock. However, the adjustment in the household sector hits the enterprise sector hard through reduced demand and weakened profitability. In addi on we have assumed a reduc on in the value of collateral in me with the fall in housing prices. Even though our work on stress tes ng is at an early state, I fully agree with Craig and Sundararajan that such tests are a valuable addi on to the surveillance of FSIs. The paper could have discussed in somewhat more detail, though, the limita ons that are intrinsically linked to stress tests. As pointed out in the paper, the payment system can be a source of large short-term credit exposures and liquidity risks. The risk of loss arises if a par cipant is unable to meet obliga ons and payment se lement is delayed or rejected. If a bank has large exposures to other banks, a delay or cancella on of se lement can reduce the bank's liquidity, thus preven ng it from mee ng its own obliga ons. In this way, liquidity problems can spread through the payment system and at worst threaten financial stability. In view of this central banks, other authori es and the industry itself try to construct and regulate the payments system to reduce risk to an acceptable level. But how do you check if you have succeeded? If you have access to data on the individual bank's posi on vis-a-vis other banks on a con nuous basis, you can check the robustness of the payment system. Norges Bank has analysed se lement data from a 10-day period in 2000 and looked at the liquidity shor all connected with the failure of one counterparty to meet his obliga ons. The poten al liquidity shor all is compared with the banks' available funds in Bank of Norway Se lement system to determine the likelihood of problems connected with the failure to pay. The analysis was in our Financial Stability Report no. 1 for 2001. In the Norwegian case, it indicates that banks seldom have large exposures to several counterpar es in the same ne ng or large exposures to the same counterparty in several ne ngs. Why do we do all this? Why do we devote considerable resources to this exercise? Because, like Mr. Ferguson remarked earlier this morning, financial stability is a fundamental objec ve of a central bank. The objec ves of monetary stability (low and stable infla on) and financial stability are interdependent. High and variable infla on can threaten financial stability. Financial instability would reduce the effec veness of monetary policy. At mes, however, there could be a trade off between monetary and financial stability. I think it is fair to say that financial stability is included in our loss func on, but since a financial crisis hopefully is a low probability event, it could be regarded as a constraint of monetary policy that at most mes would be non-binding. How do our Financial Stability reports and other studies and analysis contribute to financial stability? First, it improves the authori es' awareness and insight in financial sector developments. We present and discuss our reports in mee ngs with the Supervisory authority and the Ministry of Finance. We also write a formal le er to the Ministry summing up the conclusions of the forthcoming Financial Stability report. We put a lot of effort into informing the financial ins tu ons of our assessments. We are transparent with regard to our analy cal tools and invite others to employ them. (Both the Supervisory authority and individual banks have used our bankruptcy models to assess the quality of the por olio in individual banks). Establishing a dialogue with the financial services industry on factors that may create imbalances in the financial system well in advance of any problems is of substan al importance. Our Financial Stability Reports give us a suitable framework for this dialogue. 17. september 2002 13:00

Title: Current monetary policy issues
text: Current monetary policy questions Governor Svein Gjedrem. given at the University of Tromso and in Sparebank1 Nord-Norway, Tromso, 20 September 2002 Subject to changes during the performance. The speech is based on the assessments given at Norges Bank's press conference, which is the Monetary Policy Meeting of the Executive Board on 18 September, as well as on discussions. Monetary policy is exercised by Norges Bank's guidelines (forkri ) established by the Government. The most important instrument in monetary policy is the interest rate on banks' deposits (the sight deposit rate) in Norges Bank. The sight deposit rate forms a floor for the short-term interest rates in the money market and affects banks' lending and deposit rates. Norges Bank's Executive Board assesses the interest rate at a separate meeting every 6 weeks. The Bank shall conduct its activities in accordance with the economic-policing guidelines established by the state authorities and in accordance with the international obligations of the country. A year and a half ago, the Government and the Storting adopted new guidelines for economic policing. A plan was drawn up for the use of petroleum revenues over the state budget. Government petroleum revenues are invested in the Government Petroleum Fund. Each year, the plan is to use the expected real return on the Petroleum Fund, i.e. 4 per cent of the Fund. The government established a new opera mandate for monetary policy. Norges Bank shall view the interest rate with a view to low and stable inflation. The first sentence of the mandate refers to the value of the krone. Stability in the krone's national value means that inflation shall be low and stable. Low and stable inflation contributes to economic growth and stability in the financial and property markets. It also states that monetary policy should be aimed at stability in the international value of the krone. The krone exchange rate fluctuates from day today, from week in week and from month in month. We have open trade with foreign countries and free capital movements. We don't have instruments l fine-tune the krone exchange rate. However, when monetary policy is aimed at low and stable inflation, this will contribute to a stable krone exchange rate above d. The first of the mandate appears to be a purpose. Varig lavere lnnsvekst vil g hnd i hnd med mindre forskjell i renten og det kan snu utviklingen i kronekursen. Det konkurranseutsa e nringslivet vil f et srskilt l dersom lnnsveksten skulle avta. Renten vil kunne se es ned. Kronen vil kunne svekkes slik at inntjeningen og sysselse ngen styrkes y erligere. Utviklingen i sommer tyder p at oppgangen ute kan bli svakere og komme senere enn vi dligere har ventet. Aksjekursene har falt markert. Fallet i aksjekursene vil dempe veksten i det private forbruket og i konomien for vrig. N er de internasjonale konjunkturene svake sam dig som oljeprisen er hy. De e bidrar l at veksten hos vre handelspartnere og markedene for norsk ekspor ndustri svekkes sam dig som deler av norsk konomi fr en s mulans. I de tre nordligste fylkene samlet har oentlig sektor en mer dominerende rolle enn ellers i landet mlt i antall arbeidstakere lkny et de ulike nringene. Nr vi ser de tre fylkene samlet er nringer som industri og forretningsmessig tjenestey ng rela vt mindre representert. De e kan tyde p at nedgangen i det konkurranseutsa e nringslivet ikke vil ramme Nord-Norge like tungt som industrifylkene i Sr-Norge. Blant de tre nordligste fylkene skiller likevel Nordland seg ut som e av vre vik gste industrifylker. Det er fortsa sterk vekst i e ersprselen i Norge. Vedvarende hy lnnsvekst bidrar l hy prisvekst p norskproduserte varer og tjenester. Husholdningenes inntekter vokser kra ig, og husholdningene lner mye. Mlt i verdi er veksten i detaljomsetningen hy. I Norges Banks siste inasjonsrapport fra 3. juli i r ble veksten i konsumprisene, med uendret rente p 6,5 prosent og uendret kronekurs p gjennomsni et for kursen i andre kvartal, ansl l 2 prosent om to r. Foliorenten ble hevet med 0,5 prosentpoeng, l 7 prosent p rentemte samme dag. Vi la ogs fram anslag for inasjonen med en kurs lik gjennomsni et for juni og en rente p 7 prosent. I sommer har kronen vrt i de e leiet. Konsumprisene kte noe mer enn ventet i juni og juli, men kom lbake l det nivet vi har ventet i august. Justert for endringer i avgi er og uten energivarer steg konsumprisene med 2,3 prosent i forhold l august i or. Norges Banks Hovedstyre vurderte renten p hovedstyremtet 18. september. Det ble ikke fa et vedtak om  endre renten. Norges banks styringsrente, foliorenten, oppre holdes dermed p 7 prosent. Med uendret rente ser Norges Bank det n som like sannsynlig at inasjonen p to rs sikt blir hyere enn 2  prosent som at den blir lavere. Hy vekst i lnnskostnadene bidrar l en rela vt hy priss gning for varer og tjenester som produseres i Norge. En vedvarende sterk krone vil bidra l  holde prisen p importvarer nede. Den sterke kronen vil f konsekvenser for ak viteten i det konkurranseutsa e nringslivet. Den sterke kronen er, sammen med utsikter l lav inasjon ute, den vik gste motvekten mot den kra ige veksten i innenlandske kostnader. PUBLISERT 20. september 2002 14:00

Title: The inflation target and the interaction in economic policy
text: The inflation target and the interaction in economic policing Governor Svein Gjedrem. Speech given by the Finance Group at the Norwegian School of Economics and Business Administration in Bergen, 16 October 2002 Subject to changes during the performance. The speech is based on the assessments given at Norges Bank's press conference at the monetary policy meeting on 18 September, as well as on discussions. Monetary policy is exercised by Norges Bank's guidelines (forkri ) established by the Government. The most important instrument in monetary policy is the interest rate on banks' deposits in Norges Bank (the sight deposit rate). The sight deposit rate forms a floor for the short-term interest rates in the money market and affects banks' lending and deposit rates. Norges Bank's Executive Board assesses the interest rate at a separate meeting every 6 weeks. A year and a half ago, the Government and the Storting adopted new guidelines for economic policing. Above d, the use of petroleum revenues shall correspond to the expected real return on the Petroleum Fund, i.e. 4 per cent of the Fund. When the use of petroleum revenues is tied to the structural, non-oil deficit, the so-called automa ske stabilizers are allowed to function. This means, among other things, that in a boom, higher revenues will have an impact on improved bidding balance, and contradicted in a recession. Norges Bank shall view the interest rate with a view to low and stable inflation. The inflation target is 21/2 per cent. There are good reasons why monetary policy is being used to keep inflation low and stable. High inflation costs. Households and residents are becoming more uncertain about their income and publishing. This gives rise to incorrect investments and wider fluctuations in the economy. Avoiding deflation - a decline in prices - is just as important because it laughs hand in hand with, and can amplify, a downturn there in the economy. Low and stable inflation ensures that changes in real prices are clearly apparent to households and households. This makes it easier to make rich decisions, and contributes to more stable prices in financial and property markets than elsewhere. It is the best contribution monetary policy can make to growth and stability in the economy. We have had four periods of really high inflation over the last 100 years, during the two world wars and the Korean War, as well as a 15-year period from the first half of the 1970s in the second half of the 1980s. At Norway, really high inflation is a war phenomenon and a 1970s and 1980s phenomenon. In the wake of high inflation, we have experienced substantial real economic losses and financial instability. Inflation was expensive. The pea period of high inflation was different from the previous three. In the 1970s and 1980s, inflation gradually accelerated. It was not as high as during the world wars, but it took a long d before inflation came down. E is its fixed exchange rate system, the so-called Bre on Woods system, broke down in 1971. A couple of years later came the Yom Kippur War, with opec countries' supply halts and the first oil crisis. The sharp rise in oil prices resulted in a drop in productivity growth and led to stagnation and higher unemployment in western economies. In many countries, inflation gained traction. In Norway, the welfare state and transfers in the business sector were developed rapidly, partly because we expected substantial petroleum revenues. The economic policing sought to bridge what was expected to be a huge downturn in the global economy. This led to a battle over real resources in the economy, between the business sector and the public sector, and between competition and sheltered sector. Economic developments in Norway were characterised by high and variable inflation. This also resulted in wide fluctuations in production and employment. With low interest rate policy and devaluations, inflation remained high. The Norwegian economy lacked a nominal anchor during the low interest rate and devaluation period in the 1970s and 1980s. The fixed exchange rate policy from 1986 rebuilt monetary policy and laid the foundation for more stable economic developments later. With the free flow of capital, deep capital markets and the phasing in of petroleum revenues in the Norwegian economy, managing the interest rate e is an inflation target. The interest rate influences inflation through the effect on domestic demand and through effects in the NOK market. When interest rates rise, it becomes more profitable to save and more expensive to borrow. This dampens consumption and investment and thus the overall demand. In turn, lower demand l helps to curb the rise in prices and wages. Higher interest rates make it more of a priority to invest in NOK and borrow in other currencies. Normally, a higher interest rate will therefore lead to a stronger krone. It makes imported goods cheaper. In the first quarter, a stronger krone dampens the share of the stock, profitability and wage capacity in the internationally exposed business sector. It is important to be aware of the relationships between employment, output and inflation. If there is a shortage of jobs and other real resources, a tight monetary policy will reduce inflation through the effects on overall demand. Conversely, when unemployment is high, low interest rates will increase demand and sustain wage growth and inflation. When monetary policy is aimed at stabilising inflation, we will therefore also contribute to stability in total output and employment. In the long term, monetary policy determines the current level of inflation. Production is determined by the progression of work crashes , capital and technology, and by the production of knowledge. Attempts to increase output beyond the overall capacity of the economy will lead to inflation in the long run. What monetary policy can do is contribute to the most stable development possible, without unnecessarily wide fluctuations in production and employment. Total employment is also affected by wage formation. If wages grow more than is the basis for, employment will decline and unemployment will increase. Monetary policy cannot prevent an increase in unemployment caused by such a wage-driven cost shock. The inflation target provides a framework that ensures that policymakers in the economy have a nominal anchor. When the authorities delegate the exercise of monetary policy in a central bank's mandate, it helps to ensure credibility, llit and consistency, because the central bank is bound by its mandate. This makes monetary policy more effek v, and also increases the possibility that monetary policy may contribute to stability in the economy. They are probably the main reason l that the implementation of monetary policy has been delegated to a central bank in all the countries we can compare ourselves with. When it is clear that monetary policy contributes to low and stable inflation above d, monetary policy in the short term - under certain conditions - can contribute to smoothing fluctuations in output and demand. In the short term, there is a trade-off between considerations of stability in inflation on the one hand, and on the other hand, the consideration of stability in output and employment. An aggressive monetary policy will quickly bring inflation to target. It provides large fluctuations in the real economy. The interest rate may also be changed more gradually. This has a smaller impact on the real economy, but wider fluctuations in inflation. By influencing inflation above d, we avoid that too aggressive monetary policy in itself causes unnecessary disturbances to the economy. Money polity works with a dse erslep. Our analyses indicate that a substantial share of the effects of an interest rate change will occur within two years. Two years is therefore a reasonable dsperspek v for achieving the inflation target. Nevertheless, it is conceivable that if inflation should be very high, and economic developments are weak, we may choose to spend somewhat longer than two years to achieve the target of inflation of 21/2 per cent. The choice of dshorisont for monetary policy reflects the fact that there are real economic costs associated with getting inflation back quickly in the target. Indirectly, this horizon is an unearth for the trade-off between the consideration of stable output on the one hand and low and stable inflation on the other. In the National Budget, the Government has expressed dis hope that it is the monetary policy that should react in the first place if the outlook for economic developments changes. Nevertheless, situations may arise where the use of the bidding policy is required, either because capacity growth is particularly low, or because pressures in the economy are very high. Different factors may cause the interaction between monetary and financial policing to not work. Good interaction is based on the fact that the bodies that make the decisions are aware of how their own decisions affect the decisions the others will make. If this recognition is not present, the result of one's own decisions will not be as planned. The economy could move in a very small direction, with high interest rates, low economic growth and weakening of the state's financial woes. Without coordination, however, the result could be good if the financial policing acts as a "leader" and the money-laundering "follows," to use the unsymobed game theory. The financial authorities can internalise the monetary policy response pattern. The pattern of action in the central bank must then be known, so that the financial authorities can take this into account. When the response pattern in monetary policy is known and remains fixed above d, the social partners can take into account any monetary policy sanction when wages are determined. The "leader" in the interaction - that is, the social partners - can take into account l "follower's" - that is, Norges Bank '- reactions. The e-viewpoint is most relevant when wage formation is centralized. With decentralised wage formation, monetary policy will instead influence wage growth via market mechanisms by stabilising overall demand. A precondition for good interaction is that monetary policy is known and remains firm. U all of this year's settlement, which resulted in wage growth of 53/4 per cent, suggests that the parties have not internalised the monetary policy response pattern. Perhaps the choice of federal settlement and the large sums of expenses outside the LO-NHO area stand in the way. High wage growth also for groups whose wages are fixed through individual agreements suggests that the labour market has been tight. Developments in official salaries may also be inconsistent with the fact that the management of costs in bedri is weak and enterprises are weak in a long upturn. In the long run, wages must be in proportion to the values created by the employed. Growth in real wages is therefore determined by developments in the labour market. If historical product growth persists, a rise in labour costs of around 41/2 per cent in the long term will be consistent with the inflation target. Developments we have seen in income settlements in recent years are not consistent with such a balance sheet. To date, the effects of high wage growth on price inflation have been offset by low imported inflation. With little available resources in the Norwegian economy, strong growth in household consumption is putting pressure on prices and wages. A stable exchange rate and cost inflation among our trading partners were long anchored for wage formation. However, since 1998, the rise in labour costs in Norway been around 2 percentage points higher than among our trading partners. High wage growth is hitting manufacturing hard, along with bad ones out there and a strong krone. Overall, it appears that wages in Norway will be about 15 per cent higher than in the years from 1998 to 2003. The krone is now around 9 per cent stronger than in the 1990s. Developments in the krone are probably reversible, but the loss of competitiveness and jobs caused by the particularly Norwegian wage growth is difficult to recover. Developments in the interest rate differential between Norway and abroad have contributed to the appreciation of the krone. This year, wage settlement developments in particular appear to have pushed up interest rate expectations and thereby contributed to a stronger krone. There is a correlation between wage growth, interest rate expectations and the krone exchange rate. The appreciation of the krone dampens inflation and weakens the profitability, employment and wage capacity of international enterprises. Developments in the world economy and in international financial markets may also be behind the recent appreciation of the krone. With share prices now falling so much, investors are looking to see if e is a "safe haven." In this way, the Norwegian krone, with high interest rates and oil wealth, may appear to be a rake alterna v. Investing in the Norwegian krone can be considered to be a good guard against a recession in the world economy caused by high oil prices and fears of war. Nevertheless, there are risks associated with investing in NOK. Norwegian money markets are not very liquid, and if something should indicate that it is a good thing to withdraw from the Norwegian krone, the port may be tight. Those who have invested in NOK therefore assume a considerable risk of poor liquidity in the krone market. Oil prices have risen considerably since the new year, and it appears that the strong upturn this year has coincided with the appreciation of the krone. Although there is no clear correlation between developments in oil prices and developments in the krone exchange rate, it is possible that the situation in the Middle East has had an impact on the krone recently. In Norges Bank's most recent Inflation Report from 3 July this year, consumer price inflation, with an unchanged interest rate of 6.5 per cent and an unchanged krone exchange rate on the basis of the exchange rate in the second quarter, was estimated at L 23/4 per cent in mid-2004. The sight deposit rate was raised by 0.5 percentage point, l 7 per cent at the monetary policy meeting on the same day. We also presented projections for inflation at a rate equal to that of June and an interest rate of 7 per cent. This summer, the crown has been in the e rented. Consumer prices increased somewhat more than expected in June and July, but came back to the level we have expected in August and September. Adjusted for changes in emits and excluding energy products, consumer prices in September were 2.2 per cent higher than in September in or. Norges Bank's Executive Board will not have a decision to change the interest rate at the last Executive Board meeting on 18 September. Norges Bank's key policy rate, the sight deposit rate, was thus raised to 7 per cent. With an unchanged interest rate, Norges Bank saw it as just as likely that inflation two years ahead will be higher than 21/2 per cent as it will be lower. We showed that a high rise in labour costs contributes to a high price increase for goods and services produced in Norway. Together, a persistently strong krone will help keep the price of imported goods down. The strong krone will also have consequences for the acoustics of the internationally exposed business sector. The strong krone, together with the prospects of low inflation abroad, is the most important counterweight to the sharp rise in domestic costs. The Government's proposal l Statsbudsje for 2003 includes a real increase in the use of petroleum revenues of about NOK 2 billion from 2002 in 2003. They entail a structural non-oil deficit in 2003 of more than NOK 30 billion. Measured as a share of mainland GDP Norway, the structural deficit increases by just over 0.1 percentage points from 2002 to 2003. The increase in the e-deficit was 0.4 percentage points this year. The bidding period means that growth in the State Budget is down from 2002 in 2003, both in real terms and measured in current prices. In 2003, the total number of sledges and deliveries was about NOK 10.6 billion. The majority of the e kny is a decision that will take full effect in 2003. The effects of the Government Budget for 2003 on developments in the variables that affect monetary policy and interest rate developments will be included in the analysis in Inflation Report 3/02, which will be presented on 30 October. 16 October 2002 14:00

Foredraget bygger p vurderingene gi p Norges Banks pressekonferanse e er rentemtet 18. september samt p dligere foredrag. Det frte l en kamp om realressursene i konomien, mellom nringslivet og det oentlige, og mellom konkurranseutsa og skjermet sektor. Den konomiske utviklingen i Norge ble preget av hy og variabel inasjon. Det ga store svingninger ogs i produksjon og sysselse ng. Med lavrentepoli kk og devalueringer festet inasjonen seg. Renten pvirker prisveksten gjennom virkningen p e ersprselen innenlands og gjennom virkninger i markedet for norske kroner. Nr renten ker, blir det mer lnnsomt  spare og mer kostbart  lne. Det demper forbruket og investeringene og dermed den samlede e ersprselen. I neste omgang bidrar lavere e ersprsel l  dempe veksten i priser og lnninger. Hyere rente gjr det mer a rak vt  plassere i norske kroner og lne i andre valutaer. Normalt vil derfor en hyere rente fre l en sterkere krone. Det gjr importerte varer billigere. Det gjr pengepoli kken mer eek v, og ker ogs muligheten for at pengepoli kken kan bidra l stabilitet i konomien. Det kan likevel tenkes at dersom prisveksten skulle vre svrt hy, og den konomiske utviklingen sam dig svak, vil vi kunne velge  bruke noe lenger d enn to r p  n mlet om en prisvekst p 2 prosent. Valget av dshorisont for pengepoli kken gjenspeiler at det er realkonomiske kostnader forbundet med  f inasjonen raskt lbake l mlet. Indirekte er denne horisonten et u rykk for avveiningen mellom hensynet l stabil produksjon p den ene siden og lav og stabil inasjon p den andre siden. Regjeringen har i Nasjonalbudsje et gi u rykk for at det i frste omgang er pengepoli kken som br reagere hvis utsiktene for den konomiske utviklingen endrer seg. Det kan likevel oppst situasjoner der en ak v bruk av budsje poli kken er pkrevet, enten fordi kapasitetsutny ngen er srlig lav, eller fordi presset i konomien er svrt hyt. Hvis ikke denne erkjennelsen er l stede, vil ikke resultatet av egne beslutninger bli slik man selv hadde planlagt. konomien vil kunne bevege seg i en svrt lite guns g retning, med hye renter, lav konomisk vekst og svekkelse av statens nansielle s lling. Uten koordinering kan likevel resultatet bli godt hvis nanspoli kken opptrer som "leder" og pengepoli kken som "flger", for  bruke u rykk fra spillteorien. De nanspoli ske myndigheter kan internalisere det pengepoli ske reaksjonsmnsteret. Handlingsmnsteret l sentralbanken m da vre kjent, slik at de nanspoli ske myndighetene kan ta hensyn l det. Nr reaksjonsmnsteret i pengepoli kken er kjent og ligger fast over d, kan partene i arbeidslivet lsvarende ta hensyn l en eventuell pengepoli sk reaksjon nr lnningene fastse es. "Lederen" i samspillet - det vil si partene i arbeidslivet - kan ta hensyn l "flgerens" - det vil si Norges Banks - reaksjoner. De e synspunktet er mest relevant nr lnnsdannelsen er sentralisert. Med en desentralisert lnnsdannelse vil pengepoli kken i stedet pvirke lnnsveksten via markedsmekanismene, gjennom  stabilisere samlet e ersprsel. The speech is based on the assessments given at Norges Bank's press conference, which is the Monetary Policy Meeting of the Executive Board on 30 October and a discussion. Norway is an oil economy. Petroleum revenues provide us with an economic starting point that many other countries do not have. How are we going to live (well) with the oil? The e-mails are the economic policing of several indiscibles. Wealth must be distributed among generations in a good way. This means that the practitioners of the authorities must have discipline in their spending, and assess this in light of long-term considerations. The size of the revenue stream from petroleum activities varies. This may have a major impact on the question impulses in the Norwegian economy and may contribute to amplifying cyclical fluctuations. The use of petroleum revenues affects the competitiveness of Norwegian industry. Large fluctuations in income use can have major consequences for the framework for international industries. It is therefore important that we manage to maintain an industry structure that promotes learning, innovation and development. Petroleum activities form a significant part of the Norwegian economy. In recent years, petroleum revenues have accounted for 25-30 per cent of government revenues. The sense of economic policing and high oil prices have collectively contributed to the highest surpluses on the bidding balance recorded in any OECD country. Even in 1998, when oil prices were down to USD 10 per barrel, we had a surplus of 4 per cent of GDP measured by government ne ne ne yfinansinvesteringer. Experience from other countries shows that great natural riches can be a mixed blessing. Communities that suddenly gain access to large resources tend to spend the money and then decay. Access to rich natural resources can lead to lower growth. Explanations for the e may be that such a lgang leads l that d and resources are res against having as much of the wealth as possible. In llegg, le jent wealth o e will lead l weakened insen v l innovation and work. The result will be a weakening of the competitiveness of the business sector. They are in themselves unfortunate for developing value creation because more learning and development is created in a large competitive sector than in a small one. Historical experience thus states that it is important to have a decision-making system that provides protection against special interests enjoying strong control over petroleum wealth. In the first instance, we must preserve and develop information about new knowledge and drive innovation work. It is also important that we relate to the question of distribution between the generations. The largest part of Norway's national wealth is not the oil, but the value of work crashes in the country. The large petroleum revenues we are now using are not revenues in the usual sense, but the relocation of petroleum wealth in financial wealth. In light of these, oil revenues do not make us richer. Such a prediction could affect the rest of the wealth. Should oil wealth lead to l that we work less or become less production, the decline in the rest of our wealth will quickly become as large as the entire petroleum wealth. On 29 March 2015, the Stoltenberg Government issued new guidelines for monetary policy and presented a fiscal rule for fiscal policy. The fiscal rule for fiscal policy would entail that the government budget deficit should be answered in the expected real return on the Petroleum Fund. In Stor nget there was a broad agreement in this restructuring guidelines for the economic policing. The fiscal rule was followed up in the bidding for 2002 and in proposal l budsje for 2003. Monetary policy was to be resentable to low and stable inflation. The inflation target was 21/2 per cent. The fiscal rule entails that the non-oil deficit will increase in the years ahead. It will give a s mulance every year. However, an unpredictable and more expansionary fiscal policy than the fiscal rule would increase uncertainty In order to maintain the balance in the Norwegian economy, the phasing in of petroleum revenues in the economy must be counteracted by tighter monetary policy than otherwise. They can be achieved through a higher interest rate than otherwise or through an appreciation of the krone exchange rate, or both. High inflation costs. Households and households are becoming more uncertain about their future incomes. This gives rise to incorrect investments and wider fluctuations in the economy. It is also important to avoid deflation - or a decline in prices, because it o e goes hand in hand with amplifying the decline there. Low and stable inflation ensures that changes in real prices are clearly apparent to households and households. This makes it easier to make rich decisions, and contributes to more stable prices in financial and property markets than elsewhere. It is the best contribution monetary policy can make to growth and stability in the economy. We have had four periods of really high inflation over the past 100 years: during the two world wars and the Korean War, as well as a 15-year period from the first half of the 1970s in the second half of the 1980s. At Norway, really high inflation is a war phenomenon and a 1970s and 1980s phenomenon. In the wake of high inflation, substantial real economic losses and financial instability occurred. Inflation was expensive. The pea period of high inflation was different from the previous three. In the 1970s and 1980s, inflation gradually accelerated. It was not as high as during the world wars, but it took a long d before inflation came down. History shows that in the long run we will not experience higher growth and lower unemployment in the city against higher inflation. A monetary policy that contributes to inflation does not generate higher economic growth. On the contrary, it lays the foundation for later decline and unemployment. Without nominal stability, we also do not have stability in employment and production. The economy must have a nominal anchor. They're the job of money laundering. The Norwegian economy lacked a nominal anchor during the low interest rate and devaluation period in the 1970s and 1980s. The fixed exchange rate policy from 1986 rebuilt monetary policy and laid the foundation for more stable economic developments later. With the free flow of capital, deep capital markets and the phasing in of petroleum revenues in the Norwegian economy, managing the interest rate e is an inflation target. Monetary policy is being exchanged for low and stable inflation. The inflation target is 21/2 per cent. Put simply, we can say that the response pattern for monetary policy is: If it appears that inflation with an unchanged interest rate will be higher than 21/2 per cent, the interest rate will be increased. If it appears that inflation with an unchanged interest rate will be lower than 21/2 per cent, the interest rate will be reduced so much. Inflation in Norway is determined by both domestic and international price impulses. Domestic price impulses are influenced by the situation in the Norwegian economy. International price impulses come via the prices of the consumer goods and intermediate goods we import. These price impulses will be influenced, among other things, by developments in international commodity prices, consumer prices and the exchange rate. Money polity works with a dse erslep. Our analyses indicate that a substantial share of the effects of an interest rate change will occur within two years. Two years is therefore a reasonable dsperspek v for achieving the inflation target. Nevertheless, it is conceivable that if inflation should be very high, and economic developments are weak, we may choose to spend somewhat longer than two years to achieve the inflation target of 21/2 per cent. The choice of dshorisont for monetary policy reflects the fact that there are real economic costs associated with getting inflation back quickly in the target. Indirectly, this horizon is an unearth for the trade-off between the consideration of stable output on the one hand and low and stable inflation on the other. The inflation outlook for the next two years is characterised by two contradictory figures. On the one hand, high wage and cost inflation will keep the rise in prices for domestically produced goods and services high. On the other hand, the impact of the appreciation on the krone will result in a huge fall in prices for imported goods. If the krone exchange rate remains at the level from the last few months, the effect of the krone appreciation will be greatest towards mid-2003. The rise in the consumer price index adjusted for emits is and excluding energy products (CPIJAE) is projected to slow to 13/4 per cent next summer. At the end of 2004, inflation is estimated at 21/2 per cent. The phasing in of petroleum revenues will have consequences for the industry structure in Norway. Increased use of petroleum revenues on goods and services requiring domestic resources requires increased employment in the sheltered sector. This work crash must be taken from the competitive sector or by the natural growth in the labour force finding its way in the sheltered sector. We expect a significant fall in manufacturing employment in the coming year. One reason is the deteriorating competitiveness of Norwegian bedri. International economic conditions have weakened. Low growth among our trading partners is hitting markets for Norwegian exporters through lower demand and falling prices. In the face of cyclical fluctuations and competitive conditions, employment in manufacturing is likely to be reduced as a result of product improvements. In Norway and other OECD countries, manufacturing's share of total employment has been reduced trend-wise over the past 30 years. From the first half of 2001 in the first half of 2002, the largest change in industrial employment occurred in the workshop and transport industry. In these two sectors alone, employment increased by 2,400 from the first half of this year. In the process industry, the metal industry and wood processing experienced the largest decline, totalling 1200 people. Lower employment in manufacturing is not peculiar to Norway. There is a trend decline in manufacturing employment in all countries. The decommissioning takes place with different urgency and has different consequences for different countries. The U.S. has suffered the sharpest decline in manufacturing employment as a share of total employment. A stable exchange rate and cost inflation among our trading partners were long anchored for wage formation. However, since 1998, the rise in labour costs in Norway been around 2 percentage points higher than among our trading partners. They have few consequences for profitability in international industries. Overall, it appears that wages in Norway will be about 15 per cent higher than in the years from 1998 to 2003. We have expensive experiences with such a development. Both in the mid-1970s and the mid-1980s, the Norwegian economy was out of step with the countries around us. In the periods 1975-1978 and 1982-1988, wage growth in the Norway was substantially above wage growth among trading partners. The consequences of such a development were a significant deterioration in the competitiveness of internationally exposed enterprises. This resulted in each economic downturn with low real wage growth and higher unemployment, including in sheltered industries. They are a mechanism we must expect to take effect again. The cyclical difference between Norway and abroad is reflected in the differences between interest rates in Norway and in Germany and the US. International interest rates are currently very low to counteract the downturn. The wide interest rate differential has contributed to an appreciation of the krone. In llegg, the sharp fall in the share price internationally contributes to a focus on "safe" investments. Then the Norwegian krone, with a high interest rate and oil wealth, may appear to be a rake alterna v. The krone has appreciated by 15-20 per cent against our most important trading partners since summer 2000. The appreciation of the krone contributes to worsening the competitiveness of Norwegian manufacturing. The appreciation of the krone is probably reversible, but the loss of competitiveness and jobs resulting from the particularly Norwegian wage growth is difficult to recover. The international downturn has also resulted in weaker provision opportunities for many export industries. Norwegian manufacturing is buoyed by lower demand and falling prices for victorian exports. The situation internationally is unclear. Growth may pick up again, but it is uncertain when the upturn will come. Norwegian industry must be prepared for weak demand in the coming year. Even if employment and production in manufacturing in Norway are weakened, developments for Norwegian enterprises do not have to be nega v. Some bedri are able to be at the forefront of technological developments and increase the efficienk in line with the particularly Norwegian cost increase. Work crashes can be located abroad. Nevertheless, we take a risk when manufacturing is reduced. This makes the economy more vulnerable  the fertile ground for learning, innovation and development can be weakened when less of the business sector is exposed to intense international competition. It should be possible for us to live well with the oil. It requires us to deal with multiple misinditions. We must distribute wealth among generations in a good way. The fluctuating revenue flow must be managed in such a way that we avoid creating unnecessary fluctuations in the economy and in competitiveness.
