I llegg l konjunktursvingninger og konkurransemessige forhold, vil sysselse ngen i industrien trolig reduseres som flge av produk vitetsforbedringer. Bde i Norge og andre OECD-land er industriens andel av total sysselse ng trendmessig redusert over de siste 30 rene. Fra frste halvr 2001 l frste halvr 2002 skjedde den strste endringen i industrisysselse ngen i verkstedindustrien og transportmiddelindustrien. I disse to sektorene alene kte sysselse ngen med 2400 personer fra 1.halvr i or l 1.halvr i r. Innen prosessindustrien er det metallindustrien og treforedling som opplevde den strste nedgangen, l sammen 1200 personer. Lavere sysselse ng i industrien er ikke sregent for Norge. Det er en trendmessig nedgang i industrisysselse ngen i alle land. Nedbyggingen skjer med ulik has ghet og har ulik konsekvens for ulike land. USA har ha den kra igste nedgangen i industrisysselse ngen mlt som andel av total sysselse ng. Stabil valutakurs og kostnadsveksten hos vre handelspartnere var lenge ankerfestet for lnnsdannelsen. Men siden 1998 har veksten i lnnskostnadene i Norge vrt rundt 2 prosentenheter hyere enn blant vre handelspartnere. De e har f konsekvenser for lnnsomheten i konkurranseutsa e nringer. Samlet ser det ut l at lnningene i Norge vil s ge vel 15 prosent mer enn ute i rene fra og med 1998 l 2003. Vi har dyrkjpte erfaringer med en slik utvikling. Bde p midten av 70-tallet og p midten av 80-tallet var norsk konomi i utakt med landene rundt oss. I periodene 1975-1978 og 1982-1988 l lnnsveksten i Norge vesentlig over lnnsveksten hos handelspartnerne. Flgene av en slik utvikling var vesentlig forringelse av konkurranseevnen for konkurranseutsa e virksomheter. Det resulterte i hvert lfelle i konjunkturnedgang med lav reell vekst i lnningene og kt ledighet, ogs i skjermede nringer. De e er en mekanisme vi m vente at vil gjre seg gjeldende igjen. Konjunkturforskjellen mellom Norge og utlandet reekteres i dieransene mellom rentene i Norge og i Tyskland og USA. De internasjonale rentene er i dag svrt lave for  motvirke nedgangskonjunktur. Den store rentedieransen har bidra l en styrking av kronen. I llegg har det sterke aksjekursfallet internasjonalt bidrar l fokus p "trygge" plasseringer. Da kan norske kroner, med rela vt hy rente og oljerikdom, fremst som et a rak vt alterna v. Kronen har styrket seg med 15-20 prosent mot vre vik gste handelspartnere siden sommeren 2000. Styrkingen av kronen bidrar l  forverre konkurranseevnen y erligere for norsk industri. Styrkingen av kronen er trolig reversibel, men det tapet av konkurranseevne og arbeidsplasser som skyldes den srnorske lnnsveksten, er vanskelig  hente inn. Den internasjonale nedgangen har ogs frt l at avsetningsmulighetene er bli svakere for mange eksportnringer. Norsk industri er bli m av lavere e ersprsel og fallende priser p vik ge eksportvarer. Situasjonen internasjonalt er uklar. Veksten kan ta seg opp igjen men det er usikkert nr oppgangen kommer. Norsk industri m vre forberedt p svak e ersprsel ogs i den som kommer. Selv om sysselse ng og produksjon i industrien i Norge blir svekket, behver ikke utviklingen for norske foretak bli nega v. Enkelte bedri er vil kunne vre i forkant i den teknologiske utviklingen og ke eek viteten i takt med den srnorske kostnadskningen. Arbeidskra intensive virksomheter kan lokaliseres i utlandet. Likevel tar vi en risiko nr industrien bygges ned. Det gjr konomien mer srbar - grobunnen for lring, innovasjon og utvikling, kan bli svekket nr mindre av nringslivet blir utsa for intens internasjonal konkurranse. Det br kunne vre mulig for oss  leve godt med oljen. Det krever at vi hndterer ere u ordringer. Vi m fordele rikdommen mellom generasjoner p en god mte. Den varierende inntektsstrmmen m styres slik at vi unngr  skape undige svingninger i konomien og i konkurranseevnen. Sam dig vil bruk av oljeinntekter innebre en svekkelse av konkurranseevnen. Det er derfor svrt vik g at vi klarer  beholde en nringsstruktur som fremmer lring, nyskapning og utvikling. PUBLISERT 2. desember 2002 14:00

Title: The Norwegian economy in transition
text: The Norwegian economy in the resuscitation Governor Svein Gjedrem. Speech at Sparebank1 Nord-Norway, Bodo, 3 December 2002 The speech is based on the assessments given at Norges Bank's press conference, which is the Monetary Policy Meeting of the Executive Board on 30 October, as well as other talks. The llegg provides a preliminary assessment of some new features of cyclical developments. Changes are subject to change during the performance. A year and a half ago, the Government and the Storting adopted new guidelines for economic policing. Above d, the use of petroleum revenues shall correspond to the expected real return on the Petroleum Fund, i.e. 4 per cent of the Fund. The use of petroleum revenues is reflected in the structural deficit in the Government Budget excluding petroleum revenues. According to the fiscal rule above d, the structural non-oil deficit shall be four per cent of the fund's value. This means, among other things, that in a boom, higher revenues will have an impact on improved bidding balance, and contradicted in a recession. The e means that the so-called automa ske stabilizers are allowed to work. Norges Bank shall view the interest rate with a view to low and stable inflation. The inflation target is 21/2 per cent. In the National Budget, the Government has expressed dis hope that it is the monetary policy that should react in the first place if the outlook for economic developments changes. Nevertheless, situations may arise where the use of the bidding policy is required, either because capacity growth is particularly low, or because pressures in the economy are very high. There are good reasons why monetary policy is being used to keep inflation low and stable. High and variable inflation costs. Households and residents are becoming more uncertain about their income and publishing. This gives rise to incorrect investments and wider fluctuations in the economy. Avoiding deflation - a decline in prices - is just as important because it laughs hand in hand with, and can amplify, a downturn there in the economy. Low and stable inflation is the best contribution monetary policy can make to growth and stability in the economy. We have had four periods of really high inflation over the last 100 years, during the two world wars and the Korean War, as well as a 15-year period from the first half of the 1970s in the second half of the 1980s. At Norway, really high inflation is a war phenomenon and a 1970s and 1980s phenomenon. In the wake of high inflation, we have experienced substantial real economic losses and financial instability. The pea period of high inflation was different from the previous three. In the 1970s and 1980s, inflation gradually accelerated. It was not as high as during the world wars, but it took a long d before inflation came down. E is its fixed exchange rate system, the so-called Bre on Woods system, broke down in 1971. A couple of years later came the Yom Kippur War, with opec countries' supply halts and the first oil crisis. The sharp rise in oil prices resulted in a drop in productivity growth and led to stagnation and higher unemployment in western economies. In many countries, inflation gained traction. High and variable inflation contributed to wide fluctuations in output and employment. The wide fluctuations in the economy culminated with the borrowing and consumption boom in the mid-1980s. It was followed by a deep recession and high unemployment in the late 1980s. The wide fluctuations in the 1970s and 1980s were related to the lack of a nominal anchor in the Norwegian economy, in the form of stable prices or a stable exchange rate. High and variable inflation was countered by frequent devaluations. This was a poor starting point for stability in the economy. History shows that in the long run we will not have lower unemployment in the city against higher inflation. A monetary policy that contributes to inflation does not generate higher economic growth. On the contrary, it lays the foundation for later decline and unemployment. The world's capital markets are e is each becoming more integrated. Investing across national borders is less risky and less risky. The foreign exchange market has been given an increasingly important role in financial markets. Today, the world economy is characterized by the re-end trade and cross-border flow not only of goods and services, but also of capital. The opening up of capital markets and Norway's trade opportunities in the rest of the world have a significant impact on economic policing, particularly in two areas. First, Norway's large petroleum deposits in a world of free trade may be converted into substantial revenues for our country, and the surplus can be invested abroad. They're going to stabilize politics in the face of special inconveniences. Norway's export rate and government revenues can be expected to be very high as long as production remains high. Sam dig has experienced that revenues can vary greatly from year this year. The high level and fluctuations in revenues mean that the most important contribution financial policy can make to stabilising the Norwegian economy is to follow a prudent plan for the use of petroleum revenues. Attempts to use the state budget to fine-tune the economy may seem destabilizing if the attempt is dismissed as a violation of the long-running plan for phasing in oil revenues. It is necessary to show that the bidding policy is applied symmetrically in the upturn and downturn there. Second, economic agents look ahead when they have decisions about consumption and investment, wages and prices. They will take into account the economic policing not only as it is today, but also as they expect it to be tomorrow and the day after tomorrow. They are particularly pronounced in foreign exchange and financial markets, where exchange rates and interest rates are affected when participants are investing substantial funds based partly on their expectations of how economic policing will be and developments in the economy. The topics that are followed and that govern exchange rate and interest rate developments are changing. It is then important that the authorities do not sow doubt, but on the contrary act in a way that is predictable. The authorities need to be credible and create ill. There must be a good correlation between what is said about the objectives of policing and what is being done to achieve them. Here we find the most important reason l that the implementation of monetary policy has been delegated to the central bank in Norway, as well as in other countries with which we can compare ourselves. The settlement on the state budget for 2003 between the Government and The Progress Party is to reallocate approximately NOK 6.3 billion in accrued value and NOK 4.4 billion in book value. The real underlying growth in the share of the budget is estimated at about 1/2 per cent in 2003, and the structural non-oil deficit is estimated at L30.7 billion. These figures are the same as in the Government's original proposal in the state budget. In the settlement, the economy in the municipalities in isolation will be strengthened by NOK 1 billion. They account for about 1/2 per cent of the municipalities' revenues. But the municipalities are now forecasting NOK 1 billion lower in 2002, and with the possibility of lower revenues next year. In the state budget for 2003, the estimates for the use of petroleum revenues up to 2010 have been revised downwards considerably since the Lang d programme, the National Budget for 2002 and the Revised National Budget for 2002 were presented. This may mean that the phasing in of petroleum revenues will take place more gradually than envisages. The krone has appreciated considerably since summer 2000. There can be many reasons in this development. Relationships in the foreign exchange market are unstable. Nevertheless, there are some fundamental fundamentals that influence the krone exchange rate. The phasing in of petroleum revenues and cyclical developments is affecting the exchange rate. In llegg, the real exchange rate tends to reverse if there are large deviations above d. Moreover, the krone may be affected by whether there are skies and changes in the way wages are formed, and the krone exchange rate can also be influenced by factors that do not have much to do with Norway isolated see . More use of petroleum revenues or expectations of more use of petroleum revenues may strengthen the krone. Increased use of petroleum revenues over the government budget means increased demand. The battle for real resources will then lead to more competition in the business sector, leaving room for more sheltered activities. With low and stable inflation, this restructuring may occur through a stronger krone exchange rate. Such exchange rate movements will typically occur in waves. When petroleum revenues are phased in, there will be a tendency for the real interest rate to be higher. The real exchange rate may strengthen, i.e. a deterioration in competitiveness. In the short term, the real exchange rate may move more than will be needed in the long term. There will then be grounds for expectations that the krone will depreciade again later, because higher real interest rates, together with expectations of a depreciation of the krone, contribute l that the expected real return will be the same for capital invested in the Norway and abroad. In the outlay, there may be additional fluctuations in the exchange rate if market expectations concerning the use of petroleum revenues deviate from what is realised. There is reason to believe that foreign exchange market participants with the current exchange rate have already taken into account that the use of petroleum revenues will increase. Cyclical developments are reflected in the difference between interest rates in Norway and in Germany and the US. What is unusual now is the extremely low foreign interest rates. Interest rates abroad are so sharply down to counteract a downturn. A high and widening interest rate differential against other countries has probably contributed to the appreciation of the krone. Even though the krone exchange rate is strong, expectations concerning the krone exchange rate in the period ahead are not particularly strong. If you buy NOK for delivery in a couple of years, and agree on the exchange rate now, it will be in a krone exchange rate that is in line with the current krone exchange rate in the 1990s. Cyclical inequalities reflected in the krone exchange rate can hardly be seen completely independent of our position as an oil economy. At least since the slush of the 1990s, it appears that bedri is, households and wage earners have been adjusting to expectations of strong earnings growth. They may have contributed both to developments in the krone exchange rate and to increase cyclical differences between Norway and abroad. If the current krone exchange rate is already taking into account that the use of petroleum revenues will increase, both the longitudinal trend in the real exchange rate and expectations concerning interest rate developments ahead suggest that the krone exchange rate will each return to a more natural longitudinal level. During the 1990s, unemployment declined as long as wage growth in the Norway was lower than wage growth among our trading partners. They took cunning in 1998. At that time, the social partners said no in the line of moderation. The decline in unemployment came to a halt. The sharp rise in labour costs in recent years is a factor in higher unemployment. The interest rate is a key instrument for meeting changes in demand and keeping inflation low and stable. With low and stable inflation, changes in the interest rate can also contribute to stability in output and employment. But there is little monetary policy that can be done to prevent an increase in unemployment that is driven by high cost inflation. A stable exchange rate and cost inflation among our trading partners were long anchored for wage formation. However, since 1998, the rise in labour costs in Norway been around 2 percentage points higher than among our trading partners. Overall, it appears that wages in Norway will be about 15 per cent higher than in the years from 1998 to 2003. High wage growth is hitting manufacturing hard, along with bad ones out there and a strong krone. The krone is now around 9 per cent stronger than in the 1990s. The appreciation of the krone is probably reversible, but the loss of competitiveness and jobs resulting from the particularly Norwegian wage growth is difficult to recover. Over d, the size of the internationally exposed sector will be affected by how much petroleum revenues are absorbed into the Norwegian economy, but will be independent of the monetary policy. Any appreciation of the krone may nevertheless influence how quickly changes in the business sector occur. Industries that export abroad contribute to obtaining foreign exchange revenues to finance imports of goods and services. Having industries that are exposed to competition from abroad is also important for the growth capacity of the economy. That is why we take a risk when the industry is reduced. This makes the economy more vulnerable. The growth capacity of the economy  the breeding ground for learning, innovation and development  may be weakened when less of the business sector is exposed to intense international competition. If we look at the last three years, the industry has been built up in waves. Especially in the years from 1977 l 1984 and from 1987 l 1992 there was kra ig peeling. Profitability in manufacturing had deteriorated in the past. It may take d before such a weakening strikes lower production and employment ng. But once the cover arrives, it often happens quickly and quickly. Norway,i mean, you're not alone. There is a trend decline in manufacturing employment in all countries. The decline occurs with varying urgency. The U.S. has had the sharpest decline. Developments in recent years may herald a new round of industry resuscitations. A downturn in the world economy amplifies the restructuring and contributes in isolation to weakening the economic outlook. On the other hand, oil prices, investment and the accumulation in the petroleum sector have so far remained high. Weak international economic developments over the past couple of years are reflected in equity prices. Prices on most exchanges have fallen significantly since the end of the year. Equity prices in different countries tend to follow each other. The effects of the fall have affected several countries. Developments this summer indicate that the upturn in the world economy may be weaker and come later than expected this year. The fall in global equity prices has also forged a transition to the Norwegian stock market. There is a close relationship between share prices in the US and in Norway. A sharp fall in equity prices may also dampen the impact on the Norwegian economy, even though the impact is considerably smaller here. Households that own equities will have their wealth reduced, and they will reduce their consumption. Developments in equity prices may also have an impact on household expectations and make it less of a stretch to invest in new production capacity. American consumers are becoming more pessimis about economic developments. The last one, however, there has been some more posi ve of numbers from the US. E is having fallen through the summer and autumn, expectations rose somewhat from October this year. In Europe, expectations have weakened over the past year. Developments in Germany in particular give cause for some unease. Growth is stagnating, and households and households are looking at it darker. Expectations in manufacturing and among households are also weaker in Norway. A decline in the equity market, a weaker outlook for global growth and higher interest rates in the Norway have so far not hampered the willingness of Norwegian borrowers to see themselves in debt. The total debt burden in the household sector is high, but quickly lower than in the slush one of the 1980s, measured against household disposable income. The debt burden for the group with lower and middle incomes is currently higher than ever before. In the event of income drilling or an increase in the interest rate, households in this group may have difficulty servicing their debt. Household financial savings (ne ofinance investments) have fallen close to zero in the past couple of years. Combined with high wage growth, this has resulted in strong growth in household consumption. However, weaker expectations may be a first sign that households will be more insured than they are. There is some slowdown in the labour market. Registered unemployment has risen somewhat over the past year, and was 3.3 per cent in October (seasonally adjusted 3.5 per cent). Unemployment has risen in all counties and among all occupational groups excluding primary industries. However, unemployment is particularly rising in some service industries. So far, there are no signs of substantially higher unemployment in typical industrial counties. The increase in unemployment is particularly tied up in individual sectors, including the IT sector, transport and parts of the private service sector. We have not yet seen the full impact of the weak competitiveness on manufacturing and on industries and regions that are particularly dependent on manufacturing. In the work on the Inflation Report, information from the regional network established in the autumn was renewed. Through six rounds a year, we will have conversations with contacts from business and society about the economic development of their bedri er and industries, a total of around 200 visits in each round. We have divided the country into 7 regions and for six of them we have tied up regional research programmes that conduct contact meetings on behalf of Norges Bank. Nord-Norway is covered by Kunnskapsparken here in Bodo. From region north, it is reported that the strong krone combined with a costly wage settlement contributes to reducing competitiveness in export-ed manufacturing. Lately, they have created significantly lower demand and turnover at the bedri's that supply goods and services in this industry. The North reports reduced demand and declining profitability. The trend is the same in most industries except retail trade and other private services compared to the household sector. The retail sector has experienced an increase in turnover in the last 12 years. It is expected that this development will continue in the coming months as well. We get a report of a significant trade leak in Sweden. In building and construction, manufacturing, services and trade in capital goods, we report a shift towards the public sector. The table shows the economic outlook as assessed by Norges Bank's Executive Board before the meeting on 30 October this year. The figures and assessments are from the Inflation Report presented on the same day. Norges Bank projected high growth in private consumption. This is partly due to high wage growth in the public sector. Investment on the mainland is growing little, while petroleum investment is likely to be high next year. Mainland GDP growth was expected to Norway pick up somewhat during the projection period and reach 21/4 per cent in 2004. The projections for inflation were revised down from the Inflation Report in summer. This was due to higher interest rates and a stronger krone exchange rate. Inflation was projected to reach 21/2 per cent two years ahead. The effects of high wage growth on inflation were expected to be offset by the appreciation of the krone. Norges Bank assesses economic developments and the interest rate at regular monetary policy meetings of the Executive Board. The next monetary policy meeting is 11 December. We will then review developments since the last time and in the usual way make an overall assessment that is presented at the press conference e is the meeting. 3 December 2002 14:00

The projections have been revised downwards due to weaker economic conditions in the world economy, a sharp decline in international interest rates and a strong krone. Title: Inflation targeting with a fluctuating exchange rate
text: Infla on targe ng with a fluctua ng exchange rate Address by Deputy Governor Jarle Bergo. Conference arranged by Pareto Securi es in Oslo, 27 March 2003 The address is based on the assessments presented at Norges Bank's press conference following the Execu ve Board's monetary policy mee ng on 5 March and on previous speeches and publica ons. Please note that the text below may differ slightly from the actual presenta on. My subject today is the conduct of monetary policy in an environment where the exchange rate fluctuates. I will discuss why the exchange rate is important also in an infla on targe ng regime and how we take exchange rate fluctua ons into account when making infla on forecasts and se ng the interest rate. The Government has defined an infla on target for monetary policy in Norway. The opera onal objec ve is an infla on rate of 2 per cent over me. The key interest rate is set on the basis of an overall assessment of the infla on outlook, normally with a view to achieving an infla on rate of 2 per cent two years ahead. Forward-looking infla on targe ng contributes to smoothing fluctua ons in the economy. Pressures in the economy and risks of higher infla on will normally be met with a ghtening of monetary policy. Conversely, sluggish growth and lower infla on pressures will normally induce a relaxa on of monetary policy. Hence, the monetary policy response to changes in the infla on outlook will in most cases also promote the stabilisa on of the real economy. The krone is floa ng. We no longer have an exchange rate target. In fact, the experience of the last half of the 1990s showed that monetary policy does not have the instruments necessary to pursue an exchange rate target. But developments in the krone exchange rate are important to the infla on outlook and must be taken into account when se ng the interest rate. Exchange rate fluctua ons influence consumer price infla on through several channels: It affects infla on through a direct effect on prices for imported consumer goods in the CPI. An apprecia on of the krone reduces prices for imported goods measured in Norwegian currency. The exchange rate also influences infla on through an indirect effect via prices for imported intermediate goods, which in turn influence prices for domes cally produced goods and services in the CPI. Furthermore, the exchange rate has in impact on infla on through a profitability effect. Changes in the exchange rate may influence both the ac vity and the profitability of interna onally exposed industries and thereby wage growth. Changes in wage growth will in turn influence the CPI. In addi on, fluctua ons in the exchange rate may affect infla on through a price- wage spiral. Tradi onally, higher infla on has been met by demands for compensa on in order to maintain a given growth in real wages. Over me, it is likely that a las ng change in the krone exchange rate passes through fully to the level of prices for imported goods, when adjusted for indirect taxes, du es and freight costs. There are many reasons, however, why import prices are not adjusted immediately in response to a change in the exchange rate. First, with a floa ng exchange rate, it may be difficult for enterprises to assess the dura on of a change in the exchange rate. They may want to wait and see if it lasts before adjus ng the price to the consumers. Meanwhile, the exchange rate movements only affect the enterprises' margins. Second, many enterprises and importers hedge against movements in the exchange rate in the short to medium term, either by means of financial instruments or price agreements. Third, markets with monopolis c compe on will o en be subject to strategic price se ng. One example of this is the car market where foreign producers o en price cars in NOK in the short term, thereby assuming full or par al exchange rate risk. In this case, it may take me before the direct effects of changes in the exchange rate are reflected in the CPI. One would assume that it takes even longer for exchange rate movements to feed through to prices for domes cally produced goods and services via imported intermediate goods, not to speak of the lags in the profitability channel. Using two different models- the macroeconomic RIMINI model and a sub-index model - we have quan fied the most direct effects of a shi in the krone exchange rate on consumer prices.1The RIMINI model is based on es mated rela onships in the Norwegian economy over the past 30 years, while the sub-index model is es mated using data for the last 20 years or so. Imported consumer goods account for about 20 per cent of the CPI adjusted for specific taxes. In the sub-index model, we have es mated separate equa ons for around 10 sub-indices of the CPI. The exchange rate is incorporated as a direct explanatory factor in the es mated equa ons for the prices for imported consumer goods. Consequently, we capture the direct effects of a change in the exchange rate on the CPI. In addi on, we would expect changes in the exchange rate to have an indirect impact on prices for domes cally produced goods and services in the CPI. In the more comprehensive macroeconomic RIMINI model of Norges Bank, the exchange rate operates through a broader range of import prices. The RIMINI model captures both the direct effect from imported consumer goods, and the more indirect effect on domes c prices through imported intermediates. However, in the calcula ons presented here we have excluded any indirect effects through reduced ac vity and profitability in interna onally exposed enterprises. The cumula ve effects of a shi in the exchange rate differ somewhat between the two models, with the broader RIMINI model indica ng the largest impact. In the sub-index model, a 1 per cent change in the exchange rate will change the CPI by a good 0.2 per cent, while the RIMINI model indicates an effect on the CPI in the area of 0.4 per cent. The model using sub-indices may underes mate the indirect effects of a change in the exchange rate, for example because prices for imported intermediate goods may change. On the other hand, we have not found empirical support for a direct effect of an exchange rate change on prices for domes c goods and services (which accounts for a good 70 per cent of the CPI) in this disaggregated model. This may indicate that the RIMINI model to some extent overes mates the effects. Based on these results, we may tenta vely assume that a sustained apprecia on of the effec ve krone exchange rate of 5 per cent may reduce CPI infla on by about percentage point the first year, close to percentage point the second year and about percentage point the third year. Both models indicate that the pass-through to consumer price infla on is strongest the second year and then declines gradually. The es mates are subject to considerable uncertainty. First, there is model- uncertainty. The models are es mated using data from a period dominated by a monetary policy regime with a fixed exchange rate. Interna onally, it has been argued that the pass-through from exchange rate changes to infla on is diminishing. New Zealand, Australia and Canada have experienced wide exchange rate fluctua ons in recent years. A weaker pass-through in these countries has been explained in part by the introduc on of an infla on target which provides an anchor for expecta ons forma on and thereby contains price-wage spirals. In Norway, the period of a floa ng exchange rate and infla on targe ng is s ll too short to provide empirical evidence of such effects. Second, there is uncertainty about the ming of the pass-through. The two models indicate that the effects are strongest a er two years. However, these es mates are based on a long-las ng apprecia on. Different exchange rate expecta ons will have different implica ons for the pass-through to infla on. If the exchange rate is expected to return to a more "normal" level, the pass-through may prove to be negligible at least in the short and medium term. Wider exchange rate fluctua ons have probably also induced enterprises to take a more wait-and-see' a tude to changing prices. The value of the Norwegian krone will vary, as most exchange rates do. Changes in the exchange rate can be desirable when they contribute to stabilising infla on. The exchange rate may also act as an automa c stabiliser. In periods when economic ac vity is too high - or there are expecta ons of overhea ng - the exchange rate may appreciate, even if Norges Bank does not change its key rates. Similarly, the exchange rate may depreciate if the ac vity level is too low. However, fluctua ons in the exchange rate can also be a source of economic disturbances. Sen ments in the foreign exchange market may at mes be excessively posi ve towards a currency while at other mes they are overly nega ve. This can trigger large and unnecessary fluctua ons in the exchange rate. Norges Bank's reac on to a change in the exchange rate will depend on an assessment of the effect on infla on. This requires an evalua on of the reasons for and the expected permanence of the change. There is reason to believe that short- term fluctua ons in the krone exchange rate have li le impact on infla on. When the changes are poten ally more las ng and thus may be assumed to have a greater impact on infla on, the Bank will set the interest rate with a view to stabilising infla on. However, it is difficult to establish whether exchange rate fluctua ons are persistent or temporary and thus what the impact on infla on will be. Therefore, Norges Bank will normally proceed with cau on in connec on with any interest rate changes in response to fluctua ons in the exchange rate. Any monetary policy reac on to changes in the exchange rate will be built on an analysis of the factors behind the exchange rate developments, so that the overall stance of monetary policy is in accordance with the objec ve of low and stable infla on. What causes exchange rate movements? In the long run exchange rates reflect economic fundamentals. There is a tendency for the real exchange rate to return to its long-term average level in accordance with the purchasing power parity hypothesis. If our infla on rate is consistently higher than that of our trading partners, our nominal exchange rate will tend to fall. When PPP holds, the real exchange rate is a constant in the long run. Movements in the real exchange rate represent devia ons from PPP. The view of the PPP as a long-term interna onal parity condi on is supported by recent empirical literature tes ng the validity of the PPP hypothesis. Among the studies suppor ng PPP, there appears to be a consensus that the magnitude of the half-life of devia ons from PPP is about three to five years.2 A measure of the real exchange rate is the trade-weighted exchange rate index (TWI) in rela on to rela ve price developments between Norway and its trading partners. The real krone exchange rate has fluctuated around a long-term average level over the past 30 years. The krone exchange rate has tended to return rela vely quickly to its normal level when it has deviated from the long-term average level. Studies indicate that the size of the half-life of devia ons from PPP is about 1 years.3 Differences in price infla on between Norway and other countries have gradually been evened out by changes in the krone exchange rate. This rela onship has been robust even with considerable changes in economic policy over the years. However, it is s ll too early to say whether the revision of economic policy in spring 2001, with the introduc on of a new fiscal guideline and an infla on target for monetary policy, may have an impact on how quickly differences in price infla on narrow in the future. Economic theory serves as a guide to predict long-term movements in exchange rates. A central bank, assessing the infla on outlook, is concerned about exchange rate movements within a horizon of a couple of years. Within this horizon, several factors may affect the exchange rate. Generally these factors are outside the control of the central bank. The krone exchange rate is the price of our currency measured in terms of a foreign currency. Developments in other countries are just as important for the krone as developments in the Norwegian economy. Commodity-expor ng countries tend to experience wide fluctua ons in their exchange rate. Australia is one example, and New Zealand another. Fluctua ons in commodity prices lead to changes in countries' terms of trade, which measures the ra o of export to import prices. Fluctua ons in the terms of trade affect the exchange rate. This dampens the effects of commodity price changes on profitability in business and industry. The exchange rate thus serves as a buffer against changes in the terms of trade. In Norway, the petroleum fund mechanism and the fiscal guidelines dampen the effect on the exchange rate of changes in oil prices. Oil and gas account for the largest share of Norwegian exports. A substan al por on of the revenues from the sale of oil and gas is invested in foreign equi es and bonds through the Government Petroleum Fund. As a result, shortterm fluctua ons in the oil price have less impact on the domes c use of petroleum revenues. In the last 20 years, fluctua ons in the terms of trade have been three to four mes greater for the Norwegian economy including the petroleum sector than for the mainland economy. The Petroleum Fund thus relieves pressure on the krone exchange rate. Nevertheless, fluctua ons occur. The trade-weighted krone appreciated by around 20 per cent from May 2000 un l January 2003. The apprecia on was par cularly pronounced through 2002. The apprecia on was the subject of media headlines and caused concerns among exporters. Importers were more subdued in their comments. Since end-January the krone has depreciated by around 4 per cent. How do we explain the strong apprecia on of the krone in the period between summer 2000 and January 2003? Market par cipants have pointed to several factors that may have contributed to the strengthening of the krone: The apprecia on occurred in tandem with a high and widening interest rate differen al between Norway and other countries. Foreign interest rates fell while Norwegian interest rates remained high. This boosted demand for the Norwegian krone. The fall in interna onal stock markets led to increased risk aversion and expecta ons of a further decline in equity prices. As a consequence, many investors wanted to shi por olios from equi es to interest-bearing securi es. According to market par cipants, the Norwegian krone, with a rela vely high interest rate, may have seemed a good alterna ve. The krone exchange rate has been highly correlated with US equity prices over the last few years. Market expecta ons concerning fluctua ons between major currencies, measured by an indicator based on op ons prices, the Global Hazard Indicator4, fell. According to market par cipants, expecta ons of reduced exchange rate fluctua ons between major currencies provide less scope for specula ve gains in the foreign exchange market. In such periods, investors have placed greater emphasis on interest rate differen als and invested a higher por on of their por olios in high interest rate currencies, such as the Norwegian krone. Oil prices rose markedly from the end of 2001. Market par cipants point out that, ceteris paribus, higher oil prices make the Norwegian krone more a rac ve. Last year, the Norwegian krone was, again according to market par cipants, in periods considered a safe-haven currency. During turbulent periods, investors seek out safe investments. Tradi onally, such investments have been gold, the Swiss franc and the US dollar. Some investors may have perceived the Norwegian krone as a temporary, safe alterna ve in a situa on with uncertainty associated with a possible war in Iraq. In order to examine the importance of these factors, Norges Bank has developed an econometric model of the tradeweighted exchange rate index (TWI).5 The model includes effects of the interest rate differen al against other countries, developments in US equity prices, the magnitude of expected variability between major currencies (GHI) and the oil price. The model is es mated using monthly data from July 1999 to January 2003 and fits actual developments rather well. The interest rate differen al, RDIFF, is important in explaining short-term movements in the exchange rate. But, as the two last components of the equa on indicate, the importance of the interest rate differen al increases in periods of reduced expected variability between major currencies and nega ve growth in equity prices. Rises in equity prices are represented in the model only mul plied by the interest rate differen al. Hence, equity prices will, according to this model, have no effect when the interest rate differen al is zero. The model is well-specified judged by standard criteria. The t-sta s cs of the es mated coefficients are generally high. Accordingly, the standard devia on of the residuals is quite low. The focus of a en on, or "themes", in foreign exchange markets shi s over me. The autumn of 1998 was marked by turbulence in interna onal financial markets. Despite a high interest rate in Norway, investors shi ed out of the Norwegian krone and into the Swiss franc and US dollar. In the last half of the 1990s, capital flows were heavily influenced by investor focus on stock market returns. During the period of the krone apprecia on, which began in May 2000, investors placed considerable emphasis on interest rate differen als. The effect of the high and widening interest rate differen al on the krone was amplified by condi ons in interna onal capital markets. We have used the model to study how the different factors have influenced the krone exchange rate since May 2000. The model indicates that the widening interest rate differen al can explain about 40 per cent of the krone apprecia on between May 2000 and January 2003. The stock market decline and falling variability between major currencies can explain about 55 per cent of the krone apprecia on in the period. These factors contributed because the interest rate differen al was posi ve. Higher oil prices also made some contribu on to the apprecia on of the krone in this period. The factors make a varying contribu on over me. As some of the condi ons have changed markedly within the period, it is interes ng to look at also a shorter sub- sample, beginning at the end of 2001. At that me, oil prices started to increase. According to the model, higher oil prices can explain about 35 per cent of the apprecia on between December 2001 and January 2003. This may partly reflect the effects of the percep on of the krone as a safe-haven currency. Developments in the interest rate differen al explain some 30 per cent of the apprecia on of the krone in the period, while the stock market decline and reduced vola lity between major currencies can explain the remaining 35 per cent. The model implies that the interest rate differen al has a greater impact on the exchange rate the more equity prices are falling and the lower expected variability is between major currencies. The expected gain from specula ng in equi es or currencies may be limited when equity prices are falling and when exchange rates are rela vely stable. In this situa on, investors will place greater emphasis on interest rate differen als than when equity prices are rising and exchange rates fluctuate widely. The effects of a change in the interest rate differen al at different points in me vary considerably. The interest rate effect increased markedly between March 2000 and January 2003. In March 2000, there was high expected variability between major currencies and equity prices had risen sharply. In January 2003, on the other hand, expected variability between major currencies was low and equity prices had fallen sharply. The es ma on results, as already men oned, showed the model to be well-specified. The model fits the historical data very well. Looking backwards, the model tells a sensible story. However it should be kept in mind that although the model fits historical data very well, it is not necessarily suitable for forecas ng purposes. We know the historical values of equity prices, the oil price, interest rate differen als and the measure of expected variability between major currencies. But in order to forecast future movements in the exchange rate, we need to predict the future values of these other variables as well. This is certainly not easy. Exchange rate movements are important in determining future infla on. We need to take account of this in our infla on projec ons. But what should be our point of departure with regard to the exchange rate assump on? It would be nice to have a reliable and well-specified forecas ng model for the exchange rate. Unfortunately, as we have seen, such models are not easily available. Empirical research indicates that the be er projec on for exchange rates in the short term is a random walk.6 Thus, assuming a constant exchange rate for the next couple of years may be simple but nevertheless defendable. In our infla on reports, we have mostly assumed a constant rate equal to the average exchange rate for the last three months, or some mes the last month. Very short term fluctua ons in the krone will therefore have limited influence on the infla on forecast. If a shi in the krone exchange rate lingers on it will gradually feed through to the exchange rate assump ons and thus have an effect on the infla on projec ons and monetary policy decisions. The impact on infla on of exchange rate fluctua ons is, however, strongest at around 4-6 quarters ahead. By se ng interest rates with a view to achieving an infla on rate at the opera onal target two years ahead, the importance of krone movements is reduced. With a shorter horizon for monetary policy, interest rates would have been changed more frequently. This would imply more fluctua ons in demand and produc on. Alterna vely, the exchange rate assump on could be based on economic theory. The uncovered interest rate parity condi on is o en used as a reference when "projec ng" exchange rates. One could also use different defini ons of equilibrium (real) exchange rates as a star ng point, assuming the exchange rate, if it is perceived to be over- or undervalued, in turn will return to its equilibrium level. Although such assump ons may be a rac ve from a theore cal viewpoint, it is highly uncertain if the exchange rate will return to its equilibrium level within a two-year horizon. Turning to our latest Infla on Report, the baseline scenario is based on the technical assump on of a constant sight deposit rate of 5 per cent and a constant krone exchange rate equal to the average for February. Norges Bank's projec ons must be understood as condi onal on these assump ons. With an exchange rate equal to the average for February, prices for imported consumer goods were projected to fall gradually. The nega ve contribu on to underlying infla on was expected to be most significant around summer and into late autumn. In the course of 2004 and 2005, the effect would gradually be reduced. In this scenario, infla on could reach 2 per cent two years ahead. As an alterna ve to the baseline scenario, we also examined a possible scenario where the interest rate was reduced and the krone depreciated in line with market expecta ons. The forward rate for the Norwegian krone indicated a deprecia on of about 7 per cent up to end-2005 compared with the baseline scenario in the report, corresponding to a further fall in short-term interest rates of a good 1 percentage point. Even though the forward rate is not necessarily a good predictor of actual developments, a deprecia on of the krone of this magnitude was reflected in the expecta ons survey conducted by Consensus Forecasts. In such a scenario, underlying infla on could reach 2 per cent two years ahead. Looking beyond the two-year horizon, infla on might edge up further. By using different technical assump ons, we indicated different paths for infla on. Actual developments may, however, deviate from both paths. Norges Bank will con nuously assess developments in the global economy, the Norwegian economy and the krone exchange rate, and set interest rates with a view to achieving the infla on target. Norges Bank has reduced the sight deposit rate from 7 to 5.5 per cent since 11 December. A narrowing interest rate differen al has been followed by a deprecia on of the krone. Monetary policy has been relaxed. Summary Although we have models that can explain historical developments in the exchange rate well, such models are not necessarily suitable as forecas ng models. In the short-term, the exchange rate can fluctuate widely. However much we may understand what has driven the exchange rate ex post, it must be admi ed that economists do not have a great track record for forecas ng exchange rates in the short and medium term. Rela onships in the foreign exchange market are unstable. The effect on the exchange rate from a change in the interest rate varies over me. The impact of exchange rate fluctua ons on infla on will also vary. Experience has shown that monetary authori es do not have the means to control the exchange rate. Monetary policy has nevertheless been successful in keeping infla on low and stable. It is the overall stance of monetary policy that will determine the path of infla on. The key interest rate is set on the basis of an overall assessment of the infla on outlook, normally with a view to achieving an infla on rate of 2 per cent two years ahead. Fluctua ons in the exchange rate are important in the conduct of monetary policy to the extent that they can be expected to have an impact on infla on. By having a two-year horizon for monetary policy and including changes in the exchange rate gradually in the infla on forecasts, monetary policy contributes to reducing variability in economic ac vity. Title: The economic situation in Norway and abroad
text: The economic situa on in Norway and abroad Address by Central Bank Governor Svein Gjedrem. Invited foreign embassy representa ves, Norges Bank 27 March 2003. The address is based on the assessments presented at Norges Bank's press conference following the Execu ve Board's monetary policy mee ng on 5 March and on previous speeches. Please note that the text below may differ slightly from the actual presenta on. Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen Today, I will discuss some of the forces that are shaping the economic outlook in Norway. The weak external environment is affec ng the Norwegian economy. War is contribu ng to increased uncertainty. At the same me, wage developments in Norway have mirrored a ght labour market. In recent years, real wage growth has exceeded produc vity growth. The different cycles in Norway and abroad contributed to a substan al strengthening of the krone last year. Compe veness for mainland businesses has weakened. Since last autumn, however, the outlook for the Norwegian economy has changed. The combina on of global stagna on and the high Norwegian cost level is causing job losses and higher unemployment. As this in turn affected the outlook for infla on, monetary policy was eased and the apprecia on of the krone has in part been reversed. Cyclical divergence and the krone exchange rate The krone exchange rate fluctuates. This is not surprising, as other countries' currencies also vary. The Swedish krona depreciated sharply in 1992. Since then it has remained weak, but has shown wide varia ons. Pound sterling appreciated by more than 20 per cent between 1996 and 1998, reflec ng solid growth in the UK economy from the mid-1990s. A currency that has exhibited wider swings than most is the New Zealand dollar. A sharp apprecia on up to the mid-1990s was subsequently reversed. Over the past two years, this currency has moved in tandem with the Norwegian krone. The effec ve krone exchange rate is the price of Norwegian currency measured in terms of foreign currency. Developments in other countries are just as important for the krone as developments in the Norwegian economy. Capital flows freely and flows can change rapidly. This can spill over to exchange rates and interest rates as well as output and employment. Currency swings are driven by cross-border capital movements. Capital flows were heavily influenced by investor focus on stock market returns un l the downturn began. In the US, equity prices almost trebled between 1995 and 2000. Stock markets in other countries followed suit. Capital inflows into the stock market resulted in a strong dollar. However, expecta ons concerning corporate earnings were higher than later proved to be warranted. When expecta ons were lowered, equity prices fell. The decline was amplified a er the downturn in the global economy deepened as a result of terror and fears of war. Investors sought to avert the risk in the stock market. Demand for bonds increased, resul ng in low long-term interest rates. As equity prices fell, investors started seeking alterna ve investments. This made the krone market more a rac ve. The krone appreciated at the same me that foreign stock markets and domes c equity prices fell. Bonds and other interestbearing securi es have been of par cular interest. In recent years, the krone has shadowed the difference between Norwegian and foreign short-term rates. This is why the krone has been strong. In addi on, high oil prices have had an influence. The effect of the interest rate differen al has been intensified by condi ons in capital markets. Investors have been favouring carry trades. The interest rate differen al has contributed to a strengthening of the krone. Monetary policy has since been relaxed. Norges Bank has reduced the key interest rate from 7 to 5.5 per cent since 11 December last year. The krone depreciated from mid-January, partly reflec ng expecta ons of lower interest rates. Market par cipants weigh the interest rate differen al between Norway and other countries against the likelihood of a deprecia on of the krone in the future. Cyclical divergence can cause the krone to overshoot its long-term level in the short term. In mid-March, cost compe veness in the manufacturing sector was around 10 per cent weaker than the average over the past 30 years. Historically, following such substan al devia ons, compe veness has always returned to the average fairly rapidly. In the ten years that have passed since the banking and currency crisis in 1992, the Norwegian economy featured a long period of balanced growth. However, towards the end of the upturn, the economy was facing labour shortages, higher wage growth and a sharp increase in household consump on and debt. Interest rates had to be kept high. While the slowdown abroad started two years ago, the Norwegian economy con nued to show a high level of ac vity. This led to a widening of the interest rate differen al against other countries. The main explana on for the wide interest rate differen al is not that interest rates are high in Norway, but that interest rates are at a historic low abroad. Interest rates in the US have not been at such a low level since the 1960s. A further jump in wages in 2002 amplified the imbalances in the economy and fuelled the rise in prices for goods and services produced in Norway. This is why monetary policy in Norway has been ght. The oil market and the interna onal outlook In response to heightened uncertainty and fears of war, tradi onal safe havens for capital, such as the Swiss franc and gold, became increasingly a rac ve this winter. The Swiss franc appreciated a er the events of 11 September 2001 and towards the end of last year. Gold prices moved up sharply a er UN Security Council Resolu on 1441 was adopted on 8 November last year. Oil prices fell markedly a er 11 September 2001, but have since risen. Prices for other raw materials and staples, such as metals, also seem to be holding up, in spite of low ac vity in the world economy. These are symptoms of high uncertainty and stock-building in the face of large global risks. However, prices are vola le. Last week, new op mism led to a decline in some of these prices. It is likely that this vola lity will con nue to reflect percep ons of the developments in Iraq. Oil prices have been high this winter, in spite of subdued economic ac vity in major industrial countries. Several factors have kept oil prices high. Fears of war in Iraq increased the uncertainty surrounding global oil supplies. In addi on, strike among oil workers in Venezuela reduced oil supply. The strike has now ended, but produc on in Venezuela is s ll below pre-strike levels. Commercial stocks of crude oil and refined products were already low when the strike in Venezuela started, especially in the US. The reduced supply of oil reduced stocks further. Combined, these factors exerted considerable upward pressure on oil prices. Since the outbreak of war in Iraq, oil prices have been vola le. Ini ally, prices fell sharply. However, uncertainty and fears of a prolonged war have recently offset some of the ini al fall. The present war in Iraq may cause an immediate reduc on in oil supply of about 10 per cent of OPEC's total produc on, including a likely reduc on in both Iraq and Kuwait. Oil supplies are stretched. The major swing supplier - Saudi Arabia - is probably producing close to capacity. During the Gulf War in 1990-91, the oil price peaked at 36 dollars per barrel in October, and remained high throughout the year. When US and allied forces moved into Kuwait on 16 January 1991, oil prices fell sharply. Strategic oil reserves were released to the market at the same me and pushed down prices. Stocks of crude oil in the US are considerably lower than normal levels. The picture is similar for the OECD as a whole. However, strategic oil reserves are high. In December last year, total strategic oil reserves of OECD countries corresponded to 114 days of import for the net impor ng OECD countries. New increases in oil prices would further dampen global economic ac vity. Major economies such as the US, Germany and France are struggling with stagna on and fears of recession. Substan al tax relief and low interest rates are holding up ac vity in the US. The Japanese economy has been in a defla onary recession for a long period. On the other hand, it may well be that the ailing world economy will exert considerable downward pressures on oil prices when the war in Iraq ends. Over the years, a period of low oil prices has tended to follow a downturn in the world economy. This may happen again, at least when produc on in Iraq is phased into the world oil market. The US has been the driving force in the world economy. The US economy has historically been very resilient. Growth tends to pick up rapidly a er short periods of contrac on. Most likely this will prove to be the case this me as well. A posi ve aspect is that confidence in the financial system has not been impaired. There is some evidence of a recovery in investment. Investment in both the euro area and the UK fell at a slower pace during 2002. Investment rose slightly in the fourth quarter in the US. However, capacity u lisa on in manufacturing remains low in many countries. In the US, produc vity growth and further tax cuts will fuel con nued growth in real disposable income. This may provide scope for moderate growth in consump on. On the other hand, the saving ra o of US households will probably need to rise to achieve more sustained growth. All in all, we s ll expect global growth to rise gradually to a more normal level, although the recovery will come later than previously expected. However, we cannot exclude the possibility of a fairly long period of stagna on in the global economy. Low interest rates in the US and Europe are a reflec on of this risk. The level of investment in the US was high during the expansion, which may have resulted in excess capacity in the business sector. The fall in equity prices is having a nega ve effect on household wealth. In addi on, US household saving is low and low interest rates have induced households to build up debt. The fall in the value of the dollar may make a contribu on, but growth in the business sector is s ll not self-driven and the deprecia on of the dollar is reducing other countries' exports. The impetus from the US economy may be weak for several years ahead. Nor is the rest of the world showing clear signs of an imminent recovery. Japan is dragging down growth in the world economy. The large European economies, in par cular Germany, are stagna ng. Unemployment is high, but the growth poten al appears to be low. Interest rates in the US and Japan have been reduced to such low levels that there is li le room for further s mulus. The monetary policy authori es could use more unorthodox measures. For example, the central bank could purchase massive volumes of long-term bonds - as seen in Japan - or other assets. It is uncertain how effec ve such measures are. Tradi onal fiscal policy instruments may also prove to be ineffec ve when budget deficits are rising sharply. This may fuel expecta ons of future fiscal ghtening and tax increases. If the world economy con nues to stagnate over a longer period, the effects will also spill over to the Norwegian economy. The decline in tradi onal exports will then persist. Sooner or later, the oil market will also feel the effects of the downturn, and oil prices will decline. If the world economy experiences prolonged stagna on, a lower interest rate and a weaker krone will reduce the effects for Norway. On the other hand, any fiscal slippage will contribute to maintaining a strong krone. A stagna ng global economy has changed the domes c infla on outlook in recent months. It does not appear that interest rates in the US and Europe will increase in the near future. They may even be reduced further before the recovery starts. In Norway, the interest rate has also been reduced and the krone has weakened. The infla on target and economic stability The opera onal target of monetary policy as defined by the Norwegian government is infla on of close to 2.5 per cent over me. The infla on target provides economic agents with an anchor for their decisions concerning saving, investment, budgets and wages. The responsibility for implemen ng monetary policy has been delegated to the central bank. This is also the case in other countries. The central bank shall exercise professional judgement within the framework of its mandate. Assessments of economic developments and the basis for interest rate decisions are presented to the public. This makes it possible for others to gain insight into the assump ons and analyses underlying interest rate decisions. Norges Bank sets the interest rate to achieve the infla on target of 2 per cent. The infla on target is broadly in line with the targets of our trading partners. It is also an anchor for developments in our exchange rate. The krone fluctuates. We have open trade with other countries and free capital movements. We do not have the instruments to fine-tune the exchange rate. As long as infla on remains low and stable, any substan al devia ons in the krone over me will have a considerable impact on ac vity in business and industry. As a result, the krone will tend to return towards its long-term mean following any substan al devia ons. Wide cyclical differences and differences in wage forma on between Norway and other countries have always had an impact on the krone and on compe veness. The central bank alone cannot, with the instruments at its disposal, steer the exchange rate. This is especially the case during periods of interna onal turmoil and uncertainty, when exchange rate movements tend to be vola le. The infla on target of 2 per cent was introduced in March 2001. At the same me, new guidelines for fiscal policy were adopted. The fiscal rule s pulates that the central government budget deficit shall over me be equivalent to the expected real return on the Government Petroleum Fund. The rule is robust to varia ons in government revenues and provides a stable framework for economic developments. The fiscal rule has been followed, which in itself makes a considerable contribu on to stability. Wage forma on and unemployment High labour costs and global stagna on are leaving a mark on Norway's interna onally exposed sector. Many enterprises will not be able to sustain ac vity given current market condi ons and cost levels. Labour costs are also squeezing margins in some private service industries. More enterprises are compe ng on interna onal markets. Moreover, even if alloca ons are growing, public en es have limited capacity for increasing employment because wage expenses have risen so sharply. Unemployment has edged up recently. The current unemployment rate of 4 per cent is more or less on a par with unemployment in 1997. It is also 2 percentage points lower than the average in the 1990s. For manufacturing, the effect of weak profitability has not yet come into full evidence. Unemployment is therefore expected to increase somewhat in the period ahead. In spite of the high level of wage growth, infla on is low. Condi ons have allowed for a gradual narrowing of the interest rate differen al between Norway and abroad. How ght monetary policy will be is essen ally con ngent on how fast wage growth is brought down. The infla on targets adopted by Norway and our trading partners imply that total wage growth of about 4 per cent is consistent with li le or no change in business sector compe veness. This is based on the assump on that produc vity growth in Norway is around 2 per cent, or about the same as the average for the past 20 years. Both companies and employees can take as a given that infla on will be 2 per cent over me. This reduces uncertainty and makes it possible for the social partners to disregard brief spells of somewhat lower or somewhat higher infla on. Infla on does not have to be higher than 2 per cent in Norway to achieve growth and high employment. The experience of the 1990s demonstrates this. During that period, unemployment fell and growth was strong. Even with major restructuring and changes in industry structure, infla on was close to 2 per cent. Growth in real wages is now markedly higher than the underlying growth in produc vity. This is why unemployment is rising. Businesses must adjust their workforces to sustain profitability. This leads to a fall in employment, but also con nued opera ons in Norway. The alterna ve is that companies are not able to adjust their workforces quickly enough. If higher costs cannot be passed on to customers, earnings will fall and the wage share rise. This may lead to closures or reloca on of produc on. The wage share in Norwegian manufacturing has increased. The situa on in service industries is more mixed. Import firms have wider margins. We know that employment in some service industries has fallen. This may indicate that many service enterprises have adjusted their workforces. To some extent, higher costs can more easily be passed on to customers. This picture is typical of the final phase of an expansion. A ght labour market and the contest for economic resources lead to a sharp increase in real wages. This results in high growth in household income, consump on and housing investment. The propensity to borrow increases and house prices rise sharply. On the other hand, the business sector faces pressures on profitability, a high cost level and declining investment. Commercial property prices fall. At the same me, corporate restructuring brings growth in employment to a halt. When costs reach a high level, employment starts to fall. The period of expansion has then come to an end. The cost level must be adjusted to restore balance in the labour market. In the manufacturing sector, employment is now declining. In the public sector, where employment growth has been strong the last few years, budgets will only allow a moderate increase in employment in 2003. Overall, employment is projected to fall by per cent in 2003 and remain unchanged in 2004. Labour force par cipa on in Norway is at a record-high level. Consequently, labour force growth may be low in the years ahead. More people may choose to withdraw from the labour market un l the situa on improves. Some may exit the labour market on re rement schemes. Nevertheless, we expect unemployment to rise somewhat, especially in manufacturing. The increase through 2002 primarily reflects a rise in unemployment in the service sector. In the manufacturing sector, unemployment remained stable un l the end of last year, but has increased substan ally in the last few months. More lay-offs and lower confidence point to increased unemployment. However, laxer monetary condi ons may improve the balance in the labour market and prevent a further decline in employment. The economic outlook in Norway The outlook for the Norwegian economy weakened during last autumn and winter. Overall economic policy remained ght because of the strong krone. Reduced interest rates and the deprecia on of the krone since January will s mulate overall demand. Nevertheless, the weak world economy and a high cost level will restrain growth. In 2002, infla on was 2.3 per cent, which is close to the infla on target, but it has been somewhat lower in recent months. This reflects the strong krone we had last year. The rise in prices for domes cally produced goods and services is being influenced by our high wage growth. Wage growth moved up further last year, even in industries where profitability had weakened considerably. Developments over recent years show that monetary policy is effec ve and that infla on can be kept at a low and stable rate, even when growth in labour costs is high. However, if developments in the economy are to be sa sfactory over me, real wage growth must be adapted to underlying produc vity growth. Norwegian industrial leaders have become increasingly pessimis c in recent months. Sluggish developments in some service industries in Norway have persisted for a longer period than previously assumed. Higher wage growth has also reduced demand for labour in the public sector. A sharp increase in petroleum investment could provide posi ve growth impulses to the offshore-related industry. The demand impulses from petroleum investment to the mainland economy may, however, be weaker than has been the case earlier. Imports for construc on and installa ons will pick up substan ally from 2002 to 2003. Due to the high cost level in Norway, a growing number of contracts are also being awarded to foreign companies. At the same me, Norwegian shipyards are increasingly using foreign subcontractors in low-cost countries. This is having an impact on the Norwegian engineering industry. Investment in service sectors has fallen sharply, and is expected to con nue to fall. There is also considerable excess capacity in the commercial building market. Household income growth is expected to slow this year and next, partly as a result of low growth in employment and lower wage growth. The sharp rise in electricity prices has reduced real disposable income. Households' financial posi on is s ll solid. Increased uncertainty in the labour market will nevertheless lead to greater cau on among households. Households' confidence in their own financial situa on and the domes c economy has fallen over the last half year. The interest rate cuts this winter will s mulate household demand. Private consump on may nevertheless move on a weaker path than we assumed last autumn. Growth in mainland GDP is projected to be lower than trend growth, at 1 per cent in 2003. Further ahead, the economic situa on will depend on interna onal developments, household expecta ons, cost levels and monetary condi ons. Despite high wage growth, the year-on-year rise in underlying infla on will most likely range between 1 per cent and 2 per cent un l this summer. Subsequently, infla on will depend on developments in wages, the exchange rate and the interest rate. In our last Infla on Report, in March, we presented two alterna ve paths for the Norwegian economy. In one scenario, the ght monetary policy stance was held unchanged. Infla on then, as shown in this chart, fell below target over the next few years. In the other scenario, monetary policy was relaxed in line with market expecta ons. Infla on then moved up and was higher than the infla on target. Based on this analysis, a gradual easing of monetary policy seemed appropriate. Norges Bank will con nuously assess developments in the global economy, the Norwegian economy and the krone exchange rate, and set the interest rate with a view to achieving the infla on target. Thank you for your a en on. 27. mars 2003 14:00

Prisveksten p importerte konsumvarer har vrt trukket ned av den sterke kronekursen. Men ogs vridning i klesimporten fra hykostland l Asia og st-Europa har bidra . Det nrmeste ret vil den underliggende prisveksten preges av at kronen har vrt sterk. Til tross for hy lnnsvekst vil tolvmnedersveksten i konsumprisene justert for avgi er og uten energivarer (KPI-JAE) med stor sannsynlighet ligge mellom 1 og 2 prosent fram l sommeren. Utviklingen videre vil blant annet avhenge av den konomiske utviklingen ute, eektene av det hye kostnadsnivet for nringslivet, kronekursen og hvordan endringer i kursen slr igjennom p konsumprisene i Norge. I referansebanen som er presentert i inasjonsrapporten, hvor renten holdes p 5 prosent og kronekursen lik gjennomsni et siste mned, ansls inasjonen  holde seg under 2 prosent i hele prognoseperioden. I den alterna ve banen, hvor det er lagt inn pengepoli ske le elser i trd med forventningene hos markedsaktrene, vil det vre utsikter l at inasjonen kommer noe over mlet to r fram i d. P bakgrunn av analysene i inasjonsrapporten sa e Norges Bank ned styringsrenten med 0,5 prosentpoeng l 5,5 prosent p mtet i hovedstyret 5. mars. P pressekonferansen e er mtet u alte visesentralbanksjef Jarle Bergo at "Med en rente p 5,5 prosent ser Norges Bank det som mer sannsynlig at inasjonen p to rs sikt blir lavere enn 2 prosent enn at den blir hyere".
