Title: Global Infrastructures Are Becoming a Reality.What Are the Industry Consequences?
text: Global Infrastructures Are Becoming a Reality.What Are the Industry Consequences? Presenta on by Mr. Jarle Bergo, Deputy Governor of Norges Bank, at the Global Electronic Payments Conference, London, 20-21 January 2004. I would first like to thank our hosts for the invita on to this important conference giving me the opportunity to present some of Norges Bank's experiences in promo ng safe and efficient payment systems. Globalisa on is increasing and rapid, efficient and secure payment systems are more and more in demand. I will par cularly address the major challenges par cipa on in CLS poses to financial infrastructure and liquidity management, and how Norges Bank, in partnership with the industry, has facilitated the inclusion of the Norwegian krone in CLS. Finally, I will make some observa ons on cost developments in the retail payment system in Norway as the use of electronic services has increased.. The introduc on of Con nuous Linked Se lement in autumn 2002 in many ways marked the end of more than two decades' efforts to manage foreign exchange se lement risk in a global context. The establishment of CLS was ini ated and driven forward by the banking industry, although in close coopera on with the central banks of the currencies concerned. It is also the central banks that ul mately approve the par cipa on of their na onal currency in the system. In 1999 Norges Bank's Execu ve Board agreed in principle to allow the Norwegian krone to be se led in CLS. Norges Bank has since then been working together with CLS and the Norwegian banking industry to facilitate such an inclusion, which became a reality in September of last year. The adapta ons to CLS have necessitated changes in the way Norges Bank operates its se lement system to improve liquidity condi ons during the morning period for CLS se lement. Norges Bank has also ghtened the requirements for back-up solu ons in the banks' systems. Through CLS the par cipa ng countries' Real Time Gross Se lement systems are more closely linked. This implies that liquidity problems or lack of opera onal stability in one se lement system can more easily spread to se lement systems in other countries. Despite the liquidity saving mechanisms in CLS, situa ons in which there is a shortage of liquidity vis-a-vis CLS cannot be ruled out. For a currency to be included in CLS, there must be a sufficient number of liquidity providers - banks that are obliged on short no ce to provide liquidity in the currency in ques on if a shortage should arise. CLS recommends that there be at least three liquidity providers in each currency. Norway is a small country with limited liquidity in its currency, but with a rela vely large volume of currency trading. Thus, Norway faces many of the same challenges as our nearest neighbours Denmark and Sweden, not least in respect of liquidity management. Several of the Scandinavian banks also operate in all three Scandinavian countries. The prepara ons to include Norwegian kroner have largely taken place in collabora on with the central banks of Sweden and Denmark and the Scandinavian banking industry. In the Scandinavian countries, as in most countries, banks obtain intraday liquidity by deposi ng securi es, which gives them borrowing rights at the central bank. Norges Bank accepts a broad range of Norwegian and foreign securi es as collateral for borrowing, including. Securi es registered in Clearstream and Euroclear, or in other Scandinavian central securi es depositories. Since the Norwegian central government's financial posi on has generally been favourable, there is a rela vely small volume of government securi es in circula on. This has made it necessary for Norges Bank to accept many different types of securi es to ensure that the banks have sufficient access to intraday liquidity throughout the day. Furthermore Norges Bank sees merit in including a wide range of papers as this increases liquidity and thus the efficiency of the se lement system. However, in order to avoid exposing the central bank to undue risk, an appropriate system for calcula ng the loan value of collateral is required, including se ng haircut levels correctly in rela on to the uncertainty connected with the various securi es pledged. The haircut levels at Norges Bank appear to be high rela ve to those in many other central banks. There are two main reasons for this. First, Norges Bank uses face value when calcula ng the value of the banks' securi es por olios. This means that the real value of the pledged securi es may deviate from the value Norges Bank uses to calculate the bank's borrowing facility. Second, within the constraints of current bankruptcy legisla on, Norges Bank may risk having to wait for up to six months before pledged securi es can be sold, which further increases the risk of a reduc on in the collateral's value. The implementa on of the Collateral Direc ve in Norwegian legisla on will make possible the immediate realisa on of collateral. Furthermore, Norges Bank is in the process of conver ng its system for calcula ng lending value into a system based on the securi es' market value. The new loan collateral system will thus enable the Bank to set a lower haircut level. Norges Bank's es mates show that conver ng the system to one based on market values means that the average haircut can be reduced by almost 50 per cent. This will significantly improve liquidity in Norwegian kroner. The available liquidity in Norges Bank's se lement system and the liquidity needs in Norwegian kroner in CLS vary over me. The chart shows that liquidity in Norges Bank's Se lement System (NBO) is normally more than sufficient to meet liquidity needs in CLS. From October to December 2003, the amount of liquidity available in Norges Bank's Se lement System to the twenty largest banks in Norway typically varied between 60 and 90 billion Norwegian kroner. (One euro is equivalent to around 8,5 Norwegian kroner.) The use of liquidity in CLS is represented by the largest amount on deposit on CLS's account in the course of the day. This amount varied between approximately 1 billion Norwegian kroner and 11 billion Norwegian kroner. Even though there is normally more than enough liquidity in Norges Bank's Se lement System, one can not disregard the possibility of a liquidity shortage situa on in Norway, for instance if the payment of oil tax coincides with a pay-in failure in CLS. A par cular challenge has been to a ract a sufficient number of liquidity providers in Norwegian kroner. In a small market like the Norwegian one, there are few banks with a sufficiently large capital base to be able to take on such a role. At an early stage in the prepara ons for the inclusion of the Scandinavian currencies in CLS, the banking industry called for improvements in the exis ng model for cross-border collateral in Scandinavia, so that banks par cipa ng in se lements in more than one of the Scandinavian countries could be er u lise their liquidity. Some banks set this as a condi on for serving as a liquidity provider in more than one of the Scandinavian currencies. Against this background the central banks of Sweden, Denmark and Norway jointly considered several alterna ves. Since a model was needed that could be implemented in the short term, the Cash Collateral model emerged as the logical choice. In the Scandinavian Cash Pool (SCP), banks use deposits in one of the central banks as collateral for loans in another central bank. Let me illustrate this with an example in which a Danish bank wishes to pledge collateral in Denmark to increase liquidity in its subsidiary in Norway. 1. At the request of the Danish bank, Danmarks Na onalbank reserves a por on of the bank's available liquidity in the Danish Real Time Gross Se lement System, and transfers the deposit in Danish kroner to an account in Danmarks Na onalbank that is pledged in favour of Norges Bank. The account is in the name of the Danish bank. 2. Norges Bank receives a message from Na onalbanken that an amount in Danish kroner has been pledged as security for an increase in drawing rights for the subsidiary in Norway. Norges Bank converts the amount to Norwegian kroner, deducts a five per cent haircut against exchange rate fluctua ons and updates the subsidiary bank's account in the Norwegian Real Time Gross Se lement System with the amount in ques on. 3. The Norwegian subsidiary bank's available liquidity has been increased. The Scandinavian Cash Pool is built on exis ng structures and systems and is based on the individual country's rules and procedures. Communica on between the central banks is automated and is based on exis ng SWIFT standards. This structure ensures that cross-border collateral within the Scandinavian Cash Pool can be pledged in seconds. The Scandinavian Cash Pool may only be used to move intraday liquidity between the Scandinavian countries. Banks are obliged to redeem loans and ensure that deposits in pledged collateral accounts in Norges Bank are released the same day. In the example outlined above this means that: 1. The Norwegian subsidiary no fies Norges Bank that the collateral deposit is to be released. Norges Bank checks that the collateral has not been borrowed against, then reduces the subsidiary bank's drawing rights, adds the haircut and converts the amount in ques on from Norwegian to Danish kroner. 2. Norges Bank no fies Danmarks Na onalbank that the reserved amount can be released. Danmarks Na onalbank releases the amount by transferring from the pledged account to the Danish bank's current account in Danmarks Na onalbank. 3. The reversed liquidity is now available to the Danish bank. As I men oned before, the system is based on each of the Scandinavian countries' own procedures and rules. In Norway, collateral may be pledged and funds borrowed within the scheme from the me Norges Bank's Se lement System opens in the morning un l 3:00 pm. Similar rules apply in Sweden, whereas in Denmark, borrowed or pledged liquidity must be reversed by 1:30 pm. The central banks require same day reversal so that the use of the system does not affect monetary policy. If these deadlines are not met, a penalty is charged, which in Norway is equivalent to about 0.05 per cent of the pledged or borrowed amount. Norges Bank assumes that such a high penalty will give par cipants an incen ve to comply with the rules. Danmarks Na onalbank and Sweden's Riksbank have their own deadlines for reversals and penal es for failure to meet these deadlines. The scheme is open to all banks wishing to par cipate and may be used regardless of whether the need to move liquidity arises in connec on with CLS or banks' obliga ons as liquidity providers. As of today the system is used only between banks belonging to the same group, but the regula ons do not prevent the scheme from being used across banking groups. The costs connected with the development of the Scandinavian Cash Pool have been fully covered by the banks par cipa ng in the scheme. If new banks eventually wish to join the system, the original par cipa ng banks will be reimbursed accordingly. The Scandinavian Cash Pool has been in daily use since the summer of last year. Before the Scandinavian currencies were included in CLS, rela vely small amounts were transferred in this manner. Since the Scandinavian currencies were included in CLS, the volume has grown somewhat. In the period from September to December 2003, on average of the equivalent of some 600 million euro was transferred daily in the Scandinavian Cash Pool. The highest amount transferred in a single day was about 2 billion euro. So far, the Scandinavian Cash Pool has primarily been used to pledge security in Denmark in order to increase liquidity in Norway and Sweden. Chart 1 shows net liquidity flows to Norway through the SCP and pay-ins in Norwegian kroner to CLS. The amount of liquidity transferred through the SCP appear to coincide with the CLS pay-in requirements. Even though the average turnover in the SCP is not that high, we see that the Scandinavian Cash Pool is in regular use and that on some days considerable sums are transferred via this scheme. The Scandinavian Cash Pool is also considered to be an important back-up system. So far, liquidity providers have not been needed in CLS, and the SCP has thus not been put to the test under such circumstances. But if a liquidity crisis should arise, it is reassuring to know that the scheme can be used to transfer liquidity from one country to another in seconds. Cross-border collateral and liquidity management are issues that are drawing more and more a en on interna onally. Along with other European central banks, Bundesbank and Clearstream have devised a scheme for transferring liquidity from other countries for securi es se lement in Germany. The scheme has been opera onal since November 2003. In this model, par cipants make liquidity available for the German market by means of deposits in cash or securi es at their na onal central bank, which submits a cross-border guarantee to the Bundesbank. As in the SCP, liquidity is made available to par cipants in one country based on deposits or pledged securi es in another central bank. However, there are also differences. In the SCP, the transfer of liquidity from one country to another is not related to a specific se lement and the liquidity can flow to and from each of the par cipa ng systems. In March of last year, the US Payment Risk Commi ee (PRC), comprising representa ves of the largest global banks, the report "Managing Payment Liquidity in Global Markets: Risk Issues and Solu ons". The report recommends that the private sector develop new, well-constructed services that over me will enable market players to respond effec vely to ever-increasing demands for intraday liquidity in the global markets. Among the alterna ves listed are crossborder collateral pools. The report also urges central banks to broaden the range of foreign securi es accepted as collateral for intraday liquidity and to facilitate the use of cross-border collateral. The establishment of the Scandinavian Cash Pool is a measure in line with the inten ons underlying the recommenda ons of the PRC report. Let me add that the central banks also considered a common central securi es depository model as an appropriate model for cross-border collateral provision in Scandinavia. This model requires each central bank to set up a depository of securi es in a common central securi es depository, for example, in Clearstream or Euroclear, and to arrange for informa on exchange in real me between the lending central bank and the central securi es depository in ques on. Unlike the Scandinavian Cash Pool, the model also requires agreement among the par cipa ng countries on, among other things, the securi es that may be pledged as collateral at any given me. Nevertheless,these seems to be a preference amongst the Scandinavian banks to move towards a common CSD model. The feasibility of such a model may be assessed in the longer term. It is debatable whether it is within the central bank's responsibili es to assist in the establishment of schemes that may poten ally operate in compe on with private schemes. The report from August 2003, "The Role of Central Bank Money in Payment Systems" from BIS' Forum for central banks, the Commi ee on Payment and Se lement Systems (CPSS), discusses the use of central bank money as part of the underlying issue of the balance between payment services provided by central banks and those provided by commercial banks in the payment system. The report shows that while the objec ves and main principles of central banks in the CPSS have much in common, the implementa on of central bank policies varies widely in this area. Sec on 1 of the Norges Bank Act states that Norges Bank shall " promote an efficient payment system domes cally as well as vis-a-vis other countries ". It is not always easy to define where the industry's responsibility ends and the central bank's begins. Norges Bank considers it important to be always mindful of the balance between allowing the market to "sort things out" on its own and intervening in order to facilitate the market's ability to func on, as well as to periodically review the central bank's own role in the payment system. In our experience, the Scandinavian Cash Pool is a very secure, efficient and cost efficient scheme for moving liquidity across na onal borders, thus expanding Scandinavian banks' access to intraday liquidity. In our opinion, the establishment of the Scandinavian Cash Pool is also a good example of a successful collabora on and a balanced division of responsibility between the central banks and the industry. Returning to the CLS I find this an excellent example of how banks have jointly developed a global infrastructure, how central banks have coordinated their oversight of this infrastructure and how central banks and banks have responded to the challenges CLS poses to se lement systems in the par cipa ng currencies. CLS has reduced risk and contributed to improving the efficiency of interna onal clearing and se lement ac vi es. The efficient payment services of the future will require the development of infrastructure across na onal borders in many areas, involving substan al investment. It is es mated that payment services in industrialised countries account for between 1 and 3 per cent of GDP. A more efficient organisa on of payment services may thus yield considerable savings, freeing up resources for other purposes. Norges Bank has conducted surveys of banks' prices and costs for payment services for several years1. The reason I would like to take this opportunity to present some of the findings of these surveys is not that Norway has a unique payments system. Nor can we draw any conclusions about the general cost level connected with payment services in Norway compared with other countries. What the findings of our surveys may help to illustrate, however, is the poten al cost savings that may be achieved with the increased use of electronic services within an infrastructure that enables par cipants to u lise economies of scale. And prices reflec ng the costs of the different services appear to be an important instrument in bringing this about. Norway, like most countries, has seen a profound change in the public's payment habits in recent years. This is primarily reflected in the increased use of electronic services and a decline in the use of manual, paper-based services. This development has reduced the banks' costs and has been a key contributor to the produc vity gains recorded by the financial services industry which were quite impressive in the 90's. Norges Bank conducted surveys of the costs incurred by banks providing payment services in 1988, 1994 and 2001. Direct as well as indirect costs were included. The most recent survey covered seven banks: two large banks and five smaller ones. Together these represented 38 per cent of the volume of payment service transac ons in Norway. During the period for which we have data, the number of transac ons has risen sharply, while total costs have remained fairly stable. Since 1988, unit costs have fallen by over sixty per cent measured in constant prices. In 2001 the average unit cost, excluding cash withdrawals over the counter, was approximately five kroner. In recent years, banks have increased their direct pricing so that the degree of cost coverage has increased substan ally from 1988 to 2001. In 2001, cost recovery through direct prices had risen to 70 per cent. How has this affected the prices that consumers are charged? The overall picture is one of a rather sharp rise in prices for paper-based services, whereas the price of electronic services has remained stable at a much lower level (the scales of the two charts are very different). Despite the rise in prices for paper-based services, the increased use of electronic services has reduced the weighted average price per transac on since 1994. We believe that a key contributor to this development is that increased prices be er reflec ng the high costs of manual services have influenced customers' choices in the direc on of more costeffec ve electronic services. For most services, the prices customers are charged are lower than the banks' unit costs. Unit costs apparently remain high for one of the services that is currently growing the fastest, bill payment over the Internet. In 2001, the prices customers were charged covered less than a quarter of the costs reported by banks for providing this service. It appears that the banks are pricing this service on the basis of a long-term strategy to induce customers to use new and more efficient payment instruments by offering low prices in the introductory phase. Even though prices in the short term do not therefore reflect the rela ve costs of providing the service, we expect that this will contribute to increased efficiency in the payment system because economies of scale are exploited at an earlier stage. Since 2001 interest payments have increased drama cally, according to anecdotal evidence. As Norges Bank sees it, the most important factors for achieving a more efficient payment system in Norway have been: an infrastructure that facilitates economies of scale, which in Norway has meant a high degree of coordinated solu ons, prices that reflect the costs of providing the services, and effec ve compe on among service providers. We believe that this has meant gains for banks, consumers and business and industry, as well as for society as a whole. What has been the central bank's contribu on to this? Most importantly I think by consistently suppor ng the banking industry in their efforts to price services correctly, o en in the face of popular protest. Concluding remarks Globalisa on and technological change will increasingly affect how central banks carry out the tasks related to promo ng financial stability and efficient payment systems. With CLS and the way the central banks and the banking community have responded to the new challenges that have arisen as a result, I am confident that we will con nue to work together to reach solu ons that improve services and reduce risks in the payment system. We all have a common goal: a more efficient and secure payment system. Thank you for your a en on. Footnotes 1See for further details 21. januar 2004 14:00

Title: The conduct of monetary policy
text: The implementation of monetary policy Speech by Governor Svein Gjedrem of Norges Bank, 26 March 2004 Subject to changes during the performance. The is based on Norges Bank's report and accounts in 2003 and on several s. The most important contribution monetary policy can make to sound economic developments in the long term is low and stable inflation. In the shorter and medium term, monetary policy can also contribute to smoothing fluctuations in production and demand. We can choose our own inflation target above d. Inflation may be low and stable even if inflation abroad should be high or very low. The operatic target set by the Government for monetary policy is inflation of close to 21/2 per cent. Norges Bank has assumed that the objective is symmetrical - it is just as important to avoid too low as too high inflation. The inflation target provides economic agents with an anchor for expectations of higher inflation. This provides a point of contention for choices about savings, investments, bidding and wages. The inflation target anchors long-range inflation expectations. Norges Bank has assumed that inflation targeting shall be flexible. Weight is given to both variability in output and employment and inflation when the interest rate is viewed. Flexible inflation targeting bridges the long-term task of monetary policy, which is to keep inflation in check, and the stabilisation task. The inflation target is a limit and not an obstacle to monetary policy contributing to smoothing fluctuations in output. Normally, Norges Bank will view the interest rate with a view to inflation being 21/2 per cent two years ahead in d. There are two reasons in that: On the one hand, this provides a reasonable balance between stabilising inflation and, on the other hand, smoothing developments in output and employment. Interest rate changes affect inflation with a dse erslep. In general, it would have been possible to achieve the inflation target in the shorter term than two years by changing the interest rate more quickly and more strongly. This could also have a more impact on production and employment. The choice of a horizon longer than two years may result in a persistent deviation from the inflation target. In the interest rate period, the entire path for inflation and the real economy ahead will be included in the assessments. For example, in situations where the central bank's forecasts suggest that inflation is equal to the target two years ahead, but there are considerable available resources, it may be appropriate to raise money policy so that inflation projections can overshoot the target somewhat to address imbalances in the real economy. We have also expressed hope that this may have an impact on the assessments of the ds horizon if growth in the overall credibility should run wild and equity prices, property and house prices were to be scrapped. In cases where there is a risk that inflation may deviate considerably from the target over a longer period d, or when strong turbulence in financial markets or a negotiation-driven cost shock indicate that the monetary policy is in jeopardy, it may be rich to change the interest rate rapidly and markedly. With the inflation target in financial markets, Norges Bank has a greater opportunity through monetary policy than otherwise l also to safeguard the consideration of stability in output and employment. Similarly, the opportunities will increase as the inflation target is incorporated as an anchor for wage formation. Assessment of monetary policy In 2003, the interest rate was reduced by 4.25 percentage points. The sight deposit rate fell to 2.25 per cent in December. The cut in the interest rate since December 2002 has contributed to a weakening of the krone. Measured by an index of 44 import countries (I44), the krone depreciated through 2003 by almost 11 per cent from its strongest level in January of that year. In the annual report, we give an assessment of the implementation of monetary policy by answering the following questions: Was inflation in 2003 close to the target of 21/2 per cent? What was the background for any deviations from the target? To what extent has monetary policy strengthened the outlook l that inflation two years ahead in d comes close to the inflation target? Has monetary policy contributed to stability in production and employment? Has monetary policy in 2003 understify a lliten l that forward inflation will be 21/2 per cent? Was monetary policy in 2003 predictable for financial market participants? Assessment of developments in inflation and output In the years 1998-2002, the Norwegian economy was characterised by labour shortages and significantly higher growth in labour costs than among trading partners. 2002 was the fifth consecutive year of very high annual growth. The wage gap was considerably higher than above d's, which would be consistent with the inflation target and with normal growth in manufacturing. The wages were very different for different groups. This is why Norges Bank's view is that there is a high risk of new wage-wage spirals. Several rounds of such strong wage increases could lead to significant declines in production and employment. The monetary policy was therefore tightened l through an interest rate increase in 2002 together as the krone remained strong. In the e-year horizon, the strong krone would pull the price swing below 21/2 per cent, but you are the wildest effect of strong wage growth. Monetary policy was expected to contribute gradually to curbing pressures in the domestic economy. It was thus expected and wanted inflation to be low in 2003. In the Inflation Report in October 2002, the price glg in summer 2003 was estimated to fall to 13/4 per cent. Even in the 1/2 - 1 year horizon, price developments are uncertain. There was a possibility that inflation could fall even lower than projected and more than one percentage point below the inflation target. Nevertheless, the discrepancy between un all and forecast was unusually large. Consumer price inflation in Norway slowed considerably through 2003. Underlying price inflation (as measured by the CPI-ATE) rose by 1.1 per cent from 2002 in 2003. As of May 2003, the year-to-year growth in the CPI-ATE has been more than one percentage point below the target. The year-to-year growth fell to -0.1 per cent in February 2004. The large discrepancy between the U.S. economy and forecasts is due to the economy being exposed to major unexpected disturbances. A stronger krone through 2002 contributed to low prices for imported goods. A major reason for the strong krone was developments abroad. Growth in the world economy in 2003 took a different direction and was considerably weaker than Norges Bank and other observers had expected. Weak developments in the global economy led to lower interest rates abroad and an increased interest rate differential between Norway and abroad. Among other things, nega ve events such as the accounting scandals at large US companies, fears of terrorism and war in Iraq and the spread of SARS disease contributed to weak growth and low price growth in other countries. Developments in international equity markets and the risk of higher oil prices also contributed to strengthening the krone. Sam dig has changed trading patterns and global economic conditions have resulted in an unexpectedly sharp fall in import prices, even when measured by what Norwegian importers pay in foreign currency. The change in the trading pattern contributes in particular to a fall in prices for clothing, shoes and sound and video equipment. For audio and video equipment, rapid technological progress is also contributing to the fall in prices. In Norway, competition in retail trade, transport and other services is likely to intensify in recent years. Increased competition initially affects profit margins in the first place. But businesses will respond by reducing costs. This will partly take place in your own business. In llegg there will be a requirement for lower prices and to effek hands also at subcontractors. Intensified competition therefore normally triggers higher growth in manufacturing output in the economy. The low price range may therefore be partly equivalent to a lie in manufacturing. Under flexible inflation targeting, monetary policy shall contribute to stability both in inflation and in output. The Norwegian economy has landed softly in the long period of strong cost increases in Norway and weak global economic growth. The output gap is a measure of the difference between the factual level of output in the economy and the level of output that is consistent with stable inflation above d. The output gap is not directly observable, but needs to be narrowed. A simple method is to measure the difference between the factual production and the production capacity. It is common to assume that production capacity is trending above d because the workforce is growing and because manufacturing is increasing. The trend may vary because the growth in the labour force varies. New technology and new forms of organisation can also affect the growth of manufacturing. Developments in the output gap provide a starting point for assessing cyclical developments and can shed light on domestic price and cost pressures in the economy. The output gap, as calculated by Norges Bank, shows that capacity growth has narrowed from a high level and is now in line with the level in the years 1995-1997, before cost inflation accelerated. The output gap was only narrow in 2003. Wage growth is a direct indicator of how the social partners assess employment and the scarcity of work crashes . Above d, real wage growth must correspond to manufacturing growth. If real wage growth is higher than underlying growth in manufacturing, corporate profitability will deteriorate. The wage gap is defined as the difference between wage growth in Norway and wage growth above d is consistent with stable economic developments. From 1990 to 1995, when unemployment was high in Norway and faecal output was below production capacity, wage growth in the Norway was lower than among trading partners. From 1997, the wage gap becomes posi vt. During this period, resource renewal increased markedly. Against cunning one of the periods, the wage gap narrows in line with the fact that resource renewal is approaching a more durable level. There appears to be a close relationship between the wage gap and the capacity gap in the economy as Norges Bank measures it with the output gap. Unemployment has increased somewhat in 2002 and 2003, but is nevertheless considerably lower than at the beginning of the 1990s and is now approximately on a par with the 1990s, measured by the number of registered unemployed and at the LFS. The number of registered unemployed and persons on the roof is lower than in the 1990s. Wage growth in the 1990s was 41/2 per cent, while consumer price inflation was 21/2 per cent, in line with the current inflation target. Equilibrium unemployment is an impediment to the level of unemployment that results in wage growth consistent with stable and sustained economic developments. Equilibrium unemployment may therefore change over d, and will depend, among other things, on the ability to l'm cirizing the labour market and wage formation. We have no firm opinion on what the level of equilibrium unemployment is at any point. The frequency of employment, i.e. employment as a share of the working age population, has shown a trend since the 1970s. This is primarily due to increased occupational participation among women. The frequency often varies with the cyclical cycle and is higher than normal during a boom. The frequency of employment was above a linear trend from 1996 to 2003. Kredi growth is an indicator of the public's demand that, in an equilibrium, may be assumed to grow approximately in line with nominal GDP. Underlying growth in the public's credibility from domestic sources (C2) has fallen steadily from 9 per cent at the beginning of 2003, to 7.1 per cent at the end of the year. The year-to-year growth in the public's total bridge and sea transport (K3 Mainland Norway) fell from 7.3 per cent in December 2002 to 5.2 per cent in late December 2003. Developments in overall creed growth therefore do not indicate strong pressure. Nevertheless, developments in credi give ambiguous signals. Household borrowing growth has been strong, while the bedries have reduced their debt. Has monetary policy strengthened the outlook for inflation two years ahead in d near the inflation target? The cash rate is aimed at bringing inflation up to the target of 21/2 per cent. In the period ahead, underlying inflation will nevertheless be lower than the inflation target. The period of a strong krone exchange rate in 2002 and 2003 will quickly contribute to low inflation in imported goods and services. There's a quick outlook for low-cost outdoor prices. Wages in the wage settlement in 2003 were lower than Norges Bank had estimated. The break with the particularly high wage growth in 1998-2002 must be seen on the basis of the tightening of monetary policy in 2002 and weak developments in the global economy. It is also likely to have a significant impact on the expensive wage settlement in 2002, which had a strong nega veer on the economy and the public sector, and that these experiences were drawn on in the wage settlement in 2003. In many service industries, the possibility of overturning higher labour costs on prices has probably been more limited than before. Consumer price inflation was expected to be well below the target in 2003, but as discussed, the year-to-year rise in inflation came below 1 per cent in the summer of 2003. Without significant easing of monetary policy, inflation could be too low for too long. This, in turn, could lead to expectations of very low inflation. In such a situation, it may also become more demanding to increase the ak viteten in the economy. The Executive Board therefore considered it rich to reduce the interest rate substantially. Nevertheless, prices fell by 0.4 per cent in December 2003 and -0.1 per cent in February 2004. The 2003 monetary policy easing also reflected that the impact of the interest rate cut appeared to be less than expected . The effect on the exchange rate was dampened by low interest rates or a decline in other countries. In assessing the inflation outlook, emphasis must be placed on the fact that low inflation can mainly be attributed to developments in prices for imported consumer goods and Norwegian-produced goods sold in competition with foreign goods. The rise in prices for other domestically produced goods and services has remained high to a greater extent. If the fall in prices for imported consumer goods in particular can be attributed to the strong krone exchange rate in 2002 and then in 2003, this suggests that much of the fall in inflation will be funds. On some imported consumer goods, we have seen that there is a downward trend in prices as a result of changes in the trading pattern. They will be able to contribute quickly to low inflation in the period ahead. As mentioned, increased competition has also increased production and reduced the price of domestically produced goods and services. In Inflation Report 1/04 presented on 11 March 2004, the inflation outlook was assessed. On the assumption that the interest rate and the exchange rate will develop as expected in the futures market, the projections in the Inflation Report indicate that the price move will be close to the inflation target within two years. Inflation will pick up considerably during the e-year. In the short term, the effect will be particularly due to the gradual depletion of the appreciation. The krone has now returned, so that the effect of the appreciation can be reversed. In the somewhat longer term, the reductions in the interest rate will also contribute to stronger demand in the Norway. Overall, the 2003 monetary policy easing could make a significant contribution to bringing inflation back In the target. Sam dig expects Norges Bank's global interest rate to rise and prices abroad to pick up somewhat. Trust and predictability With the inflation target, monetary policy can to a greater extent smooth fluctuations in the economy. Expectations concerning inflation in the Norway ahead give an indication of whether the inflation target is being achieved. The survey from TNS Gallup from the first quarter of 2004 shows that expected inflation in two years is generally just below the inflation target of 21/2 per cent. Analysts, academics and employers' organisations have revised down their inflation expectations somewhat in two years over the past year. These groups' expectations concerning inflation five years ahead in d have remained stable around the inflation target. Inflation expectations in employee organisations appear l to swing quite a bit from one survey l the next. Consensus Forecasts Inc. provides a monthly overview of various incentives' forecasts for consumer price inflation in Norway. The estimates are given for two years to come. In the survey in February, the estimate for 2004 and 2005 was 1.2 per cent and 2.3 per cent respectively. The low estimate for 2004 must be viewed in connection with the path for electricity prices. Twice a year, in October and April, estimates with a longer ds horizon are published. Estimates released in October 2003 showed that price inflation was expected to pick up. In both the 5- and 10-year horizons, the price range was estimated at 2.4 per cent. They were 0.1 per cent lower than in October 2002. The difference between forward rates in Norway and Germany may also give an indication of developments in price expectations in Norway. The inflation target for Norway may be somewhat higher than in the euro area.1 In the euro area, the longitudinal expectations are l inflation barely below 2 per cent.2 With the inflation target, forward rates in Norway should therefore be somewhat higher than in Germany. The differences between forward rates also reflect premiums for differences in liquidity in the Norwegian and German markets. The difference between Norwegian and German long-term interest rates was just under 1 percentage point in 2002 and fell somewhat in 2003. Overall, pricing in the fixed income market so far indicates that the inflation target will be achieved. Based on information from expectations surveys and longitudinal interest rates, there are signs that inflation is expected to be lower than 21/2 per cent in the coming year. Expectations further ahead in d do not appear to deviate substantially from the inflation target. The easing of monetary policy this year has contributed to the fact that expectations of a rise in inflation around the inflation target have remained stable. The impact on Norwegian market interest rates was substantial at monetary policy meetings in 2002 compared with other countries with inflation targeting. In 2003, the impact was considerably lower. The decisions at monetary policy meetings were therefore somewhat more predictable for market participants. Conclusion It is not only Norway who are experiencing a sharp fall in inflation. In Sweden, underlying inflation has fallen 0.1 per cent in recent months. Excluding energy prices, underlying prices are 0.7 per cent in Sweden. Inflation is also falling in Finland and Denmark. A fall in prices for imported goods is pushing down prices, but high product growth may also have contributed . Inflation has also slowed in the US and the euro area, but in the euro area the impact is less pronounced than in Scandinavia. Cyclical developments in the Norwegian economy have reversed, and the economy has landed softly in the long period of sharp cost increases in Norway and weak growth abroad. Production is back on trend. Employment is back on trend. Unemployment is the same as in 1996 and equal through the 1990s. Wage growth is at a level consistent with stable competitiveness above d. Overall creed growth is balanced. The costs of wages between Norway and our trading partners are now lacy at a long time. The nominal krone exchange rate measured by I-44 is in line with that of the 1990s. The interest rate level is in line with the level among our trading partners. Inflation expectations are approximately equal to the inflation target. This is an equilibrium in the Norwegian economy right now. But inflation is low. E are the effects of the strong krone in 2002. Sam dig contributes to a change in trading patterns and cyclical developments abroad in the fall in import prices, also when measured by what Norwegian importers pay in foreign currency. In Norway, tighter competition appears to be resulting in high product growth. This probably contributes to low inflation. In other years, inflation is expected to pick up substantially during the year. In the short term, the effect will be particularly good in that the appreciation is gradually emptied out. In the somewhat longer term, the interest rate reductions will also contribute to stronger demand in the Norway. But the Norwegian economy is facing several uncertain terms. It may take d before interest rates abroad are substantially increased. We have found that the krone is heavily influenced by developments in the difference between interest rates abroad and at home, and this must be taken into account in our interest rate. But the themes of foreign exchange markets can ski e. The effect on the exchange rate of changes in the interest rate may be dampened. House prices and developments in households influence consumption and housing investment. We seek to take these indirect effects into account when we see the interest rate level. Rising asset prices and building up debt may be a risk to economic stability. But now only households have strong debt growth. Enterprises borrow little. House prices seem to be recovering. But office space prices are stable. We have limited scope l to slow down the structural changes that occur when households increase their debt over several years to invest in housing and other properties and aquily. The interest rate can be used to reduce the demand for loans. Today , with low interest rates abroad and a close relationship between our interest rate and the krone, a tighter monetary policy would curb credit demand primarily because jobs would become more uncertain. The fall in the value of the krone over the past year has strengthened Norwegian business and industry. But the business sector is bearing the brunt of the effects of a sharp rise in labour costs over several years. Labour costs measured in a common currency are in line with the level in 1990, but about per cent higher than in the mid-1990s. There has been a sell-off in the competitive e-business sector. Those who are now in a dare may be in better condition to carry the high level of pay. Nevertheless, the costs can hamper accompaniment and employment ng. Thank you for listening. Footnotes 1 The Norwegian inflation target is tied to the consumer price index, while the ECB follows the harmonised consumer price index (HICP). On Norwegian data, the harmonised index has been somewhat lower than the consumer price index. 2 Se ECBs Monthly Bulle n, january 2004. 26 March 2004 14:00

Pengepoli kken ble derfor strammet l gjennom en rentekning i 2002 sam dig som kronen holdt seg sterk. P e rs sikt ville den sterke kronen trekke priss gningen under 2 prosent, men dere er ville virkningene av den sterke lnnsveksten veie tyngst. Det var ventet at pengepoli kken kunne bidra l gradvis  dempe presset i den innenlandske konomien. Det var sledes ventet og villet at inasjonen ville bli lav i 2003. I inasjonsrapporten i oktober i 2002 var priss gningen sommeren 2003 ansl  falle ned l 1 prosent. Selv p  - 1 rs sikt er det usikkerhet i prisutviklingen. I det l det en mulighet for at prisveksten kunne komme enda lavere enn ansl og mer enn e prosentpoeng under inasjonsmlet. Avviket mellom u all og prognose ble likevel uvanlig stort. Veksten i konsumprisene i Norge avtok vesentlig gjennom 2003. Den underliggende priss gningen (mlt ved KPI-JAE) steg med 1,1 prosent fra 2002 l 2003. Fra og med mai 2003 har tolvmnedersveksten i KPI-JAE vrt mer enn e prosentpoeng under mlet. Tolvmnedersveksten falt l -0,1 prosent i februar 2004. Det store avviket mellom u all og prognoser har sammenheng med at konomien ble utsa for store uventede forstyrrelser. Sterkere krone gjennom 2002 bidro l lav priss gning p importerte varer. En vik g rsak l den sterke kronen var utviklingen ute. Veksten i verdenskonomien i 2003 tok en annen retning og ble vesentlig svakere enn det Norges Bank og andre observatrer hadde ventet. Svak utvikling i internasjonal konomi frte l lavere rente ute og kt rentedieranse mellom Norge og utlandet. Blant annet nega ve hendelser som regnskapsskandalene i store amerikanske selskaper, frykt for terror og krig i Irak og spredning av SARS-sykdommen bidro l svak vekst og lav priss gning i andre land. Utviklingen i de internasjonale aksjemarkedene og risiko for kte oljepriser bidro ogs l  styrke kronen. Sam dig har endret handelsmnster og konjunkturene ute gi et uventet sterkt fall i importprisene, ogs nr de mles ved det norske importrer betaler i utenlandsk valuta. Endringen i handelsmnsteret bidrar srlig l at prisene p klr, sko og lyd- og bildeutstyr har falt kra ig. For lyd- og bildeutstyr bidrar ogs rask teknologisk fremgang l fallet i prisene. I Norge er trolig konkurransen i varehandel, transport og annen tjenestey ng bli skjerpet de senere rene. kt konkurranse rammer i frste omgang fortjenestemarginene i bedri ene. Men virksomhetene vil svare med  redusere kostnadene. Det vil dels skje i egen virksomhet. I llegg blir det s lt krav om lavere priser og om  eek visere ogs hos underleverandrer. Skjerpet konkurranse utlser derfor normalt kt vekst i produk viteten i konomien. Den lave priss gningen kan derfor dels ha si motstykke i et l i produk viteten. Under eksibel inasjonsstyring skal pengepoli kken bidra l stabilitet bde i inasjon og i produksjon. Norsk konomi har landet mykt e er den lange perioden med sterk kostnadskning i Norge og svak ak vitet ute. Produksjonsgapet er et ml p forskjellen mellom det fak ske nivet p produksjonen i konomien og det nivet p produksjonen som er forenlig med stabil inasjon over d. Produksjonsgapet er ikke direkte observerbart, men m es meres. En enkel metode er  mle forskjellen mellom den fak ske produksjonen og produksjonskapasiteten. Det er vanlig  legge l grunn at produksjonskapasiteten s ger trendmessig over d fordi arbeidsstyrken vokser og fordi produk viteten ker. Trenden kan variere fordi veksten i arbeidsstyrken varierer. Ny teknologi og nye organisasjonsformer kan ogs pvirke veksten i produk viteten. Utviklingen i produksjonsgapet gir et utgangspunkt for  vurdere konjunkturene og kan belyse det innenlandske pris- og kostnadspresset i konomien. Produksjonsgapet, slik Norges Bank beregner det, viser at kapasitetsutny elsen har avta fra et hyt niv og n er p linje med nivet i rene 1995-1997, fr kostnadsveksten ltok. Produksjonsgapet var bare svakt nega vt i 2003. Lnnsveksten er en direkte indikator p hvordan partene i arbeidslivet vurderer sysselse ngen og knappheten p arbeidskra . Over d m reallnnsveksten samsvare med produk vitetsveksten. Er reallnnsveksten hyere enn den underliggende veksten i produk viteten, vil lnnsomheten i nringslivet svekkes. Lnnsgapet er denert som forskjellen mellom lnnsveksten i Norge og en lnnsvekst som over d er forenlig med en stabil konomisk utvikling. Fra 1990 l 1995 da ledigheten var rela vt hy i Norge og den fak ske produksjonen l under produksjonskapasiteten, var lnnsveksten i Norge lavere enn hos handelspartnerne. Fra 1997 blir lnnsgapet posi vt. I denne perioden kte ressursutny ngen markert. Mot slu en av perioden avtar lnnsgapet i trd med at ressursutny ngen nrmer seg et mer oppre holdbart niv. Det synes  vre en nr sammenheng mellom de e lnnsgapet og kapasitetsutny elsen i konomien slik Norges Bank mler den med produksjonsgapet. Arbeidsledigheten har kt noe i 2002 og 2003, men er likevel vesentlig lavere enn p begynnelsen av 1990-tallet og er n om lag p niv med gjennomsni et for 1990-tallet mlt ved antallet registrert ledige og ved AKU. Antallet registrerte ledige og personer p ltak er lavere enn gjennomsni et p 1990-tallet. Lnnsveksten p 1990-tallet var i gjennomsni 4 prosent, mens konsumprisveksten i gjennomsni var 2 prosent, p linje med det som n er inasjonsmlet. Likevektsledigheten er et u rykk for det nivet p arbeidsledigheten som gir en lnnsvekst som er forenlig med en stabil og oppre holdbar konomisk utvikling. Likevektsledigheten kan derfor endre seg over d, og vil avhenge blant annet av evnen l oms llinger i arbeidsmarkedet og av lnnsdannelsen. Vi har ingen fast oppfatning om hva nivet p likevektsledigheten er p ethvert dspunkt. Sysselse ngsfrekvensen, det vil si sysselse ngen som andel av befolkningen i arbeidsdyk g alder, har vist en s gende trend helt siden dlig p 1970 tallet. Det har frst og fremst sammenheng med kt yrkesdeltaking blant kvinner. Frekvensen varierer gjerne med konjunktursykelen og er hyere enn normalt i en hykonjunktur. Sysselse ngsfrekvensen l over en liner trend fra 1996 fram l 2003. Kredi veksten er en indikator p publikums e ersprsel som i en likevekt kanskje kan antas  vokse om lag i takt med nominelt BNP. Dersom vi tar utgangspunkt i at BNP for fastlandskonomien vokser trendmessig med opp mot 2 prosent reelt og med en priss gning lik inasjonsmlet, kan kredi veksten vre rundt 5 prosent. Den underliggende veksten i publikums kredi fra innenlandske kilder (K2) har falt jevnt fra 9 prosent ved inngangen l 2003, l 7,1 prosent ved utgangen av ret. Tolvmnedersveksten i publikums samlede bru ogjeld unnta oljevirksomhet og utenriks sjfart (K3 Fastlands-Norge) falt fra 7,3 prosent i desember 2002 l 5,2 pro-sent i desember 2003. Utviklingen i den samlete kredi veksten tyder derfor ikke p sterkt press. Utviklingen i kredi en gir likevel tvetydige signaler. Husholdningenes lnevekst har vrt sterk, mens bedri ene har bygget ned sin gjeld. Har pengepoli kken i 2003 styrket utsiktene l at inasjonen to r fram i d kommer nr inasjonsmlet? Le elsene i pengepoli kken har ta sikte p  bringe inasjonen opp mot mlet p 2 prosent. I en periode fremover vil den underliggende prisveksten likevel vre lavere enn inasjonsmlet. Perioden med sterk kronekurs i 2002 og dlig i 2003 vil fortsa bidra l lav prisvekst p importerte varer og tjenester. Det er fortsa utsikter l lav priss gning ute. Lnns lleggene i lnnsoppgjret i 2003 ble lavere enn det Norges Bank hadde ansl . Bruddet med den srnorske hye lnnsveksten i 1998-2002 m ses p bakgrunn av lstrammingen i pengepoli kken i 2002 og svak utvikling i internasjonal konomi. Det har trolig ogs ha vesentlig betydning at det dyre lnnsoppgjret i 2002 kk sterke nega ve virkninger p konomien og ak viteten i oentlige virksomheter og at det ble trukket p disse erfaringene i lnnsoppgjret i 2003. I mange tjenesteytende nringer har muligheten for  velte kte lnnskostnader over p priser trolig vrt mer begrenset enn fr. Konsumprisveksten var ventet  ligge godt under mlet i 2003, men som omtalt dligere, kom tolvmnedersveksten i inasjonen under 1 prosent sommeren 2003. Uten vesentlige le elser i pengepoli kken ville inasjonen kunne bli for lav for lenge. Det ville i sin tur kunne lede l forventninger om fortsa svrt lav inasjon. I en slik situasjon kan det ogs bli mer krevende  ke ak viteten i konomien. Hovedstyret vurderte det derfor som rik g  redusere renten vesentlig. Likevel falt priss gningen y erligere l 0,4 prosent i desember 2003 og -0,1 prosent i februar 2004. Le elsene i pengepoli kken gjennom 2003 gjenspeilte ogs at virkningen av reduksjonen i renten syntes  bli mindre enn anta . Virkningen p valutakursen ble dempet av at rentene ble holdt lave eller sa ned i andre land. I vurderingen av inasjonsutsiktene m det legges vekt p at den lave prisveksten i hovedsak kan lskrives utviklingen i prisene p importerte konsumvarer og norsk-produserte varer som selges i konkurranse med utenlandske varer. Veksten i prisene p andre norskproduserte varer og tjenester har i strre grad holdt seg oppe. Dersom prisfallet p importerte konsumvarer srlig kan lskrives den sterke kronekursen i 2002 og dlig i 2003, trekker det i retning av at mye av fallet i prisveksten vil vre midler dig. P enkelte importerte konsumvarer har vi imidler d se at det er en nedadgende trend i prisene som flge av endringer i handelsmnsteret. De e vil kunne fortse e  bidra l lav prisvekst fremover. Som nevnt har kt konkurranse ogs kt produk viteten og redusert priss gningen p norskproduserte varer og tjenester. I Inasjonsrapport 1/04 som ble lagt fram den 11. mars 2004, ble utsiktene for inasjonen vurdert. Med en forutsetning om at renten og valutakursen utvikler seg som forventet i terminmarkedet, tyder anslagene i inasjonsrapporten p at priss gningen kommer nr inasjonsmlet innen to r. Inasjonen vil ta seg vesentlig opp i lpet av de e ret. P kort sikt vil virkningen srlig komme ved at virkningen av appresieringen gradvis tmmes ut. Kronen har n vendt lbake, slik at virkningen av appresieringen kan bli reversert. P noe lengre sikt vil reduksjonene i renten ogs bidra gjennom sterkere e ersprsel i Norge. Samlet se kan le elsene i pengepoli kken i 2003 gi et vesentlig bidrag l  bringe inasjonen lbake l mlet. Sam dig venter Norges Bank at ak viteten internasjonalt fortse er  ke, og at priss gningen ute tar seg noe opp. Tillit og forutsigbarhet Med llit l inasjonsmlet kan pengepoli kken i strre grad jevne ut svingninger i konomien. Forventninger om prisveksten i Norge fremover gir en indikasjon p om det er llit l at inasjonsmlet ns. Sprreunderskelsen fra TNS Gallup fra 1. kvartal i 2004 viser at forventet inasjon om to r gjennomgende er i underkant av inasjonsmlet p 2 prosent. Analy kere, akademikere og arbeidsgiverorganisasjonene har gjennom det siste ret nedjustert sine forventninger noe om inasjonen om to r. Disse gruppenes forventninger om inasjonen fem r fram i d har imidler d ligget stabilt rundt inasjonsmlet. Inasjonsforventningene l arbeidstakerorganisasjonene ser ut l  svinge noks mye fra en underskelse l den neste. Consensus Forecasts Inc. gir en mnedlig oversikt over ulike ins tusjoners prognoser for konsumprisveksten i Norge. Anslagene gis for inn l to r fremover. I underskelsen i februar var det gjennomsni lige anslaget for 2004 og 2005 p henholdsvis 1,2 prosent og 2,3 prosent. Det lave anslaget for 2004 m ses i sammenheng med forlpet for strmprisene. To ganger i ret, i oktober og april, publiseres anslag med lengre dshorisont. Anslagene som ble gi i oktober 2003, viste at priss gningen var forventet  ta seg opp. Bde p 5- og 10-rs sikt var priss gningen ansl l 2,4 prosent. De e var 0,1 prosent lavere enn i oktober 2002. Dieransen mellom terminrentene i Norge og Tyskland kan ogs gi en indikasjon p utviklingen i prisforventningene i Norge. Inasjonsmlet for Norge kan vre noe hyere enn i euroomrdet.1 I euroomrdet er de langsik ge forventningene l inasjonen s vidt under 2 prosent.2 Med llit l inasjonsmlet br terminrentene i Norge derfor ligge noe hyere enn i Tyskland. Forskjellene mellom terminrentene gjenspeiler dessuten premier for forskjeller i likviditet i det norske og det tyske markedet. Dieransen mellom norske og tyske langsik ge terminrenter l i underkant av 1 prosentpoeng i 2002 og falt noe i 2003. Samlet se tyder prisingen i rentemarkedet s langt p at det er llit l at inasjonsmlet vil ns. Basert p informasjon fra forventningsunderskelser og langsik ge renter er det tegn l at det forventes lavere inasjon enn 2 prosent det nrmeste ret. Forventningene lengre fram i d ser ikke ut l  avvike vesentlig fra inasjonsmlet. Le elsene i pengepoli kken i r har bidra l at forventningene om en frem dig inasjon rundt inasjonsmlet har vrt rela vt stabile. De gjennomsni lige utslagene i de norske markedsrentene var rela vt store ved rentemtene i 2002 sammenliknet med andre land med inasjonsstyring. I 2003 var utslagene betydelig lavere. Vedtakene p rentemtene var derfor noe mer forutsigbar for aktrene. Avslutning Det er ikke bare Norge som opplever kra ige fall i inasjonen. I Sverige har den underliggende inasjonen falt kra ig de siste mnedene l 0,1 prosent. Utenom energipriser er den underliggende priss gningen 0,7 prosent i Sverige. Ogs i Finland og Danmark er inasjonen p veg ned. Prisfall p importvarer trekker prisene ned, men ogs hy produk vitetsvekst kan ha bidra . Inasjonen har avta ogs i USA og euroomrdet, men i euroomrdet er utslagene mindre markert enn i Skandinavia. Konjunkturene i norsk konomi har snudd, og konomien har landet mykt e er den lange perioden med sterk kostnadskning her hjemme og svak ak vitet ute. Produksjonen er lbake p trenden. Sysselse ngen er lbake p trenden. Arbeidsledigheten er som i 1996 og lik gjennomsni et p 1990-tallet. Lnnsveksten er p et niv som med en normal produk vitetsvekst er forenelig med stabil konkurranseevne over d. Den samlede kredi veksten er balansert. Kredi en vokser om lag som den trendmessige veksten i nominelt BNP. De rela ve lnnskostnadene mellom Norge og vre handelspartnere er n lbake p et langsik g gjennomsni . Den nominelle kronekursen mlt ved I-44 er p linje med gjennomsni et p 1990-tallet. Rentenivet er p linje med nivet hos vre handelspartnere. Inasjonsforventningene er om lag lik inasjonsmlet. Slik er det en likevekt i norsk konomi akkurat n. Men inasjonen er lav. E ervirkningene av den sterke kronen i 2002 trekker prisveksten ned. Sam dig bidrar endret handelsmnster og konjunkturene ute l fall i importprisene, ogs nr de mles ved det norske importrer betaler i utenlandsk valuta. I Norge ser skjerpet konkurranse ut l  gi hy produk vitetsvekst. Det bidrar trolig l den lave prisveksten. Vi venter imidler d at inasjonen vil ta seg vesentlig opp i lpet av de e ret. P kort sikt vil virkningen srlig komme ved at eekten av at appresieringen gradvis tmmes ut. P noe lengre sikt vil rentereduksjonene ogs bidra gjennom sterkere e ersprsel i Norge. Men norsk konomi str ovenfor ere u ordringer. Det kan ta d fr rentene ute blir kt vesentlig. Vi har erfart at kronen dvis blir sterkt pvirket av utviklingen i forskjellen mellom rentene ute og hjemme, og det m vi ta hensyn l i vr rentese ng. Men temaene i valutamarkedene kan ski e. Virkningen p kursen av endringer i renten kan bli dempet. Boligprisene og utviklingen i kredi l husholdninger pvirker forbruk og boliginvesteringer. Disse indirekte virkningene sker vi  ta hensyn l nr vi se er nivet p renten. Kra ig vekst i formuespriser og oppbygging av gjeld kan vre en risiko for den konomiske stabiliteten. Men n er det bare husholdningene som har en sterk gjeldsvekst. Foretakene lner lite. Boligprisene ser ut l  ta seg opp. Men prisene p kontorlokaler er stabile. Vi har begrenset mulighet l  bremse de strukturelle endringene som skjer nr husholdningene ker sin gjeld over ere r for  investere i boliger og andre eiendommer og ak va. Renten kan brukes for  redusere e ersprselen e er ln. I dag - med lave renter ute og nr sammenheng mellom vr rente og kronen - ville en strammere pengepoli kk dempe e ersprselen p ln frst og fremst fordi arbeidsplassene ville bli mer usikre. Fallet i verdien av kronen det siste ret har styrket norsk nringsliv. Men nringslivet brer fortsa med seg virkningene av kra ig vekst i lnnskostnadene over ere r. De rela ve lnnskostnadene mlt i felles valuta er p linje med nivet i 1990, men om lag prosent hyere enn p midten av 1990-tallet. Det har skjedd en avskalling i det konkurranseutsa e nringslivet. De bedri ene som n er i dri , kan vre i bedre stand l  bre det hye lnnsnivet. Likevel kan kostnadene hemme ak vitet og sysselse ng. Takk for at dere ville hre p. Title: Flexible inflation targeting
text: Flexible inflation targeting Speech by Governor Svein Gjedrem of the STOCK Exchange Group BI on 29 March 2004 Subject to changes during the performance. The speech is based on the assessments given at Norges Bank's press conference e is the monetary policy meeting of the Executive Board on 11 March, Inflation Report 1/04 and on the previous speech. The mandate for monetary policy In many countries, the implementation of monetary policy has been delegated to a central bank. In Norway, responsibility for interest rate decisions was delegated to Norges Bank in 1986. The mandate for the implementation of monetary policy has been edified by the Ministry of Finance in the forecrimination of 29 March 2001. The first sentence of the mandate for monetary policy refers to the value of the krone. Stability in the krone's national value means that inflation shall be low and stable. It also states that monetary policy should be aimed at stability in the international value of the krone. The krone exchange rate fluctuates from day today, from week in week and from month in month. We have open trade with foreign countries and free capital movements. We don't have instruments l fine-tune the krone exchange rate. However, when monetary policy is aimed at low and stable inflation, this will contribute to a stable krone exchange rate above d. The inflation target is a framework, not an obstacle, for monetary policy to contribute to stabilising developments in output and employment. The purpose also comes in the forecrimination of the monetary policy. If e demand is goods and services are high and there is a shortage of jobs , there will normally be prospects of higher inflation. When the interest rate is raised, e demand is reduced and inflation is kept down. If e-demand is low and unemployment rises, there will be prospects of lower inflation. Then look at the interest rate down. The mandate entails that inflation targeting shall be flexible, so that weight is placed on both variation in employment and inflation. The second subsection of the mandate states more specifically what Norges Bank shall do. The operative target set by the Government for monetary policy is inflation of close to 2.5 per cent. The objective is symmetrical - it is just as important to avoid inflation that is too low as it is for high inflation. The inflation target provides economic agents with an anchor for expectations of higher inflation. It then affects their choices about savings, investments, bidding and wages. History shows that in the long run we will not have lower unemployment or stronger economic growth in the city against higher inflation. We saw this in the 1980s, when growth was low and inflation was high. The task of monetary policy is to provide the economy with a nominal anchor. Low and stable inflation is such an anchor. In the long term, the production of the lgangen on work crashes and capital and the ability l to resuscitate, but in the short and medium term, monetary policy can also have real economic effects. The economy is growing above d. Production moves in waves. Production will alternately be above and below the longitudinal trend. We call the output gap the discrepancy between the trend and the fak sk production gap. Stabilising developments in output means seeking to keep fak ske production close to trend. The output gap is causing pressure on real resources in the economy. Developments in the output gap provide a starting point for assessing output stability and may shed light on domestic price pressures in the economy. A high-gear economy provides a posi vt output gap. A low-gear economy leaves a nega vt gap. We have seen clear cyclical waves in the Norwegian economy. The recession at the beginning of the 1990s was followed by an upturn from 1993. This increase peaked in 1998. You're the economy transitioning from an upturn in a boom. Growth stalled in the winter of 2002. Now it's a rise. The output gap is one of several indicators that Norges Bank has as a whole says something about growth and the level of growth in the economy is high or low in relation to trend developments. These indicators show that the economy has landed softly in the long period of strong cost increases in Norway and weak global economic growth. The wage gap is one of the indicators used in the output gap. The wage gap is an indicator of how the social partners assess employment and the scarcity of work crashes . The wage gap is defined as the difference between wage growth in the Norway and wage growth above d is consistent with stable economic developments. From 1990 to 1995, when unemployment was high in Norway and fak ske production was below the potential for production, wage growth in the Norway was lower than among trading partners. From 1997, the wage gap becomes posi vt. During this period, resource renewal increased markedly. Against cunning one of the periods, the wage gap narrows in line with the fact that resource renewal is approaching a more durable level. There appears to be a close relationship between the wage gap and resource renewal in the economy as measured by Norges Bank with the output gap. Normally, the interest rate is determined with a view to inflation being 21/2 per cent two years ahead in d. Norges Bank has assumed that inflation targeting shall be flexible, so that weight is placed on both variability in inflation and variability in output and employment. Moreover, the money policy works with a dse erslep. Thus, behind the choice of the two-year horizon lies a trade-off between variability in inflation and variability in output and employment, as well as a perception of how the interest rate affects the path for these variables. If special circumstances should be If Norges Bank assumes a different ds horizon than two years, the Bank will account for this. It will also do so if special emphasis is placed on developments in financial markets. Norges Bank's instrument is the interest rate. Norges Bank's key policy rate (the sight deposit rate) influences short-term money market rates1, and expectations concerning future developments in the key policy rate are decisive for banks' deposit and lending rates and bond market rates. You may want to distinguish between three channels through which monetary policing works: The e-demand channel: When interest rates fall, consumption and investment in households and municipalities will tend to pick up. This is because they get more money when the debt is serviced, and that it becomes cheaper to borrow. Bedri's economy is strengthening, and they may become more interested in investing. Increased demand leads to greater production and employment ng. Wage growth may pick up. Combined with higher margins in the economy, this will result in stronger price growth. The exchange rate channel: The effect of interest rate changes may be amplified because the interest rate also affects the krone exchange rate. With lower interest rates, more loans and fewer will invest in NOK. Normally, a lower interest rate will therefore result in a weaker krone. Imported goods then become more expensive, and inflation is rising. In this case, a weaker krone l leads to increased exports and improved profitability in the Norwegian business sector. The effect of the interest rate on the krone exchange rate will vary with shading themes and sentiments in the foreign exchange market. The expectations channel: We believe expectations play a important role when prices and wages are seen. And not least in the foreign exchange market, expectations of substantial inflation and stability in the economy are of considerable importance. Expectations concerning inflation in the period ahead also affect wage demands and influence when the companies adjust prices. It can be difficult to form an opinion of how expectations will be l. Confidence in the inflation target may provide an anchor. The inflation we have behind us may also influence what we think about rising inflation. This results in an interaction between inflation expectations and inflation. If monetary policy is low, the expected rise in prices will be equal to or close to the inflation target. They contribute to stabilising inflation around the target. Thus, the expectations channel contributes to amplifying the effects of monetary policy. Therefore, we attach great importance to ensuring that households, bedri er, the social partners and those trading in financial markets, should have little effect on low and stable inflation. The effect of a change in interest rates on inflation comes with a dse erslep. The effect will vary in strength. The most up-to-date and correct picture of the current situation is necessary to make good forecasts for the person to come. In the autumn of 2002, Norges Bank established a regional ne work as an aid to take the pulse of the ak viteten in the Norwegian economy. Public scrutiny and assessments of developments in financial markets will soon be the main basis for our assessments, but the towing and revisions of such stubbornness make it new to supplement with other information. The regional ne verket gives us updated information about the level of the Norwegian economy. This shall contribute l that petroleum revenues are allocated not only by this, but also by future generations. The Fund is a buffer between current petroleum revenues and the use of these revenues in the Norwegian economy. As a result, the economic impact is shielded from fluctuations in prices and recovery rates in the petroleum sector. Petroleum revenues can be phased gradually into the Norwegian economy. The fund is also a savings fund. The increase in the proportion of elderly people in the population will in a few years require greater public funding than can be financed at current levels. The socioeconomic costs of a significantly higher level than today would be substantial. It is therefore important that the state has savings capital to draw on. The Act on the Government Petroleum Fund stipulates that the Petroleum Fund shall mo a all government revenues from petroleum activities, and that funds from the fund shall only be used above the state budget. The Act prohibits the use of funds from the Fund in any other way. This provision ensures that the state authorities take a stand once a year in terms of how much it is in favor of using from the Fund. It also ensures that all use of state funds is subject to the same assessment, so that alterna ve purposes must be prioritized against each other. Ordinary pension funds have precisely defined obligations in the form of forward-looking pension payments. The purpose of the funds is to fulfil these obligations with a reasonable degree of certainty. The authorities regulate the activities of the funds, among other things, with a requirement that the funds shall have funds that are highly likely to be sufficient l to cover long-term obligations. Such a formulation of objectives is of great importance for the choice of investment strategy in ordinary pension funds. In recent years, returns in capital markets have been weak, and in many countries the value of pension funds' funds has decreased in relation to liabilities. The decline in the contribution ratio of pension funds has led to clear changes in the portfolio composition of some funds. The Pensions Commission proposed that the Government Pension Fund should not be such a purely pension fund. The government has substantial current income and can therefore cover pension obligations from sources other than from any Government Pension Fund. The government's taxation policy means that it will not be op malt to leave the investment strategy in such a fund completely governed by the pension obligations. We can look at the Government Pension Fund as part of the government's general wealth and the government pension obligations as part of the government's general obligations. The government has the opportunity to maintain a long investment horizon even if the coverage ratio of a large Government Pension Fund should fall below what is deemed desirable in periods. Dersom de ikke gjorde det, kunne vi f betydelige kostnader ved at prosjekter som ikke er samfunnskonomisk lnnsomme likevel kk nansiering. En markedssvikt er det mest eek vt  avhjelpe med selek ve virkemidler, spesielt re et mot dem som rammes av svikten. Staten har derfor oppre et spesielle fond eller selskaper som gir nansiering l private bedri er, enten ved  skyte inn egenkapital eller ved  gi ln som det ordinre kapitalmarkedet ikke vil gi. Det er vanskelig  f full oversikt over omfanget av slik statlig kapital lfrsel. Et grovt anslag er at minst 20 milliarder statlige kroner n er investert i utviklingsprosjekter i private bedri er. Tilfrsel av kapital p rimeligere be ngelser enn i det vanlige kapitalmarkedet har lenge vrt et virkemiddel i distriktspoli kken. E er hvert har de e utviklet seg l  bli et landsdekkende virkemiddel. Tilfrsel av risikokapital innebrer en betydelig sannsynlighet for tap. Men for at lfrselen skal kunne kalles vellykket, m den ogs innebre en betydelig sannsynlighet for uvanlig god lnnsomhet. Investeringene i utviklingskapital br i gjennomsni gi posi v avkastning for investorene, ogs for staten. Dersom staten i gjennomsni tjener penger kan en med stor sikkerhet si at staten avhjelper en markedssvikt.
