Title: Management of the Government Pension Fund Global
text: Management of the Government Pension Fund Global Governor Svein Gjedrem. Introduction to a hearing of the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs on 18 May 2010. Figures in pdf format Changes are subject to change during the performance. Thank you to the Chairman of the Committee, and thank you for giving us the opportunity this year to explain Norges Bank's management of the Government Pension Fund Global (GPFG), in connection with the Storting's large-scale report on the management of the fund. The Government at the Ministry of Finance has mandated Norges Bank to do so in the management of the GPFG. The management mandate has been specified in the forecrimination and in unsubstaged guidelines from the Ministry. The Ministry of Finance stipulates, among other things, one benchmark portfolio for equities and one for bonds, which Norges Bank will be fairly close to. A management agreement has also been entered into. This model, which will now be further developed, contributes to clear division of responsibility, l transparency and sets limits for a high degree of professionalism in the management of the fund. Figure 1: Organisation of the management of the fund (1) The Executive Board has the executive authority of Norges Bank and sees the objectives and frameworks for the Bank's operatic management of the Fund. In recent years, the Executive Board has strengthened its follow-up. We have chosen a model where the Bank's asset management department  Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM)  is in a different location than the other two business areas in Norges Bank; monetary policy and financial stability. The CEO of NBIM has a clear role as CEO of NBIM and reports the Executive Board in accordance with the e. The Governor and the Deputy Governor then have duties as working chairmen. Chart 2: Governing documents for investment management The Executive Board stipulates principles for the management of risk in investment management. E are these principles placed different types of risk in one of four categories: market risk, credaceous risk, counterparty risk and operational risk. We need risk to be measured in different, unsubstowed ways. We also see requirements in managing the risk. The principles are inconsistent with more concrete frameworks for the activities in an investment mandate. These limits are partly a tightening of the rules established by the Ministry of Finance. Among other things, the Executive Board's limits state that the allocation to equities in the Fund shall be 60 per cent plus/minus 2.5 percentage points (1), while the Ministry will report deviations of up to 10 percentage points. Similarly, the limit for a measure of the normal deviation (2) between the return on the Fund and the benchmark portfolio has been reduced from the Ministry's limit of 1.5 percentage points, in 1.1 percentage points. Risk measures calculated on the basis of fairly short-term fluctuations in prices in the market did not capture the factual risk at the time of the crisis. Therefore, the Executive Board in the investment mandate has also established limits in areas that are not regulated by the Ministry. Among other things, there are limits to how similar the factual portfolio should be to the benchmark portfolio. The Executive Board has also said rules limit the scope of leverage and the sale of equities and bonds with settlement. There are rules for lending securities. Such sizes are suitable for control level regulation. NBIM reports monthly on the Executive Board. This reporting reflects the investment mandate. The instructions for NBIM's leader describe the professional and administrative responsibilities he has, and the requirements for systems, control and reporting. Figure 3: Organisation of the management of the fund (2) The Executive Board has appointed an advisory committee consisting of international experts in asset management. The Committee and the Executive Board have all-day meetings four times a year. The Executive Board has also established a two committee that will be preparating bodies in matters concerning audit and compensation. The audit committee was established in 2006, in coordination with the Bank's internal audit. The Committee consists of three of the Executive Board's external members and prepares matters concerning risk management and internal control for the Executive Board. In or, the Executive Board established a remuneration committee as a preparating body for the Executive Board. Among other things, the Committee shall submit to the Executive Board the framework for remuneration in the CEO of NBIM, and in managers who report directly to him. From autumn 2009, nbim's entire management team will receive all their remuneration as a fixed salary. The reason for the deviation from what is practice in the industry is that we want the managers to have a longitudinal perspek v. Other NBIM employees receive remuneration that is partly based on results, preferably over something d. Each year, the Remuneration Committee shall prepare a submission to the Executive Board on the principles for this remuneration, as well as a submission for the total limits on salary. Title: Management of the Government Pension Fund Global
text: Management of the Government Pension Fund Global Yngve Slyngstad's introduction in Stor nget's consultation on the Government Pension Fund Global. Subject to changes during the performance. Figures in PDF format (939 kB) A broad upturn in international equity and fixed income markets contributed to a 9.6 per cent return on the Government Pension Fund Global. Equity markets in particular were strong, and the return on the fund's equity investments was 13.3 per cent. The contribution from fixed-income investments was also 4.1 per cent, despite the crisis in southern European government debt that characterised the news for parts of the year. Chart 1: The fund's market value The fund's market value is now about NOK 3 150 billion. In recent years, we have seen steady growth in the fund's value measured in NOK. In the first quarter, the return was 2.1 per cent. The stock market has also made the largest contribution to the fund's return this year. Despite the fall in the fund's Japanese investments, the return on equity investments was 2.9 per cent in the first quarter of the year. The return over the past two years has been good. The results must be viewed in the context of weak figures in the crisis year 2008. The fund has now won back all the lost and more l. Chart 2: Share purchases and share prices The purpose of the fund is to distribute purchases from oil wealth over several generations. Langsik gheten is reflected both in the fund's strategy and in the management of the fund. Thanks to this longitudinality, the fund was able to buy 0.6 per cent of the world's listed equities in two years through the financial crisis. This gives a significant share of the world's value creation. Chart 3: Expected fluctuations in the fund The fund's market values will vary over d. During the financial crisis, the expected annual fluctuations in the fund were up to NOK 550 billion measured by the method based on daily price observations. Even though expected fluctuations are now somewhat lower, there is reason to expect considerable variation in the fund's values in the period ahead. Even for what many considered safe investments, such as government bonds, the risk has increased over the past two years. Transparency in the management of the fund means that we use common available benchmark indices. However, the benchmark indices are not necessarily fit for purpose in all contexts. We must therefore have an accompaniment to how the indices are so together, and consider whether they reflect the owner's target and provide the best possible relationship between return and risk. The Bank's management must also be opposed to the long-running return on the Fund. They must be reflected both through the strategy advice we provide and in the factual implementation of our management. Chart 4: Currency weights in the benchmark portfolio for fixed income investments The most commonly used benchmark indices for fixed income investments are market-weighted. This means that we are borrowing more and more in those who take out new debt. E iswhich increased debt itself can reduce the ability l to service the loans, provides such a market shift ng you wording for the Fund. We have therefore proposed using GDP weights as a basis for how much government debt from individual countries the Fund should have. Investments in nominal bonds now account for close to 40 per cent of the fund. At the current interest rate level, these investments will not generate a high real return. In funds d, a broad purpose of fixed-income investments is to reduce fluctuations in the fund's overall return. Government debt in particular contributes to achieving this target. Norges Bank has proposed that 70 per cent of fixed-income investments be invested in government debt, while 30 per cent is invested in corporate debt. Corporate debt will have a different role and should be given a different distribution than government debt. The management of the fund is to achieve the highest possible international purchase risk within the risk limits drawn up by the owners. In order to do this, we must take part in growth in the world economy. We should therefore consider whether today's regional weights, where Europe in particular is of great weight, are appropriate. The fund has two characteristics: its size and length. Both give the fund advantages that can be used to increase returns. In the future, we will place great emphasis on longitudinal work and competence building. All our investment units aim to increase knowledge about the underlying values of what we invest in. Norges Bank has recently completed its first investment in real estate. In a few years, real estate investments will account for 5 per cent of the fund's value, with a corresponding reduction in bond holdings. We expect investments in real estate to improve the relationship between return and financial risk in the fund. Real estate represents a new type of investment for the fund, at large positions in private markets. For these investments, it is demanding to create good benchmarks. Only through analysis of underlying economic values can we judge whether the investments will generate the desired real return above d. Chart 5: Ac ace external equity mandates per strategy Purchasing services is an important element of our business strategy. We purchase management services in areas where it is not appropriate or realis sk for the Bank to build up external expertise. They are mainly specialist expertise in special industries or specific emerging markets. The objective of the external management mandates is to place too high a longitudinal return on the lowest possible cost and risk. It is important that the agreements lead to the highest possible level of interest between Norges Bank and the management companies, and a long-term management relationship on the part of the managers. Chart 6: Highest fee in external managers The contractual fees in external managers are based on purely business assessments. The fee structure in most agreements has a performance-dependent element. The return achieved by the management company is compared with an index imposed at a minimum rate. Until the return is higher than the benchmark, the company will not receive a performance-dependent fee. All agreements now have an upper limit on annually paid fees, and rules that keep the fee earned if they are overlooked by the upper limit. We hope that the fee structure we have now established can help to change market practices and that we are able to enter into agreements with the best management organisations. It can be costly for the fund to be in a position where we are cut off from buying high-quality external expertise. Figure 7: Eierskapsutovelse. Forven ngsdokumentene At the end of 2010, the fund held shares in 8,500 companies worldwide. The fund is now among the largest shareholders in many companies. The role of significant shareholder requires us to know the companies' activities well. Sam dig will be a minority shareholder, and we need to win over other owners to get a say in our positions. The exercise of ownership rights must therefore be clear and lengthy. As a shareholder, we work in principle. We have chosen to concentrate our efforts on six priority areas where we can expect to gain an impact, and where we can develop high competence. The exercise of ownership rights is based on international guidelines recommended by the UN and the OECD. We prepare expectations documents as a means of promoting our interests as an owner. Every year we conduct surveys on how the companies we have invested in have met these expectations. We also hope that the companies themselves will take up a place within these in their corporate governance. The fund's owners have laid down a framework with a long-way strategy. Norges Bank will further develop our expertise in order to safeguard the consideration of longitudinal values and the preservation of the fund's values. 20 May 2011 11:15

Disse investeringene vil med dagens renteniv ikke gi en hy realavkastning. Imidler d er et vik g forml med renteinvesteringene  redusere svingningene i fondets samlede avkastning. Det er srlig statsgjeld som bidrar l  n de e mlet. Norges Bank har foresl at 70 prosent av renteinvesteringene plasseres i statsgjeld, mens 30 prosent plasseres i selskapsgjeld. Selskapsgjeld vil ha en annen rolle, og br gis en annen fordeling enn statsgjeld. Mlse ngen med forvaltningen er  oppn hyest mulig internasjonal kjpekra innenfor risikorammene som eierne trekker opp. For  klare det, m vi ta del i veksten i verdenskonomien. Vi br derfor vurdere om dagens regionvekter, hvor srlig Europa er gi en stor tyngde, er hensiktsmessige. Fondet har to vik ge kjennetegn: strrelsen og langsik gheten. Begge deler gir fondet fortrinn som kan brukes for  ke avkastningen. Vi vil fremover legge stor vekt p langsik ghet og kompetansebygging. Alle vre investeringsenheter sikter mot  ke kunnskapen om de underliggende verdiene i det vi investerer i. Norges Bank har nylig gjennomfrt den frste investeringen i fast eiendom. Eiendomsinvesteringene vil i lpet av noen r utgjre 5 prosent av fondets verdi, med en lsvarende reduksjon i obligasjonsbeholdningen. Vi forventer at investeringer i eiendom vil bedre forholdet mellom avkastning og nansiell risiko i fondet. Eiendom representerer en ny type investeringer for fondet, ved store posisjoner i private markeder. For disse investeringene er det krevende  lage gode mlestokker. Bare gjennom analyse av de underliggende konomiske verdier kan vi bedmme om investeringene vil gi nsket realavkastning over d. Figur 5: Ak ve eksterne aksjemandater per strategi Innkjp av tjenester er et vik g element i vr forretningsstrategi. Vi kjper inn forvaltningstjenester p omrder det ikke er hensiktsmessig eller realis sk for banken  bygge opp lsvarende intern kompetanse. I hovedsak er de e spesialistkompetanse innenfor srskilte nringer eller spesikke fremvoksende markeder. Mlse ngen med de eksterne forvaltningsmandatene er  legge l re e for hy langsik g avkastning l lavest mulig kostnad og risiko. Det er vik g at avtalene frer l hyest mulig interessesamsvar mellom Norges Bank og forvaltningsselskapene, og en langsik ghet i forvaltningen fra forvalternes side. Figur 6: Hyeste honorar l eksterne forvaltere De avtalefestede honorarene l eksterne forvaltere er basert p rene forretningsmessige vurderinger. Honorarstrukturen i de este avtaler har et avkastningsavhengig element. Avkastningen forvaltningsselskapet oppnr, sammenlignes med en indeks llagt en minimumssats. Fr avkastningen er hyere enn mlestokken, vil ikke selskapet f et avkastningsavhengig honorar. Alle avtaler har n en vre grense p rlig utbetalt honorar, og regler som holder lbake opptjent honorar dersom de overs ger den vre grensen. Vi hper at den honorarstrukturen vi n har etablert kan bidra l  endre markedspraksis og at vi sam dig er i stand l  inng avtaler med de beste forvaltningsorganisasjonene. Det kan vre kostbart for fondet  s lle seg i en posisjon der vi er avskret fra  kjpe ekstern kompetanse av hy kvalitet. Figur 7: Eierskapsutvelse. Forven ngsdokumentene Ved utlpet av 2010 hadde fondet aksjer i 8500 selskaper verden over. Fondet er n blant de strste aksjonrene i svrt mange selskaper. Rollen som betydelig aksjonr krever at vi kjenner selskapenes virksomhet godt. Sam dig vil fondet all d vre en minoritetsaksjonr, og vi er avhengige av  vinne andre eiere over p vr side for  f gjennomslag for vre standpunkter. Eierskapsutvelsen m derfor vre tydelig og langsik g. Som aksjonr arbeider vi prinsipielt. Vi har valgt  konsentrere innsatsen om seks satsingsomrder der vi kan forvente  f gjennomslag, og der vi kan utvikle hy kompetanse. Eierskapsutvelsen er basert p internasjonale retningslinjer anbefalt av FN og OECD. Vi utarbeider forventningsdokumenter som et virkemiddel for  fremme vre interesser som eier. Hvert r foretar vi underskelser om hvordan selskapene vi har investert i, har forholdt seg l disse forventningene. Vi hper ogs at selskapene selv tar ini a ver innenfor disse i virksomhetsstyringen. Fondets eiere har lagt et rammeverk med en langsik g strategi. Norges Bank vil utvikle vr kompetanse videre for  ivareta hensynet l langsik ghet og bevaring av fondets verdier. Title: Launch of Norges Bank's timeline
text: Launch of Norges Bank's dslinje Deputy Governor Jan F. Qvigstad gave an introduction on the occasion of the launch of "Norges Bank's dslinje". Dear Minister, Students and Teachers, We invite school classes twice a year to such events. We want to communicate to you what we do here at Norges Bank what social task we manage. It's a task we've had for almost 200 years. Today is a special day. We present a first edition of "Norges Bank's dslinje" on internal . There we show events from the bank's history, stubborn and economic history along a ds line. We show how the social task has evolved over d. We want to further develop this line together with you so that it can become a new g in teaching. I'm excited to hear what you think of the first version. At the heart of what we do is look after the monetary system. The Reichstag men at Eidsvoll already thought that this task was important. This should lead to "supervision of Rigets Paengevaesen", section 75c of the Constitution states. When it became clear during the summer of 1814 that the great powers were serious about the Kiel Treaty, and that we were going into union with Sweden, the representatives were very careful. They didn't want a monetary union with Sweden. Therefore, they wrote into the revised Constitution, which was adopted on 4 November 1814, a new Article 110, which the Explis said that we should have our own central bank, and thus a separate monetary system under the supervision of the Great NGET. Based on Section 110 of the November Constitution, Norges Bank was amended in 1816. In the early years of 1814, there was no order for the monetary system. There were many different banknotes in circulation. It was the old Rigsdale courant notes from the union with Denmark, as well as certificates issued by the government commission that ruled Norway during the blockade. In llegg, the stubborn holder of the Norway, Prince Chris an Fredrik, had issued the so-called princess notes. It was therefore not so laugh to know what was money. Inflation was very high. The price level increased during the Napoleonic Wars in the eleven-double. When a price increased, it was difficult to know whether that item was becoming more expensive, or if it was only the general price level that increased. The basis for a market economy was therefore weakened. The money partially lost its function as a unit of measure. They are described, for example, in Karlsoy and Helgoy village book. It happened that accounts were kept in goods such as cod liver oil, storsei or flour, on this one. Moreover, there was not a good market for loans with a long installment d. Those who invested in farm buildings or in mills did not receive loans with installments d that matched the physical life of the farm building or mill d. These investments were financed by card-only bills. It hampered investment that would build the country. You know the principle of division and the division of the executive, judiciary and the legislative and appropriating power. In the present, the monetary system had many times been destroyed by kings - the executive power. When he was unable to put people to the limit l to raise the need for beatings and wars, or when no one would rather lend him money, sometimes only an alterna v, money from his own bank. The bank was forced l to print banknotes without coverage in silver or gold. Another alterna v was to reduce the metal content of the coins and to sell them for the same price. The greatest master of this art was Henry 8th of England. He reduced the silver content of the coins from 75 percent l 25 percent between 1542 and 1551. That, of course, led to hyperinflation. But the king made large sums of money from the e and was able to develop the English fleet. It was also probably expensive with all the wives. In Norway, Stor nget therefore decided to commit, and not least the king, l mast. The headquarters of Norges Bank was therefore laid in Trondheim, more than day trips away from the government and large ng. There had been chaos as a result of the blockade and the Napoleonic wars. Some of you may remember Henrik Ibsen's poem about Terje Vigen rowing in Denmark to get grain in his family. He was brought up by English ships and must say e many years in the "prison" as the English prison was called. In the years e is 1814 slow order in the monetary system. In 1822, it was allowed to exchange the notes on the promised silver, rich in bad prices, that one must e give two speciedaler in banknotes for a speciedaler in silver. It wasn't until 1842 that you got what you promised. The notes could be exchanged for par in silver as it is called. Stability in the monetary system laid a solid foundation for growth in Norway. Money has no value in itself in a society. But money and the monetary system are prerequisites for prosperity and growth. Growth in Europe took off in earnest when trade and investment were lost. When the boats left Venice and Genoa, it took a while for them to return with goods. It required someone to lend money. Likewise, it took a monetary system of banking to save and others to borrow to invest in manufacturing. In this way, trade and production were financed. Monetary services with loans, repayments and savings require llit, credibility and discipline. You have to keep your word. Back then, there were very harsh punishments for those who did not keep their word. A description we find in Shakespeare's "The Merchant of Venedig" with Shylock and Antonio. Shylock demanded li of Antonio's "flesh" when he did not settle the debt. We have also had harsh penalties  and have  in Norway. Those who mess with money get in trouble. As you know, it doesn't cost much to produce a banknote  about 50 cents. And we sell it for 50 kroner, 100 kroner, 200 kroner, 500 kroner or 1000 kroner. It gives us a tremendous profit. Our profits are in the state and the community. Of course, it is tempting to get in the industry. For a long time, the death penalty was for that. In 1825, Jens Amundsen Fenstad became a banknote forgery. There are harsh penalties. There is a minimum of 2 years imprisonment for banknote counterfeiting. Now the monetary system is in order in Norway. Price stability is defined as low and stable price inflation close to 21/2 per cent above d. This means that the prices of individual goods act as signals to manufacturers and consumers. We all agree to use kroner as a calculation. Imagine if someone used yard and other meters as a unit of measurement about each other and without disclosing which device one was using? There exists a capital market where some save and others borrow. Those who buy a house can get a loan with a run d of 2025 years. Buying a car gets a car loan. And if you buy a TV, you can get a consumer loan. The loan is fit for purpose. On September 11, 2001, we had the tragedy at Manha an. The World Trade Center was the neighboring building in the U.S. Central Bank's New York office that is at the heart of the U.S. monetary system. The computer system was shut down. They had a reserve site in New Jersey, which worked, but the people who were supposed to be operating the reserve site were locked in lower Manha an because the bridges were closed. The monetary system and payments were about to stop. If things went bad in New York, it meant the dollar was stalling. Then the international monetary system would stop - including the Norwegian one. Then what would we pay with? Sigare is? We were nervous for a while. But the Federal Reserve agreed to guarantee all payments into the system in New Jersey. But we're not going to take ng like of course. In October 2008, the money market between banks did not function. Norges Bank must step in. Banks also had problems obtaining loans. Then we got the "gold card" where the Governor and Finance Minister were central. Even these days, we pay extra attention to European banks and whether they have enough capital l to withstand the Greek crises. Money is a means of payment. Money is a unit of reckoning. Money ensures that there are savers and those who invest. A stable and well-functioning monetary system is a prerequisite for a well-functioning welfare state. It is the central bank's job to protect the monetary system. I hope you use the Timeline on our pageswhich you will soon see, and that you engage both in our history, but also in our main tasks. As I said, we are facing many inconveniences ahead. That's why it's important that we acquire knowledge and knowledge in our society's economy. Learning is the greatest value Norway has. You are forward and will look after the country's values going forward. The human knowledge in Norway is sometimes worth more than the oil wealth! I now give the word l councillor of state Kris n Halvorsen. She has now for many years practised in two of the most important social developments, the Grand ng and the Government. How did she learn about the social issues? Does she have any advice in you how to proceed? Deputy Governor Jan F. Vi nsker  videreutvikle denne dslinjen sammen med dere slik at den kan bli ny g i undervisningen. Jeg er spent p  hre hva dere synes om frsteversjonen. Kjernen i det vi driver med, er  passe p pengevesenet. Den oppgaven syntes allerede riksdagsmennene p Eidsvoll var vik g. Stor nget skulle fre opsyn over Rigets Pngevsen str det i Grunnlovens paragraf 75 c. Da det i lpet av sommeren 1814 e er hvert ble klart at stormaktene mente alvor med Kiel-traktaten, og at vi skulle i union med Sverige, var stor ngsrepresentantene aktsomme. De ville ikke ha en pengeunion med Sverige. Derfor skrev de inn i den reviderte grunnloven, som ble vedta 4. november 1814, en ny paragraf 110, som eksplisi sa at vi skulle ha egen sentralbank, og dermed et eget pengevesen under Stor ngets oppsyn. Med utgangspunkt i november-grunnlovens paragraf 110, ble Norges Bank oppre et i 1816. De frste rene e er 1814 var det ikke var orden p pengevesenet. Det eksisterte mange ulike pengesedler i sirkulasjon sam dig. Det var de gamle rigsdaler courantsedlene fra unions den med Danmark, dessuten assignasjonsbevis utstedt av regjeringskommisjonen som styrte Norge under blokaden. I llegg hadde sta holderen i Norge, prins Chris an Fredrik utstedt de skalte prinsesedlene. Det var derfor ikke s le  vite hva som var penger. Det var svrt hy inasjon. Prisnivet kte under napoleonskrigene l det elleve-dobbelte. Nr en pris kte, var det vanskelig  vite om den varen var bli dyrere, eller om det bare var det allmenne prisnivet som kte. Grunnlaget for en markedskonomi var derfor svekket. Pengene mistet delvis sin funksjon som mleenhet. De e er for eksempel beskrevet i Karlsy og Helgy bygdebok. Det hendte at regnskap ble frt i varer som tran, storsei eller mel, p denne den. Dessuten var det ikke et godt marked for ln med lang avdrags d. De som investerte i grdsbygninger eller i mller, kk ikke ln med avdrags d som samsvarte med grdbygningens eller mllens fysiske leve d. Disse investeringene ble nansiert med kortsik ge veksler. Det hemmet investeringene som skulle bygge landet. Dere kjenner l mak ordelingsprinsippet og tredelingen mellom den utvende, dmmende og den lovgivende og bevilgende makt. I dligere der hadde pengevesenet mange ganger bli delagt av konger - den utvende makt. Nr han ikke klarte  ska legge si folk i lstrekkelig grad l  oppre holde si behov for slo og kriger, eller nr ingen heller ville lne ham penger, stod det enkelte ganger bare igjen et alterna v, penger fra egen bank. Banken ble tvunget l  trykke sedler uten dekning i slv eller gull. Et annet alterna v var  redusere metallinnholdet i myntene og  selge dem for samme pris. Den strste mester i denne kunsten var Henrik 8. av England. Han reduserte slvinnholdet i myntene fra 75 prosent l 25 prosent mellom 1542 og 1551. Det frte selvsagt l hyperinasjon. Men kongen tjente store summer p de e og kunne bygge ut den engelske ten. Det var ogs sikkert dyrt med alle konene. I Norge bestemte Stor nget seg derfor for  binde seg, og ikke minst kongen, l masten. Hovedkontoret l Norges Bank ble derfor lagt l Trondheim, mer enn dagsreiser borte fra regjering og stor ng. Det hadde vrt kaos som flge av blokade og napoleonskrigene. Noen av dere husker kanskje Henrik Ibsens dikt om Terje Vigen som rodde l Danmark for  skae korn l familien. Han ble oppbrakt av engelske skip og m e si e mange r i prisonen som det engelske fengselet ble kalt. Det ble i rene e er 1814 langsomt orden i pengevesenet. I 1822 ble det lov  veksle sedlene om l det lovte slvet, rik gnok l drlige kurser at en m e gi to speciedaler i sedler for en speciedaler i slv. Frst i 1842 kk man det man hadde lovet. Sedlene kunne veksles inn l pari kurs i slv som det heter. Stabilitet i pengevesenet la et godt grunnlag for vekst i Norge. Penger har ikke verdi i seg selv i et samfunn. Men penger og pengevesenet er forutsetning for velstand og vekst. Veksten i Europa tok for alvor av da det ble handel og investeringer. Nr btene gikk ut fra Venezia og Genova, tok det jo en stund fr de kom lbake med varer. Det krevde at noen lnte ut penger. Likeledes krevdes det et pengevesen med bankvirksomhet for at noen kunne spare og andre kunne lne for  investere i produk v virksomhet. P den mten ble handel og produksjon nansiert. Pengevesen med utln, lbakebetaling og sparing, krever llit, troverdighet og disiplin. Man m holde ord. Den gang var det svrt strenge straer for dem som ikke holdt ord. En beskrivelse vi nner i Shakespeares Kjpmannen i Venedig med Shylock og Antonio. Shylock krevde li av Antonios esh da han ikke gjorde opp gjelden. Strenge straer har vi ogs ha  og har - i Norge. De som tuller med penger gr det ille med. Som dere vet, koster det ikke mye  produsere en seddel  vel 50 re. Og vi selger den for 50 kroner, 100 kroner, 200 kroner, 500 kroner eller 1000 kroner. Det gir oss en enorm fortjeneste. Vrt overskudd lfaller staten og fellesskapet. Det er selvflgelig fristende  g oss i nringen. Det var det lenge ddsstra for. I 1825 ble Jens Amundsen Fenstad henre et for seddelforfalskning. Fortsa er det strenge straer. Det er minimum 2 rs fengsel for seddelforfalskning. N er det orden i pengevesenet i Norge. Det er prisstabilitet denert som lav og stabil priss gning nr 2 prosent over d. Det betyr at prisene p enkeltvarer fungerer som signaler l produsenter og forbrukere. Vi er alle enige om  bruke kroner som regneenhet. Tenk dere hvis man noen brukte yard og andre meter som mleenhet om hverandre og uten  opplyse om hvilken enhet en brukte? Det eksisterer et kapitalmarked hvor noen sparer og andre lner. De som kjper et hus kan f et ln med lpe d p 2025 r. Kjper en bil fr en et billn. Og kjper en TV kan en f forbruksln. Lnet er lpasset formlet. 11. september 2001 hadde vi tragedien p Manha an. World Trade Center var nabobygningen l den amerikanske sentralbankens New York-kontor som er kjernen i det amerikanske pengesystemet. Datasystemet ble sl ut. De hadde et reservested i New Jersey, som fungerte, men folkene som skulle betjene reservestedet, var lst fast p nedre Manha an fordi broene var stengt. Pengesystemet og betalinger var i ferd med  stoppe opp. Gikk det i st i New York, betydde det at dollar stoppet opp. Da ville det internasjonale pengesystemet stoppe - ogs det norske. Hva skulle vi da betale med? Sigare er? Vi var en stund nervse. Men den amerikanske sentralbanken beslu et  garantere for alle betalinger inn l systemet i New Jersey var oppe og stod. Men vi skal ikke ta ng som selvsagt. I oktober 2008 fungerte ikke pengemarkedet mellom bankene. Norges Bank m e tr l. Bankene hadde ogs problemer med  f innln. Da kk vi gullkortet hvor sentralbanksjef og nansminister var sentrale. Ogs i disse dager flger vi ekstra nye med p de europeiske banker og om de har nok kapital l  st i mot greske kriser. Penger er betalingsmiddel. Penger er en regneenhet. Penger srger for at det nnes de som sparer og de som investerer. Et stabilt og velfungerende pengevesen er en forutsetning for en velfungerende velferdsstat. Det er sentralbankens oppgave  verne om pengevesenet. Jeg hper dere tar i bruk Tidslinjen p vre ne sider  som dere snart skal f se, og at dere engasjerer dere bde i vr historie, men ogs for vre hovedoppgaver. Vi str som sagt overfor mange u ordringer framover. Derfor er det vik g at vi skaer oss kunnskap og kjennskap l vrt samfunns konomi. Det at dere lrer, er den strste verdien Norge har. Dere er frem den og skal passe p landets verdier fremover. Den menneskelige kunnskapen i Norge er ganger mer verdt enn oljeformuen! Jeg gir n ordet l statsrd Kris n Halvorsen. Hun har n i mange r prak sert i to av de vik gste samfunnsins tusjonene, Stor ng og regjering. Hvordan legnet hun seg kunnskap om samfunnsins tusjonene? Har hun noen rd l dere hvordan dere skal g frem? Visesentralbanksjef Jan F. Qvigstad foreleser for skoleklasser i Norges Bank Kunnskapsminister Kris n Halvorsen PUBLISERT 31. oktober 2011 13:00

Title: Management of the Government Pension Fund Global
text: 05/08/2022, 14:13 Management of the Government Pension Fund Global Management of the Government Pension Fund Global Governor oystein Olsen. Introduction to a hearing of the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs on 17 April 2012. Subject to changes during the performance. Hearing on online TV (Stortinget, Horingssal 1) Figures in pdf format (238 kB) Thank you to the Chairman of the Committee, and thank you for giving Norges Bank this year the opportunity to explain our management of the Government Pension Fund Global (GPFG), in connection with the consideration of the White Paper. As an investor, the Government Pension Fund Global differs from most others. The fund does not rely on borrowing to invest and there are no short-term liquidity requirements. We are able to manage the fund with a long-term perspective  to have ice in our stomachs during periods of great uncertainty. At the same time, the Government Pension Fund Global has grown sharply. The size means that we can take advantage of investment opportunities all over the world, in several asset classes. Figure 1: Transparency Norges Bank maintains its ambition to exercise great transparency, also with regard to the management of the Fund. The Executive Board's mandate for the head of Norges Bank Investment Management  NBIM  has been revised and in 2011. So are documents describing risk management, corporate governance, organisation, management and remuneration. NBIM has principles and guidelines for all important parts of its operations. In the report for 2011, the accounts are reported for the first time fully according to the international standard IFRS. This ensures that the fund's accounting rules follow best international practice, among other things, the note information has been significantly expanded. Chart 2: The fund's operating costs 1/2 05/08/2022, 14:13 Management of the Government Pension Fund Global Norges Bank has realised economies of scale in its management of the fund in recent years. During this period, the fund's equity share has increased. We invest more in smaller markets, in small companies and now also in real estate. Nevertheless, management costs as a share of the Fund have fallen. Chart 3: Norges Bank's letter advising on investment strategy One of Norges Bank's important tasks in the management of the Fund is to advise on the investment strategy. Management must be adapted to the framework conditions. The world's economic geography is changing. While growth in traditional advanced economies has been weak and slowing, growth has long been solid in Latin America and Asia. Over the past year, we have advised the Ministry on how the fund's equity and fixed income investments should be distributed between countries and regions. We believe that global weights according to the companies' market value should be the starting point for equity investments. For investments in government bonds, we have recommended that the currency distribution be determined based on the size of the countries' economies. The change means, among other things, that the share of European bonds will be reduced over time. Studies conducted by Norges Bank show that a systematic reversal of the equity share to the strategic weight  so-called rebalancing  has been a profitable strategy. The rebalancing should be continued through a publicly established rule. Let me now give the word to NBIM's ceo, Yngve Slyngstad, who will also elaborate on the Bank's proposal for changes to the fund's investment strategy. 17 Apr, 2012 12:15 2/2

Som investor skiller Statens pensjonsfond utland seg fra de fleste andre. Fondet er ikke avhengig av  lne for  investere og det er ingen kortsiktige krav til likviditet. text: Management of the Government Pension Fund Global Yngve Slyngstad's introduction in Stor nget's consultation on the Government Pension Fund Global. Subject to changes during the performance. Hearing on ne -TV (Stor nget, Consultation hall 1) Figures in pdf format (888 kB) Figure 1: Fund return The return on the Government Pension Fund Global was -2.5 percent. They are the third weakest result in the fund's history. The year was marked by the sovereign debt crisis in southern Europe, and this summer is a growing turbulence in financial markets. The fund's equity portfolio returned -8.8 percent. The fall was due in particular to weak European and Asian equity markets. Chart 2: The fund's market value The fund's market value currently is NOK 3,450 billion. Since the big hearing on 20 May 2011, it has grown by NOK 300 billion. The fund's real return from 1998 to the end of the year was 2.5 per cent annually. With a good first quarter, we now have a return on inflation, ska , and management costs of 2.8 per cent annually. It is mainly developments in the equity market that determine how good the fund's return will be in the long term. The return ahead is a result of considerable uncertainty. Figure 3: Realavkastning 1900-2011 Historically, equities have returned significantly higher than other investment alternations. The return on equities varies considerably, also from the year this year. The past year has been weak, but Norges Bank nevertheless believes that it is important to maintain the equity share in the fund. Chart 4: Inflows into the Fund The fund is funded every month. In or, total imports amounted to NOK 271 billion. That was the highest rate since 2008. The inflows are used in the purchase of equities and bonds. The distribution depends on developments in the markets. In the autumn, e is that the stock market had fallen, the whole export was used in the purchase of equities, essentially in Europe. In some situations, AK VA is also sold. In the run-up to falling equity prices, the fund's equity share will decline. In order to maintain the share of 60 percent, the fund must be weighted back in the first place  through so-called rebalancing. This strategy means that the Fund buys shares when stock values have fallen, and sell when share prices have risen considerably. Figure 5: Tilbakevek ng In the fund's history, we have only carried out full lbakevek ng twice. The first time was in the first quarter of 2003, with share purchases of NOK 4 billion. The second time was in the first quarter of 2009, where we bought shares for NOK 136 billion in lbakevek ng. The decline in spring 2009 alone has contributed to increasing the annual return on the fund since 1998 by about half a percentage point. In our Investment Advice, Norges Bank has proposed that a rule be established on lbakevek ng when the equity share is higher than 63 per cent or lower than 57 per cent. A rule will increase the likelihood that lbakevek ng fak sk is implemented when they are the most unsuitable and the risk seems greatest. The return on the Fund will also depend on the markets in which it is invested. More than half of the fund has been invested in Europe. Chart 6: Equity investments with different weights European equities have a high share relative to the size of the region, which means that good returns for the Fund are particularly dependent on market developments in Europe. Norges Bank has advised that the European weight should be reduced. They result in increased investment in other parts of the world, not least in the so-called emerging markets. They are markets that will occasionally have large fluctuations, as the legal charge of investors is weaker. Figure 7: Markedsstorrelse In these markets, a smaller part of the economy is also investable to financial investors. E is an overall assessment, we believe it is appropriate for the Fund to increase its investments in these markets, now and above d. Chart 8: The fund's bond portfolio The long-term objective of the management of the fund is to preserve the international purchase of the fund. A natural starting point for the bond index is to weight the markets with each country's bridge international product. Such a wicket will also better distribute the fund's risk to developments in the world's economies. Figure 9: Interest rates on 10-year real-rate bonds Norges Bank has proposed including government debt from emerging economies in the benchmark index for bonds. Real interest rates for 10-year government bonds in developed markets are currently nega ve, while real interest rates in emerging market bonds are considerably higher. Chart 10: New benchmark index for bonds In the first instance, 7 per cent of the fund's bond holdings will be in emerging markets. As more large countries such as China, India, Brazil and Russia become more open to foreign investment, the share will increase above d. The fund has a long investment horizon, and we should be able to withstand wide fluctuations in market value from e year to year in the next. This means that the fund, in order to ensure a good return above d, should firstly have a high equity share. Second, we should stick to a strategy of lbakevek ng when markets have fallen. They mean that we will buy equities when the risk seems high and the market value of the fund has fallen. The e sikre e is Norges Bank's assessment best in that a public rule is established for lbakevek ng. Third, the fund's investment strategy must be developed in line with changes in the world economy. This means that a higher share of the fund now and in the years to come will be invested in emerging economies. 17 Apr, 2012 12:15

Title: Welcome remarks
text: SPEECH Welcome remarks Workshop on Wri ng Central Bank and Monetary History arranged by Norges Bank and The Graduate Ins tute in Geneva. Dear par cipants, It is a great pleasure for me to welcome you all to this interna onal workshop on Wri ng Central Bank and Monetary History, sponsored by Norges Banks Bicentenary Project. It is an honour for Norges Bank and the Graduate Ins tute here in Geneva to host a workshop with par cipa on from such a prominent group of interna onal experts in central banking and monetary history. Norges Banks Bicentenary Project was ini ated in order to mark Norges Banks two hundred years of existence in 2016. But why did Norges Bank take the ini a ve to arrange a series of workshops here in Geneva? In short, why are we here? To answer this ques on we first have to go back in me to the birth of Norges Bank right a er the Napoleonic Wars. Six laws about the Norwegian monetary system laid the framework for the establishment of Norges Bank. The Norwegian Cons tu on of 17 May 1814 specified that the Stor ng (Norwegian parliament) should oversee the monetary system but made no explicit reference to a central bank. The Cons tu on was amended in November 1814 a er Sweden showed some military muscle to enforce the Treaty of Kiel. The amended Cons tu on was in place on 4 November 1814, and the main changes reflected the fact that Norway had entered a loose union with Sweden under a common monarch. A change, o en overlooked, was that a new paragraph has been added which explicitly stated that Norway should have its own bank and monetary system, both under the auspices of the parliament. Hence the Norwegian parliament preserved an independent legal authority to decide on Norways monetary system and ins tu ons in the union with Sweden. Since then, Norges Bank has evolved, as have central banks worldwide, in the face of shi ing paradigms, crises and o en in tandem with interna onal developments. Norges Bank has throughout its existence pursued objec ves similar to those of most other central banks, primarily the twin goals of price stability and financial stability. But the role of the central bank and its ac vi es has changed over me. Today, the central bank pursues price stability by determining and implemen ng a path for short-term interest rates with view to maintaining a low and stable rate of infla on over me. Under the gold standard, or prior to that the silver standard, the central bank pursued price stability by guarding the conver bility of paper notes on demand into gold or silver, ensuring that the money supply, and hence the price level, would not vary much. It was taken for granted that financial stability was a major concern and responsibility of the central bank and preserving it implied concerns for upholding the payment system. Let us, as an alterna ve, consider the different func ons of central banks. Firstly, central banks were typically chartered with a role in suppor ng a states financing needs as the designated banker for the government. In that pursuit, the central bank had to reconcile the governments desire for cheap finance with the demands of holders of government debt to receive their promised value. Secondly, central banks would also, in many cases provide credit to the general public, alone or in compe on with private banks. Central banks were banks of issue, o en with a chartered monopoly, and were responsible for maintaining conver bility of their notes (which were gradually granted the status of legal tender) into metal (silver or gold). However, during the course of years central banks would become specialised as the banker of private banks, facilita ng transac ons between banks, and their role as a direct credit provider to the general public would subsequently be scaled down to a minimum. Central banks interconnectedness with correspondent banks and their large reserves enabled them to take on a key role in the clearing system. During financial crises these factors allowed central banks to act as lender of last resort and provider of short-term liquidity to the banking system. During financial crises central banks have also expanded into new territories as the market maker of last resort, typically when credit markets are in disarray. The balance between the different central bank func ons has also changed over me. While the func ons for private banks have been upheld, the central banks func ons as banker for the government have typically been toned down. From a historical perspec ve, the domina ng concern for central banks has typically varied between normal mes (price stability) and extraordinary mes (financial stability). What seems to draw the most interest today, in light of the recent financial crisis, is indeed this shi ing balance between price stability and financial stability. The future role of central banks is again on the top of the agenda. Are we actually entering a new epoch? Charles Goodhart iden fied three epochs during which the interpreta on of central banks role was stable; the Victorian era (the 1840s to 1914); the decades of government control (the 1930s to 1960s); and the triumph of the markets (the 1980s to 2007). Following the financial crisis we now face the challenge of finding appropriate ways to implement macropruden al policy and supervision, and jointly, to find the right balance between the responsibili es of central banks, financial supervisory authori es and ministries of finance. Four years ago we met (at least some of us) here in Geneva at a workshop in October 2008. We outlined the ambi ous targets we had set for Norges Banks Bicentenary Project. Earlier anniversaries had usually given birth to a book, wri en in Norwegian, by a former governor, focusing on Norways own economic history. We stated here four years ago and reiterate today: this me is indeed different. This me we want our history to be wri en by academic experts, and we have underlined the need for a strong interna onal perspec ve. Firstly, for the obvious reason that we want to achieve a high degree of objec vity, but also for benchmarking purposes. Central banking in a na onal perspec ve is a lonely business. It is easy to become a na onal champion. So we are mee ng in Geneva, and not in Oslo, to underline the interna onal aspect of central banking and wri ng central bank history. Another reason for the interna onal dimension is that in substance central banking has indeed always been an interna onal ac vity, with its inherent links to the interna onal monetary system. Developments in one country can come before, at the same me or a er those of other countries, but it is always a part of an interna onal development. The financial crisis had its roots in the US but quickly engulfed the world and was met with interna onally concerted measures, both at government level and by central banks. We want to give birth to three high-quality books: The History of Norges Bank 18162016; The Monetary History of Norway 18162016; and last but not least a book on central banking viewed from an interna onal historical perspec ve, What is a useful Central Bank? Evolu on over two centuries, in the form of a conference volume. All three books will be focused on the same substance: central banking over the past two centuries, but wri en from different angles. The first book is to be wri en by economic historians in their tradi on. The second book is being wri en by economists focusing on the economic analysis of the monetary history of Norway, and finally we have the book that a empts to answer the perennial ques on of what is the role of the central bank today and how that role has evolved over the past two centuries. Norway will only appear in the la er book if we have contributed something special to the evolu on. In addi on to the end product, the three books, it was stated at the very beginning of the project that the road towards the end products would also be an end in itself. There are two aspects of this, competence and communica on. Firstly, the first phase of the project has produced numerous research publica ons, in books and journals, ten master theses at Norwegian universi es, and two PhD projects which are in progress. Hence, the project has already increased our insights in central banking and monetary history. Secondly, inspired by the Swiss 100-year anniversary project, which we learned about at the 2008 workshop here in Geneva, we have recently the first version of Norges Banks historical me lines on the internet. We will con nue to develop this applica on, it will be translated into English, and Norges Banks Bicentenary Project will con nue to document high-quality historical data and sources, and supply more long me series and broader data sets. Before ending my opening remarks, let me elaborate a bit on the third book. This book will be based on contribu ons to a Norges Bank conference on ques ons surrounding the role of a central bank from an evolu onary perspec ve. In a world where publica ons on central banking tend to become outdated very quickly (some, even before they go to press!), this choice will ensure that the value of the book will be resilient to the wearing effect of me. One of the very few publica ons of the kind which has maintained popularity over the years is the Bank of Englands tercentenary volume (edited in 1994 by Forrest Capie, Stanley Fischer, Charles Goodhart and Norbert Schnadt), which precisely adopts an evolu onary perspec ve. However, it can be argued that an updated book on the evolu on of central banking is of relevance today. Firstly, an addi onal 20 years give rise to new experiences, insights and perspec ves. Secondly, the 1994 book by Capie et al. was centered on the Bank of England. Thirdly, it had a strong focus on the recent evolu on of the monetary policy regime to infla on targe ng and central bank independence. We believe that there is now room for revisi ng the evolu onary aspects of central banking and making a valuable contribu on to the literature. Our aim is to have a pre-conference here in Geneva next year and a real conference in Oslo in June 2014. But we are star ng already today with this warm-up session for next years conference. Todays workshop has been divided into four sessions in the following order; monetary policy implementa on and money market opera ons; regional aspects of central banking; mes of war and instability; crisis management. I would like to thank all of you for devo ng a share of your valuable me to preparing your contribu ons to this workshop. Thank you for your a en on. 26 April 2012 13:00

Title: Countercyclical capital buffer  criteria for use and interaction with monetary policy
text: Countercyclical capital buffer d0 criteria for use and the interaction with monetary policy Speech by Governor afystein Olsen at ACI Norway's annual meeting in Oslo. Figures in PDF format (311 kB) Financial crisis and some lessons learned Chart: GDP in advanced economies The financial crisis brought the world economy into its deepest recession since the war. Five years on, the economic ripple effects are evident. GDP in advanced economies is far below the pre-crisis trend, and unemployment in many countries has risen at worryingly high levels. A mechanical calculation of trend growth in the years before the crisis probably exaggerates the potential of the economies. Households, enterprises and states lived above capacity for several years. There is little doubt that the crisis has clearly left advanced economies behind. Developments in recent years are therefore a good illustration of the fact that financial crises can have substantial real economic costs. Chart: Consumer price inflation in advanced economies The financial crisis is also a new reminder that price stability is not a stretching constraint on stability in the financial system. The 1970s and 1980s were characterised by high and variable inflation in advanced economies. Since the beginning of the 1990s, inflation has generally stabilised at a low level. Sam dig built financial imbalances up during this period. When the imbalances burst, the financial system was not resilient in being able to cope with the disturbances that occurred. A modern economy is entirely dependent on well-functioning banks. If banks' ability to communicate financing, uninfavourable payments and redistributive risk is impaired, the ripple effects in the rest of society may be considerable. Therefore, a framework is required to ensure that the financial system is robust. The financial crisis showed that the framework for banks was not good enough. Not least, the need for better regulation and macro-level vision became apparent. The individual bank may appear solid, but this does not mean that the system as a whole is robust in the face of disturbances. Systemic risk can occur in several ways. The risk can be built up over d through strong growth in asset prices and debt. It may be the result of increased dependence between incentives, or it may be due to many people being exposed to the same risk factors, for example on the funding side. Expectations that the government will not let the fiscal deficit end may contribute to increased risk-taking. Based on these weaknesses, the regulatory framework for banking and finance is now changing internationally. New liquidity buffers and capital adequacy requirements are on the way in line with changes in eea regulations. When requirements are iowed in the individual bank, the overall risk in the financial system shall also be taken into account. Therefore, the new framework contains macro ltak that can be looked in if needed. This will result in a banking system that is steadier when losses increase and financial markets are in tatters. Macro vision and countercyclical buffer The EU Parliament this week passed a new regulation on banks' capital adequacy. Before Easter, the Government presented a bill on new capital requirements for banks. The proposal is in line with the EU's new regulations. Chart: New requirements in pure tier 1 capital ratio d0 phasing in Central to the new regulations are capital buffers that are included in the llay in the minimum requirement. It strengthens the ability l to bear losses. When banks do not meet these, they will face restrictions on the distribution of awards and bonuses. The preservation buffer and The requirements for systemic risk and systemic complexity shall be permanent. At the top comes a countercyclical capital buffer d0 a capital requirement that can be increased during upturns and taken away in bad ones there. The buffer shall consist of pure core capital and shall normally be between 0 and 2.5 per cent of the calculation basis. This shall apply to the activities of all banks in Norway, including foreign banks and branches. The capital adequacy requirements specify how much capital banks must hold as a share of their risk-weighted assets. The lower the risk weights, the less capital is required. The regulations and methods used to determine risk weights therefore have an impact on how much capital banks must hold. The Government has also announced that changes will take place here. The Government's new capital requirements bill is due to be considered in the UK before the summer. The Ministry of Finance will prepare a foreclos charge that gives Norges Bank the main responsibility for preparing the basis for the decision on the countercyclical capital buffer. In our work, we will cooperate with Finans lsynet and exchange relevant information. The Ministry of Finance will determine the buffer rate. When the regulations are clear, probably over the summer, Norges Bank will present concrete advice on the level of the buffer. You will have an updated assessment basis and advice on the buffer being presented four times a year. The council will build on three criteria. Chart: Criteria for a good countercyclical capital buffer The first criterion states that banks should build an additional buffer when financial imbalances increase, so that they are better equipped against periods of higher losses. The size of the capital buffer must be viewed in the light of other requirements for banks. This is especially true when new requirements are introduced. That's the second criterion. The third criterion applies when the requirement is switched off. In the event of a downturn in the economy and the outlook for bank losses, the buffer shall be able to be consumed. This could prevent austerity in banks' credibility from intensifying The back cover. The capital buffer will thus contribute to increased stability in the economy. The capital buffer should not be reduced without further ado, even if there are signs that financial imbalances should decline. E is a period of high risk and an increased countercyclical buffer, it will probably cost little for banks to pass on the buffer. The benefits of having it there can turn out to be huge. In practice, it is demanding to identify financial imbalances. But economic theory and experience from more crises can help us. Chart: Key indicators of the countercyclical capital buffer Norges Bank's advice on the countercyclical capital buffer will as a general rule be based on four key indicators. The indicators cover debt growth, house and commercial property prices and banks' market funding. In the chart, we have highlighted our own banking crisis at the beginning of the 1990s and the financial crisis of 2008. The four indicators have shown clear signs of leading the way. We have similar experiences from crises in other countries. Taken together, the four indicators may signal a build-up of financial imbalances. Hensikten er  sikre at det analy ske grunnlaget er konsistent med u ormingen av pengepoli kken. Den motsykliske bueren og styringsrenten har to forskjellige ml. Bueren har som sikteml  gjre bankene mer solide for  kunne motst tap i en lavkonjunktur. Pengepoli kken skal srge for lav og stabil inasjon over d. Inasjonsmlet avveies mot hensynet l  jevne ut svingninger i produksjon og sysselse ng. P tross av ulike ml virker bde styringsrenten og kapitalbueren gjennom bankenes lpasning. Bueren vil bli fastsa ut fra en vurdering av risikoen for at nansielle ubalanser bygger seg opp og utlser eller forsterker lbakeslag i konomien. Kravet l kapitaldekning  og hvordan det virker p bankenes valg av rentemarginer  vil vre n av mange faktorer som vil ligge l grunn for den pengepoli ske analysen. Beslutningsgrunnlaget for kapitalbueren vil bygge p den aktuelle situasjonen i norsk konomi, med srlig vekt p ulike kredi - og formuespriser. Selv om regelverket for nye kapitalkrav frst vedtas senere i r og innfases gradvis, er virkningene av nye reguleringer trolig allerede synlige. Som ledd i gjennomfringen av pengepoli kken flger Norges Bank lpende med p hvordan bankene lpasser seg regelverket. Den motsykliske bueren bidrar l  ke bankenes soliditet i oppgangs der. Den kan ogs i noen grad bidra l  motvirke at nansielle ubalanser bygger seg opp. Men virkningen er usikker. Norges Bank kan derfor ikke se bort fra hensynet l nansielle ubalanser nr styringsrenten fastse es. Kriteriene for gjennomfringen av pengepoli kken ligger fast ogs e er innfring av en motsyklisk kapitalbuer. Takk for oppmerksomheten. PUBLISERT 18. april 2013 18:00

Title: Management of the Government Pension Fund Global
text: Management of the Government Pension Fund Global Director Yngve Slyngstad. Introduction to consultation on the management of the Government Pension Fund Global 2013 in the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs. Subject to changes during the performance. Figures in PDF format (900 kB) Thank you to the chairman of the committee, and for giving me the opportunity to talk about our stewardship in 2013. Chart: The objective of the management of the fund Our goal is to achieve the highest possible return in the long term. We aim to achieve the e-goal of acceptable risk in our investments, and attach great importance to being a responsible investor. Norges Bank seeks to achieve high returns without investing in companies that violate basic e.e. norms. We carry out the management assignment with an effek v organization. Our ability to invest in the long term depends on how we manage the fund. A high degree of transparency will contribute l achieve the e. Chart: Return on the Fund The return on the Government Pension Fund Global was 15.9 per cent. They were the second highest percentage return in the fund's history. The return was NOK 692 billion measured in international currency, and a total of NOK 983 billion if we take into account the depreciation of the krone  the highest return on the krone ever. The fund's return over the past five years has been good with an annual return of 12 percent. Since 1998, the fund's annual return is 5.7 percent. Chart: Accumulated return Norges Bank aims to create added value in the management of the Fund. Compared with the broad markets illustrated here by showing the fund's factual value development and the benchmark index's development, the excess return is 0.3 percentage point per year since 1998. In the last five years, the annual excess return is 1.2 percentage points, and all main strategies in our management have contributed to the results. Norges Bank's management is at the forefront of the fund's benchmark index, which is combined by broad indices from leading index providers. Public indices have significant weaknesses and are not fit for the fund's particular needs. Therefore, Norges Bank has created internal benchmark portfolios that take into account to a greater extent in the fund's characteristics as a large and long-time investor. The goal is to get the best possible urban relationship between expected return and risk over d. Our management of the fund has created considerable added value without increasing the fund's overall risk. As discussed in the white paper, Norges Bank has proposed a moderately higher risk limit. The proposal will support the fund's long investment horizon and pave the way for further development of the investment strategy. The proposal does not imply any change in the fund's total risk. A change in risk may as well reduce as increase the risk in the management of the fund. Chart: Effek v management Norges Bank attaches importance to operating a cost-effective management sector where costs must be kept under control. The Bank's bidding and accounts are determined by the Supervisory Council. Management costs have been reduced as a share of total assets in recent years. Compared with other funds, costs are low. We have reduced the scope of external management, and in recent years we have announced a major benefit to the management of the fund. We have reduced total costs despite a higher equity share, increased investments in several smaller limited companies, several new markets and countries, as well as unlisted investments in real estate. Chart: Trades in the export of funds Nevertheless, the most important part of our cost-effective management is something else  the ability to trade at low costs in the market. Over the past 10 years, we have received NOK 2 500 billion, i.e. we have invested about NOK 1 billion in the market every trading day. During the same period, there have been major changes in the fund's composition, primarily changing the geographical composition of the fund's investments, but also changes in the benchmark indices for equities and bonds. We have in llegg completed a leak of the equity share under challenging market conditions with low liquidity in the first quarter of 2009, and a lbakevek ng under considerably simpler market conditions in the second quarter of 2013. The changes in the strategy amount to a total trade of NOK 2 500 billion. In its management, Norges Bank has taken total trading costs for imports, leakage and changes in the strategy without adjusting the benchmark indices for the costs. They are our most significant contribution to cost-effective management of the fund. Chart: Ak vt and responsible ownership The work on responsible investments is important for the Fund. They are a longitudinal work where the results must be assessed above d. The starting point is to hedge the fund's financial assets. Good returns in the long term depend on sustainable developments in the economic, environmental and social sense, as well as well-functioning, legi me and effek ve markets. We attach great importance to voting, contact with companies and analysis of the companies we own in order to safeguard the value of the fund for future generations. We have a long-term horizon for our investments and we work principle-based, but acquiest, to achieve results in active ownership. If we are to have a breakthrough as a minority shareholder, we must assume norms that other shareholders will also emphasise. The exercise of ownership rights is based on internationally recognised standards for investors. We are working to improve standards. In 2013, we continued to work on CDP's water program, which aims to improve companies' information and reporting of their water resources. Furthermore, we have ongoing industry-ini to refer to businesses' impact on rainforests and the need for industry standards when extracting metals. In 2013, we worked to ensure that UNICEF's principles for children and business were implemented as a member of an advisory working group. We continue to work to improve our principles for the exercise of ownership rights, such as principles for voting. In the coming year, we will also strengthen international research in the field, and ownership is one of the priority areas in "Det norske finansini a vet (NFI)". The instruments in our corporate governance activities are voting and dialogue with companies, investors, regulators and other standards. We vote at general meetings and put forward shareholder proposals. In 2013, we voted at almost 9 600 general meetings in large part see all 8 200 companies in which we have ownership interests. As of the third quarter of 2013, the voting is on our ne pages the day e is that the general meeting has been held. We had 2,300 meetings with the companies. In an increasing share of the meetings, we took up ownership, and a larger share was with the chairman of the companies. In recent years, we have increasingly integrated ownership issues into our investment business, and we have systema sert data on ownership conditions for 4 100 companies. Chart: Responsible investor We work particularly, but not exclusively, with our focus on children, climate, water, well-functioning markets, equal treatment of shareholders, and the board's responsibilities. We have set up an advisory committee for ownership work. The e-committee provides important input in our work in this area. Chart: Divestments in some sectors In 2013, we quickly began our efforts to acquire the portfolio in terms of risk and social conditions that may have an impact on the fund's return. The adjustments were based on sectoral and company analyses that will identify business models that are considered less sustainable and profitable over d. We have carried out a risk assessment of sectors where environmental inequalities are particularly large. The e applies to mining companies and companies involved in the production of palm oil. In 2012 and 2013, we sold out of 65 companies as a result of the work. Figure: Miljorelaterte investeringsmandater Since 2009, Norges Bank has divided environment-related investment mandates into internal and external managers. In total, these investments amounted to NOK 31.4 billion at year-end skiing. Of the 166 companies in this part of the portfolio, the main emphasis was on water, energy efficiency and renewables and alterna v energy. Norges Bank's investments in environment-related mandates are made in listed companies. We have recently begun investing in environment-related bonds. The investment universe is complex and under rapid change both in the market and in framework conditions. The environment-related investments are therefore well suited for management. The proposal to consolidate the instruments for responsible investments may make ownership work more impact-hardened. We will increase our reporting, strengthen our expertise and improve our work in the area of responsible investment in the years to come. 25 April 2014 12:15
