Title: Money and freedom  the importance of trust
text: 05/08/2022, 14:14 Speech by Governor oystein Olsen at the Museum of Cultural History on 3 June 2014. Thank you very much for your invitation to talk about an important topic for a central bank  the importance of confidence in the value of money. At the same time, I must commend the Museum of Cultural History for an exhibition that is both exciting and thought-provoking. Some of you may have visited Norges Bank's hall and read the story of the dramatic gold transport in 1940. Back then, gold was the country's most important international reserve and it was important to get it out when the country was occupied. The Government of London could easily trade the gold into more walkable coins. It gave freedom of action in exile. Metal as a means of exchange has a long history, dating back to ancient Mesopotamia 5,000 years ago. There, for the first time, people began to use small pieces of metal with stamped weight as a means of exchange. Mesopotamia was, for its time, a well-developed society. Agriculture was extensive, and in the cities people specialized in various professions. Trade in goods and services resulted in a need for a generally accepted means of exchange. The pieces of metal were a useful contribution to making the trade in goods and services efficient. From Mesopotamia we have to make a long timely leap  to Lydia on the west coast of present-day Turkey 2,600 years ago. Here we find for the first time identically designed pieces of metal with a piston in which the king guarantees the weight. This is considered the first money. Today, money takes many forms. We still carry coins around, but we also have banknotes, and access to deposit money. With bank cards and mobile phones, we can quickly move money from one account to another. The transactions are only seen as numbers on a screen. Nevertheless, we have confidence in them. Money fills three basic tasks; They act as generally accepted means of payment, they make use as a value gauge and accounting unit, and they are well suited for storing values. A well-functioning monetary system is an important foundation for an economy. It gives us the freedom to manage the values we create. When we can sell our labor or the item we have produced for money, it allows for trade and specialization. Long-term purchase and sale agreements can be entered into when we have confidence that the value of the money will remain. Money is also impersonal. We're not tied to trades. We are free to decide where and how the money will be spent. 1/7 05/08/2022, 14:14 With a stable monetary value, we also have the freedom to choose when the use should take place. Earned funds can be saved, as a collateral against unforeseen events, or to be invested in real estate or production equipment. High inflation results in an arbitrary redistribution from those who have saved to those with debt. The incentives to save are destroyed. Deflation or a fall in prices is also problematic. This results in burdensome debt burdens, which we saw during the parity policy in the 1920s and during the Depression in the 1930s. Both high inflation and deflation affect investments in productive capital. In periods of high and fluctuating inflation, the information contained in the price of an item is covered. It becomes unclear whether a price change is due to an increase in the general price level or whether the cost of producing the item has increased. This can lead to incorrect investments. High inflation also has a self-reinforcing effect. Once inflation has taken root, people get used to prices rising rapidly, taking that into account both in wage settlements and when prices are set. This became a major problem in the 1970s and 1980s. If money is to fill its tasks, we must trust that its value stays over time. The history of the monetary system is about how the authorities have at various times tried to build confidence in the value of money. But it is also the story of how trust has in many cases been undermined. In Norway coins came first as foreign currency  a result of the Vikings' extensive trading activities. After Harald Hardrade established the first Norwegian mint, Norwegian coins quickly took over. The coins carried the king's seal as a guarantee of the silver content. When new kings took the throne, the ancient coins were collected and exchanged for coins with the new king's seal. Thus, the coins also served as a vindication of the incumbent king's power. There are several examples of the medieval kings releasing coins with increasingly inferior silver content. By reducing the silver content, or offering a poor price when old coins had to be exchanged, the throne gained income. The Kings limited the use of other coins through laws. The Norwegian kings were not the only ones who undermined confidence in the coins by reducing the silver content. Most famous is Henry 8. who developed this into a  not so noble  art. During the 18th century, many countries introduced banknotes as a forced means of payment. The notes were a security that entitled the owner to a certain amount of silver from the issuer. The right to issue banknotes was granted as a royal privilege. The use of paper money was effective, but at the same time made it easy to water down the value of money. While the mint of silver and gold coins was limited by the amount of available precious metal, printing paper money was cheap. There was little to prevent an unequivocal king from starting the banknote press if the temptation or the need for money became too great. Europe was far from a peaceful continent. Wars occurred frequently and had to be financed. This often led to the suspension of the redemption obligation. 2/7 05/08/2022, 14:14 In denmark-Norway, the banknote bank's duty to exchange banknotes for silver was revoked in 1757 after the outbreak of the Seven Years' War. In the years that followed, constant wars and conflicts were financed by printing new banknotes. Attempts to clean up the monetary system were half-hearted and often led to more disorder. The Napoleonic wars brought chaos to the monetary system. When the Denmark Norway was dragged into the war, two banks - both with royal privilege - issued banknotes: Riksdaler courant and riksdaler. King Frederick VI continued to finance public expenditure by printing money. In Norway, the blockade made it difficult to obtain banknotes from Denmark. To remedy the money shortage, the government commission issued monetary reparations that could be used against public coffers, so-called "certificates of allocation." The country was also hit by years of ineffination. The combination of shortages of goods and several banknotes in circulation led to hyperinflation and a lack of confidence in the monetary system. From 1806 to 1813, the price level more than doubled. In 1813, the value of money was written down by almost 90 percent, at the same time that a new banknote bank was created and a new monetary unit was introduced; riksbankdaler. But the chaos in the monetary system and people's lack of confidence in the value of the notes persisted. The postings in the accounts between merchant Poul Hansen in Tromso and guest thom'son on Buroy were kept in varieties such as cod liver oil or storsei. The monetary system was close to collapse. The separation from Denmark involved a split of the Danish-Norwegian monetary union. At Eidsvoll, Christian Magnus Falsen stated: No state can pass without a well-functioning monetary system. A separate currency would be a symbol of the country's sovereignty and freedom. The elected representatives themselves took responsibility for the monetary system. Section 75c of the Constitution states: "Storthinget is granted:[..] that lead Opsyn over Rigets Pengevaesen". In the November Constitution, it was established that Norway should have its own bank and monetary system. The King should no longer be authorised to print money at his discretion. Behind this decision were bitter memories of the decay of the monetary system during the Union era and inspiration from The Thinkers of the Enlightenment and the revolutions in the United States and France. The Danish King's sole selection was to be replaced by popular sovereignty and power distribution. Institutions with clearly defined roles should prevent arbitrary use of force and build trust. The Storting gave the task of overseeing the country's monetary system to Norges Bank, which was established in 1816. The bank's headquarters were initially added to Trondheim  twelve day trips from the Government of Christiania, and even further from Stockholm. This gave a geographical  and not only formal  distance from state power. 3/7 05/08/2022, 14:14 It was urgent to get the economy back on its feet. Without confidence in the monetary system and the currency, the country's economic freedom would be limited. But it would take time to restore confidence in the value of money. The first years after 1814 are characterised by many and different banknotes in circulation, new rounds of devaluation and sharp inflation. From 1814 to 1817, prices more than doubled. During the financial debate at Eidsvoll, 13 May 1814, the National Assembly had decided to print up enough riksbank valleys to cover the state's deficit. Members of the National Assembly personally guaranteed both government debt and banknote courses. This was referred to as the "Eidsvoll Guarantee". But the guarantee was not followed up by concrete measures. The economic foundation for a stable monetary value was also not present. The guarantee was rejected by the Storting after two years, and the riksbankdaler was replaced with speciedaler. The monetary value should be guaranteed by an inventory of silver. A separate silver tax was discharged. For a young nation, breaking the promises of stable monetary values was costly. The breach of the Eidsvoll Guarantee was noticed internationally. When the government had to take out loans, it was difficult to find lenders. Loans that were eventually granted were granted on tough terms. The introduction of speciedaler did not give the necessary confidence in the monetary system. In addition, it proved difficult to collect the silver tax. The value of speciedaler fell. In 1822, the Storting decided to lay down a longer-term strategy. The redemption rate should gradually increase to par value. At the same time, a strict economic policy was pursued that brought the state's finances into balance, and the national debt was paid. Only after twenty years  in 1842  was the trust established and it became possible to exchange money for par silver courses. The latter half of the 19th century was a period of solid economic growth and stable prices. During this period, more and more countries switched to tying their currency to gold, and an international fixed exchange rate system with gold standards emerged. Norway introduced the gold standard in 1874 at the same time as we entered into a coin union with Denmark and Sweden. The crown took over from the speciedaler. The First World War quickly ended the stable monetary system established in the decades before. In many countries, the authorities again fell for the temptation to finance the war using the banknote press. High inflation again became a problem. Norway did not participate in the war. But monetary and fiscal policy nevertheless got out of control. People stood in long queues outside Norges Bank's premises to exchange for gold. Gradually, the benefits from the financial crisis are letting go. But the picture is mixed. In many places, inflation is low and interest rates are kept at a fast low level. In order to counteract the risk of a marked decline in the Norwegian economy as a result of the fall in prices, Norges Bank lowered the key policy rate before Christmas. When we presented our latest Monetary Policy Report in March, the interest rate was kept unchanged. But we were also clear that if developments are as forecast , there are prospects that the interest rate will be so high. I'll be back in the analysis from the march report later in the . But before we get this far, I'd like to say a few words about where the oil has brought us and how we've handled the revenue. Among other things, I would like to explore the oil fund mechanism and Norges Bank's exchange of foreign exchange on behalf of the government. Chart: GDP per capita When the first oil was recovered in 1971, the income level in Norway was low compared to other Western countries. Today, the picture has been reversed. We have gradually regained the edge the richest countries had on us. Measured by GDP per capita, Norway is now at the very top. The emergence of oil and gas activities has been decisive for the strong economic growth in the Norway over the past 40 years. The knowledge on the NCS has had ripple effects in other parts of the business sector. More and more people are  not just in the workshop industry  have made an accusation towards deliveries in the oil sector. An advanced supplier industry has emerged. New products and technological solutions have been developed. For many, the assignments on the Norwegian shelf have been a springbre in new export markets. The last 15 years stand out. From the 1990s, the price of North Sea oil rose from about USD per barrel above USD per barrel. High oil prices and good profitability in the extraction of oil and gas have led to a steady rise in petroleum investment in recent years. Increased use of petroleum revenues over public couriers has contributed to growth in domestic demand. Employment has remained high and unemployment low, even when the financial crisis hit in 2008. The large profits from petroleum activities are managed well. It was established that the oil and gas resources belong to the community. Ska esystem and framework conditions for the petroleum activities were uns wormed so that the large surpluses imposed on the state. We made serious mistakes, but also won lessons in our first two years as an oil nation. E is each we put in place the mainstays of the economic policing. With the Petroleum Fund and the fiscal rule for the use of petroleum revenues, we have avoided making public couriers dependent on aviation revenues. The fiscal rule gave us a long-run strategy for the use of petroleum revenues. Revenues would be phased into the economy gradually, in line with the expected real return on the Fund. Over d, as long as the fund grows, this may contribute to a stronger real exchange rate. The petroleum fund mechanism and the fiscal rule mean that the use of petroleum revenues is decoupled from the current revenue stream. Figure: Real value course They have contributed to stabilising the krone exchange rate and limiting real appreciation. Compared with other commodity currencies, the krone has been stable, even in periods of wide fluctuations in oil prices. Chart: Government revenues from the petroleum sector  and how they are used Let me elaborate on the li around the foreign exchange transactions lkny an oil fund mechanism. All revenues from the sale of oil and gas are in foreign currency. The petroleum companies exchange a share of their revenues in nok, in order to pay ska and utby e l the state. The government will generate substantial foreign exchange revenues from its direct ownership interests on the Norwegian shelf (SDFI). Chart: Government revenues from the petroleum sector  in 2014 As long as government revenues in NOK, from the petroleum sector, are greater than the annual use of petroleum revenues over the government budget, the government is left with a surplus of NOK. They were the situation until 2014. On behalf of the government, Norges Bank exchanged the e krone surplus for l currency, which was later transferred to the Petroleum Fund. The exchange from NOK l currency to some extent offset the effect of the krone purchases made by oil companies to pay the oil tax. These operations are thus neutral with regard to the impact on the foreign exchange market. It is the use of petroleum revenues over the government budget that may affect the real krone exchange rate. Chart: Government revenues from the petroleum sector  in 2015 In 2015, the use of petroleum revenues is estimated to be higher than government revenues in NOK. The non-oil deficit in the government budget has increased above d, as the petroleum fund has become larger. Sam dig is the cash flow from petroleum activities on the way down. As a result, Norges Bank has refrained from selling NOK, l selling foreign exchange to finance the use of petroleum revenues. But it is quickly how much petroleum revenues are spent over the government budget that determines the effect on the real exchange rate. In other words, Norges Bank does not wish to influence the krone exchange rate through its foreign exchange transactions. Therefore, krone purchases are also distributed evenly throughout the year. On the last business day of each month, Norges Bank announces the size of the daily transactions in the coming month, based on estimates of petroleum revenues and the use of revenues. Let me reverse the current situation for the Norwegian economy. Chart: Oil prices We have left behind 15 years of strong economic growth. The Norwegian economy has a tailwind. The opportunities we have few have been used. The flip side of the medal is an economy that is gradually becoming more dependent on oil, and thus vulnerable to changes in oil prices and revenues from the shelf. This vulnerability has now become apparent, as we know, oil prices have fallen by almost 50 per cent since the summer last year. Large parts of the business sector and the labour market are currently tied to the oil industry. Few are employed directly in the extraction of oil and gas. However, if we count everyone who delivers in the sector, about one in nine jobs in the Norway  around 300 000 in total  can tie up the oil industry. An increasing share of this accumulation is based on deliveries in oil extraction in other countries. Figure: Petroleumsinvesteringer Petroleum investment has risen considerably over several years and been a driving force for the upturn in the mainland economy. Growth slowed through 2014, and even before oil prices began to fall this autumn, we projected that investment would fall significantly in 2015. The fall in oil prices over the past six months has accelerated and amplified the recovery. The decline in oil prices significantly weakens the expected profitability of investment projects. Some projects will no longer be very profitable l to be carried out, and cost-reducing ltak can push other projects into d. The decline in investments is exacerbated by a deterioration in cash flow in oil companies as a result of the decline in oil prices. Lower aquities in the petroleum industry do not mean that the oil age is now moving towards a sluggish one. Fortsa remains to recover almost half of the known reserves of oil and gas on the Norwegian shelf. Major new discoveries have been made over the past couple of years. One of them  Johan Sverdrup  is ready for development. New assignments can be expected for the Norwegian supplier industry. Nevertheless, the Norwegian economy must now have a markedly lower e-demand from the oil sector. The ripple effects will be felt in the mainland economy. Earnings in the bedries are weakening and the need for work crashes is diminishing. Companies that supply in the oil sector must apply for entry into new markets. Other competitive activities must emerge. A high cost level can make that job demanding. E is many years of particularly Norwegian wage growth, the cost level in Norway must again be adjusted to the level among our trading partners. A necessary adjustment of the cost level can take place in two ways: through lower wage growth than in other countries and by a weaker krone exchange rate. The monetary policy in Norway is aimed at keeping inflation low and stable. The operatic target is consumer price inflation of close to 2.5 per cent. The inflation target provides the economy with a nominal anchor. When inflation expectations are firmly anchored, monetary policy may be the first line of defence when economic conditions slow down. Chart: Oil prices and the krone exchange rate Monetary policy can only affect inflation. It cannot take primary responsibility for the necessary restructuring of the economy. But through the effect on the exchange rate, monetary policy can help the business sector get started. As long as inflation remains low and stable above d, a marked depreciation of the krone may coincide with low interest rates. The krone has depreciated markedly since September 2014, and is now about 10 per cent weaker than in the first half of 2014. Developments in the krone exchange rate must be viewed in the context of lower oil prices and weaker growth prospects for the Norwegian economy. Figure: Lonnskostnader rela vt l handelspartnerne The depreciation of the krone contributes to sustaining inflation and dampens the impact on the Norwegian economy of lower oil prices. Even though the cost level in the Norway is rapidly high compared with other countries, a weaker krone l is contributing to strengthening the competitiveness of Norwegian bedri is meeting competition from abroad. Sam dig has wage growth in Norway slowing, and there are prospects that real wage growth this year will be the weakest in 20 years. Chart: Mainland exports and import growth among trading partners Improved competitiveness over the past two years as a result of a weaker krone makes exporters better able to maintain their market share. Exports from mainland Norway excluding oil activities may thus increase in line with e-demand from export markets. Together, petroleum-related exports may be curbed by weaker developments in global offshore investments. Chart: Unemployment It will probably take d before the effects of lower oil prices are fully reflected in the mainland economy. A flexible labour market appears to be limiting the rise in unemployment. So far, unemployment has increased little nationwide. But we are seeing a more pronounced increase in regions and industries that are close to an oil industry. Growth in employment has so far remained high, but various expectations indicators point in the direction of low employment growth ahead. The ratio between the number of unemployed and unemployed persons also indicates that the labour market is becoming less tight. In the period ahead, unemployment is expected to increase somewhat. Weaker growth prospects and rapid uncertainty about economic developments may be holding back on investment decisions. On the other hand, improved competitiveness will provide a basis for increasing production capacity in parts of the business sector. llegg it appears that housing investment will contribute l keeping the overall investment stock up. Chart: Households In recent years, household consumption has increased moderately, and the saving rate has reached a high level despite the low interest rate level. Pension reform, high labour immigration and uncertainty about economic developments are likely to contribute ln increased savings. Household indicators have remained at low levels since autumn 2009. In addition, lower real wage growth is likely to dampen household purchasing rates. This is why there are prospects of moderate growth in consumption and high saving. Chart: House prices and credibility Over several years, high petroleum revenues and residual spin-off effects from the oil sector have driven up house prices and household debt. Debt has grown far faster than income. Fast-moving low interest rates may increase the risk that debt and asset prices will be kept above d. Together, the prospects of weaker income growth and somewhat higher unemployment may each curb house price inflation. Norges Bank emphasises the consideration of financial stability in the interest rate period. The aim is to avoid an abrupt downturn in the economy and higher unemployment at a later date. As a result, we have chosen to keep the key policy rate li higher than if we had not taken into account the balance of risks. We have "leaned against the wind". Figure: Trading partner terminrenter A small open economy such as The Norwegian economy is largely influenced by economic developments abroad. Growth in the world economy has pick up somewhat over the past couple of years, but the picture is mixed. In the euro area, growth and inflation are still low. Household consumption is rising and there are signs that consumer investment will continue in the period ahead. Sam dig is likely to high unemployment and further deleveraging in the private and public sectors will contribute to curbing the ak vitet for a long time d. In the US, the recovery has gained some traction, although Americans this year, as in or, appear to have experienced a slowdown in the first quarter. An expansionary monetary policy appears to be working, and both consumption and investment have pick up. Unemployment has fallen. Increased economic growth has contributed to a substantial reduction in the government budget deficit. There are also large volumes of Norwegian exports in the UK and Sweden. But low inflation is an unconsyndary one. Key rates are close to zero in many countries and are expected to be low for a long period. Over the winter, several foreign central banks have resorted to new unconventional ltaks to shred the acrosanction and counteract the risk of deflation. Market participants' expectations of key rates have continued to fall. Low interest rates abroad influence developments in the krone and thus the inflation outlook, and also contribute to low interest rates in Norway. Figure: Appropriations Pengepoli sk report 1/15 In other words, the outlook for the Norwegian economy weakened through autumn or. In December, Norges Bank raised its key policy rate by 0.25 percentage point, to 1.25 per cent, to reduce the risk of a marked downturn in the Norwegian economy as a result of the sharp fall in oil prices. At the monetary policy meeting in March, emphasis was placed on the fact that developments in the Norwegian economy over the winter had been broadly in line with expectations. Inflation had remained close to 2.5 per cent and unemployment had remained stable. The impact on the real economy of the fall in oil prices had so far been small. Nevertheless, the outlook for the Norwegian economy weakened somewhat in December. Oil prices had continued to fall, and the accompaniment in the petroleum industry seemed to be declining more than expected . Wage growth in 2014 was lower than assumed in December, and there were prospects that wage growth in the period ahead will also be lower than projected . This weakens the driver of inflation further ahead. In our latest report, we emphasized that house prices have rapidly increased. This may make households more vulnerable and may trigger or amplify a downturn in the economy further ahead in d. An overall assessment by the Executive Board at the March meeting is that the key policy rate should be kept unchanged at 1.25 percent. It was also emphasised that if developments in the economy in the period ahead are broadly in line with projections, there are prospects that the key policy rate will be reduced so much. The analyses in Monetary Policy Report 1/15 imply a key policy rate of about 1 per cent over the next few years. You are the interest rate estimated to increase gradually. With such a development in the key policy rate, the analyses in the report suggest that inflation will increase somewhat in the coming quarters before decreasing and remain above 2 per cent during the projection period. Capacity growth in the mainland economy is considered to be slowing somewhat before it recovers towards a more normal level against sluggish one of the projection periods. Let me cancel. Since last summer, oil prices have almost halved. The fall in prices comes on top of a planned rescheduling of a lower level of oil prices in the oil sector. In other countries, deliveries to oil activities in other countries may be lost. So far, the effects on the mainland economy have been fairly small. Nevertheless, the Norwegian economy must now see lower demand from the oil sector and lower petroleum revenues. The transition to an oil-driven economy with high wage capacity has been a pleasant journey. The return, where the supplier industry will shrink and other competitive activities must emerge, will be more demanding. But the starting point for dealing with the restructuring is good. We have room for manoeuvre in economic policing. Inflation expectations are firmly anchored, and the krone exchange rate acts as a stabiliser. And perhaps most importantly, Norwegian businesses and the social partners have shown more abilities in the field. It will be decisive this time, too. Thank you for your attention. Figur: Lnnskostnader rela vt l handelspartnerne Svekkelsen av kronen bidrar l  holde inasjonen oppe og demper utslagene i norsk konomi av en lavere oljepris. Selv om kostnadsnivet i Norge fortsa er hyt sammenliknet med andre land, bidrar en svakere krone l  styrke konkurranseevnen for norske bedri er som mter konkurranse fra utlandet. Sam dig har lnnsveksten her hjemme avta , og det er utsikter l at reallnnsveksten i r blir den svakeste p 20 r. Figur: Fastlandseksporten og importvekst hos handelspartnerne Bedret konkurranseevne de siste to rene som flge av svakere krone, gjr eksportbedri ene bedre i stand l  oppre holde sine markedsandeler. Eksporten fra Fastlands-Norge utenom oljevirksomheten vil dermed kunne ke i takt med at e ersprselen fra eksportmarkedene ltar y erligere. Sam dig vil den petroleumsrelaterte eksporten kunne dempes av svakere utvikling i globale oshoreinvesteringer. Figur: Arbeidsledighet Det vil trolig ta d fr virkningene av lavere oljepris kommer fullt ut l syne i fastlandskonomien. Et eksibelt arbeidsmarked ser ut l  begrense oppgangen i arbeidsledigheten. S langt har ledigheten kt lite p landsbasis. Men vi ser sam dig en mer markert kning i regioner og nringer som er nrt lkny et oljevirksomheten. Veksten i sysselse ngen har s langt holdt seg oppe, men ulike forventningsindikatorer peker i retning av lav sysselse ngsvekst fremover. Ogs forholdet mellom antall arbeidsledige og ledige s llinger indikerer at arbeidsmarkedet er bli mindre stramt. Fremover venter vi at arbeidsledigheten vil ke noe. Svakere vekstutsikter og fortsa usikkerhet om den konomiske utviklingen kan f bedri er l  holde igjen p investeringsbeslutninger. P den andre siden vil bedret konkurransekra gi grunnlag for  ke produksjonskapasiteten i deler av nringslivet. I llegg ser det ut l at boliginvesteringene vil bidra l  holde den samlede investeringsak viteten oppe. Figur: Husholdningene De siste rene har husholdningenes konsum kt moderat, og spareraten har kommet opp p et hyt niv p tross av det lave rentenivet. Pensjonsreformen, hy arbeidsinnvandring og usikkerhet om den konomiske utviklingen har trolig bidra l kt sparing. Husholdningenes llitsindikatorer har holdt seg p lave niver siden hsten i or. I llegg vil trolig lavere reallnnsvekst dempe husholdningenes kjpekra . Det er derfor utsikter l fortsa moderat vekst i konsumet og hy sparing. Figur: Boligpriser og kredi Gjennom ere r, har hye oljeinntekter og omfa ende ringvirkninger fra oljesektoren drevet opp boligpriser og husholdningenes gjeld. Gjelden har vokst langt raskere enn inntektene. Fortsa lave renter kan ke risikoen for at gjeld og formuespriser s ger l niver som ikke kan oppre holdes over d. Sam dig vil utsikter l svakere inntektsvekst og noe hyere arbeidsledighet e er hvert kunne dempe veksten i boligprisene. Norges Bank vektlegger hensynet l nansiell stabilitet i rentese ngen. Siktemlet er  unng en br nedgang i konomien og kt arbeidsledighet p et senere dspunkt. Det har frt l at vi dvis har valgt  holde styringsrenten li hyere enn dersom vi ikke hadde hensynta risikobildet. Vi har lent oss li mot vinden. Figur: Handelspartnernes terminrenter En liten pen konomi som den norske pvirkes i stor grad av den konomiske utviklingen ute. Veksten i verdenskonomien har ta seg noe opp de siste par rene, men bildet er blandet. I euroomrdet er ak viteten i ferd med  ke, men veksten og inasjonen er fremdeles lav. Husholdningenes forbruk ker og det er tegn l at bedri enes investeringer vil lta fremover. Sam dig vil trolig hy arbeidsledighet og videre nedbelning i privat og oentlig sektor bidra l  dempe ak viteten i lang d. I USA har oppgangen f godt feste, selv om amerikanerne i r, som i or, ser ut l  ha opplevd en avdemping i frste kvartal. En ekspansiv pengepoli kk ser ut l  virke, og bde forbruk og investeringer har ta seg opp. Arbeidsledigheten har kommet ned. kt ak vitet i konomien har bidra l at underskuddet p statsbudsje et er betydelig redusert. Ogs i Storbritannia og Sverige, som er store mo akere av norsk eksport, er det posi ve utviklingstrekk. Men lav inasjon er en u ordring. Styringsrentene er nr null i mange land og forventes  vre lave lenge. Gjennom vinteren har ere utenlandske sentralbanker tydd l nye ukonvensjonelle ltak for  s mulere ak viteten og motvirke faren for deasjon. Markedsaktrenes forven nger l styringsrentene har falt videre. Lave renter ute pvirker utviklingen i kronen og dermed utsiktene for inasjonen, og bidrar l lave renter ogs her hjemme. Figur: Anslag Pengepoli sk rapport 1/15 Utsiktene for norsk konomi svekket seg alts gjennom hsten i or. I desember i or ku et Norges Bank styringsrenten med 0,25 prosentenheter, l 1,25 prosent for  redusere risikoen for en markert nedgang i norsk konomi som flge av det kra ige fallet i oljeprisen. I rentemtet i mars ble det lagt vekt p at utviklingen i norsk konomi gjennom vinteren hadde vrt om lag som ventet. Prisveksten hadde holdt seg nr 2,5 prosent og arbeidsledigheten hadde holdt seg stabil. Utslagene i realkonomien av oljeprisfallet hadde s langt vrt rela vt sm. Utsiktene for norsk konomi var likevel noe svekket i forhold l desember. Oljeprisen hadde falt videre, og ak viteten i petroleumsnringen s ut l  avta mer enn dligere anta . Lnnsveksten i 2014 ble lavere enn lagt l grunn i desember, og det var utsikter l at veksten i lnningene ogs fremover blir lavere enn dligere ansl . Det svekker drivkre ene for inasjonen lenger frem. Sam dig la vi i vr siste rapport vekt p at boligprisene har fortsa  ke. Det kan gjre husholdningene mer srbare og kan utlse eller forsterke et lbakeslag i konomien lenger frem i d. E er en samlet vurdering beslu et hovedstyret p marsmtet at styringsrenten holdes uendret p 1,25 prosent. Det ble sam dig understreket at dersom utviklingen i konomien fremover blir om lag som ansl , er det utsikter l at styringsrenten vil bli sa ned. Analysene i Pengepoli sk rapport 1/15 innebrer en styringsrente p om lag 1 prosent de neste rene. Dere er er renten ansl  ke gradvis. Med en slik utvikling i styringsrenten lsier analysene i rapporten at prisveksten vil ke noe de nrmeste kvartalene fr den avtar og blir liggende li over 2 prosent utover i prognoseperioden. Kapasitetsutny ngen i fastlandskonomien vurderes  avta noe fr den ltar mot et mer normalt niv mot slu en av prognoseperioden. La meg avslu e. Siden i or sommer er oljeprisen nr halvert. Prisfallet kommer p toppen av en planlagt oms lling l et lavere ak vitetsniv i oljesektoren. Sam dig kan leveranser l oljevirksomheten i andre land falle bort. S langt har eektene p fastlandskonomien vrt noks sm. Likevel m norsk konomi n lpasse seg lavere e ersprsel fra oljesektoren og lavere oljeinntekter. Overgangen l en oljedrevet konomi med hy lnnsevne har vrt en behagelig reise. Returen, hvor leverandrnringen skal krympe og annen konkurranseutsa virksomhet m vokse frem, blir mer krevende. Men utgangspunktet for  hndtere oms llingene er godt. Vi har handlingsrom i den konomiske poli kken. Inasjonsforventningene er godt forankret, og kronekursen fungerer som en stabilisator. Og kanskje aller vik gst: Norsk nringsliv og partene i arbeidslivet har dligere vist evner l oms lling. Det blir avgjrende ogs denne gangen. Takk for oppmerksomheten. PUBLISERT 16. april 2015 18:00

Title: Management of the Government Pension Fund Global
text: Management of the Government Pension Fund Global Director Yngve Slyngstad. Introduction to consultation on the management of the Government Pension Fund Global 2014 in the Executive Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs. The hearing will be broadcast live on Stor nget's ne pages Subject to changes during the performance. Thank you to the chairman of the committee, and for giving me the opportunity to talk about our stewardship in 2014. Chart: Return on the Fund The return on the Government Pension Fund Global was 7.6 per cent measured in international currency, equivalent to NOK 544 billion. Since 1998, the fund has an annual return of 5.8 percent. E is a deduction of inflation and costs, the real return on the first krone has been 3.8 per cent. The through-the-crown has a real return of 4.5 per cent. The return has been solid in recent years, but we must also be prepared for periods of decline in value. Chart: Accumulated change in market value At the end of the first quarter of this year, the fund had a market value of NOK 7 012 billion. Since its establishment in 1996, the fund has invested NOK 3 459 billion. The return has been NOK 2 743 billion. Inlay comes movements in the krone exchange rate. The return represents a significantly larger share of the fund's market value today than it was a few years ago. We aim to create added value in our management of the fund. Compared with the benchmark indices against which the fund is measured, the excess return is 0.25 percentage point per year since 1998 until the end of 2014. In 2014, the return was 0.8 percentage point lower than the return on the benchmark index. They can mainly be explained by a higher proportion of European equities and a shorter duration of the fund's fixed income investments compared to the benchmark index. Figure: Forvaltningsmal Our goal is to achieve the highest possible return in the long term, with an acceptable level of risk. We attach great importance to being a responsible investor, and that is an integral part of our management assignment. We have a good management with low costs, and emphasize as much transparency as possible about the management of the fund. They are strategic choices that influence how we manage the fund. Chart: Three pillars of responsible investment As part of this transparency, we have this year a separate report on our work on responsible investment in 2014. The steady work is up about the management's target ng  the highest possible return in acceptable risk. The work is based on three main principles: We will help improve the standards for corporate governance, we will exercise our ownership rights responsibly, and we will monitor and manage the risk in the fund's investments. International standards are particularly important for us as a minority shareholder. If we are to have a breakthrough, we must assume norms that other shareholders will also emphasise. We are steadily developing selected international standards, and place particular emphasis on standards anchored in bodies such as the UN and the OECD. In 2014, for example, we provided input from the OECD on the development of the OECD principles for corporate governance. We steady are also more limited standards. We are a member of the Carbon Disclosure Project, which aims to improve company reporting on climate risk. Furthermore, this year we have launched a new expectation document on climate. We are here to explain to companies our starting point and what our expectations are. We are the owner and minority shareholder in more than 9000 companies. Our increasing ownership interest in individual companies has meant that more is expected of us as an owner. We place great emphasis on voting, contact with companies and analysis of the companies in order to safeguard the fund's value. We also need to make priorities in order for ownership work to have the best possible effect. We will have a good contact with the boards, and have participated in nomination processes on companies' boards. Our voting is available on our pages together with the inventory lists. This year, we are increasing this transparency by publicly announcing our voting intentions in advance of the general meeting of some peers. Sam dig we publicly explain our mo vation and justification. We believe they can give us greater impact. Chart: Environment-related mandates Through the fund's environment-related mandates, we invest extra in environmental technology. At the end of 2014, we had NOK 42 billion invested in environment-related equity mandates. We also invest in so-called green bonds. We invest in companies in various areas, such as low-emission energy solutions and alterna ve fuels; energy-affect display; and natural resource management. The return on the environment-related mandates was 5.0 per cent, which was somewhat lower than the return on the fund as a whole in 2014. We must be prepared for the fact that the return on these investments may fluctuate more than the fund as a whole and the broad equity market. The Ministry of Finance plans to increase the limit for environment-related mandates somewhat. The environment-related mandates are currently concentrated in parts of the equity market that may be suitable for management. Our managers have achieved better results than the environmental indices we use as a benchmark. Nevertheless, the environment-related mandates have a return of 7 per cent annually than the fund's benchmark indices for equities since inception in 2009. The environment-related mandates increase the distance in the benchmark index and thereby the real risk in the management of the fund. The Ministry plans to increase the limit for real fluctuations in 1.25 percentage points, which is appropriate when the limit for environment-related mandates is also increased. Chart: Divestment and undisclosing of companies In 2014, we fast-moving our work on risk-based divestments. Some sectors have special environmental and social implications. Based on a financial overall assessment, we can divest from individual companies. In the last three years, we have divested out of a total of 114 companies based on such reviews. Chart: Risk-based divestments in recent years So far this year, we have issued y-12 companies. In recent years, we have looked specifically at deforestation, water and greenhouse gas emissions. Chart: The fund's holdings in coal extraction At the end of 2014, the fund had only smaller holdings in coal mining. Furthermore, at the beginning of the year we have sold ourselves down in some of these companies. The fund is quickly invested in companies where coal is only one of several business areas, including large mining conglomerates. Chart: Fund holdings in selected sectors The fund is also invested in companies in kra supply and oil and gas extraction. At the end of the first quarter of 2015 the fund had NOK 228 billion invested in companies in oil and gas extraction, NOK 109 billion in kra supply and NOK 31 billion in general mining. Chart: Kra supply and energy sources Companies in the field of kra supply beny are o e several different energy sources. We've sent letters to our largest companies in the field of kra supply. We are asking for a strategy and ds line to phase coal out of the crag production. Chart: Letter l companies in general mining We have also sent letters to the largest companies in general mining. Here we are asking for a strategy for transition into a low-carbon energy system. We also raise questions about separating the coal business out of the company. Chart: New real estate investments in 2014 The fund's real estate investments are growing rapidly. In 2014, we started buying properties in the US and Europe. We've never made as many real estate investments as we have in or. The share of the fund invested in real estate increased by 2.2 per cent over the year, and we will in the next few years accelerate to increase investments in real estate. In order to achieve the objectives, we have set up a separate management team for real estate management that will build up a separate organisation in the Bank for real estate investments. The strategy is to invest in big cities in the US, in Europe and in Asia. We plan to invest about 1 per cent of the fund in real estate each of the next few years. An assessment of the 5 percent limit is therefore appropriate. Increased investments in real estate and any infrastructure may contribute to improving the relationship between risk and return in the fund. Our task as manager of the fund is to preserve and further develop the financial wealth that belongs to the Norwegian people. We do them in a responsible way, so that both today's and future generations benefit from oil wealth. 4 May 2015 10:15
text_original: FOREDRAG Forvaltningen av Statens pensjonsfond utland Direktr Yngve Slyngstad. Innledning l hring om forvaltningen av Statens pensjonsfond utland 2014 i Stor ngets nanskomit. Hringen overfres direkte p Stor ngets ne sider Med forbehold om endringer under fremfringen. Takk l komiteens leder, og for at jeg fr anledning l  snakke om vr forvaltning i 2014. Figur: Fondets avkastning Avkastningen for Statens pensjonsfond utland var i or 7,6 prosent mlt i internasjonal valuta, lsvarende 544 milliarder kroner. Siden 1998 har fondet ha en rlig avkastning p 5,8 prosent. E er fradrag av inasjon og kostnader har realavkastningen p den frste kronen vrt p 3,8 prosent. Gjennomsni skronen har ha en realavkastning p 4,5 prosent. Avkastningen har i de siste rene vrt god, men vi m ogs vre forberedt p perioder med verdifall. Figur: Akkumulert endring av markedsverdi Ved utgangen av frste kvartal i r hadde fondet en markedsverdi p 7 012 milliarder kroner. Siden etableringen i 1996 er fondet lfrt 3 459 milliarder kroner. Avkastningen har vrt 2 743 milliarder kroner. I llegg kommer kronekursbevegelser. Avkastningen utgjr en betydelig strre andel av fondets markedsverdi i dag enn for noen r siden. Vi har som ml  skape merverdi i vr forvaltning av fondet. Sammenlignet med referanseindeksene som fondet mles mot, er meravkastningen 0,25 prosentpoeng per r siden 1998 og frem l utgangen av 2014. I 2014 isolert se var avkastningen 0,8 prosentpoeng lavere enn referanseindeksens avkastning. De e kan i hovedsak forklares av en hyere andel europeiske aksjer og en kortere varighet p fondets renteinvesteringer sammenlignet med referanseindeksen. Figur: Forvaltningsml Vrt ml er  oppn hyest mulig avkastning p lang sikt, med et akseptabelt niv p risiko. Vi legger stor vekt p  vre en ansvarlig investor, og det er en integrert del av vrt forvaltningsoppdrag. Vi har en eek v forvaltning med lave kostnader, og legger vekt p strst mulig penhet om forvaltningen. De e er strategiske valg som preger hvordan vi forvalter fondet. Figur: Tre brebjelker i ansvarlig forvaltning Som ledd i denne penheten, har vi i r gi ut en egen rapport om vrt arbeid med ansvarlig forvaltning i 2014. De e arbeidet st er opp om forvaltningens mlse ng  hyest mulig avkastning l akseptabel risiko. Arbeidet bygger p tre hovedprinsipper: Vi vil vre med og forbedre standardene for virksomhetsstyring, vi vil utve eierskapet vrt p en ansvarlig mte, og vi vil overvke og hndtere risikoen i fondets investeringer. Internasjonale standarder er spesielt vik g for oss som minoritetsaksjonr. Hvis vi skal ha gjennomslagskra , m vi legge l grunn normer som ogs vrige aksjonrer vil vektlegge. Vi st er utviklingen av utvalgte internasjonale standarder, og legger srlig vekt p standarder forankret i organer slik som FN og OECD. Vi gir faglige innspill og annen type st e. I 2014 leverte for eksempel innspill l OECD om utviklingen av OECDs prinsipper for selskapsstyring. Vi st er ogs mer avgrensede standarder. Vi medlem av Carbon Disclosure Project som har som ml  forbedre selskapsrapporteringen om klimarisiko. Videre har vi i r lansert et ny forventningsdokument p klima. De e beny er vi for  forklare selskaper vrt utgangspunkt og hva vre forventninger er. Vi er eier og minoritetsaksjonr i mer enn 9000 selskaper. Vr kende eierandel i enkeltselskaper har medfrt at det forventes mer av oss som eier. Vi legger stor vekt p stemmegivning, selskapskontakt og analyse av selskapene for  sikre verdiene i fondet. Vi er ogs avhengige av  gjre prioriteringer for at eierskapsarbeidet skal ha best mulig eekt. Vi vil ha en te ere kontakt med styrene, og har i utvalgte lfeller delta i nominasjonsprosesser l selskapers styrer. Vr stemmegivning er lgjengelig p vre ne sider sammen med beholdningslistene. I r ker vi denne penheten ved at vi oentligjr vre stemmeintensjoner i forkant av generalforsamlingen i enkelte lfeller. Sam dig forklarer vi oentlig vr mo vasjon og begrunnelse. Vi mener de e kan gi oss strre gjennomslagskra . Figur: Miljrelaterte mandater Gjennom fondets miljrelaterte mandater investerer vi ekstra i miljteknologi. Ved utgangen av 2014 hadde vi 42 milliarder kroner investert i miljrelaterte aksjemandater. Vi investerer ogs i skalte grnne obligasjoner. Vi investerer i selskaper innen ulike omrder, slik som lav-utslipp energilsninger og alterna ve drivstoer; energieek visering; og naturressursforvaltning. Avkastningen av de miljrelaterte mandatene var i or 5,0 prosent, som var noe lavere enn avkastningen p fondet totalt se i 2014. Vi m vre forberedt p at avkastningen p disse investeringene vil kunne svinge mer enn fondet totalt se og det brede aksjemarkedet. Finansdepartementet legger opp l  ke rammen for miljrelaterte mandater noe. De miljrelaterte mandatene er i dag konsentrert l deler av aksjemarkedet som kan egne seg godt for ak v forvaltning. Vre forvaltere har oppndd bedre resultater enn miljindeksene vi beny er som mlestokk. Likevel har miljmandatene ha 7 prosent rlig lavere avkastning enn fondets referanseindekser for aksjer siden oppstart i 2009. De miljrelaterte mandatene ker avstanden l referanseindeksen og dermed den rela ve risikoen i forvaltningen. Departementet legger opp l  ke rammen for rela ve svingninger l 1,25 prosentenheter, noe som er hensiktsmessig nr rammen for miljrelaterte mandater ogs kes. Figur: Nedsalg og u rekk av selskaper I 2014 fortsa e vi vrt arbeid med risikobaserte nedsalg. Enkelte sektorer har srskilte milj- og samfunnsmessige u ordringer. Basert p en nansiell helhetsvurdering kan vi selge oss ut av enkeltselskaper. De siste tre rene har vi solgt oss ut av totalt 114 selskaper basert p slike vurderinger. Figur: Risikobaserte nedsalg de siste rene S langt i r har vi ta ut y erligere 12 selskaper. Vi har de siste rene se spesielt p avskoging, vann og klimagassutslipp. Figur: Fondets beholdninger innen kullutvinning Fondet hadde ved utgangen av 2014 kun mindre beholdninger innen kullutvinning. Videre har vi i starten av de e ret solgt oss ned i enkelte av disse selskapene. Fondet er fortsa investert i selskaper der kull kun er e av ere forretningsomrder, blant annet i store gruvekonglomerater. Figur: Fondets beholdninger i utvalgte sektorer Fondet er ogs investert i selskaper innen kra forsyning og olje- og gassutvinning. Ved utgangen av frste kvartal 2015 hadde fondet 228 milliarder kroner investert i selskaper innen olje- og gassutvinning, 109 milliarder kroner innen kra forsyning og 31 milliarder kroner innen generell gruvedri . Figur: Kra forsyning og energikilder Selskaper innen kra forsyning beny er o e ere ulike energikilder. Vi har sendt brev l vre strste selskaper innen kra forsyning. Vi e erspr en strategi og dslinje for  fase kull ut av kra produksjonen. Figur: Brev l selskaper innen generell gruvedri Vi har ogs sendt brev l de strste selskapene innen generell gruvedri . Her e erspr vi en strategi for overgang l et lavkarbon energisystem. Vi tar ogs opp sprsml om  skille kullvirksomheten ut av selskapet. Figur: Nye eiendomsinvesteringer i 2014 Innslaget av eiendomsinvesteringer i fondet er i sterk vekst. I 2014 fortsa e vi  kjpe eiendommer i USA og Europa. Vi har aldri gjort s mange eiendomsinvesteringer som i or. Andelen av fondet som er investert i eiendom kte l 2,2 prosent i lpet av ret, og vi vil de neste rene fortse e  ke investeringene i eiendom. For  n mlene har vi oppre et en egen ledergruppe for eiendomsforvaltningen som skal bygge opp en egen organisasjon i banken for eiendomsinvesteringene. Strategien er  investere i storbyer i USA, i Europa og e er hvert i Asia. Vi legger opp l  investere om lag 1 prosent av fondet i eiendom hvert av de neste rene. En vurdering av 5 prosent-grensen er derfor hensiktsmessig. kte investeringer i eiendom og eventuelt infrastruktur kan bidra l  bedre forholdet mellom risiko og avkastning i fondet. Vr oppgave som forvalter av fondet er  ta vare p og videreutvikle den nansielle formuen som lhrer det norske folk. Vi gjr de e p en ansvarlig mte, slik at bde dagens og frem dige generasjoner fr nyte godt av oljeformuen. PUBLISERT 4. mai 2015 10:15

Title: Economic perspectives
text: SPEECH Economic perspec ves Address by Governor oystein Olsen to foreign embassy representa ves in Oslo, 5 March 2015. An oil-driven economy To Norway, the sea has always been of great importance. It has been our lifeblood, and it has been a main artery. Fishing, shipping and trade have been a source of living for many. With its changing face and magical power, it has also inspired ar sts. As the well-known 19th century novelist Alexander Kielland wrote: "Nothing is so boundless as the sea, nothing so pa ent." 1 Kielland, who was born and raised in Stavanger, could hardly suspect the inconceivable wealth the sea was so pa ently concealing under the sea floor. Chart: GDP per capita in 1971 The discovery of oil was the start of an amazing era for the Norwegian economy. When the first oil was brought to the surface in 1971, income levels in Norway were low compared with other western countries. Chart: GDP per capita in 2013 The picture has reversed since then. We have gradually caught up to the wealthiest na ons. Measured by GDP per capita, Norway now ranks at the top. From the beginning, it was established that the oil and gas resources belong to the Norwegian people. The tax system and framework condi ons for the petroleum industry were designed so that the large revenues would accrue to the state. The stage was set for greater prosperity, with prospects for growth in both public and private consump on. Developing a new industry and spending the associated revenues also entailed challenges. The challenges were discussed in a white paper in 1974, Report no. 25 to the Stor ng, en tled "The role of the petroleum industry in Norwegian society". If room was to be provided for supplying the oil sector other industries would have to give way. The changes would come about through domes c cost pressures. Wage earners would find be er paid jobs, while companies who could not bear increased costs, would be forced to downscale. The country was indeed braced for structural changes and the a endant costs. But the white paper made it clear that restructuring was a necessary precondi on for reaping the benefits of economic growth. We now know, more than 40 years later, that the structural changes did indeed come to pass. The industry structure of our economy has changed. A growing number of firms, not only manufacturing companies, have targeted the oil industry. Labour shedding in some sectors has released labour for other uses. Chart: Wages per full- me equivalent (FTE) by industry Oil companies have shown the capacity and the willingness to pay. Tax rules have favoured investment spending. Earnings have been solid. The companies' employees have been wage winners here in Norway. A state-of-art oil service industry has emerged. New products and technological solu ons have been developed. For many, the contracts on the Norwegian con nental shelf have been a springboard to new export markets. The oil and gas industry has been decisive for the strong growth in the Norwegian economy over the past 40 years. The past 15 years stand out. From the end of the 1990s, the price of North Sea oil rose from about USD 10 per barrel to over USD 100 per barrel. Chart: Business investment High oil prices and a profitable petroleum produc on industry have been accompanied by record-high oil investment in recent years. The level in 2014 was equivalent to total investment in domes c non-oil industries. Employment has remained high and unemployment low, even when the financial crisis hit in 2008. The Norwegian economy has made use of the tailwinds and seized the opportuni es offered. The other side of the coin is an economy that has become increasingly dependent on oil, and thereby more vulnerable to changes in oil prices and petroleum revenues. About 1 in 9 jobs in Norway, a total of 300 000, are linked to the oil industry.2 Exports from Norway to the oil industry in other countries account for a growing share of this ac vity. Chart: Labour costsrela ve to trading partners Moreover, labour costs in Norway have reached high levels. The cost level in the business sector has increased sharply in rela on to our trading partners. With lower ac vity and earnings from the petroleum sector, oil service companies must seek other markets, which may be demanding with a high cost level. From a unique economic posi on to restructuring Oil prices have fallen by nearly 50 percent since last summer. The price decline comes on top of a planned adjustment to a lower ac vity level in the Norwegian oil sector. Low growth in the world economy has restrained growth in oil consump on, while the high prices prevailing in recent years have led to increased supply and more energy-efficient produc on methods. Last year, growth in global oil demand hit a five-year low, while non-OPEC produc on was record-high. Chart: US crude oil produc on New shale oil extrac on technology has boosted the global supply of oil. Over three years, US oil produc on rose by more than 50 percent. The addi onal supply from US shale oil is more than twice as high as Norwegian oil produc on. Looking ahead, we must prepare ourselves for an environment of lower oil prices compared with the levels seen in recent years. It would be unwise to act on the assump on that oil prices will again se le around USD 100 per barrel. This does not mean that Norway's oil age is coming to an end. Nearly half of known oil and gas reserves on the Norwegian con nental shelf have not yet been extracted.3 Over the past few years, large new discoveries have been made. One of them  Johan Sverdrup  is soon ready for development. The Norwegian oil service industry can expect new orders. Nonetheless, the Norwegian economy must adapt to considerably lower demand from the oil sector. From being in a unique economic posi on, Norway now faces a period of restructuring. The Norwegian business sector showed a high degree of willingness and ability to shi to oil-related ac vity during the boom. The shi to an oil-driven economy with a high wage capacity has been a comfortable journey. The journey forward, where the oil service industry must downscale and other trade-exposed industries must grow, will be more challenging. Chart: Labour costsrela ve to trading partners A er many years of rela vely high wage growth in Norway, the domes c cost level must again be brought more into line with that of our trading partners. A necessary adjustment of the cost level in Norway can occur by two means; lower wage growth in Norway than in other countries and a deprecia on of the krone exchange rate. The economic policy pursued will be of importance for how the adjustment takes place. Without our own na onal currency the situa on would be more challenging. The social partners would then have to do the job alone. The experience of other countries shows that this can be demanding. Chart: Labour costsrela ve to trading partners with 2015 With a floa ng exchange rate, the necessary adjustment of the cost level can take place faster, and may prove less painful. The krone exchange rate can func on as a stabiliser. The deprecia on of the krone through autumn last year indicates that this mechanism is func oning. The monetary policy credibility built up over the years is now of considerable benefit. Con nued confidence that infla on will remain low and stable over me is a necessary precondi on for a pronounced weakening of the krone concurrent with a low key policy rate. The benefit associated with a currency of our own disappears if the temporary rise in infla on associated with a krone deprecia on is countered by higher wage increases. The result would be a higher key policy rate and a stronger exchange rate than would otherwise be the case and, not least, higher unemployment. The social partners have a par cular responsibility in this regard. Norwegian government finances are solid. This has been of great benefit, par cularly during the financial crisis. It may be temp ng to increase public spending to so en the impact of a fall in oil prices on the real economy. The risk is that this may hold back the restructuring needed if oil prices remain low for a long period. Increased public spending may push up the cost of labour and crowd out other exposed industries. When the economy meets a severe downturn, with a pronounced rise in unemployment, fiscal policy can help support economic ac vity. But the Norwegian economy is presently far from being in a crisis situa on. Unemployment remains low. The interna onal economic picture is mixed Six years have now passed since the global economy was severely hit by the financial crisis. The Norwegian economy quickly rebounded, supported by robust public finances and strong growth in the petroleum sector. Other advanced economies have experienced a more difficult me. Excessive debt, in both the private and public sector, has led to weak ac vity and high unemployment in many of those countries. Chart: Gross domes c product The situa on in the euro area appears to be par cularly problema c. A large por on of the workforce is idle alongside produc on equipment. Infla on is worryingly low. Elevated uncertainty surrounding economic developments, high corporate debt and ght bank credit standards are holding back the willingness and ability to invest. The result is a selfreinforcing mechanism that is difficult to escape. Even though growth in the world economy is gradually picking up, it is unlikely that we will again see the high growth rates observed in the years prior to the financial crisis. Perhaps this is not something to wish for either. Recent high growth was partly driven by unsustainable borrowing. Chart: Produc vity growth in the OECD area Several condi ons suggest that the tradi onal advanced economies are facing more deep-rooted challenges. Produc vity growth has declined since the 1970s. Through several decades to the end of the 20th century, an expanding labour force and higher educa on a ainment contributed to driving the economy forward. Growth was accompanied by solid returns and considerably higher real interest rates than observed in recent years. These growth impulses are fading away. The labour force is expanding at a slower pace in many countries. If produc vity and labour force par cipa on do not increase by a considerable margin, the return on fixed investment will fall. Low growth and low real interest rates may be the new norm. The Government Pension Fund Global  further growth depends on future returns Over the past 20 years, Norway has accumulated considerable foreign financial assets. The Government Pension Fund Global (GPFG) represents our collec ve savings and is to be managed to the benefit of both current and future genera ons. As an investor, the fund makes capital available for economic ac vity in other countries. The return on our capital will thereby be a result of the value added in those countries. So far, our na on has earned a solid return on its financial assets. The cumula ve return on the fund since its incep on amounts to over NOK 2 000 billion. This is equivalent to about a third of the fund capital at the end of 2014. Chart: Exports and the GPFG's dividend, interest and rental income Given its increasing size, the fund's cash flow  dividend and interests - has also become substan al, and is now higher than the revenues from major exports such as fish and metals. Chart: Interna onal real interest rates Over a third of the fund is invested in bonds. The real interest rate on high-grade government bonds is the star ng point for calcula ng the rate of return. In recent years, those yields have been close to zero. Historically, equi es have yielded higher returns than bonds. We also expect that to be the case ahead. But it is doub ul that equity prices will con nue to rise at the same pace as in recent years. Weak or moderate growth in the real economy will feed through to the return on equi es. So far, the fund has earned an annual real return of 3.8 percent. We must be prepared for the possibility that it will be lower, perhaps below 3 percent. Chart: Petroleum revenues and petroleum revenue spending Since the turn of the millennium, the government has received substan al revenues from the petroleum sector. A large share has been saved and transferred to the pension fund. At the same me, the spending of petroleum revenues over the fiscal budget has increased. The revenue stream from the con nental shelf is now declining. Chart: Transfers to GPFG We are approaching the point where government spending of petroleum revenues will exceed the revenues deriving from the petroleum sector. At today's oil price, transfers to the fund will quickly fall towards zero, soon leading to a situa on where its current income is limited to interest and dividend income. Next year, it may be necessary to spend some of the return to cover the non-oil budget deficit. The GPFG is nearing the peak The decline in oil revenues ahead gives rise to new challenges for the Norwegian economy. But we must not forget that we have a good star ng point. During a period of high oil prices, we have transformed oil in the ground into financial wealth. We have avoided making public sector budgets dependent on vola le income. The fund and the fiscal rule have been the main elements of the policy pursued. Under the fiscal rule, government spending over the annual budget, on average over an economic cycle, should equal the expected real return on the Fund  es mated at 4 percent annually. This way, the capital will also benefit future genera ons. Recent years have been characterised by wide fluctua ons in returns, with extreme variability during the financial crisis. Vola lity on the world's stock exchanges and in financial markets impacts the market value of the fund and thereby the anchor for fiscal policy. Although the deprecia on of the krone has increased the fund's current value in krone terms, this veils the fact that its interna onal purchasing power is unaffected by changes in the krone's value. Such vola lity has become more difficult to manage as the fund has grown in size. At an oil price of around USD 60 per barrel, transfers to the fund may come to a halt. Rather, it seems that at today's level of petroleum revenue spending there will soon be a need to make transfers from the fund to the fiscal budget. Measured as a share of GDP, the oil fund may have already reached the peak. Chart: Different return and oil price scenarios for the GPFG The broken red line shows the trajectory for fiscal space assuming a real return of 4 percent. The es ma on is based on the oil price level prevailing late last summer. If the return is closer to 3 percent, there will be li le room for increasing petroleum revenue spending over the fiscal budget. On the contrary, in the course of a couple of decades, petroleum revenue spending as a share of GDP will have to be reduced. Fiscal policy will have to be ghtened. If the oil price se les more permanently around the level observed so far this year, fiscal policy must be adjusted earlier. If petroleum revenue spending follows the real return, we will be heading for a period of sizeable fiscal retrenchment each year. At the same me, pension obliga ons will show a pronounced rise further ahead. The fall in oil prices has been a reminder of the uncertainty surrounding future petroleum revenues. The same applies to the return on the fund. The three paths illustrate the uncertain es we are facing, but they also illustrate another important point. Spending the return will ul mately lead to a fla ening of the fund capital, which will then decline as a percentage of GDP. It has always been clear that this will happen at some point in the future. What is new is that this may be the case here and now. At today's oil price, the fund may have reached the peak. In that case, petroleum revenue spending as a percentage of GDP must be reduced to avoid using more than the return on the fund. Even if the oil price and the rate of return follow a path that allows the fund to grow for a period ahead, petroleum revenue spending should be restrained. By keeping spending well below the upper bound, the need for fiscal retrenchment further ahead can be reduced. The fiscal rule has func oned as a long-term guideline for fiscal policy for nearly 15 years. It has served its purpose. The me has now come to show restraint. A sensible risk strategy is now to refrain from increasing petroleum revenue spending further from today's level. The era of rising petroleum revenue spending may be behind us. Conclusion The more than forty-year-old white paper on the role of the petroleum industry in Norwegian society was far-sighted and proved to be on the mark. The structural changes described in it have come to pass. The growth in prosperity was more difficult to predict. The development of an advanced oil service industry is an industrial adventure in its own right. We have extracted large quan es of oil and gas at very favourable prices, and have set aside a sizeable por on of the revenues  to the benefit of future genera ons. Norway's oil age is far from over. But ac vity in the petroleum sector has passed the peak. In addi on, we must be prepared for lower returns in the oil industry. The white paper also provides a glimpse into a me when belief in government interven on in the economy was far greater than today. That regulatory op mism has diminished significantly. We are le with an important recogni on: The key to economic progress is the ability to restructure. We cannot rely solely on the sea to carry us forward: Let me again quote Kielland: "It is not true that the sea is faithless, for it has never promised anything..." Where our journey takes us is our own responsibility. Thank you for your a en on. Footnotes 1 1 Alexander Kielland (1880): Garman & Worse (Transla on by W.W. Ke lewell). 2 Es mate based on calcula ons in Blix Prestmo, Strom and Midsem (2015): Ringvirkninger av petroleumsnaeringen i norsk okonomi [Spillovers from the petroleum industry to the Norwegian economy]. Forthcoming report from Sta s cs Norway. Petroleum-related exports from mainland Norway are also included. 3 Including reserves that have been approved for development by holders of oil rights and other proven resources in fields and discoveries. Source: The shelf in 2014, Norwegian Petroleum Directorate 5 March 2015 15:00

Title: Management of the Government Pension Fund Global
text: Management of the Government Pension Fund Global Governor oystein Olsen. Introduction to consultation on the management of the Government Pension Fund Global 2015 in the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs. Hearing on ne -TV (Stor nget, Consultation Hall 1) Subject to changes during the performance. Thank you for your invitation to talk about the management of the Government Pension Fund Global. The framework for the management of the fund ensures a clear division of responsibilities and roles between the owner and the manager. Central frameworks and road choices are anchored in Stor nget and determined by the Ministry of Finance. Norges Bank's role is to manage the fund and advise on further development of the strategy. The mandate from the Ministry of Finance specifies the scope of Norges Bank's management: The Bank shall seek to achieve the highest possible return on capital within specified e limits. The fund has grown and its complexity has increased over d. The Executive Board's role is to follow up the operatic management of the Fund, and to exercise strategic management. The Executive Board's capacity has been expanded. In the autumn, the Executive Board will form two new subcommittees, a risk and investment committee and an ownership committee. Both are headed by the new Deputy Governor. A restructuring system for managing and controlling asset management has been established. The ongoing management has been delegated to Norges Bank Investment Management, which reports on return, risk and compliance with the Executive Board. Internal Audit is the Executive Board's supervisory body. The Supervisory Council has a important role as Stor nget's supervisory and control body. Norges Bank attaches great importance to transparency in the management of the Fund. In the annual report and a separate report on responsible investments, we have two new reports this year  an expanded report on return and risk and a report on unlisted real estate investments. Unlisted investments are one of the topics in this year's big report. The Ministry proposes a comprehensive management of market and foreign exchange risk in the GPFG. The return on unlisted real estate shall now be measured against the return on equities and bonds. At year-end, 2.4 per cent of the fund was invested in unlisted real estate. The properties are owned through then companies. Norges Bank has raised a number of companies in several countries, including the UK, the US and Luxembourg. When choosing jurisdictions, we emphasize whether legal frameworks are predictable and proven. By investing through then companies are accusations that we are the fund against claims that may arise in unlisted investments. Local rules and bilateral agreements are also important. The Executive Board has established principles for handling ska , based on the Bank's mandate from the Ministry of Finance. Norges Bank follows sound market practice and blames the SPU's position as a sovereign wealth fund invested abroad. There is full transparency about Norges Bank's redress and the use of companies in the management of real estate investments. The supervisory bodies, including the Supervisory Council and the Bank's auditor, have full access, in the same way as in other parts of the management of the fund. In a letter to the Ministry of Finance from November, we described the Bank's experience with unlisted real estate investments, investments in partnerships and the use of companies. The letter states that the Bank is investigating the possibility of also cheating Norwegian companies. Finally, I'd like to tie some comments in the fund's results. The annual return on equities and the bond portfolio since inception is 0.25 percentage point e is the first quarter of this year. They are a good result providing the limits that have been established for the management of the fund. Management costs are low and measured as a share of assets in management, they have fallen above d. The costs amounted to 0.06 per cent of the capital in 2015. In the extended return and risk report, in March, the excess return is broken down into overall investment strategies. The report also analyses the costs and compares the return with different measures of risk. The Executive Board believes that the analyses are firmly in line with the conclusion of good management performance. TIME 29 APR 2016 9:30AM
