Title: Management of the Government Pension Fund Global
text: Management of the Government Pension Fund Global Director Yngve Slyngstad. Introduction to consultation on the management of the Government Pension Fund Global 2015 in the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs. Hearing on ne -TV (Stor nget, Consultation Hall 1) Subject to changes during the performance. Thank you to the chairman of the committee, and for giving me the opportunity to talk about our stewardship in 2015. Chart: The fund's annual return The return on the Government Pension Fund Global was 2.7 per cent measured in international currency, equivalent to NOK 334 billion. Since 1998, the fund has an annual return of 5.6 percent. E is a deduction of inflation and costs, the real return on the first krone has been 3.7 per cent. The through-the-crown has a real return of 4.2 per cent. Returns have been solid in recent years, even though the market has been uneasy. Periods of impairment may occur. Chart: Accumulated change in market value At the end of the first quarter of this year, the fund had a market value of NOK 7 079 billion. Since its establishment in 1996, the fund has invested NOK 3 475 billion. The return has been NOK 2 591 billion. Inlay comes movements in the krone exchange rate. In recent years, movements in the krone exchange rate have resulted in a resulting value of the fund measured in NOK. The return represents a significantly larger share of the fund's market value today than it was a few years ago. We aim to create added value in our management of the fund. Compared with the benchmark indices against which the fund is measured, the excess return is 0.26 percentage point per year since 1998 and up to the end of 2015. In 2015, the return was 0.5 percentage point higher than the return on the benchmark index. All our main strategies contributed to the result in 2015. Figure: Forvaltningsmal Our goal is to achieve the highest possible return in the long term, with a moderate level of risk. The e-goal should be achieved with an effek v organization and low costs. We attach great importance to being a responsible investor  as an owner in companies, and as a manager on behalf of the Norwegian people. And we want to be as open as possible. Chart: New expectation document Clear expectations in companies in which we are invested, based on internationally recognised principles, form the basis for our work on responsible investment. We expect companies to take into account a broad and long-range risk picture in their investment plans, risk management and reporting. In 2015, we released a new expectation document on human gheter. They were the result of dialogue with companies, experts and organizations. The document deals with the companies' strategy, risk management, reporting and transparency, and it is a starting point for our dialogue with the companies. Chart: The work on climate change Our work on climate change has been ongoing since 2006. In recent years, we have carried out risk-based divestments in return for, among other things, greenhouse gas emissions and deforestation, including coal companies. We have also started by measuring carbon footprints in the portfolio. In 2015, we initiated various research and analysis to refer to climate risks and consequences for companies and the fund. Chart: 52 coal companies excluded The new product-based coal criterion was introduced in the guidelines for observation and exclusion on 1 February this year. The Bank has already carried out the first exclusions in line with the e. Earlier this month, we announced the exclusion of 52 companies in coal mining and coal crab production. During the year, we will analyse more relevant companies that may be affected by the criterion. And we will publish lists of companies that are excluded in accordance with the product-based coal criterion. Chart: Contributions in public discussion We contribute to an open public discussion on key topics for the Fund. We send letters in the Ministry of Finance on investment strategy. As for the last year, in 2015 we discussion papers supporting the advice we provide. We have also something we call managerperspek ver, which is our input in the development of well-functioning financial markets. Furthermore, we are, as mentioned, expectations documents for companies in which the fund is invested. Our views on key ownership issues are also as notes. For example, here we provide justification for our voting at companies' general meetings. Chart: reports Another important part of our transparency is the public reports on our activities. This year we have three unsubstaged reports in the annual report. Chart: Three pillars of responsible investment In our report on responsible investment in 2015, we describe our accompaniment within standards ng, ac vt ownership and risk management. Chart: Return and risk report 2015 We have also an unprecedented report with information and analysis of the fund's return and risk. The report is a further development of analyses that have been on a regular basis. The report deals with equity and fixed income investments. Yesterday we issued an unprecedented report with information and key figures for the unlisted real estate investments. Figure: Timeline Property This year it has been five years since we completed the first property investment, which was in Regent Street in London. Since then, we have gradually built up our real estate portfolio, with more investments in the largest European markets and the US. Today, we manage a global but concentrated real estate portfolio with investments in selected major cities and global distribution of works. The majority of the investments are in office properties, which are followed by logis kk and trading. By investing in both unlisted and listed real estate, the fund has a broader look at investment opportunities. The distribution between unlisted and listed real estate investments will vary over d and depend on local market conditions. Real estate investments have resulted in broader diversification than investment in equities and interest rates. Chart: New real estate investments in 2015 In 2015, we announced 10 new real estate transactions. They were in the UNITED States, The United Kingdom and in Kon nental-Europe. We are continuing our strategy of investing a few major global cities. The share of the fund invested in real estate increased from 2.2 L 3.1 per cent in 2015. Chart: The fund's current revenues In line with the increase in the fund's value, cash flow from the fund's investments has also increased. This stream consists of equity dividends, interest income and rental income. While interest income dominated, the declining interest rate level internationally has contributed to reversing the e. The fund's market value has increased in recent years. With a large fund, we must expect to see considerable fluctuations ahead. Our task is to manage the people's financial assets in a responsible, efficient and open manner. TIME 29 APR 2016 9:30AM

Good corporate governance and well-functioning boards are important for our ownership strategies. As a shareholder, we are interested in understanding the companies' framework for corporate governance and handling of carrier crashes, in areas such as bold and financing strategy. Clear expectations in companies we are invested in, based on internationally recognised principles, are part of the work. Our expectations are primarily against the companies' boards, and are a starting point for dialogue. In the past, we have expectations documents on children's health, water management, climate change and human rights. Earlier this year we a new expectation document on ska and transparency. We expect mule national companies to have a appropriate, well-considered and open system. Chart: Management costs fall Management costs in the fund are falling rapidly. The downward trend over the past few years has quickly accelerated. Internal management costs accounted for 0.04 per cent of managed capital in 2016. We have extracted significant major benefits in recent years. In recent years, Sam dig has built up real estate management, which costs more per krone managed, compared to equity and fixed income investments. Norges Bank has adopted a strategy plan for the period 2017 in 2019. Our goal is to keep internal management costs below 0.05 per cent of managed capital, even with expected changes in allocation. Chart: All public information can be found on the website In our annual report, we publish unsubstaged information about responsible investment, real estate investments, and return and risk. All public information about the Fund can be found on our website. There are a number of publications, data and background information. We send letters in the Ministry of Finance on investment strategy. These advice is supported by discussion notes. We also publish something we call managerperspek v, which is our input in the development of well-functioning financial markets. In our communication with companies, we are expectations documents, and furthermore, we present our view on key ownership issues through position notes. Earlier this year, for example, we a position paper on executive remuneration. Taken together, they provide a great deal of transparency in the management of the fund. Our task is to manage the people's financial assets in a responsible, efficient and open manner. 2 May 2017 13:00

Title: Who determines the interest rate in Norway?
text: Who determines the interest rate in Norway? Director of Norges Bank Pengepoli kk, Ida Wolden Bache, gives a speech at the Economist Currency Seminar in Oslo. Changes are subject to change during the performance. Thank you for your invitation l to speak at this year's Currency Seminar. The theme this year is "Stabilization policing and u ordnants tie a l financial stability". The role of monetary policy in stabilisation policing and in promoting financial stability is discussed both in Norway and in other countries. At Norges Bank, we have emphasised that the responsibility given to the central bank must be proportional to the opportunities we have in achieving the objectives that are said. And that's the theme of my post here today: What opportunities does monetary policy have in a small open economy l to pursue domestic goals? To what extent can monetary policy dampen fluctuations in the real economy and financial markets in a world where capital flows freely across national borders? Put another way, who really decides the interest rate in Norway? One of the most famous theories in economics is nobel laureate Robert Mundell's so-called "trilemma". A trilemma is a situation where one has to make a choice between three alterna ver, in which each of the altar veins has its inevitable costs. The trilemma in international finance means that a country cannot have both a free flow of capital, a stable exchange rate and an independent monetary policy. According to Mundell, a country can only get two of these: with full capital mobility, the country must choose between an independent monetary policy and a stable exchange rate. If one chooses a stable exchange rate, a co-operative waives the opportunity l see an interest rate based on domestic needs. With a floating exchange rate, monetary policy can play a greater role in stabilisation policing. This was also part of the reason why Norway switched from an exchange rate target in an inflation target in 2001. In the period before the introduction of the inflation target, there had increasingly been a conflict between the objective of keeping the exchange rate stable and the objective of curbing fluctuations in the real economy. The money pole became cocyclical. We last saw this in autumn 1998, when oil prices fell markedly and the interest rate was terminated by 3 percentage points. With the introduction of the inflation target and the fiscal rule for fiscal policy, Norges Bank was given greater responsibility in cyclical targeting. The monetary policy was to be resentment towards low and stable inflation and would contribute to smoothing fluctuations in output and employment. E is the transition to a floating exchange rate, one might expect that the interest rate differential between Norway and trading partners would be larger and vary more over d. As shown in the chart, there has been a terdence between money market rates abroad and in Norway, and the shift in inflation targeting has also been linked. Does this mean that Norwegian interest rates are actually determined in Washington and Frankfurt? Is the choice between free capital flows and an independent monetary policy? Or, in other words, are the authorities in small open economies facing a dilemma, not a trilemma? One who has answered yes to the last question is the French economist Helene Rey. In a at the Jackson Hole Symposium in 2013,[1] she showed the correlation between asset prices, capital flows and creed growth across countries. According to Rey, the financial conditions of a small open economy are determined by the financial conditions of the major international financial centers, regardless of the exchange rate regime. There can be many reasons l that interest rates, and financial conditions more generally, correlate between countries. However, a high correlation does not mean that Mundell's thesis is invalid or that the independence of the monetary policy is illusory. When asked if we have an independent monetary policy in Norway, the answer is an unequivocal yes. We may see a key policy rate that deviates from key rates in other countries; the question is to what extent it is desirable to do so. As a small open economy, Norway are naturally affected by disturbances from abroad and international developments. In a study by researchers at Norges Bank, it is estimated that almost 80 per cent of mainland GDP fluctuations may Norway Iscribed to international relations. [2] It is therefore not unnatural that interest rates in Norway correlate with the interest rates of our trading partners. We are responding to the same disturbances to a large extent. Over the past three years, there has been a trend decline in both nominal and real interest rates internationally. The decline in real interest rates is related to long-term developments that have influenced global saving and investment. Large savings surpluses in emerging economies, particularly in China and oil-exporting countries, have probably been one factor. In many countries, saving has probably increased as a result of a more uneven income distribution and retirement savings among large e-war cohorts. In llegg, manufacturing growth has slowed and resulted in a lower return on real capital. These structural factors are mainly outside the control of central banks and contribute to a correlation between international interest rates regardless of monetary policy. Nevertheless, they have consequences for monetary policy by affecting the level of the real interest rate that is consistent with the balance of the economy, the so-called neutral real interest rate. Economists at the Federal Reserve find that the neutral real interest rate has fallen markedly over the past 25 years in the US, the euro area, the UK and Canada. [3] They find a significant degree of correlation between the es mats on the neutral real interest rate in the countries they are looking at, and interpret them as a sign that common global factors are important for understanding developments in neutral real interest rates. In the shorter term, monetary policy will also be affected by international conditions. Developments abroad influence the outlook for inflation and the real economy in Norway through many channels. Increased demand abroad results in higher demand for Norwegian goods and services, which in turn can increase pressures in the labour market and contribute to higher wage and cost inflation in Norway. Higher wage and price inflation in the countries we trade with will normally result in higher prices for the goods and services we import. This may also result in higher prices for domestically produced goods that compete with imports. In isolation, both higher demand and higher inflation abroad will point to higher interest rates both among our trading partners and in Norway. With a fixed exchange rate, changes in monetary policy abroad will normally affect the interest rate at home closest to the one-L. But also with a floating exchange rate, changes in monetary policy abroad will also affect interest rates in Norway. Some may interpret them as a lack of monetary policy. The fact that interest rates in small open economies are responding to money policy abroad is in line with the current level of monetary policy under an inflation target. A lower interest rate abroad will, all else being equal, cause the Norwegian krone to appreciate. A stronger krone will normally contribute l a slowdown in imported inflation, and lower e demand e are domestically produced goods and services both from abroad and domestically. With an inflation target for monetary policy, Norges Bank will lower the key policy rate to curb the fall in inflation even if we do not have a specific exchange rate target. However, the change in interest rates will typically be less than the one-L. Unlike under a fixed exchange rate regime, some of this will take place through the exchange rate. Unconventional monetary policy may also have forged effects in other countries. When the major central banks buy government bonds, this will put downward pressure on long-term interest rates. The fall in long-term interest rates may result in appreciation pressures on the currencies of other countries, which central banks, for the sake of the domestic economy, may wish to counteract with a lower key policy rate. Unconventional monetary policy may also have forging effects that are not normally matched by exchange rate changes. Lower returns on government securities abroad may result in higher returns in other markets. The willingness to accept lower compensation for risk will push asset prices up and risk premiums in bond markets down, even in countries that do not lead to a more expansionary monetary policy. Several studies find that term premiums above d are more correlated between countries and tea correlated with term premiums in the US. [4] It illustrates a more general point, namely that changes in financial conditions, in the sense of ease of obtaining financing, can forge through many channels, regardless of the monetary policy framework. In its Global Financial Stability Report in April, the IMF raised questions about how much influence countries have over domestic financial conditions in a world of tea-intertwined financial markets. [5] In line with the results of Rey and her co-publishers, the IMF finds that common global factors explain a significant part of the variation in domestic financial conditions in the countries they are looking at. The importance of global factors is particularly high in emerging economies. The common global component moves in line with US financial conditions and measures of global risk such as the VIX index. But the IMF also does not believe that a high degree of covariance across countries is an impediment to countries losing control of domestic financial conditions. Their conclusion is that through monetary policy, countries have a great influence over the financial conditions of their own country. Interestingly, the IMF also does not find that the importance of global financial cycles has increased above d. At Norges Bank, we take into account developments in financial conditions in the exercise of monetary policy. In the monetary policy reports, we follow developments in risk premiums, lending margins and banks' credibility. Changes to these, as in some Traps can be driven by international conditions, affecting interest rates. In autumn 2016, for example, uncertainty about the effects of money market reform in the US l contributed to a rise in US money market rates. This forges a premium in the Norwegian money market. Norges Bank can mitigate the impact of higher premiums on the Norwegian economy by lowering the key policy rate. A floating exchange rate and the freedom to see our own interest rate mean that we can to a greater extent mitigate the impact on the Norwegian economy of disturbances in international capital markets than if we had an exchange rate target. Let me summarize what I have said so far: In a tea intertwined global economy, countries will be affected by many of the same disturbances, and developments in the major countries will have a major impact on developments in other countries. The more equal and the more integrated the economies are, the greater the correlation between interest rates will be, even if monetary policy is aimed at stabilising the economy in each country. In other words, a high correlation between interest rates or financial conditions in different countries is not necessarily a sign of a lack of independence in monetary policy. With a floating exchange rate, we can see an interest rate that deviates from interest rates abroad and uses monetary policy to stabilise the economy. Of course, it cannot be ruled out that large-scale mergers between countries can be unsurprising for a "fear of floating" and a desire to curb exchange rate fluctuations, even if the countries officially have a floating exchange rate. The exchange rate may also become a source of disturbances, and for some countries it may be rich to give up some monetary policy in the city against a more stable exchange rate. In emerging economies where it has been common to take out loans in foreign currency, fluctuations in the exchange rate and abrupt slide in capital flows may have wealth effects with potentially large ripple effects in the real economy and the financial sector. In Norway, households, banks and businesses collectively take a limited currency risk. Experience in This Country is that the exchange rate in the period of inflation targeting has acted as a shock absorber when we have been exposed to major disturbances. Even though the interest rate level in Norway is largely influenced by interest rates abroad, this does not mean that we might as well have a fixed exchange rate. A floating exchange rate has been particularly volatile in curbing the effects of wide fluctuations in oil prices. The fact that we have a floating exchange rate and freedom l see an interest rate that deviates from interest rates abroad does not mean that monetary policy can solve all stabilisation inequalities. With several objectives and only e-instruments, the central bank must weigh different considerations against each other. The extent to which a conflict of objectives arises depends on disturbances in which the economy is exposed and how interest rate changes affect the economy. This applies to both closed and open economies. In a small open economy, monetary policy must take international considerations into account to a greater extent, and the exchange rate channel becomes weaker. One lesson is that in a small open economy, many of the disturbances will be of such a nature that the central bank must weigh the objective of bringing inflation back quickly in line with the objective of avoiding wide fluctuations in the real economy. If the real economy is to be fully shielded, the interest rate must be increased, but not as much as the interest rate abroad, so that the effect of a higher interest rate and a weaker exchange rate level level each other. Title: Economic perspectives
text: SPEECH Economic perspec ves Address by Governor oystein Olsen to foreign embassy representa ves in Oslo, 10 April 2018. Introduc on Your excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. Firsts of all, I would like to thank you for taking the me to a end this event, which provides me with an opportunity to present Norges Banks view of the economic situa on and some of the challenges ahead. The advanced economies have emerged from another challenging period. Ten years ago the world economy was hit by a shock and thrown into the deepest recession since the 1930s. Chart: Economic growth following the financial crisis The economic downturn that followed the financial crisis stands apart from earlier recessions.[1] It was both deeper and longer. Potent measures were deployed to address the crisis, but it has s ll taken me to get the world economy back on its feet. Monetary policy had to take on substan al responsibility. Without powerful economic policy measures, there was a risk of a self-reinforcing recession. In the past few years, advanced-economy growth has steadily strengthened. Unemployment has fallen back, in Europe too. In parallel with this, longer-term structural developments have changed the economic landscape. A more closely integrated world economy and technological changes are transforming aspects of everyday life and also have consequences for economic policy. Trade and technology Chart: Global trade as share of GDP Over the past fi y years, global trade has more than doubled as a share of global GDP. The scaling back of trade barriers has been an important driving force. In the past decades, lower transport costs and new technological solu ons have fostered new ways of organising produc on and trade. Global trade has generated substan al welfare gains. As consumers, we have gained access to cheaper and be er products. More importantly, over one billion people have been li ed out of poverty.[2] Many people would be nega vely affected if the tendency is reversed towards higher trade barriers. Chart: Produc vity growth in Norway and abroad Society is being transformed by advances in informa on and communica on technology. We are living in an increasingly digital world. From the comfort of our sofas, we can now access an unprecedented array of music, film and literature. From a tablet or a mobile phone, we can order groceries or control the temperature in our holiday home. Ar ficial intelligence and the increasing use of robots are also in focus. By managing processes using machine learning, work can be made more efficient. But even if technology appears to be advancing more rapidly than ever before, there is li le visible effect on produc vity growth for the economy as a whole. Both in Norway and among our trading partners, produc vity growth has declined. Produc vity growth may be lagging because the diffusion of new technology into goods and services produc on takes me. Produc vity growth will only increase once the use of informa on technology and digital solu ons reduces the use of labour. Chart: Produc vity for fron er firms and other firms Behind the average figures we also find an interes ng pa ern. In many sectors; the gap between the most produc ve firms and the rest has increased.[3] The chart shows the gap within the service sector, but the same picture applies to other sectors. While produc vity growth for fron er firms has remained robust, it has been substan ally weaker in the rest of the economy. This may indicate that it is not the rate of innova on that has slowed, but rather the diffusion of new technology from fron er firms to laggard firms. In the past decade, the fallout from the financial crisis has probably had a dampening impact on produc vity growth. Weak economic growth and increased uncertainty have reduced businesses willingness to invest. In addi on, banks in many countries held back on lending for a long period. This may have discouraged new entrants and slowed the replacement of outdated produc on equipment. The legacies of the financial crisis are now fading. Investment is picking up across countries. This could li produc vity ahead. But this will not materialise of its own accord. It is up to us to take advantage of the possibili es provided by technological innova on. In order to profit from new technology, work must become less labour-intensive. When labour flows into other profitable ac vi es, we get more out of our resources.[4] This is part of the restructuring needed to generate growth. A flexible labour market, high educa on levels and a solid social safety net are precondi ons for successful restructuring. In Norway, much of this is in place, but we too must be prepared to adapt to changing circumstances. In addi on, we are lucky to be endowed with natural resources, which it will be important to build on, also in the years to come. Low price and wage infla on Not everyone benefits from a more closely integrated global economy and new technology. In many countries, the compe on for low-skilled jobs has intensified, depressing wages for these workers. On the other hand, technological advances have pushed up demand for high-skilled labour for which there is a wage premium. The result is wider wage gaps. Chart: Labour share The income distribu on between labour and capital has also changed. It had long been a widely-held view among economists that the labour share of income would remain fairly constant over me. Keynes described the stability of the labour share as one of the most surprising, yet best-established, facts in the whole range of economic sta s cs.[5] Yet since 1980, corporate profits have risen faster than wages. Technological advances have reduced the rela ve cost of capital goods. Tasks have been taken over by robots and other capital equipment. This probably explains some of the decline in the labour share.[6] Chart: Worlds largest listed companies The emergence of global technology companies is also reducing the labour share. With broad pla orms and vast numbers of users, they dominate the market, which translates into both market power and substan al profits. The winner takes all. A few technology companies stand out by virtue of their size. Alphabet is one example. 80 percent of the worlds web searches are done through its Google search engine. The decline in the labour share can primarily be explained by the fundamental transforma on of the global labour market in recent decades. More countries are par cipa ng in global trade, labour mobility has increased, and offshoring produc on to low-cost countries has become easier. When China, India and Eastern Europe joined the global market economy, the labour force of countries par cipa ng in world trade doubled.[7] The result is that workers in advanced economies face compe on from new groups, which pushes down wage growth and affects the income distribu on between labour and capital. Lower unionisa on levels have also weakened workers bargaining power. Low wage growth puts downward pressure on prices for goods and services. Many firms also face compe on from firms that have relocated produc on to lower-cost countries. The scope for passing on higher costs to prices is narrowing. The tendency of lower global price and wage infla on has consequences for monetary policy. On the one hand, infla on is likely to show smaller fluctua ons than earlier. But this also means that it may be more difficult to bring up infla on once it has fallen to a low level. Chart: Unemployment and wages The Phillips curve  the rela onship between unemployment and wage and price infla on  may have changed. In many countries, wage growth has been fairly weak, even though unemployment has fallen. The reason for this, among other things, is the global driving forces I have just men oned. But the rela onship between wages and unemployment has not broken down. There are now signs in many countries that wage growth is again rising against the background of a broadening upturn and a ghtening labour market. Expansionary monetary policy in many countries Chart: Global real interest rates Never before have global interest rates been as low as today over such a long period. The interest rate level was moving down long before the 2008 crisis. The trend is explained by several structural changes. Diminished growth in advanced economies has dampened the willingness to invest. At the same me, groups and countries with a high saving rate account for a larger share of income growth. Both lower investment and higher saving have contributed to depressing real longterm interest rates. When the financial crisis hit the global economy in 2008, central banks responded forcefully. Many central banks s ll found it difficult to provide a sufficiently accommoda ve monetary stance, and the room for further interest rate cuts was gradually exhausted. Central banks were led into unknown territory and implemented unconven onal measures. The strong medicine has worked. Unemployment in major economies is lower than before the financial crisis. Price and wage infla on is rising from low levels. The need for monetary accommoda on is thus diminishing. The global interest rate rise will probably be gradual. A er a long period of very low rates, the effect of higher interest rates on the economy is uncertain. It is also uncertain how quickly wage and price infla on will rise as ac vity gains momentum. As condi ons normalise, interest rates will likely remain lower than they were a few decades ago. The structural condi ons that have depressed the global neutral interest rate will not reverse overnight.[8] Monetary policy  lessons from the financial crisis Ten years of historically low interest rates and large-scale asset purchases give cause for reflec on. An important ques on is what responsibili es should rest with a central bank. A related theme is what is meant by the objec ve of low and stable infla on. Let me take a closer look at these ques ons. The primary objec ve of monetary policy is to maintain monetary stability, as part of the central banks responsibility for the monetary system. Infla on that is either too high or too low has undesired consequences, such as arbitrary wealth redistribu on, underinvestment and resource misalloca on. The result is lower ac vity and lower welfare. Since 1990 an increasing number of countries have chosen to link monetary stability to a numerical infla on target. Since the financial crisis, all of these countries have maintained their infla on targe ng regimes. This reflects the overall posi ve experience with this framework. It did not get in the way of a powerful response to the financial crisis. Chart: Infla on in Norway In Norway too, infla on targe ng has func oned well. Infla on has remained low and stable since it came down in the early 1990s. Despite major shocks to the Norwegian economy, employment variability has been lower since 2001 than in previous periods. Lessons have been learned along the way. Ini ally, central banks had high ambi ons to steer infla on to target within a clearly defined me horizon. But experience with these regimes provided useful insight. When confronted with shocks, small open economies in par cular experienced that a rapid return to the infla on target could have undesired consequences for the real economy.[9] Norges Bank has addressed this concern by giving greater weight to output and employment. The infla on target horizon has been extended and monetary policy has gradually become more flexible. A few weeks ago, on 2 March, the Norwegian Government adopted a new, modernised regula on on monetary policy. In Norges Banks assessment, the new regula on will not result in significant changes in the conduct of monetary policy. Let me elaborate somewhat on the implica ons of the new regula on. Monetary policy, according to the new regula on, shall maintain monetary stability by keeping infla on low and stable. The regula on thus clarifies the primary task of monetary policy. Price stability is the best contribu on that monetary policy can make towards sound and stable economic developments over me. According to the new regula on, the opera onal target of monetary policy shall be annual consumer price infla on of close to 2 percent over me. It is not possible to quan fy precisely an op mal infla on target for the Norwegian economy. A numerical target of 2 percent is, however, consistent with the infla on target of most of Norways trading partners. In 2001, when infla on targe ng was introduced, the Norwegian economy faced the prospect of gradually increasing oil revenue spending. It was widely expected that the phasing-in of revenues would entail an apprecia on of the real exchange rate. At the me, the nominal target was set at 2.5 percent. An expected real apprecia on could then occur partly in the form of wider price and cost differen als between Norway and its trading partners. The period of rising oil revenue spending now appears largely to be over. Thus, it is difficult to find compelling arguments for se ng an infla on target in Norway today that differs from that of trading partners. The new regula on underpins the Banks flexible approach to infla on targe ng. The regula on states that: Infla on targe ng shall be forward-looking and flexible so that it can contribute to high and stable output and employment and to counteract the build-up of financial imbalances. As long as there is confidence that infla on will remain low and stable, monetary policy can contribute to stabilising the economy. When the economy is exposed to shocks, the central bank can respond rapidly by adjus ng the key policy rate, preven ng downturns from becoming deep and protracted. This can reduce the risk of unemployment becoming entrenched at a high level following economic contrac ons. Nevertheless, monetary policy cannot assume primary responsibility for high output and employment. The level of output and employment over me depends on overall economic policy. Monetary policy is only one component of such an overall framework. The importance of financial markets and financial stability was underes mated before the crisis - also by central banks. The financial crisis revealed how harmful financial imbalances can be. Monetary policy can in given situa ons take account of the risk of a build-up of financial imbalances. But monetary policy cannot take primary responsibility for heading off a gathering storm. Regula ons and supervision of financial ins tu ons are the primary means of addressing shocks to the financial system. The build-up of financial imbalances has in recent years been given li le weight in monetary policy by the major central banks. Their focus has been on counterac ng a deeper and more prolonged downturn and on preven ng defla on. In countries that were less affected by the financial crisis, more a en on has been devoted to financial stability considera ons. In high-tech, global financial markets, capital moves rapidly between different currencies. A wide interest rate differen al could have a substan al impact on the exchange rate, with repercussions on infla on, output and employment. This is why low interest rates in large economies that were severely hit by the financial crisis quickly led to lower rates in countries where the cyclical situa on, in isola on, would have implied higher rates. This was the case in Norway un l oil prices fell. Other small open economies have been in the same situa on. Chart: House prices These countries have imported low interest rates and experienced rapidly rising house prices and debt. They have introduced measures to limit elevated debt in order to prevent imbalances from building up further. In Norway, stricter mortgage lending requirements have been imposed on banks. These measures have probably contributed to the recent correc on in Norwegian house prices. The exchange rate places a limit on how far Norwegian interest rates can deviate from foreign rates. But with a floa ng exchange rate, monetary policy can help to stabilise the economy when it is exposed to shocks. How Norges Bank will react to movements in the exchange rate will depend on how these fluctua ons affect the outlook for infla on, output and employment. A recent example is the monetary policy response to the nega ve oil price shock in 2014. The exchange rate served as a shock absorber. With confidence in the infla on target, monetary policy was able to underpin a weaker krone. The krone deprecia on, combined with moderate wage se lements, contributed to a marked improvement in business profitability and compe veness. At the same me, an expansionary fiscal policy and lower interest expenses have been important in sustaining domes c demand. Chart: Mainland GDP This brings me to the current situa on. Two years a er the cyclical trough was reached in Norway, growth has gained a firm foo ng. There are prospects for solid growth in business investment and consump on and renewed op mism in the petroleum industry. A number of large development projects will contribute to a rebound in oil investment in the coming years. The impetus from abroad has strengthened and exports are picking up. On the other hand, housing investment has fallen, and is likely to decline further. While underlying infla on is s ll low, rising capacity u lisa on will probably push up price and wage infla on further out. Chart: The Execu ve Boards assessment and interest rate forecast At its monetary policy mee ng in March, the Execu ve Board gave weight to the sustained upturn in both global and Norwegian economy. The Execu ve Board decided to keep the key policy rate unchanged at 0.5 percent. The Boards current assessment is that the key policy rate will most likely be raised a er summer this year. That would be the first increase in seven years  and should be taken as a good sign. Footnotes 1. Data are from Jorda, O., M. Schularick, and A. M. Title: Should central banks be governed?
text: Should central banks be governed? Speech by Deputy Governor Jon Nicolaisen at the Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters on 12 April 2018. Changes are subject to change during the performance. 1 Delegation of the instruments How should central banks be managed? The usual answer is through delegated authority, combined with Democrats" views and evaluation in e-mail. This requires a trade-off between the bank's independence on the one hand and the need for the policing authorities to follow up the bank's activities. The work of the Central Bank Act Committee  chaired by the finance council and Governor Svein Gjedrem  is relevant to the problem. [1] The Commission's proposal to separate the Government Pension Fund Global  the "Oil Fund"  is probably what has received the greatest public attention. I'm going to leave that question tonight. The Commission also presents a number of proposals for the management of the central bank. Some of the proposals touch on the core of the relationship between the policing authorities and the Bank. This should arouse interest far beyond Norges Bank, at least for those who are concerned with state customs and organisation. Let me first go back in the mid-1980s, when the current Central Bank Act was passed by stor nget. The Norwegian economy went through some challenging years. The liberalisation of the credice market resulted in a crash in household debt accumulation. During 1985, consumption grew by 10 per cent. Sam dig skyrocketed house prices. The wage settlement in 1986 led to a lock-out and oil production in the North Sea was shut down in April. Sam dig fell the price of oil considerably  at USD 10 per barrel. The fall in oil prices and high consumption growth resulted in substantial trade balance deficits abroad. In the spring of 1986, the Norwegian krone  which was then tied to a fixed exchange rate against a basket of currencies  came under pressure. In Stor nget's consideration of a separate "Easter package" of austerity proposals, the government asked Willoch cabin questions and resigned. On 11 May 1986  re e is that the new Brundtland government resigned  the Norwegian krone was devalued by 10 per cent. [2] The government felt it had no choice. The pressure on the krone was too great. E is a year of high cost inflation and frequent devaluations, the krone and credibility in the fixed exchange rate system were weakened. Inflation was high and variable. How could the economic policing have failed so fundamentally? On it, most instruments were gathered in the government apparatus, and especially in the Ministry of Finance. The Government determined the exchange rate for the krone and determined the interest rate. Norges Bank carried out the Government's policing by intervening in the foreign exchange market. In the 1960s and 1970s, economic policing was marked by considerable governance optimism. Great emphasis was placed on maintaining accompaniment and employment in the short term. Episodes of crashing inflation were met with compensation in wage settlements. Each time domestic cost growth threatened the country's competitiveness, the exchange rate was adjusted. The result was wage and price spirals and repeat devaluations. E is the devaluation in May 1986, the Government decided that the value of the Norwegian krone should quickly be stabilised against a collapsed basket of currencies. Sam dig understood that they must take action to resurrect the crown. Story with constant devaluations and high inflation could not have been hasted e. In order to ensure credibility on monetary policy, the authorities must commit. The krone was to be defended, and this meant a more accompli to the use of the interest rate. Norges Bank was responsible for determining the interest rate. It increased credibility in the new policing. Inflation was combated, and the economy came e is each in balance, but not without large costs. The Norwegian economy has to go through a crash. We went into a deep recession. It would take several years for the arrows to point upwards again, and the nominal anchor was resurrecting one. The crisis the Norwegian economy went through showed how costly it can be to lose a stable value of money. Trust and credibility can be torn down quickly, but can take a long time and require great sacrifices to rebuild. Even before the crisis, Stor nget had  in 1985  passed a new Central Bank Act, e is many years of selection work. One important feature was that the Act raised the threshold for overriding Norges Bank in interest rate terms. Under the new Act, Norges Bank was given considerable formal authority to determine the interest rate. Nevertheless, the bank's real freedom of action was not obvious when the law came into play. During the work on the law, there had been a broad debate about the central bank's place in the governing body, and deba a fort in the years e is that the law was in the works . Governor Hermod Skanland said that Norges Bank's reseal was unclear. In particular, he showed that the bank was richly responsible for determining the interest rate, but the bank should be the law "... conduct their activities in accordance with the economic-policing guidelines established by the state authorities..." [3] He described it as follows: "... while the text of the Act laid down the competence in the use of an instrument in Norges Bank, the Bank's freedom of action was bound up by guidelines for the same instrument". [4] Professor  and later highest sevens arius  Carsten Smith participated in the committee that drafted the Central Bank Act. He had a different view than Skanland. By placing the responsibility for determining the interest rate in Norges Bank, the Act gave the Bank an independent responsibility in the implementation of monetary policy. [5] Sam dig pointed out that monetary policy was part of the overall economic policing that was the responsibility of the government and the Great NGET. The bank must be able to be managed. But the threshold for reviewing the Bank's decisions should be high. E is the law, only the Government  not the Ministry of Finance alone  can instruct the Bank, and there must be a specific procedure: The Bank shall be heard before the instruction decision is made, and notification shall be sent in Stor nget as soon as possible. The bank's instruction can thus only take place in full public view. Perhaps both Skanland and Smith had re. U jerk used in the law  "... in accordance with the economic-policing guidelines established..."  is undeniably not precise. Different authorities such as the Government, the Ministry of Finance and Norges Bank may have different opinions about what they actually entailed. In e is d, we know that the provision had significance  at least when the law was new. [6] The Governor believed that the Bank's freedom of action was limited. He argued that if the Bank had been allowed to decide - interest rates would have been raised more easily. It might have limited the crisis. [7] The ambiguity of the legislation thus had significant consequences for the exercise of monetary policy. Today, there is no doubt about what Carsten Smith pointed out: The Norges Bank Act gives Norges Bank authority l  and the responsibility for  exercising monetary policy. Any conflict with the policing authorities shall e is the law handled e are the procedures for instruction. Here it is on them to stop li. What exactly was the point of delegating the fixed key policy rate to the central bank? If the authorities had first made up their minds, why couldn't they even carry out the policing that was supposed to l? There are several reasons why the authorities delegate tasks. [8] If the exercise of discretion required is primarily professional and should not be characterised by policing choices, it is appropriate that authority is delegated to a professional body. In addition, delegation can contribute to prioritisation of important considerations. It may be necessary, but demanding, to accept victims in the short term in order to achieve a better balance in the economy over d.[9] A delegated mandate with a clear objective can both clarify the division of labour in the economic policing and determine the priority of longitudinal stability. In turn, it can strengthen the credibility of policing, thus contributing to the success of policing. Internationally, it was common to give central banks the responsibility for reducing inflation. Central banks were seen as well suited to exercise the professional judgement that was to be exercised. In order to have room l to exercise professional judgement and give credibility in the exercise of discretion, the authorities jointly acknowledged that central banks themselves must be given responsibility for the use of instruments. The independence of the central banks in the US and Germany was highlighted as examples. In 1990, New Zealand as the first country introduced an exploding inflation target for the central bank, and they soon became the result of more. Inflation has been lower in most Western countries, and it has since remained fairly low and stable. Central banks are not alone in managing long-run targets on behalf of society and with authority established in law. The starting point in Norwegian re is that the superior authority can instruct subordinate agencies. The degree of independence varies. The strict procedures for instruction see is Norges Bank's independence in a special way. 2 Hordan run a central bank? With independence, a new problem arises: How can the government secure Democrat control of an independent inquiry? Basically, the words "control" and "independent" sound undeniably like two mutually exclusive concepts. [10] How policing authorities govern Norges Bank will have an impact both on the central bank's real independence, for the Bank's exercise of authority, and for how the Bank is held accountable. The management of Norges Bank must take place within the framework of the Norges Bank Act. The Act is adopted by stor nget, which thus establishes the overarching principles for the central bank's activities. The Government determines the division of labour in the overall economic policy, including the authority of the central bank and the specific objectives it will govern. This is done through the pre-crisis basis pursuant to the Central Bank Act. In particular, there are two aspects of the act that are important. First, the Act gives the Bank authority over some instruments, such as the key policy rate. Secondly, as I have already mentioned, the Government can only instruct Norges Bank's procedures and in full transparency. It makes the threshold of instruction high. The Central Bank Act Committee proposes strengthening Norges Bank's formal independence by tightening the right to instruct Norges Bank: The Government may quickly set targets for the Bank's activities. However, in individual cases, the Bank should only be instructed in extraordinary situations. Other provisions of the Act also under the Bank's independence. The government cannot take out loans from Norges Bank, and the Bank's bidding is determined independently of the Ministry and the Government. In llegg, the Bank has re and duty l to advise the Ministry when the Bank believes that there is a need for ltak by anyone other than the Bank. In other words, Norges Bank has a high degree of independence in its use of instruments. However, the objectives against which the Bank shall steer clear, and the framework for which instruments it can use, are set by the policing authorities. The central bank's objectives are of great importance to the central bank's real influence and responsibility. The greater the scope for the exercise of discretion, the more the policing authorities leave the central bank. In Norway, they can be illustrated by the difference in monetary policy mandates under exchange rate targeting and inflation targeting. text: Management of the Government Pension Fund Global Governor afystein Olsen. Introduction to consultation on the Government Pension Fund in the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs. Hearing on ne -TV (Stor nget) Consultation Hall 1 Subject to changes during the performance. Norges Bank manages the Government Pension Fund Global with the goal of achieving the highest possible return above d, providing acceptable risk. The Executive Board is satisfied that the return on both 2017 and above d has been good, and higher than the return on the benchmark index determined by the Ministry of Finance for the management of the fund. It is important to stick to the target for investments. Restrictions and orders that are seen in the side of the trade-off between return and risk will reduce the possibility l achieve good results over d. The most important variables that are decisive for the fund's long-term performance have been determined by the Ministry of Finance and anchored in the Stor nget. Norges Bank, for its part, has developed management in light of the fund's growth and in line with the mandate from the owner. Norges Bank follows several investment strategies. The strategies can be divided into allocation, securities selection and market exposure. The strategies don't make each other any good. We do not expect that all strategies in any d will generate an excess return. The goal is that they collectively, and above d, give meravkas ng. In 2017, the return measured in the fund's currency basket was 13.7 per cent before management costs. The return was 0.7 percentage point higher than in the benchmark index. Over the entire 20-year period from 1998 on year, the annual return measured in the same way has been 6.1 per cent, or 0.3 percentage points higher than in the benchmark index. In recent years, the fund's management costs have been 0.06 per cent of the fund's value. The fund is large, and although management costs account for a small share of the fund's value, the figures are measured in NOK. Norges Bank aims for the highest possible return e is costs. The Fund shall be managed with satisfactory control and risk management, and in a responsible and efficient manner. The Executive Board's three-year strategy plan describes how the Bank seeks to achieve this target. The strategy plan for 2017-2019 included increasing the share of external management of equities in emerging markets and small companies. This results in somewhat higher management costs, but the experience so far is that the fund's revenues are increasing more. Furthermore, the strategy has been laid out in the necessary further development of the investment plaque for the management of the fund. A new and more secure model for delivering IT services will mean higher costs in the short term, but a safer and more eff00 management of the fund over d. Norges Bank will be a global leader in responsible investment. The work is an integral part of the management of the fund and the surrounding area includes active ownership and exclusions on an e sk basis. The work is described in the annual report on the management of the Government Pension Fund Global and in a separate publication on responsible investment of the Fund. In its management of the Fund, Norges Bank has both a re-and-a-duty to advise on the most important choices in the management of the Fund. This is a key part of the Bank's mission, and this year's major report on the Fund shows several advice that the Executive Board gave the Ministry of Finance through 2017. In its annual report, the Ministry of Finance announced that it would increase the equity share in the fund's benchmark index from 62.5 percent. Seventy percent. An increased equity share was in line with advice from Norges Bank, among others. The change is large, and the Ministry has, in consultation with Norges Bank, established a plan for phasing in an increased allocation to equities. By investing broadly in equities, the Fund takes part in economic growth and value creation in large parts of the world. Based on historical experience, we can assume that equities will make a significant contribution to the return over d. Together, we must be prepared to deal with wide fluctuations in the fund's value in the years to come. 4 May 2018 08:30

text: Management of the Government Pension Fund Global Director Yngve Slyngstad. Thank you to the Chairman of the Committee, and for giving me the opportunity to talk about the management of the Government Pension Fund Global. Chart: NOK 8 488 billion in the fund The Government Pension Fund Global had a market value of NOK 8 488 billion at the end of 2017. The fund returned 13.7 percent during the year. 2017 was characterised by very good equity markets. In NOK, the return was more than NOK 1 000 billion, the largest annual return in NOK ever. Since 1998, the fund has an annual return of 6.1 percent. E is a deduction for inflation and costs, the real return on the first krone has been 4.2 per cent. The through-the-crown has a return of 6.8 per cent and a real return of 4.9 per cent e is a deduction for inflation and costs. Chart: Total return greater than total lforsel Since its establishment in 1996 at the end of 2017, the fund has totalled NOK 3 495 billion, while the uke has been NOK 162 billion. The total return amounts to NOK 4 141 billion, which is a larger amount than what is said in the fund. The largest part of the increase in the fund's value has come from an exceptionally good return over the past five years. Three out of four kroner in returns have come in this period. llegg has seen an increase in the fund's value of about NOK 1 000 billion due to the depreciation of the krone in recent years. They do not affect the fund's international purchasing crater. The fund is significantly larger than the estimated value of the oil reserves on the Norwegian shelf, and has a size no one had expected when the first funds were announced more than 20 years ago. Chart: 208 billion in current revenues in 2017 In line with the increase in the fund's value, the current income in the fund from investments has also increased. These come from equity dividends, interest income and rental income. Total current revenues amounted to about NOK 200 billion in 2017 alone. A falling interest rate level internationally means that equity dividends are from companies in which the fund is invested that are now making the largest contribution. Chart: New property purchases in 2017 A major change in management in or was the introduction of a new management model. The change means that the fund's real estate investments are no longer part of the benchmark index. The benchmark index currently consists only of equities and bonds. The Fund may soon invest in real estate, but it is delegated to Norges Bank to composition of real estate investments. In 2017, the fund made the first unlisted real estate investment in the Asian market, with the purchase of five buildings in Tokyo. The changes in the management model for the Fund ensure a holistic approach to a management assignment that includes both listed and unlisted investments, and facilitate further development of the investment strategy. Figure: Forvaltningsmal The management objective is to achieve the highest possible return in the long term. The share of equities in the fund is the most important decision in terms of expected return and risk. The equity share has been discussed and changed approximately every year, most recently in 2017, when it was said to be 70 percent. At the end of the year, the share was 66.6 per cent. Another important decision is which classes the fund can be invested in. The e have been discussed regularly, and most recently in this year's Great Notice. The management model has a high return in the long term as a target. However, we must implement the management of the fund with an acceptable risk, an effective organisation and in a responsible manner. We will share information with the public, and be transparent about all aspects of the management of the fund. We attach great importance to those e in our management of the fund. In terms of risk, we have our own annual publication with analyses and assessments. An effek v organization ensures low costs, which we report quarterly and annually through accounting closes with notes. Our work on responsible investment is covered through a separate annual publication. In our management, we follow several investment strategies that give way to each other. The objective is that the total and above d give a higher return than the benchmark indices. The different investment strategies are part of a whole that has delivered good results over d. One investment strategy is to enrich external managers in areas where we believe local knowledge is necessary to ensure high returns, acceptable risk and responsible investment. This is especially true in emerging markets, and in small and medium-sized companies. Costs in external managers have accounted for about 40 per cent of the costs. The higher return from external management has made significant contributions to the fund's total excess return. Figure: Stable internal forvaltningskostnader We attach importance to maintaining high quality management and ensuring good control and cost-effectiveness. Total management costs measured as a share of the fund's capital have been low and remain stable in recent years, despite the build-up of a portfolio of unlisted real estate investments and an increased share of equities. Sam dig's management has been expanded in terms of the number of markets in which we are invested. We have extracted significant major benefits in recent years. Our goal is to keep internal management costs below 0.05 per cent of managed capital. Inlays come costs in external management. In 2017, total management costs were 0.06 per cent of managed capital. They are very low compared to other funds. Chart: Responsible investment Good corporate governance and well-functioning boards are important for the fund's return in the long term. Clear expectations of companies in which we are invested, based on internationally recognised principles, are part of the e. Our expectations are primarily against the companies' boards, and are a starting point for dialogue with the companies. We have already expectations documents on children's health, water management, climate change, and human rights. In 2017, we issued an expectation document on ska and transparency. In the first quarter of this year, we also issued a new expectation document on an "corruption". Later this year we will provide an update on the expectation document on water management. Until now, they have been about fresh water, but we will include the oceans in the future. Another issue we raised in 2017 was executive remuneration, which we a position paper on. In the memorandum, we point out that remuneration should be linked to value creation and ensure common interests between senior executives and shareholders. Chart: All public information can be found on ne All public information about the Fund can be found on our website. In our quarterly and annual reports, we publish unsubstained information about responsible investment, unlisted real estate investments, and return and risk. On our pages there are also a number of publications, data and background information. Taken together, they provide a great deal of transparency about the management of the fund. We manage financial assets for future generations in a secure, efficient, responsible and transparent way. But we must never lose sight of the fact that the target is a high return. 4 May 2018 08:30

Title: Management of the Government Pension Fund Global
text: Management of the Government Pension Fund Global Director Yngve Slyngstad. Introduction to consultation on the management of the Government Pension Fund Global in the Executive Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs. Subject to changes during the performance. Thank you to the Chairman of the Committee, and for giving me the opportunity to talk about the management of the Government Pension Fund Global. Chart: NOK 3 666 billion total return The Government Pension Fund Global had a market value of NOK 8 256 billion at the end of 2018. The year was characterised by wide fluctuations in the fund's value. On this, the fund's market value was less than NOK 8 000 billion, the lowest level of the year. E are the e rose value again, before we suffered broad market falls in the autumn. E's good return at the beginning of 2019 is the fund's market value today higher. The fund has a total of NOK 3 327 billion, while the return has been NOK 3 666 billion. Chart: Trading volume and stock prices The share of equities in the fund is the most important decision in terms of expected return and risk. The equity share was last discussed and changed in 2017, when it was said to be 70 percent. We bought shares worth NOK 250 billion at year-end, and we currently have an equity allocation of 70 per cent. A higher equity share results in a higher expected return, but also a higher risk of a fall in the fund's value. If we had invested only in government debt, the expected real return would have been close to zero per cent, i.e. not the 3 per cent assumed in the fiscal rule today. In the long term, this would not provide a good return, nor security for our savings. With the new equity share, the Ministry also plans to establish new lbakevek ng rules. We will now have 70 percent already when we are 2 percentage points away from 70 percent. Even if they are a change from a broader band, there will still be significant amounts traded in the event of a rebalancing. With the current fund value, such a rebalancing will entail the purchase and sale of securities of about NOK 360 billion. With a changed equity share, it was also natural to see the framework for fixed income investments. The Ministry is now proposing to have fewer markets in the benchmark index. Investments in government bonds in emerging markets are reduced. When we reduce fixed-income investments in emerging markets, it is common to preserve the diversification characteristics that emerging markets have in the overall portfolio. A characteristic of our management model is that the fund is invested in the whole world, and half of the world's value creation takes place in emerging markets. We mainly make such equity investments through external managers. Their local knowledge has ensured high returns, acceptable risk, responsible investment, and management that has delivered good results over d. Chart: Different investment strategies We are enriching various investment strategies in the management of the fund. First of all, we're together a long-range benchmark portfolio. This shall be adapted to the fund's characteristics, and is the starting point for the fund's investments. The benchmark portfolio should be assessed over a long ds horizon. It includes investments in emerging income markets and systema ske risk factors in the axis investments. Our company investments are based on thorough analyses, and have proven successful over d. So have our enhanced indexing strategies, which provide effk v market exposure. They're our best strategy. The investment strategies are different, and they are used to varying degrees in different submarkets. The objective is that the l together and above d give a higher return than the benchmark indices against which the fund is measured. But it is not a goal for them to generate an excess return on the same d and under the same market conditions. The various investment strategies are part of a whole that has delivered good results over d. Chart: Return on environmental mandates At year-end 2018, we had NOK 43.3 billion invested in environment-related equity mandates. The mandates have been managed both internally and externally since start-up in 2009. The mandates are currently managed internally, e is that in 2018 we will cancel an externally managed mandate to reduce management costs. In the period ahead, investments in so-called green bonds may constitute a larger share of these investments. Such investments have low costs for us as a manager. The environment-related mandates have a return that has been somewhat weaker than the broad markets and our general equity investments. Chart: Impact from return exclusions The fund's return is also influenced by decisions concerning the exclusion of companies and sectors from the fund's investment universe. Historically, product-based exclusions have incurred costs for the fund, in the form of weaker returns. Exclusion of companies and sectors reduces the spread of risk in the fund. It is therefore a premise that there should be a high threshold for exclusion. The fund is also conducting risk-based divestments, where we believe businesses are not carriers in the long term. Such divestments are based on long-downward financial risk and have improved the return on the fund. The Treasury will take out of the fund companies the index provider FTSE Russell classifies as upstream companies. We do not know which companies they are applying today, as the index provider is planning changes in the sector division. We assume that there will be an implementation period that spans longer d. Chart: New property purchases in 2018 We invested a total of NOK 12.7 billion in unlisted real estate in 2018. At year-end, such investments amounted to NOK 246 billion, or 3 per cent of the fund. Norges Bank has delegated the size and composition of real estate investments within the mandate's 7 percent limit. In 2018, Norges Bank decided to hold on to the unlisted real estate share of around 3 percent, and introduced a simplified strategy for unlisted real estate to keep costs down. Figure: Stable internal forvaltningskostnader Total management costs measured as a share of the fund's capital have been low and remain stable in recent years, despite the build-up of a portfolio of unlisted real estate investments and an increased share of equities. We have extracted significant large-scale benefits and keep internal management costs below 0.05 per cent of managed capital. They are very low compared to other funds, and are due in part to very low costs in internally managed aquicalypse strategies. These have close to the same cost as the index-oriented internal strategies. The scope of external management was reduced in 2018, and a new strategy for real estate was adopted, among other things, to reduce costs. Chart: All public information can be found on ne All public information about the Fund can be found on our website. In our quarterly and annual reports, we publish unsubstained information about responsible investment, unlisted real estate investments, and return and risk. On our pages there are also a number of publications, data and background information. Taken together, they provide a great deal of transparency about the management of the fund. We manage financial assets for future generations in a secure, efficient, responsible and transparent way. The management objective is to achieve the highest possible return in the long term. 25 April 2019 08:00
