Title: Liquidity and financing of banks during crisis management
text: Liquidity and financing of banks during crisis management Speech by Torbjorn Haegeland, Director of Financial Stability at Norges Bank, at Finance Norway's seminar on crisis management regulations 12 September 2019. Thank you for your invitation l to talk about a topic during crisis management of banks. As we have heard from the previous talks today, from our colleagues in finans lsynet, in bankenes sikringfond and in Denmark, the new crisis management regulations are well rigged to ensure that a bank is solvent again e is a possible crisis management process. But a bank, crisis-managed or not, must not only have icy capital, it must also have icy liquidity. Communicating payments is at the heart of banks' core tasks. Being a bank is participating in the payment settlement. To participate there, the bank must be liquid. How liquid is a bank that opens on a Monday morning e is having been crisis managed over the weekend? Even if a bank is in crisis-managed, it may not be liquid. There are several reasons in it: Prior to crisis management, the Bank will probably have emptied its liquid holdings, including the securities approved as collateral for Norges Bank's standing liquidity facilities. Immediately, other players in the money market may also be uncertain about the Bank  despite the recapitalisation that has taken place through the decision of the crisis management authority. They can especially be in the same way if it has been a long time since the last time a bank was handled in crisis. The market will then have no experience of how crisis management works and what a crisis-managed bank looks like. As a result, the Bank will have difficulty obtaining loans in the money market. In such a situation, it will need liquidity steady. For the Bank itself, the central bank will appear as an obvious source of such steady e.e. Liquidity steady in crisis-managed banks is a problem that several central banks are occupying. Among other things, the ECB is working on this problem for it. And so do Norges Bank. The theme of my presentation here today is: How should Norges Bank learn that a bank that is being dealt with in a crisis is applying for extraordinary liquidity or loans on special terms, so-called S-loans? Before I answer those e question, let me just briefly say what not to talk about today. I'm not going to talk about the F-loans that we use to provide the money market with general extra liquidity or the standing facilities, that is, D-loans or intraday loans. These loans are provided only against full collateral in certain securities and with a loan basis that is updated daily. Banks must have security in advance. The loan basis for each bank is then automatically included in Norges Bank's loan system. So lbake l S loan. The possibilities for S-loans are limited. Norges Bank will process S-loan applications only from banks that are domiciled in Norway. Norges Bank will not consider an S-loan application from a branch of a foreign bank. It is the central bank in the foreign bank's home country that must handle any application for an S-loan from that bank. This is evident in the Memorandum of Understanding between the Nordic-Balese central banks, where it is stated in section 5.4 (a): A request for Emergency Liquidity Assistance from a Bank within a Cross-Border Banking Group would be dealt with by the Bank's Home-Country Central Bank. [1] Furthermore, Norges Bank can only provide S-loans in very special situations. There will be a situation where financial stability is threatened if such a loan is not granted. A bank that the Ministry of Finance has decided to manage in crisis will most likely meet that criterion if it has liquidity problems. However, Norges Bank must make several demands: A bank that has to make S-loans must be solvent, and it must be reassuringly secure. If we let go of these remarks, it will mean that we give solidity to the e, and that is not our task. This is clarified in the guidelines adopted by Norges Bank in 2004.[2] These guidelines will soon be based also under the new Norges Bank Act. Norges Bank shall not contribute to steady banks that are insolvent. Section 3-1 fifth paragraph of the new Norges Bank Act now states that Norges Bank can only provide loans against satisfactory collateral. Let me say li more about the requirement l solvency, before I talk further about collateral for S-loans. A fundamental  and in this context almost existential  question is: Can a bank during crisis management be considered solvent? As the Bank enters crisis management, there is strong doubt at best about the bank's solvency. However, the moment there is a decision on the recapitalisation of the bank, the bank must be considered solvent. This means that Finans lsynet has decided to write down part of the bank's debt  and not least convert a small portion of the bank's remaining debt into equity. Moreover, the crisis fund or the government may have decided to deposit extra equity in the bank. The decisions must be made quickly and have a very solid basis. This underlines how important it is that the crisis plans are so well prepared that there can be no doubt about the validity of the write-down decisions and conversion decisions that Finans lsynet has received. Without the recapitalisation in order, Norges Bank will not be able to contribute to securing liquidity. The next question is whether Norges Bank can provide loans to a bank without the new equity in place, that is, it has been paid in? Yes, when it is decided that equity will be invested, we can give the bank a loan. The conclusion is that a crisis-managed bank is solvent in that a valid decision on recapitalisation is received in accordance with the Norwegian regulations on crisis management. Then let me go over l to talk about security. If a bank, whether it is in crisis management or not, applies to Norges Bank for S-loans, it is because it does not have a tenacious system with liquid deposits and ordinary collateral in being able to participate in the settlement of payments. This means that in an S-loan situation, only collateral other than that provided in Norges Bank's liquidity facilities or in the case of F-loans is relevant. Securities that do not meet the requirements for being used as collateral in ordinary loans may be relevant. But the bank may also not have a hard time with such papers. If so, it will be appropriate to resort to nontraditional security. A type of nontraditional collateral that may be relevant for S-loans is part of a bank's lending portfolio. There are many practising indisclamations associated with accepting such security. And in an S-loan situation, it is hardly d, especially if the bank is also in crisis management. But a change in the Financial Security Act starting in 2017 has made the pragmatists significantly less than worse off. It is no longer necessary to inform each borrower if Norges Bank is to pledge a portfolio of mortgages. Norges Bank may now be resealed for collateral in a mortgage portfolio and collateral in the underlying objects, i.e. the dwellings in question. In order for Norges Bank to pledge a portfolio of mortgages, the Act requires that the Bank in question send Norges Bank a list of all the loans in the portfolio. Norges Bank has begun to look at how they can be done in practice. This has partly been done in cooperation with representatives of Finans Norway and some banks. Here we do not envisage an automa cert system for processing security a la what is used in our standing facilities. We aim to establish a system that we can be ready to use in a crisis situation even if it is not to be used in normal there. Norges Bank will require that a mortgage portfolio to be used as collateral for S-loans only contains non-default loans. Thus, we can use very simple decors for the pledged e portfolio. Such a rough valuation method will save d, l advantage for both parties, in a probably very croch ng situation. In the period ahead, Norges Bank will test, in cooperation with several banks, how it can be done to transfer loan information about all the loans in a portfolio of many thousands of loans. We will prepare a plan for how this information will be processed at Norges Bank. We will contact banks and finance Norway about this in not everything for ern forward d. The experience gained from this thesis will form the basis for updating Norges Bank's S-loan reforms. What happens during a crisis management is dskri sk. text: The role of money politics in a corona d Speech by Governor oystein Olsen at a seminar organized by the Centre for Monetary Economics (CME)/BI Norwegian Business School, 6 October 2020. Introduction Thank you l Centre for Monetary Economics (CME) and BI for also hosting the event this year. I see a great price on this occasion l to elaborate on how we at Norges Bank think about monetary policy. Chart: Historic fall in GDP Since then, the corona pandemic has turned the world upside down. From being close to the peak of an upturn, both Norway and large parts of the world are now in a historically deep recession. In order to limit the spread of forging, in virtually all countries, strict forging has been required. Internationally, we are talking about "the great lockdown" - a shutdown of society. This has had major economic consequences. In Norway, the downturn was exacerbated by a fall in oil prices. In many countries, the GDP fall in the second quarter was the largest ever measured. In the UK, the ak vitet fell by as much as 20 per cent. In Norway, the decline has been smaller, but we are also experiencing the sharpest economic downturn in a single year since World War II. In this year's talks, the theme was the toolbox of money policing. L want to remind you of two messages that I emphasized. First, there is a difference between which monetary policy instruments we use in normal settings there and which may be relevant during a crisis. Secondly, not all the ceilings in use outside are equally suitable for Norway. Over the past six months, we've been using a lot of the toolbox I was talking about the last time I was here. In today's , I would like to remind you of what we have done. I'd also like to get into some indisctives we're facing in a longer perspek v. But first, I would like to say a few words about where we stand now and how we envisage further developments in the economy. A historically deep decline Chart: A half-year drama The corona pandemic is a worldwide health disaster with few historical parallels. We have to go back 100 years  in the Spanish flu  to find a very serious epidemic. Globally, more than 35 million people are now infected with the coronavirus, and about one million have died. In Norway, the first trap was discovered on February 26. Two weeks e is, large parts of the community were shut down. So far, we have managed to keep the forging and mortality rates at a very low level, but the situation has been difficult to deal with for Norwegian health authorities as well. Chart: Gradual improvement The first forge e-wave quickly came under control. From late April through the summer, many of the forges could be laughed at. Better control over the forging situation, reopening parts of society and cracking down on economic output contributed to a recovery in the economy. But the pandemic is rapidly affecting both the Norwegian and international economies. Here at home, the ak vitete is fast lower than at the start of the year. Although many permi peas have returned to work in recent months, unemployment is still high. Less than two weeks ago, li new projections for further developments. Ak viteten has recovered, but it will take d before it is back to the level from before the pandemic broke out. First towards 2023, we expect capacity renewal in the Norwegian economy will be close to normal. According to our estimates, unemployment will then be somewhat above the level from the beginning of March. There is considerable uncertainty as to how quickly the recovery in the economy will take place. Not least, the uncertainty revolves around the further forging spread and how quickly a vaccine becomes broadly available. Looking further ahead, the uncertainty is about what lasting traces the pandemic is leaving. In recent weeks, we have seen that forge has flared up again in several places  both in Norway and among our trading partners. This has led to further deaths in ltak being put on hold, and it has been tightened in some areas. This may slow the recovery in the economy the closest it can be. Chart: Private consumption during the pandemic Households account for about half of the total demand from the mainland economy. The strict forging led to a crash in private consumption. We also had a clear shift away from services and towards goods. Many journeys must be put on hold, and much of the cultural hub was shut down. Although consumption has clearly increased since spring, the level is rapidly lower than at the beginning of the year. The reflection is a marked increase in household saving. The increased savings are partly due to restrictions on what we can or want to spend money on. But this must also be seen in the light of considerable uncertainty about the economic outlook. It is likely that the savings rate will return to a more normal level. The increase in consumption can come quickly if many people want to use the means they have said l side. On the other hand, we cannot rule out that the seriousness of the crisis has created an uncertainty that leads to a structural skies in saving for an extended period of time. People can "bake in" a higher likelihood of serious crises in the future, and also the behaviour you are. The shift in demand also causes the economic downturn to affect differently. The services sector in particular has been hit hard by the forging. In tourism and culture, many people have lost much of their revenue. Service consumption is clearly lower than before the outbreak of the virus. This twisting has an impact on production and employment. The impulses from service consumption in the rest of the economy are far greater than from consumption of goods. Figure: Corona pandemic leads l... Service providers are also affected by lower demand from the bedris market. Events have been cancelled and travel activity is low. Norges Bank recently asked the company in our regional ne work what the corona pandemic will lead in the coming year. Four out of five responded that they wanted to reduce travel. One in three envisa lower investment rates. Among these we find many service providers bedri is. Chart: Higher unemployment among younger people Like many young jobs in service occupations that were closed down in March, younger age groups were particularly affected by permutations and redundancies. They also have shorter seniority and work experience than the elderly, and must therefore go first when downsizing. Those who are now entering the labour market face a labour market where it is more difficult to gain entry. Several studies show that unemployment at a young age may have particularly nega ve consequences for employment later on, especially if unemployment lasts above anything d.[2] They emphasise that it is important to limit both the depth and length of the downturn in the economy. Economic downturns there have accelerated structural changes. It could also happen this time. In the long term, this may lead to increased production. However, within a somewhat shorter horizon, we expect both the production and employment potential to be lower than before the coronavirus outbreak. Despite steady schemes that are directly opposed to bedri are in the public interest in industries, businesses will have to close down. Workers need to get into new jobs. Experience shows that it can take d. If unemployment remains high for a longer period d, the risk of people falling permanently out of the labour force increases. Closures and bankruptcies can result in permanent loss of production capital. Combined with lower investment stocks, it could reduce manufacturing stocks. Kra full financial ltak The authorities have been struggling with massive ltaks to counter the negro woes of the pandemic and forge the ltaks. During the shutdown phase in March and April, it was particularly important to secure workers and people who were affected financially. Unnecessary bankruptcies must be avoided, and ties between employer and employees should be maintained. Key instruments were financial steady packages and amended permi ering rules. As long as the pandemic and forging restrictions keep e-mail demand against some industries down, it is the fiscal policy that is best suited to meet the ineptitudes of ansa e and bedri one meeting. Measures can be measured against industries and groups of workers who are hardest hit. Sam dig's use of petroleum revenues has reached a high level. Chart: Measures from Norges Bank Monetary policy has also helped to counteract the nega ve economic effects of the crisis. We have reduced the key policy rate from 1.5 l 0 per cent. The interest rate has not been this low before. Most likely, it will remain at zero for some time to come. The economic downturn is strong, and there is considerable uncertainty about future developments. This means that the interest rate is kept at rest until there are clear signs that conditions in the economy are normalising. Low interest rates improve the liquidity situation for bedri are and households affected by income drilling all. This year's interest rate cuts are likely to have sculpted the economy, including in the housing market. A marked fall in house prices would have amplified the decline. As society gradually opens up, low interest rates can help the economy recover more quickly at a normal level. This reduces the risk of unemployment becoming entreasing at a high level. Norges Bank must also work along a different front in the pandemic. In March and April, there was considerable turbulence in the financial and credice markets. It was important to avoid the health crisis and the real economic downturn also developing in a financial and banking crisis. Norges Bank initiated several ltaks to improve liquidity in the market. We lbod banks extraordinary Flan. The loans had a longer run d than normal, up this year, and banks could borrow what they wanted in an interest rate equal to or li above the key policy rate. We also laughed at the demands of security. A key objective has been to ensure that the cow's key policy rate had an impact on both money market rates and banks' lending rates. A similar approach to strengthening liquidity and improving the functioning of financial markets was initiated by other central banks. Overall, this has led to an abnormally high risk premium in the financial markets. At one point, we also chose to go in the unusual way of intervening in the foreign exchange market. Market turbulence and low liquidity in the krone market sent the krone to a historically weak level. In order to ensure a well-functioning market, Norges Bank announced that we were ready to enter with steady purchases. The purpose was to ensure that the market functioned as normal. The krone exchange rate has appreciated since the days of drama in March. This has happened as uncertainty in international financial markets has subsided and oil prices have risen. But the krone is weaker than it was at the beginning of the year. Chart: Central bank balance sheets have increased Other central banks have stretched monetary policy further than Norges Bank has done. Since the financial crisis, they have made large acquisitions of government bonds and other securities. The aim is to make monetary policy more expansive by bringing the cost of longer-running loans down. Over the past six months, existing programs have already been expanded, and new ones have arrived l. In this year's CME speech, I justified why quakes are not appropriate in Norway. The reasons are that the market for government bonds is much thinner in Norway than in many other countries, and that fixed-rate loans are relatively low in Norway. Our assessment is that the costs of using such instruments may be overlooked. Refa end purchases of securities have increased central bank balance sheets. However, as shown in the chart, Norges Bank's balance sheet has also increased during the pandemic. One important explanation is the sharp increase in F-loans in banks. In llegg, the depreciation of the krone l resulted in an increase in the value of our foreign exchange reserves, measured in NOK. In the spring there was also a need for ltak towards the banking system  but primarily of a preventive nature. E is advice from Norges Bank, the Ministry of Finance reduced the size of the countercyclical capital buffer that banks are required to hold. The purpose was to reduce the risk of banks tightening lending standards and thereby amplifying the downturn in the economy. Pengepoli ske was ordlinger Chart: Key rates close to zero So in the way forward and some indiscibles we face in the money policy. Central banks have also reacted quickly and harshly this time to counter the severe economic downturn. We are not alone in having said the interest rate far down; central banks in many other countries now have interest rates in the range of around zero per cent. But despite the fact that the pandemic has led to even deeper falls in accompaniment levels than what happened at the end of the financial crisis in 2008, the size of central banks' interest rate cow has been considerably smaller in this crisis. It's due to two ng. First, interest rates in most other countries were already at a low level when the pandemic broke out. That wasn't the case at the start of the financial crisis. Second, there is a limit to how far down it is appropriate to see the key policy rate. If the interest rate is already at a low level when disturbances occur, it limits the central bank's ability to counteract a downturn. Before the financial crisis, most macroeconomic economists regarded zero as the lower limit for the interest rate. Sam dig was this frontier most of theore sk interest. The experience of the past year has meant that the view of the lower limit has changed, and that we are now talking about "The Effec ve Lower Bound" instead of "The Zero Lower Bound". The lower limit for the key policy rate is not a sharp limit. It is more apt to see it as an area where the key policy rate has a gradually less impact on the interest rates faced by households and the interest rate, and where the interest rate has uncertain, and in some cases undesirable, effects on financial markets. These conditions may vary between countries. When the key policy rate approaches zero, central banks must therefore make demanding assessments on the question of a further interest rate decline. Central banks that did not already have nega v key policy rate have been reluctant to cross the nul line during the corona pandemic. Norges Bank does not envisage that the interest rate will be so higher than today's level. However, we do not rule out the possibility of going further down. This may, for example, be relevant in periods of strong turbulence in financial markets and a sharp rise in risk premiums. Chart: Norges Bank's forward dsguiding A key monetary policy instrument beyond the actual fixed interest rate is forward guidance. This means that the central bank is signalling a large interest rate rise. The purpose is to strengthen the impact of long market rates, as well as to provide key signals to actors who will make investment decisions. Most central banks are signalling a rise in monetary policy primarily through verbal inecursions, and extended with forecasts for inflation and output. However, some central banks, including Norges Bank, are more express; we publish our own interest rate forecasts. On this level, you can see our latest interest rate forecast together with projections for inflation and the output gap. As envisages the outlook and balance of risks, the key policy rate will be kept at zero percent for some time to come. Let me take a closer look at how our interest rate path should be understood in light of the lower limit for the interest rate. To do that, I will show some model simulations in a simplified, sized version of our main model NEMO. Figure: Assume No Lower Limit The starting point for the calculations is that there is a crash in shock, such as the corona pandemic. First, assume that there is no lower limit, and that the interest rate works in much the same way when it is nega v as when it is posi v. De e is a simplification done in most macro models, including NEMO. Then the model describes a development as illustrated by the dark blue lines. The low interest rate means that the economy normalises and inflation is each on target. But this trajectory is, of course, completely hypothetical. We know that the interest rate will not function as normal at such low nega levels. We also believe that there are costs associated with possible side effects in financial markets when interest rates fall below zero and that are not safeguarded by our analytical apparatus. Instead, in order to seek to safeguard factors that the model cannot take into account, the central bank stops at zero percent and keeps the interest rate there for a while. Based on the model, which has much of the same mechanisms as in NEMO, we get a development that is illustrated by the light blue path. The downturn will be deeper, and it will take li longer d before the economy normalizes and inflation reaches its target. Therefore, the interest rate is also li later than in the dark blue path. According to the model analysis, achieving the target appears to be deteriorating when the central bank keeps the interest rate at zero percent. However, as mentioned, such model exercises do not capture all factors that are important in the interest rate period. When we choose a specific interest rate path, we make all d a trade-off between different considerations. A lower interest rate path may result in a faster rise in the accompaniment level as illustrated by the model analysis. However, even lower interest rates can lead to a build-up of financial imbalances and thereby an increased risk of a downturn. The risk associated with very low interest rates is very demanding to model and quantify. Although research and model developments, both internationally and internally at Norges Bank, are making progress on the e-mails, they are e assessments that in practice must be made "outside the model". The dark blue path is "op template" only in a model technical sense, but it does not take into account that the interest rate acts differently when it is nega v or that such a path may increase the risk of instability. The light blue path can therefore be interpreted as the actual "op paint" path when these considerations are taken into account . The type of development in the interest rate that central banks raise l is anchored in the monetary policy framework and in the strategy. Several central banks are reviewing, or have recently reviewed, their monetary policy strategies. These processes started before the pandemic broke out, but the pandemic has actualized some of the indiscrimination rings, such as the u ordrings tying a l the lower limit. The Federal Reserve, the Fed, announced in August some interesting changes to its policy framework. [3] One of the changes is that they now focus on the fact that inflation should be 2 per cent above d. This means that they aim to bring inflation above 2 per cent if it has been below 2 per cent for a period. They are underwred by their forward dsguiding at the last monetary policy meeting in September. It said the rate was expected to remain fixed "at 2 per cent and is on track to moderately exceed 2 per cent for some me." [4] One important development in this change in the Fed's strategy was to contribute to better anchoring of inflation expectations. When people expect periods when monetary policy is limited by the lower limit to occur more frequently in the period ahead, inflation expectations may fall. Aims the central bank to over-target when the economy normalises, rather than simply bringing it up in the target can counteract inflation expectations being too low. When a central bank succeeds in anchoring inflation expectations around the target, it has greater room for manoeuvre l to influence the real economy and thereby contribute to high and stable output and employment. Figure: Gjennomsni lig inflasjon som mal A strategy of focusing on consistent inflation can be illustrated by the purple path in the chart. Here, the interest rate is kept at zero even longer than in the light blue. As a result, each output gap is posi vt, and inflation shoots above target. They can also make monetary policy more expansive today through the expectation channel. In the model simulations, it is assumed that the actors are partly forward-looking and rational. Expectations that the interest rate will remain at zero longer than in the light blue path mean that e-demand and inflation will rise somewhat faster. This effect is highly uncertain, and depends in particular on how credible the strategy is. An inflation path that shoots clearly above the target may lead the central bank to raise interest rates anyway to counteract more severe wage and price pressures. That's the credibility problem the Fed seeks to address by changing strategy. As mentioned, a volatility behind the Fed's new strategy is a desire to anchor inflation expectations better. The combination of an economic downturn and an interest rate that is limited by the lower limit poses a risk that inflation in the US will fall and remain low. Chart: Weaker krone at the back of the pound For a small, open economy like the Norwegian one, this inevision is smaller. Title: Management of the Government Pension Fund Global
text: Management of the Government Pension Fund Global Director Nicolai Tangen. Introduction to consultation on the management of the Government Pension Fund Global in the Executive Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs. Subject to changes during the performance. Thank you to the Chairman of the Committee, and for giving me the opportunity to talk about the management of the Government Pension Fund Global. First, I would like to start by saying that it is a pleasure to finally get to meet the members of the committee. It's now been two months since I stepped down as oil fund manager. There are big shoes to fill e is my predecessor Yngve Slyngstad and it is with great respect that I have got on the e work. Let me start by talking about financial markets. 2020 has been a very special year for all of us. In financial markets, we have seen considerable movements. The Government Pension Fund Global had a market value of about NOK 10 100 billion at the end of 2019. E is that the fund returned close to 20 percent in 2019, and markets fell abruptly in March due to the coronavirus pandemic. The value is now about 10 600 billion. In the management of the fund, we try to do better, i.e. make more money, than the indices against which we are measured. With a professional organization and a clear goal to reach out to, we have shown that we can do it. Since inception, we have achieved an excess return, i.e. a return higher than these benchmarks, of about 0.2 percentage point. They emit more than NOK 100 billion extra in the fund due to our management. Comparisons made by the Fund with other similar funds show that we have a good deal lower costs than everyone else it is natural to compare ourselves with. But low costs in themselves are not a goal if it compromises the possibilities of achieving good returns. It is the return e is costs that ultimately come to the fund's owners l dildo. About 10 per cent of the fund's equity investments are in emerging markets. We have found that proximity in the markets is important in order to assess the risk associated with investments here. The fund has made money from enriching external managers. This has also meant that the fund has avoided certain companies with reputational risk. By developing the fund's characteristics, and our experience and knowledge, we gain through the fund's external managers Bake a lot more than we pay for your services. It's also something I think we should build on. The external equity managers have so far given us an additional return of more than NOK 60 billion. As oystein said, the Ministry plans to change the composition of the benchmark index. This means that we will sell shares in Europe and buy shares in North America, especially the US. In order to get the lowest possible transaction costs and reduce the risk of trading at the wrong point, it is best to spread the restructuring over d. As stated in the White Paper, the Ministry will draw up a plan for the uninhabitation in consultation with Norges Bank. At the hearing here in the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs in 2019, one of the topics was investments in unlisted renewable energy infrastructure. Almost a year ago we were given a mandate l to invest in the e. We have built up a group with expertise in the e-area, and we are ready to make investments in a good way. Our experience so far is that many investors see e are such investments, and that the pricing is therefore not all right for us. We will carry out these investments with the same requirements in return and risk as other investments. In the short term, it can be challenging to find projects that meet these requirements. It is a very impressive technology machinery that must l to dri e de e fund. All our operations are aircraft one up in the 'clouds'. We have automa sert most of the processes in the IT area and combined insourced from our more external IT provider. The e are among the most important things we have done over the past year and which both increase the quality of our work and will be cost-saving in the long term. When the Corona pandemic came this year, it was an advantage for us to have a global place, with offices in different parts of the world. Among other things, we have an office in Shanghai that was affected more than the head office in Oslo. This allowed us to have a lot of experience with the operational indiscrimination, and made us better able to cope with the further development. To manage investments, the organization must trade in over 250 marketplaces, provide settlement, valuation, custodian, risk management, etc. We had about 30 million share trades, that is, in about 100,000 per day. That's more than the Oslo Stock Exchange combined. This machine has been rolling and running around the clock, even with all the operational irreconditions due to the Corona pandemic, and the significant movements in the markets. Within the area of responsible investment, we work on a number of topics. I want to point out someone here. We've been working on climate for a long time. We launched a document with our expectations of companies we are invested in in terms of climate. Since then, we have worked with standards for reporting greenhouse gas emissions, dialogue with companies, and we have divested from some smaller companies that we believe have too high a climate risk. Another topic that is important to us is ska and transparency. As an investor, we are buoyed by real value creation above d, and not the potential short-term gains that some companies can achieve through aggressive shaky planning. We are therefore clear about what we expect from the companies we are invested in. We have recently divested from some companies that we see have very weak or no reporting ties et l ska and transparency. As a responsible owner, we must also make many decisions. This means, among other things, that we all work to know the companies as best as possible, and buy companies we believe in, and sell others. When we know the companies and sectors we invest in, we can also have a meaningful dialogue with them, and we can vote at general meetings based on good information. In 2020, we voted on approximately 115 000 issues on the agenda, in almost 12 000 general meetings. Next year we will start publishing how we will vote before the general meetings. Here we will be a world leader. I have three priorities for the organization going forward: return, communication and talent development. The highest possible return e is cost is the main goal for us. We get a mandate from the Ministry of Finance, they are anchored with you in Stor nget. Then it is our task to create as good a return as possible. And that's something that me and we in the fund are really passionate about. My second priority is communication. This applies upwards in the management model and internally in the management organisation. This also applies to the Norwegian population and the markets in the world. We will quickly develop transparency about the management of the Fund. And the latter is talent development. l want to develop the organization l to become more diverse and colorful. I think it will give more credib, more dynamism. And we need that to create returns in the future. The oil fund has an incredibly large and important mandate, and is a fantasist's workplace. It's the place where everyone wants to work, and we want the best in their areas to apply to the fund. 30 October 2020 09:00
