Percent 5 5 4 4 3 3 2 2 KPI 1 Anslag PPR 4/21 1 Inflas jons m eel 0 0 2015 2016 2017 2018 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 Sources: Statistics Norway and Norges Bank 11 In our economic analyses, monetary policy dominance  not fiscal dominance  is implicitly used both in Norway and among our trading partners. Nevertheless, the assumption of monetary policy dominance in Norway is not particularly controversial, because Norway, unlike most other countries, has a large public wealth. Even if monetary policy dominance is used as a basis, the theory points to an important point: Price stability is not necessarily something monetary policy can take responsibility for alone. Fiscal policy must be oriented so that it does not undermine the main task of monetary policy. Until now, I have talked about the importance of the interaction between monetary and fiscal policy for price stability. Let me now talk about the importance of the interaction for real economic stability. Over the past 30 years, there has been a relatively large professional consensus that monetary policy is well suited as a first-line defence in stabilisation policy. The interest rate can be changed rapidly to mitigate the effects of economic shocks. Fiscal measures, on the other hand, often take longer to decide and implement (although the support measures during the pandemic showed that it can also be done quickly). In addition, it may be difficult to reverse some expansionary fiscal measures. An active fiscal policy may therefore conflict with the consideration of sustainable government finances in some countries. Experience from the financial crisis and the pandemic has to some extent changed the view of fiscal policy in the academic community. Previously, there was a focus on securing sustainable government finances through rule-driven budgetary policies. Experience in recent years, however, has been that in the event of major, special disturbances, monetary policy and fiscal measures will be needed. What is an appropriate policy composition generally depends on the type of disruption the economy is exposed to. Let me take the pandemic as an example. We interpreted the disruption as both a negative supply and demand shock, but that the net effect was too low in relation to production potential in the short term. (This is also referred to as a "Keynesian offer shock"2). If the problem is too low demand in relation to the potential for output, an expansionary monetary policy will normally contribute to stabilising both the real economy and inflation. Another characteristic of the "pandemic shock" is that it affected different industries and groups of the population very differently; it was an asymmetric shock. It was industries that are based on close contact with or between customers, such as culture, tourism and the restaurant industry, that were clearly hardest hit by the infection control measures. Using a small stylised model, let me illustrate some points about the interaction between monetary and fiscal policy in a situation that can be interpreted as a simplified description of the shocks of the pandemic. In the model, we have two groups of the population  those who work in industries that were shut down and those who work in industries that were not directly affected. For your convenience, I call them "waiters" and "office workers", respectively. The disruption to the economy is a negative demand shock to the "waiter" industry. 2 Se Guerrieri, V. m. fl. (2022) Macroeconomic implications of Covid-19: Can negative supply shocks cause demand shortages?. American Economic Review (kommende). First, let me look at the case where only monetary policy responds. This can be seen as an illustration of the traditional view where monetary policy is the first line of defence in stabilisation policy. Monetary policy response only Ko n to ra rb e i d e re Se rvi tore r 12 This chart shows the effects of the shock on interest rates, inflation, output and demand for "waiters" and "office workers", respectively. The central bank conducts a normal monetary policy in which the interest rate responds to inflation and overall activity (as measured by the output gap). Although the shock affects only one sector, it has aggregated effects. The central bank reduces the interest rate and reduces the fall in the output gap. Even if the output gap falls, inflation increases. This is because the exchange rate depreciating as a result of lower interest rates, and this contributes to higher inflation in imported goods. The interest rate reduction counteracts some of the fall in demand among "waiters". But at the same time, lower interest rates stimulate demand for "office workers", who have not been affected by the shock. They thus end up having marginally higher demand than they had before the shock occurred. Monetary policy can thus counteract the aggregate effects of the shock, but it cannot be targeted. Therefore, it also cannot affect the distribution between "waiters" and "office workers". In this case, it is assumed that the central bank may cut interest rates considerably. In practice, however, the room for interest rate reductions may be limited, either because there is a limit to how low the key policy rate may be before it loses influence on market rates, or because there may be other reasons why the central bank may not want to set the key policy rate below a certain level. For example, several central banks, including Norges Bank, are very reluctant to set a negative key policy rate, because this can lead to undesirable and unintended effects in financial markets. The lower bound on the interest rate is implied by the dotted line in the chart. If this limit is binding, monetary policy will be less able to counteract the economic downturn. Monetary policy and traditional fiscal policy Ko n to ra rb e i d e re Se rvi tore r 13 Now assume that fiscal policy supplements monetary policy in the form of a traditional aggregate counter-cyclical policy, which responds to aggregate demand. This case is shown in this figure. We see that with an expansionary fiscal policy, the need for a reduction in interest rates will be reduced, and the lower limit for the interest rate is no longer binding, as specified in fiscal policy. But even if such a policy is favourable with regard to the lower limit, a traditional expansionary fiscal policy will not contribute to more even demand between "waiters" and "office workers". 14 Unlike monetary policy, fiscal measures can be targeted. In this figure, I assume that the authority is concerned with distribution, and implements targeted support for the "waiters". We see that demand for "waiters" is falling less. In these model exercises, I have assumed that there is some redistribution from the "office workers" to the "waiters", so that demand among the "office workers" falls somewhat. Support for the "waiters" also has an effect on aggregate demand, and the need for very low interest rates is also diminishing here. (The green line is on top of the red one). In this model exercise, there are therefore potentially substantial gains from having a targeted fiscal policy in addition to monetary policy. Being able to target the instruments is generally a beneficial characteristic when asymmetric shocks occur. In the model exercise here, I have assumed that it is easy to identify which group is affected by the shock. This is perhaps a natural assumption to illustrate the support measures during the pandemic. However, it is often very difficult to identify how different groups are affected. In addition, in practice, it is not always obvious whether it is a temporary shock, as assumed here, or a lasting shock. If it turns out to be a lasting shock, targeted measures could prevent a necessary restructuring. There are several dimensions of the policy composition that have not been taken care of in the simple model exercises I have shown, but which we want to look into in the future. For example, the composition of policy may be important in order to prevent stabilisation of the real economy from leading to a build-up of financial imbalances. I have now illustrated that there may be gains from good interaction between monetary and fiscal policy. It is important that the central bank is independent. Nevertheless, it is an advantage if the two policy areas have a good knowledge of each other's reaction patterns in order to make the right decisions. The exchange of information between the Ministry of Finance and Norges Bank contributes to this.3 Norges Bank's monetary policy strategy 15 In December, Norges Bank the monetary policy strategy to the Monetary Policy and Financial Stability Committee. The strategy bridges the mandate for monetary policy to practical conduct. Monetary Policy Handbook 1 16 3 This was also pointed out in the National Budget for 2022, where the Government writes that "(d)et is particularly important that the formulation of fiscal policy and monetary policy is based on a common understanding of the economic situation and how policy works, both individually and in interaction". The scientific basis for monetary policy in general, and the strategy in particular, has now been compiled in the form of norges bank's handbook in monetary policy, which we publish today. The ambition is that the manual can be seen as a kind of "woodpecker book" in monetary policy. If you have any questions about monetary policy in Norway, refer to the manual. We hope that the publication of both the strategy and the manual will give authorities and other interested parties better insight into our monetary policy assessments, response patterns and decision basis. In addition, we wish to discuss academic issues of relevance to monetary policy with you and other external academic communities. The strategy and manual will hopefully be useful in that respect.

Og ekspansiv finanspolitikk  gjennom kte overfringer og kt offentlig ettersprsel  virker ogs stimulerende. Men at sistnevnte blir finansiert av pengetrykking og ikke av gjeld, frer ikke ndvendigvis i seg selv til kt inflasjon. I praksis kan det likevel vre mekanismer som gjr at finansieringen kan f betydning. Kanskje vil folk forvente, med rette eller ikke, at budsjettunderskudd finansiert av pengetrykking vil fre til hyere inflasjon og lavere realrente, slik at de vil bruke pengene tidligere? Kanskje sitter ogs pengene lsere hos en del i form av bankinnskudd enn i form av obligasjoner? Kanskje kan det ogs tenkes at politikere vil, igjen med rette eller ikke, se p pengetrykking som billig finansiering og dermed fre en mer ekspansiv finanspolitikk? Jeg har n diskutert virkningen p inflasjonen av kvantitative lettelser og finanspolitikk p kortere sikt. I et lengre tidsperspektiv vil inflasjonen i stor grad bestemmes av noen grunnleggende egenskaper ved de pengepolitiske og finanspolitiske regimene. Hvis pengepolitikken er innrettet mot  sikre lav og stabil inflasjon, og sentralbankene har virkemidler og uavhengighet til  oppfylle mandatene sine, er det naturlig  tenke at kningen i inflasjonen er midlertidig. Sprsmlet da er ikke om inflasjonen skal komme ned igjen, men hvor mye det vil koste i form av kte renter og redusert aktivitetsniv. I faglitteraturen om samspillet mellom penge- og finanspolitikken analyseres det imidlertid ogs situasjoner der pengepolitikken ikke vil vre i stand til  srge for prisstabilitet. Et begrep som ofte brukes for  beskrive en slik situasjon er fiscal dominance - finanspolitisk dominans.1 Under finanspolitisk dominans er ikke budsjettpolitikken brekraftig. Sentralbanken m da fr eller senere oppgi mlet om prisstabilitet og i stedet bruke pengepolitikken til  finansiere budsjettunderskuddene med pengetrykking. Det er da i praksis finanspolitikken som bestemmer inflasjonen. Hva skiller dette fra drftingen jeg hadde i sted av ekspansiv finanspolitikk, der sentralbanken kjpte opp obligasjonene? Da argumenterte jeg for at dette ikke ndvendigvis 1 Distinksjonen mellom finanspolitisk dominans og pengepolitisk dominans gr tilbake til den toneangivende artikkelen Some Unpleasant Monetarist Arithmetics fra 1981 av Nobelprisvinneren Thomas Sargent og hans medforfatter Neil Wallace. ga kt inflasjon, i hvert fall ikke utover det at ekspansiv finanspolitikk i seg selv virker stimulerende. I den statiske analysen av privat sektors balanser antok jeg imidlertid implisitt at det var pengepolitisk dominans og ikke finanspolitisk dominans. Under pengepolitisk dominans tilpasser myndighetene sine utgifter og skatter slik at finanspolitikken er brekraftig. Pengepolitikken kan da ta ansvar for prisstabilitet. Formlet med kvantitative lettelser i balanseanalysen var  stabilisere inflasjonen og realkonomien  ikke  finansiere budsjettunderskuddene. Under finanspolitisk dominans, derimot, mtte sentralbanken ha kjpt opp stadig flere statsobligasjoner og ville ikke kunne bruke styringsrenten til  motvirke inflasjonen. Statsgjelden har kt Statsgjeld. Andel av BNP. Prosent 160 140 USA Tys kland Frankrike 120 100 80 60 40 20 0 2005 2008 2011 2014 Kilde: IMF Italia 2017 160 140 120 100 80 60 40 20 0 2020 10 Det er ikke vanskelig  finne eksempler p finanspolitisk dominans i historien, og ogs i dag i enkelte land. Finanspolitiske stttetiltak under pandemien har frt til en kning i statsgjelden i mange land, fra niver som i flere av dem allerede var blitt hye i kjlvannet av finanskrisen. Er det en risiko for at finanspolitisk dominans blir mer utbredt? Dersom sentralbankene i gjeldstyngede land ker renten, vil budsjettunderskuddet isolert sett kunne ke som flge av kte renteutgifter, og myndighetene kan bli tvunget til  stramme inn i finanspolitikken. Hvis ikke sentralbankene er villige til  ke renten tilstrekkelig til  f inflasjonen under kontroll av hensyn til virkningen p myndighetenes budsjetter, kan en havne i en situasjon som i praksis kan karakteriseres som finanspolitisk dominans. Som jeg nevnte tidligere, tilsier Norges Banks prognoser at inflasjonen i Norge og internasjonalt vil komme ned igjen i lpet av innevrende r. Venter nedgang i inflasjonen Konsumprisindeksen (KPI). Firekvartalersvekst. Prosent 5 5 4 4 3 3 2 2 KPI 1 Anslag PPR 4/21 1 Inflas jons m l 0 0 2015 2016 2017 2018 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 Kilder: Statistisk sentralbyr og Norges Bank 11 I vre konomiske analyser legger vi implisitt til grunn pengepolitisk dominans  ikke finanspolitisk dominans  bde her hjemme og blant vre handelspartnere. Antagelsen om pengepolitisk dominans i Norge er uansett ikke srlig kontroversiell, fordi Norge, i motsetning til de fleste andre land, har en stor offentlige formue. Selv om vi legger pengepolitisk dominans til grunn, peker teorien p et viktig poeng: Prisstabilitet er ikke ndvendigvis noe pengepolitikken kan ta ansvar for alene. Finanspolitikken m vre innrettet slik at den ikke undergraver pengepolitikkens hovedoppgave. Jeg har til n snakket om betydningen av samspillet mellom penge- og finanspolitikken for prisstabilitet. La meg n snakke om betydningen av samspillet for realkonomisk stabilitet. Det har de siste 30 rene vrt relativt stor faglig enighet om at pengepolitikken er godt egnet som frstelinjeforsvar i stabiliseringspolitikken. Renten kan endres raskt for  dempe virkningene av konomiske forstyrrelser. Finanspolitiske tiltak, derimot, tar det gjerne lenger tid  beslutte og implementere (selv om stttetiltakene under pandemien viste at det ogs kan gjres raskt). I tillegg kan det vre vanskelig  reversere en del ekspansive finanspolitiske tiltak. En aktiv finanspolitikk kan derfor komme i konflikt med hensynet til brekraftige statsfinanser i en del land. Erfaringene fra finanskrisen og pandemien har i noen grad endret synet p finanspolitikken i fagmiljet. Tidligere var det fokus p  sikre brekraftige statsfinanser gjennom regelstyrt budsjettpolitikk. Erfaringene de siste rene har imidlertid vrt at ved store, srskilte forstyrrelser, vil det vre behov for bde pengepolitiske og finanspolitiske tiltak. Hva som er en hensiktsmessig politikksammensetning avhenger generelt av hva slags type forstyrrelse konomien utsettes for. La meg ta pandemien som et eksempel. Vi tolket forstyrrelsen som bde et negativt tilbuds- og ettersprselssjokk, men at nettoeffekten var for lav ettersprsel i forhold til produksjonspotensialet p kort sikt. (Dette er ogs omtalt som et keynesiansk tilbudssjokk2). Hvis problemet er for lav ettersprsel i forhold til produksjonspotensialet, vil normalt en ekspansiv pengepolitikk bidra til  stabilisere bde realkonomien og inflasjonen. En annen egenskap ved pandemisjokket er at det rammet ulike nringer og grupper av befolkningen svrt forskjellig; det var et asymmetrisk sjokk. Det var nringer som er basert p nrkontakt med eller mellom kunder, slik som kultur, reiseliv og restaurantnringen, som ble klart hardest rammet av smitteverntiltakene. La meg ved hjelp av en liten stilisert modell illustrere noen poenger ved samspillet mellom penge- og finanspolitikken i en situasjon som kan tolkes som en forenklet beskrivelse av sjokkene under pandemien. I modellen har vi to grupper av befolkningen  de som jobber i nringer som ble stengt ned og de som jobber i nringer som ikke ble direkte rammet. For enkelhets skyld kaller jeg dem henholdsvis servitrer og kontorarbeidere. Forstyrrelsen som treffer konomien er et negativt ettersprselssjokk til servitr-nringen. 2 Se Guerrieri, V. m. fl. (2022) Macroeconomic implications of Covid-19: Can negative supply shocks cause demand shortages?. American Economic Review (kommende). La meg frst se p tilfellet der det kun er pengepolitikken som responderer. Det kan sees p som en illustrasjon av det tradisjonelle synet der pengepolitikken er frstelinjeforsvaret i stabiliseringspolitikken. Kun pengepolitisk respons Ko n to ra rb e i d e re Se rvi tre r 12 Denne figuren viser virkningene av sjokket p rente, inflasjon, produksjon og ettersprselen til henholdsvis servitrene og kontorarbeiderne. Sentralbanken frer her en normal pengepolitikk der renten responderer p inflasjonen og den samlede aktiviteten (mlt ved produksjonsgapet). Selv om sjokket bare rammer den ene sektoren, har det aggregerte effekter. Sentralbanken setter ned renten, og det reduserer fallet i produksjonsgapet. Selv om produksjonsgapet faller, ker inflasjonen. Grunnen til det er at valutakursen depresierer som flge av lavere rente, og det bidrar til hyere prisvekst p importvarer. Rentenedsettelsen motvirker noe av fallet i ettersprselen blant servitrene. Men samtidig stimulerer lavere rente ettersprselen til kontorarbeiderne, som ikke er rammet av sjokket. De ender dermed med  ha marginalt hyere ettersprsel enn de hadde fr sjokket inntraff. Pengepolitikken kan alts motvirke de aggregerte effektene av sjokket, men den kan ikke mlrettes. Derfor kan den heller ikke pvirke fordelingen mellom servitrer og kontorarbeidere. I dette tilfellet er det antatt at sentralbanken kan sette ned renten mye. Men i praksis kan rommet for rentenedsettelser vre begrenset, enten fordi det er en grense for hvor lav styringsrenten kan bli fr den mister gjennomslag til markedsrentene, eller fordi det kan vre andre grunner til at sentralbanken ndig vil sette styringsrenten under et visst niv. For eksempel er flere sentralbanker, inkludert Norges Bank, svrt tilbakeholdne med  sette en negativ styringsrente, fordi det kan fre til unskede og utilsiktede virkninger i finansmarkedene. Den nedre grensen for renten er antydet ved den stiplede linjen i figuren. Hvis denne grensen er bindende, vil pengepolitikken vre mindre i stand til  motvirke det konomiske tilbakeslaget. Pengepolitikk og tradisjonell finanspolitikk Ko n to ra rb e i d e re Se rvi tre r 13 Anta n at finanspolitikken supplerer pengepolitikken i form av en tradisjonell aggregert motkonjunkturpolitikk, som responderer p samlet ettersprsel. Dette tilfellet er vist i denne figuren. Vi ser at med en ekspansiv finanspolitikk, blir behovet for rentenedgang mindre, og den nedre grensen for renten er ikke lenger bindende, slik vi har spesifisert finanspolitikken. Men selv om en slik politikk er gunstig med hensyn til den nedre grensen, vil heller ikke en tradisjonell ekspansiv finanspolitikk bidra til jevnere ettersprsel mellom servitrer og kontorarbeidere. Pengepolitikk og mlrettet finanspolitikk Ko n to ra rb e i d e re Se rvi tre r 14 I motsetning til pengepolitikken, kan finanspolitiske tiltak mlrettes. I denne figuren antar jeg at myndigheten er opptatt av fordeling, og iverksetter mlrettet sttte til servitrene. Vi ser at ettersprselen til servitrene faller mindre. I disse modellvelsene har jeg antatt at det er en viss omfordeling fra kontorarbeiderne til servitrene, slik at ettersprselen blant kontorarbeiderne faller noe. Sttten til servitrene har ogs en effekt p samlet ettersprsel, og behovet for svrt lav rente blir mindre ogs her. (Den grnne linjen ligger opp den rd). I denne modellvelsen er det derfor potensielt store gevinster ved  ha en mlrettet finanspolitikk i tillegg til pengepolitikken.  kunne mlrette virkemidlene er generelt en gunstig egenskap nr asymmetriske sjokk inntreffer. I modellvelsen her har jeg antatt at det er lett  identifisere hvilken gruppe som er rammet av sjokket. Det er kanskje en naturlig antagelse for  illustrere stttetiltakene under pandemien. Ofte er det imidlertid svrt krevende  identifisere hvordan ulike grupper pvirkes. I tillegg er det i praksis ikke alltid opplagt om det er et midlertidig sjokk, som antatt her, eller et varig sjokk. Hvis det viser seg  vre et varig sjokk, kan mlrettede tiltak kunne hindre en ndvending omstilling. Det er flere dimensjoner av politikksammensetningen som ikke er ivaretatt i de enkle modellvelsene jeg har vist, men som vi nsker  se nrmere p i fremtiden. For eksempel kan politikksammensetningen vre av betydning for  unng at stabilisering av realkonomien kan fre til oppbygging av finansielle ubalanser. Jeg har n illustrert at det kan vre gevinster ved et godt samspill mellom penge- og finanspolitikken. Det er viktig at sentralbanken er uavhengig. Det er likevel en fordel om de to politikkomrdene har god kjennskap til hverandres reaksjonsmnster for  treffe riktige beslutninger. Informasjonsutvekslingen mellom Finansdepartementet og Norges Bank bidrar til dette.3 Norges Banks pengepolitiske strategi 15 I desember publiserte Norges Bank den pengepolitiske strategien til Komiteen for pengepolitikk og finansiell stabilitet. Strategien bygger en bro fra mandatet for pengepolitikken til den praktiske utvelsen. Hndbok i pengepolitikk 1 16 3 Dette ble ogs ppekt i Nasjonalbudsjettet for 2022, der regjeringen skriver at (d)et er srlig viktig at utformingen av finanspolitikken og pengepolitikken bygger p en felles forstelse av den konomiske situasjonen og hvordan politikken virker, bde hver for seg og i samspill. Det faglige grunnlaget for pengepolitikken generelt, og strategien spesielt, har vi n samlet i form av Norges Banks hndbok i pengepolitikk, som vi publiserer i dag. Ambisjonen er at hndboken skal kunne sees p som en slags hakkespettbok i pengepolitikk. Hvis det er noe dere lurer p om pengepolitikken i Norge, kan dere sl opp i hndboken. Vi hper at publiseringen av bde strategien og hndboken vil gi myndigheter og andre interesserte bedre innsikt i de pengepolitiske vurderingene, reaksjonsmnsteret og beslutningsgrunnlaget vrt. Dessuten nsker vi  diskutere faglige problemstillinger av relevans for pengepolitikken med dere og andre eksterne fagmiljer. Strategien og hndboken vil forhpentligvis vre nyttig i s mte.

Title: Economic perspectives
text: SPEECH Economic perspec ves Address by Governor Ida Wolden Bache to foreign embassy representa ves in Oslo, 31 March 2022. Intro Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. It is a great pleasure for me to welcome you to Norges Bank for the first me since 2019. Todays event is taking place against the backdrop of the dark shadow cast over Europe by Russias invasion of Ukraine. Russias invasion has caused large-scale destruc on and immense human suffering. On behalf of all the staff at Norges Bank I would like to express my deepest sympathy for the suffering of the Ukrainian people. The economic situa on The war is also having an impact beyond Ukraines borders. The invasion has led to vola lity in financial markets and heightened uncertainty about the global economic outlook. Prices for energy, metals and agricultural products are soaring. Poor countries are being hard hit by the rise in commodity prices, and higher living costs are causing unrest in some countries. At the same me, the global Covid-19 pandemic, which has been affec ng the world economy for two years now, is by no means over. This week, parts of Shanghai went into lockdown. Chart: Higher interest rates When the pandemic hit Norway in spring 2020, we cut the policy rate to zero. The aim was to cushion the downturn and mi gate the risk that the pandemic would leave las ng scars on the labour market. Now that we can look at the years 2020 and 2021 in the rear view mirror, we can see that economic ac vity in Norway picked up more quickly than expected. Employment exceeded the pre-pandemic level in autumn 2021, and the same degree of monetary policy s mulus was no longer needed. In September, we started a gradual normalisa on of the policy rate. Ac vity in the Norwegian economy has con nued to rise a er containment measures were li ed in February, and labour demand is high. At the same me, price and wage infla on has been higher than projected, and wage expecta ons have risen. Rising wage growth and imported goods infla on are expected to push up underlying infla on ahead. Norges Banks primary objec ve under our mandate is low and stable infla on, and our target is infla on of close to 2 percent over me. Our infla on targe ng regime is flexible. This means that in addi on to maintaining price stability, we also set monetary policy to support high and stable output and employment. However, there is a limit to how high output can be and how far unemployment can fall before prices and wages start to accelerate. In our assessment, the objec ve of stabilising infla on around the target somewhat further out suggests a higher interest rate. Last week, the policy rate was raised from 0.5 to 0.75 percent. As the chart shows, we also signalled that we intend to raise the policy rate further. If the economy develops roughly in line with our projec ons, the policy rate will reach 2.5 percent by the end of next year. Higher interest rates will ease the pressures in the Norwegian economy, but employment will likely remain elevated. Chart: High infla on in many countries and higher commodity prices. Infla on among our trading partners has risen sharply. In the US and the UK, infla on has not been as high for decades. Higher infla on and higher infla on expecta ons have led to expecta ons of a rise in global policy rates. Some countries have already started ghtening monetary policy. Globally, infla onary pressures were already on the rise before Russias invasion of Ukraine. Demand for energy and commodi es has rebounded as the global economy started to recover from the pandemic. An increase in the pace of climate transi on has also pushed up demand for many metals used in, for example, car ba eries, solar panels and wind turbines. With Russias invasion of Ukraine, already rising energy and commodity prices have risen further. Russia is a major exporter of a range of commodi es and is not least a main supplier of oil and gas to Europe. Russia is a leading exporter of industrial metals such as aluminium, nickel and steel. And Russia and Ukraine are major exporters of agricultural products such as corn and wheat. The outlook for commodity prices is highly uncertain. Futures prices suggest that energy and other commodity prices will eventually fall, but that they could remain at a higher level than before the pandemic for quite some me. The expansionary monetary and fiscal policies of recent years are s ll making a posi ve contribu on to ac vity in most countries. On the other hand, high infla on, disrup ons in export markets and greater uncertainty among households and firms are expected to weigh on growth ahead, especially in Europe. Chart: Norway: Rise in infla on In Norway, 12-month consumer price infla on has risen well above 2 percent. Unusually high electricity prices through winter were a key driver, resul ng in large electricity bills for households and firms alike. In the conduct of monetary policy, we look through, or disregard, temporary changes in infla on. Our focus is on underlying infla on, which excludes prices that tend to show temporarily large varia ons, such as energy prices. In the chart, underlying infla on is illustrated by the index called the CPI-ATE, which is the consumer price index adjusted for tax changes and excluding energy products. Underlying infla on has picked up from the low levels of last autumn. Prices for both imported goods and for domes cally produced goods and services are rising more rapidly, and we expect underlying infla on to con nue to rise ahead. Chart: Economic ac vity expected to rise Since the Covid-19 outbreak in spring 2020, ac vity in the Norwegian economy and the number of unemployed have fluctuated in step with changes in infec on rates and the scale of containment measures. Higher infec on rates and containment measures led to a dip in ac vity in the Norwegian economy around the turn of the year. But ac vity rebounded as the containment measures were removed in winter. The sectors most affected by restric ons, such as tourism, hospitality and entertainment, have recovered rapidly, and we expect the upswing in the Norwegian economy to con nue. However, the war in Ukraine has led to heightened uncertainty about the economic outlook. Although our trade with Ukraine and Russia is limited, the war is s ll affec ng the Norwegian economy. On the one hand, high energy prices provide large government revenues and may boost petroleum investment and exports related to electricity and oil and gas extrac on. But on the other hand, high energy prices also mean higher costs for household and firms. Some firms may also face supply problems and faltering foreign demand or be more reluctant to invest when price developments and other market condi ons are uncertain. Chart: Low unemployment Unemployment has fallen to a low level. In fact, unemployment is at its lowest level since before the 2008 financial crisis. At the same me, the number of employed has risen considerably and the employment rate has increased to the highest level in more than ten years. Norwegian firms are now repor ng capacity constraints. For many firms, produc on is being constrained by labour shortages. Never before has the number of registered job vacancies been so high. As I men oned earlier, with a ght labour market and higher infla on, wage expecta ons have increased. Chart: Strong consump on growth, but moderate house price infla on ahead Over the past two years, the pandemic has restricted consumers spending op ons. Many consumers have shi ed spending away from services and towards goods. Many households have also saved more than usual. As society has gradually reopened, spending has picked up, and not least services consump on has increased. This year, solid growth in private consump on is expected to boost domes c ac vity. Looking further ahead, growth in private consump on will likely be dampened by higher interest rates. House price infla on and credit growth are also expected to moderate. Chart: Business investment expected to grow Over the coming years, ac vity in the Norwegian economy will also be supported by growth in business investment. In par cular, I want to men on investment in ba ery factories and hydrogen plants, which is expected to pick up strongly ahead. This will not only boost output and employment but is also a sign that the transi on to a more sustainable economy is underway. The transi on will probably lead to higher and more vola le energy prices than we have been used to. At the same me, higher prices for carbon-based energy may spur the transi on to a net-zero economy. Climate change and central banks Chart: Climate change and central banks And the transi on is necessary. Climate change is one of the greatest challenges of our me. The prime responsibility and the most effec ve tools to mi gate climate change lie with governments. However, carbon emissions and the increased frequency and severity of extreme weather events will affect our economy and the financial system. As such, climate change is relevant to Norges Banks core responsibili es as central bank. Like other central banks, we have over the past few years intensified our efforts to understand the effects of climate change and manage the risks from the physical effects of climate change and the transi on to a low-carbon economy. In the years ahead, climate change and the transi on to net-zero economies will involve structural changes and periods of considerable uncertainty. Delivering on the objec ves of price stability and economic stability will then be more important than ever. Structural changes in the payment system Chart: Structural changes in the payment system In addi on to promo ng economic and price stability, the Banks responsibili es also include ensuring that the payment system is safe and efficient. The payment system is now undergoing a deep transforma on driven by digital technology and increased compe on. Money and payments are evolving rapidly. Norway is one of the countries where the use of physical cash has declined most. Most of us prefer digital alterna ves such as payment cards and apps on our mobile phones. Interna onally, compe on among financial service providers is intensifying. Payment intermedia on is no longer the sole preserve of banks. Compe on comes from both specialised Fintech companies and from global tech giants such as Apple and Google. Tradi onal money is also mee ng compe on from new forms of money such as e-money, stablecoins and cryptocurrencies. Lately, the invasion of Ukraine and the sanc ons against Russia have brought cryptocurrencies into the spotlight. Norges Bank wants to be a driving force for change that enhances the efficiency and safety of the payment system. As the central bank, we take a precau onary approach and keep a close eye on the poten ally far-reaching implica ons for the financial system of some of the changes that are underway. Among other things, we must ask ourselves whether measures will be needed to ensure that we can con nue making payments in Norwegian kroner efficiently and safely in the future. A key issue in that context is whether Norges Bank should launch a central bank digital currency. We have not yet reached a conclusion, but we want to be ready to launch it, should it be necessary to do so. Conclusion Norges Bank will do its part to ensure that paying in Norwegian kroner will con nue to be an a rac ve and safe alterna ve in the future. Being adap ve and responsive to technological developments in the payment system is one necessary condi on. Keeping infla on low and stable is another. Chart: Infla on to move close to target With last weeks policy rate hike and the further increases indicated by our policy rate forecast, we expect infla on in Norway to move close to target somewhat further out. Our projec ons are uncertain. The war in Ukraine has triggered vola lity in financial and commodity markets. There is considerable uncertainty as to how severe the economic consequences of the war will be and how long they will last  in Norway as well as among our trading partners. Growth may turn out to be slower than projected while infla on accelerates. There is also a risk that capacity constraints in the economy and persistent global price pressures will lead to higher wage and price infla on than currently expected. If developments in the economy should differ from our current projec ons, then the policy rate forecast may also be adjusted. But our mandate remains unchanged: to keep infla on low and stable and contribute to high and stable output and employment. Thank you for your a en on. 31 March 2022 15:00

Title: The conduct of monetary policy
text: The implementation of monetary policy Governor Ida Wolden Bache holds an introductory hearing on the Financial Markets Report 2022 in the Grand NGET Finance Committee on 28 April 2022. Subject to changes during the performance. Introduction Thank you for the opportunity l account for the implementation of the monetary policy. My introduction here today is based, among other things, on Norges Bank's annual report for 2021 and our monetary policy assessments until the monetary policy meeting in March this year. It is now more than two years since the corona pandemic brought the Norwegian economy into a crash. In the spring of 2020, Norges Bank cut the key policy rate by zero percent. The countercyclical capital buffer for banks was reduced from 2.5 per cent to 1 per cent. During the pandemic, The Great News has adopted a turnaround in financial policy. The purpose of The ceilings have been to mitigate the economic consequences of the pandemic for bedri er and households. In e is d we can ascertain that the accompaniment came back faster than expected. During the year, conditions in the economy became more normal again, and there was no longer a need for an equally expansive monetary policy. During the autumn, it also became clearer that the objective of stabilising inflation around the target in the somewhat longer term meant that the key policy rate should be raised to a more normal level. Since this summer, the key policy rate has been raised from zero to 0.75 per cent, and we envisage a further rise in the key policy rate. In line with the normalisation of the economy, the countercyclical capital buffer has also been terminated again. Russia's invasion of Ukraine has severely affected us all in recent months. The war causes great destruction and great human suffering. It also creates uncertainty about the economic outlook, both internationally and in Norway. Normalisation of the Norwegian economy throughout the year First, let me say more about developments here at home. Chart: Ak viteten is higher than before the pandemic The pandemic and forging have caused wide fluctuations in the number of people in the world over the past two years. Increased forging and new forges resulted in a huge drop in the accumulation around the year,but the consequences of the omikron variant of the virus were less than we envisaged when we made forecasts against cunning one of the. Over the past year, high electricity prices have resulted in inflation, and annual consumer price inflation is now clearly above the inflation target of 2 per cent. When we determine the interest rate, we tend to see through monetary fluctuations in inflation and are more absorbed by what we describe as underlying inflation. Underlying inflation can be measured in different ways, but here it is illustrated by the CPI-ATE, which is consumer price inflation adjusted for changes in prices and excluding energy products. Underlying inflation has risen from low levels in autumn. Both the rise in prices for the goods we import and the rise in prices for domestic goods and services have risen. Underlying inflation is expected to continue, both as a result of high inflation in imported goods and because there is little spare capacity in the Norwegian economy and the prospects for higher wage growth. Monetary policy objective Chart: Target of low and stable inflation The Monetary Policy and Financial Stability Committee was conducting a review of the monetary policy strategy. The strategy, in December, describes the committee's interpretation of the mandate for monetary policy and how the committee will weigh the various considerations against each other. The overall target for monetary policy is low and stable inflation, defined as annual consumer price inflation of close to 2 per cent. Having an exceptional inflation target provides economic agents with an anchor for inflation expectations. Persistently high inflation is costly for society, partly because it creates uncertainty about the value of money and makes economic planning difficult. As long as it is important that inflation will be low and stable, fluctuations in inflation around the target will probably not have substantial socio-economic costs. In the interest rate range, we place emphasis on avoiding large and persistent deviations from the inflation target, both on the above and below sides. The mandate states that inflation targeting shall be flexible. This means that monetary policy will also contribute to high and stable production and employment. While high unemployment has direct costs for both society and the individual who cannot find work, high employment or very low unemployment only has indirect costs in the form of excessive wage and price inflation. The consideration of getting as many people as possible into work must therefore be weighed against the risk that inflation will be too high. If interest rates are kept low for a long time to keep the economy low, the pressures in the economy will sooner or later be so high that prices and wages are accelerating. The mandate for monetary policy also states that we will contribute to counteracting the build-up of financial imbalances. Typical signs that financial imbalances are building up are high house price inflation and a rapid rise in household debt. This could in turn amplify a rebound in the economy. We must therefore not be too short-sighted in the interest rate period, but also think about how the policing we are conducting today may affect stability in the economy in the longer term. This means, among other things, that we are aware that a period of very low interest rates may lead to an increase in financial imbalances. In general, monetary policy cannot take the main responsibility for counteracting the build-up of financial imbalances. The first line of defence against disturbances in the financial system is regulation and monitoring of financial incentives. Requirement l the countercyclical capital buffer and systemic risk buffer in banks are part of macroprudential regulation of the financial system, also known as macroprudential supervision. In September this year, Norges Bank was given decision-making responsibility for the countercyclical capital buffer, and formalised advisory responsibility for the systemic risk buffer. Since then, the countercyclical capital buffer has been increased twice. The monetary policy trade-offs in March Chart: Higher interest rates ahead At the last monetary policy meeting in March, we raised the interest rate to 0.75 per cent and presented an interest rate forecast that indicated that the key policy rate will be raised gradually to around 2.5 per cent at the end of next year. The forecast means that the mortgage rate, which is now above 2 per cent, could each rise to around 4 per cent. In March, we also raised the buffer rate to 2.5 per cent with effect from 31 March 2023. The rise in interest rates reflects a high level of interest rates in the Norwegian economy and that there is a high level of demand for jobs . Inflation has increased, and higher wage growth and higher inflation in the goods we import are likely to result in underlying inflation ahead. We believe that the upturn in the Norwegian economy is rapid, but the war in Ukraine is contributing to uncertainty about the growth prospects. High energy prices generate substantial revenues in the state and can result in investments and exports related to kra and oil and gas extraction, but this entails a jointly increased release for households and enterprises. Sam dig seems that the war could exacerbate disturbances in the international value chains. Chart: Further upturn in the economy and inflation close to the target in the somewhat longer term Our main task is to ensure low and stable inflation. At the monetary policy meeting in March, the Committee's assessment was that the objective of stabilising inflation around the target in the somewhat longer term is a higher key policy rate. If we had not raised the interest rate, there would have been an increasing risk that inflation will be too high. There could then be a need for higher interest rate increases in the d, which in turn could increase the risk of a downturn in the economy. There is uncertainty about economic developments and how households will see higher interest rates. This means that the interest rate will be raised gradually. A gradual rise in interest rates will contribute to inflation being close to the target in the somewhat longer term. Higher interest rates will slow the economy, but unemployment is expected to remain low. Higher interest rates result in higher costs for those who have loans and will contribute to curbing household consumption. There were many people who saved more than normal during the pandemic. We believe that the high saving, together with higher wage growth and increased employment, will contribute to an accerawing in consumption. Solid growth in mainland investment is also expected to continue in the period ahead. Much of the investment growth we envisage will come in manufacturing, partly driven by climate and energy consumption at home and abroad. Conclusion La meg avslu e. Two years is when the pandemic started, we can note that the Norwegian economy has so far fared well. The economy is high, and the increased pressures in the economy are likely to result in higher inflation in the period ahead. The interest rate is therefore on the rise. But the forecasts are uncertain. If the economy develops differently than currently envisages, interest rate developments may also be different. The outlook for the world economy is weighed down by the war in Ukraine. There is considerable uncertainty about how large and how lasting the consequences for the economy of the war will be  both among our trading partners and in Norway. Global growth may deteriorate more than projected as inflation picks up. Capacity constraints in the economy and persistent global price pressures may also result in higher wage and price inflation than currently envisaged. While rising trade and competition between countries have long contributed to keeping inflation down, globalisation has slowed in recent years. The pandemic probably reinforced a trend where more businesses want to secure their own supply lines and have a larger part of the production chain closer to customers. The war in Ukraine has resulted in high commodity prices and led many countries to make themselves less dependent on Russian energy and commodity imports. This could accelerate the transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy. During this transitional phase, energy and commodity prices may remain higher than we have been accustomed to in recent years. Going forward, we may face more difficult trade-offs in monetary policy. But we have a clear social mission, and we will do our part to ensure low and stable inflation and stable economic developments in the years to come. Thank you for sheltering me. 28 Apr, 2022 10:15

Title: Norges Bank's management of the Government Pension Fund Global
text: Norges Bank's management of the Government Pension Fund Global Head of Norges Bank Investment Management, Nicolai Tangen. Introduction to consultation on the Government Pension Fund in the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs. Subject to changes during the performance Finance Minister, committee chair and members. Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM) worked at the end of the first quarter of this year for 528 people. As manager, it is our job to invest petroleum revenues that enter the fund in the best possible way, and to try to deliver a return that is better than the markets [within the limits we have for deviations from the benchmark index provided by the Ministry of Finance]. Since inception, the return has been 0.29 percentage point higher than the return on the benchmark index. They involve an additional return of NOK 308 billion. The first quarter of this year gave us a nega v return on the fund, but far less than we could have  thanks to an excess return in the aquivy part of the fund, and brilliant efforts from my colleagues. The fund's return in the first quarter was 0.66 percentage point, or NOK 82 billion better than the return on the benchmark index. This means that each estimate in the fund generated value of NOK 155 million each in the first quarter. I must say we're pretty proud of that. Of course, they are not numbers we should count on every quarter and it is the long lines that count, but they give you a sense of what sums we are talking about here. Since its first deposit in 1996, the Fund has delivered an absolu annual return of 6.3 per cent. They represent a total return of NOK 7,355 billion. "Now we have a book," then-Finance Minister Sigbjorn Johnsen said at the time more than 25 years ago. But the money is not "on book." They are invested in stocks, bonds, unlisted real estate and in a wind farm. The return on our investments has meant that the Norwegian people have a fund that is three times larger than if we had just sold the oil and said the money on book. Of course, Johnsen knew that at the time, but he hardly imagined that the overall return a few years later would contribute to each pea krone on the state budget. Or that we should own 1.3 percent of all listed shares worldwide. How big and complex have they become. I have now been head of Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM) for more than a year and a half. It's been a d-feeling pandemic and working from the kitchen counter. It took me more than a year to visit our offices in New York and Singapore and greet our people there. So, when we started putting the pandemic behind us and thought that everything is going to be "normal", it slammed again . Just as the pandemic has affected the fund and the job we are doing, Russia's invasion of Ukraine will do the same. Not only directly on investments in Russia, but also through increased inflationary pressures. The fund is invested broadly in international markets. That's the basic idea. This means that what is happening in the world affects the fund. There's nowhere to hide. In our world, risk is something we have to live with. It's our job to deal with it. When asked what I think are the biggest indiscibles for the fund in the years to come, I have answered inflation and geopolics. Inflation was already on the rise before the war in Ukraine broke out. Since then, it's just risen. The geopolic consequences of the war are difficult to say, but we are probably facing the biggest changes we have seen in 30 years. There is little doubt that increasing friction between major powers and the reversal of globalisation will affect markets. Today, the situation is that interest rates are very low and an expensive stock market. All they are together means that it's going to be rough going forward. So is the new normal for the fund greater uncertainty and more risk than we have seen? I think I'll answer "yes" to that. We have to prepare ourselves for that reality. Then there are two ng that are particularly important: The first is that we have an organisation with a lot of resources to manage the risks and uncertainties we are in  because there is a lot of money to be made from. It's not that hard to make money in good ones there. What's hard is doing it in bad. The second is that we communicate well with our owners  the Norwegian people. We're totally dependent on what we're doing. And there is a direct connection between knowledge and llit. That's why we sound and think more now than before. In order to generate the greatest possible return for current and future generations, we must all be able to stay in the world elite of asset management environments. In many ways, the fund is a money bag that we fly around the world. We have to deal with trades and transactions around the clock. It starts in Europe in the morning, flights are on in New York in the evening and in Singapore in one, before we get it back in Europe again. In total, this money works 23 of the 24 hours a day, on behalf of the Norwegian people. At the end of 2021, around 50 per cent of the fund is invested in North America, 30 per cent in Europe, 15 per cent in Asia. They are by far our three largest markets. We have international offices to be close to where it happens. We need to be able to feel the markets on the pulse of building knowledge and be able to make those decisions at the richest points. A more unstable situation internationally makes them just even more volatile. But we also want to strengthen our asset management environment in Oslo. We have started both a Graduate and summer cracking program, where we bring in a number of young people from school. Some fortse are in the fund, while others take the knowledge from us and enter other parts of the Norwegian investment management environment. We will safeguard the wealth of future generations and must have the wisest heads. I will dwell on some considerations as to why we are strengthening our stable in the future. The first thing I want to talk about is ownership. We are already an ak v owner who follows up the companies we own and builds knowledge about the markets in which we operate. Now we're going to do more. We need to have an in-depth knowledge of markets and companies in order to be an owner. Lately, for example, we have a particular focus on finding what we call "rotten apples" and getting these out of the fund's portfolio. Some companies are less good investments. Others may have a business that is not good. They're not all d so le e to find. For li d lbake, we considered four accounting and fraud specialists. We believe that they will pay off in the long run. A important part of our ownership is our work on responsible investment. Children's resources, water management, human rights, corruption, ska and transparency, the use of the ocean, biodiversity and ecosystems, and climate change are among the areas where we have clear expectations in the companies we own. We do these through dialogue with the companies and voting. To say something about the breadth of the work, we held about 3,000 company meetings and voted on about 120,000 proposals. Through the voting process, we have a right to give clear disduity to our views as an owner. We are now in the middle of the busiest period for our ownership group, since the bulk of the companies' annual general meeting takes place before the summer. This year we are particularly focused on executive pay, skills diversity on boards, and climate change. Let me dwell on the latter  climate change  and say something about how we work with climate risk. The Fund is exposed to a number of different risks, and climate risk is one of these. The fact that the companies we are owners in handle the transition in a low-emission society in a good way is, for us, important  financially. Companies that do not take climate risk seriously are a financial risk to the fund. In a scenario where the world is unsuccessful in a low-emission economy, the risk also increases for the fund, because the consequences will be felt everywhere. We want to be a driving force for these to be cirred against zero emissions over d. Why not just sell these companies? We think it's not a good solution. Rather, we believe that the best way we can contribute to safeguarding the fund's financial objectives is to be an owner. One that sounds and seems good in the companies. One that works to establish good common international standards for reporting, which is absolutely necessary to understand the companies' climate risks. Ownership is a long way off. Changes may take d. Then it is posi vt that we also see results through concrete measurements from years this year. Every year we make around 4,000 detailed assessments of the companies' management structure, strategy, risk management and targeting of carrier collars. We're seeing better goals. And the companies we have contacted are improving more than the rest of the companies. That doesn't mean we're going to own every company. We want to be able to sell out of companies that we believe do not have a sustainable business model, and where our opportunities to influence are minimal. In llegg, we began by reviewing the carrier risk in the companies before they are included in our benchmark index, so that we can not buy companies with high risk. In sum, we believe that they reduce the carrier risk in our portfolio and provide more opportunities l follow up the companies' efforts. In this year's Great Ngsmelding, it is proposed to err on the environmental mandates. We're behind the proposal. Together we have built expertise in environmental technology and investments. This expertise is important in a world that is to be cirrped in zero emissions, and it is natural that we build on it. We have a mandate to invest two percent of the fund in renewable infrastructure. In April last year, we made our first investment. Competition is fierce, and there are few good projects for so long. It will therefore take d to build up this portfolio. We are now working on our strategy for managing climate risk that will take into consideration the changes that are being formalised e is the Great ngsmeldingen has been processed. It's important to point out that we don't start from scratch. We have been working on climate risk for 15 years. In order to raise the level of ambition, more resources will be needed than we have today. Not only because we want to strengthen and develop the work, but also to ensure that the work does not compromise other companies. Climate risk is a financial risk to the Fund. But we are also exposed to operational risk. One of these comes from the cyber domain The world's largest sovereign wealth fund is a target to attack and hit, and the war in Ukraine has increased the risk of cyberattacks against the Oil Fund. A successful attack on our IT systems may see these out of action over shorter or longer d with the consequences it will have for one of the fund. It may drain us of market information and other sensi v information, and damage our reputation and reputation, which is why we work with information security in all our IT processes. The battle for the best IT heads is fierce - both in Norway and internationally. We have to become more of an employer in technology and IT. We know that NBIM is not all on the employer radar of the foremost technology students in Norway. We're going to do something about that! But we don't just use technology l to defend ourselves in the cyber domain. We also spend it on getting better at making money. Ago, we introduced a test version of an investment simulator in the fund. With the help of millions of historical data points with which we provide the simulator, we will be able to extract valuable information that enables our ansa e to make better decisions. De e is an innova v way to see e information in system and we hope that it can help l make our people better. It's a good team of professionals that 23 more a day creates i fantasizing results, with very low costs. I am incredibly proud and humbled to be your colleague. Title: Interest rates are now unchanged
text: Lecture Interest rate to be kept unchanged now Governor Ida Wolden Bache's introduction to the press conference on the interest rate decision on 19 January 2023. Chart 1: Interest rate to be kept unchanged now Norges Bank's Monetary Policy and Financial Stability Committee has unanimously decided to keep the key policy rate unchanged at 2.75 percent. Norges Bank's task is to ensure low and stable inflation. The target is inflation of close to 2 per cent over time. At the same time, we will help to ensure that as many people as possible are in work and to stable economic development. Price stability is important for the smooth functioning of the economy. When prices increase quickly and unexpectedly, it particularly affects those who have little to go on. Ensuring low and stable inflation is the most important contribution monetary policy can make to promoting high employment over time. Chart 2: Inflation is too high Last year, inflation accelerated both internationally and in Norway, and since last spring we have raised the interest rate rapidly. The aim of the interest rate hikes is to bring down inflation. At the same time, we want to avoid slowing down growth in the economy more than is necessary to control inflation. Inflation is now about 6 per cent and well above the inflation target. The annual rise in the consumer price index has slowed somewhat from the very high levels in autumn, but excluding energy prices, inflation has been fairly stable in recent months. Price developments have been in line with our expectations when we presented our forecasts in December. Chart 3: Unemployment has remained low Activity in the Norwegian economy is high, and unemployment is still very low. At the same time, high inflation and higher interest rates are weakening household purchasing power, and many enterprises expect a fall in activity ahead. Based on the Committee's current assessment of the outlook, there will be a need to raise the policy rate somewhat further in order to bring inflation down towards target. The labour market appears to have been slightly tighter than projected in December. Continued high pressures in the Norwegian economy may contribute to sustaining inflation. This could indicate that the interest rate should be raised at this meeting. On the other hand, there are prospects that energy prices will be lower ahead than envisaged in December, and there are signs that inflation has peaked in a number of the countries with which we trade. The interest rate has been raised substantially in a short period of time, and monetary policy has begun to have a tightening effect on the economy. This may indicate a more gradual approach to interest rate setting. We therefore chose to keep the interest rate unchanged at this meeting. Chart 4: Likely to raise the policy rate further in March The interest rate path will depend on economic developments. The outlook is more uncertain than normal, but we will most likely raise the policy rate in March. At that time, we will also present the first Monetary Policy Report of the year with new forecasts for the Norwegian economy. The Committee has also decided on the countercyclical capital buffer and unanimously decided to maintain the 2.5 percent rate with effect from 31 March 2023. Title: We raise interest rates to bring down inflation
text: Lecture We raise interest rates to bring down inflation Governor Ida Wolden Bache's introduction to the press conference on the interest rate decision on 4 May 2023. Chart 1: Interest rate raised by 0.25 percentage point Norges Bank's Monetary Policy and Financial Stability Committee has decided to raise the policy rate by 0.25 percentage points to 3.25 per cent. Norges Bank's task is to ensure low and stable inflation. The target is inflation of close to 2 per cent over time. At the same time, we will help to ensure that as many people as possible are in work and to stable economic development. Chart 2: Inflation is too high Inflation is now clearly above target. In March, consumer prices were 6.5 per cent higher than a year earlier. High energy prices are one important reason for the high inflation, but prices for other goods and services have also risen rapidly. Price stability is important for the smooth functioning of the economy. We set the interest rate with a view to bringing inflation back to 2 per cent. At the same time, we want to avoid slowing down growth in the economy more than is necessary to control inflation. We have not yet seen the full effects of the interest rate hikes we have behind us. Our forecast in March indicated a policy rate increase to around 3.5 per cent this summer. We have not prepared new forecasts for this monetary policy meeting, but we have assessed new information against the projections we presented in March. Chart 3: Global inflation has slowed Inflation among our trading partners is also high, but in many countries it has slowed in recent months. Gas and power prices have fallen from the very high levels last year. Problems at some banks in the US and Switzerland led to large movements in financial markets in March. Global equity indices have risen since the March Report, and bond market risk premiums have fallen. In the US and Europe, it appears that it has become slightly more difficult for households and businesses to obtain loans. Chart 4: The krone has depreciated High inflation has led central banks in many countries to raise key rates rapidly, and more than in Norway. The Norwegian krone has depreciated in recent months and is now at its weakest since the outbreak of the coronavirus pandemic in the spring 2020. The krone is weaker than projected in March. Chart 5: Unemployment remains low Activity in the Norwegian economy is high. Household consumption has continued to increase despite high inflation and higher interest rates. A high proportion of the population is in work, and employment has risen further so far this year. The labour market is tight. Recently, however, economic growth has slowed. Unemployment rose slightly in April, and fewer positions are being advertised than before. The tight labour market has contributed to a pick-up in wage growth. Wage growth last year was the highest since 2011, and it seems that it will increase further this year. The outcome of the wage settlement so far may indicate that annual wage growth will be slightly higher than projected in March. Higher wage growth leads to higher costs for companies and may result in higher prices for what we produce in Norway. The depreciation of the krone means that imported goods will become more expensive in the period ahead. Chart 6: Interest rate likely to be raised again in June The Committee's assessment is that a higher interest rate is needed to curb inflation. Since the publication of our forecasts in March, overall economic activity has been broadly in line with expectations. Excluding energy prices, consumer price developments have also been as projected. The rise in wage growth and the depreciation of the krone will contribute to sustaining inflation ahead. If the krone remains weaker than assumed or pressures in the economy persist, a higher interest rate may be necessary than previously envisaged. The future path of the interest rate will depend on economic developments, but we will most likely raise the policy rate again in June. At that time, we will also present updated forecasts for the Norwegian economy. Presentation at the press conference on 4 May 2023 (pdf) Published: 4 May 2023, 10:30
